questions.explanation: Co-creating one product vision with the teams and sponsors gives everyone the same definition of success and, because the teams help author it, genuine ownership; keeping it visible where planning and trade-offs are argued makes it the reference point that unblocks those stalled discussions. Explicitly connecting each team's backlog items to the customer and business outcomes they serve during planning and reviews turns the vision from a wall poster into a working tool, so members repeatedly see how their daily work contributes to the product winning. Having each team write its own vision independently would deepen the silo the survey exposed, arming every team with an even stronger local story to argue from in cross-team trade-offs. Broadcasting the executive strategy deck with a read-confirmation is one-way push: reading a deck produces neither shared understanding nor commitment, which is precisely why the survey result looks the way it does even though the strategy is already documented. Routing trade-off decisions to the program manager substitutes authority for alignment — decisions get made, but members still cannot connect their work to the product's purpose and their empowerment shrinks.
questions.concept: Building shared purpose across multiple teams
questions.question: A hybrid program has five teams building one freight-pricing platform. A recent engagement survey shows members can describe their own team's next milestone but few can explain how the product is meant to win in its market, and cross-team trade-off discussions routinely stall because each team argues from its own milestone. Which TWO actions would most effectively strengthen shared vision and purpose across the program? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Have each team write its own team-level vision statement independently so every group owns a vision it created
Co-create a concise product vision with the teams and sponsors together, and keep it visible in the spaces where planning and trade-off discussions happen
Distribute the executive strategy deck to all members and require confirmation that each person has read it
During planning and reviews, explicitly connect each team's backlog items to the customer and business outcomes they serve
Route cross-team trade-off decisions to the program manager so alignment no longer depends on the teams agreeing

questions.explanation: A voluntary community of practice creates a durable, practitioner-owned channel where the people doing integration work exchange techniques directly, and rotating facilitation keeps ownership with the members rather than with management. Publishing blameless post-incident summaries in an open, searchable space and reviewing notable ones at a cross-team event makes failure knowledge findable at the moment another team needs it; together the two move knowledge through people and through transparency. Standardizing every team on one framework mistakes uniformity for learning — the repeated mistakes are integration-technical, not framework-specific, and forced convergence discards the tailoring each team has earned. A central approval board is gatekeeping rather than sharing: it slows every team's flow and concentrates the knowledge in the gatekeepers instead of spreading it. Manager-compiled monthly email reports push second-hand, filtered information on a slow cadence, and lessons buried in inboxes rarely change how practitioners actually work.
questions.concept: Communities of practice and transparent failure learning
questions.question: An organization runs twelve delivery teams across Scrum, Kanban, and a Lean-hybrid approach. Different teams keep repeating the same integration mistakes, and the agile practitioner has been asked to help knowledge flow across team boundaries. Which TWO actions would BEST promote knowledge sharing across the teams? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Standardize all twelve teams on a single framework so that lessons transfer more easily between them
Sponsor a voluntary community of practice on integration, meeting on a regular cadence with rotating facilitation drawn from the teams
Establish a central architecture board that must approve every team's integration design before implementation
Have each team's manager compile a monthly lessons-learned report and distribute it to all teams by email
Make failure learning visible by publishing blameless post-incident summaries in an open, searchable space and reviewing notable ones at a cross-team demo day

questions.explanation: The riskiest assumption is whether the mapping is clinically correct, and a text dump of real records answers that question perfectly well; feedback is worth far more when it arrives before three more weeks of work are layered on a possibly wrong foundation. Waiting until the screen is built delays the answer to the highest-risk question purely to protect appearances, and any mapping defect found then is far more expensive to unwind. Asking the specialist for her twenty hardest record examples is the strongest alternative and worth doing as well, since hard cases make excellent test data, but it trades away thirty minutes with the expert in the room, where a raised eyebrow at an unexpected value teaches the team more than a list checked in her absence. Having the product owner review the mapping rules substitutes a proxy for the person with the clinical knowledge, which is the very situation early feedback exists to prevent.
questions.concept: Low-fidelity early validation of the riskiest assumption
questions.question: A team modernizing a hospital's lab-results interface has just finished a large data-mapping component. The clinical informatics specialist who will use it is available for a thirty-minute walkthrough tomorrow, but the component has no user interface yet — only a command-line harness that prints mapped records. A developer argues it would be embarrassing to show a raw text dump and suggests waiting three weeks until the screen is built. What is the BEST response?
choices: Run the walkthrough tomorrow using the command-line harness so the specialist can check the mapping against real cases
Wait until the screen is built so the specialist can judge the mapping the way clinicians will encounter it in practice
Ask the specialist for her twenty hardest record examples and check the mapping against them after the walkthrough slot
Have the product owner review the mapping rules on the specialist's behalf so the team keeps moving this week

questions.explanation: Pairing and rotating others through real release work spreads tacit knowledge in the flow of work, reduces the bus factor sustainably, and relieves the engineer's load over time — knowledge transfer through doing is far more effective than transfer through artifacts alone. Pausing everything to write comprehensive documentation is a big-bang approach: it delays releases, produces documents that go stale quickly, and captures little of the tacit judgment that makes her effective. Hiring a contractor adds capacity but not shared knowledge — the silo remains, and may even deepen if the contractor becomes a second silo. A checklist-and-approval gate lets people execute steps without understanding them, which adds process while leaving the team unable to handle anything the checklist did not anticipate.
questions.concept: Reducing single-point knowledge risk through pairing and rotation
questions.question: In a hybrid program, only one platform engineer understands the release pipeline. She is overloaded, releases queue up behind her, and she was unreachable during the last production incident. She says she has "no time to teach anyone." What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Have her step off feature work for an iteration to write full pipeline documentation the other engineers can follow next release
Bring in a contractor with comparable pipeline skills to absorb the release queue while she keeps doing the work only she can do
Add a release checklist and an approval step so other engineers can run releases from the procedure rather than from knowledge
Work with the team to schedule pairing and rotation on upcoming release tasks so others learn the pipeline by doing it with her

questions.explanation: Bringing both teams together to examine their real needs and invent options is collaborating — the only conflict mode that searches for a solution satisfying both parties — and the history here, a compromise that caused both teams to miss commitments, shows why splitting the difference is not enough. Asking the sponsor to rank deliverables escalates to a forcing decision before the teams have attempted joint problem solving, producing a winner and a resentful loser. Reinstating the alternation schedule repeats a compromise that has already demonstrably failed both teams. Telling the Kanban team to yield is accommodation built on the false assumption that flow-based work carries no date pressure, and it settles the conflict by sacrificing one team's needs rather than examining either team's actual constraints.
questions.concept: Conflict modes — collaborating versus compromising, accommodating, and forcing
questions.question: Two teams — one using Scrum, one using Kanban — share a single performance-test environment. Last quarter they "split the difference" by alternating access weekly, and both teams missed their commitments. Now both need the environment during the same two weeks, and tension is rising in the shared channel. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Reinstate the alternating schedule so that each team gets one of the two weeks, then hold a joint review at month's end to confirm the arrangement is working better this time
Facilitate a joint session where both teams map their actual test needs and explore options that could satisfy both, such as staggering test types or virtualizing part of the environment
Have the two product owners rank their competing deliverables against portfolio value, then grant the shared test window to whichever team is carrying the greater customer impact this quarter
Ask the Kanban team to run its performance tests against a scaled-down copy of the environment, accepting the lower fidelity so that the Scrum team keeps the shared instance uninterrupted

questions.explanation: The gap here is confidence, not competence, and that is exactly the gap coaching closes: open, non-directive questions help the person recognize that they already hold the answers, which builds self-efficacy and ends the dependence on the practitioner. A formal course targets a skills deficit that the two successful releases prove does not exist, and it consumes time the launch does not have. Step-by-step instruction, even with a stated plan to taper it, deepens the dependency now and keeps the practitioner as the decision-maker at the moment the developer most needs to decide. Sharing the practitioner's own experience and recommending the same moves is mentoring — useful when experience is genuinely missing, but here it again locates the answers outside the developer and does nothing to build trust in judgment the developer already demonstrates.
questions.concept: Coaching vs. mentoring vs. training vs. directing — selecting the development approach for a confidence gap
questions.question: A developer has successfully led two internal releases and clearly possesses every skill needed to coordinate the upcoming customer launch, yet keeps asking the agile practitioner to make each call. Which development approach BEST fits this situation?
choices: Training — enroll the developer in a formal release-management course before the launch
Directing — give step-by-step instructions for this launch and reduce the direction on future releases
Mentoring — share detailed accounts of how the practitioner handled similar launches and recommend the same moves
Coaching — ask open questions that help the developer surface and trust their own judgment

questions.explanation: Co-created working agreements with one shared definition of done give the merged group a jointly owned way of working and make quality everyone's responsibility, dissolving the two-backlog mentality at its root. Cross-specialty pairing on single items builds shared context and grows generalizing specialists, so collaboration happens inside the work instead of across an inbox. Nominating a coordinator to triage the inbox optimizes the request-routing mechanism — it makes the separation more efficient rather than removing it, and inserts an intermediary between people who should talk directly. Phased delivery with a formal handoff review reintroduces sequential, predictive-style stage gates and hardens the specialty boundary the merger was meant to erase. Mandating tickets for every cross-specialty request replaces conversation with documentation, adding process overhead that further discourages direct collaboration.
questions.concept: Working agreements and generalizing specialists in newly merged cross-functional teams
questions.question: An organization merges its application developers and machine-learning engineers into a single product team. Each specialty still keeps its own backlog and tooling, and members route requests to the "other side" through a shared inbox. Which TWO actions by the agile practitioner would best promote a collaborative team environment? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Facilitate co-creation of team working agreements, including a single definition of done that spans both specialties
Nominate a technical coordinator to triage the shared inbox so cross-specialty requests are routed faster
Split delivery into a machine-learning phase and an application phase with a formal handoff review between them
Encourage pairing across specialties on single backlog items so members gradually become generalizing specialists
Require every cross-specialty request to be logged as a ticket to improve traceability

questions.explanation: A band that widens while the upstream bands stay parallel means work is accumulating in front of a constrained downstream step, and the flat completion rate confirms development throughput is not the limitation; walking the deployment step with the team surfaces the actual waiting time and its cause before anything is changed. Adding developers feeds a non-constraint, inflating the queue that is already growing and lengthening lead time further. Lengthening the iteration hides the delay inside a longer reporting window without removing a minute of waiting. Splitting stories more finely is generally healthy, but here it pushes even more items into the queue ahead of the constrained release step and would make the widening band worse.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation and constraint identification
questions.question: A team builds maintenance-scheduling software for offshore wind farms. Its cumulative flow diagram over the last ten weeks shows the arrival and departure lines for Analysis and Build running roughly parallel, while the band for "Ready for Deployment" widens steadily week over week. Average lead time from commitment to production has grown from nine days to twenty-one, although the number of items the team finishes each iteration is unchanged. A delivery manager proposes adding two developers to "speed things up." What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Support adding the two developers, since a lead time that has more than doubled shows the team lacks capacity to keep up with demand.
Ask the team to slice stories more finely so smaller items move through the deployment step and lead time comes back down.
Bring the diagram to the team and walk the deployment step as a value stream, timing where work waits, before proposing any change.
Lengthen the iteration so that more of the queued items can reach production inside a single iteration boundary and lead time stops growing.

questions.explanation: Raising the pattern with the whole team and facilitating an update to the working agreements on how ideas are challenged is best, because psychological safety is a property of the team system rather than of one person: the team must own the norm, and a respectful, facilitated conversation restores safety while preserving self-management. Private feedback to the senior developer is likely to land better than a public correction and may still be worth doing, but on its own it leaves everyone who watched the dismissal with no sign that anything changed. Inviting the analyst to co-facilitate gives her a platform without changing how her ideas are treated once she uses it, and it asks one person to carry a team-wide problem. A round-robin turn in every meeting guarantees that each person speaks, but it engineers around the conflict instead of through it; compelled turns produce compliance while the norm that made her idea unsafe to raise stays in place.
questions.concept: Psychological safety and working agreements
questions.question: During a Kanban replenishment meeting on an insurance-claims platform team, a junior analyst suggests splitting a large regulatory work item. A senior developer laughs and says, "That's not how real systems work." Team members exchange glances, and over the following weeks the analyst — and two other quieter members — stop offering ideas in meetings. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Give the senior developer private feedback on how the remark landed, since he is likelier to change when he is not corrected in front of the whole team
Invite the junior analyst to co-facilitate the next replenishment meeting so her splitting idea gets a fair hearing and quieter members see a way back in
Introduce a round-robin turn in every meeting so each member speaks in order, ensuring the quieter voices are heard without anyone having to confront the senior developer
Raise the pattern with the whole team and facilitate an update to the working agreements on how ideas are challenged, addressing the dismissive interaction directly but respectfully

questions.explanation: Privacy and regulatory attributes are quality characteristics of a releasable increment, not debt to be carried forward, so the agile response is to surface the risk transparently and collaborate on an option that preserves both value and compliance — discarding location metadata at upload is a small change that removes the exposure without sacrificing the release date. Logging it as a follow-up item ships a known privacy exposure to real policyholders and justifies that by the absence of a regulatory finding rather than by the actual harm. Holding the release three weeks for counsel is the strongest alternative and is defensible caution — but other privacy and security stakeholders are available now, and delay is not the only remedy. Amending the Definition of Done and re-auditing everything is a worthwhile follow-on that leaves this exposure untouched today.
questions.concept: Privacy and compliance as non-deferrable increment quality
questions.question: A regional insurer's team is two iterations from a release that will let policyholders upload claim photos from their phones. During refinement, a developer mentions that uploaded images carry embedded location metadata that the current design stores indefinitely and exposes in the internal adjuster view. Legal counsel is on leave for three weeks. The product owner wants to release on schedule and log a follow-up item for "privacy metadata handling" to be addressed in a later increment, arguing that no regulator has raised it and the feature's value is high. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Log the follow-up item the product owner proposes and rank it first for the increment after the release, since no regulatory finding exists yet and the location metadata is visible only inside the internal adjuster view used by staff today

Hold the release until legal counsel returns in three weeks and can rule on the metadata question, since a privacy determination of this kind belongs with counsel rather than with the product owner or the team

Add a rule that no unnecessary personal data is retained or exposed to the team's definition of done, and re-verify every previously released item against that rule before the team takes any further feature work into an iteration

Make the risk visible with the product owner and the available privacy or security stakeholders now, and work through options — such as stripping location metadata on upload — that keep the release viable while removing the exposure

questions.explanation: Walking the board right-to-left and inspecting aging cards is the diagnostic step: a persistently full downstream column with a growing queue upstream is the classic signature of a bottleneck, and the team needs to understand the cause — a single verifier, environment waits, rework returning from Verify — before it changes the system. Raising the limit to eight, even framed as a one-week experiment with a before-and-after comparison, admits more work into the constrained step; more work in progress at unchanged throughput lengthens cycle time, and a single week cannot separate the effect from ordinary variation. Lowering the Build limit is the strongest rival, because subordinating upstream work to the constraint is right in principle and would stop the queue growing, but it is a system change made before anyone knows why Verify is slow. Adding start dates and blocked markers improves the data yet defers action to next week, when the board has already shown three weeks of a full column.
questions.concept: WIP limits, bottleneck identification, and Little's Law
questions.question: A logistics team runs a Kanban board with a WIP limit of 4 in the "Verify" column. For three weeks the column has sat at its limit while "Build" cards pile up behind it, and average cycle time has grown from 6 days to 14. In the daily standup a developer proposes raising the Verify limit to 8 so cards stop being blocked. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Ask the team to walk the board right-to-left and examine why cards are aging in Verify before changing any limit
Raise the Verify limit to eight for one week as an experiment, then compare cycle time before and after the change
Lower the Build limit so fewer cards arrive at Verify, keeping the downstream queue from growing further
Add start dates and blocked markers to every card so aging in Verify can be measured at next week's review

questions.explanation: Facilitating a joint outcome-ranking session is best because it makes the competing stakeholders resolve the alignment problem together against the shared product vision, produces transparent trade-offs the team can trust, and strengthens the product owner's ordering going forward — collaboration plus transparency attacks the root cause of the weekly goal churn. Splitting each release sixty-forty looks balanced but papers over the disagreement: neither stakeholder's concern is examined, the vision still is not doing the prioritizing, and the ratio becomes the next thing they fight over. Holding one decision point per release and freezing the backlog between them is the strongest alternative and would give the team a stable goal, yet it only buffers the symptom — the stakeholders remain unreconciled and reopen the argument at each decision point. Requiring written requests with a business case improves the inputs but leaves the product owner alone in arbitrating two agendas with no agreed measure of value.
questions.concept: Stakeholder alignment through collaborative, vision-anchored prioritization
questions.question: A team building a patient-scheduling product is whipsawed between two influential stakeholders: the clinical operations director pushes throughput features, while the compliance officer insists the next two releases focus on audit trails. The backlog order reflects whichever stakeholder last spoke to the product owner, and team members say the goal 'changes weekly.' What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Advise the product owner to split each release roughly sixty percent throughput features and forty percent audit work, so both stakeholders see steady progress and the weekly reordering stops
Facilitate a working session where both stakeholders and the product owner rank desired outcomes against the product vision and make the trade-offs explicit and visible to the team
Coach the product owner to hold one decision point per release and freeze the backlog order between those points, so the team is shielded from mid-release lobbying
Ask both stakeholders to submit requests in writing with a stated business case, so the product owner can rank them consistently instead of answering whoever spoke last

questions.explanation: The item isolates what happens after the emotion has been recognized: choosing to pause, reframe, and respond constructively is regulation of one's own emotional impulse, which is self-management. Naming it self-awareness describes the earlier step — the stem says he has already recognized the irritation, so the noticing is not what the pause demonstrates. Empathy would require sensing what the stakeholder feels or the pressure he is under, and nothing in the described behavior reaches toward his state; the lead is governing his own. Relationship management is the strongest distractor, because the neutral question does keep the workshop productive and the two abilities often travel together, but relationship management describes influencing and steering the interaction with others, whereas the behavior asked about here is the internal act of checking his own impulse before it reaches the room.
questions.concept: Emotional intelligence: self-awareness vs self-management boundary
questions.question: During a heated quarterly planning workshop, a delivery lead notices his irritation rising as a stakeholder dismisses the team's forecasts. Having already recognized the feeling, he deliberately pauses, reframes his reaction, and asks a neutral clarifying question instead of firing back. The pause-and-reframe itself BEST demonstrates which emotional intelligence ability?
choices: Self-awareness, because he recognizes the irritation as it rises during the exchange
Empathy, because he attends to the pressure the stakeholder is working under
Relationship management, because he keeps the workshop conversation productive
Self-management, because he consciously regulates his impulse before responding

questions.explanation: The dispute is not really about which number is bigger; it is about how much either number can be trusted. Surfacing the assumptions and sequencing the work so the highest-uncertainty assumption is tested by an early releasable slice converts an argument about forecasts into a decision fed by evidence, and it preserves the sponsor's authority while improving their information at each checkpoint. Proceeding as directed accepts a three-year model built on a borrowed enrollment rate and locks ten months of investment before anyone learns whether customers enroll. Recommending the billing initiative because incremental delivery carries less risk substitutes a method preference for economic reasoning. Asking finance for a sensitivity analysis on enrollment is the strongest alternative and is exactly what that technique is for — but it yields a range of forecasts, where a released slice yields observed enrollment.
questions.concept: NPV assumptions, value uncertainty, and incremental validation
questions.question: A retail energy company must choose between two initiatives for the coming year. Finance modeled a smart-thermostat program at a net present value (NPV) of USD 4.2 million over three years, but its design requires a single integrated launch roughly ten months out before any revenue appears. A self-serve billing initiative models at USD 1.6 million NPV and can put usable capability in customers' hands roughly every month. The sponsor directs the team to take the thermostat program "because the NPV is nearly three times higher." The team notes that the thermostat model rests on an assumed 30 percent enrollment rate drawn from a vendor case study in a different market, with no local evidence. What is the BEST response?
choices: Proceed with the thermostat program as the sponsor directed, since net present value is the organization's accepted investment criterion and a decision of this size belongs to the sponsor rather than the delivery team.

Recommend the self-serve billing initiative instead, since capability that reaches customers every month carries far less delivery risk than a single integrated launch ten months out, whatever the two financial models currently say.

Ask finance to re-run the model with a sensitivity analysis on the enrollment assumption and bring the revised numbers back to the sponsor, so the choice between the two initiatives rests on a sounder forecast.

Make the model's key assumptions explicit with the sponsor and finance, then sequence the thermostat program as releasable slices that test the enrollment assumption first, with checkpoints to re-run the numbers on observed data.

questions.explanation: The conflict has escalated from a disagreement about facts to personal attack and side-taking, so prompt, skilled intervention is required: private facilitation with active listening lowers the emotional temperature, reframes the issue around the shared goal of a safe and timely release, and then lets the two parties settle the substance themselves against the release criteria that already exist. Waiting four days for the retrospective is tempting because retrospectives are a legitimate venue, but personalized conflict deepens fast and is already pulling the team apart — delay is the real risk, and a public forum can harden positions further. Proposing a split-the-difference release with prominent release notes imposes the practitioner's own compromise on a question the parties have never examined together, and on a medical-device program that compromise may not even satisfy the documented release criteria. Briefing the sponsor for a decision hands the question upward before any collaborative resolution has been attempted, strips both parties of ownership, and signals that the team cannot manage its own conflicts.
questions.concept: Recognizing conflict escalation levels and intervening with emotional intelligence
questions.question: On a hybrid medical-device program, the lead verification engineer and the product owner disagree about releasing with a known minor defect. Over the past week the exchange has shifted from debating test data to sarcastic remarks — yesterday the engineer said 'people like you never care about patients' — and team members are beginning to take sides. The retrospective is four days away, the sponsor is available, and documented release criteria exist. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Hold the conversation at the retrospective in four days, where the whole team can weigh the defect evidence together in a structured setting and agree how release disagreements will be handled in future

Meet with the two privately, use active listening to de-personalize the dispute and reconnect them to the shared release goal, then facilitate a joint review of the defect data against the agreed release criteria

Propose a middle path yourself: release on the committed date with the known defect documented prominently in the release notes and a fix scheduled for the next iteration, so each of them gets part of what they want

Ask the sponsor for a release decision now, since the exchange has turned personal and a call from outside the team is the fastest way to stop the two positions and their supporters from hardening further

questions.explanation: The root problem is that two months of work accumulated before anyone who actually uses the kiosk saw it. Putting working software in front of museum staff and real visitors every week or two shrinks the amount of work at risk between feedback events and lets the team correct course while change is cheap. Asking the operations director to sign off detailed usability requirements assumes he can predict what will confuse an elderly visitor, which is exactly what documents fail to do. A usability review stage with specialist sign-off adds a gate and a queue without making feedback arrive sooner. Having museum staff try the weekly staging build is the strongest alternative and genuinely shortens one loop, but staff are proxies for the visitors whose confusion caused the rejection.
questions.concept: Frequent delivery of working software to real users as the primary feedback mechanism
questions.question: A Kanban team building a self-service ticketing kiosk for a science museum deploys to an internal staging environment every week, but museum staff and visitors only see the software at a quarterly showcase. At the latest showcase, the operations director rejected two months of work because the checkout flow confused elderly visitors. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the operations director to sign off on detailed usability requirements for the checkout flow before the team resumes building
Arrange for museum staff and a sample of visitors to try working versions of the kiosk at much shorter intervals, such as every week or two
Add a usability review stage to the Kanban board so nothing reaches a showcase until an accessibility specialist has signed off on the flow
Have museum staff try the weekly staging build, keeping the quarterly showcase as the point at which actual visitors first see and use the kiosk

questions.explanation: A team that still waits to be directed needs a deliberate, supported transfer of authority. Co-designing a pull-and-swarm working agreement gives the team a concrete mechanism to replace the practitioner's daily assignments, explicit decision boundaries make the delegated authority safe for a mixed contractor-employee group, and stepping back gradually matches the leadership style to the team's current readiness. Appointing a rotating daily facilitator keeps stand-ups running when the practitioner is away — the most practical alternative — but it preserves the assignment mechanism itself, simply rotating who hands work out. Pairing every contractor with an employee builds trust across the blended group, yet the pairs still wait to be told which story to take, so the dependency survives. Publishing a charter of roles and asking members to pick items matching their listed role narrows each person's pool, discourages swarming, and mistakes role-matching for self-organization.
questions.concept: Situational leadership and progressive delegation
questions.question: An agile practitioner has spent three months with a newly blended team of contractors and employees on a hybrid insurance program. Every morning the members still wait for the practitioner to say who works on what, and stand-ups stall whenever the practitioner is absent. The practitioner wants the team to become self-organizing. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Appoint a rotating daily facilitator from within the team to hand out the morning's work, so assignments still happen and stand-ups keep running when the practitioner is away
Facilitate a working session where the team designs how it will pull and swarm on work, agree explicit decision boundaries with them, and step back gradually while coaching
Pair each contractor with an employee on every story and let the pairs divide the work between them, since the unblended mix of the two groups is what stalls self-organization
Publish a team charter listing each member's role and responsibilities, then ask members to pick up whichever waiting item matches their listed role each morning

questions.explanation: The "Negotiable" quality means a backlog item deliberately stops short of being a contract, preserving the conversation between the team and the customer about how the need is best met. A Definition of Ready is a lightweight, team-owned agreement about the shared understanding an item should have before work starts — useful as a guideline, harmful when it hardens into a gate that blocks collaboration or demands up-front detail. The Definition of Done sits at the opposite end of the same idea: a shared quality bar applied to completed work so that "done" means potentially releasable rather than "coded on my machine." A "Could have" item is genuinely wanted but explicitly expendable — the first scope released under pressure without endangering the goal, which is exactly what separates it from a "Should have." The common trap is swapping the two agreements: readiness governs the shared understanding before the team pulls work, while the completeness bar governs the quality of what the team delivers.
questions.concept: Distinguishing INVEST qualities, Definition of Ready, Definition of Done, and MoSCoW categories
questions.question: A team maintaining a hospital equipment-tracking product is tightening how it refines its backlog. Match each refinement or prioritization concept on the left with the description on the right that most accurately captures its purpose.
pairs: The "Negotiable" quality in INVEST
The item records the intent of a need rather than a fixed specification, leaving deliberate room for a conversation about how it is best satisfied
A team's Definition of Ready
A working agreement describing the shared understanding an item should have before the team pulls it — a guideline for conversation, not a gate that blocks it
The Definition of Done
A shared quality and completeness bar that every increment must meet before it can be called finished and potentially releasable
A "Could have" item in MoSCoW prioritization
Desirable scope that is the first to be dropped if the iteration or release comes under pressure, without causing the goal to be missed

questions.explanation: Releasing a minimum viable slice to willing early users converts five months of assumption into six weeks of evidence: the team learns which of the remaining seven capabilities actually matter, and the clinics receive value sooner. Laying both options out and asking executive leadership to choose looks properly deferential, but it hands over the decision without the evidence that would make it real; making the value and risk trade-off visible is the practitioner's own work. Building all nine for one launch defers all value and all learning to a single risky event and treats the executive's assumption about confusion as fact when three clinics have volunteered to test it. Demonstrating each increment to the sponsor and the clinics is the strongest alternative, yet a demonstration collects opinions about software nobody can use — no clinic changes its workflow and the five-month bet stands.
questions.concept: MVP and early validated value delivery
questions.question: A veterinary telehealth product has nine planned capabilities. The sponsoring executive wants a single launch in five months with all nine present, arguing that a partial product will confuse clinics. The team estimates it could deliver appointment booking and secure video consultation to production in about six weeks, and three regional clinics have offered to use whatever is ready. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Lay the single-launch and the incremental options out for the executive leadership team along with the trade-offs of each, ask them to choose between the two, and have the team proceed on whichever release plan they select for the telehealth product.

Build all nine capabilities and release them together on the five-month date, since a partial telehealth product would confuse the clinics and damage its reputation with patients and staff before the full value of the service is actually available.

Work with the product owner and the three volunteer clinics to define a minimum viable slice of booking plus secure video, release it to those clinics in six weeks, and use their real usage data to order the remaining capabilities.

Keep the five-month launch date but demonstrate each two-week increment to the executive sponsor and the three volunteer clinics, so that their feedback arrives steadily across the whole build without putting an incomplete product in front of real patients.

questions.explanation: Showing real users a working slice now shortens the feedback loop, replaces assumptions with evidence while change is still cheap, and does not conflict with governance — informal demos and formal gates can coexist, which is exactly how agile practitioners tailor within hybrid constraints. Waiting for the quarterly gate delays learning by months and lets assumption-driven design harden. Demanding that the PMO dismantle the stage gates picks an organizational fight instead of delivering value, and it is unnecessary since early demos violate nothing. Circulating a specification for sign-off substitutes documents for working software and yields far weaker feedback than watching adjusters react to the real thing.
questions.concept: Early stakeholder feedback within hybrid governance
questions.question: An agile team inside a hybrid program is building an internal claims-processing dashboard. Program governance requires formal stakeholder review only at quarterly stage gates. Three weeks in, the team has a working slice showing live claim queues, and developers are debating design choices based on assumptions about how claims adjusters work. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Arrange short informal demonstrations of the working slice with a few claims adjusters now, feed what is learned into the backlog, and still meet the gate requirements
Wait for the first quarterly stage gate so that stakeholder feedback arrives through one consolidated official channel rather than through scattered informal conversations
Ask the program office to remove the stage gates from the governance model, so the team can validate directly with adjusters without a duplicate review step
Write a detailed dashboard specification describing the planned screens and ask the adjusters to review and sign it before the debated design work continues

questions.explanation: Contradictory signals, expert disagreement, and cause-and-effect visible only in retrospect are the signature of the complex domain, where the fitting approach is probe-sense-respond: cheap safe-to-fail experiments, observing real responses, and amplifying what works. Analyzing with experts and applying good practice fits the complicated domain, where cause and effect are discoverable through analysis, but here the experts themselves disagree. Applying best practice with checklists fits the clear domain of well-understood, repeatable work, which a never-served market with unproven technology is not. Acting first to impose stability is the response to chaos, where there is an active crisis demanding immediate action, not an exploratory product decision.
questions.concept: Cynefin complex domain: probe-sense-respond through experimentation
questions.question: A team is asked to create a wellness feature for a market segment the company has never served, using a recommendation technology it has never applied. Interviews produce contradictory user opinions, and experts disagree about what will work; the team suspects cause and effect will be clear only in hindsight. Applying the Cynefin framework, which approach best fits this situation?
choices: Bring in domain experts to analyze the new segment, then apply the good practice their study identifies
Adopt the industry's established best practice for wellness features and run it with standard checklists
Run small safe-to-fail experiments, sense how users actually respond, and amplify the approaches that show promise
Act decisively to put one workable recommendation approach in place, then assess results once usage stabilizes

questions.explanation: MoSCoW loses its power when "Must have" becomes a synonym for "important." The discipline is the consequence test: a true Must is one whose absence makes the release unviable, unlawful, or unsafe. Facilitating that test with the product owner and stakeholders re-establishes real distinctions and usually collapses sixteen Musts to a handful, freeing capacity for Shoulds and for the delighters. Promoting the three delighters to the top misreads Kano — delighters produce disproportionate satisfaction only once must-be qualities are present; excitement features on a release missing basics still disappoint. Fusing MoSCoW and Kano into one numeric score gives false precision by mathematically blending an ordinal viability judgment with a satisfaction-response category; the two answer different questions, and combining them hides which constraint is actually driving the order. Imposing a quota of eight applies arbitrary process to a definition problem — it forces an equally unexamined cut and takes prioritization ownership away from the product owner.
questions.concept: MoSCoW rigor and its relationship to Kano categories
questions.question: A team building a museum-membership renewal experience has finished a lightweight release plan. The product owner asks the practitioner to help sort forty candidate backlog items for the next release. She has classed each item under MoSCoW and separately run a survey scoring items on the Kano dimensions. Sixteen items came back as "Must have" — more than the release could plausibly hold — and three of those sixteen score as delighters in the survey. What is the BEST way for the practitioner to help?
choices: Convert the MoSCoW classes and Kano scores into numeric weights and rank all forty items by the combined score, so release contents fall out of the data
Facilitate a conversation that tests each "Must have" against what would actually happen if the release shipped without it, then re-sequence the genuinely mandatory ones first
Cap the Must have list at eight items the team can deliver, and ask the product owner to choose which eight of the sixteen survive
Move the three delighters to the top of the release, since the survey shows they excite members, and push the Must have items into later releases

questions.explanation: The derived figures show items sitting in Code Review climbing from 1 to 24 while weekly completion falls from 8 to 2 — a steadily widening band on the diagram, which is the signature of a queue building in front of a step nobody is pulling from. Because Code Review carries no limit, nothing signals the team to stop starting and start finishing, so the right first move is to understand why reviews are not being pulled and then consider limiting that state. Calling Development the constraint misreads the picture: it holds 4 items against a limit of 5 and pushes 7 downstream every week, so raising that limit feeds the queue. Adding a second reviewer is the strongest alternative, since capacity at a constraint is legitimate, but it buys people before anyone has asked why reviews lose to new starts. Average cycle time cannot be read straight off a widening band, and publishing a target from a degrading system commits to a number that worsens weekly.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation and unlimited queues
questions.question: An agile practitioner reviews the cumulative flow diagram below for a content-platform team that pulls work through four states. The board carries a WIP limit of 5 on Development and no limit on Code Review. Arrival into the system has been steady. Based on the exhibit, what should the agile practitioner raise with the team first?
choices: Development is the real constraint, since its band stays flat against the limit of 5, so the team should raise that limit and let more items through the system
The Code Review band is widening every week while completion falls — the team should examine why reviews are not being pulled and consider a WIP limit on that state
Work is arriving faster than the team can finish it, so the team should add a second reviewer temporarily until the review queue has drained back to its earlier size
Average cycle time can be read directly off the widening bands, so the team should publish that figure and agree on a delivery target with stakeholders before it changes anything else

questions.explanation: The root problem is a months-long feedback loop between endpoint finished and consumer actually using it. Putting a thin working slice in a real consumer's hands early, backed by consumer-written contract tests that fail in the platform team's own pipeline, converts integration discovery from a quarterly surprise into continuous, automated feedback. A more rigorous specification formally approved by all three consuming teams is the strongest alternative, since it does engage the consumers before coding, but approval proves everyone read the same words, not that they read them the same way, which is exactly how field semantics diverge. An architecture review checkpoint validates designs against standards, adds queue time, and still leaves real integration for months later. Reference examples and richer documentation improve the odds of correct interpretation without ever testing it.
questions.concept: Thin slices and consumer-driven contract testing as early feedback
questions.question: A platform team builds an internal pricing API consumed by three product teams. In the last two quarters, consuming teams discovered mismatched field semantics only during their own integration work, months after the platform team had finished the endpoints. The platform team asks its agile practitioner how to prevent this pattern. What should the agile practitioner recommend first?
choices: Expose each new endpoint to one consuming team as a thin working slice, with consumer-written contract tests running in the platform team's pipeline
Write a more rigorous interface specification and have all three consuming teams review and formally approve it before any endpoint development begins
Add an architecture review checkpoint where a governance group validates every API design against the organization's integration standards before the endpoints are released
Publish reference examples and richer field-level documentation for every endpoint, so the three consuming teams interpret the semantics correctly when they build against it

questions.explanation: Kano thinking holds that basic and performance needs must be met before excitement features pay off, because their absence produces dissatisfaction no amount of delight offsets — the loudly-missed status page and the must-have statement archive are those needs, the unexpected but high-impact document upload is the excitement attribute worth investing in next, and a mascot that annoys as many users as it pleases is a low-confidence bet rather than a reliable delighter. Building the mascot first inverts the model by chasing delight while known dissatisfiers remain unaddressed. Building all four in one release abandons prioritization altogether, paces every increment to the slowest item, and forfeits the early feedback that would test the document-upload bet. Sequencing strictly by development cost ignores customer value entirely; Kano exists precisely to inform order, and cost belongs in the decision only weighed alongside value.
questions.concept: Applying the Kano model to sequencing decisions
questions.question: A product team must choose which of four candidate features to build first for a bank's small-business lending app. Analysis shows: automated document upload has high customer-satisfaction impact but customers do not expect it; a faster status page is expected as standard and customers complain loudly when it is slow; an animated onboarding mascot delights a few users and annoys others; and a downloadable statement archive is something customers list as a must-have but rarely mention when it is present. Applying Kano thinking, which sequencing decision is BEST supported?
choices: Build the animated mascot first, since the attribute that delights users is what differentiates the app from competing small-business lending products
Satisfy the faster status page and the statement archive first, then invest in automated document upload as a differentiator, and treat the mascot as optional
Deliver all four of the candidates in a single release so the app is competitive on every dimension the analysis identified on the day that it launches
Sequence the four candidates strictly by development cost, since the Kano model describes customer satisfaction rather than the order in which the work should be built

questions.explanation: Releasing a minimum viable slice to real users converts months of untested build into measured behavioral evidence, and framing the riskiest assumption as a testable hypothesis with success metrics ensures the team knows what that evidence must show; together they restart the build-measure-learn loop. A comprehensive market-research study is big-bang analysis that pauses delivery and yields opinions rather than observed behavior. Lengthening iterations moves in exactly the wrong direction, enlarging batches and stretching the interval between building and learning. A steering-committee sign-off gate adds an internal approval delay that produces no customer evidence at all, substituting stakeholder judgment for market feedback.
questions.concept: Build-measure-learn: MVP release plus hypothesis-driven development
questions.question: A startup product team says it follows Lean Startup, yet it has spent four months building a full-featured customer portal without exposing any part of it to users, and its assumptions about sign-up conversion remain untested. Which TWO actions would most effectively shorten this team's feedback loops? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Commission a comprehensive market-research study to be completed before development continues
Release a minimum viable slice of the portal to a small cohort of real users and measure their actual behavior
Lengthen the team's iterations so each one can deliver more scope for validation at once
Introduce a steering-committee sign-off gate for every remaining feature before it is built
Restate the riskiest assumption as a testable hypothesis with explicit success metrics before building further

questions.explanation: Value is broader than revenue: cost of delay, regulatory exposure, and sustainability commitments all change the true value of doing work now versus later, so reordering with stakeholders on those combined factors produces a defensible sequence. Publishing the deadline and the commitment as explicit roadmap constraints supplies the timing information that reordering depends on, since a constraint nobody can see gets discovered late and forces reactive replanning. Promoting the largest customer's export request confuses one loud voice with customer value overall and would starve a legally mandated item; satisfaction matters, but not as an override of obligations. Pushing the retention and energy work into a separate technical backlog splits ownership of one product's priorities across two lists, which reliably means the second list loses every trade-off. Reducing every item to a single revenue figure forces false precision onto items whose value is avoided penalty or reduced footprint, and prioritization debate is where shared understanding is built, not waste to be engineered away.
questions.concept: Value-based prioritization beyond revenue, including compliance and sustainability
questions.question: A team building a wildlife-tracking data platform is preparing its next quarterly release. The product owner has ordered the backlog by expected revenue only. During refinement, the team surfaces three concerns: a data-retention obligation with a legal deadline, an architectural change needed to keep server energy consumption within the organization's sustainability commitment, and a request from the largest customer for a custom export format. Which TWO actions BEST help the team prioritize responsibly? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Reorder the backlog with stakeholders so cost of delay, regulatory deadlines, and sustainability commitments are weighed alongside expected revenue
Move the largest customer's custom export request to the top, since customer satisfaction is the primary measure of value
Defer the retention obligation and the energy work into a separate technical backlog owned by the architecture group
Make the retention deadline and the sustainability commitment visible as explicit constraints on the roadmap so their timing drives sequencing
Have the product owner assign each item a revenue figure and re-sort, since a single comparable number removes prioritization debate

questions.explanation: Running Five Whys on the actual escapes and then fixing the cause is best because the evidence already points at environment drift, and building parity into the pipeline removes the defect class instead of adding inspection downstream of it; the team keeps ownership and the fix pays back on every future release. Adopting the checklist and freeze adds process and delays feedback while leaving configuration drift fully intact — the freeze would simply make each release larger and riskier. Handing sign-off to the release manager moves accountability away from the people who can prevent the defect and adds a hand-off queue. Extra exploratory testing is valuable in general but here it inspects for a problem that only appears in production configuration, so it is unlikely to catch these escapes and does nothing to stop them recurring.
questions.concept: Five Whys root-cause analysis versus adding inspection process; quality built in
questions.question: Three of the last five releases of a payments service were followed by a production hotfix within 48 hours. In the retrospective, the team proposes a pre-release sign-off checklist and a two-day code freeze before every release. Reviewing the incident notes, the agile practitioner sees that all three escapes involved configuration values that differed between staging and production. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Adopt the proposed sign-off checklist and the two-day code freeze for every release, then measure across the next quarter whether the number of hotfixes that follow a release drops below the current rate.

Ask the release manager to take ownership of final sign-off on every release, so that an independent reviewer confirms the configuration values in each environment before a change ever reaches production.
Add a timeboxed exploratory testing session against the staging environment before each release, so more of the configuration differences are found by the team before the payments service ships.

Facilitate a Five Whys on the three escapes with the team, then act on what it exposes — such as bringing environment configuration into the deployment pipeline so staging and production cannot drift.

questions.explanation: Unknown rules, poorly understood behavior patterns, and pilots that keep surprising the team are the signature of Cynefin's complex domain, where cause-and-effect relationships can only be understood retrospectively; the fitting strategy is probe-sense-respond — run safe-to-fail experiments, observe what emerges, and amplify what works. Treating the problem as complicated assumes experts can analyze their way to a correct answer up front, but expert analysis requires discoverable cause-and-effect, which the repeated surprises show is absent here. The chaotic-domain response of acting immediately to impose order applies to genuine crises with no discernible patterns at all, not to a product development effort that can afford deliberate experimentation. The clear-domain response of applying established best practice assumes an obvious, well-understood problem — the opposite of a situation where even the detection rules are unknown.
questions.concept: Cynefin complex domain and probe-sense-respond
questions.question: A team is asked to build a fraud-detection capability for a payments product where neither the effective detection rules nor customer behavior patterns are well understood, and every small pilot release has revealed unexpected results. Using the Cynefin framework, which reasoning BEST supports how the team should proceed?
choices: The work sits in the complex domain, where cause and effect are visible only in hindsight, so the team should probe with safe-to-fail experiments, sense the outcomes, and respond
The work sits in the complicated domain, so the team should bring in recognized fraud analysts to study the payment patterns fully and then build the detection design they recommend
The work sits in the chaotic domain, so the team should act at once to stop losses and impose stability, and analyze the detection patterns only after conditions settle
The work sits in the clear domain, so the team should adopt the established industry rule sets for fraud detection and apply them consistently across every payment channel

questions.explanation: A 3-to-40 point spread is a knowledge problem rather than an estimating problem, and a timeboxed spike buys that knowledge cheaply by generating early empirical feedback on the riskiest unknown before anyone commits. Averaging the estimates manufactures a false number: the mid-point of a spread driven by ignorance carries no more information than either extreme, and presenting it as a commitment quietly transfers the hidden risk to the sponsor. A full architecture workshop is up-front big-bang analysis on a problem nobody has hands-on experience with, so it yields confident-looking design decisions that have never met real data or real sync conflicts. Bringing in an outside expert purely to produce the estimate outsources learning the team will need across two quarters of build, delays feedback while the engagement is arranged, and leaves the team no better able to forecast its own work.
questions.concept: Spikes for reducing technical uncertainty before commitment
questions.question: A team is starting a two-quarter effort to add offline capability to a field-inspection application. Nobody on the team has built conflict resolution for offline data sync before, and estimates for the sync stories range from 3 points to 40 points depending on who is asked. The sponsor wants a committed date next week. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Run a short, timeboxed spike to build a throwaway prototype of the riskiest sync behavior, then re-estimate with what was learned
Average the team's estimates and give the sponsor the mid-point as the committed date, noting the spread as a known risk
Hold a detailed architecture-design workshop to specify the conflict-resolution approach fully before any sync story is estimated again
Bring in a consultant experienced in offline data sync to produce the estimate the sponsor is asking for by next week

questions.explanation: Every option would move work forward, but only one restores customer engagement, transparency, and flow at once. Convening the three voices with the team surfaces the conflict where it can be reconciled, ties each signal to value measures everyone has already agreed to, keeps the decision horizon small — the next few items rather than the whole roadmap — and uses a real release to test the choice. Prioritizing by analytics alone treats one signal as truth; analytics show where users struggle but not why, and identity-verification drop-off in a regulated context may be deliberate friction. Holding the sequence until the clinical director returns is the strongest rival, because settling competing customer demands is exactly the proxy's job — but the team has already stopped pulling feature work for three weeks, and waiting leaves one absent person as the program's single point of failure. Building thin versions of all three multiplies work in progress and delays every outcome, spending real capacity on what one session and a small release could reveal sooner.
questions.concept: Reconciling conflicting customer signals with shared value measures and short validation cycles
questions.question: A regulated telehealth program delivers on a continuous-flow cadence. Three customer channels now disagree about what comes next: support tickets point to appointment-rescheduling errors, a clinician advisory board wants e-prescribing, and usage analytics show most drop-off occurs at identity verification. The clinical director who serves as customer proxy has been unavailable for three weeks, and the team has stopped pulling new feature work while it waits for a decision. What is the BEST response?
choices: Prioritize from the usage analytics alone, since measured behavior is a more objective signal than stakeholder opinion, and begin with the identity-verification step where the drop-off is heaviest.

Hold the current sequence until the clinical director returns and can rank the three signals as customer proxy, since the customer proxy role exists precisely to settle competing customer demands of exactly this kind.

Convene representatives of all three channels with the team to map each signal against the program's agreed value measures, re-sequence only the next few items, and validate the choice with a small release.

Build a thin version of all three areas and release them together behind a controlled comparison, so measured customer preference rather than argument decides where the team invests its capacity next.

questions.explanation: Turning both onboarding designs into cheap, measurable experiments is best: when opinions conflict and nobody has evidence, the agile response is to stop arguing and start learning, and the smallest workable version of each flow plus real activation data resolves the question quickly and objectively. Letting the senior developers decide privileges internal seniority over customer behavior, which is the same bias that produced three sessions of stalemate. Commissioning an external usability study is slow, costly analysis when the product itself can generate live evidence, and it measures reactions in a research setting rather than activation in real use. Building the guided tour first because it is smaller and revisiting the gallery only if activation fails is the strongest alternative — shipping and watching beats debating — but with one flow released the team cannot attribute the result, and waiting a quarter for an ambiguous signal costs more than running both thin versions now.
questions.concept: Hypothesis-driven development; A/B experimentation
questions.question: A product team using XP practices has spent three consecutive planning sessions debating whether new users should be onboarded through a guided tour or a template gallery. Each faction cites its own past experience, and the standoff is now delaying other work. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Frame each option as a testable hypothesis, release the smallest workable version of both to a subset of new users, and let activation data settle the debate
Let the senior developers decide, since they carry the most delivery experience and will build whichever onboarding path is put in front of new users
Commission a usability study with an external research firm so the choice rests on professional research rather than the competing personal experiences in the room
Build the guided tour first because it is the smaller option, and revisit the template gallery only if activation fails to improve over the next quarter

questions.explanation: Matching leadership style to readiness is the key: this team has high capability but low confidence after years of directive leadership, so supported delegation — frame the decision, supply context, hand over ownership, remain available, then widen the decision space as confidence returns — grows real autonomy without setting the team up to fail. Collecting private preferences, merging them, and presenting the result back as the team's own decision manufactures ownership rather than building it; the practitioner still authors the plan, and members recognize the pretense. Inviting the previous leader to walk through the reasoning behind past decisions is the most defensible alternative, because decision criteria are worth transferring, but it re-centers the person whose style created the dependency and keeps the team receiving answers instead of forming them. Settling the sequence with a timeboxed spike answers a technical question while quietly avoiding the real one, which is who decides.
questions.concept: Situational leadership; delegation matched to team readiness after directive leadership
questions.question: An agile practitioner inherits a long-tenured platform team whose previous leader personally made every design and estimation decision. The team is technically strong, but when the practitioner asks how members want to sequence an upcoming migration, they glance at each other and wait to be told. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask each member privately for a preferred sequence, merge the answers into one migration plan, and present it back as the team's own decision so members feel genuine ownership
Frame the migration decision, share the relevant context, ask the team to propose the approach, and stay available for support — widening their decision space as confidence grows
Invite the previous leader to walk the team through the reasoning behind past design calls, so members absorb the decision criteria before they are asked to sequence anything
Run the sequencing as a timeboxed technical spike and let the measured results settle the order, since evidence spares the team an unfamiliar and uncomfortable group decision

questions.explanation: The two-night shadow trial and the instrumented thin slice both convert an assumption into measured behavior inside the two-week window, and they do it where the risk actually lives — on a night shift, with real carts and real staff. The shadow trial costs almost nothing and exposes the physical constraints of moving carts with two people on a floor; the thin slice produces a scan-success rate per shift that either retires the risk or triggers a design change while months of runway remain. A specification section signed off by ward managers records intent rather than behavior, and managers are not the people scanning at 2 a.m. Usability testing after feature completion teaches the same lesson months later, once the inventory model has already been built on the untested assumption. Raising the risk score and taking it to the steering meeting documents and escalates the risk without reducing it by a single point; a risk-adjusted backlog exists so high-uncertainty items are pulled forward and tested, not so scores are updated on a register.
questions.concept: Reducing a high-impact assumption through early empirical validation and risk-adjusted sequencing
questions.question: A team is replacing the tote-tracking system for a hospital laundry service on a five-month runway. The team's own pre-mortem identified the riskiest assumption: that ward staff will scan tote barcodes reliably during night shifts, when two people cover a floor and carts move fast. If the assumption is wrong, the entire inventory model fails. Which TWO actions best reduce this uncertainty within the next two weeks? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Add a detailed barcode-handling section to the requirements specification and walk ward managers through it for sign-off.
Run a two-night shadow trial on one ward using a handheld device and a paper fallback, observing what staff actually do with the carts.
Schedule usability testing once the system is feature complete, so testers experience the full workflow as it will ship.
Raise the assumption's risk score on the risk register and table it for discussion at the next steering meeting.
Release a thin end-to-end slice covering one tote type to a single ward and instrument the scan success rate per shift.

questions.explanation: Coaching draws the answer out of the person being coached: the coach asks powerful questions, and the product owner owns both the thinking and the decision, which builds durable capability. Sharing one's own past experience and advice is mentoring — valuable, but a different stance in which the expert's history rather than the coachee's context shapes the answer. Delivering a structured curriculum of techniques is training, which transfers defined skills on the trainer's schedule rather than developing the person's own judgment against live decisions. Making the calls on her behalf is not development at all; it creates dependency, delays her growth, and quietly takes back the decision authority the role requires.
questions.concept: Coaching vs mentoring vs training distinctions
questions.question: An agile practitioner wants to help a newly appointed product owner grow into the role and deliberately chooses a coaching approach rather than mentoring or training. Which behavior is consistent with that choice?
choices: Sharing how the practitioner worked through similar prioritization dilemmas in two earlier product roles
Walking the product owner through a structured curriculum covering backlog-management techniques and metrics
Making the harder prioritization calls on the product owner's behalf until her confidence builds up
Asking questions that help the product owner examine her options and reach her own prioritization decision

questions.explanation: Average cycle time equals average work in progress divided by average throughput, so thirty divided by six gives about five weeks, matching the stakeholders' experience; of the two terms, work in progress is the one the team can change immediately by committing to fewer items and finishing what is started, whereas throughput moves only slowly through improvements to the system. Treating higher weekly commitment as the lever confuses starting more with finishing more and would raise work in progress, lengthening cycle time rather than shortening it. Claiming the law cannot be applied ignores that Little's Law is a relationship among averages over a period and needs only aggregate figures for a rough, decision-useful estimate. Inverting the ratio yields throughput per item rather than time per item, then invents an off-board explanation for a delay the figures already account for.
questions.concept: Practical application of Little's Law to cycle time
questions.question: A support-and-enhancement team for a university financial-aid portal completes an average of six work items per week. Its board consistently holds about thirty items between the commitment point and Done. Stakeholders complain that a request accepted today is typically not delivered for more than a month, and they ask the team to "work faster." Applying Little's Law to these figures, which statement best explains the situation and identifies the most effective lever?
choices: Average cycle time is roughly five weeks, since thirty items in progress divided by six completed per week gives five; the fastest lever available to the team is to reduce the number of items in progress.

Average cycle time is roughly five weeks, and the fastest lever available to the team is to raise the number of items it commits to each week so that throughput rises far enough to meet the demand arriving.
Cycle time cannot be derived from these averages, because Little's Law needs the individual start and finish timestamps of every single item before an average can be quoted to stakeholders.
Average cycle time is roughly 0.2 weeks, since six completions per week divided by thirty items in progress gives 0.2, so the month-long wait must come from work queued before commitment.

questions.explanation: The systemic problem is anchoring: whoever speaks first — especially with seniority — sets the range of acceptable opinion, and distributed members have the least power to break in. Silent simultaneous writing equalizes airtime structurally, so the design concern (and every future concern) can surface on its own merits, while private coaching helps the senior engineers see their unintended silencing effect; this fixes the mechanism, not just this incident. Raising the concern by proxy gets one issue heard once but leaves the team dependent on the practitioner as a courier and does nothing to make the next concern speakable — and thin anonymity on a small team risks exposing the source. Escalating to the manager frames well-intentioned seniors as offenders, bypasses the team, and teaches everyone that candor triggers management intervention. Splitting the retrospective by location institutionalizes the divide: the people who most need to hear the feedback are excluded from the room where it is said.
questions.concept: Facilitation techniques that neutralize anchoring and power gradients in distributed retrospectives
questions.question: In the retrospectives of a distributed data-platform team, the two most senior engineers speak first on every topic, after which the remote members briefly agree and the discussion moves on. Privately, a remote member tells the agile practitioner that a recurring production defect traces back to a design the senior engineers championed, but says 'there is no point raising it in the retro.' Several responses are technically possible. Which is BEST?
choices: Raise the design concern in the next retrospective yourself without naming anyone, so the recurring production defect finally gets discussed openly while the member who first reported it stays protected

Restructure the retrospective around silent, simultaneous written input that the team reviews together before anyone speaks, and separately coach the senior engineers on how speaking first shapes what others will say
Tell the engineering manager that the senior engineers are shutting down dissent, so the pattern is handled through the management chain and the remote members are not left to challenge it themselves
Hold a separate retrospective for the remote members where concerns surface freely, then carry the agreed items into the main session so the quieter half of the team still reaches it

questions.explanation: Keeping the radiator where it is and turning the visit into a conversation about how surfaced blockers attract help is the point of an information radiator: honest, ambient information that prompts action — including from executives who may be exactly the people able to remove two-week-old impediments. Building a separate digital board of throughput and cycle time for the tour creates one view for leadership and another for the team; even with the corridor wall retained, the executives are shown curated metrics instead of the aging blockers, which is selective transparency. Moving the wall into the team room as instructed is honest in its briefing but still removes the ambient signal from the corridor where it was doing its work, and it complies with a request whose purpose is to make the impediments less visible. Working the aging blockers hard so the column reads well by the visit is the clearest anti-pattern: it manages the appearance of the board for an audience rather than the system that produced two-week blocks, and the underlying impediment returns as soon as the executives leave.
questions.concept: Information radiators and visible impediments
questions.question: An insurance claims team manages its work on a large Kanban wall in a corridor. Several blocked items have visible aging indicators showing they have been stuck for more than two weeks.
