A department head tells the agile practitioner to move the wall into the team room before a group of executives tours the floor next week, saying the blocked column 'makes the department look bad.' What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Keep the wall where it is and use the executive visit as an opportunity to show how visible blockers attract help and get resolved faster.
Build a digital board for the executive tour that shows throughput and cycle time, and keep the corridor wall as the team's own working view.
Move the wall into the team room as asked and brief the executives with a progress summary that names the blocked items honestly.
Work the aging blockers hard this week so the column is clear by the time the executives walk the floor and the wall reads well.

questions.explanation: Little's Law ties work in progress, throughput, and cycle time together — 18 items in the system at 12 completed per iteration puts average cycle time near 1.5 iterations — and that same throughput history says 58 items need roughly 4.8 iterations against the five that remain, a result with essentially no margin for normal variability. The honest output is a forecast expressed as a range with its assumptions stated, paired with a conversation about which must-haves genuinely have to ship on the regulatory date. Dividing 58 by 12 dresses a point estimate as a certainty and forecloses the scope conversation a fixed date demands. Re-estimating the 58 items in story points is the strongest rival, because sizing matters when items vary — but the stem says sizes are broadly similar, so it buys no accuracy and spends scarce iterations measuring rather than delivering. Raising the throughput target to 15 changes no capacity in the system; targets are not a delivery mechanism, and pressure on a stable system usually buys apparent speed by quietly cutting quality.
questions.concept: Practical Little's Law and probabilistic forecasting
questions.question: A team delivering a utility-billing rewrite works in two-week iterations, has held a stable throughput of roughly 12 work items per iteration, and typically has about 18 items in the system at any time. A regulator has just confirmed a hard cutover date 10 weeks — five iterations — away. The product owner asks whether the 58 remaining must-have items will be done, and wants a single number. Historical item sizes are broadly similar and the team's WIP has been stable for two months. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Use the team's throughput and current WIP to derive an expected cycle time, present a forecast as a range with its assumptions, and discuss scope options with the product owner
Give the product owner the single number requested by dividing the 58 remaining items by a throughput of 12, which puts the work finishing comfortably inside the five iterations
Re-estimate the 58 must-have items in story points and burn down against the cutover date, since item counts hide the size variation the team has already observed
Raise the team's throughput target to 15 items an iteration and hold daily checkpoints against it, so the remaining must-have scope fits inside the regulator's window

questions.explanation: A first increment has to be genuinely releasable, which for a regulated financial product means the mandatory anti-money-laundering checks are inside it, not deferred. A single account type with verification working end to end is a thin vertical slice a real applicant can complete, and it puts the riskiest assumption — the verification step where abandonment concentrates — in front of real users fastest. A design prototype of the whole journey produces opinions rather than evidence about a flow that must work against real identity data, and no account is opened. The polished wizard is the strongest alternative, because saved progress does attack the abandonment point the data identifies — but it invests in breadth before verification is proven and pushes learning past eight weeks. Deferring the anti-money-laundering checks leaves an increment compliance has already said cannot go live.
questions.concept: MVP definition as a thin vertical slice with non-negotiable regulatory scope
questions.question: A product team at a savings-and-loan is planning the first increment of a mobile account-opening flow. Data shows applicants abandon most often at identity verification. The product owner drafts three candidate first increments: a polished multi-step onboarding wizard with saved progress; a single-path opening flow for one account type with identity verification and required anti-money-laundering checks working end to end; and a design prototype of the whole journey with no working verification. Compliance confirms that any live account opening must include the anti-money-laundering checks. The sponsor wants something in customers' hands within eight weeks. What is the BEST guidance from the agile practitioner?
choices: Recommend the design prototype, since it exercises the whole journey within days and puts the identity verification step in front of applicants soonest
Recommend the polished wizard, since saved progress attacks abandonment at the exact step the data identifies as the largest source of loss
Recommend the single-path flow with working identity verification and the required anti-money-laundering checks as the first releasable increment
Recommend the single-path flow but defer the anti-money-laundering checks to a later increment, so identity verification is proven with real applicants first

questions.explanation: Stopping new starts and swarming the full column is best: it moves capacity to the constraint, drains the queue that is inflating lead time, and puts the team in position to see why testing is slow before changing anything structural. Raising the Test limit from three to six deletes the signal without touching the constraint, and pushing more cards into the slowest step lengthens lead time further. Adding an unlimited buffer between Build and Test does make the wait visible, which the board should do, but visualization alone relieves nothing: the six-day wait simply moves one column upstream while developers keep starting work, so lead time is unchanged. Escalating for a new hire is a slow external fix that treats headcount as the only lever and skips the improvement the team can make today.
questions.concept: WIP limits, bottlenecks, and swarming the constraint
questions.question: A support-and-delivery team runs a Kanban board with column limits of Analysis 3, Build 4, Test 3, Done. For nine straight days the Test column has been full, and cards there wait an average of six days while cards clear Build in about one day. Developers keep pulling fresh items into Analysis because, as one says, "we can't sit idle." Average lead time has doubled over the last month. What is the BEST response?
choices: Raise the Test column limit from three to six so cards stop stacking against the limit and developers can keep pulling new work into Analysis
Add an unlimited Waiting for Test buffer column between Build and Test, so the queue that is really forming becomes visible and its waiting time measurable
Ask the developers to stop starting new work and swarm on finishing the cards already in Test, then inspect with the team what makes testing slow.
Ask the functional manager for a second tester and hold current policies until that person joins, since testing is plainly the constrained step in the team's workflow

questions.explanation: Making the block visible with its start date and then going directly to the group that owns the constraint is the first move: it creates transparency about aging work and resolves the impediment through collaboration with the people who actually control the rig. Escalating to the director first skips the peer conversation, spends political capital before it is needed, and damages a working relationship the team will depend on again next month. A policy that returns blocked cards to the backlog hides the impediment rather than removing it — the wait is still real, it is simply no longer measured, and the item loses its place in the queue. Continuing to pull around the block and deferring the discussion to the retrospective lets the item age silently, inflates work in progress, and delays feedback on a problem that is actionable today; retrospectives improve the system, they are not the queue for live blockers.
questions.concept: Impediment visualization and resolution at the lowest effective level
questions.question: On a Kanban team at a coastal ferry-booking company, a card for "passenger manifest export" has sat in Build for three days because the only shared hardware test rig is controlled by the onboard-systems department and is booked solid. The developer mentioned it once in standup; since then the team has simply pulled other cards around it, and the card carries no marking on the board. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Ask the onboard-systems director to reassign the shared test rig to this team for the remainder of the iteration, so the manifest export card can finish quickly.
Introduce a policy returning any card blocked more than two days to the backlog, so the board shows only work that is genuinely moving through the system.
Mark the card blocked on the board with the date the wait began, then go with the developer to the onboard-systems team to agree access and a resolution date.
Keep the team pulling other cards so throughput holds steady, and bring the shared test-rig constraint to the next retrospective for a more lasting fix.

questions.explanation: A continuously visible, team-owned board radiates current, unfiltered information to everyone, replacing stale monthly snapshots, and demonstrating working increments while openly discussing impediments gives stakeholders direct evidence of real progress and real problems. Adding a red-amber-green slide to the monthly deck still delivers curated, month-old information through an intermediary, which is the root cause of the complaint. Limiting access to raw metrics is gatekeeping dressed up as helpfulness; the agile answer to misinterpretation is shared context, not restricted data. Reporting only completed items is selective disclosure that manufactures false confidence and guarantees stakeholders learn about trouble "too late," exactly the failure they described.
questions.concept: Information radiators, working software as honest status, unfiltered communication
questions.question: An agile practitioner joins a hybrid program where sponsors complain that they "never know the real status until it is too late." Status has been communicated through monthly slide decks assembled by a coordinator. Which TWO actions would best build transparency for this program? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Have the coordinator add a red-amber-green summary slide to the monthly deck so executives can scan status faster
Establish a team-owned board, visible to all stakeholders, that continuously shows workflow states, work-in-progress, and current blockers
Limit stakeholder access to raw team metrics so the data cannot be misinterpreted without context
Report only fully completed items to stakeholders so confidence in the program remains high
Demonstrate working product increments at regular reviews and openly discuss impediments and risks in the same forum

questions.explanation: Taking the diagram to the team, confirming the constraint together, and agreeing a change is best because a single widening band with stable arrival and departure rates is the classic signature of a bottleneck, and the effective responses — subordinating upstream work to the constraint and moving capacity toward it — are decisions the team should make with the data in front of them. Asking analysts for far more detailed test cases prescribes a solution before the cause is understood and adds documentation work upstream of the step that is already overloaded. Splitting In Test into finer states is the strongest rival, since knowing where inside testing the wait falls would sharpen any countermeasure, but it spends two more weeks observing a band that has already grown from two days' worth of work to eleven, and finer reporting changes nothing in the system. Raising the iteration commitment pushes more work into a system that already cannot drain its test queue, lengthening cycle time further.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation and bottleneck response
questions.question: On an insurance claims-automation team, the cumulative flow diagram for the past six weeks shows the arrival line and the completion line running roughly parallel, but the "In Test" band has widened steadily from about two days' worth of work to about eleven days' worth. All other bands are stable. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Ask the business analysts to write far more detailed test cases up front, so that testers spend less of their time working out intent and the widening band closes without anyone new being added.
Split the In Test column into several finer states so that the diagram shows precisely where inside testing the items are waiting, then decide what to change once another two weeks of data is in.
Show the widening band to the team, confirm together that testing is the current constraint, and help them agree on a change such as limiting upstream pull and having developers pair into testing.

Raise the team's iteration commitment so that more items are completed each week, which should pull the accumulated work through the testing step and bring that widening band back toward its earlier width.

questions.explanation: The strongest response protects the blameless container while still honoring the director's legitimate need for confidence that the outage is being addressed: pausing to restate the systemic purpose resets the room, and offering a follow-up on improvement actions gives leadership a proper channel without sacrificing safety. Naming the individual in the name of transparency confuses openness about work with scapegoating people — it would teach the team permanently that candor in retrospectives is dangerous. Ending and rescheduling the session dodges the tension, delays learning while the outage is fresh, and leaves the director's question unanswered, inviting a repeat. Ejecting the director enforces the rule but does so confrontationally, escalating conflict with leadership and wasting a chance to educate a senior stakeholder about how blameless learning works.
questions.concept: Blameless retrospectives and managing leadership intrusion
questions.question: Minutes into a blameless retrospective following a payment outage, a senior director joins unannounced and asks the team to identify "who pushed the faulty configuration." Team members exchange glances and stop speaking. The agile practitioner is facilitating. Several responses are technically possible — which is BEST?
choices: Answer the director from the deployment record, since transparency is a core agile value and the team should not appear to shield one of its own members
Close the session and reschedule the retrospective for a time when the director is elsewhere, so the team can speak candidly about the payment outage without an outside audience
Ask the director to leave the room, citing the team agreement that retrospectives belong to the team alone, and send the improvement actions once the session has finished
Pause, restate that the session examines how the system allowed the failure rather than who acted, and offer to walk the director through the resulting improvement actions afterward

questions.explanation: The iteration goal is a commitment about value, and only the person accountable for product value can trade against it — with the requester present so the trade-off is explicit rather than absorbed silently. That conversation may end in a swap, a deferral, or a decision that the prospect matters more; what matters is that it happens openly with the team's remaining capacity in view. Quietly accepting the work because it sounds small is how a second unplanned item erodes the goal, and the retrospective surfaces the damage only after it is done. Letting the product owner rule alone is the strongest alternative, since ordering is their accountability — but the deal context arrives second-hand and the requester learns nothing. Declaring the goal protected treats the timebox as a rule and closes a legitimate value discussion.
questions.concept: Protecting the iteration goal through transparent scope trade-offs
questions.question: An XP-influenced team building a farm-equipment telematics service is midway through a two-week iteration whose goal is "a mechanic can see why a machine stopped without calling the depot." On day five a regional sales director asks the team to add a fleet-utilization export for a prospect demo the following week, saying it is only a few hours of work and the deal is significant. The team has already absorbed one unplanned item this iteration. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Accept the export because it is small, and record its effect on the iteration goal in the retrospective so the pattern becomes visible to everyone
Bring the sales director and product owner together to weigh the export against the current iteration goal and decide openly what enters and what leaves
Have the product owner decide alone whether the export replaces planned work, since ordering value against the iteration goal is the product owner's accountability
Tell the sales director the iteration goal is protected and offer to make the export the first item of the next iteration, ahead of the prospect demo

questions.explanation: Working with the manager and the team to replace morning assignments with a pull policy is best because it removes the idle time and the overload at their common source — a single dispatcher deciding who works on what — and restores the team's ability to self-organize around the flow of work. Publishing the next day's assignments each evening changes only the timing of the same push system: members still wait to be handed work, and the uneven loading survives. A work-in-progress limit of two per person caps the overloaded member but keeps the manager as sole dispatcher, and limits attached to people reinforce individual ownership of tickets instead of team ownership of flow. Asking the two idle members to take tickets off the overloaded one is the most immediately helpful option and worth doing today, but it is a manual rebalance inside the same system that needs someone to intervene every morning.
questions.concept: Pull systems and self-organizing teams
questions.question: A Kanban team maintains a logistics platform's integration services. Every morning, the operations manager reviews the incoming ticket queue and assigns each ticket to a named team member. The agile practitioner notices that two members finished their tickets by midday yesterday and then waited idle until this morning's assignments, while another member is overloaded. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the manager to publish the following day's assignments each evening, so that nobody starts the morning idle while the incoming ticket queue is still being reviewed
Work with the manager and the team to replace morning assignments with a pull policy in which members select the next ticket themselves as their capacity frees up
Introduce a work-in-progress limit of two tickets per person, so that no individual can be loaded beyond capacity while others finish early and then sit waiting
Ask the two members who finished early to take some tickets off the overloaded member, so that the day's assigned work is completed by the team as a whole

questions.explanation: Bringing the reviewer into the team's design sessions attacks the waste directly: a six-day wait that changes roughly one submission in forty is pure queue time created by a handoff, and moving the review into the moment of creation removes the queue while preserving the compliance outcome the organization wants. Capping the brand-review column at three limits how much waiting work accumulates but does not shorten the wait itself; the handoff, not the queue depth, is the root of the six-day delay. Sampling one submission in five is the strongest rival, since a one-in-forty change rate genuinely argues for lighter inspection — but it is a unilateral reduction of someone else's control, decided without them, and the sampled screens still sit in the same queue. Requiring brand sign-off on every mockup before development moves the gate earlier without removing it, front-loads documentation, and turns a six-day wait into a precondition for starting work at all.
questions.concept: Handoff and waiting waste in the value stream
questions.question: A five-person team building scheduling software for veterinary clinics must route every screen change through a separate brand-compliance reviewer who works from static mockups. The board shows nine items parked in an "Awaiting brand review" column, where they wait an average of six days. Over the last quarter, the reviewer requested a change to only one of forty-one submissions. What is the BEST course of action for the agile practitioner?
choices: Set a work-in-progress limit of three on the brand review column so the queue is capped, and leave the separate reviewer handoff itself otherwise unchanged.
Ask the reviewer to sample one in five submissions, given that only one of forty-one needed a change, and let the remaining screens pass through untouched.
Invite the brand reviewer into the team's design working sessions so compliance feedback happens while the design is being created rather than in a queue afterward.
Require brand sign-off on every mockup before a screen is allowed to enter development, so that the review happens up front and the team avoids reworking finished code.

questions.explanation: Running a time-boxed spike against the sandbox is best because the risk burndown is flat precisely because nobody is buying information — a spike converts an unknown into evidence within the teams' own control without waiting on procurement, and the anti-corruption layer limits the blast radius if the assumed API shape is wrong, which also protects the speculative integration code already written. Re-scoring from real learning is what actually makes a risk burndown move. Moving the item to a procurement-owned dependency log hides the largest exposure from the very forum that has the authority to act on it; it satisfies the request to stop alarming the committee at the direct cost of transparency. Seeking approval for an in-house contingency is a large, expensive commitment made before anyone has tested whether the vendor works at all — a response chosen ahead of understanding. Deferring all identity-verification stories delays learning further, leaves the already-written integration code unvalidated, and concentrates the entire exposure at the end of the program, when there is no time left to respond.
questions.concept: Risk burndown stagnation, spikes as risk-reduction experiments, risk-adjusted backlog
questions.question: A regulated fintech program has three teams contributing to one release train. A risk-adjusted backlog and a risk burndown chart were established at program start; the risk burndown has been flat for five iterations. Investigating, the practitioner finds that the single largest remaining exposure — an unproven third-party identity-verification vendor whose contract signature is controlled by procurement — has been carried as "monitor" every iteration because the teams believe they cannot act until the contract closes. Meanwhile teams have been building integration code against an assumed API shape. The program manager wants the risk removed from the chart to "stop alarming the steering committee." What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Move the vendor item off the risk burndown onto a program dependency log owned by procurement, so the exposure sits with the group controlling the contract signature
Facilitate the teams in running a time-boxed spike against the vendor's public sandbox behind an anti-corruption layer, and re-score the risk from what the spike learns
Have the teams start building an in-house identity-verification capability now as a hedge, so the program is covered whichever way the vendor contract finally goes
Defer every identity-verification story until the contract is signed and fill the freed capacity with other release-train work, then plan the integration once terms are known

questions.explanation: Dividing active time by elapsed time gives 4.5 over 18, or roughly 25 percent, which means about three quarters of the delivery time is spent waiting -- in queues, on handoffs, on blocked dependencies -- so attacking those wait states offers far more leverage than pressing people to work faster during the quarter of the time that is already active. Treating 100 percent as the target misreads the measure and the remedy that follows from it: keeping everyone busy on more items at once raises work in progress, lengthens queues, and drives flow efficiency down rather than up. Concluding that the team should slow delivery for quality does not follow from these two numbers, which say nothing about defect rates or rework. Insisting that velocity must come first confuses a capacity-forecasting measure expressed in story points with a time-based diagnostic that has already localized where the elapsed time goes.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency calculation and diagnostic use
questions.question: A team measures two numbers on every work item: total elapsed time from commitment to delivery, and the portion of that elapsed time in which someone was actively working on the item. Last quarter the averages were 18 days elapsed and 4.5 days active. The team wants to shorten delivery time and is choosing where to focus. The most useful interpretation of these figures is that:
choices: Flow efficiency is about 25 percent, so the largest opportunity lies in reducing waiting and handoffs rather than in working faster
Flow efficiency is about 25 percent, and since 100 percent is the goal the team should raise utilization by starting more items
The team is spending too little active time on each item, so it should slow delivery to improve quality first
These figures cannot guide improvement until the team also knows its velocity in story points, since a percentage alone says nothing

questions.explanation: Situational leadership matches leader behavior to follower readiness: a team high in enthusiasm but low in competence needs directive guidance paired with strong support, with autonomy expanding deliberately as capability develops. Borrowing a seasoned engineer from another group is genuinely useful help, but keeping the familiar hands-off posture alongside it dodges the adjustment the situation calls for, and the loan ends while the leadership gap remains. Setting detailed standards and reviewing every change is the right stance today but the wrong stance to hold for the engagement — fixed control blocks the team from ever growing into the autonomy the practitioner should be handing back. Cutting scope for the first few iterations lowers pressure without addressing competence; a smaller amount of unfamiliar work still needs direction and support the team is not currently getting.
questions.concept: Situational leadership and growing team autonomy
questions.question: An agile practitioner known for a hands-off servant-leadership style takes on a newly formed team of enthusiastic junior engineers adopting a technology stack none of them has used before. Applying situational leadership, how should the practitioner adjust?
choices: Pair the team with a seasoned engineer from another group and otherwise keep the familiar hands-off posture in place
Set detailed standards and review every change until the stack is mastered, holding that level of control for the engagement
Cut the team's scope for the first few iterations so members can learn the new stack before anything is committed
Provide close direction and structured support now, and progressively hand decisions over as the team's competence grows

questions.explanation: A joint end-to-end mapping session with shared working agreements is best because systems thinking says the failure lives in the interaction between the teams, not inside either one: visualizing the whole flow together dissolves the blame narrative and lets the teams own a shared integration cadence — collaboration before escalation. Escalating to the engineering director to assign fault entrenches the adversarial framing and strips both teams of ownership of a problem only they can solve day to day. Inserting an integration manager adds an intermediary and a handoff, weakening the direct cross-team communication agile favors and creating a new bottleneck. A formal change-control log adds process to compensate for missing collaboration — it documents changes after the fact but slows feedback and does nothing to align the teams' rhythms.
questions.concept: Cross-team coordination and systems thinking
questions.question: In a logistics company, the mobile-app team and the routing-engine team are distributed across two continents. Integration fails at nearly every iteration boundary, and each team's retrospective concludes the other team is at fault. The mobile team's lead asks the agile practitioner to "get management to make the routing team fix their API discipline." What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Bring both teams together virtually to map the full integration flow end to end and jointly create shared working agreements on interfaces and integration cadence
Ask the engineering director to weigh both teams' evidence and rule on which side owns the integration failures, so the blame in retrospectives finally stops
Introduce a dedicated integration manager who owns the handoff between the two teams, so that neither side has to coordinate the shared interface across time zones itself
Require both teams to record every API change in a shared change log before merging, so nothing surprising turns up at the next iteration boundary

questions.explanation: An effective shared vision paints a vivid, customer-centered future state that is short enough to remember and concrete enough to arbitrate everyday trade-offs, and the picture of any neighborhood pharmacy filling any prescription in under two minutes with no paperwork does precisely that — any team member can hold a proposed story up against it and judge whether it moves the world closer to that state. Committing to fourteen roadmap features by quarter-end within budget is a scope-and-schedule commitment: it names what will be built rather than why it matters, invites feature-count thinking, and becomes meaningless the day the quarter closes. Improving response time by thirty percent and cutting defects states internal quality targets that describe the system's condition, not the customer's changed world, so they cannot settle a debate about which capability to build next. Following the product owner's ranking is a process working agreement; it locates purpose inside one person's ordering rather than in a shared outcome the whole team owns, which is exactly the dependency a shared vision exists to remove.
questions.concept: Qualities of an effective product vision
questions.question: A product owner drafts four candidate statements to align a newly formed cross-functional pharmacy-tech team around its purpose. Which statement will function BEST as a shared product vision?
choices: Deliver the fourteen features on the approved roadmap by the end of the third quarter, within the approved budget
Improve system response time by thirty percent and reduce the defect count in every release
Every neighborhood pharmacy can fill any prescription in under two minutes, with zero paper forms
Follow the prioritized backlog so the team always works on whatever the product owner has ranked highest

questions.explanation: An explicitly delegated decision is being taken back, and the team is responding by surrendering the rest of its authority — a fast path to learned helplessness. The practitioner should bring the department head and team together to re-examine the boundary: what changed, what the overrides were protecting, and what information or guardrails would let him honor the delegation. Endorsing the pre-approval emails buys short-term calm but institutionalizes the disempowerment, making permission-seeking the team's new normal. Routing his requests through backlog refinement is a process workaround that manages the symptom while leaving the broken trust and the unclear boundary unaddressed. Waiting for the retrospective delays a live leadership problem, and framing the choice as whether to escalate skips the collaborative conversation that should come first.
questions.concept: Delegation and decision boundaries
questions.question: A Scrum team at an insurance carrier agreed with its department head that the team decides which defects to fix within each sprint. In the last three sprints, the department head has twice replaced the team's defect selections with his own list after sprint planning ended. Team members have now begun emailing him their proposed selections for pre-approval before planning. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Endorse the pre-approval emails as a practical safeguard, since they surface the department head's concerns before planning rather than after it has already ended
Facilitate a conversation between the department head and the team to revisit the agreed decision boundary and understand what he needs in order to trust it
Ask the product owner to route the department head's defect requests through backlog refinement, so his priorities reach the team before planning starts
Raise the repeated overrides at the next retrospective and let the team decide how it wants to respond the next time its defect selections are replaced

questions.explanation: A steadily widening band on a cumulative flow diagram while every other band stays constant is the visual signature of a bottleneck: arrivals into sign-off exceed departures, so work accumulates there and throughput falls. Making that visible to the team and letting them design the countermeasure honors transparency and team empowerment, and it corrects the lead's misdiagnosis of adding capacity upstream of the constraint, which only inflates the queue. Requesting a dedicated reviewer from another manager escalates before the team has diagnosed the problem together and presumes staffing is the only remedy, when batching reviews, pairing during sign-off, or simplifying the sign-off criteria may work faster and cost nothing. Subdividing the sign-off column changes reporting granularity but not flow, since the same queue simply appears as several smaller queues, and reporting was never the problem. Lengthening the iteration hides the delay inside a larger batch, increasing feedback latency and work in progress, which is the opposite of what a flow problem needs.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation and bottleneck identification
questions.question: A hybrid team maintaining a hospital scheduling platform runs two-week iterations but pulls defects continuously from a Kanban board. Over the last four iterations, the cumulative flow diagram shows the "Awaiting Clinical Sign-off" band growing steadily wider while all other bands stay constant. Throughput has dropped from nine items per iteration to five. The team lead has been adding capacity to development because "the developers look busiest." What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Walk the team through the cumulative flow diagram so they see that the widening band identifies sign-off as the constraint, then facilitate a session on relieving it
Ask the clinical reviewers' manager for a dedicated reviewer until the sign-off backlog clears, since a queue growing for four iterations is plainly a capacity shortfall
Split the sign-off column into finer stages so review progress can be reported precisely and stakeholders can see exactly where each waiting item currently stands
Extend the iteration to four weeks so more sign-offs complete inside one boundary and throughput per iteration returns to the nine items the team used to show

questions.explanation: The team has been paying for speed with debt and is now slower than when it started, which means the current trajectory will not reach the date; transparency plus a scope conversation gives the sponsor a real decision — which capabilities are essential by the compliance date — and treats scope as the flexible variable when date and quality are constrained. Agreeing to eight more weeks and promising a hardening iteration compounds the debt during the period when the build is already unstable, and post-date cleanup iterations are routinely canceled by the next urgent request. Silently restoring the practices is right on the technique and wrong on the behavior: it is a material change to the forecast, and concealing it from the sponsor forfeits the trust the team will need for the scope conversation. Overtime and weekend work sacrifices sustainable pace to protect a scope commitment, and an exhausted team on a failing build produces more defects, not more delivery.
questions.concept: Technical debt, sustainable pace, and transparency with sponsors
questions.question: A team delivering a regulated payments feature has been asked by the sponsor to hit a fixed compliance date eight weeks out. To keep pace the team has been merging without the agreed pair review, skipping the writing of automated tests for "simple" changes, and deferring a growing list of refactorings. Cycle time has crept from four days to eleven, the build fails several times a day, and two developers have said they are exhausted. The sponsor asks the team to sustain this pace for the remaining eight weeks. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Make the accumulated technical debt and its measured effect on cycle time and build stability visible to the sponsor, and facilitate a scope conversation about what will actually fit by the date
Commit the team to the sponsor's eight-week date and schedule a dedicated hardening iteration immediately afterward to repay the debt, since the compliance deadline is genuinely immovable
Have the team restore full pair review and test-first practices at once without raising it with the sponsor, since how the work is engineered is the team's own professional responsibility to protect
Ask the sponsor to fund overtime and weekend work for the remaining weeks so the team can keep its quality practices and still meet the date the regulator has already fixed in place

questions.explanation: Making the team's real workflow and every in-flight item visible on a shared, team-updated board creates transparency at the source: duplicated work like the billing integration becomes obvious the moment the second card appears, and the board reflects how the team actually works rather than an imposed template. Refreshing the spreadsheet twice a day and emailing a consolidated list keeps information second-hand and stale between updates, and makes the shared picture depend on one person's handoff. Daily written updates produce individual reports rather than one shared picture — two people could both write "working on the billing integration" and never notice. Rolling out a workflow tool is the strongest alternative and may be where the team ends up, but it copies the spreadsheet's columns, the very model that hid the duplication, and defers transparency behind accounts, permissions and migration.
questions.concept: Workflow visualization and shared team boards
questions.question: A distributed platform team tracks its work in a spreadsheet that one member updates every Friday afternoon. During the daily sync, people repeatedly ask each other what is currently being worked on and what is blocked. This week two developers discovered they had each spent three days building the same billing integration. The agile practitioner is asked to help. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Have one member refresh the spreadsheet twice a day and email a consolidated list of in-flight items, so everyone can see who holds what without waiting for the Friday update.
Facilitate a short working session where the team maps the workflow states it actually uses and puts every in-flight item onto a shared board that all members can see and update in real time.
Ask every member to post a written daily update covering finished work, planned work, and blockers, so duplicated effort like the billing integration surfaces within a day rather than at week's end.
Select a workflow tool that mirrors the spreadsheet's columns and roll it out to all locations, then migrate the in-flight items once accounts and permissions have been arranged for everyone.

questions.explanation: Changing the facilitation structure acts immediately, inside the team's own event, and fixes the system for everyone: silent idea-writing followed by round-robin sharing guarantees airtime for every voice without singling anyone out, which is how a practitioner grows psychological safety in practice. Private feedback to the senior developer after the session is a legitimate follow-up and probably belongs in the plan, but it works on one person after the fact while the next retrospective keeps losing the quiet members' ideas. Asking the product owner to judge whether past improvement items were the highest-value ones misreads the problem — the concern is who is generating items at all — and imports an outside arbiter into the team's own inspect-and-adapt loop. Rotating the facilitator role spreads ownership over time, but changing who runs the meeting does not stop interruptions inside it.
questions.concept: Psychological safety and inclusive facilitation techniques
questions.question: During an XP team's retrospective, the agile practitioner notices that whenever a junior tester starts to propose an idea, a senior developer talks over her and the discussion moves on. Reviewing notes from the last three retrospectives, the practitioner sees that nearly every improvement item came from the same two people. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Meet with the senior developer after the session to describe the interrupting pattern and agree how he will make room for other voices next time
Shift the retrospective to a structured format, such as silent idea-writing followed by round-robin sharing, so every member's input is captured equally
Ask the product owner to review the improvement items from the last three retrospectives and confirm whether the team has been choosing the highest-value ones
Introduce a rotating facilitator role so a different member runs each retrospective and no one person is left shaping what the group talks about

questions.explanation: Visualizing work means the board reflects reality, and the first move is to make the invisible waiting time visible by mapping the real workflow with the team, including handoff and queue states — once waits have a place on the board, the team can see and attack them. A required daily status note on each card records commentary about delays without exposing where work actually sits, so the same eight-to-eleven day gaps persist behind more paperwork. Agreeing turnaround expectations with the data team and the meter vendor is the strongest alternative and may well follow, because those handoffs are where the time goes — but negotiating before the waits are measured means bargaining on anecdote. A five-day age limit that pushes cards back to To Do applies policy before understanding and destroys the very history that shows the delay.
questions.concept: Workflow mapping and making queue/wait states explicit
questions.question: A hybrid team maintaining a municipal water-billing platform works from a physical wall board with columns To Do, In Progress, and Done. The delivery lead notices that the board says almost nothing about actual progress: cards sit in In Progress for eight to eleven days, and when anyone asks why, the answer is always "it's with the data team" or "waiting on the meter vendor." The board is accurate — it just hides where the time is going. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Facilitate a session where the team maps how work actually flows today and splits In Progress into the real states, including the waiting states
Add a required daily status note to each card so the reason an item is stuck gets recorded before the stand-up rather than only being said aloud
Agree turnaround expectations directly with the data team and the meter vendor, leaving the board as it is since its columns already report status accurately
Set a five-day age limit in In Progress and return any older card to To Do, so aging work stops accumulating where nobody is actively moving it

questions.explanation: Flow efficiency is active time divided by total elapsed lead time — 3 of 12 days, or 25 percent — which says three quarters of the item's life was spent waiting in queues, blocked, or sitting between handoffs. That is where the leverage sits: even making the hands-on work twice as fast would shave only 1.5 days off 12, while draining the queues could recover most of the other nine. Concentrating on the three hands-on days is the strongest rival because it is the part the team most directly controls, but it is also the smallest slice of the timeline, and pull policies and handoff agreements give the team real influence over the waiting as well. Reading 25 percent as spare capacity confuses flow efficiency with resource utilization and would justify pulling in more work, which lengthens queues further. Waiting a quarter for more data is fair about sample size but defers action on a finding so lopsided that no realistic sample would overturn it.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency
questions.question: A team instruments one representative work item end to end. From the moment it was pulled into the workflow to the moment it reached customers, 12 working days elapsed; summing the periods when someone was actively working on it gives 3 working days. Which conclusion should the team draw from this measurement?
choices: Flow efficiency is 25 percent, so the team should concentrate on shortening the three days of hands-on work, which is the part of the process it controls.
Flow efficiency is 25 percent, meaning the team is only a quarter utilized, so it can safely pull in roughly three times as much work without adding people.
A single item is not a representative sample, so the team should keep measuring and defer any process change until a full quarter of flow data exists.
Flow efficiency is 25 percent, so the largest improvement lever is removing waiting time in queues and handoffs rather than making hands-on work faster.

questions.explanation: Facilitating a data-backed conversation between the team and the product manager repairs the broken relationship that created the shadow backlog: the slowdown evidence connects debt to customer value in terms the product manager cares about, and a jointly agreed mechanism makes the work durably visible instead of hidden. Moving the spreadsheet items into the product backlog respects her accountability for ordering and is where the work belongs eventually, but it repeats the move that already failed; without the evidence, the items are simply deleted again. Reframing debt as customer-facing outcomes is persuasion rather than transparency, and it obscures the trade-off the product manager is actually making. Quietly reserving a share of every iteration avoids the argument by keeping the work concealed, which swaps one hidden channel for another and costs more trust when it surfaces.
questions.concept: Making technical debt visible on a single shared backlog
questions.question: An agile practitioner discovers that an XP team keeps a private spreadsheet of refactoring and technical-debt items. In the past, whenever developers added such items to the product backlog, the product manager deleted them as 'not customer value.' The accumulating debt is now visibly slowing every release. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Move the spreadsheet items into the product backlog and let the product manager order them alongside features, since ordering the backlog is her accountability
Have the team reframe each debt item as a customer-facing outcome, so the product manager recognizes the value in them and stops removing them from the shared product backlog
Facilitate a conversation in which the team shows the product manager the release-slowdown data and they jointly agree how debt work will be made visible and prioritized
Coach the team to reserve a steady share of every iteration for the spreadsheet items, so the debt gets worked down without reopening the argument over the backlog

questions.explanation: The failure here is shared understanding, and refinement exists precisely to build it. Reframing the item around who benefits and what observable result signals success converts an architecture-shaped item into a value-shaped one, and slicing it exposes where the three interpretations actually diverge — the item becomes negotiable, valuable, estimable, small and testable through the conversation itself. Having the three developers settle a single technical scope with the architect afterwards is defensible and would close the estimate spread, but it resolves the disagreement outside the team and still leaves an item nobody can tie to a beneficiary or to a way of knowing it worked. Walking the team through the architecture diagram spreads one picture, but it is a picture of how the pipeline is built rather than who it serves, which is the question that stalled estimation. Slicing by ingestion, transformation and storage yields smaller pieces that are still horizontal layers — none can be demonstrated or validated on its own, so smallness arrives without value or testability.
questions.concept: Backlog refinement for shared understanding; INVEST and outcome-framed slicing
questions.question: A municipal water utility is building a leak-detection platform. The team's backlog top slice contains an item written as "Sensor telemetry ingestion pipeline — Phase 1." During refinement, three developers each describe a different scope for it, and nobody can name who benefits from it or how anyone would know it worked. The product owner insists the item is clear because the architecture diagram covers it. Estimation stalls. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the group to reframe the item around a specific beneficiary and observable outcome, then slice it into thinner items the team can confirm they understand the same way
Ask the three developers to settle on a single technical scope with the architect after refinement, then re-estimate the item once the interpretation gap between them has closed
Have the product owner walk the team through the architecture diagram in detail, so everyone holds the same picture of the pipeline before estimating again
Slice the item by technical stage — ingestion, transformation, storage — so each piece is small enough to estimate and the first stage can start next iteration

questions.explanation: Framing each design as a falsifiable hypothesis and testing minimal versions with a small real-user segment is best: it converts an opinion debate into an empirical question, produces validated learning in days rather than months, and limits blast radius through the small segment. A shortened four-week study is still a prediction exercise, and it holds development for a month to produce forecasts the team could replace with observed behavior this week. Building what the claims-handling specialists prefer trades one opinion for another; their process knowledge is real, but they are not the policyholders uploading photos, and measuring only after a full rollout settles nothing about the rejected design. Releasing one design to everyone and comparing with last quarter is the most defensible alternative because it measures real behavior, but the comparison confounds the design with everything else that changed.
questions.concept: Hypothesis-driven development and validated learning
questions.question: A product team at an insurance carrier is split between two competing designs for a claims-photo upload flow. The marketing department proposes a twelve-week market research study to settle the debate before any development begins. The team is technically able to deploy limited functionality to a small pool of policyholders within days. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Help the team express each design as a falsifiable hypothesis, release a minimal version of both to a small policyholder segment, and compare measured behavior
Support a shortened four-week version of the study, so the debate is settled with customer input without holding development back for a full quarter
Build the design the claims-handling specialists prefer, since they know the process best, then measure upload completion rates after the new flow reaches all policyholders
Release one design to all policyholders and compare completion rates against the previous quarter, then try the other design in a later release if results disappoint

questions.explanation: The accusation moved the conflict from a problem to a person, and the room's silence shows psychological safety has just collapsed, so the intervention has to happen in the moment. Pausing, re-anchoring to the agreement the team itself authored about critiquing work rather than people, and steering toward observable facts about how defects are recorded and closed de-personalizes the issue while keeping the underlying concern — which may be real and important — on the table where the whole team can examine it. Ending the retrospective early and handling it in one-on-ones feels safer but teaches the team that hard topics get taken offline, draining the retrospective of exactly the candor it exists to produce. Pressing on with the agenda ignores that no honest data will surface in a room this frozen; the remaining time is already lost, and the unaddressed accusation hardens into a private grudge. Bringing in functional managers escalates a team-level conflict outside the team at the first spike, takes resolution away from the people who must keep working together, and signals that the team cannot manage its own tensions.
questions.concept: In-the-moment de-escalation and psychological safety
questions.question: A team's working agreements include "critique the work, not the person." Midway through a retrospective, a tester says a developer "quietly buries defects to keep his numbers clean." The developer goes silent and stares at the table; two teammates start checking their phones, and the facilitator's next prompt gets no response from anyone. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: End the retrospective early and meet the tester and the developer separately, so that each can speak openly without the rest of the team present
Move on with the planned agenda and raise the exchange privately with both members once the immediate tension in the room has had time to cool
Ask both members' functional managers to look into how defects are being handled, so the accusation is settled by someone outside the team
Pause the session, restate the team's working agreements, and refocus the discussion on observable facts about how defects are being handled

questions.explanation: The rework is a symptom of a quarter-long feedback loop between the team and its real users. Bringing actual dispatchers into iteration reviews and piloting thin slices with one depot shortens that loop to weeks, so misunderstandings are caught while they are cheap to fix. A big upfront requirements workshop is predictive thinking: it tries to eliminate feedback by getting the specification right once, which rarely survives contact with real use. Bolting a user-acceptance phase onto the end of the quarter keeps the feedback exactly as late as it is today and merely formalizes the delay. Lengthening iterations moves in the wrong direction entirely, making each feedback cycle slower and each batch of potential rework larger.
questions.concept: Real-user feedback each iteration vs. proxy customers
questions.question: A team using XP practices is building a route-optimization API for a trucking company. Iteration demos are attended only by an internal business analyst acting as a proxy customer; the dispatchers who will actually use the system first see features after each quarterly release, and nearly a third of delivered work comes back as rework. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Work with the proxy to bring actual dispatchers into iteration reviews and release small slices to a pilot depot sooner
Run a requirements workshop with dispatch supervisors before the next quarter so the rework is designed out up front
Add a formal acceptance-testing phase for dispatchers at the end of each quarterly release, before the depots switch over
Lengthen the iterations so features are further along before the business analyst reviews them at the demo each time

questions.explanation: On a cumulative flow diagram the vertical width of a band is the amount of work sitting in that state, so a steadily widening In Test band means arrivals into testing exceed departures — a constraint downstream of Build. Naming that honestly and letting the team investigate and relieve it is both transparent and empowering, and it is the only option that can actually change the Done slope. Halting intake into build for a full iteration is the strongest alternative and would drain the queue, but it prescribes a remedy before anyone has asked why testing cannot keep up, and resuming the old intake rate afterwards guarantees the band widens again. Requesting two more testers accepts the sponsor's framing and buys capacity before the constraint has been examined — it may be environments or a pull policy rather than people. Counting completed items instead of points is a better measure, but it answers a reporting question while the system quietly degrades.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation
questions.question: A claims-platform team at a regional insurer reviews a cumulative flow diagram covering the past ten weeks. The Done band rises at a steady, unchanging slope, while the In Test band has grown steadily wider week over week. The Build band's width is roughly unchanged. In the review, a business sponsor points at the flat Done slope and asks the team to "raise velocity next quarter." What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Recommend the team stop pulling new items into build for one full iteration so the testing queue drains, then resume the previous intake rate once the Done slope steepens.
Explain that the widening In Test band shows work arriving into testing faster than it leaves, and facilitate a working session with the team to find and relieve that constraint.
Agree with the sponsor and request two more testers next quarter, since the widening In Test band shows the testing group is understaffed for the rate at which build hands work over.
Explain that story points are a poor measure of throughput and propose the team count completed items instead, so the sponsor sees a truer picture of the delivery rate.

questions.explanation: The exhibit shows rework cost climbing steeply with loop length: a defect caught in 15 minutes costs 0.5 hours to fix, while one caught nine weeks later in production costs 40 hours — roughly 80 times more. Seventy-five defects per quarter (44 in hardening plus 31 in production) are currently found by the two slowest, most expensive loops. Studying what kinds of defects escape and extending the fast automated checks to catch those classes moves detection left, converting weeks-long expensive discoveries into minutes-long cheap ones. Adding manual regression testers invests in the slow 6-week loop, making late detection bigger rather than making detection earlier. Lengthening hardening to eight weeks stretches the feedback loop further and delays release learning for every change, defect or not. A triage committee manages production defects after they have already incurred the 40-hour cost — added process with no effect on when defects are found.
questions.concept: Cost of delayed defect feedback and shifting detection left
questions.question: A retail loyalty-app team reviews the escaped-defect analysis shown in the exhibit. Based on the data, which improvement should the agile practitioner advocate?
choices: Add manual regression testers so the hardening phase catches a larger share of the defects that currently escape it and reach loyalty-app customers in production after every release
Extend the hardening phase from six weeks to eight, so more of the escaping defects are found before the release rather than by customers after it has shipped
Stand up a triage committee for the production-reported defects, so the ones with the heaviest customer impact are diagnosed and repaired in the next release
Analyze the defect classes escaping to hardening and production, and extend the commit-time and nightly automated checks to catch those classes within minutes or a day

questions.explanation: Continuous integration with automated tests collapses the technical feedback loop from weeks to minutes, so defects are caught while the change is still fresh and cheap to fix; weekly demonstrations of working increments to real end users collapse the requirements feedback loop, catching misunderstandings one cycle after they occur instead of weeks later. Lengthening the cadence does the opposite — bigger, less frequent releases widen every loop and raise the cost of each discovered problem. A monthly quality council batches feedback, adds a hand-off, and delays learning behind a committee. More detailed upfront documentation attempts to prevent misunderstanding by prediction rather than shortening the loop that detects it, and heavier documents are a weaker communication channel than working software in front of users.
questions.concept: Technical and customer feedback loop mechanisms
questions.question: A Lean software team finds that defects and requirement misunderstandings routinely surface weeks after the related work was finished, making them expensive to correct. Which TWO actions would MOST effectively shorten the team's feedback loops? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Adopt continuous integration so automated tests report failures within minutes of every code change
Lengthen the delivery cadence so each release contains more functionality for stakeholders to review at once
Route all completed work through a monthly quality council that returns consolidated feedback
Demonstrate small working increments to actual end users at the end of every weekly cycle
Require developers to write more detailed upfront design documents to prevent misunderstandings

questions.explanation: Making the participation and late-discovery pattern visible to the whole team, then facilitating co-created working agreements for inclusive design decisions, treats the silence as a property of the team's system, gives the team ownership of the fix, and turns the pattern into shared evidence rather than an accusation. Introducing a design record the architect drafts and the other sites comment on is the strongest alternative and would probably help, since asynchronous review suits a three-country team; it loses because the practitioner imposes it and because the architect still authors every decision while the other sites react to a frame already set. Rotating the design call between time zones assumes inconvenient hours are the cause, but testers who suspected gaps during the call and said nothing were not asleep, they were unsafe. Having the remote testers route concerns through the practitioner makes candor depend on an intermediary and confirms that speaking directly is not viable.
questions.concept: Psychological safety and inclusive participation in distributed teams
questions.question: A cross-functional medical-device software team spans three countries. Across several retrospectives an agile practitioner observes the same pattern: a senior architect at the head office makes most design decisions during live calls, members at the other sites rarely speak, and testers at one remote site keep surfacing requirement gaps late that they apparently suspected during design. What is the BEST response?
choices: Introduce a design record the architect drafts and the other sites comment on before any decision is confirmed, giving remote members a channel that does not depend on speaking up live
Rotate the design call between the three time zones so each site hosts within its own working hours, since inconvenient meeting times are what keeps the remote members quiet

Present the observed participation and late-discovery pattern to the whole team and facilitate them in co-creating working agreements for inclusive design decisions, such as round-robin input and asynchronous review windows

Ask the remote testers to bring their requirement concerns to the practitioner directly between calls, and relay those concerns into the design discussion while decisions can still change without rework

questions.explanation: The cheap probe with a small pilot group tests the riskiest assumption — will nurses act on automated recommendations? — before significant money is spent, embodying build–measure–learn: it generates behavioral evidence quickly, is safe to fail, and gives leadership real data instead of competing opinions. Presenting the interviews and recommending a pause treats qualitative signals as conclusive and frames the decision as build-versus-stop when a small test could resolve the uncertainty either way. Building the full funded scope and measuring adoption only after release defers all learning to the most expensive possible moment. The quarter-long trial across every hospital is genuine experimentation but is neither early nor safe-to-fail — it requires building substantial capability first and exposes the entire customer base to an untested change, making it a big-bang test dressed up as an experiment.
questions.concept: Lean Startup build–measure–learn and riskiest-assumption testing
questions.question: Leadership at a hospital-scheduling software company has funded a major initiative to add AI-generated shift recommendations, convinced it will reduce nurse overtime. The delivery team's own discovery interviews suggest charge nurses distrust automated schedules and may ignore them. The product manager asks the agile practitioner how the team should proceed. What is the BEST response?
choices: Take the discovery findings to leadership and recommend pausing the initiative until the charge nurses' distrust of automated scheduling has been understood and worked through with the nursing units at customer hospitals

Proceed with the funded build and measure whether the charge nurses act on the recommendations once the first full release ships, since leadership has already weighed the business case and committed the budget
Design a cheap probe — such as offering a small pilot group recommendations produced behind the scenes — to test whether nurses actually act on them, and let the results shape the investment

Run a controlled trial in every customer hospital for a full quarter, comparing AI-generated schedules against the ones charge nurses build manually today, so the adoption evidence is statistically defensible before the build proceeds

questions.explanation: A timeboxed spike buys empirical information about the specific unknown at a bounded cost, and it does so before the team commits to a design, which is how agile teams retire technical risk. Expanding the design document invests more analysis in a behavior nobody has observed; more pages about an unverified assumption do not reduce the uncertainty. Recording the risk in a register and reviewing it at the iteration boundary makes the risk visible but takes no action to reduce it, and the two iterations of runway elapse with the unknown intact. Splitting the migration into smaller stories is sound delivery practice, but slicing work whose central unknown is still unresolved distributes the uncertainty rather than resolving it, and the slices cannot be sized sensibly until the provider's behavior is known.
questions.concept: Spikes to retire technical uncertainty
questions.question: A team is two iterations from starting a migration of a customer identity store that no one on the team has done before. The architect has produced a fifteen-page design document and asks for sign-off. The practitioner notices the team has more questions after reading it than before, particularly about how the legacy provider behaves under concurrent session refresh. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Have the architect add a concurrency section to the design document and recirculate it, so the team's questions are answered before sign-off
Propose a timeboxed spike that exercises concurrent session refresh against the legacy provider and reports findings to the team
Sign off the design as written and record concurrent session refresh as a high-impact item to be reviewed at the iteration boundary
Split the migration into thinner stories so the concurrency unknowns are met a little at a time across several iterations

questions.explanation: A widening band with a flat departure slope means arrivals exceed departures and WIP is growing in testing; making that visible to both the team and the stakeholder reframes the conversation from "start more" to "finish more," which is the only change that moves the flat Done line. Accepting a higher target and pulling more stories pushes additional work into a system that already cannot drain its testing queue, growing the queue and lead time further. Redefining done to push testing into the next iteration makes the velocity number tidier while hiding undone work; it degrades transparency and inflates a metric that no longer represents releasable value. Adding a test lead is a plausible capacity move, but it prescribes a solution before the cause is understood and before the team has seen the data; the accumulation may stem from environment waits, defect rework, or batch handoffs that a new person would not fix.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation and metric integrity
questions.question: A payments team's cumulative flow diagram over the last eight weeks shows the "In Testing" band widening steadily while the "Done" band's slope stays flat and the arrival line into the system keeps its original slope. Velocity reported to the steering committee has held at roughly 30 points per iteration because points are counted at the end of development. The delivery manager wants the practitioner to raise the velocity target to 35. What should the practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Accept the higher target and ask the team to pull extra stories each iteration so the reported figure moves toward what the committee now expects
Walk the CFD with the team and the delivery manager to show that work is accumulating in testing, then focus improvement on finishing rather than starting
Change the definition of done so testing falls into the following iteration, which makes the reported velocity consistent with the point at which work is counted
Add a dedicated tester to work the testing queue down, and keep reporting velocity as it stands until the widening band on the diagram narrows again

questions.explanation: Bringing the testers together voluntarily lets the people closest to the problem exchange what they have learned, discover the overlap, and decide together how to converge; a lightweight community of practice grows knowledge sharing organically and leaves ownership with the practitioners. Publishing one of the solutions as a mandated organizational standard imposes a decision the testers never made together, discards the learning embedded in the other two attempts, and discourages future sharing. Asking a manager to appoint a single owner concentrates the knowledge in one person, which is the opposite of spreading it, and escalates a problem the testers can solve among themselves. Mandatory training presumes a skill gap that has not been diagnosed: the testers already produced workable solutions, so what is missing is a channel for sharing them, not instruction.
questions.concept: Communities of practice as a vehicle for cross-team knowledge sharing
questions.question: An agile practitioner supporting three Kanban product teams notices that the testers on each team have independently built partial solutions to the same flaky test-automation problem, and none of them know about the others' work. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Document the strongest of the three approaches as an organizational standard and ask each team to adopt it in the coming iteration
Invite the testers from all three teams to a voluntary session to compare approaches and explore forming a community of practice
Ask the quality manager to name one tester as the single owner of test-automation tooling across all three of the teams
Schedule required test-automation training for every tester so the three teams reach a common level of skill in the practice

questions.explanation: Agreeing on lightweight readiness conditions gives the team a shared, self-applied filter that catches missing acceptance criteria and unknown dependencies without creating a gate, and regular refinement conversations are where oversized items get split and dependency questions get raised in time to resolve them. A formal product-owner sign-off converts a team agreement into an approval bottleneck, adding process and removing team ownership of readiness. Reserving buffer capacity absorbs the symptom while leaving every cause in place — items still enter the iteration with no acceptance criteria, with unknown dependencies, and too large to finish — so blockage recurs and usable capacity simply shrinks. Assigning an analyst to write full specifications up front reintroduces big-bang documentation, moves understanding out of the team, and still does not make items smaller.
questions.concept: Contextual readiness conditions and ongoing refinement practices
questions.question: A team refining the backlog for a school-transport routing product finds that items pulled into iterations are frequently blocked mid-iteration: some lack any way to tell when they are finished, others depend on a data feed whose availability is unknown, and a few are so large they cannot be completed within an iteration. The team wants to reduce mid-iteration blockage without adding a heavyweight gate. Which TWO actions best address this? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Agree as a team on a lightweight, contextual set of readiness conditions — such as clear acceptance criteria and known external dependencies — and apply them during refinement
Introduce a formal approval step where the product owner signs off each item as ready before it can be pulled
Reserve a fixed buffer of capacity in each iteration to absorb items that become blocked mid-iteration
Hold regular refinement conversations in which the team splits oversized items and surfaces dependency questions early enough to resolve them before the item is pulled
Assign a business analyst to write full specifications for every backlog item before refinement begins

questions.explanation: The real damage here is to psychological safety: public ridicule taught the team that visible mistakes are punished, and the developer's withdrawal from integration work is the predictable symptom. Refreshing working agreements and treating build breaks as signals about the system, such as why the pipeline let the change through, repairs the norm for everyone rather than this one incident. Assigning integration tasks only to senior developers ratifies the joke, shrinks cross-functionality, and makes the withdrawal permanent. Privately suggesting the developer run the full suite locally is reasonable technical advice that still treats the person who was mocked as the problem. A rule that whoever breaks the build fixes it first is a legitimate XP norm about pipeline health, but introduced days after a joke about supervision it reads as a penalty and reinforces the individual-fault framing.
questions.concept: Blameless response to failure and working agreements
questions.question: On an XP team building medical-device firmware, a developer's commit broke the overnight build. At the next standup, two teammates joke that 'someone needs supervision,' and over the following days the developer stops volunteering for integration tasks. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Assign integration tasks only to the more senior developers until the overnight build has become stable enough to trust again
Speak privately with the developer and suggest running the full test suite locally before committing, so the build stops breaking
Add a rule that whoever breaks the build fixes it before starting any new work, so that accountability for the pipeline is clear to everyone
Guide the team to revisit its working agreements and treat build breaks as signals about the system to learn from, not personal failures

questions.explanation: Demonstrating the item while labeling it clearly as unfinished preserves both transparency and the feedback opportunity: the sponsor still gets to react to the design, and the release metrics still tell the truth about what is actually releasable. Counting merged code as complete and deferring the accessibility checks quietly redefines Done under stakeholder pressure and turns an accessibility obligation into invisible debt on a burn-up that now overstates readiness. Letting the sponsor decide whether it counts respects his authority over the release, which makes it the strongest alternative — but Done is the team's shared quality agreement, not a stakeholder preference, and someone who has seen a screenshot cannot judge whether accessibility criteria are met. Finishing the checks before showing anything protects the metric while discarding the inspection and feedback the review exists to create.
questions.concept: Definition of Done integrity and transparency during increment review
questions.question: At the review for an insurance claims-intake product, three of five planned items meet the team's agreed Definition of Done. A fourth is coded and merged but has not passed the accessibility checks the team included in its Definition of Done. The sponsor, who has seen a screenshot, asks the team to demonstrate that fourth item and count it on the release burn-up "since it's basically finished." What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Show the item honestly as work still in progress, keep it out of the completed count, and use the demonstration to collect the sponsor's feedback on it.
Count the item as complete because the code is merged, and put the accessibility checks on the backlog as a follow-up so the burn-up reflects the work delivered.
