Demonstrate the item and let the sponsor decide whether it counts, since he owns the release and has already seen the screen working in the screenshot.
Finish the accessibility checks before showing anything, so the only work the sponsor sees at the review is work that genuinely meets the Definition of Done.

questions.explanation: The best move is to surface the riskiest assumption — will drivers act on predictions? — and test it cheaply before four months of capacity is spent. A manual, small-scale probe that sends hand-generated congestion predictions to a handful of drivers is a classic Wizard-of-Oz experiment: it produces validated learning in days and lets the product owner decide with evidence instead of conviction. Back-testing the model against two years of dock records proves the predictions can be accurate, which is not the doubt on the table; accuracy and driver trust are different assumptions, and only one is untested. Slicing the capability into iteration-sized items with reviews at every replenishment is the strongest distractor, since incremental delivery with regular inspection is sound practice — but it still commits to building the capability before anyone knows drivers will use it. Raising the concern and then proceeding defers learning to the most expensive moment.
questions.concept: Hypothesis-driven development (Lean Startup validated learning)
questions.question: A product owner at a freight logistics company asks a Kanban team to spend the next four months building a machine-learning feature that predicts loading-dock congestion, convinced it will cut driver wait times. The team's data scientist privately doubts drivers will trust the predictions enough to change their routes. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Have the data scientist back-test the model against two years of historical dock records and present the accuracy figures to the product owner, so the four-month build begins only once the predictions are proven reliable enough

Ask the product owner to slice the capability into iteration-sized backlog items so congestion predictions reach drivers steadily across the four months, and review how the drivers are actually reacting at every replenishment meeting as the work proceeds

Help the team frame the riskiest assumption as a testable hypothesis and run a small, inexpensive experiment — such as sending manually generated congestion predictions to a handful of drivers — before investing in the full build

Have the data scientist raise the trust concern openly at the next replenishment meeting so the product owner can weigh it against the roadmap, then proceed with the ranked work and gather driver feedback after the release

questions.explanation: Talking directly with the manager addresses the root cause collaboratively: he almost certainly does not see the cost of the interruptions, and agreeing that new requests arrive through the product backlog protects the team's focus while still getting his genuine needs prioritized transparently. Coaching the developers to decline and redirect him to the product owner is right in principle but delegates the confrontation to the people with the least positional power, in a relationship that touches their careers. Absorbing the requests into the sprint backlog and showing their effect on capacity at the review has real merit, because it makes the cost visible with data, but it lets the disruption run for a whole sprint and stages the conversation in a semi-public forum instead of having it directly. Reserving a fixed slice of capacity for his urgent work legitimizes a channel that bypasses the product owner and encodes mid-sprint interruption as normal.
questions.concept: Servant leadership: resolving organizational impediments that disrupt team flow
questions.question: A functional manager regularly sends direct messages to individual developers on a Scrum team asking them to handle 'quick urgent tasks' in the middle of the sprint. The developers feel unable to refuse, and the team's sprint progress is suffering. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Meet with the manager to explain the impact on the team's flow and sprint commitments, and agree that new requests will come through the product backlog
Coach the developers to decline mid-sprint requests and to redirect the manager to the product owner whenever one of these messages arrives
Add the urgent requests to the sprint backlog as they arrive and show the manager their effect on the team's remaining capacity at the review
Reserve a fixed slice of capacity in every sprint for unplanned urgent work, so that the manager's requests can be absorbed without disturbing the sprint plan

questions.explanation: A WIP limit that blocks is doing its job: it is a signal to finish before starting. Having the team swarm the oldest review card converts idle capacity into flow, shortens the age of the most at-risk item, and keeps lead time stable — the pull-system behavior of "stop starting, start finishing." Pulling the next Ready item and deferring the topic to a retrospective ignores the signal, grows WIP, and delays feedback on work already nearly done. Raising the limit to four removes the very constraint that surfaced the problem; limits are changed deliberately after evidence, not to relieve momentary discomfort. Asking a manager to designate a dedicated reviewer escalates and adds a role before the team has even tried to drain a queue it can clear itself, and it creates a new single-point handoff that will bottleneck later.
questions.concept: WIP limits, pull systems, and swarming to relieve a queue
questions.question: A five-person team maintaining tide-prediction services runs a Kanban board with a work-in-progress limit of three in the "Peer Review" column. A developer finishes coding a sensor-calibration item and finds Peer Review already holding three cards, the oldest of which has been sitting untouched for four days. The developer's next item is sitting in "Ready." What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Let the developer pull the next Ready item so no one is idle, and raise the review queue as a topic for the next retrospective.
Temporarily raise the Peer Review limit to four for the rest of the week so the finished item can move forward.
Ask the team to stop starting and swarm on the oldest card in Peer Review so the queue drains before anyone pulls new work.
Ask the delivery manager to designate a full-time reviewer so review never becomes a constraint again.

questions.explanation: Making the delay visible with its measured size and then talking directly to the group that owns the constraint applies the agile sequence of transparency first, collaboration next, escalation only if collaboration fails — and the eleven-day measurement is exactly the shared data a joint fix needs. Going to the CIO first skips the people who can actually change the process, frames a colleague team as a problem to be policed, and spends escalation credibility that may be needed later. Re-sequencing the backlog to dodge rotation work buys two iterations of relief while leaving the systemic constraint fully intact, so the same impediment returns with less time to solve it. Building an eleven-day buffer into every affected story makes forecasts honest but institutionalizes the waiting time as permanent, which is the opposite of impediment removal.
questions.concept: Impediment transparency and resolution through cross-team collaboration before escalation
questions.question: A team integrating a new payment gateway discovers that every encryption key rotation must be approved by a shared cryptography group; the last two requests took eleven days each. The next two iterations both contain work that needs a rotation. The delivery manager tells the agile practitioner to raise it with the CIO straight away, since delivery dates are at risk. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Log the eleven-day wait as a visible, measured impediment and meet the cryptography group's lead to agree a faster path, such as a standing weekly slot or a delegated approval for non-production keys.

Follow the delivery manager's instruction and take the eleven-day wait straight to the CIO, since two iterations of delivery are exposed and senior attention moves a shared group faster than a peer request does
Re-sequence the backlog so that nothing needing a key rotation falls in the next two iterations, buying time to work on the dependency once the current delivery pressure has eased off
Add an eleven-day allowance to every story that touches key rotation so the forecasts given to stakeholders stay honest about what the approval step actually costs the team each time

questions.explanation: Per team-week, the exhibit ranks the slices at roughly $60,000 for paperless consent, $30,000 for auto-renewal reminders, $14,000 for the fee-schedule rewrite and $12,000 for the dashboard, and only the first two switch benefit on the moment they go live; taking them first buys $300,000 of annualized benefit for a single iteration of capacity, after which the rewrite can be attacked as slices. Starting the rewrite chases the largest absolute number while ignoring effort and timing: as an indivisible 30-team-week block it consumes almost the whole window and returns nothing until the end. Building the dashboard first buys political goodwill at the worst ratio in the table. Starting all four in parallel is the most defensible alternative, but 43 team-weeks of work will not fit 32 — parallel starts only push every completion later.
questions.concept: Benefit-per-effort sequencing and avoiding large indivisible batches
questions.question: The product owner proposes starting with the fee-schedule rewrite because it carries by far the largest benefit figure. Interpreting the exhibit, what should the agile practitioner recommend?
choices: Start the fee-schedule rewrite immediately and give it the entire 32-week window, since its $420,000 annualized benefit exceeds the other three slices put together and releasing a pricing engine only part-built would risk inconsistent fee calculations for every one of the members.

Build the executive dashboard refresh first to secure the vice-president's visible sponsorship for the release, then take the fee-schedule rewrite with whatever capacity remains and hold the consent and reminder slices for the following quarter.

Start all four slices in parallel so that every benefit stream begins accruing at the same time, releasing each one as it finishes rather than sequencing the window by benefit per team-week and leaving three of the slices waiting behind the largest item.

Deliver paperless consent capture and auto-renewal reminders first — 8 team-weeks that switch on $300,000 of annualized benefit within the first iteration or two — then work with the product owner to find a thin, independently releasable slice of the fee-schedule rewrite.

questions.explanation: Unclear user needs plus a novel combination of technologies means cause and effect can only be understood in retrospect — the complex domain — where the appropriate pattern is probe, sense, respond through safe-to-fail experiments. Expert analysis followed by good practice fits the complicated domain, where cause and effect are discoverable through expertise; here there are no experts in this market because it does not yet exist. Categorizing against best practice suits the clear domain of well-understood, repeatable work, which this is not. Acting first to impose order is the response to chaos — an actual crisis with no discernible patterns — and applying it here would substitute arbitrary decisions for available learning opportunities.
questions.concept: Cynefin framework — matching approach to the complexity domain
questions.question: A team is building a product for a market with no comparable offerings: user needs are unclear, and although the underlying technologies are individually proven, they have never been combined in this way. Applying the Cynefin framework, how should the team primarily approach this work?
choices: Probe with safe-to-fail experiments, sense the outcomes, and respond by amplifying what works and dampening what does not
Have recognized experts analyze the combination thoroughly, then apply the good practice that their full analysis produces
Categorize the work against industry best practice and run the matching playbook consistently across the build
Act decisively to impose order on the unknowns first, then assess the situation once the delivery has stabilized

questions.explanation: The conflict is escalating from problem-focused disagreement toward personal attack, and bystanders are withdrawing — the facilitator must intervene in the moment. Pausing, invoking the team's own working agreements, and re-anchoring on the shared cost target and observable facts de-escalates and depersonalizes the conflict so root-cause analysis can resume. Closing the session and meeting the two separately is defensible, since heated people often talk better one-to-one, but it leaves the remarks standing in front of the group and lets the camps harden offline before anyone reconvenes. Moving straight to countermeasures assumes progress will dissolve the friction; in a polarized room the countermeasures belong to whoever is still speaking, and the quiet members stay quiet. Dot-voting on the most likely cause forces premature convergence while the group is split, picking a winner instead of rebuilding collaborative inquiry.
questions.concept: Conflict de-escalation and levels of conflict
questions.question: During a Lean team's kaizen session on a missed cost target, the discussion shifts from the process to the people: an engineer declares that the analyst's estimates 'are the real problem,' and the analyst responds with a sarcastic remark about the engineer's 'gold-plated designs.' Several members go quiet, and the practitioner senses the room hardening into camps. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Close the session for the day and meet the engineer and the analyst separately, so the personal remarks are worked through calmly before the group reconvenes on the target
Move the group straight to countermeasures for the cost variance, on the view that visible progress against the target will dissolve the friction between the two members
Ask the group to dot-vote on the most likely cause so that shared data, rather than the two loudest voices in the room, decides where the kaizen effort goes next
Pause the session, remind the group of its working agreements, and reframe the discussion around the shared cost target and observable facts rather than individuals

questions.explanation: Making the wait an explicit queue on the board is correct because flow efficiency of roughly 18 percent means the problem is invisible waiting, not idle people, and management cannot stop prescribing "more focus" until the board shows where the 11.5 lost days actually go. Reducing the review batch size or embedding a reviewer is correct because a weekly batch creates an average half-week of pure queue time on every item; smaller, more frequent reviews attack the delay directly at its source. Asking for longer days compresses only the 2.5 active days, so even heroic effort buys almost nothing while eroding sustainable pace and quality. Inflating estimates documents the delay rather than removing it and quietly normalizes the waste in future plans. Starting more stories in parallel raises WIP, which by Little's Law lengthens lead time for everything in the system and merely grows the pile in front of the same weekly review.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency, queue visibility, and batch-size reduction at an external constraint
questions.question: A team measures an average cycle time of 14 days on compliance-facing stories. Of that, roughly 2.5 days involve anyone actively working the item; the remainder is spent waiting for an external security group that reviews submissions in one weekly batch. Management's suggestion is "more focus and fewer meetings" for the team. Which TWO actions will most improve flow? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Ask the team to work longer days during compliance cycles until cycle time comes down.
Make the security-review wait an explicit queue column on the board so the delay is visible and measurable to everyone, including management.
Inflate story point estimates on compliance-facing stories so plans reflect the longer duration.
Work with the security group to review in smaller, more frequent batches — for example a short review slot two or three times a week, or a reviewer embedded with the team.
Start more compliance stories in parallel so something is always ready whenever the weekly review runs.

questions.explanation: Facilitating a direct conversation that moves both developers from positions — refactor first versus tests first — to underlying interests, since both actually want safe, high-quality code, uses the collaborating conflict mode and produces a working agreement the two of them own, which is the most durable outcome and keeps resolution at the lowest possible level. Rebuilding the rotation so they never pair is avoidance: the conflict festers, XP's collective code ownership weakens, and the team learns that hard conversations get engineered around. Choosing the approach yourself and publishing it as the coding standard is forcing; it may settle the technical question but leaves the relationship damaged and makes the practitioner the arbiter of engineering disputes. A team vote is the most attractive alternative, because the decision at least stays with the team, yet counting preferences settles a rule without surfacing either interest and repairs nothing between the two.
questions.concept: conflict management modes (collaborating vs. avoiding, forcing, escalating)
questions.question: On an XP team, two developers repeatedly clash while pair programming: one insists on aggressively refactoring legacy code before adding new tests, while the other calls that approach reckless. Yesterday one of them refused to pair at all, and other developers are now quietly avoiding both of them. The team asks the agile practitioner to "sort it out." What is the BEST response?
choices: Bring the two developers together, use active listening to surface the interests behind each position, and help them shape a working agreement they both own
Rebuild the pairing rotation so these two never pair together, protecting the rest of the team from a clash neither developer seems able to settle on their own
Choose the refactoring approach yourself and publish it as the team coding standard, so both pairs have one rule and stop relitigating it in every session
Put the two approaches to a team vote and record the majority choice as a working agreement, so the decision is made collectively and the pairing can resume

questions.explanation: Making the blocker visible with a named owner and a running age, then acting on it with the developer the same day, is impediment management as practiced: transparency, ownership, and removal at the team's own cadence rather than someone else's. Pulling another backlog item keeps a person busy but raises work in progress, hides the blocked story, and lets its age grow unnoticed while nobody owns the removal. Sending it to a monthly steering report escalates before anyone has attempted a direct, collaborative resolution and postpones removal by weeks for a problem that may take one phone call. Trimming the iteration commitment adapts the plan to the impediment instead of removing it, so the same credentials will still be missing next iteration.
questions.concept: Impediment board, blocker aging, and direct removal versus workaround
questions.question: A hybrid team building a warehouse robotics dashboard has one story sitting in the "waiting on external" column for four days because a partner firm never issued the data-feed credentials. At the daily coordination huddle the developer mentions the wait for the third time and the team moves on to other topics. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Have the developer pull another backlog item so that capacity keeps flowing while the credentials request stays open with the partner firm.
Make the blocker visible on the impediment board with a named owner and its age, and work the partner contact with the developer today.
Add the credential delay to the monthly steering report so leadership can decide who owns the partner relationship going forward.
Reduce the iteration commitment with the product owner to absorb the four lost days and re-plan the remaining work realistically.

questions.explanation: Expedite is a class of service, and a class of service without an explicit policy and a WIP cap degrades into a fast lane everyone uses. Writing the policy with the requesters in the room makes the cost of interruption visible to the people creating it, the cap of one restores predictability for the other 59% of demand, and tracking usage turns the argument into data the team can inspect and adapt. Abolishing the lane outright removes a legitimate mechanism for real emergencies and prescribes a cure before anyone understands why urgent demand is so high — the pattern simply reappears as informal corridor pressure. Routing every request through the operations director escalates a team-and-stakeholder policy question to a manager, adds a queue in front of the queue, and lengthens lead time further. Splitting two people onto a standing expedite rotation is tempting because it does protect the others' focus, but it hard-wires 41% expedite demand into the team's capacity, starves ordinary work of people, and still asks no requester to justify an interruption.
questions.concept: Classes of service and WIP limits in a Kanban system
questions.question: A regional insurance operations team runs a Kanban board with a permanent "expedite" lane. Over the last quarter, 41% of completed items traveled through that lane, and average lead time for ordinary items has roughly doubled. Team members admit they have stopped pulling normal work with any energy, because "it will just get interrupted anyway." What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Facilitate a working session with the team and its requesters to make the expedite policy explicit — what qualifies, who may invoke it, and a hard cap of one expedite item at a time — then make usage visible on the board.

Remove the expedite lane entirely so that every request follows the same single path through the system, since one queue is the simplest way to restore the predictable lead times for the ordinary work that has been starved of capacity for months.

Ask the operations director to personally approve each expedite request before it reaches the board, so that the volume of urgent work falls once a senior manager is accountable for every single interruption the team is asked to absorb each week.

Dedicate two of the team members to a standing expedite rotation and let everyone else pull only ordinary work, so that urgent requests stop interrupting the flow of normal items and the doubled lead time on that ordinary work comes back down again.

questions.explanation: Having the team author its own working agreements about how ideas are debated, reinforced with facilitation techniques that guarantee every voice airtime, addresses the norm rather than one person, is owned by the team, and creates safety without public blame — the silent retrospective itself signals safety is already low, so structure is needed. Escalating to a functional manager outsources a team-norm problem to hierarchy, likely deepening fear and silence. Telling the quieter members to toughen up places the burden on those being silenced and leaves the dismissive behavior untouched. Isolating the experienced developer on solo work removes a voice, weakens collective ownership of design, and treats a systemic interaction pattern as an individual defect.
questions.concept: Working agreements and inclusive facilitation
questions.question: On an XP team, a highly experienced developer routinely interrupts and dismisses ideas from two quieter teammates during collective design sessions. Delivery metrics look healthy, but pairing rotations show most people now avoid pairing with that developer, and the last retrospective produced no comments at all about team dynamics. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Raise the pattern of interruptions with the developer's functional manager as a performance matter, since delivery metrics are healthy and the team has not asked for change
Facilitate a session in which the team co-creates working agreements on how ideas are raised and challenged, and introduce structured techniques such as round-robin input into design discussions
Coach the two quieter developers privately on techniques for holding the floor, so they can carry their own ideas through design discussions without the practitioner intervening for them
Assign the experienced developer to solo architectural spikes and leave collective design to the team, protecting the healthy delivery numbers while the tension between him and the others eases

questions.explanation: Collaborating, or problem solving, is indicated when both the substance of the outcome and the relationship are high-stakes: a years-long architectural commitment deserves a solution that integrates both developers' legitimate concerns, for example through a short time-boxed spike that tests both designs, and the extra effort is justified by the durability of the decision. Imposing a decision trades a lasting architecture choice for schedule convenience and leaves one senior developer overruled and disengaged; an upcoming hardening period is schedule pressure, not a genuine emergency. Splitting the difference on architecture typically yields an incoherent halfway design that placates the people but harms the system, sacrificing quality precisely where durability matters most. Yielding to preserve harmony suppresses a technical concern that will resurface in the code for years, and it wrongly treats the outcome as the lesser stake when the outcome matters greatly here too.
questions.concept: Selecting a conflict-management mode by outcome stakes and relationship importance
questions.question: Two senior developers on an XP team have argued for a week over whether to adopt an event-driven design for a core service. The choice will shape the codebase for years, the two developers' continued collaboration is essential, and the team's planned hardening period begins in two days. Which conflict-handling mode is MOST appropriate for the agile practitioner to encourage, and why?
choices: Accommodating, because the two developers must keep collaborating, so yielding to the one with deeper service experience protects the partnership
Compromising, because a hybrid design gives each developer part of their approach and settles the argument before hardening starts
Forcing, because the hardening period begins in only two days, and an imposed decision protects the iteration's committed work
Collaborating, because the decision is long-lived and the relationship is critical, so both developers' concerns must be fully integrated

questions.explanation: Recurring incidents and 30 percent rework are a systemic problem, and the two effective moves are to understand the cause and then to make the fix real. Structured root-cause analysis with the people who did the work — Five Whys or a fishbone — is how a team gets past "someone made a mistake" to the process condition that keeps reproducing the same incident. Pulling a single improvement action into the iteration backlog, owned and with acceptance criteria, is what makes kaizen stick: retrospective actions go unfinished precisely because they never compete for capacity the way real work does. Asking the steering committee for a commitment-free quarter is a big-batch remedy handed upward before anyone has diagnosed anything, and it trades away customer value on a guess. A mandatory manager sign-off inserts an approval queue, delays feedback and substitutes end-of-line inspection for quality built in. Counting defects per developer measures individuals instead of the system, drives concealment and defensive behavior, and misattributes what is almost always an outcome of the process.
questions.concept: Root cause analysis and making kaizen actions capacity-funded
questions.question: A regional blood-bank logistics team has seen the same category of production incident recur in four of the last six iterations. Cycle time has stayed stable, but roughly 30 percent of the team's capacity now goes to unplanned rework, and the improvement actions named in retrospectives are rarely finished. Which TWO actions should the agile practitioner take? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Escalate the rework percentage to the steering committee and ask for a full quarter free of feature commitments so the team can stabilize.
Facilitate a Five Whys or fishbone analysis of the most recent incident with the people who actually did the work, so the team moves past the symptom to a systemic cause.
Introduce a mandatory manager sign-off before any deployment so that defects are caught before they can reach production.
Start tracking defects created per developer so the team can see where in the group the errors originate.
Have the team pull one improvement action into the iteration backlog with an owner and acceptance criteria, sized and tracked like any other work item.

questions.explanation: The original item's fatal weakness is that it is not testable and not small — "work well" and "goes smoothly" cannot be demonstrated or bounded, so no one can agree it is finished. The revision naming a specific actor, a specific action at a specific moment, and an observable result gives the item testable acceptance and a size the team can handle, satisfying the criteria that were violated. Adding adjectives such as fast, reliable and intuitive across all tasks leaves the item just as unverifiable while making it larger. Rewriting the story from the product owner's perspective removes the user whose need justifies the work and still states no observable behavior. Attaching a point estimate assigns a number to something nobody can define, which creates false precision rather than making the item valuable or testable.
questions.concept: Applying INVEST — testable and small over vague quality wording
questions.question: A team writing stories for a hotel housekeeping app drafts: "As a housekeeper, I want the app to work well so my shift goes smoothly." Applying INVEST criteria, which revision BEST addresses the item's most serious weakness?
choices: "As a housekeeper, I want to mark a room as cleaned from the room's doorway so the front desk sees availability without me returning to the service station"
"As a housekeeper, I want fast, reliable, and intuitive app performance on every housekeeping task so my whole shift goes smoothly from the first room to the last"
"As a product owner, I want the housekeeping app's room-status screen streamlined so housekeepers finish more rooms per shift without needing extra training"
"As a housekeeper, I want the app to work well, sized at eight points and pulled into the next iteration, so that my shift goes smoothly on every floor"

questions.explanation: The sarcasm shows a task-level design disagreement escalating toward personal conflict, and it is already chilling the rest of the team's willingness to work in that code. Facilitating a direct conversation is the collaborating mode: it surfaces the legitimate design interests underneath the sniping and converts them into shared design guidelines the whole team owns, which is what collective code ownership requires to function. Giving each developer separate modules is avoidance — it suppresses the symptom, dismantles collective ownership, and leaves the rift intact. A general reminder at the daily meeting names no one, settles nothing about the design, and signals that the practitioner will not deal with conflict openly. Asking a third senior developer to judge the two approaches would stop the re-refactoring, which makes it tempting, but it settles design by verdict rather than agreement and ignores the personal edge driving teammates away.
questions.concept: Collaborative problem-solving mode for task conflict
questions.question: On an XP team practicing collective code ownership, two senior developers have begun re-refactoring each other's code and exchanging increasingly sarcastic pull-request comments about 'fixing amateur design choices.' Other team members are starting to avoid touching the modules involved. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Assign each developer clear ownership of separate modules so their work no longer overlaps and the sarcastic comments have nothing left to attach to
Remind the whole team at the daily coordination meeting that comments like these are unprofessional, and ask both developers to keep reviews focused on the code
Facilitate a direct conversation between the two developers to surface the design concerns behind the comments, and help the team agree on shared design guidelines
Ask a third senior developer to review both approaches and pick the one the team keeps, so the repeated re-refactoring of shared modules finally stops

questions.explanation: An agile mindset treats a change like this as new information that improves the plan, not as a threat to it: collaborating with the sponsor and product owner to reorder the backlog preserves the relationship, redirects effort to what is now valuable and compliant, and keeps delivery flowing. Delivering the approved scope and putting the regulatory work at the front of the next annual cycle knowingly builds items the rule has already invalidated, and an annual cadence is a poor match for a regulator's timetable. Pausing delivery for a full impact analysis across every affected system is the most defensible alternative, because the rule genuinely needs interpreting, but it stops value delivery for one big batch of analysis when the highest-priority regulatory items could be examined first. Splitting the team looks like a compromise, yet it halves capacity on both fronts and still funds scope the regulation has made worthless.
questions.concept: Responding to change over following a plan
questions.question: Midway through an initiative, a Lean delivery team at an insurance company learns that a new regulatory rule invalidates roughly a third of the remaining backlog. The sponsor insists the team complete the originally approved scope first "so the business case stays intact," then handle the regulation afterward. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Deliver the approved scope as the sponsor directs and place the regulatory work at the front of the next annual planning cycle, so the business case holds
Pause delivery until a full impact analysis across every affected system is complete, so any replanning rests on a verified reading of the new rule
Split the team so half continues the approved scope while half starts the regulatory work, satisfying sponsor and regulator at the same time
Work with the sponsor and product owner to reprioritize the backlog so upcoming work reflects the new regulatory reality and the remaining value

questions.explanation: A blameless, cross-team root-cause session is best because recurring incidents across a shared value stream are almost always systemic — handoffs, feedback gaps, environment mismatches — and only a joint, blame-free analysis will surface those causes and produce countermeasures both teams own; bringing the director countermeasures reframes his request from punishment to improvement. Separate reviews compared side by side keep the two accounts apart and still answer the question of where defects originate, so causes that live in the handoff between the teams fall into the gap between two write-ups. Coaching the director on why blame suppresses reporting is sound in itself, but withholding all analysis until leadership issues a no-blame policy makes customers wait on a governance decision, and that coaching lands far better carried by the results of a review already done. A joint sign-off checkpoint adds a control-heavy gate that slows flow and treats the symptom while the causes stay untouched.
questions.concept: Blameless root-cause analysis across a value stream
questions.question: Two teams share a value stream in a Lean service organization: a development team and an operations team. After the sixth customer-facing incident this quarter, operations blames defective code, development blames configuration changes, and a senior director asks the agile practitioner to "find out who is responsible so we can hold them accountable." What is the BEST response?
choices: Have each team run its own incident review and compare the write-ups, so the director can see where defects originate without either group feeling singled out
Coach the director privately on why blame suppresses reporting, and hold off on any incident analysis until leadership commits to a no-blame policy for the organization
Facilitate a blameless root-cause session with both teams focused on systemic causes across the whole value stream, and bring the director the agreed countermeasures
Add a joint approval checkpoint so no code or configuration change ships without both teams signing it off, cutting the incident rate while the causes are still studied

questions.explanation: Learning cycles are sequenced by risk and by the date of the commitment they inform, not by delivery value. The field-logging cycle wins on all three counts: coverage is the assumption an irreversible 4,000-modem order depends on in nine weeks, a two-week instrumented drive across representative fields is the cheapest way to get a real answer, and naming the coverage level that would trigger a store-and-forward design makes the experiment capable of disconfirming rather than merely reassuring. The willingness-to-share survey names a genuinely larger business risk, which is what makes it tempting, but no commitment rides on it inside the horizon and stated preference is weak evidence for a behavior change; it is a later cycle behind a stronger test, not the first one. Ordering learning by the approved backlog confuses value sequencing with risk sequencing and would spend the nine weeks learning about the least uncertain part of the system. The thin end-to-end slice demoed to dealers is the most expensive option and confounds three variables at once: a successful demo run near a well-served pilot site says nothing about cadence in the target counties, so the team would pay two iterations and still sign the modem order on an untested assumption.
questions.concept: Sequencing learning cycles by decision deadline and risk rather than backlog value
questions.question: A farm-equipment manufacturer is launching a subscription telematics service that streams machine data from combines to a cloud dashboard. The backlog is ordered by customer value: dashboard views first, then in-season alerts, then dealer service integration. Three assumptions underpin the business case: growers will agree to share machine data; rural cellular coverage in the target counties supports the 30-second telemetry cadence the alerts depend on; and dealers can complete retrofit installs inside the winter service window. Modems carry a 14-week lead time, so the purchase order for the first 4,000 units must be signed nine weeks from now. No other commitment in the plan falls due for six months. How should the team sequence its first learning cycle?
choices: Follow the value-ordered backlog and spend the first cycle building the dashboard views, since delivering the highest-value capability first is what the business case promised and early grower reaction will teach the team the most.

Run a two-week cycle logging signal strength and packet loss from instrumented loaner machines across a representative sample of target-county fields, agreeing beforehand the coverage level that would send the team to a store-and-forward design instead.

Build a thin end-to-end slice from combine to dashboard across the next two iterations and demo it to three dealers and a panel of growers, so all three assumptions are exercised together in one working pass.

Survey two hundred growers across the target counties about their willingness to share machine data, since adoption is the assumption the whole subscription business case rests on and it can be tested now without instrumenting any machines.

questions.explanation: The valuable feedback here concerns sensing accuracy, sampling behavior, calibration and power profile — none of which depend on the enclosure. A bench rig or simulator lets stakeholders see and challenge real firmware behavior every iteration, so wrong assumptions surface while they are still cheap to change, and it answers the product owner's unease directly. Waiting for one comprehensive demonstration stores up ten weeks of unvalidated work and makes any correction expensive; a polished-looking reveal is not worth the risk of having built the wrong behavior. Substituting a written status report trades feedback for reporting — nobody reacts to working software, and a signature on a document is not validation. Pressing the supplier attacks a constraint that is not actually blocking feedback, spends the sponsor's influence on the wrong problem, and still leaves the team unvalidated for ten weeks if the date does not move.
questions.concept: Sustaining short feedback loops under hardware and dependency constraints
questions.question: A team building firmware for an agricultural soil sensor works in two-week iterations. The moulded enclosure will not arrive from the supplier for another ten weeks, so the team has decided to postpone all demonstrations until they can show the device "properly." The product owner is uneasy but does not want to disrupt the team. What is the BEST response?
choices: Demonstrate the sensor's behavior each iteration on a bench rig or simulator so stakeholders can react to working firmware now
Continue building and hold one comprehensive demonstration when the enclosure arrives, to avoid confusing stakeholders with an unfinished device
Replace the demonstrations with a detailed written status report each iteration, reviewed and signed off by the product owner
Ask the sponsor to press the supplier to expedite the enclosure so the demonstration schedule can resume

questions.explanation: A community of practice creates an ongoing, voluntary channel through which the duplicated knowledge can flow, converge, and keep evolving — the engineers who care about accessibility decide together what to standardize, which earns real adoption. Publishing a mandatory standard built on the earliest utility imposes a solution before the teams have compared approaches and breeds quiet workarounds rather than shared ownership. Appointing an accessibility lead with authority over tooling centralizes a decision the teams can make collaboratively and installs a gatekeeper where a peer network is needed. A one-time demonstration transfers a snapshot of knowledge but nothing sustains the exchange afterward — the next duplicated utility appears a quarter later.
questions.concept: Communities of practice as durable cross-team knowledge channels
questions.question: An agile practitioner supporting four product teams at a museum-technology vendor discovers that three of the teams have independently built nearly identical accessibility-testing utilities during the past quarter. What is the BEST response?
choices: Publish an organizational standard naming the earliest of the three utilities as the version every team must adopt from now on
Ask the program office to appoint an accessibility lead holding authority over every team's tooling choices, so the duplication cannot recur
Book a one-time session in which the first team demonstrates its utility so the other teams can decide whether to reuse it
Help interested engineers launch a community of practice with regular protected time to share and converge their accessibility work

questions.explanation: An MVP conversation grounded in validated need and the real cost of delay lets the group decide together what the smallest releasable product is, and here the evidence points strongly at the out-of-range alert. Asking marketing to sequence its own four capabilities accepts the premise that all four belong in the first release and only rearranges them. Reducing the depth of all four spreads effort thinly across capabilities with no evidence of demand and risks shipping four half-products instead of one that works. Estimating everything first supplies cost data but leaves the decision framed as "how much does the wish list cost" rather than "what is the smallest thing that solves the validated problem," and it consumes team time before the framing is fixed.
questions.concept: MVP definition using validated need and cost of delay
questions.question: A hardware-plus-software team is planning the first commercial release of a cold-chain sensor for vaccine transport. Stakeholders have supplied a candidate list of capabilities. Marketing insists that a mobile alerting app, a web dashboard, historical trend analytics, and multi-tenant fleet management must all be in the first release. Field interviews with three logistics operators showed that their single unmet need is knowing within minutes when a shipment goes out of temperature range. Manufacturing lead time means each additional capability pushes the release by roughly six weeks. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask marketing to rank its four capabilities so the team builds them in that order and ships the highest-ranked ones first, letting the remaining ones follow in later releases as engineering capacity becomes available

Facilitate a working session with marketing and the product owner to define the minimum viable product against the validated operator need, using the interview evidence and the six-week cost per added capability
Propose building all four capabilities at reduced depth so the announced release date holds, then deepening whichever ones the logistics operators turn out to use once the sensor is in the field

Have the team estimate all four capabilities first, so the product owner can weigh the full six-week-per-capability cost against the fixed release date before any conversation about cutting scope begins

questions.explanation: Coaching the team to pull work using the board's explicit policies builds the self-organization a pull system depends on: members learn to select the highest-priority item they can advance, and the practitioner's role stays that of an enabler rather than a dispatcher. Assigning the cards personally, even as a temporary measure while the team gains Kanban experience, creates dependence and teaches the team that work selection is someone else's job — the opposite of the maturity it is meant to build. Having the functional manager publish a weekly allocation moves the decision even further from the people doing the work and reinstates command-and-control over a system designed for pull. A fixed rotation by column merely swaps one form of external assignment for another and prevents the team from flexing to wherever flow is blocked.
questions.concept: Self-organizing teams and pull-based work selection
questions.question: A ferry-booking platform has just moved its support-and-enhancement group to a Kanban system. Each morning, several team members stand at the board and ask the agile practitioner to tell them which cards to take. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Assign the cards each morning yourself, handing selection over as the team's Kanban fluency grows
Coach the team to pull work themselves based on the board's explicit policies and priorities
Have the functional manager publish a weekly allocation naming who works on which cards
Set a fixed rotation so each member always works the same column of the board each week

questions.explanation: The stakeholders are arguing because they have no shared model of the product. A story map gives them one: activities across the backbone, detail beneath, and a visible first slice that runs end to end. Slicing to "sell, scan, refund one real ticket" turns three competing wish lists into one usable increment that every group has a stake in, and the remaining rows fall naturally into later slices. Applying MoSCoW to 240 rows produces a ranked list without a shared narrative — the same argument, now expressed as Must-versus-Should, and a "Must" pile that will swallow most of the list. Estimating all 240 items is a big-bang analysis exercise that consumes weeks on items that will be reshaped or dropped, and a forecast built on an unvalidated scope is false precision. Sequencing by component builds the engine, then access control, then the portal — meaning nothing works end to end for months, no feedback is possible, and integration risk is pushed to the end.
questions.concept: Story mapping and walking-skeleton release slicing
questions.question: A stadium ticketing replatform inherits a 240-row spreadsheet of features harvested from the legacy system. Box office staff, season-ticket holders' representatives and the security team each insist their rows must come first. The team has no shared picture of what a first release would even contain, and every refinement session turns into a debate about relative importance. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the product owner to apply MoSCoW across all 240 rows so the team pulls from a single ranked list, settling the competing claims of the three groups before any release content is discussed further.

Run a relative estimation session across the 240 rows so a credible release date can be forecast, then let the three stakeholder groups negotiate scope against that shared date and their own internal deadlines.

Facilitate a story mapping workshop with all three groups to lay out the fan, box-office and security journeys, then slice the thinnest release in which a real ticket can be sold, scanned and refunded.
Sequence the work by component with the architects, taking the ticketing engine first, then access control, then the customer portal, so each release rests on a stable technical base.

questions.explanation: Flow efficiency here is roughly 23 percent, so nearly four-fifths of lead time is waiting. Attacking that wait — the dominant Lean waste in this system — is where the leverage sits, and declining the extra hour protects sustainable pace, which agile treats as a condition for durable delivery rather than a nice-to-have. Endorsing more calls and longer days adds coordination overhead and fatigue to a system whose constraint is queueing, not effort: working harder inside a 2.5-day active window cannot compress an 8.5-day wait. Recalculating velocity on active time only produces a tidier internal number while the customer still waits 11 days; changing the measurement does not move the constraint. Asking the other group's manager to jump this team's requests escalates before collaborating and seeks a preferential queue position rather than removing the queue, which likely just displaces the delay onto another consumer of the same environment.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency, wait-time waste, and sustainable pace
questions.question: A distributed team modernizing a freight-tracking service has 11 days of average lead time, of which measurement shows only about 2.5 days are active work — the rest is queue and wait, mostly waiting for a shared integration environment owned by another group. The team wants faster delivery. In their next iteration they plan to add a second daily coordination call and ask each developer to work an extra hour to "catch up." What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Support the plan for one iteration and compare lead time before and after, so the team learns for itself whether tighter coordination and extra hours actually compress delivery
Redirect the team toward reducing the wait itself — negotiating environment access, automating provisioning, or shifting some verification left — and treat the extra hours as unsustainable
Recalculate the team's capacity from active work time and republish the delivery dates, so forecasts rest on the 2.5 days of real effort rather than queue time
Ask the other group's manager to place this team's environment requests ahead of other consumers, so the queue dominating lead time shortens from the next iteration

questions.explanation: Agreeing explicit decision boundaries and expanding them as capability grows applies situational leadership: a forming team with mixed experience genuinely needs more guidance today, and empowerment is grown in deliberate delegation steps rather than switched on. This keeps her in a coaching stance while handing the team an ever-larger decision space it can actually handle, and it makes the growth path visible to everyone. Declaring the team fully empowered and refusing to answer questions is abdication rather than empowerment — a low-maturity team left unsupported stalls or makes avoidable mistakes, and that failure then becomes the evidence that empowerment "does not work here." Continuing to make every decision until the deadline optimizes short-term throughput while training the team into permanent dependence, which is the opposite of her stated goal and only postpones the same problem. Importing a technical lead to own the team's decisions inserts a hierarchy layer and outsources the team's growth, entrenching the very learned helplessness she is trying to cure.
questions.concept: Situational leadership and delegation levels for a forming team
questions.question: A servant leader supports a newly formed data-migration team whose members have never worked together and have mixed experience levels. They bring her nearly every routine decision — library choices, task sequencing, even naming conventions. She wants the team to become self-organizing but recognizes that abruptly withdrawing support could leave them stuck. What should she do FIRST?
choices: Declare the team fully empowered from today and step back from all routine technical questions, so that the members build their own confidence by making every call themselves
Work with the team to make decision boundaries explicit — which decisions it owns now, which are made jointly, and how its authority will expand as confidence grows
Keep making the routine decisions until the migration deadline has passed, then begin handing them over once delivery pressure eases and the team has settled
Ask the PMO to place an experienced technical lead on the team who owns the library and sequencing choices while members focus on learning the migration domain

questions.explanation: Average cycle time equals average WIP divided by average throughput, so 18 divided by 9 gives roughly 2 weeks — and the law's assumptions are the important half of the answer, because it describes a stable system over a period and the estimate degrades the moment arrivals outrun departures, WIP drifts, or aged items sit uncounted. Treating two weeks as a durable property that survives a climb to thirty items misses the law's most useful implication: cycle time scales with work in progress, which is why limits work. Dividing throughput by work in progress inverts the relationship and produces a figure with no meaning as a duration. Refusing to answer at all is the strongest wrong option because its premise is true — the law gives a system average, not a per-item prediction — but the stakeholder asked what is likely, and an average offered with its stability caveat is both honest and useful.
questions.concept: Practical application of Little's Law and its stability assumptions
questions.question: A municipal utility's support-and-enhancement team pulls all work through a single Kanban system. Over the last quarter the team completed an average of 9 items per week and carried an average of 18 items in progress. A stakeholder asks how long a newly pulled item is likely to take from pull to done. Applying Little's Law, which statement is the most defensible answer?
choices: About 2 weeks, and because the figure rests on a full quarter of observation it will keep describing this team's delivery even if work in progress climbs to thirty items or more
About 2 weeks on average, and that figure holds only while the system stays stable — arrivals roughly matching departures, WIP staying near 18, and no items quietly aging outside the count
About 4.5 days, obtained by dividing the average weekly throughput of 9 items by the average work in progress of 18 items, since throughput is what the team actually delivers to stakeholders
It cannot be answered from these averages, because Little's Law describes the behavior of the system as a whole and supports no statement about any single newly pulled item

questions.explanation: The exhibit shows that the loops verifying the product is built right are already short, while the only loop validating that the right product is being built, real customer usage, runs to 74 days because feedback arrives only with quarterly releases. Releasing smaller increments more often and instrumenting usage attacks the longest and most valuable loop. Moving stakeholder demonstrations to weekly genuinely halves a real loop and is worth doing, but stakeholders are proxies whose reactions predict customer behavior rather than measure it. Exploratory testing every iteration strengthens verification and catches defects earlier, yet a defect-free feature nobody wants is still the wrong feature. Pairing brings design feedback within hours, optimizing one of the shortest loops on the exhibit while the validation gap stays untouched.
questions.concept: Prioritizing which feedback loop to shorten using cycle-time evidence
questions.question: An agile practitioner reviews the feedback-delay data shown in the exhibit with the team. The team can invest in exactly one improvement this quarter. Based on the exhibit, which change would MOST improve the team's ability to validate that it is building the right product?
choices: Release smaller increments to production more frequently and instrument the product to capture customer usage data
Move stakeholder demonstrations to weekly, so proxy feedback on each increment arrives twice as often as it does now
Add exploratory testing every iteration so defects are found and fixed before the increment ever reaches a customer
Adopt pairing across the team so design feedback lands within hours and rework is caught well before integration

questions.explanation: MoSCoW only creates information when "Must have" is constrained; bounding it to demonstrated capacity and forcing each item to declare the outcome it serves and the cost of omission converts private preference into a shared, value-based decision the stakeholders own and will defend later. Having the product owner rank all fifty on value alone and take twenty is fast and does end the argument, which makes it the strongest alternative — but it discards the stakeholders' knowledge of consequence and the buy-in that survives the first hard trade-off. Asking each group to halve its own tags reaches the right arithmetic with no cross-group comparison, so one group's least important must-have can survive while another's most important is cut. Planning all forty and letting weekly progress expose reality spends much of the release proving what demonstrated throughput already shows.
questions.concept: MoSCoW discipline and capacity-bounded, value-based prioritization
questions.question: During release planning for a credit union's card-dispute portal, five stakeholder groups apply MoSCoW to a candidate list of fifty items for a three-month release. Forty come back tagged "Must have," including three requested by a single branch manager. The team's demonstrated throughput suggests it can finish roughly twenty items of this size in the release window. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Have the product owner rank all fifty items by business value alone and take the top twenty into the release, since a single ranked list ends the argument over what counts as a must have.
Ask each stakeholder group to halve its own must-have tags, so the total lands near the team's demonstrated throughput without anyone having to compare their own items against another group's list.

Facilitate a working session that bounds "Must have" to the capacity the team can realistically deliver and requires each candidate to name the release outcome it serves and the consequence of its absence.

Plan all forty tagged items and publish progress weekly, letting the stakeholders withdraw items themselves once actual throughput shows how much of the tagged list the team is really able to finish in the window.

questions.explanation: More than one action here has merit, so the discriminator is what must happen first. The award is unintentionally teaching the organization that firefighting pays and prevention is invisible, and only the vice president can change that signal — so the first move is a private conversation that seeks her intent before offering impact, backed by incident-trend data so the feedback is evidence rather than opinion. Proposing rewritten award criteria at the next leadership meeting prescribes a remedy before anyone has understood her reasoning, and a group forum invites defensiveness. Routing it to the team retrospective hands an organizational-leadership problem back to the people with the least authority over it. Coaching the two members to make their prevention record visible in the release report is constructive and worth doing later, but on its own it accepts that visibility is the team's problem and leaves the recognition signal unchanged.
questions.concept: Hero-culture anti-pattern and influencing upward with data
questions.question: At a retail bank's quarterly all-hands, a vice president presents a 'Firefighter of the Quarter' award to a developer who worked three consecutive nights patching a broken release. The XP team whose test-first discipline has quietly prevented production incidents for two quarters is not mentioned. Afterward, two of its members ask the agile practitioner why they bother with disciplined engineering when heroics get the recognition. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Assemble the incident-prevention data and propose at the next leadership meeting that the award criteria be rewritten around sustainable, quality-focused engineering behavior
Meet privately with the vice president to understand the intent behind the award, and share — supported by incident-trend data — how the recognition landed with the team
Bring the two members' question into the team's next retrospective so the group decides together how it wants to respond, keeping the issue with the people closest to it
Acknowledge the unfairness with the two members and coach them to make their prevention record visible in the next release report, so the discipline gets noticed

questions.explanation: The team's real deficiency is a weeks-long, ticket-driven feedback loop, and the agile response is to shorten the loop, not to predict harder. Releasing changes first to a small group of pilot clinics and adding in-product usage analytics gives the team direct signals from real use, so usability problems surface within days and shape the next change. Backing more detailed upfront specifications is predictive thinking applied to the one class of problem documents cannot anticipate, because usability emerges from how real clinicians interact with working software. Adding an extended acceptance testing stage is the most defensible alternative, since it does move some discovery before release, but it lengthens cycle time and tests in artificial conditions rather than genuine clinical use. Having each clinic nominate a representative to send a consolidated report at month end keeps the loop a month long and filters raw user signal through an intermediary, costing both speed and fidelity.
questions.concept: Empirical product feedback via pilot releases and telemetry versus predictive documentation
questions.question: A distributed team maintaining a telehealth scheduling product currently learns about usability problems only when clinics raise support tickets, often weeks after a release. A program manager proposes solving this with more detailed upfront specifications for every change. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Support the proposal, since precise upfront specifications catch usability problems in review before a change ever reaches a clinic
Suggest instead releasing changes first to a small group of pilot clinics and adding in-product usage analytics so the team learns within days
Add an extended acceptance testing stage before each release, so trained testers find the usability defects rather than clinics finding them weeks later
Ask each clinic to name a representative who gathers usability issues and sends the team a consolidated report at the end of every month

questions.explanation: Delivering every committed item while the funded outcome stays flat is evidence that the team is producing output nobody is benefiting from; the review is exactly where that evidence belongs, and reframing the next increment as a small, measurable experiment tests the cause cheaply before more money is spent. Funding a second team and splitting the backlog scales the rate of producing unvalidated features — it multiplies the output problem rather than solving the outcome problem, and adds coordination cost. Raising work-in-progress limits and shortening iterations is a flow intervention aimed at a throughput problem this team does not have; delivery is already reliable. Commissioning research and pausing delivery replaces short empirical feedback with a long analysis cycle, stops value flowing entirely, and yields opinions weeks later when a one-iteration experiment would produce behavioral data sooner.
questions.concept: Outcomes versus outputs in value measurement
questions.question: A municipal water utility's leak-reporting app has been delivered by the same team for six iterations; every committed item has shipped, and the sponsor praises the team's consistency in reviews. However, the outcome the program was funded to move — verified leak reports per week from residents — has been flat since launch. The sponsor's proposed remedy is to fund a second team so features ship faster. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Accept the sponsor's offer and split the existing backlog across the two teams, on the reasoning that the fastest way to move a flat outcome is to get more of the planned features in front of residents and find which one finally lifts reporting.

Raise the team's work-in-progress limits and shorten the iteration to one week so that features reach residents sooner, on the basis that a faster feedback loop will reveal why reports are not converting without any change to what the backlog contains today.

Bring the flat outcome data into the next review and work with the sponsor and product owner to reframe the coming increment around a testable hypothesis about why reports are not converting, delivering a small slice to check it before adding capacity.

Commission market research into what residents expect from the app and hold backlog delivery until the findings arrive, so the next increment is shaped by evidence about resident behavior rather than by the team's own assumptions about the flat trend.

questions.explanation: Putting the newest increment in front of a few real clinicians on real handover scenarios shortens the feedback loop from ten weeks to days, and because the software is already staged, the cost is arranging the session rather than building anything new. A usability sign-off gate adds an approval queue, substitutes one person's opinion for the experience of the clinicians who actually do handovers, and slows flow. Producing wireframes and an interaction specification for the whole release front-loads analysis and still validates against assumptions instead of against clinicians in a live handover. Extending the cycle to 12 weeks budgets for rework instead of preventing it and pushes real feedback even further from the moment the work is done.
questions.concept: Incremental delivery and early customer feedback on working increments
questions.question: A hospital scheduling product is built by a team using a continuous-flow approach. Working software reaches a staging environment every few days, but the only demonstration to clinicians happens at the end of each 10-week release. At the last one, clinicians rejected the new triage screen because it added four taps to the shift-handover routine. Reworking it consumed the first three weeks of the following release. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Arrange short, frequent sessions in which a few clinicians use the newest staged increment on real handover scenarios, and feed what is learned directly into the next items the team pulls.
Introduce a usability sign-off that the clinical director completes before any screen enters development, so problems are caught by a clinical decision maker rather than at the release demonstration.
Have the team produce detailed wireframes and a written interaction specification for every screen before coding starts, so the handover routine is settled on paper rather than discovered late.
Extend the release cycle from ten weeks to twelve so there is room to absorb rework found at the final demonstration without it consuming the opening weeks of the following release.

questions.explanation: The best first step is a direct, collaborative conversation with the manager that explains why pull beats push — team members selecting their own next item keeps flow moving, respects WIP limits, and builds ownership — and invites the manager to observe the evidence on the board together. Taking over ticket triage personally simply swaps one push-assigner for another and makes the practitioner the new bottleneck. Posting a working agreement that only the team may pull or reassign tickets states the right policy, and explicit policies are good Kanban practice, but aimed at a manager nobody has spoken to it is confrontation by notice board and invites him to overrule it. Raising the WIP limits so pre-assigned tickets keep moving removes the visible queue while discarding the very signal that push assignment is causing the blockage and the idle time.
questions.concept: Pull systems and self-organizing teams
questions.question: A customer-support engineering team uses a Kanban board with explicit WIP limits. A newly hired engineering manager, wanting to "balance the load fairly," starts assigning every incoming ticket to a named individual before it reaches the board. Within two weeks, blocked items pile up while some engineers sit idle waiting for "their" tickets. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Take over ticket triage yourself so assignments at least come from someone who reads the board daily, and let the manager watch how the limits work
Meet with the manager, explain how pull-based flow lets members select the next highest-priority item, and observe the board together for a week
Add a working agreement that only the team may pull or reassign tickets, and post it beside the board so the new manager can see the policy
Raise the WIP limits so the pre-assigned tickets keep moving and the idle engineers always have something available, then review the flow data in two weeks

questions.explanation: Facilitating a conversation that surfaces the underlying interests — consumer migration cost, maintenance burden, security exposure — and then converging on objective decision criteria is collaborative problem solving: it resolves the substance, repairs the team dynamic, and keeps the decision with the people closest to the work. Asking the enterprise architect for a binding ruling against the API standard escalates before the team has attempted to resolve its own disagreement and teaches that disputes get outsourced upward. Raising the sarcasm at the retrospective and agreeing communication norms first is the strongest alternative, because the relational damage is real — but it separates the tone from its cause, defers the deprecation decision that consumers are waiting on, and the sarcasm will return with the unresolved trade-off. Splitting ownership so the two never have to agree is avoidance dressed up as a structural fix; it institutionalizes the disagreement and fragments the design.
questions.concept: Collaborative problem solving and interest-based facilitation
questions.question: A Kanban platform team maintains payment APIs for internal product groups. Two senior engineers disagree about whether to deprecate an aging API version immediately or support it for one more quarter. Over three days the debate has spilled into the team channel, replies have turned sarcastic, and other members have stopped commenting altogether. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the enterprise architect to rule on the deprecation date against the organization's API standard, so the team has an authoritative answer and the channel debate ends today
Raise the sarcasm at the next retrospective so the team can agree on communication norms before anyone reopens the question of when the aging version is deprecated
Bring the two engineers together, help each articulate the interests behind their position, and facilitate agreement on objective criteria the team can use to decide
Divide ownership so that one engineer holds the aging version and the other the replacement, letting each move at their own pace without needing the other's agreement

questions.explanation: The widening band on a cumulative flow diagram is the visual form of a growing queue: arrivals outpacing departures in that stage stretch lead time and point at a constraint just downstream. The burnup's rising upper line is the scope line, so a steady completion slope beneath a climbing target means delivery capacity is fine and scope growth is what pushes the date out — a distinction a burndown alone hides by conflating the two movements in a single line. The weekly throughput histogram is a distribution rather than a single average, which is precisely what makes it usable for a range-and-confidence forecast. Item age is the one signal in this set that looks forward on a specific piece of work: the cumulative flow diagram and the histogram describe the system after the fact, while an aging card invites action today, before that item becomes a late delivery.
questions.concept: Distinguishing cumulative flow diagrams, burnup scope lines, throughput distributions, and work-item age
questions.question: Match each flow or progress signal on the left to what it tells the team on the right. Provide your answer as pairs (for example, 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D).
pairs: A steadily widening horizontal gap between the arrival and departure curves of a single band on a cumulative flow diagram
Lead time through that stage is growing because items are entering faster than they leave, signaling a queue forming ahead of a constraint
A burnup chart whose upper line steps up repeatedly while the completed line climbs at a consistent slope
Team output is steady, but the target keeps moving because scope is being added faster than it is being absorbed, so the projected finish date recedes
Six months of weekly completed-item counts plotted as a histogram
The basis for a probabilistic forecast: how often the team has delivered various counts, used to express a delivery date as a range with confidence levels
The age of each item currently in progress, shown on its card on the board
A leading indicator that lets the team intervene on an item that is aging past its usual cycle time while the outcome can still be changed

questions.explanation: Thanking the tester for openness and steering the team into a blameless, systems-focused discussion is the best first move: the repeated apologies and the team's silence are signals of fear, and the practitioner must model in that moment that mistakes are treated as learning about the system, not as personal failings. Introducing a mandatory peer-review checklist prescribes a control before anyone has understood the problem, and an imposed process communicates distrust rather than learning. Privately advising the tester to be more careful locates the cause in one person's carelessness and quietly reinforces a blame culture. Reporting the incident to the QA manager escalates outside the team and teaches everyone that admitting a mistake triggers managerial consequences, which guarantees future problems will be hidden.
questions.concept: Blameless response to failure
questions.question: A tester on a Kanban team supporting an insurance-claims platform pushed a configuration change that briefly took down the staging environment. At the next daily sync she apologizes repeatedly, and the rest of the team falls silent. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Introduce a peer review on every configuration change, so that a single person can no longer take the staging environment down
Speak with her privately after the sync and suggest she take more care the next time she changes a shared environment
Thank her for surfacing the issue openly and guide the team into a blameless discussion of what the system allowed to happen
Record the outage with the QA manager so that accountability for the lost staging time is documented and assigned

questions.explanation: A community of practice is the only structure that is voluntary and cross-team, organized around a shared discipline rather than a single team's work — that boundary-crossing character is its distinguishing mark. Pair rotation is the deliberate re-partnering of two people inside a team; the rotation, not the pairing alone, is what spreads tacit system knowledge so no module belongs to one person. An information radiator shares knowledge passively and ambiently — no meeting, no request — which distinguishes it from every interactive structure in the list. A blameless post-incident review converts failure into shared learning; removing personal fault is what makes people reveal the real systemic causes, which distinguishes it from a fault-finding audit. Confusing the cross-team scope of a community of practice with the intra-team scope of pair rotation, or the passive broadcast of a radiator with the facilitated dialogue of a review, are the classic errors this distinction set tests.
questions.concept: Knowledge-sharing structures: communities of practice, pairing, radiators, blameless reviews
questions.question: Match each knowledge-sharing structure (1-4) with the description (A-D) that best distinguishes it from the others.
pairs: Community of practice
A voluntary group that crosses team boundaries so people in the same discipline can exchange techniques and lessons over time
Pair rotation
Regularly changing which two people work together on a task so knowledge of the system spreads across the whole team
Information radiator
