A display kept in the team's workspace that passively broadcasts the current state of work to anyone who looks at it
Blameless post-incident review
A structured discussion after a failure that seeks systemic causes and improvement actions without assigning personal fault

questions.explanation: Value-based prioritization weighs risk reduction alongside revenue: losing the servicing license destroys the entire revenue stream, so the disclosure carries value far beyond its own feature payoff. Convening the parties who hold the risk information, the funding authority, and the delivery knowledge makes that trade-off visible and produces a jointly owned sequence rather than a practitioner's unilateral call. Accepting late sequencing treats a fixed regulatory date and an existential risk as ordinary backlog items and leaves no schedule buffer if the work proves larger than assumed. A sizing spike is not wrong in itself, but it delays the decision that actually matters, the prioritization conversation, and an effort estimate does not change the fact that the deadline is immovable. Asking the regulator for an extension outsources the problem, is rarely granted for a published rule, and gambles the license on someone else's decision.
questions.concept: Risk-adjusted value prioritization for regulatory and compliance needs
questions.question: Midway through refinement for a student loan servicing platform, a regulator publishes a rule taking effect in five months that requires borrowers to be shown a standardized repayment-comparison disclosure before any plan change. The current roadmap for that period is full of retention features with strong projected revenue. The compliance officer says non-compliance risks the servicing license. The sponsor asks the practitioner to "fit it in somewhere late, after the revenue work." What is the BEST response?
choices: Accept the sponsor's sequencing, since the retention features carry quantified revenue and the disclosure rule still has five months of runway before it takes effect
Add a spike next iteration to size the disclosure work, then reopen the roadmap conversation once the team can bring the sponsor a credible estimate
Bring the compliance officer, sponsor, and team together to make the license risk explicit in prioritization and re-sequence the roadmap on risk-adjusted value
Have the compliance officer request an extension from the regulator so the retention features can ship before the disclosure work enters the roadmap

questions.explanation: The root problems are a handoff-shaped workflow and an us-versus-them dynamic; both are best addressed by the team itself agreeing on how it will collaborate — a small overlap window, pairing a developer and tester on each story, and treating quality as shared — then inspecting the results empirically after a few cycles. Adding a coordinator institutionalizes the handoff instead of shrinking it, inserting an intermediary where direct conversation is needed. Asking management to consolidate testing escalates a collaboration problem into a reorganization the team has not tried to solve itself, and discards people rather than improving the system. Splitting the backlog by location may reduce friction but hardens the two sites into separate silos, walking away from cross-functional teamwork rather than building it.
questions.concept: Working agreements for distributed, cross-functional teams
questions.question: A hybrid-delivery team has developers in Lisbon and testers in Manila with almost no overlapping hours. Finished stories routinely wait a full day for test feedback, and the latest retrospective dissolved into each location blaming the other for missed commitments. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Add a coordination role that owns the handoff between Lisbon and Manila, so every finished story has one person tracking it through test feedback and back to its author
Recommend that management consolidate all testing in Lisbon so the handoff disappears entirely and finished stories get test feedback on the same working day they are built
Split the backlog so each location owns its stories end to end, removing the cross-site dependency that both sites blamed for the commitments missed in the last retrospective
Facilitate the whole team in drafting working agreements — overlap windows, developer–tester pairing on each story, shared ownership of quality — and trying them for a few cycles

questions.explanation: Taking the wait-time data to the DBA lead and co-designing a working agreement is correct because it addresses the impediment at the level closest to the work, uses objective flow data rather than complaint, and treats the other group as a partner whose constraints also matter — often producing a cheap fix such as earlier notice, pairing, or a pull trigger. Escalating first asks a sponsor to arbitrate a problem the two groups have never discussed, burns political capital, and is unlikely to yield a dedicated specialist across nine teams. Adding a waiting column plus a higher WIP limit makes the blockage look normal and increases work in process, lengthening cycle time while the root cause survives. Logging it for a quarterly review defers action by months on an impediment that is costing the team every iteration.
questions.concept: Impediment resolution at the lowest level with shared-service dependencies
questions.question: A team's board shows that database schema changes sit in a "Ready for DBA" state for an average of six days, and the last four iterations each ended with two items unfinished for that reason. The DBA group is a shared service supporting nine teams and has never been part of the team's refinement. The team is frustrated and has begun asking the practitioner to "get management to give us our own DBA." What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Put a request to program leadership for a DBA assigned full time to the team, since six-day waits and unfinished items justify the headcount
Add a Waiting for DBA column and lift the team's work-in-process limit so members can start other items instead of sitting idle while blocked
Record the dependency in the risk register and raise it at the quarterly cross-team governance review alongside the program's other shared-service constraints
Bring the measured wait-time data to the DBA team lead and jointly design a working agreement, such as a pull signal and a DBA joining refinement

questions.explanation: This situation has several technically defensible moves, and the best one harnesses the change without breaking faith on the dated commitment. Bringing the product owner and sponsor to the evidence and validating a thin, toggled slice with real nurses turns the discovery into cheap validated learning, keeps the contractual release on track, and gives the sponsor data instead of a demand — collaboration before escalation, experiment before commitment. Merely recording the item for next release treats late-breaking, high-value learning as an inconvenience and delays feedback by months. Swapping the release scope immediately acts on a single usability signal without validation and unilaterally overrides a sponsor constraint, risking trust and the contract date. Invoking change control now and pausing work adds process and idles the team before anyone knows whether the new workflow actually holds up, surrendering the chance to bring evidence to the decision.
questions.concept: Harnessing late-breaking change through low-risk validation
questions.question: Two sprints before a contractually dated release of a hospital staff-scheduling product, usability sessions reveal that charge nurses have built a spreadsheet workaround exposing a scheduling workflow far more valuable than one feature still on the release plan. The sponsor reminds everyone that scope changes go through change control after the release ships, and the product owner is torn. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Route the change through the change control board and pause work on the scheduling module until a formal decision is recorded, so the team never builds scope that is later reversed
Advise the product owner to drop the remaining planned feature and start building the new scheduling workflow now, since the usability evidence already shows where the greater value lies

Help the product owner and sponsor examine the usability evidence together, and propose validating a thin, feature-toggled slice of the new workflow with nurses while the committed release items continue
Capture the nurses' workaround as a well-formed backlog item with the usability evidence attached, so the product owner can prioritize it properly when planning begins for the next release cycle

questions.explanation: Splitting by permit type produces slices that each move an applicant from start to submitted permit, so every slice is independently demonstrable, independently valuable, and testable against a real clerk's expectations; sequencing by applicant volume with the people who know the demand puts the largest share of citizen value in the earliest release. Splitting into a data model, a service layer, and a front end produces pieces that fit an iteration but deliver nothing anyone can use or judge until all three land, which hides risk and defers feedback to the very end. Front-loading two weeks of analysis across all fourteen types is big-bang requirements work that spends capacity before a single type has been validated in use, and much of what it documents will change once the first type is live. Estimating the whole item in ideal weeks makes the roadmap look precise while leaving an undemonstrable, unfinishable item in the backlog — the accuracy of the number is not the problem, the size and shape of the work is.
questions.concept: Vertical slicing and value-based sequencing of decomposed items
questions.question: A team is building an online permitting platform for a city. During refinement, the product owner brings forward the item "Applicants can submit any of the 14 permit types online." The team's rough sizing puts it at roughly five times the largest item it has ever completed in one iteration, and no one can describe how it would be demonstrated. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Split the item by permit type with the team, and sequence the highest-volume type first with the product owner and a permit clerk
Have the team split the item into a data-model item, a service-layer item, and a front-end item so each piece fits inside one iteration
Ask the product owner to fund a two-week analysis effort documenting the rules for all fourteen permit types before any splitting is attempted
Leave the item whole and have the team estimate it in ideal weeks so the roadmap shows a realistic completion date

questions.explanation: Publicly appreciating the developer's open acknowledgment and steering the team toward a blameless examination of what happened reinforces that honest reporting of failure is safe, and it converts the incident into team learning. Reassuring the developer privately after the daily scrum and reminding the team that mistakes are expected early on is kind and defensible, but it is the weaker version of the same intent: the anxiety and the silence happened in front of everyone, so the repair has to happen there too, and a private word leaves the rest of the team still guessing how failure is treated here. Asking for a peer check before shared-environment changes prescribes control before anyone understands the cause and treats a systemic gap as a discipline problem. Moving on and holding a separate incident review later protects the timebox at the cost of the moment that mattered, signaling that failure is something this team does not discuss together.
questions.concept: Blameless response to failure
questions.question: During an iteration, a recently hired developer on a Scrum team pushes a configuration change that briefly brings down the shared test environment. At the next daily scrum the developer apologizes repeatedly and looks visibly anxious, and the rest of the team falls silent. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Reassure the developer privately after the daily scrum and remind the team that mistakes are expected during anyone's first few weeks
Ask the team to add a peer check before shared-environment changes so a new joiner cannot break it alone
Thank the developer for acknowledging the issue openly and guide the team to examine it as a blameless learning opportunity
Move on with the day's plan and hold a separate incident review later so the scrum stays inside its timebox

questions.explanation: Technical debt is a risk to value rather than a separate category of work, so the agile move is to surface it transparently with its risk and cost of delay attached and let the team and product owner make one integrated prioritization decision. That separates debt that endangers the regulated billing calculation — thin coverage on that logic, a slow manual deploy that makes any late fix risky — from cosmetic cleanup that can safely wait, and it keeps the regulatory outcome central. A blanket two-iteration freeze converts an economic trade-off into an all-or-nothing stance and consumes most of the remaining runway while two mandatory requirements sit unbuilt, which puts the go-live itself at risk. Deferring all debt until after go-live is the mirror-image error: it accepts unverified billing logic into a regulated release, where a calculation defect is the single failure that matters most. Scheduling a hardening iteration at the end pushes quality into a late big-bang activity, contradicts building quality in, and leaves the least possible time to react if that iteration uncovers deep problems.
questions.concept: Technical debt as prioritized, risk-weighted backlog work
questions.question: A team replacing a utility company's meter-reading app is three iterations from a hard regulatory go-live. Automated test coverage on the new billing calculation is thin, deploys are manual and take four hours, and the team has logged nine "we will clean this up later" shortcuts. In the retrospective the team proposes freezing all new features for two full iterations to pay down technical debt. The product owner objects that two of the remaining regulatory requirements are not yet built. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Endorse the two-iteration feature freeze, since quality has to be built in before any further requirements are added, and the team is closest to the code and best placed to judge how much repair the nine shortcuts actually need

Support the product owner and defer all nine shortcuts until after go-live, when the regulatory pressure has lifted and the team can repair the billing calculation without competing against a date that cannot move for anyone

Help the team and product owner make the debt visible as prioritized items carrying explicit risk and cost of delay, then decide together which debt directly threatens the regulatory outcome and sequence that alongside the remaining requirements

Add a hardening iteration immediately before go-live and keep feature work at the current pace until then, so the debt is repaid in one dedicated block once the remaining regulatory requirements have actually been finished and accepted by the product owner

questions.explanation: The distinctions turn on timing and purpose. A pre-mortem is anticipatory: the team assumes failure has happened and works backwards, which surfaces threats that ordinary risk brainstorming misses because it licenses pessimism before any damage is done. Five Whys is retrospective: it starts from an event that already occurred and drills through symptoms to the underlying cause, so it belongs with incident reviews and retrospectives rather than with threat identification. A spike is neither identification nor analysis but action — a timeboxed experiment or investigation that converts an unknown into knowledge so the team can estimate or commit responsibly. The risk burndown is a metric rather than a technique for finding or reducing risk: it aggregates remaining exposure over time and tells the team and its stakeholders whether the mitigations they chose are actually working. Confusing the anticipatory technique with the retrospective one, or the investigation with the trend chart, leads teams to analyze causes for problems that have not happened yet, or to assume that plotting risk is the same as reducing it.
questions.concept: Distinguishing risk identification, root-cause analysis, uncertainty reduction and risk trend reporting
questions.question: Match each risk and problem-solving technique to the description that best characterizes what it does and when it is used.
pairs: Pre-mortem
A forward-looking exercise in which the team imagines the effort has already failed and reasons backwards to surface threats while there is still time to act
Five Whys
An iterative questioning technique that traces a problem which has already occurred back to its underlying cause
Spike
A timeboxed investigation that buys information about an unknown so a commitment can be made with less uncertainty
Risk burndown chart
A trend view of total remaining exposure across iterations, showing whether threats are genuinely being retired over time

questions.explanation: The system is behaving worse than the board admits because its largest source of delay is not represented on it. Mapping the real flow and adding the wait state plus item age makes the queue and the aging visible, which is the precondition for any sound decision about what to change. Imposing a work-in-progress limit on Build prescribes a countermeasure before the team understands the constraint; the queue forms after Build, so capping Build may simply move the pile-up upstream without shortening cycle time. Escalating for a dedicated reviewer requests a solution from outside before the team has evidence about the size and pattern of the delay, and it skips the collaboration with the security group that may resolve it cheaply. Logging wait hours for a quarter-end report defers insight by months, adds administrative burden, and produces a document instead of a visible signal the team can act on daily.
questions.concept: Making queues, wait states, and item aging visible
questions.question: A bank's mortgage-origination team pulls work across a board with the columns Analysis, Build, Test, and Done. Over one quarter, average cycle time rose from 6 days to 17 days, yet the board looks healthy and no card carries a blocked marker. Walking the board, the agile practitioner learns that finished Build items routinely sit for four to nine days awaiting a shared enterprise security-review group before anyone moves them to Test, and that wait exists nowhere on the board. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Facilitate the team in mapping how work actually flows, then add the hidden wait state and item age to the board.
Set a work-in-progress limit of three on the Build column to stop the queue of finished items from growing.
Raise a risk to the program office requesting that a dedicated security reviewer be assigned to the team.
Ask team members to log the hours they spend waiting so that an accurate delay report can be produced at quarter-end.

questions.explanation: Facilitating a session where product leadership and the teams co-create a shared release outcome is best: the root cause is local optimization against team-level goals with no unifying purpose, and shared vision is built through joint ownership, not instruction. Inserting mandatory integration milestones through the program office and reporting compliance adds control without alignment — teams will tick the box while still treating integration as someone else's problem. A dedicated integration team creates a hand-off, adds a dependency, and reinforces the 'not our job' mindset that caused the slippage. Adding an integration story to every backlog with a weekly cross-team sync is the most practical alternative and would catch slippage earlier, but the quarterly objectives still do not count that work, so the story is the first thing dropped under pressure, and a sync detects the symptom rather than removing the incentive conflict producing it.
questions.concept: Countering local optimization by connecting team goals to shared purpose
questions.question: In a hybrid delivery program at a logistics company, three feature teams each consistently meet their own quarterly objectives, yet the integrated release has slipped twice because every team deprioritizes cross-team integration work as 'not on our objectives.' Leadership is frustrated, and the teams each blame the other two. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Ask the program office to add mandatory integration milestones to each team's quarterly plan and report compliance, so the work cannot be deprioritized
Propose a dedicated integration team that owns the cross-team work, so each feature team keeps meeting the objectives it is measured on
Add an integration story to every team's iteration backlog and hold a weekly cross-team sync so slippage is caught earlier in the release
Facilitate a working session where product leadership and all three teams co-create a shared release outcome and trace each team's objectives to it

questions.explanation: Regulatory constraints are product requirements, and the person who holds that knowledge belongs in the conversation that converts them into testable acceptance criteria — this is collaboration and shared understanding applied to compliance, and it keeps the story small enough to be genuinely done rather than nominally done. Building the happy path and waiting for auditors to reveal the gaps at the launch review gets feedback far too late on work whose rework cost is highest, and treats an already-known requirement as an unknown. Parking the story until auditors issue a formal written interpretation surrenders the team's ability to make progress, converts a conversation into a document exchange, and stalls delivery on information the compliance officer can already supply today. Deferring all exception behaviors to a compliance hardening story at the end creates an undone-work batch on the critical path just before launch — the classic pattern that turns a regulated release into a crisis — and it means every increment until then falsely appears complete.
questions.concept: Acceptance criteria for regulatory and compliance requirements
questions.question: A payments team is three iterations from a regulated launch. During refinement, a developer points out that the strong-customer-authentication story has acceptance criteria describing only the happy path, while the compliance officer's e-mail lists eleven mandated exception behaviors. The product owner says "the auditors will tell us at the launch review whether we got it right" and wants the story pulled into the next iteration as-is. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Bring the compliance officer into a working session with the team and the product owner to turn the mandated exception behaviors into testable acceptance criteria before the story is pulled

Hold the story back until the auditors supply a formal written interpretation of all eleven mandated exceptions, so the team builds the authentication flow against a reading that nobody can dispute afterwards
Build the happy path now and raise a separate compliance hardening story for the final iteration, so the authentication flow is available for integration testing much earlier
Pull the story into the iteration as written and log the mandated exceptions as defects once the auditors have responded, since running software shows everyone where the gaps are

questions.explanation: The belief statement paired with a measurable outcome, a bounded test population, a timebox, and an explicit abandonment threshold is a complete, falsifiable hypothesis — it defines in advance what evidence will confirm or refute the value assumption and what decision follows. The user-story phrasing is a sound expression of need but asserts value without any measure or decision rule, so building it teaches the team nothing testable. The delivery target with a quarter-end date is a pure output commitment that would be declared successful merely by shipping, regardless of whether behavior changed. The open-ended investigation names a curiosity but specifies no prediction, metric, or threshold, so it can never be proven wrong — and an unfalsifiable statement is not a hypothesis.
questions.concept: Well-formed, falsifiable hypotheses in hypothesis-driven development
questions.question: A grocery-delivery team wants to adopt hypothesis-driven development for an upcoming reorder capability. Which backlog artifact best positions the team to practice it?
choices: "We believe one-tap reorder for returning shoppers will raise the 30-day repeat-purchase rate by at least 5%; we will expose it to 10% of traffic for two weeks and abandon or rework it if the lift is under 2%."

"As a returning shopper, I want one-tap reorder so that checkout is faster; it is done when any past order can be repeated in a single tap from the home screen and an order confirmation appears on the same screen."

"Deliver one-tap reorder to all shoppers by the end of the third quarter, then measure the 30-day repeat-purchase rate across the quarter that follows and report the change we observe to the product council at its next meeting."

"We believe returning shoppers want a faster way to reorder; we will release one-tap reorder to everyone and gather feedback through in-app surveys and support tickets until the team is confident it works for shoppers who use it most."

questions.explanation: Psychological safety is rebuilt inside the team, not around it. Refreshing working agreements makes respectful treatment of ideas an explicit norm, techniques such as silent idea-writing immediately lower the cost of speaking up, and a private conversation gives the principal engineer a chance to change without public shaming. Speaking privately with the engineer and asking each junior member separately what would help is part of the credited answer and genuinely useful, but on its own it leaves the team's norms untouched and puts the burden on three quiet people to describe what frightens them. Switching permanently to anonymous written feedback lowers the immediate cost of speaking while conceding that speaking openly is unsafe. Reopening the two-month-old incident so the principal engineer apologizes in front of the team stages accountability as theater, exposes the junior developer a second time, and invites defensiveness; safety is not restored by an audience.
questions.concept: Psychological safety and inclusive retrospective facilitation
questions.question: During retrospectives on a payments team using a hybrid approach, the practitioner notices that ever since a principal engineer sarcastically dismissed a junior developer's suggestion two months ago, the three most junior members have not spoken once. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Speak privately with the principal engineer about the effect his remark had on the room, and ask each of the three junior members separately what would make it easier for them to contribute during a retrospective

Switch the team's retrospective to anonymous written feedback gathered before each session, so the junior members can raise whatever concerns they have without ever having to voice them in front of the principal engineer

Open the next retrospective by revisiting the incident from two months ago so the principal engineer can apologize to the junior developer in front of the team, then turn to improvements from the current iteration

Revisit the team's working agreements on how ideas are treated, use facilitation techniques such as silent idea-writing so every voice is captured, and speak privately with the principal engineer about the impact of the behavior

questions.explanation: Coaching the VP privately is best because the root cause is leader behavior and its perceived consequences — only a change in what the VP does, and is seen to do, can restore safety, and the VP's genuine intent makes coaching likely to succeed. Asking the team to raise the reassignment directly with the VP in the next retrospective is right in principle and wrong in sequence: candor does have to return to that room, but requiring the most exposed people to confront a powerful leader before anything has changed asks them to take the exact risk they just watched a colleague pay for. Moving to anonymous written input treats the symptom, institutionalizing the fear rather than removing it, and face-to-face candor never returns. Having the VP open each retrospective by confessing a mistake models vulnerability usefully, but as a scripted ritual it says nothing about the reassignment the team believes it witnessed.
questions.concept: Leader behavior as the primary driver of psychological safety
questions.question: An agile coach notices that since a new VP began attending a platform team's retrospectives, spoken contributions have dropped sharply. Two engineers privately tell the coach they stay quiet because a colleague who challenged an architecture decision was recently moved off a high-profile initiative. The VP genuinely wants to stay close to the team. What is the BEST response by the coach?
choices: Coach the team to raise the reassignment concern with the VP directly in the team's next retrospective, since candor is rebuilt by practicing it in the room where it broke down
Move the retrospective to anonymous written input, so engineers can raise the architecture and reassignment concerns openly without the VP being able to tell which person wrote which item
Meet privately with the VP, share the observed impact without naming individuals, and agree on concrete behavior changes — including possibly stepping back while the team rebuilds candor
Ask the VP to open each retrospective by describing a recent mistake of their own, so the team sees for itself that admitting an error openly carries no career penalty here

questions.explanation: The ruling restricts one method of feedback, not the need for feedback, and a joint design session produces legally acceptable ways to put working software in front of real clinicians within days rather than months. Waiting four months while cataloguing assumptions makes the exposure visible but leaves every assumption unretired; a risk-adjusted backlog orders work by exposure, it does not reduce exposure. Seeking an exception for anonymized live records attacks the regulatory boundary instead of working inside it, and even a granted exception would take longer than running a synthetic-data walkthrough this iteration. Treating the IT project sponsor as a stand-in swaps the actual user for a convenient proxy, which is precisely the substitution that produced the assumption backlog.
questions.concept: Designing feedback loops within regulatory constraints
questions.question: A team builds a companion app for a regulated medical device. Its real users are hospital clinicians, but the organization's legal counsel has ruled that unreleased software may not touch live patient data in any form. For three iterations the team has shipped increments with no clinician input and has accumulated a long list of untested assumptions about clinical workflow. The product owner proposes waiting for the formal validation phase, which begins in four months. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Follow the product owner's plan and log every untested assumption on a risk-adjusted backlog, so exposure stays visible and can be retired once validation opens.
Ask legal for an exception permitting a small clinician pilot on anonymized patient records, since anonymized data no longer identifies any individual patient.
Convene clinicians, legal, and the team this iteration to design feedback methods that fit inside the constraint, such as synthetic-data walkthroughs and clickable prototypes.
Demonstrate each increment to the hospital's IT sponsor and clinical informatics manager, treating their sign-off as a proxy for clinician feedback until validation opens.

questions.explanation: An assumption that could invalidate the design is bought down by learning, and the cheapest learning available is a small timeboxed experiment against the real service; re-sequencing so that high-exposure work is proven early is exactly how a risk-adjusted backlog is ordered, with value and risk reduction together driving sequence. Building against a mock generated from the draft documentation is the strongest rival, because it unblocks work immediately and mocks are legitimate practice — but a mock built from the draft encodes the very assumption in doubt, so the team validates its own guess and may rebuild the quote flow anyway. Waiting for a final signed contract makes progress hostage to an external party and treats a document as evidence, whereas one successful call against the running service is evidence. Padding the integration estimates reserves money for rework but still discovers the problem in the final iteration, when change is most expensive.
questions.concept: Spikes and risk-adjusted backlog sequencing
questions.question: An insurance quoting product must integrate with a partner's rating engine. The partner has supplied only draft API documentation and nobody on the team has ever called the live service. Release is six iterations away, and the integration stories are sequenced into the final iteration because the pricing screens come first. During refinement a developer says, "If their contract is not what the draft says, we rebuild the whole quote flow." What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Have the team build a mock of the partner's rating engine from the draft documentation and develop the integration against it, so the work can start now without waiting on the partner's availability or a final contract
Ask the partner to confirm a final written API contract and keep the integration stories in the last iteration, so the team builds once against a specification that will not move underneath it later

Work with the product owner to pull a short timeboxed spike into the coming iteration that calls the partner's live service with real data, and re-sequence the backlog so the highest-exposure work is validated early
Add a contingency buffer to the integration estimates so the final iteration can absorb the rework if the partner's live contract turns out to differ from the draft documentation the team was given

questions.explanation: Net present value discounts future cash flows into today's terms, and discounting is the only thing that separates these two options: their undiscounted totals and costs are effectively the same, so the difference in value lies entirely in timing. Pairing that financial view with risk reduction and knowledge gained is what makes the decision agile rather than purely accounting-driven. Choosing on the shorter payback period is the strongest alternative and would probably pick the same initiative, but payback is a crude risk screen that ignores everything happening after the cash is recovered, so it supports a decision rather than justifying one. Relying on internal rate of return alone is unsafe: IRR can rank options misleadingly when cash-flow shapes and durations differ, and a percentage says nothing about the magnitude of value created. Treating the two as financially equivalent because their undiscounted totals match is precisely the error discounting exists to prevent, and it settles a real economic question on team capacity instead.
questions.concept: Applying NPV versus IRR in value-based prioritization
questions.question: A product owner for a subscription audiobook service is choosing between two candidate initiatives. Initiative A is expected to return most of its cash within the first year; Initiative B returns its cash evenly across five years. The two initiatives have similar total undiscounted cash inflows and similar cost. Applying value-based prioritization, what is the most defensible way to use financial measures here?
choices: Select the initiative with the shorter payback period, since recovering cash inside the first year limits exposure if the market shifts underneath
Compare the initiatives on net present value so the timing of cash flows is reflected, alongside non-financial factors such as risk and learning
Select whichever initiative shows the higher internal rate of return, since a percentage return normalizes their differing cash timing
Treat the two as financially equivalent and decide on team capacity, since undiscounted inflows and costs are close to identical in both cases

questions.explanation: Proposing a pilot release of the first working dashboard engages the sponsor's concern while creating the short feedback loop that makes agile work: real users interacting with real software reveal whether the team is building the right thing while course correction is still cheap, and a small, friendly pilot group directly answers the fear of being judged on half-done work. Holding the portal back until all twelve dashboards are polished defers learning to the most expensive moment and risks delivering twelve dashboards nobody uses. Walking finance users through clickable prototypes is genuinely useful discovery and the closest call here, but a prototype tests reactions to a layout, not whether the numbers answer the questions finance actually asks. Monthly sponsor reviews of finished dashboards put feedback on a long cycle, filter it through one person who is not the end user, and arrive after the build cost is already sunk.
questions.concept: Feedback loops and early incremental delivery
questions.question: A Kanban team is building an internal analytics portal for the finance department. The sponsor tells the agile practitioner, "Let's not show anyone until all twelve dashboards are finished — I don't want people judging half-done work." What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Agree to hold the portal back until all twelve dashboards are polished, since partial work invites unfair judgment
Propose releasing the first working dashboard to a small pilot group of finance users and gathering their feedback
Walk a group of finance users through clickable prototypes of the dashboards so input arrives before any release
Ask the sponsor to review each finished dashboard monthly so issues surface early without exposing partial work

questions.explanation: A Minimum Viable Product is aimed at validated learning — its return is knowledge about whether an assumption holds, which is why the learning-focused description fits it and the saleable-offering description does not. A Minimum Marketable Feature is the smallest chunk genuinely worth putting in front of customers as usable or saleable value, which distinguishes it from the MVP's experimental intent; teams confuse the two because both begin with "minimum." The Definition of Done is a team-wide quality agreement applied uniformly to every increment — not a per-item entry condition and not a statement of purpose. The iteration goal is the cohesive outcome statement that binds the selected work together within the time-box; it expresses intent, whereas the Definition of Done expresses completeness. The distinctions that matter on the exam are learning versus marketable value, and quality agreement versus outcome intent.
questions.concept: Distinguishing MVP, MMF, Definition of Done, and iteration goal
questions.question: Match each product-planning artifact or practice on the left with the description that best distinguishes it from the others.
pairs: Minimum Viable Product
The smallest build that generates validated learning about a product assumption, where the primary return is knowledge rather than revenue
Minimum Marketable Feature
The smallest coherent piece of functionality that delivers enough benefit to be worth releasing to customers as a saleable or usable offering
Definition of Done
A shared quality agreement applied to every increment, describing the conditions that must hold before work is considered complete and potentially releasable
Iteration goal
A short cohesive statement of the outcome the team intends to achieve in the current time-box, giving the selected work a common purpose

questions.explanation: The exhibit isolates one dramatic change: decision-making autonomy collapsed from 4.2 to 2.1 in exactly the quarter the mandatory architecture sign-off was introduced, while psychological safety, clarity of purpose, and technical practices stayed essentially flat; the morale drop to 2.7 and the doubling of median cycle time from 6 to 14 days are downstream effects. Convening the team with the architecture board to negotiate decision boundaries — pre-agreed guardrails in place of per-release sign-off — addresses the cause collaboratively. Batching approvals into one weekly submission is a sensible flow tactic that would cut some waiting, but it optimizes the queue in front of the gate instead of questioning the gate, and authority stays where it fell. A morale offsite treats the symptom while the constraint remains. Discarding the self-assessment throws away the instrument that localized the problem, and the cycle-time figures corroborate it.
questions.concept: Self-assessment interpretation and root-cause analysis of empowerment erosion
questions.question: An agile practitioner reviews the team self-assessment shown in the exhibit. Based on this data, what should the practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Coach the team to batch its release approvals into one weekly submission to the architecture board, so the added sign-off costs less waiting time in each iteration
Arrange a team offsite focused on morale and trust, since the empowerment scores will recover once confidence in the team's own judgment has been rebuilt again
Bring the team and the enterprise architecture board together to examine the new sign-off step and negotiate decision boundaries that restore the team's release authority
Replace the self-assessment with objective delivery metrics such as cycle time and deployment frequency, because perception scores cannot show whether the sign-off slows decisions

questions.explanation: With average work in progress of 12 items and throughput of 3 items per week, average cycle time is about four weeks; holding throughput steady and halving items in progress to 6 gives about two weeks, which is exactly the relationship the law expresses. Saying cycle time stays near four weeks inverts the relationship: with throughput fixed, cycle time moves in proportion to work in progress. Claiming a fall to one week assumes that halving work in progress doubles throughput; less context switching often does lift throughput indirectly, but the law predicts no such doubling and the question explicitly holds the completion rate steady. Rejecting the law because item sizes vary and support work is mixed in confuses precision with validity: variability makes the result an average and an approximation rather than a guarantee for any single item, and the two months of stable figures are exactly the condition the practical form of the law needs.
questions.concept: Practical application of Little's Law to cycle time, WIP, and throughput
questions.question: A team maintaining a claims portal keeps an average of 12 work items in progress and finishes an average of 3 items per week, and both figures have been stable for two months. Leadership asks what would happen if the team held its completion rate steady but cut the number of items in progress to 6. Which statement BEST applies Little's Law to this situation?
choices: Average cycle time would fall from about four weeks to about two weeks, because average cycle time equals average work in progress divided by average throughput.
Average cycle time would stay near four weeks, because throughput is what sets cycle time and the team is still completing an average of three work items every single week.
Average cycle time would fall to about one week, because halving the work in progress doubles the number of work items the team is able to complete in a week.
Little's Law cannot be applied here, because the team's work items vary widely in size and unplanned support work keeps the arrival rate unstable.

questions.explanation: A blocked pull is the WIP limit doing its job: it converts a personal-utilization problem into a system conversation. The best response is to teach the underlying idea — optimize flow, not individual busyness — and then let the team define its own blocked-pull behavior, whether swarming, pairing, reviewing, unblocking upstream, or improving tooling, which respects self-management and makes the agreement stick. Raising the limit to six dissolves the constraint that generated the improvement signal and simply legitimizes higher WIP and the longer cycle time that follows. Having the team lead enforce the limit treats the breach as a discipline problem and imposes authority where understanding is needed; the cycle-time evidence is genuinely useful, but the developer is still left with no better option than the one he took. Tracking breaches as a weekly flow metric is sound practice and makes the cost visible, yet counting violations answers none of the developer's real question about what to do instead.
questions.concept: WIP limits, blocked-pull behavior, and resource utilization versus flow
questions.question: A Kanban team at a veterinary-diagnostics company has a WIP limit of 4 in Development. A senior developer finishes a card, finds all four Development slots occupied by teammates' in-progress items, and rather than idling starts a fifth card, saying "my alternative was doing nothing, and idle developers are pure waste." Two other developers see this and do the same over the next week. Cycle time rises noticeably. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Raise the Development limit to six so that the policy matches the team's real capacity and no developer has to sit idle waiting for a teammate's slot to open
Coach the team that a full column is a signal to swarm on existing work, and facilitate a session to agree what members do when the limit blocks a pull
Ask the team lead to enforce the agreed limit and show the developers that the extra cards they started are what drove the team's cycle time up
Track limit breaches as a weekly flow metric and review the trend with the team so everyone can see the cost of overloading a column that is already full

questions.explanation: A minimum viable product exists to answer a question: it is the least build that yields trustworthy evidence about an assumption, and it is legitimate for it to be thrown away once the answer arrives. A minimum marketable feature exists to be sold or adopted: the emphasis is not on learning but on standing alone as something a customer will take up, which is why it is the natural unit of a release rather than of an experiment. The two are frequently confused because both are small; the distinction is intent — evidence versus marketability. A definition of done is a quality agreement that spans all work in the increment, not a description of any one item's behavior, which is what separates it from acceptance criteria. An iteration goal is a statement of intended value for a timebox, and its purpose is to let the team trade scope while keeping direction — it is not a list of committed items and not a quality standard.
questions.concept: Distinguishing MVP, MMF, definition of done, and iteration goal
questions.question: Match each product term (1-4) to the description (A-D) that most precisely defines it. Each description is used exactly once.
pairs: Minimum viable product
The smallest thing the team can build to produce validated learning about a product assumption, kept or discarded based on what it reveals
Minimum marketable feature
The smallest coherent piece of functionality that stands on its own well enough that a customer would adopt or pay for it
Definition of done
A shared set of quality conditions every item must satisfy before it counts as complete, applied uniformly across the increment
Iteration goal
A single agreed statement of the value the team intends to achieve within the current timebox, giving room to adjust scope while holding purpose

questions.explanation: Thanking the analyst for rapid, honest disclosure and steering the team into a blameless review protects the behavior the team most needs: people admitting mistakes fast so they can be fixed and learned from. If public criticism goes unanswered, the lesson everyone absorbs is to hide errors. Messaging the two senior engineers privately about their tone addresses the right problem in the wrong place — the discouraging exchange happened in front of the team, so a private word leaves every witness with the impression that questioning her access was acceptable. Starting work on a pipeline safeguard is a sound engineering response and the strongest distractor, but choosing it first answers the technical failure while leaving the social one running: the analyst is still being second-guessed in the channel. Opening a formal incident review with named action owners and organization-wide distribution escalates a brief outage into a process event and attaches her name to it publicly, which is precisely how candor becomes a career risk.
questions.concept: Blameless response to failure as the foundation of psychological safety
questions.question: The newest analyst on a Kanban-based platform support team pushes a configuration change that briefly takes the client portal offline. She immediately posts in the team channel describing exactly what she did and what broke. Within minutes, two senior engineers reply questioning whether she should be allowed near production at all. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Message the two senior engineers privately about the tone of their replies, and let the incident thread run its own course without any further comment
Publicly acknowledge the analyst for surfacing the problem so quickly and redirect the team toward a blameless review of how the failure happened
Start work on a pipeline safeguard so that a bad configuration change cannot reach production again without passing an automated safety check
Open a formal incident review with a written timeline and named action owners, and share the findings with the wider platform organization

questions.explanation: The evidence shows the roadmap is producing outputs, not outcomes; bringing the usage and support data directly to the people who own the roadmap and facilitating a value-based reprioritization is the fastest route to redirecting investment toward what customers demonstrably need. Completing the committed feature sets first honors the plan over the goal — it knowingly spends two more quarters building features the data says customers do not use. Going to the steering committee for descoping approval before discussing the evidence with the sponsor escalates past the closest decision-makers and turns a collaborative product decision into a governance fight. A retrospective on forecasting accuracy looks inward at estimation process when the urgent question is outward-facing: where should the next quarter of investment go — it improves future predictions while the current misallocation continues.
questions.concept: Outcomes versus outputs and evidence-based roadmap reprioritization
questions.question: Three releases into a product roadmap, telemetry shows that a heavily requested feature set delivered last quarter is used by fewer than 2 percent of customers, while support tickets reveal fast-growing demand for capabilities that are not on the roadmap at all. The sponsor reminds the team that the roadmap was formally approved and that two more feature sets in the same theme are committed for the next two quarters. What is the BEST response?
choices: Deliver the two committed feature sets as approved, then bring the adoption and support evidence to the next annual planning cycle for the roadmap refresh
Share the telemetry and support data with the product owner and sponsor, and facilitate reprioritizing the roadmap toward the outcomes customers now need
Ask the steering committee to formally approve descoping the remaining feature sets before the telemetry is discussed with the sponsor or the product owner
Run a team retrospective on why the original adoption forecasts were so far off, so the next roadmap's value estimates are better grounded

questions.explanation: Collaborating is most appropriate: the allocation drives quarter-long commitments for both teams and the teams must keep working together afterward, so both the outcome and the relationship are high-stakes — precisely the conditions where a joint win-win exploration pays off — and the meeting slot tomorrow makes the time investment feasible. Having the senior lead decide trades a quarter of consequences for two days of convenience and leaves lasting resentment between the teams. Splitting the designer's time evenly is the tempting trap here, since deadline pressure invites a quick 50/50 answer, but an even split may serve neither team's real need and converts one solvable problem into two half-losses. Having one team accommodate the other sacrifices that team's legitimate quarter-long needs merely to avoid tension, smoothing over the contention rather than resolving how a shared specialist should be allocated.
questions.concept: Conflict-management modes (collaborating versus compromising) applied to shared-specialist contention
questions.question: Two delivery teams both need their shared UX designer for most of the coming iteration, and the outcome will shape both teams' commitments for the entire quarter. The iteration starts in two days, and both team leads and the designer are free to meet tomorrow. Applying conflict-management theory, which approach to resolving the designer's allocation is MOST appropriate?
choices: Forcing — with the iteration starting in two days, let the more senior team lead simply decide the allocation so both teams can commit to their work on time
Compromising — split the designer's hours evenly across the coming iteration, so that each team gets a predictable share and both can still commit in two days
Smoothing — have one team accommodate the other for this iteration, since preserving the long-running working relationship matters far more than either team's delivery plan for this quarter
Collaborating — use tomorrow's meeting for both teams to jointly explore needs and options, because the stakes are high for both the outcome and the ongoing relationship

questions.explanation: The diagram already says what is wrong: arrivals exceed departures, so work in progress is growing, and with throughput flat, cycle time must rise in proportion. Limiting WIP at the widening stage and finishing started work before starting more is the fastest, cheapest, fully reversible lever the team itself controls, and re-checking cycle time turns it into a real experiment rather than an opinion. Having developers help with testing is the strongest alternative — subordinating the system to the constraint is sound — but returning to the current way of working once the band drains guarantees it refills, because no pull policy has changed. Slowing acceptance onto the board manages demand at the front door while the constraint sits in test, so without a limit there the team can still start everything it accepts. Measuring cycle time by work type sharpens the picture but delays action on a signal that is already unambiguous.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram diagnosis driving a WIP-limit change
questions.question: Eight weeks of a cumulative flow diagram show the arrival line climbing steadily, the "in test" band widening week over week, and the departure line flattening. Average cycle time has risen from 6 days to 15; items completed per week is unchanged. In the improvement session the test lead asks for a contract tester, the product owner asks the team to commit to more items per iteration so that more gets finished, and a developer wants the test column split into four sub-columns to see where the time really goes. What is the BEST next move?
choices: Have developers help with testing until the widening band drains, then return to the current way of working once cycle time comes back down toward six days.
Walk the team through the diagram, agree a WIP limit on the test stage, stop starting new items until the test band drains, then inspect cycle time again after two weeks.
Slow the rate at which new items are accepted onto the board so that arrivals match departures, since the diagram shows demand outrunning what the team has been able to absorb.
Measure cycle time separately for each type of work first, so the team can see which items are driving the increase before it changes any of its flow policies.

questions.explanation: The wellness offering sits far from certainty on both axes that matter for suitability, what to build (an unserved segment means unvalidated needs) and how to build it (unfamiliar technology), which places it in the complex zone where empirical iteration is the only reliable way to converge on a working answer. The regulatory reporting change is certain on both counts, with statutory requirements and a platform the team has run for years, so disciplined execution beats discovery. The loyalty rebuild is the strongest alternative, since an unfamiliar infrastructure stack is real technical uncertainty, but its business rules are settled, so architectural spikes resolve it without empirical product discovery. The mobile refresh has the mirror problem, contested scope on familiar frameworks, so only one dimension is genuinely in doubt.
questions.concept: Agile suitability — Stacey Matrix / Cynefin domain fit
questions.question: An agile practitioner is advising a portfolio committee on which initiative would benefit MOST from an empirical, iterate-and-learn approach rather than a detailed up-front plan. Which initiative is the strongest candidate?
choices: A wellness offering aimed at a customer segment the company has never served, built on technology the team has not used before
A regulatory reporting change whose requirements are fixed by statute, delivered on a platform the team has maintained for years
A loyalty program with settled business rules that has to be rebuilt on an infrastructure stack the team has never used
A mobile refresh whose scope stakeholders still argue about, built with the same frameworks the team ships with every week

questions.explanation: The root problem is the absence of a shared definition of success, and a vision is only owned when the people who must live by it build it together; the workshop also yields an agreed trade-off yardstick, so future disputes get settled against the vision instead of by argument. Having the PMO appoint one sponsor as sole authority escalates before collaboration has been attempted and converts the other two departments into disenfranchised stakeholders whose commitment the platform still needs. Guaranteed swimlane shares institutionalize the fragmentation — capacity is divided fairly while the product still lacks direction, and value stops driving sequence. Halting intake for a comprehensive requirements study is big-bang analysis that delays feedback and gathers detail without resolving the underlying misalignment on purpose.
questions.concept: Co-created product vision and stakeholder alignment
questions.question: In a hybrid program building a citywide clinic-scheduling platform, three sponsoring departments each steer the backlog toward their own performance targets. Increments ship on schedule, but every review ends in a priority dispute, and team members privately admit they can no longer say what success for the product looks like. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask the program steering group to name a single sponsor as final prioritization authority, so every review ends in a decision rather than a standoff
Split each iteration's capacity into three fixed department shares, so every sponsor gets guaranteed throughput and the three stop competing for the same increment
Hold new intake while a consolidated requirements study reconciles all three departments' targets, so the backlog reflects a single agreed set of needs
Facilitate a chartering workshop where the sponsors and the team co-create a shared product vision and agree on how future trade-offs will be judged

questions.explanation: Reviewing the test portfolio with the team is best because duplicated slow tests are overproduction and rework — Lean waste dressed as diligence — and rebalancing toward fast lower-level tests keeps the 40% defect reduction while reclaiming capacity; naming the evening work as an impediment protects sustainable pace, which the team must be able to hold indefinitely. A dedicated test maintainer creates a hand-off and a silo, removing shared ownership of quality and leaving the wasteful suite intact. Pausing automation trades away the very practice that produced the defect reduction and lets quality debt accumulate for a whole quarter. Reporting overtime upward and cutting commitment by an arbitrary 20% bypasses the team, treats a symptom, and leaves the bloated suite consuming the same share of every future iteration.
questions.concept: Test portfolio balance, duplicated coverage as waste, sustainable pace
questions.question: A team supporting a national parks reservation system has committed to "quality built in." Over the past six iterations, defects found after release have dropped 40%, but the team is now spending an average of 55% of each iteration writing and repairing automated UI tests. Many of those tests duplicate coverage already provided by unit and service-level tests, and the UI suite takes 90 minutes to run. Two team members privately say they are working evenings to keep both the features and the suite moving. What is the BEST response?
choices: Make one team member the full-time owner of the automated tests, so the suite is maintained by a specialist and the rest of the team can concentrate on delivering features each iteration
Ask the team to stop writing new automated tests until the feature backlog is back on schedule, then restart automation next quarter using the hours that have been recovered
Facilitate a review of the test portfolio with the team to remove duplicated UI coverage in favor of faster lower-level tests, and address the overtime as an impediment to sustainable pace
Report the overtime to the functional manager and ask that the team's iteration commitment be cut by 20 percent so the test work fits inside normal hours and the two members stop staying late

questions.explanation: Continuous improvement fails when improvement items have no owner, no capacity, and no evidence of effect. Investigating why the same action stalls and then treating a single improvement as real work with an owner and a measurable outcome converts the retrospective from a venting session into a working inspect-and-adapt loop. Changing the format and rotating the facilitator is the strongest alternative after eleven identical rounds and would probably lift the mood, but the complaint is that nothing changes, and a fresh activity that again produces an unowned action item confirms exactly that. Handing the test-data work to the team lead outside the session may finish one item while teaching the team that improvement belongs to somebody else. An anonymous board treats a participation symptom and removes the dialogue in which causes surface; nothing suggests people are afraid to speak, only that speaking has led nowhere.
questions.concept: Retrospective effectiveness and actionable improvement items
questions.question: A team building a fleet-telematics product has run the same retrospective format for eleven iterations. Participation has thinned; the last two sessions produced the identical action item ("improve test data") and neither was completed. A team member says privately that the retrospective feels like "a meeting where we list things and nothing changes." What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Facilitate the next retrospective to examine why the test-data action keeps stalling, then have the team pull one improvement into the iteration backlog with an owner and a measure
Change the retrospective format and rotate the facilitator each iteration, so the sessions feel fresh and the team surfaces problems it has stopped noticing after eleven identical rounds
Have the team lead own the test-data action outside the retrospective so the improvement finally gets done without spending more of the team's session time on it each iteration
Collect observations on an anonymous board before each session so quieter members can name the reasons the improvement keeps stalling without social pressure from more vocal peers

questions.explanation: Taking ownership of the impediment and working with the operations group to restore access is the essence of servant leadership: the leader absorbs organizational friction so the team can keep delivering value, and a blocker already two days old warrants action today. Telling the tester to keep chasing it herself leaves a team member spending delivery time on organizational navigation that the practitioner is far better positioned to handle. Recording the delay in the risk register converts an active, present impediment into a passive future item and postpones any action to a meeting. Reassigning her to filler work manages around the blocker rather than removing it, normalizing the delay and hiding its true cost to flow.
questions.concept: Servant leadership and impediment removal
questions.question: During a daily sync, a tester mentions in passing that she has been waiting two days for access credentials to the new staging environment and has been re-testing old builds to stay busy. What should the agile practitioner, acting as a servant leader, do?
choices: Take ownership of the impediment and work directly with the operations group to get her access unblocked
Remind the tester that the access request is hers to chase and ask her to follow up again
Record the access delay in the risk register so it stays visible at the next review
Reassign the tester to documentation work until the credentials arrive, so her time is not wasted waiting

questions.explanation: Lead time is driven by how much work waits and how large each piece is, so limiting the review column and making review outrank starting new work drains the biggest queue on the board, while smaller items shorten the time any single piece spends in every step and expose problems sooner. Lengthening the iteration changes the reporting window, not the queue — items still wait six days for review. Keeping two items active per developer raises work in progress and directly lengthens time in process, and it is precisely the habit that let 11 items pile up unreviewed. Chasing high individual utilization optimizes each person locally and reliably increases queues, because a system run near full utilization makes everything wait longer.
questions.concept: WIP limits and batch size as lead-time levers
questions.question: A media-platform team wants to shorten lead time. Their board shows an average of 19 items in progress across 8 developers, a "Ready for Review" column currently holding 11 items with several waiting six days, and a working agreement that any team member may pull any item at any time. Which TWO actions are most likely to shorten lead time? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Set a WIP limit on the review column and make reviewing a waiting item take priority over starting new work.
Extend the iteration from two weeks to three so that more items can be completed inside a single iteration.
Ask each developer to keep two items active at all times so no one sits idle while waiting on a review.
Reduce the size of items entering the system so work moves through each step in smaller batches.
Track individual developer utilization and set a 90 percent target so available capacity is not left unused.

questions.explanation: Getting real operators in front of each small finished slice as soon as it is done shortens the feedback loop from months to days, so misunderstandings are caught while they are still cheap to fix — this is the heart of empirical, feedback-driven delivery. Demanding more detailed written requirements up front assumes the problem is insufficient specification, when the real problem is that learning arrives too late; heavier documentation lengthens the loop rather than shortening it. Inserting a user-acceptance phase before the quarterly review adds process but still delivers feedback only once a quarter, long after the work was built. Recording the quarterly reviews improves note-taking, not timing — the team would still learn about mismatches months after the fact.
questions.concept: Frequent delivery of small increments to real users
questions.question: A Kanban team maintains a dashboard used by warehouse robotics operators. Finished work is deployed to an internal staging area, but operators only see new features at a quarterly operations review, where they repeatedly say the features "aren't what we actually needed." What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the operations manager to provide more detailed written requirements before any work is pulled into the workflow
Add a formal user-acceptance testing phase in the weeks before each quarterly review
Arrange for a few warehouse operators to see and try each small finished slice as soon as it is done
Keep the quarterly reviews but record them so the team can study operator reactions in detail

questions.explanation: Psychological safety means members can take interpersonal risks — admitting mistakes, asking questions, challenging seniors — without fear of embarrassment or punishment, and a junior member volunteering her own miss while the team responds with process inquiry rather than blame is precisely that behavior in action. The architect owning last month's outage is the strongest alternative, since leaders modeling fallibility genuinely builds safety, but a senior voice risks far less than a junior one, and thanking him before moving to the next topic skips the shared examination that turns candor into learning. Energetic debate closed by a show of hands tests comfort with technical disagreement, not interpersonal risk, and voting can bury a minority concern rather than surface it. Unanimously high anonymous survey scores are self-report, and needing anonymity to collect them is itself a signal.
questions.concept: Psychological safety indicators vs. false harmony
questions.question: An agile practitioner is assessing whether psychological safety actually exists on four teams. Which observed behavior is the STRONGEST evidence that it does?
choices: A junior tester openly tells the team her own test approach missed a defect that reached production, and the team responds by examining the process together
The senior architect tells a retrospective that his own design caused last month's outage, and the team thanks him for the candor and moves to the next topic
Members debate technical options energetically in every design session, and the sharpest disagreements are consistently settled by a show of hands at the end
The anonymous survey the team runs each quarter returns unanimously high scores on the statement that mistakes here are safe to discuss openly with anyone

questions.explanation: Coaching is non-directive: the coach uses open questions to help the person define the outcome they want and discover their own answers, which builds lasting capability and self-reliance - exactly what clarifying his desired outcome and letting him find his own approach does. Walking him through a proven agenda and having him practice each stage is training: transferring a defined skill through structured instruction. Sharing the practitioner's own facilitation experience and recommending techniques is mentoring: advice drawn from greater experience in the same domain. Co-facilitating and stepping in whenever the discussion stalls is directive rescue - it may save the session but takes the learning moment away from him and builds dependence rather than capability.
questions.concept: Coaching vs. mentoring vs. training distinctions
questions.question: A business analyst preparing to facilitate his first large retrospective asks the agile practitioner for help. Which response BEST illustrates coaching, as distinct from mentoring or training?
choices: Walking him through a proven retrospective agenda step by step and having him rehearse each stage
Describing retrospectives the practitioner has run himself and recommending the techniques that worked
Asking open questions that help him clarify the outcome he wants and find his own facilitation approach
Co-facilitating the session with him and stepping in whenever the discussion stalls, so he can watch it handled

questions.explanation: Improvement work that lives on a flip chart is invisible work with no capacity behind it, which is exactly why it loses to committed features every iteration; moving a small sized slice into the same backlog makes it transparent, gives the product owner a real trade-off to accept, and delivers the improvement incrementally instead of demanding one large investment. Reserving a tenth of every iteration for improvement is a legitimate practice and the strongest alternative, but it settles a percentage instead of a decision: the allowance drifts or is reclaimed under pressure, and the test-data work itself is still neither sized nor visible to the product owner. Spending a whole retrospective on why actions never get done yields more insight and still no capacity, when this team needs one item finished more than another diagnosis. Two volunteers working quietly outside the commitment keeps the work hidden, adds unplanned load, and confirms that improvement happens only in the margins.
questions.concept: Making retrospective actions actionable through the backlog
questions.question: A municipal permitting portal team has closed its last four retrospectives with the same improvement: "make test-data setup faster." Each time, the item is written on a flip chart, and each time the iteration fills with committed features and nothing changes. In today's retrospective, two team members say openly that retrospectives are theatre. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Put the improvement into the same backlog as feature work, have the team size a small first slice, and get the product owner's agreement to pull that slice into the next iteration alongside features.

Ask the team to reserve a fixed tenth of every iteration's capacity for improvement work, so that the test-data setup gets steady attention without competing directly against the features the team already committed.
Have the team spend the whole of the next retrospective on why its improvement actions never get done, so the underlying cause is understood before another test-data action is added to the same list.

Ask two volunteers to fix the test-data setup outside the iteration commitment, treating it as a side task that the team absorbs quietly without disturbing the product owner's agreed feature plan for the coming iteration.

questions.explanation: Sanitized data breaks empiricism at its foundation: sponsors are inspecting an artifact that no longer reflects reality, so every adaptation they make, including staffing, is built on distortion. The best first move is collaborative, bringing the people doing the editing together to restore truthful data and surface why bad news feels dangerous. Rebuilding the dashboard to pull straight from the teams' boards is a strong fix that probably belongs in the eventual solution, but automating honesty without addressing the fear behind it simply moves the adjustment upstream. Asking the managers to publish the unedited data and explain it themselves hands the hardest conversation to the people most afraid of it, with nothing changed in the environment. Telling the sponsors first is defensible given the staffing decisions, yet it confirms that candor gets people burned.
questions.concept: Transparency as the foundation of empirical process control
questions.question: At a gaming studio, an agile practitioner discovers that the flow data on the program dashboard is edited before it reaches sponsors: scope carried over between iterations is quietly removed so status always shows green. Sponsors have started making staffing decisions based on these dashboards. Mid-level managers explain that 'leadership only wants a clean story.' What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Rebuild the dashboard so the figures are pulled straight from the teams' boards and no manual editing step sits between the data and sponsors
Ask the managers to publish the unedited flow data in the next dashboard cycle and to explain the change to sponsors themselves
Facilitate a working session with the managers and teams to restore the real flow data and explore why sharing bad news feels unsafe
Tell the sponsors what has been happening before the next dashboard goes out, so their staffing decisions rest on real numbers

questions.explanation: The item fails the testable and small dimensions of INVEST: nobody can state what "better visibility" means or when it is done, and cycle-time evidence shows items of this shape stall for weeks. Collaborative decomposition into thin, testable slices with agreed acceptance criteria is exactly what refinement exists to do, and it builds shared understanding among the product owner, developers, and testers in the moment. Handing the product owner a functional specification to write alone moves analysis upstream to one person, delays feedback, and swaps conversation for documentation. Sizing the item for its uncertainty and pulling it in anyway knowingly starts work the team cannot finish predictably and simply repeats the three-week pattern the data already shows. Splitting by database, service and interface is the strongest alternative because it does yield smaller pieces, but each is a horizontal layer owned by one person: nothing can be shown to a dispatcher, and the disagreement about which screens are wanted survives intact.
questions.concept: INVEST criteria and vertical decomposition during refinement
questions.question: A hybrid team building a marine-cargo tracking platform holds a refinement session. The product owner reads out a backlog item: "As a fleet dispatcher, I want better visibility of container status so that I can make good decisions." The developers say they can size it but they cannot tell when it would be finished, and two of them describe completely different screens. The team's cycle-time data shows items like this routinely spend three weeks in progress. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Facilitate the team and product owner in splitting the item into thinner slices with concrete, testable acceptance criteria before it is pulled into work
Ask the product owner to write a detailed functional specification covering every screen and bring it back to the team's next refinement session for sizing
