Have the team size the item for its uncertainty and pull it in next, letting the first days of work discover the screens
Split the item by layer so the database, service, and interface work go to separate developers and each part can be finished and measured

questions.explanation: Facilitating agreement on shared success criteria and running short time-boxed spikes of both approaches is best: it depersonalizes a conflict that has hardened around two individuals, redirects their energy toward evidence both have already agreed to accept, gives the decision to the team rather than to either developer, and puts the two back into shared work within days. Handing the decision to the architect settles the question but not the conflict — it removes ownership from the team, leaves one developer feeling overruled, and teaches everyone that escalation is how disagreements end. Letting each developer apply a preferred approach in their own area of the codebase is avoidance dressed as compromise; it institutionalizes inconsistent testing, keeps the two apart, and leaves the escaped-defect problem unsolved. Deferring the discussion until after the release lets defects keep escaping while the rift widens and more developers take sides.
questions.concept: Depersonalizing hardened technical conflict through collaborative, time-boxed experiments
questions.question: On an XP team, two senior developers have argued for two weeks about whether escaped integration defects should be attacked with consumer-driven contract tests or an expanded end-to-end suite. Their disagreement has hardened into a personal one: they now avoid pairing with each other, other developers are starting to take sides, and defects continue to escape. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Facilitate a working session where the two developers agree on shared success criteria, then run a short time-boxed spike of each approach against recent real defects so the team can decide on the evidence
Let each developer apply the preferred approach in the part of the codebase they know best and revisit the question next quarter, when there is enough defect history to compare the two fairly
Ask the technical architect to weigh both positions and issue a binding decision on contract testing, so the team stops losing delivery time to an argument that has already turned personal

Defer the testing decision until the current release has shipped, and in the meantime have the two developers jointly triage each newly escaped defect so that they are at least working from the same evidence base

questions.explanation: Stakeholder surprises come from information that is curated and lagging; an always-on information radiator — the live board with WIP and flow metrics, reinforced by reviews of working software — lets stakeholders pull an unfiltered, real-time picture, eliminating both the surprises and most of the reporting effort. Sending a daily status email increases the reporting burden the team is already complaining about and still delivers a curated snapshot. Assigning a coordinator to own reporting preserves the filtered intermediary that caused the surprises and adds a hand-off. Collecting stakeholder questions in advance shortens the deck but keeps the information mediated and delayed, so the underlying transparency problem remains.
questions.concept: Information radiators for distributed teams
questions.question: A distributed Kanban team spends several hours each week assembling a polished status deck for stakeholders. Despite the effort, stakeholders say they are repeatedly surprised by delays, and the team complains that reporting time is crowding out delivery work. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask stakeholders which decisions the deck actually supports, then cut it down to only those few slides so preparation time drops
Replace the weekly deck with a short daily email of the same content, so delays reach stakeholders days earlier than they do now
Have one member own reporting for each iteration, so delivery time is protected and the deck's quality stays consistent for stakeholders
Give stakeholders continuous access to the team's live board and flow metrics, and invite them to regular reviews of working software

questions.explanation: Scaling the streak-repair token, probing further on study groups, and setting aside the conversation partner is the only reading consistent with the pre-agreed thresholds: the token beat its threshold decisively (62% vs 40%) at the lowest cost (2 iterations), so persevere; study groups landed just under threshold (13% vs 15%), which justifies one more cheap, refined probe before committing 5 iterations; and the conversation partner missed by a wide margin (8% vs 25%) while carrying the highest cost (6 iterations), so the hypothesis is invalidated as framed. Scaling all three because each showed "some engagement" ignores the point of setting thresholds in advance — any feature produces nonzero numbers, which is why the pass line was agreed before the data arrived. Prioritizing the conversation partner because it has the most "room for growth" reads a large miss as an opportunity; the evidence says learners are not adopting it, and it is the most expensive bet on the board. Rerunning everything with larger samples treats a clear pass and a clear fail as equally uncertain, delaying validated decisions and spending another cycle to relearn what the board already shows.
questions.concept: Validated learning and pivot-or-persevere decisions against pre-set success criteria
questions.question: A product team reviews the experiment results shown in the exhibit. Based on the exhibit, what should the team do next?
choices: Scale all three of the features, since every one of the experiments produced a measurable increase in learner engagement above the baseline the team recorded
Scale the streak-repair token, run a cheaper refined probe on peer study groups before committing, and treat the AI conversation partner hypothesis as invalidated for now
Prioritize the AI conversation partner, since the size of its gap to the threshold shows where the largest headroom for improvement is still available to the team to capture
Rerun all three experiments with larger samples before any scale or drop decision is taken, so that no promising feature is cut on the strength of thin data

questions.explanation: Net present value discounts each cash flow by when it arrives, so 120,000 at the end of year one and year two (about 109,000 plus about 99,000 in today's money) is worth more than a larger amount that does not appear until year three (about 188,000). Nord clears its cost and Sud does not, which reverses the ranking a raw total would produce - exactly the reason agile prioritization favors earlier value. Comparing the undiscounted 250,000 against 240,000 ignores the time value of money and is the specific error this comparison exposes. Declaring the options equivalent and sorting by story-point size confuses effort with value; size is an input to cost, never the ranking criterion. Refusing to start either because no return lands inside the current quarter substitutes an arbitrary accounting horizon for economic analysis and would reject value-positive work outright.
questions.concept: Net present value applied to sequencing and value-based prioritization
questions.question: A product team must decide which of two funded options to sequence first. Option Nord costs 200,000 to build and is expected to avoid 120,000 of cost at the end of each of the next two years. Option Sud costs 200,000 and is expected to generate a single payment of 250,000 at the end of year three. The organization discounts at 10 percent. Applying value-based prioritization, which statement BEST supports the decision?
choices: Option Sud should go first: its single return of 250,000 exceeds Nord's combined 240,000 for the same build cost, so it produces the larger surplus across the horizon that the two options both share.
The two options are financially equivalent, since both cost 200,000 and both return more than they cost, so the team should sequence them by the size of the delivery effort instead.
Option Nord should go first: discounted at 10 percent its returns are worth about 208,000 against a 200,000 cost, while Sud's year-three payment is worth about 188,000 - less than it costs to build.
Neither option should be started, because for both of them the positive return arrives outside the current fiscal period and so cannot be recognized against this period's operating budget.

questions.explanation: Showing the working feature together with its measured cost gives the people who own the value trade-off -- the product owner and the beta users who live with the battery -- exactly the information they need, while the retrospective addresses the systemic gap that let an outcome-critical constraint go unstated. Shipping on the strength of the item's acceptance criteria alone treats the output as the goal and quietly degrades a stated customer outcome for 40 real users. Withholding the feature until battery use is optimized removes the very information stakeholders need and makes the increment look better than it is, which is the opposite of transparency. Rewriting the criteria after the fact and unilaterally failing the item punishes the team for a gap in the shared definition, hides a working capability, and still leaves the Definition of Done unchanged for next time.
questions.concept: Outcomes versus outputs and Definition of Done gaps
questions.question: A firmware team for a hearing-aid manufacturer works in two-week iterations with continuous integration and pair programming. Two days before the iteration review, integration results show the new adaptive-noise feature meets every acceptance criterion on its item but increases battery drain by about 18 percent. Battery life between charges is one of the product's three stated customer outcomes; it appears in the product goal but not in this item's acceptance criteria and not in the team's Definition of Done. The product owner wants to demo the feature and push it to the 40-person beta cohort. The QA lead wants it held back entirely. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Add a battery-consumption threshold to the item's acceptance criteria now, mark the item unfinished, and carry it into the next iteration for tuning, so that what the team demonstrates at the review is unambiguously complete against the product's three stated customer outcomes

Demo the feature at the review with its measured battery impact shown beside it so the product owner and beta users decide together what to do, and raise the missing criterion in the retrospective as a candidate addition to the Definition of Done.

Release the feature to the beta cohort as planned, since it satisfies every acceptance criterion written for the item, and the beta participants have already agreed to accept early capability that is still being tuned for battery and network use in the field

Hold the feature out of the iteration review until the team has brought the battery drain back down near its earlier level, so that the beta users and stakeholders are never shown an increment that undercuts one of the product's three stated customer outcomes

questions.explanation: The Five Whys analysis located the cause precisely: the only feedback on real integration behavior arrives in a manual window at the end, so defects are discovered days after they are introduced. Moving that feedback into the pipeline through contract tests or nightly integration runs shortens the feedback loop and builds quality in, which is exactly what the evidence points to. Adding a third manual day scales the late-detection approach rather than replacing it: defects are still found at the gate, the release cadence lengthens, and cost of delay grows. Escalating for an API freeze asks another team to stop changing so this team can avoid changing, works against collaboration, is unlikely to hold in a live program, and does nothing about the next integration change once the freeze lifts. Raising unit test coverage to 90 percent adds a process gate aimed at the wrong layer - unit tests against stubs cannot detect a mismatch with the real partner API no matter how high the coverage number goes.
questions.concept: Root cause analysis leading to continuous integration testing at the right layer
questions.question: A team on a regulated banking program releases every two weeks. Three consecutive releases have each required a hotfix within 48 hours for defects that automated tests did not catch. The team's build pipeline runs unit tests on every commit and passes consistently. In the retrospective, the team runs Five Whys and traces the defects to integration between their service and a partner team's API, which they stub in all automated tests and only exercise during a two-day manual test window before each release. The team is under pressure to add a third day of manual testing. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Add a third day of manual testing before every release and hold the release cut until that pass is signed off, since two days are demonstrably insufficient to catch the integration defects that keep reaching production within 48 hours of every release

Facilitate the team in designing an experiment that exercises the real partner integration continuously - for example a contract test suite or a nightly run against a partner test instance - so integration defects surface within hours rather than at the release gate

Ask the partner team to freeze their API between the team's release dates so the integration surface stops moving, and treat any change inside that window as an exception that both teams agree with a named owner on each side before either ships it

Raise the unit test coverage target to 90 percent and make the coverage gate blocking, so no release is cut until the pipeline has demonstrated that the team's own service code is exercised far more thoroughly than the current suite manages at present

questions.explanation: Coaching the team to establish its own pull policies builds the self-organization the team currently lacks: members choose work against transparent, jointly agreed rules, so nothing falls through the cracks and ownership stays with the team. A rotating assignment schedule still externalizes the decision into a mechanism rather than the team's judgment, and treats fairness as the problem when the real gap is shared ownership. Assigning work personally, even temporarily, trains the team to depend on the practitioner and delays self-organization rather than developing it. Handing allocation to the delivery manager moves the decision even further from the people doing the work and reintroduces command-and-control task assignment.
questions.concept: Self-organizing teams and pull-based work selection
questions.question: A newly formed Kanban team maintaining a hotel-booking platform asks the agile practitioner to assign work items to individuals every morning "so nothing falls through the cracks." What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Set up a rotating assignment schedule so the workload stays evenly spread across the team
Coach the team to pull work themselves using explicit selection policies they define together
Assign the items each morning as asked until the team has more experience of the platform
Ask the delivery manager to allocate the items according to each member's recorded skill profile

questions.explanation: Agreeing on objective evaluation criteria and running short, time-boxed spikes of each framework converts a personality contest into an evidence-based decision the whole team owns; the practitioner manages the process while the team keeps the decision. Settling it by majority vote at planning ends the deadlock quickly but creates winners and losers on a question evidence could answer, so the minority's possibly valid risks are outvoted rather than tested. Keeping the current framework and revisiting next quarter is the strongest alternative — nobody has shown the framework blocks delivery, so the migration may genuinely not be worth it — yet deciding by default leaves the deadlock and the silent daily syncs untouched. Having each developer write a proposal moves the debate out of the sync, but two advocacy documents restate positions without testing them and still ask the team to pick a side.
questions.concept: Collaborative, evidence-based resolution of technical conflict
questions.question: On an XP team building firmware dashboards for agricultural sensors, two senior developers have been deadlocked for three iterations over whether to migrate the automated test suite to a new framework. Their debates now dominate the daily sync, and the rest of the team has started staying silent. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Have the team settle the framework question by majority vote at the next planning session, so the deadlock ends and the daily sync moves on
Facilitate a session where the team agrees on objective evaluation criteria, then time-boxes a small spike of each framework against them
Keep the current test framework and revisit migration next quarter, since neither developer has shown the framework is blocking delivery
Ask each developer to write a proposal for the team to read before deciding, so the debate leaves the daily sync and becomes a document

questions.explanation: Writing acceptance criteria with the clinic staff as concrete examples before work starts makes their real workflow the shared specification rather than a reconstruction from old notes, and having a staff member exercise the feature during development shrinks the feedback loop from a fortnight to hours, so misunderstandings are corrected while the work is still cheap to change. Raising unit-test coverage only proves the code does what the team intended, and the team's intent is exactly what is wrong, so this class of failure is invisible to it. A signed scope document substitutes contractual protection for collaboration and freezes an understanding that has already proved unreliable. Tripling the length of the review gathers more feedback at the same late moment, after the rework has already been created.
questions.concept: Specification by example and continuous customer involvement in acceptance
questions.question: A team building a clinical scheduling tool finds that features pass every automated test the team writes, yet clinic staff reject roughly one in three at the review with comments like "that is not how we actually book a patient." The product owner currently drafts detailed acceptance criteria a few days after development begins, working alone from earlier notes. Which TWO actions will most improve customer acceptance? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Raise automated unit-test coverage so that fewer defects reach the review
Write acceptance criteria together with clinic staff before the item is pulled, expressed as concrete examples of real bookings
Have clinic staff sign a scope document at the start of each release so expectations are contractual
Arrange for a clinic staff member to exercise the feature with the team during development rather than waiting for the review
Extend the review from 30 to 90 minutes so more feedback can be gathered on each feature

questions.explanation: Improvement work competes with delivery work, so it only happens when it is treated as work: one item, sized, visible on the board, owned, and inspected next cycle. Limiting to one also applies work-in-progress thinking to improvement — a short list finished beats a long list admired. Changing the format every iteration is the strongest rival, since a stale session genuinely does depress engagement and rotating activities is standard facilitation, but this team is not short of ideas: it generates eight to ten a fortnight and completes none, so a fresher session produces a fresher list that still goes nowhere. Handing the list to the delivery manager removes ownership from the people best placed to change their own way of working and turns improvement into someone else's status report. Moving to a monthly cadence halves the number of feedback loops without addressing why nothing gets done, so the problems simply persist longer.
questions.concept: Making retrospective outcomes actionable (Kaizen as visible work)
questions.question: A payments team finishes every two-week retrospective with eight to ten improvement ideas captured in a shared document. Across the last three iterations, none of the ideas has been completed, and team members have begun referring to the session as "the complaint hour." What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Have the team select a single improvement, size it, pull it onto the board as a visible work item with an owner, and inspect the result at the next retrospective.

Change the retrospective format every iteration so the session stops feeling like a complaint hour, and trust that renewed engagement will carry the improvement ideas through to completion on its own.
Ask the delivery manager to own the improvement list outside the team, so the actions get followed up by someone accountable without consuming capacity already committed to iteration work.
Move the retrospective to a monthly cadence so more time passes between sessions, giving the improvement ideas room to be finished alongside delivery work without changing how they are tracked.

questions.explanation: Separate lobbying, hardened 'non-negotiable' positions, and duplicated features are the signature of a positional inter-group conflict, and the collaborative mode — getting the parties into one room to work the problem together — is the resolution approach that produces a durable win-win. Facilitating that session restores the common purpose behind one shared platform, converts a win-lose contest into a single value proposition, and still leaves room to apply economic ordering afterwards on inputs everyone accepts. Ordering the backlog by cost of delay is a sound technique applied too early: with no agreed outcome, every input to the model would itself be contested, and a practitioner-imposed ranking substitutes analysis for agreement. Escalating to the steering committee hands the conflict upward before the parties have attempted to resolve it themselves, and whatever ruling comes back will be complied with rather than owned. Helping each side polish its own case entrenches the rivalry, rewards the duplicated work, and abandons the practitioner's neutral, alignment-building role.
questions.concept: Collaborative resolution of inter-team conflict by restoring shared purpose
questions.question: Two product teams build on the same internal platform and face a joint funding review in three weeks. Stakeholders from each side lobby the agile practitioner separately to champion their roadmap, and the teams have quietly begun duplicating each other's features to strengthen their cases. Every stakeholder insists their priorities are non-negotiable. What is the BEST response?
choices: Order the two roadmaps into a single sequence using cost-of-delay economics so the funding review turns on objective numbers rather than on lobbying, and let the resulting order show which duplicated features each of the teams should drop

Ask the steering committee to set platform priorities ahead of the review, since only it holds the authority to settle a funding dispute, and use its ruling to stop the two teams from duplicating each other's features

Bring both teams' stakeholders and members into one working session to reconnect around the platform's shared purpose and customer outcomes, agree how success will be measured, and shape a single coherent proposal before the review

Coach each team to sharpen its own business case with customer evidence and delivery data, so the funding review compares two well-argued proposals and the stronger platform investment wins the decision on its merits

questions.explanation: Partnering with the governance body — armed with transparent cycle-time and cost-of-delay evidence — to tailor a pre-approved fast lane for low-risk changes improves the system for everyone while respecting controls the organization has legitimate reasons to keep; this is how agile practitioners drive organizational adaptation. Batching the small corrections into one quarterly change request cuts paperwork but multiplies the delay that is doing the damage, since each label fix would then wait up to a quarter. Reclassifying the label and validation fixes as defects is the most tempting alternative, and some of them genuinely are defects, but relabeling work so it falls outside the board's remit is an evasion that hides the real problem and costs trust when it surfaces. Treating governance as fixed and raising corrections a cycle early abandons impediment removal and assumes clerks can foresee fixes they discover only in use.
questions.concept: Organizational adaptation and tailoring governance in hybrid environments
questions.question: On a hybrid payroll-modernization program, an enterprise change control board requires a three-week approval cycle for any scope adjustment. Small corrections requested by payroll clerks — label changes, validation fixes, report tweaks — sit in the queue for weeks, and the team is increasingly demoralized watching easy value wait on paperwork. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Batch the small corrections into one quarterly change request, so a single approval covers many fixes and the queue stops growing between meetings
Reclassify the label and validation fixes as defects rather than scope changes, so they fall outside the board's remit and ship in the normal iteration
Bring cycle-time and cost-of-delay data to the change control board and collaborate on a tailored, pre-approved fast lane for low-risk changes within agreed boundaries
Treat enterprise governance as a fixed constraint and coach the team to raise the clerks' corrections a cycle early so the wait is absorbed

questions.explanation: The iteration goal represents a commitment to a specific outcome, and trading it away is a value decision belonging to the product owner in conversation with the requester. Facilitating that conversation keeps ordering with the accountable person, makes the trade-off explicit, and respects the team's real capacity. Accepting the export and pushing an alert story out removes the ordering decision from the product owner and sacrifices the goal for an unvalidated revenue claim. Declining because iteration scope is fixed is the strongest alternative, since protecting a goal mid-iteration is usually right and a next-iteration slot is a fair offer — but it turns a protective norm into a rule and settles a value question the product owner was never asked. Adding the export to the top of the backlog for the team to judge daily disguises a value trade-off as scheduling.
questions.concept: Protecting the iteration goal while allowing deliberate re-ordering
questions.question: A team building an agricultural sensor product runs a two-week cadence. The product owner has ordered the next iteration around a single goal: prove that farmers will act on a frost alert. Midway through the iteration, the head of sales asks the team to squeeze in a small CSV export requested by a prospect in a live deal, estimated at roughly one day. The team has capacity for it only if it drops one of the alert stories. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Bring the head of sales and the product owner together to weigh the export against the iteration goal, and let the product owner decide
Accept the export and move one alert story to the next iteration, since a live deal is concrete revenue and the goal survives a short delay
Decline the request because iteration scope is fixed once planning ends, and offer the export as the first item of the next iteration
Add the export to the top of the backlog and let the team judge during daily coordination whether it fits alongside the alert stories

questions.explanation: Collaborating (problem-solving) fits when the issue is important and time permits: working through both sets of legitimate concerns can yield an error-handling design stronger than either original position, and it resolves the conflict durably rather than papering over it. Compromising trades away parts of each position for speed — appropriate under deadline pressure on moderately important issues, but here it risks baking a half-measure into a reliability-critical payment service when there is time to do better. Accommodating sacrifices legitimate technical concerns for harmony, leaving the yielding engineer's valid risks unaddressed and the disagreement likely to resurface in production. Forcing a decision from the practitioner contradicts servant leadership, strips the engineers of ownership, and ends the argument without resolving the underlying technical question.
questions.concept: Selecting conflict management modes by issue importance and time available
questions.question: Two senior engineers on a Kanban team keep clashing over the error-handling design of a payment service. The design materially affects reliability, both engineers' concerns are technically legitimate, and the next release is several weeks away. Which conflict-handling mode is MOST appropriate for the agile practitioner to encourage, and why?
choices: Forcing, because reliability decisions on a payment service warrant a decisive call, and the practitioner can make it quickly so delivery is not held hostage
Accommodating, because two senior engineers must keep working together, so yielding to the one who owns the payment service protects that key relationship
Compromising, because each engineer concedes one part of the error-handling design and the team regains flow without a long technical debate
Collaborating, because the issue is high-stakes for the product and there is enough time to integrate both engineers' concerns into a better solution

questions.explanation: Going to the division head to reconnect the mandate with its underlying intent is the only response that treats the root cause: the leader wants better delivery, the checklist measures ritual instead, and gaming is the predictable symptom of measuring the wrong thing. Proposing outcome measures — cycle time, feedback frequency, value delivered — while teams tailor their own practices models the agile mindset for leadership and converts an imposed mandate into an invitation. Adding cycle time and escaped-defect rate beside the maturity scores is genuinely useful evidence and the closest call, but it leaves the gamed metric in force and defers the conversation to day ninety. Helping the two candid teams make their real practice match the checklist buys honesty at the price of legitimizing the checklist as the goal, and it reaches two teams of fourteen. Value-stream mapping would likely move cycle time, yet it routes around the mandate still driving everyone's behavior.
questions.concept: Shifting leadership from practice compliance to outcome-based measures of agility
questions.question: After a successful agile pilot, a division head mandates that all fourteen teams adopt identical two-week cadences and reach full marks on a tool-based agile maturity checklist within ninety days. By week six the dashboard shows every team compliant, yet cycle times have not moved, and two teams privately admit they update the checklist just before each audit. Several responses are technically possible. Which is BEST for the agile practitioner?
choices: Add cycle time and escaped-defect rate alongside the maturity scores on the dashboard, so the division head can see compliance scores and actual delivery results side by side when the ninety days are up
Work with the two teams that admitted updating the checklist before audits to make their real practices match it, so the dashboard becomes an honest picture of how they work
Meet with the division head to connect the mandate to the outcomes they actually want, and propose replacing checklist compliance with outcome measures while teams tailor their own practices
Ask each of the fourteen teams to map its value stream and act on the largest delay it finds, since cycle time is the measure that has not moved in the six weeks since the mandate

questions.explanation: Flow efficiency is a property of the work item, not of the people: it says the item waited three quarters of its life, so the queues, handoffs and approvals between the steps hold the recoverable time, and halving the wait shortens delivery far more than making the coding faster ever could. Reading 25% as under-utilized people inverts the measure and leads straight to the worst possible countermeasure — more parallel items raises WIP and makes each item wait even longer. Treating 100% as the target misreads the metric too; knowledge work commonly measures in the 5-25% range, and pushing toward full efficiency would require zero queues everywhere, which in practice means starving the system and removing the slack that absorbs variability. Reinterpreting the ratio as estimation bias confuses effort with elapsed time — the 40 hours of work may have been estimated perfectly well; it is the 120 hours of waiting that the estimate never covered.
questions.concept: Interpreting flow efficiency (touch time / elapsed time) as a waste signal
questions.question: A team instruments one representative work item from pull to release: 40 hours of hands-on work spread across 160 hours of elapsed time, a flow efficiency of 25%. Members disagree about what the number is telling them. Which interpretation should guide the team's next improvement?
choices: Team members are only 25% utilized, so each of them should carry more items at once to stay occupied across the 160 hours of elapsed time.
Any figure below 100% signals a broken process, so the team should adopt 100% flow efficiency as the improvement target that it works toward.
Effort estimates are running roughly four times optimistic, so the team should multiply its future effort estimates by four to make its forecasts honest.
The 120 hours the item spent in queues, handoffs and waiting for approvals — not the 40 hours of hands-on work — is where the improvement lever sits.

questions.explanation: Encouraging pairing on scheduling stories dissolves the single-person bottleneck in the most agile way: knowledge transfers through the real work itself, delivery keeps flowing, and the team grows generalizing specialists — and it respects the current owner by keeping her at the center of the work rather than working around her. Hiring a second specialist escalates outside the team, takes months, and duplicates the silo instead of removing it. Re-sequencing the backlog around one person's availability optimizes the plan to preserve the constraint rather than addressing it, and lets wait times persist. Independent documentation study is a slow, feedback-free way to learn a live codebase and produces far weaker knowledge transfer than working together on real stories.
questions.concept: Generalizing specialists and pairing to remove knowledge silos
questions.question: On an XP team building a telehealth portal, only one developer understands the appointment-scheduling module. Her queue of scheduling stories keeps growing while other developers wait, sometimes for days, and she says she prefers owning the module herself. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Encourage the team to pair on scheduling-module stories so knowledge spreads while the work continues to flow
Ask the resource manager to hire a second scheduling specialist to absorb the queue
Re-sequence the backlog so scheduling stories are batched to match the specialist's availability
Assign another developer to study the module's documentation independently until he can take over some stories

questions.explanation: Each mechanism creates transparency or feedback at a different level, and the exam expects you to keep them distinct. An information radiator makes work status transparent passively and continuously — its defining trait is that no one has to ask; if people must request the data, it is an information refrigerator instead. A working agreement makes behavioral expectations transparent: the team writes its own norms so collaboration standards are explicit rather than assumed, which is different from displaying work status. A retrospective is the team's process feedback loop — it inspects how the team works, not what the product does in the market. A minimum viable product is the outermost feedback loop: it tests a value hypothesis against real users, generating validated learning about the product itself. Confusing these — for example treating an MVP as merely a small release rather than a hypothesis test, or a radiator as a report someone pulls — is a classic exam trap.
questions.concept: Feedback loops and transparency mechanisms at work-status, team, process, and product levels
questions.question: Match each transparency or feedback mechanism (1-4) with the description (A-D) that best captures its distinct purpose.
pairs: Information radiator
A continuously updated visible display that lets anyone assess current work status without having to ask
Working agreement
A team-created, explicit set of norms making expectations about day-to-day collaboration visible to everyone
Retrospective
A recurring inspect-and-adapt session in which the team examines and improves its own way of working
Minimum viable product
The smallest releasable version of a product used to test a value hypothesis with real users and gather market evidence

questions.explanation: Facilitating a collaborative visioning exercise is best because a shared vision must be built with the people who will deliver it — co-creating an elevator statement with the product leader present reconciles the conflicting mental models and produces ownership, not just awareness. Having the product leader state the goal and the team write it on the planning board is fast and better than nothing, but it is one-way transmission: three people picturing three different customers can all nod at the same sentence and then plan from different assumptions. Surfacing each member's picture and then asking the product leader to rule is the closest alternative, since it does expose the divergence, yet it ends in a verdict the team receives rather than a goal it builds, so commitment stays shallow. Carrying on and letting the goal emerge from story discussion gambles the session, because estimating and slicing on divergent assumptions bakes the contradictions into the plan.
questions.concept: Collaborative visioning techniques (elevator statement, product vision)
questions.question: During release planning for a lean-startup analytics product, the agile practitioner notices that three team members describe three different target customers, and no one can state what problem the upcoming release is meant to solve. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Pause planning and facilitate a short collaborative visioning exercise, such as an elevator statement, with the team and the product leader so everyone constructs the release goal together
Ask the product leader to state the release goal at the start, then have the team capture it on the planning board so everyone plans from one written statement
Have each member write down the customer they picture, compare the answers openly, then ask the product leader to rule on which description the team plans around
Carry on with planning and use the discussion of individual stories to reveal which customer each item serves, capturing the release goal once it emerges from the backlog

questions.explanation: Compliance work with a legal date is not one option among equals competing on return; it is a boundary the sequence has to respect, and naming it as such frees the genuine value comparison to be made honestly on what remains. Ranking the rest by value against effort with the people who own the value and the estimates — and explicitly counting the re-partitioning's effect on future delivery cost as value rather than as overhead — produces an order the team can defend and revise as evidence changes. Sequencing purely by net present value treats a dated legal obligation as deferrable and risks discovering too late that two releases were not enough. Putting the re-partitioning first is a plausible economic argument but converts a leverage decision into a dogma, spending the nearest releases on work no customer experiences while a deadline runs. Waiting on finance for internal rate of return figures adds analytical precision to inputs that are already rough estimates, stalls a decision the team can make today, and moves ordering away from the product owner.
questions.concept: Value-based prioritization with regulatory constraints and cost-of-delay reasoning
questions.question: A payments team's backlog holds three candidate themes for the next two releases: a merchant-analytics feature with the highest modeled net present value; an accessibility-conformance package that national regulation requires within two releases; and a platform re-partitioning that developers estimate would roughly halve the cost of future changes. The product owner says "just sequence by value" and wants the order settled in today's refinement session. What is the BEST response?
choices: Sequence strictly by modeled net present value alone, and bring the accessibility package forward only when its regulatory date is close enough to put a release at risk, so that the ordering rule the product owner stated stays intact for the rest of the current two-release plan

Treat the accessibility package as a dated constraint on the plan, then work with the team and product owner to rank the remaining themes by value against effort — including the re-partitioning's effect on the cost of future delivery — and re-check the order at each refinement.

Do the platform re-partitioning first, because halving the cost of future change lifts the return on everything that is sequenced behind it in the two-release plan, then take the analytics feature and fit the accessibility package into whatever capacity remains once that work is under way

Ask the finance group to produce internal rate of return and payback figures for all three themes, and hold the sequencing decision until those numbers arrive, so that the ranking rests on comparable economics across the portfolio rather than on the team's rough estimates of relative effort alone

questions.explanation: The best response educates the analyst on the agile mindset and brings her into the work: incremental delivery with real feedback from clinic staff is how agile teams discover requirements, and inviting her to help shape thin, testable slices converts a skeptic into a collaborator. Negotiating a shorter document that is still signed off before coding keeps the approval gate and merely shrinks the waste rather than changing how requirements are learned. Asking her to convert her requirements into a ranked backlog of user stories before the first iteration is the strongest alternative, and something like it will probably happen — but done now it still treats her prose as the source of truth, when the real gap is that clinic staff have never used anything. Beginning to build while she documents alongside excludes her from the conversation that would change her mind and preserves the artifact she believes prevents rework, fixing neither the relationship nor the belief.
questions.concept: Agile vs predictive thinking — working software over comprehensive documentation
questions.question: A development team at a veterinary clinic chain is about to start building a new appointment-scheduling tool. A business analyst, newly transferred from the organization's predictive PMO, insists that development cannot begin until a complete 60-page requirements document is written and signed off, saying, "Otherwise we will build the wrong thing." What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Negotiate a shortened requirements document covering only the scheduling rules and clinic roles, signed off before coding starts, so the analyst keeps the approval gate she expects while the team avoids writing sixty pages of upfront detail

Ask the analyst to convert her requirements into a ranked backlog of user stories before the first iteration, so development starts from prioritized scope rather than from prose that clinic staff have never actually reviewed

Explain that delivering small increments of working software and gathering clinic staff feedback will reveal the right requirements faster than upfront documentation, and invite the analyst to help shape thin, testable slices of scope

Begin building the highest-value scheduling flows now and have the analyst write the requirements document alongside the code, so the organization still gets the record it wants without the team waiting on a sign-off

questions.explanation: A pipeline that fails twice daily and passes on rerun is producing information the team keeps discarding. Treating the next red build as a stop-and-investigate event and applying a structured root-cause technique preserves the pipeline's role as fast, trustworthy feedback and follows understanding before prescribing; in a payments system, intermittent failures commonly expose real timing, concurrency, or data-isolation defects that will eventually appear in production. Moving the unstable tests to a nightly job, even with a morning review, hides the signal and stretches the feedback loop the team most needs, converting a defect currently caught within minutes into one found a day later or by customers. Appointing a build steward to rerun red builds and log which tests failed institutionalizes the rerun habit and makes one person absorb a whole-team quality problem. Taking the pattern to the shared-environment group is the strongest rival, since infrastructure really is a common source of intermittent failures — but it names a culprit before any evidence and hands the team's investigation to someone else.
questions.concept: Continuous integration signal integrity and root-cause analysis
questions.question: A payments team practicing continuous integration has seen its pipeline turn red on average twice a day for a month. The usual response is that whoever notices reruns the build, and it typically passes on the second or third attempt. Nobody has changed the tests. A retrospective raises the issue, and one developer proposes moving the flaky tests to a nightly job so the main pipeline stays green. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Support moving the unstable tests into a nightly job so daytime feedback stays fast, and ask the team to review the nightly results together each morning before starting any new work
Ask the team to stop the line on the next red build and run a Five Whys on that specific failure to find what the intermittent signal is actually revealing
Assign a build steward each iteration who reruns red builds and records which tests failed and when, so a reliable pattern can be recognized over the coming few weeks
Raise the pattern with the group that owns the shared test environment, since failures that come and go with no code change often point at the shared infrastructure itself

questions.explanation: The continuously visible, team-maintained display is the genuine information radiator: it pushes honest, current information, including problems, to anyone who passes by, with no filtering, no gatekeeper, and no request required. A formatted status summary emailed each morning by a coordinator is push reporting through an intermediary, and because the tool is updated at the end of the day it is already behind when it lands. A detailed plan in a shared tool with stakeholder read access is the closest of the three, since the data is current and nobody is gatekeeping it, but information behind a login must be deliberately pulled rather than absorbed at a glance, and blockers never announce themselves. A wall chart replaced once a quarter is highly visible yet changes only at planning, so it radiates a plan rather than the work.
questions.concept: Transparency; information radiators
questions.question: A coach is assessing how four teams share information about their work. Which team is using an information radiator as intended?
choices: A team whose coordinator emails a formatted status summary every morning, drawn from the tracking tool the team updates at the end of each day
A team that keeps a detailed plan in a shared tool and grants stakeholders read access, so anyone can pull the current status whenever they need it
A team that posts a wall chart of the release plan at the start of each quarter and replaces it at the next planning session, keeping the display uncluttered
A team that keeps its board, current blockers, and key trend charts continuously visible in its work area and updates them itself as conditions change

questions.explanation: Agreeing on acceptance criteria and concrete examples up front, then automating them, removes the ambiguity that lets a developer believe a story is done when it is not, and it pulls verification back to the moment the code is written instead of days later. Test-driven development shrinks that feedback loop to minutes by making the failing test the specification, which is precisely what building quality in means. Automatically re-estimating and carrying reopened stories is bookkeeping: it makes the rework tidier to track but does nothing to stop defects being injected or found late. A sign-off gate at the end of the iteration adds an inspection step even further downstream, lengthening the loop the team is trying to shorten and making quality one person's responsibility instead of the whole team's. Buffering points for rework institutionalizes the waste, permanently consuming capacity to accommodate a cause nobody has removed.
questions.concept: Acceptance test-driven development and TDD for built-in quality
questions.question: A logistics platform team keeps missing its forecast because "nearly done" stories reopen after the iteration review. Root-cause discussion points to defects being found only when a tester picks the story up two or three days after the developer declares it complete. The team wants to build quality in rather than inspect it in later. Which TWO actions most directly address the cause? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Introduce a rule that any story reopened after review is automatically re-estimated and carried to the next iteration
Have developers and testers agree on acceptance criteria and concrete examples before coding begins, and automate those examples as acceptance tests
Add a quality-assurance sign-off gate at the end of each iteration, owned by the test lead
Adopt test-driven development for the modules with the highest reopen rate so failing tests are written before the code
Increase the story point buffer in each iteration to absorb the rework caused by reopened stories

questions.explanation: This is a high-impact technical unknown sitting underneath 40 percent of the remaining backlog; the cost of being wrong grows with every iteration of work built on it. A time-boxed spike buys the information cheaply and early, and sequencing it as a risk-adjusted backlog item is exactly how agile teams balance value delivery against risk reduction. Logging it in a risk register with a quarterly review defers the learning far past the point where the answer is still cheap to act on — documenting a risk is not reducing it. Building a parallel fallback rating engine is a large speculative investment made before the team knows whether it is needed, which is over-processing waste and may be entirely thrown away. Deferring to the product owner's authority on sequencing without surfacing the exposure abdicates the practitioner's responsibility; the product owner does own priority, but is entitled to a clear picture of the risk and the cheap experiment available, after which the decision can be made informed.
questions.concept: Spikes and risk-adjusted backlog sequencing for architectural unknowns
questions.question: A team building an insurance quoting engine faces a dependency on a third-party rating service whose behavior under high request volume is undocumented. The architecture assumes the service can sustain the peak load, and roughly 40 percent of the remaining backlog is built on that assumption. The product owner wants to keep delivering visible customer features and revisit the assumption during hardening, six iterations from now. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Record the load assumption on the risk register with a named owner and a mitigation plan, and review its status with the architecture group each quarter
Propose a short, time-boxed spike this iteration to test the rating service under representative load, and add it to the backlog as a risk-adjusted priority
Design a fallback rating engine in parallel so the team is protected whichever way the assumption turns out, and choose between them at hardening
Accept the product owner's sequencing, since ordering the backlog is the product owner's decision to make, and revisit the load assumption once hardening work begins

questions.explanation: The two actions that build transparency directly are radiating the work itself and normalizing the surfacing of problems. An organization-visible virtual board is a distributed team's information radiator: anyone can see real work state, WIP, and blockers at any moment, with no curation layer between the data and the viewer. A same-day, in-the-open impediment norm is a working agreement that makes bad news travel fast — transparency is as much about problems being visible early as about tasks being listed. A polished weekly deck is the opposite of radiation: it is filtered, delayed, and produced by one person, so leadership sees a curated snapshot rather than reality. Restricting board access to the team protects against a feared misuse by hiding information — it may feel safer, but it reduces transparency by definition; the fear of misuse is better addressed through working agreements about how metrics are used. A formal change-approval gate adds process and a control point; visibility of change requests is a side effect, and the gate slows flow without radiating the ongoing state of work.
questions.concept: Information radiators and openness norms for distributed teams
questions.question: A newly formed, fully distributed team supporting a Lean product group wants to increase transparency for both the team itself and its stakeholders. Which TWO actions would contribute MOST directly to transparency? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Have the team lead compile a polished weekly status deck for leadership
Publish a shared virtual board showing all work, WIP limits, and blockers, visible to anyone in the organization
Restrict board access to team members only, so managers cannot misuse the metrics
Add a formal change-approval step so stakeholders can see every requested change before it is accepted
Create a working agreement that impediments and risks are raised in the team's open channel the same day they are found

questions.explanation: Every option is technically possible, but only one follows agile decision rules. Surfacing the spike evidence immediately and facilitating a transparent pivot-or-persevere conversation lets the people accountable for value decide with current information, while two months still remain to act on it. Delivering the roadmap and revealing the analysis after release knowingly spends two months building diminished value and withholds material information — the opposite of transparency. Building a stealth MVP alongside committed scope splits the team's capacity without stakeholder knowledge; even though experimentation is agile, hiding it from the sponsor is not, and it makes the practitioner the one deciding product direction. Waiting three weeks for the product owner respects an accountability boundary but sacrifices a quarter of the remaining runway; accountabilities do not justify sitting on decision-critical market evidence when a facilitated stakeholder conversation can happen now.
questions.concept: Pivot-or-persevere decisions on new market evidence
questions.question: Two months before a contract-committed release, a platform team's technical spike reveals that a competitor's newly published API makes the release's core differentiating feature nearly worthless in the market. The product owner is on extended leave for three more weeks. The sponsor wants the published roadmap honored because sales has already demonstrated it to customers, and the team is split between pivoting to an alternative capability and delivering as promised. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Have the team build a thin version of the alternative capability beside the committed scope, and show the sponsor once there is something to demonstrate
Hold the scope decision until the product owner returns in three weeks, since roadmap tradeoffs are the product owner's accountability, not the team's
Share the spike findings openly with the sponsor and key stakeholders now, and facilitate an evidence-based decision on whether to pivot the remaining scope
Continue delivering the published roadmap and commission a competitive analysis of the rival interface, so its findings can shape the next quarter's planning cycle

questions.explanation: Two short spikes on real depot data replace speculation with evidence, cost days rather than weeks, keep the committed five-week feature intact, and leave the decision with the people who hold the knowledge rather than with the practitioner. Accepting the six-week study and re-planning the feature delays all customer value and buys analysis that still will not show how either engine behaves on this program's own data. Deciding from published vendor benchmarks is fast but discards the cheap experiment that would test the vendors' claims, and it makes an expensive, hard-to-reverse choice on the weakest available evidence. An abstraction layer is speculative design: it adds code and complexity now to preserve an option the team may never exercise, and it postpones the learning the spikes would deliver in a few days.
questions.concept: time-boxed spikes to reduce technical risk and uncertainty
questions.question: An architect on a logistics program wants six weeks of comparative analysis before choosing between two route-optimization engines, arguing the decision is expensive to reverse. The team estimates it could wire either engine to one real depot's data in roughly four days each. The first customer-facing route feature is committed for five weeks from now. What is the BEST response?
choices: Support the six-week comparative analysis and re-plan the customer route feature into the following quarter, since an engine choice this costly to reverse deserves rigor.
Ask the architect to choose now from the vendors' published benchmarks and reference customers, so the team can start on the route feature this same week.
Run two time-boxed spikes against real depot data, publish the findings openly, and hold a decision checkpoint with the architect and team once the spikes complete.
Build the route feature behind an abstraction layer so either engine can be substituted later, and defer the choice until production volumes are known.

questions.explanation: Shared purpose is built through co-creation and sustained through visible, everyday connection to the work: a joint visioning session with all three teams and their stakeholders generates genuine ownership of one product direction, and radiating the product goal while explicitly linking backlog items to it during refinement and planning turns purpose into a working input rather than a poster. A required strategy video is one-way communication — people can recite a message they were made to watch without owning it, and mandatory viewing invites compliance rather than commitment. Grading individuals on "adherence to the vision" converts purpose into a performance-review metric, which encourages gaming and fear, and it individualizes something that is inherently collective. Consolidating the backlogs under a single work-allocating coordinator centralizes control, strips teams of ownership of their own backlogs, and aligns activity by command instead of by shared intent.
questions.concept: Co-created vision and visible linkage of backlog work to the product goal
questions.question: Three feature teams contribute to one streaming-media platform. Members increasingly describe their objective as "finishing our own backlog," cross-team trade-offs stall, and refinement discussions rarely mention customers. Which TWO actions would most strengthen a shared sense of purpose across the teams? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Bring all three teams and key stakeholders together to co-create a single product vision and shared quarterly outcome goals
Have the sponsor record a video explaining the strategy and require every member to watch it
Add each team's adherence to the vision as a weighted factor in individual performance reviews
Make the product goal visible in each team's workspace and connect backlog items to it during refinement and planning
Consolidate the three backlogs under a single coordinator who allocates work to keep the teams aligned

questions.explanation: A 31 percent adoption rate is the product telling the team that enthusiastic sponsor sign-off is not evidence of user value. Releasing a small slice to one branch office behind a flag is a low-risk way to reach real users without asking 200 adjusters to attend reviews; it converts a quarterly one-way rollout into a fortnightly learning loop and works within the sponsor's constraint instead of fighting it. The training video assumes the only problem is unfamiliarity - an untested hypothesis that costs money and, if the workflow is genuinely wrong, teaches people a tool they will still abandon. The post-rollout survey keeps feedback a quarter late and arrives after the money is spent, which is exactly the loop that produced this outcome. Personas validated by the sponsor deepen reliance on the proxy whose sign-off has already proven unreliable; documented assumptions are not a substitute for watching someone work.
questions.concept: Reaching real users with a small-batch release (feature flag, pilot site) instead of relying on proxy approval
questions.question: A supplier team delivers a claims portal to an insurer. The insurer's business sponsor attends every review and signs off enthusiastically, but the adjusters who will use the portal see it only at quarterly training rollouts; after the last rollout, 31 percent of adjusters used the new screens and the rest went back to the legacy system. The sponsor says adjusters cannot spare time for reviews, the delivery manager proposes a polished training video, and an analyst proposes a satisfaction survey after the next rollout. The tech lead notes the portal already supports feature flags. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Produce the polished training video first, since 31 percent adoption points to unfamiliarity with the new screens rather than to any mismatch between the portal and the way adjusters handle claims in their daily work.
Send the satisfaction survey to every adjuster after the next quarterly rollout and feed the scored results into the plan for the quarter that follows, so the next release reflects them.
Build detailed adjuster personas and journey-based acceptance criteria, and have the business sponsor validate them on the adjusters' behalf during the regular quarterly review sessions.

Propose to the sponsor that the next increment go live behind a feature flag to a single branch office, observe adjusters using it in their real work, and feed what is learned into the next iteration.

questions.explanation: The board is failing at its primary job: making work and its impediments understandable at a glance to everyone who needs the information. Redesigning the cards with the team so they show customer-facing meaning, item age, and blocker signals restores transparency at the source and lets the same walkthrough answer the questions being asked. Adding a status column to a weekly report creates a second, lagging source of truth and leaves the board just as unreadable. Having the product owner answer questions between walkthroughs handles each person individually while the board that caused the confusion stays opaque, and it makes one person the interpreter of information that should be legible to all. Limiting work in progress in the verification column is sound flow practice and the strongest alternative, but it addresses throughput rather than information design: cards would still read PERM-4471 and blocked items would still carry no marker.
questions.concept: Information radiator design: customer-facing card content, item age, blocker signals
questions.question: A Kanban team maintaining a municipal permit-renewal service uses a wall with columns Ready, Build, Verify, Deploy. Stakeholders in the weekly walkthrough keep asking "is my permit-fee change done yet?" even though the card sits plainly in Verify. Investigating, the agile practitioner finds that cards say things like "PERM-4471" and nothing else, and blocked cards carry no marker. What is the BEST response?
choices: Add a status column to the weekly stakeholder report so anyone can look up where a permit change stands without having to read the team's wall
Have the product owner answer stakeholder questions between walkthroughs, so the session itself stays focused on the team's flow and its blockers
Work with the team to make each card carry the customer-facing outcome, its age, and a visible blocker signal, then review the board with stakeholders
Put a work-in-progress limit on Verify so items clear that column faster and stakeholders no longer need to ask whether their own change is finished yet

questions.explanation: Both problems are classic Lean wastes — completed-but-undelivered inventory and over-processing — and both live outside the team's own boundary, so the effective move is to map the stream with the stakeholders who own the release gate and the documentation expectation, quantify the delay, and then pilot a smaller-batch alternative that preserves the control they care about. Shortening the specification helps a little but leaves the far larger waste, five weeks of finished value earning nothing, completely untouched. Increasing capacity produces more inventory feeding the same closed gate, which lengthens the delay between build and feedback rather than shortening it. Automating the deployment pipeline is the strongest rival and is worthwhile technical work, but the constraint here is the quarterly window, not build time; assembling a release in hours changes nothing while shipping stays quarterly, so the five weeks of undeployed inventory survive intact.
questions.concept: Value-stream mapping to expose inventory and over-processing waste
questions.question: A team building agronomy dashboards for a farm-supply cooperative consistently meets its iteration goals, yet features reach growers roughly five weeks after they are marked done because deployment is restricted to a quarterly-aligned release window. The team also writes a twelve-page design specification for every story; when the practitioner asked, no one downstream could recall opening one in the past year. Which action BEST addresses the waste?
choices: Trim the twelve-page design specification down to a one-page summary and leave the quarterly release window untouched, since release timing is decided outside the team and the specification is the only waste within its control.
Raise the team's iteration capacity so a larger set of finished features is ready the moment each quarterly window opens, turning the five-week wait into a larger amount of value shipped per release.
Automate the deployment pipeline so a release can be assembled in a few hours, then keep shipping on the existing quarterly cadence until the automation has proved itself reliable in production.

Map the value stream with the release and compliance stakeholders to expose the five weeks of undeployed inventory and the unread specifications, then pilot smaller, more frequent releases behind feature toggles.

questions.explanation: Three iterations at the observed 22-point average give roughly 66 points against 79 points of Must plus Should work, a shortfall of about 13 points against a fixed date. Making that gap visible and letting stakeholders choose which Should items drop is exactly how MoSCoW is meant to work: Should items are important but not release-critical, so they are the intended flex that protects a fixed date. Reporting the release as achievable by comparing capacity to Must-haves alone silently redefines the release the stakeholders were promised and hides the shortfall until it is too late to choose. Proposing that the team lift throughput to roughly 26 points per iteration asks for about a 20 percent increase with no basis beyond the arithmetic needed to make the plan fit, and the usual way teams meet such a number is by cutting quality. Removing Could-have items frees nothing, because the 27 points of Could-have work were never inside the 79 points being compared against capacity.
questions.concept: MoSCoW prioritization and capacity-based release forecasting
questions.question: Review the exhibit. The team plans a release when all Must and Should items are complete. Iteration capacity has averaged 22 points for the last four iterations, and three iterations remain before the fixed release date. During refinement the product owner asks whether the release is achievable. Based on the exhibit, what is the BEST response?
choices: Report that the release is achievable, because the roughly 66 points of capacity remaining across the three iterations comfortably exceed the 41 points of Must-have work still left in scope
Report that the release is achievable if the team lifts its pace to about 26 points per iteration over the three remaining iterations, and ask the team what that increase would take
Show stakeholders that 79 points of Must plus Should work exceeds the roughly 66 points of remaining capacity, and facilitate a decision on which Should items move out of this release
Recommend dropping the Could-have items from the release plan, since removing them frees up the capacity the team needs to finish all of the Must and Should work in scope

questions.explanation: A recurring failure with an instantly agreed cause is the classic signal that the team is treating a symptom; a brief structured why-chain, or a fishbone, surfaces the real mechanism — perhaps device-matrix gaps, late merges, or a build configuration that only differs at submission — so the countermeasure targets something that will actually stop the recurrence. Hardening "test more" into a definition-of-done item writes process around a cause nobody has identified, and the same crash can pass the new step. Recording the action and giving the test lead ownership turns a system problem into one person's job and removes the rest of the team from responsibility for how defects escape. A store-submission dry run each iteration is the strongest rival, since it would probably surface this class of crash earlier and may well be what the team chooses — but picking it now is still a countermeasure chosen before diagnosis, and it pays for a rehearsal rather than removing whatever makes the submission build different.
questions.concept: Root-cause analysis (Five Whys) versus symptom-level retrospective actions
questions.question: For the third iteration running, a mobile team's release slips because a crash surfaces during app-store submission. Ten minutes into the retrospective the group agrees the answer is "test more before we submit," writes it on a card, and wants to move to the next topic. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Facilitate a short root-cause exploration, asking why the crash escaped layer by layer, before the team agrees a countermeasure
Accept the card as written and add a pre-submission test pass to the definition of done, making the action binding
Record the action, give the test lead ownership, and review whether the crash rate improved at the next retrospective
Ask the team to add a store-submission dry run each iteration, so the crash surfaces before the release

questions.explanation: Empirical process control rests on transparency, frequent inspection of real outcomes, and adaptation of the next steps, which is precisely what releasing frequently, examining what metrics and users reveal, and adjusting the following slice provide. Reviewing a detailed plan monthly and revising the forecast on variance inspects conformance to the original baseline rather than what the product is doing, which is defined rather than empirical control. Demonstrating finished work each iteration is genuine inspection and the strongest alternative, but logging the feedback for the next release planning breaks the adapt half of the loop; evidence that arrives too late to change the next slice buys nothing. Choosing whatever the most experienced engineer recommends substitutes prediction and authority for observation, however good the track record.
questions.concept: Empiricism: transparency, inspection, adaptation
questions.question: Which team behavior best demonstrates empirical process control?
choices: Reviewing the detailed plan monthly and revising the forecast whenever reported variance exceeds the agreed threshold
Demonstrating finished work each iteration and logging the feedback for consideration at the next release planning
Releasing frequently, examining what the metrics and users reveal, and adjusting the next slice of work accordingly
Choosing the approach the most experienced engineer recommends, since those forecasts have held up on comparable work

questions.explanation: The deeper defect is not the missed topic but the conditions that kept an entire team silent about a known cause of an outage; working with the tester to understand the fear, then adjusting retrospective techniques — anonymous input, written rounds, explicit blameless framing — repairs those conditions so the team can surface this issue and the next one itself. Raising the incident personally, even without names, spends information that was shared in confidence and teaches everyone that private disclosures to the facilitator become public — it may fix this instance while making future candor less likely. Reporting the root cause to the product owner escalates outside the team before it has had any chance to inspect and adapt, and breaches the tester's trust entirely. Mandating an incident-review step adds process, but the same silence that suppressed the topic in the retrospective will operate inside a mandated review; process cannot substitute for safety.
questions.concept: Blameless retrospectives and safe surfacing of failure
questions.question: Shortly before a distributed team's retrospective, a tester privately messages the facilitator: a recent production outage traces back to a shortcut the whole team agreed to under deadline pressure, but nobody has mentioned it in any team forum. During the retrospective, the topic never comes up. Several responses are technically possible. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Raise the outage in the retrospective yourself without naming the tester, so the team can analyze the shortcut and agree what to do differently the next time it is under pressure
Take the root cause to the product owner and the operations group so the organization can decide how the shortcut should be handled and who repairs it
Add a standing incident review to the retrospective agenda so that every outage is examined as a matter of course and nothing of this kind is missed by the team again
Talk with the tester about what makes the topic feel unsafe to raise, and introduce retrospective techniques that let concerns surface without exposing individuals

questions.explanation: Bringing the whole team together to name the friction, reset working agreements, and institute cross-site pairing is best: the root cause is eroded trust and separate communication paths, and only restored human connection and shared norms reverse silo formation. Splitting into two independent teams with separate codebases makes the divide permanent and abandons the shared product before anyone has tried to repair it. Requiring an approving comment from a reviewer at the other location is the strongest alternative, because it does force daily cross-site contact over shared code; it loses on how that contact arrives, as an approval obligation attached to a merge gate, which slows flow and tends to harden the us-versus-them line rather than dissolve it. Handing the tone problem to the two site managers escalates a team-owned dynamic outside the team.
questions.concept: Distributed teams; silo formation and trust repair
questions.question: A platform team using a hybrid Scrum-Kanban approach is split between two countries. Code-review comments have turned curt, defects are logged with notes like "their side broke it," and each location has quietly started holding its own separate planning call. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Split the group into two independent teams with separate codebases and backlogs, so each location can deliver on its own without depending on people at the other site it no longer trusts
Require every code review to carry an approving comment from a reviewer at the other location, so the two sites are put back into daily contact over the code they share
Bring the whole team together to surface the friction openly, rebuild shared working agreements, and establish routine cross-site pairing so people collaborate across locations daily
Take the curt review comments and the defect notes to the two site managers and ask each of them to address the tone with their own members, since local leaders know their people best

questions.explanation: The correct labeling is coaching, then mentoring, then training: the questions-only session is coaching because the practitioner draws the answers out of the tester rather than supplying them; the principal engineer sharing her own experience and advice is mentoring because it passes on wisdom from someone who has already walked that path; the two-day toolset class is training because it imparts a defined skill through structured instruction. Labeling the questions-only session as mentoring is wrong because withholding advice and drawing out the other person's own answers is precisely what distinguishes coaching from mentoring. Labeling it facilitation is wrong because facilitation is neutral guidance of a group's process toward a group outcome, not a one-on-one development conversation about an individual's career. Placing training second is wrong because the engineer's story-and-advice conversation has no curriculum, no defined skill objective, and no instructor role — it is classic mentoring.
questions.concept: Coaching vs mentoring vs training distinctions
questions.question: A tester wants to grow into a test-automation role.
