First, the agile practitioner holds a session using only open-ended questions so the tester discovers their own development plan. Later, a principal engineer shares stories and advice from her own career path into automation. Finally, the tester attends a two-day hands-on class covering a specific automation toolset. Which option correctly labels the three interventions in order?
choices: Mentoring, then coaching, then training
Facilitation, then mentoring, then training
Coaching, then mentoring, then training
Coaching, then training, then mentoring

questions.explanation: The real defect is not that co-located people talk — informal conversation is healthy — it is that decisions are invisible to part of the team until too late. Having the whole team revise its own working agreements addresses that systemic gap, gives remote members a voice in the fix, and produces norms the team owns and will actually follow. Telling the headquarters group to stop hallway decisions prescribes a behavior ban the practitioner cannot enforce and would suppress useful collaboration instead of making its outputs transparent. Routing decisions through a team lead inserts a bottleneck and a hierarchy that agile teams work to avoid, and does nothing to include remote members in the reasoning. Splitting into location-based sub-teams institutionalizes the silo rather than healing it, trading one coordination problem for a larger cross-team one.
questions.concept: Working agreements and decision transparency in distributed teams
questions.question: A hospital-scheduling product team is split across three time zones. Developers co-located at headquarters routinely settle design questions in hallway conversations; teammates in the other two locations discover the outcomes days later through ticket comments and have started quietly disengaging from planning discussions. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Facilitate a whole-team session to revise the working agreements, focusing on how decisions are made visible and when remote colleagues must be included before a decision is final
Ask the headquarters group to settle design questions only in scheduled team meetings, so nothing important is decided while colleagues in the other two locations are outside working hours
Route design decisions through the team lead for approval and announcement, so all three locations learn of every outcome at the same time from one reliable source
Propose reorganizing into location-based sub-teams that each own their own components, so every site can decide inside its own boundary without waiting on the other two

questions.explanation: Facilitating the two developers toward shared success criteria and a small, low-cost experiment converts a positional argument into collaborative problem solving and lets evidence, not status, decide - the essence of the collaborating conflict mode; meeting face to face also lets the practitioner reset the working agreement that disagreements stay about the work rather than the person. Handing the dispute to the architect for a binding ruling settles the immediate question but teaches the team that conflicts get outsourced rather than worked through, weakening ownership. Defaulting to the senior developer's view resolves the argument by rank rather than merit and signals that the quieter voice does not matter, which is what has already silenced the rest of the team. Deferring to the retrospective delays resolution of a live technical blocker and lets the interpersonal damage compound in the meantime.
questions.concept: Collaborating conflict mode and evidence-based resolution of technical disputes
questions.question: On an XP team, two developers are clashing in the team chat over whether integration tests for a payment feature should mock the third-party gateway or call its sandbox environment. The thread has turned personal, and other members have gone quiet. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Bring the two developers together to agree on the outcome both need and the criteria for judging it, then let them try each approach on a thin slice of the feature
Ask the technical architect to read the thread and rule on mocking versus the sandbox, so the team has an authoritative answer from outside the pair and the stalled payment work restarts
Adopt the senior developer's approach, since he holds the deepest payment-domain context, and ask the other developer to follow that convention for this feature and raise it again after release
Let the thread cool for a day and put the integration-test question on the retrospective agenda, so both developers can settle the question calmly in the team's own regular improvement forum

questions.explanation: Having the team author its own working agreements and definition of done, and delegating the how-to-meet-the-goal decision while staying available for support, both transfer genuine decision authority to the team with a safety net — the servant-leader pattern that grows self-organization. Assigning tasks by strongest skill keeps the practitioner in the director's chair and optimizes short-term efficiency at the cost of learning and shared ownership. Reviewing and approving every technical decision is a command-and-control approval loop that signals distrust and trains the team to wait for permission. Rotating a task-coordinator role still centralizes assignment in a single person each week — it changes who directs, not whether the team self-organizes.
questions.concept: delegation and servant leadership
questions.question: A newly formed hybrid delivery team asks its agile practitioner to "just tell us who does what." The practitioner wants to build the team's ability to self-organize instead of creating dependence. Which TWO actions would BEST develop the team's self-organization? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Assign initial tasks based on each member's strongest skill so the first iterations run efficiently
Ask the team to create its own working agreements and definition of done
Review and approve the team's technical decisions until members demonstrate they are ready for autonomy
Delegate to the team the decision of how to organize its work to meet the iteration goal, while remaining available for support
Rotate a "task coordinator" role weekly so each member takes a turn making the assignments

questions.explanation: Providing stronger direction now while agreeing an explicit path for progressive delegation matches leadership style to the team's real maturity in this context — individually senior people can still be a low-maturity team in a new domain — and makes empowerment a deliberate trajectory rather than a slogan. Refusing direction in the name of self-organization is abdication: the team has asked for help it genuinely needs, and dogmatic hands-off leadership at low context maturity produces thrash and erodes trust in the practitioner. Owning the decisions until delivery stabilizes, with only a vague reassessment later, is open-ended command that gives the team neither reason nor mechanism to grow, and 'a few months' quietly becomes permanent. Embedding an architect who owns the decisions moves authority further from the team and creates a dependency that outlives the ramp-up.
questions.concept: Situational leadership and the delegation continuum
questions.question: A streaming-media company forms a new team to build a rights-management service. Every member is individually senior, but all are new to the domain, the codebase, and each other. In week two the team tells the agile practitioner: 'Just set the technical direction for us until we find our feet.' What is the BEST response?
choices: Give more direction now — explicit decision guardrails and frequent check-ins — with an agreed, visible plan to hand decisions back as the team's context grows
Decline to set direction and hold the team to its own technical choices, since a self-organizing team builds ownership fastest when the coach resists filling the gap
Take the technical decisions personally through the first few releases, then revisit the arrangement once delivery has stabilized and the domain is better understood
Ask the enterprise architecture group to embed an architect who owns the technical decisions for this domain until the team has learned enough context

questions.explanation: A wide estimate spread is information: it says the item hides distinct questions, not that the team estimates poorly. Decomposing along those exact uncertainty lines — document uploads, history depth, adjuster-note visibility — turns one ambiguous item into several small ones the team can size confidently, and lets the understood slices deliver value in the release while the murky ones stay visible in the backlog. Recording the number the product owner wants destroys the signal, buries risk inside a committed item, and treats estimation as negotiation rather than shared understanding; a mid-iteration checkpoint discovers the problem after capacity is already spent. Writing a full approved requirements document is a big-batch analysis detour that delays feedback and answers questions a thin working slice would answer faster and more reliably. Spiking the entire area for an iteration over-invests in research when only a few specific unknowns exist; a targeted timeboxed investigation of one unknown may be warranted, but wholesale exploration trades delivery for study without proportionate risk reduction.
questions.concept: Estimate divergence as a decomposition trigger
questions.question: A product team building a self-service claims portal for a regional insurer has a backlog top slice containing an item titled "Claims history." During refinement, developers ask whether it covers uploaded documents, how far back history goes, and whether adjuster notes are visible to policyholders. Estimates from the team range from 3 to 21 points. The product owner, who has already promised the item for the next release, says, "Just estimate it at 13 and we'll figure the details out mid-iteration." What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Record the estimate the product owner expects and add a mid-iteration checkpoint where the team settles the open questions as work proceeds
Facilitate splitting the item along the specific unknowns the team raised so the team can size and pull the parts that are understood
Keep the item out of the next release until a written requirements specification for claims history has been reviewed and approved
Have the team spend a full iteration spiking the whole claims-history area so that the estimate which follows rests on real knowledge

questions.explanation: Encouraging pairing on the constrained skill attacks the bottleneck at its source: XP's pair programming and collective ownership deliberately spread scarce knowledge, turning a single-point specialist into a team of generalizing specialists so the queue dissolves over time. Asking the hardware engineer to write a detailed guide to the abstraction layer is the most reasonable alternative, since documentation does transfer some knowledge — but it spends the constrained person's time producing a static artifact, and firmware knowledge of this kind lives in judgment and debugging habits a document cannot carry. Spreading the abstraction-layer stories evenly across iterations levels his queue on paper while leaving every one of those stories dependent on the same person. Splitting into a hardware team and an application team with an agreed interface replaces a skill bottleneck with a permanent handoff boundary, hardening the silo the team should be dissolving.
questions.concept: Generalizing specialists and collective ownership
questions.question: An XP team building firmware for smart utility meters has one engineer who understands the hardware-abstraction layer; most stories queue behind him while other members wait for that portion of the work. A team member proposes splitting into a hardware team and an application team with a documented interface between them. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Encourage pairing on hardware-abstraction stories so ownership spreads and members grow into generalizing specialists
Have the hardware engineer write a detailed guide to the abstraction layer so other members can start those stories without him
Sequence the backlog so hardware-abstraction stories are spread evenly across iterations and his queue stays level
Support the split into two component teams with an agreed interface, so neither group has to wait on the other

questions.explanation: Reading the increments, items enter Ready at 13, 14, 15 and 16 per week while Done rises by exactly 4 every week, so demand is running roughly three to four times actual capacity and the Ready band has swollen to 56 items. At 4 completions per week, a newly accepted request waits about 14 weeks before work even starts — which is precisely why stakeholders experience long waits while the team feels busy and productive. The first conversation therefore belongs with the product owner and customer about intake rate, prioritization, and what will explicitly not be done. Calling the thin Test band a rigour problem misreads a cumulative flow diagram: band width shows how many items are sitting in that stage, not how well they are tested, and a narrow, stable band means work is not piling up there. Claiming throughput has collapsed contradicts the data, which shows Done rising by a steady 4 items every single week. Naming Build the bottleneck ignores that the Build band is flat at 6 items week over week — nothing is accumulating there — while the Ready band grows by roughly a dozen items each week; adding developers to Build would only pull faster from a queue whose real problem is that far more work is accepted than can ever be finished.
questions.concept: Interpreting cumulative flow diagram band widths; arrival rate versus throughput
questions.question: Review the exhibit. A team using a Kanban system has held a stable completion rate for weeks, but stakeholders complain that requests "take forever." The team's own view is that they are busy and productive. Based on the cumulative flow diagram data, what should the agile practitioner raise with the team first?
choices: The Test band is unusually thin for the volume being built, so the team should add a manual regression pass before Done to be sure quality is not slipping as items move through
Throughput has collapsed over the last few weeks, so the first conversation should be about why fewer items are now reaching Done each week and what has changed inside the team's own delivery process
Requests are being accepted three to four times faster than the team completes them, so the first conversation should be about intake and prioritization with the customer, not about team speed
Build is the constraint because its band is wider than Test, so the team should move its testers onto development tasks until the Build queue drains and that band narrows back to its earlier width

questions.explanation: Novel work with no organizational precedent and contradictory expert opinion sits in the complex domain, where cause and effect are only visible in hindsight — so the honest move is probe–sense–respond: run cheap, safe-to-fail experiments with clear measures and let the viable approach emerge, then plan incrementally on evidence. Hiring a consultancy to distill best practice is the seductive wrong answer: expert analysis works in the complicated domain, where good practice exists, but here even the experts contradict each other — analysis cannot substitute for probes when no one has the answer. Padding a nine-month plan with buffers dresses up a guess as a commitment; buffers absorb estimation variance, not fundamental uncertainty about whether the approach works at all. Delivering the requested plan while privately treating it as disposable might feel pragmatic, but it sacrifices transparency, sets false expectations with leadership, and destroys trust the moment reality diverges from the document.
questions.concept: Cynefin — complex versus complicated domain responses; safe-to-fail probes
questions.question: A city services department funds technology work through detailed annual plans. Leadership asks a team to commit to a nine-month plan, including guaranteed accuracy levels, for a machine-learning feature that auto-classifies resident service requests — something the organization has never attempted and about which vendors give flatly contradictory advice. Several responses are technically possible. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Engage a specialist consultancy to analyze industry best practice and produce the detailed, defensible nine-month plan that leadership is asking the team for
Propose funding a short series of safe-to-fail, time-boxed experiments with explicit success measures, committing to further plans only as results come in
Produce the nine-month plan with generous contingency buffers on every estimate and accuracy target, so the unpredictability is absorbed inside it
Give leadership the nine-month plan it wants while treating it internally as a draft the team revises as the classifier work proceeds

questions.explanation: Value is measured by outcomes, not by completed outputs; the practitioner's job is to make the gap between shipped scope and unchanged downtime transparent to the people who can act on it, and to let that evidence drive the next prioritization decision. Starting the next feature set because scope was accepted mistakes output completion for value delivery, and adding downtime to a monthly reporting pack surfaces the problem long after the capacity is committed. Redesigning the alerts so they are harder to dismiss prescribes a cause — inattentive growers — before anyone has asked why the alerts are ignored; they may be noisy, mistimed, or unrelated to what actually stops a harvester. Running a retrospective on the miss is the strongest alternative and genuine inspection, but it keeps the finding inside the team and waits for the next scheduled review, while the sponsor is asking for the next feature set today.
questions.concept: Outcomes versus outputs
questions.question: A product team at an agricultural equipment maker has an outcome goal of "cut unplanned harvester downtime for our pilot farms." Six iterations in, the team has delivered every planned feature — a telematics dashboard, an alerts feed, and a maintenance scheduler — and burn-up shows scope complete and on budget. Telemetry from the pilot farms, however, shows downtime unchanged; alerts are being dismissed unread. The sponsor is pleased with the delivery report and asks the team to start the next feature set. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Start the next feature set as requested and add downtime to the monthly reporting pack, so the outcome is tracked from now on without giving up delivery momentum
Bring the downtime and alert-dismissal data to the sponsor and team, and use it to re-examine whether the next feature set is still the highest-value work
Redesign the alerts so they are harder to dismiss and release the change before raising the downtime question with the sponsor and the pilot farms
Run a retrospective on why the delivered features missed the outcome and bring the team's conclusions to the sponsor at the next scheduled review

questions.explanation: A community of practice is the voluntary cross-team group organized around a discipline such as testing, UX, or architecture, and it exists to exchange techniques and lessons — its defining trait is spanning team boundaries by choice rather than by assignment. Mob programming is whole-team collaboration on a single work item at one station, so knowledge transfers in real time as the work is done — its defining trait is that creation and sharing happen simultaneously, which is why it does not describe the voluntary cross-team group. An information radiator is the large visible display — board, burn-down chart, build monitor — that pushes status to anyone passing by; its defining trait is passive broadcast requiring no request, which distinguishes it from every mechanism that depends on people working together. Team-member rotation moves a person, and therefore tacit context, into another team for a period; its defining trait is that the human being is the transfer medium across the organizational boundary, unlike a display or a meeting series.
questions.concept: Distinguishing knowledge-sharing mechanisms and the boundaries they cross
questions.question: Match each knowledge-sharing mechanism (1-4) to the description (A-D) that best captures what distinguishes it.
pairs: Community of practice
A voluntary group spanning team boundaries, united by a shared discipline, that meets to exchange techniques and lessons
Mob programming
The whole team works together on one work item at a single station, so knowledge spreads at the moment it is created
Information radiator
A large, highly visible display that broadcasts current status so anyone can absorb information without asking for it
Team-member rotation
An individual temporarily embeds with another team, carrying context and skills across an organizational boundary in person

questions.explanation: Hypothesis-driven development requires three things visible in the first practice: an explicit assumption, a pre-defined measure with a threshold that could refute it, and the smallest build sufficient to generate that evidence. Shipping each feature fully built and then reading support tickets and store reviews gathers evidence only after the full cost is sunk, and ticket volume is a noisy proxy for the question the team meant to ask. Iterating internal prototypes until a steering group picks the most promising validates against stakeholder preference, so the riskiest assumption is never put to a user. Testing two variants of every release is the strongest alternative because it observes real behavior, but with no measure or threshold agreed beforehand the team can read any difference as a win and has no rule for abandoning the change.
questions.concept: Validated learning and falsifiable hypotheses (Lean Startup)
questions.question: Four teams each describe how they "experiment." Which team's practice best reflects hypothesis-driven development?
choices: A team that states the assumption a feature depends on, defines the metric and threshold that would confirm or refute it, and releases the smallest slice able to produce that measurement
A team that ships each feature fully built, then reads support tickets and store reviews afterward to judge whether the change was worth making before it starts the next one
A team that builds successive internal prototypes, reviews each one against the steering group's expectations, and then develops in full the version those stakeholders judge most promising
A team that tests two variants of every release and keeps whichever one performs better, without stating beforehand which measure and threshold would decide the question

questions.explanation: Dividing average WIP by average throughput (30 items divided by 5 items per week) gives about six weeks of average lead time, and the honest conclusion is that a two-week promise requires changing one of the two inputs — usually cutting WIP, which is faster and cheaper than raising throughput. The three-week answer invents a "half finished" adjustment the relationship does not make: every item in the system counts as WIP no matter how far along it is, and partial progress is already reflected in the observed completion rate; the appeal to overtime then makes matters worse, since fatigue typically lowers throughput and raises defects. Rejecting Little's Law because item sizes vary misunderstands it: it is an averages relationship over a stable system, not a per-item prediction, and the team's two months of stability is exactly the condition that makes it usable. Concluding that the team should raise its velocity commitment confuses a delivery-rate observation with a promise about points; declaring a higher number changes no queue, and points are not the throughput unit in the calculation.
questions.concept: Practical application of Little's Law to forecast lead time
questions.question: A support-tooling team's board shows an average of 30 items in progress across all active columns, and the team completes an average of 5 items per week. Both figures have been stable for two months. A product manager has just promised a stakeholder that a newly requested item, entered at the back of the queue, will be delivered "in about two weeks." Applying Little's Law to this system, what is the most defensible conclusion?
choices: Average lead time is roughly three weeks, because items in progress are on average half finished, so the promise is achievable with overtime.
Little's Law cannot be applied here, because the items differ widely in size and complexity, so the average tells nothing useful.
Average lead time is roughly six weeks, so the two-week promise is unrealistic unless work in progress is cut or throughput rises.
Average lead time is roughly six weeks, so the promise can be met by raising committed velocity to fifteen points per week.

questions.explanation: Naming the work as complex and proposing short, funded probes matches the situation: when neither customer response nor the technology can be known in advance, cause and effect become clear only in retrospect, so the sensible approach is probe, sense, and respond. Reworking the plan into rolling waves is the strongest alternative and is real tailoring, since later phases stay coarse, but it still commits six fully sequenced months to a service no customer has used, so the first learning arrives after the largest bet is placed. A market study and feasibility review try to analyze away uncertainty that only customer contact resolves. Accepting the plan as the funding baseline and handling discoveries through a change control board turns every inevitable learning into administrative friction.
questions.concept: Cynefin complex domain — probe-sense-respond over predictive planning
questions.question: A retailer's leadership wants to launch an AI-driven personal-styling service. No competitor offers anything similar, customer response is unknown, and the recommendation technology is unproven. The sponsor asks the agile practitioner to validate a fully sequenced two-year plan produced by an external consultancy before funding is approved. What is the BEST response?
choices: Ask the consultancy to rework the plan into rolling waves, with the first six months fully sequenced and later phases left coarse until customer demand is better understood
Recommend a market study and a technical feasibility review to resolve the unknowns first, so the two-year plan can be validated against evidence before funding is released
Explain that unknowable customer response and unproven technology place this work in the complex domain, and propose funding a series of short probes whose results steer the roadmap
Accept the plan as the funding baseline and manage the unknowns through a change-control board, so the remaining scope can be reprioritized whenever customer feedback or technical findings arrive

questions.explanation: Both winning actions move a wait into the flow itself. Bringing security into refinement with an agreed checklist converts a 9-day handoff queue into work done alongside development, which is the essence of building quality in rather than inspecting it in later. Agreeing acceptance criteria with the venue operations representative before items are pulled removes the mid-stream clarification wait at its source and is direct customer engagement rather than a ticketing exchange. Increasing batch size is the classic false economy: fewer, larger reviews lengthen lead time, enlarge the change under review, and delay feedback and value. Raising WIP limits hides the wait behind busyness — with throughput unchanged, more work in progress mathematically lengthens average cycle time, so the queue grows rather than shrinks. A blocked swimlane and a weekly management report make waiting visible and push it up the hierarchy, but visibility is not elimination; the same 14 days of queue remain in the value stream.
questions.concept: Value-stream mapping and removing downstream handoff queues
questions.question: A value-stream map for a museum's ticketing platform shows an end-to-end lead time of 34 days against 6 days of touch time. The two largest waits are a 9-day queue for a shared security review performed after code is complete, and a 5-day wait for the venue operations representative to clarify acceptance criteria on items the team has already started. The team is weighing several responses. Which TWO actions best attack the mapped waste? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Increase batch size so that fewer, larger releases need to pass through the shared security review queue each month.
Invite a security engineer into the team's refinement and reviews and agree a shared checklist so most items clear security inside the flow instead of in a downstream queue.
Raise the team's WIP limits so members can start other items while security reviews and acceptance clarifications are pending.
Hold a short weekly session with the venue operations representative to work through concrete examples and agree acceptance criteria before items are pulled.
Add a blocked swimlane to the board and send management a weekly report listing every item that is waiting and for how long.

questions.explanation: Every option here is technically defensible, which is what makes the situation hard. Flow efficiency of 14 percent says the dominant problem is waiting, not working — so adding people or buying time attacks the wrong variable until the wait states are understood. Having the team map its own wait states and pick one change targeted at the specialist bottleneck empowers the team, addresses the actual constraint, and produces a measurement that makes the contractor and date questions answerable with evidence rather than opinion; pairing also spreads tariff knowledge as a by-product of delivering real items. Adding three contractors loads the constraint further — the only people who can onboard them are the specialists already blocking the queue, so short-term throughput falls exactly when it can least afford to. Asking the specialists to write documentation is well intentioned but takes the bottleneck resource off value work to produce an artifact nobody has yet needed, and documentation transfers tacit knowledge far more slowly than working together on live items. Proposing a date change may ultimately be necessary, and the climbing defect rate and ten-hour days are genuine sustainability warnings, but taking that to the sponsor before the team has attempted the improvement and re-measured means negotiating from assumption rather than evidence.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency, specialist bottlenecks, and Brooks's Law under deadline pressure
questions.question: A team of nine is six weeks from a contractual go-live for a border-clearance customs portal. Flow efficiency measured on the last 40 items is 14 percent — items sit in wait states most of their life. Two developers hold specialized knowledge of the tariff-calculation engine and every tariff item queues behind them. The team has been working ten-hour days for a month, defect escape rate is climbing, and the sponsor has just asked whether adding three contractors would help. The two specialists are the only people who could onboard the contractors. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Facilitate a session where the team maps the wait states in the tariff work and chooses one change to relieve the specialist constraint — such as pairing on the highest-value tariff items — then re-measures flow efficiency before deciding anything about contractors

Recommend the sponsor bring the three contractors on immediately, since six weeks is enough time for them to become productive on the non-tariff portions of the portal, which frees the two specialists to work the tariff queue without further interruption from other stories

Ask the two specialists to spend the whole of the coming iteration writing detailed documentation of the tariff-calculation engine, so their knowledge spreads to the other seven developers and the queue standing behind them dissolves well before the go-live crunch arrives

Propose to the sponsor that the contractual go-live be renegotiated now, since 14 percent flow efficiency, a climbing defect escape rate, and a month of ten-hour days together make the date unachievable without lasting damage to the team and the portal

questions.explanation: Using powerful open questions while deliberately withholding one's own answers is the signature of coaching: the developer holds both the goal and the raw material for the answer, and the practitioner's role is to unlock her thinking rather than populate it. Mentoring is the near-miss — a mentor intentionally shares personal experience and advice, which is exactly what this practitioner chose not to do, because a borrowed career template would substitute his answer for hers. Training closes a defined, transferable skill gap through structured instruction; "how do I want to balance coding and leading" is an ambiguous personal question, not a curriculum item. Facilitation is the tempting label, since the practitioner does supply no content, but facilitation is a content-neutral process role serving a group's own outcome, and this is a one-on-one developmental conversation aimed at growing one person's judgment.
questions.concept: Coaching versus mentoring versus training
questions.question: A capable developer on a Scrum team tells the agile practitioner she wants to grow into a lead role but cannot decide how to balance hands-on coding with guiding others. The practitioner responds almost entirely with open questions — "What does leading look like to you? What have you already tried?" — and deliberately avoids offering his own career path as the model. Which support approach is the practitioner applying, and why does it fit?
choices: Mentoring, because a developer weighing a lead role needs a more experienced person's path as her template
Coaching, because the developer owns the goal and needs help discovering her own answer rather than receiving one
Training, because moving into a lead role is a defined skill gap best closed by structured instruction
Facilitating, because the practitioner is guiding the shape of the conversation rather than supplying any of the content

questions.explanation: Live, universally visible board access and openly displayed flow metrics are the two genuine transparency moves. A live board acts as an information radiator: anyone can pull the current truth at any moment, blockers surface as they arise, and Friday surprises disappear. Visible aging and cycle-time metrics, inspected at a regular cadence, turn raw visibility into inspection and adaptation — the team sees trouble while it is still cheap to fix. Restricting board visibility to the team hides information and treats stakeholders as adversaries, worsening the surprise problem. Daily status emails are pushed, fragmentary reports that add overhead and go stale on arrival — an information refrigerator, not a radiator. Confining delay discussions to a private leads-only channel deliberately delays bad news, which is the opposite of transparency and erodes the trust the team is trying to rebuild.
questions.concept: Transparency and information radiators
questions.question: A cross-functional platform team's work status lives inside a tracking tool licensed only to the two team leads, and stakeholders learn of delays from a slide deck compiled every Friday. Stakeholders complain of surprises, and team members say they discover blockers late. Which TWO actions would MOST improve transparency? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Restrict board visibility to the delivery team only, so external pressure cannot distort estimates
Give the whole team and stakeholders live access to a board showing work states, WIP, and flagged blockers
Add a daily written status email from each team member to the project sponsor
Move all discussion of delays to a private leads-only channel until root causes are confirmed
Display flow metrics such as aging work items and cycle time where everyone can see them, and review them with the team at a regular cadence

questions.explanation: Stating a falsifiable hypothesis with a success threshold before building, shipping the smallest thing that can generate the signal, and letting measured behavior drive the decision is the build-measure-learn loop in its proper order — the metric is chosen in advance so the team cannot rationalize any outcome as success. Building the complete module first and surveying afterward maximizes investment before any learning and measures opinion rather than behavior. A three-month market study replaces cheap direct evidence with slow secondhand analysis and delays contact with real users. Logging the assumption in a risk register acknowledges uncertainty but does nothing to reduce it — the team still builds on an untested belief.
questions.concept: Hypothesis-driven development and MVP (Lean Startup build-measure-learn)
questions.question: An agri-tech product team believes vineyard managers will take protective action if they receive satellite-based frost alerts, but the belief has never been tested. Which action best applies hypothesis-driven development to this situation?
choices: Build out the complete alerting module across every planned channel first, then survey the vineyard managers about their overall satisfaction once the frost season ends, so their feedback reflects the finished experience rather than an early fragment of the design.

Commission a three-month study of regional frost-protection practices and alert tolerances among growers before the feature enters the roadmap, so the team commits engineering effort only once the underlying market behavior has been documented and properly understood.

Record the belief as an open assumption in the product risk register with a named owner and a scheduled review date, and continue building the alerting feature as planned while that risk is monitored and reported back at every iteration review.

State a falsifiable hypothesis with a predefined signal — for example, 'at least 30% of pilot vineyards act within 24 hours of an alert' — release a minimal alert to a pilot group, and decide next steps from the measured behavior.

questions.explanation: Active engagement means creating channels through which real customers influence real decisions, and for a large external population that means both a small, rotating group who touch pre-release builds and telemetry showing how the shipped API is actually used — stated preference plus revealed behavior, both flowing into the backlog. A published quarterly roadmap with a comment mailbox is one-way broadcast with an optional, slow reply path, and nobody sees software before it ships. Account-manager sentiment summaries are a second-hand monthly filter that strips out the specifics an engineering team needs to act on. An annual survey ranked by respondent count and contract value is the strongest rival, since it does reach all forty companies and ties priority to commercial weight, but once a year is far slower than the delivery cadence, it records what integrators say rather than what their code does, and majority-plus-revenue ranking buries the small integrator whose failing integration exposes a real defect.
questions.concept: Customer engagement mechanisms for large external user populations
questions.question: A platform team maintains a public API consumed by roughly 40 external integrator companies in six countries. None of them can attend the team's iteration reviews, and their engineers are not employees of the team's organization. Which approach best represents actively engaging customers in this situation?
choices: Recruit a rotating design-partner group of integrators for pre-release previews, and instrument released endpoints so real usage feeds backlog decisions.
Publish a quarterly roadmap on the developer portal and invite integrators to send comments to a shared mailbox the product owner reviews each month.
Have account managers summarize integrator sentiment in the monthly steering report so the team hears one consolidated customer voice rather than forty.
Run an annual survey of all forty integrators and rank the backlog by the capabilities the largest number of respondents ask for, weighted by contract value.

questions.explanation: A blameless analysis of the actual failures examines the whole release system — runbook clarity, environment drift, test coverage, schedule pressure — with the people closest to it, which is the only way to identify the real causes; framing it as blameless keeps the release engineer supplying information instead of defending himself. Adding a mandatory sign-off gate prescribes a control before anyone knows what went wrong, adding delay while possibly addressing nothing. Reassigning release duties treats a person as the cause on the strength of hallway rumor and leaves any systemic weakness ready to defeat the next engineer. Asking leadership to fund a pipeline rebuild commits money to a guessed solution; no analysis has yet shown the pipeline is where the failures originate.
questions.concept: Blameless root-cause analysis of systemic failure
questions.question: A Lean software team supporting warehouse robotics has had three failed releases in five weeks. Managers and some teammates have begun blaming the release engineer, and the practitioner overhears 'if he would just follow the runbook.' What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Introduce a mandatory sign-off gate before every release, so that a second engineer catches configuration mistakes before anything reaches the robots
Move release duties to another engineer until the failures stop, giving the team steadier footing before its next attempt
Fund a rebuild of the deployment pipeline first, since three failures in five weeks point squarely at the tooling itself
Facilitate a blameless analysis of the three failed releases with the people involved, tracing causes across the whole release system

questions.explanation: "Quickly" is a vague quality attribute with no measurable threshold, so the team cannot write acceptance criteria or verify completion — the story is not testable until a target such as "loads within 2 seconds under normal load" is agreed. The story is not lacking independence, because the team explicitly agreed it can be built on its own. It is not lacking negotiability; nothing in the story fixes a solution, and its details remain open to conversation. It is not lacking value, because the benefit to the warehouse supervisor is stated directly in the story itself.
questions.concept: INVEST criteria (Testable) and acceptance criteria
questions.question: During refinement, an agile team examines this user story: "As a warehouse supervisor, I want the picking screen to load quickly so that I can start orders without waiting." The team agrees the story is small and independent and clearly helps the supervisor, but no one can describe how they would confirm the story is complete. Which INVEST attribute does the story most clearly lack?
choices: Independent
Negotiable
Testable
Valuable

questions.explanation: Ready policies are contextual agreements the team owns, not immutable gates; the agile move is to make the exception explicit as a defined class of service, decided transparently with the team and the requester, so patient-safety work flows into the free WIP slot immediately while the policy stays honest and the next urgent case has a visible precedent. Holding the item until the next refinement session applies process rigidly to an active safety issue and delays value with no offsetting benefit. Pulling it unilaterally gets the fix moving but leaves the agreement silently violated and the exception invisible, so the board no longer reflects how work is actually pulled and every future judgment call is re-litigated from scratch. Logging the missing criteria as technical debt and coding while someone else writes them keeps the policy nominally intact but separates the shared-understanding conversation from the work, which is precisely what acceptance criteria exist to prevent — and on a scheduling defect, ambiguity about correct behavior is the main risk.
questions.concept: Contextual readiness agreements and classes of service
questions.question: A Kanban team maintaining a hospital scheduling system has an explicit ready policy requiring every item to have acceptance criteria, a named requester, and a test data source before it is pulled. A cardiology clinic reports that a defect is causing double-booked appointments today. The item has no acceptance criteria and no test data source. The team's WIP limit has one free slot. What is the BEST response?
choices: Hold the cardiology defect until the next refinement session so that it meets the same ready policy every other item on the team board must already satisfy before it is pulled into work
Pull the defect on your own authority right now, since patient safety plainly outweighs a team process agreement, and let the rest of the team know about the exception at standup
Ask the cardiology requester to write the acceptance criteria while a developer starts on the fix, so that the ready policy is satisfied by the time the item reaches the test column
Convene the team and the cardiology requester briefly, agree this expedite class of service bypasses the standard ready policy, pull the item, and make that class of service explicit on the board

questions.explanation: Acknowledging the analyst's candor and addressing the mocking remark in the moment, anchored to the team's working agreement, repairs psychological safety at the exact point it was damaged; the silent room is watching whether honesty is punished or protected. Turning the discussion to how the shortcut went undetected for two days is excellent systems thinking and belongs in the conversation, but taken first it steps past the put-down, and the team learns that ridicule is tolerated as long as the analysis continues. Giving the senior adjuster private feedback afterward spares him correction in front of the team, yet the people who went quiet saw the remark and need to see it answered where it happened. Converting the admission into an improvement action honors what she surfaced while leaving the interpersonal damage untouched.
questions.concept: Psychological safety in retrospectives
questions.question: During a Kanban team's retrospective at a claims-processing center, a junior analyst admits that a shortcut she took caused two days of rework. A senior adjuster laughs and says, "That's what happens when we hire rookies," and the room goes quiet. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Turn the discussion to how the shortcut went undetected for two days, so the room focuses on the system rather than the person
Thank the analyst for her openness, restate the team's working agreement on respectful dialogue, and address the mocking remark in the moment
Give the senior adjuster private feedback afterward, since correcting him before the team would harden his position and cost his cooperation
Convert the analyst's admission into an improvement action on the board, so her openness produces a change in how shortcuts get caught

questions.explanation: Little's Law in its practical flow form gives average cycle time as work in progress divided by throughput: 18 items divided by 6 items per week is about 3 weeks, and 9 divided by 6 is about 1.5 weeks. That relationship is precisely why WIP limits are the cheapest lever on lead time -- less work in the system finishes faster without anyone working harder. The claim that only extra people can shorten cycle time inverts the relationship, since adding people typically increases work in progress and, with the constraint untouched, lengthens cycle time rather than shortening it. The 0.33-week figure divides throughput by work in progress instead of the other way round, and then also reverses the direction of the effect of lowering WIP. The demand for ten iterations of velocity history confuses estimate-based iteration forecasting with flow-based forecasting; Little's Law needs only work in progress and throughput, and the caveat that actually matters is system stability -- balanced arrivals and departures and reasonably consistent item sizes -- which this team already has.
questions.concept: Practical application of Little's Law to cycle time and WIP limits
questions.question: A support-tooling team's board holds an average of 18 items in progress and the team completes an average of 6 items per week; arrivals and departures have been roughly balanced for two months. The product owner asks how long a newly pulled item is likely to take end to end, and what would happen if the team brought average work in progress down to about 9 by tightening its WIP limits, with throughput holding near 6 per week. Which response applies the data correctly?
choices: About 3 weeks today, and reducing work in progress to 9 will not shorten cycle time unless the team adds people.
About 0.33 weeks today, and reducing work in progress to 9 would roughly double the average cycle time.
About 3 weeks today, and if throughput holds near 6 items per week, average cycle time would fall to roughly 1.5 weeks.
Cycle time cannot be estimated from these figures; the team would first need at least ten iterations of velocity history.

questions.explanation: Completions are steady at four per week (12, 16, 20, 24), while commitments rise by 12, then 14, then 16 per week. Work committed but not yet done therefore climbs from 28 items in Week 1 to 58 in Week 4, with the gap widening by 8, then 10, then 12 items each week while only four leave the system. With throughput flat and work in the system rising, Little's Law says average lead time must lengthen, which is exactly what widening bands depict. Throughput is not declining: the Done column increases by a constant four every week, so that reading contradicts the numbers. Testing is not the fastest-growing band in proportional terms — the Test band goes from 4 to 10 items (2.5x) while the Development band goes from 8 to 24 (3x), so naming testing as the constraint is the familiar-looking trap rather than what these figures show. Calling flow stable confuses a steady completion rate with a healthy system; a constant Done slope alongside an accelerating intake line is the classic signature of a queue building up in front of the team.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation (WIP growth, throughput, lead time)
questions.question: A team reviews the cumulative flow data in the exhibit during a flow review. Based on the exhibit, which statement is BEST supported?
choices: Throughput is falling, because each successive week on the diagram shows fewer items crossing the line into Done than the week before it.
Intake is outpacing completion, so the amount of work in the system and the average lead time are both rising even though four items finish every week.
Testing is the binding constraint, because the Test band on the diagram widens faster in proportional terms than any other band over the same span of weeks.
Flow is stable and no intervention is warranted, because the Done line climbs by the same steady amount in every week the diagram covers.

questions.explanation: Making the invisible visible is the core move here. Waits scribbled in card corners are real process states the board pretends do not exist; turning them into explicit columns lets everyone see where time is actually consumed, and only then can the team make an informed decision about limiting concurrent work. Facilitating this with the team rather than imposing it keeps ownership of the process where it belongs. Assigning a coordinator to chase dependencies adds a role and a workaround while leaving the board — and therefore the shared understanding — just as misleading as before. Logging waits in a private spreadsheet for a month delays action, hides the information from the wall where the team makes daily decisions, and separates measurement from the workflow it should inform. Imposing a one-item-per-person limit is a prescription issued before the problem is understood; the constraint is external hand-offs, not personal multitasking, so an arbitrary limit would simply idle people without shortening the waits.
questions.concept: Making queues and wait states explicit on a visual board
questions.question: A Kanban team maintaining an insurance claims platform has a wall showing To Do, In Progress, and Done. Cycle time has drifted from 4 days to 11 days over two months. Standing at the wall, the practitioner sees 14 cards in In Progress across six people, and several cards have handwritten notes like "waiting on actuarial" or "needs legal sign-off" scribbled in the corner. Team members say they "pick up something else while they wait." What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Facilitate the team in redrawing the board so the hidden wait states become explicit columns, then discuss limits on work in progress
Assign a coordinator to chase the actuarial and legal approvals every day so that cards stop waiting, leaving the wall itself unchanged
Ask the team to log the reason and duration of every wait in a spreadsheet for a month, then analyze that data before altering the wall
Set a firm limit of one card per person straight away so the fourteen in progress fall, then check cycle time again in two weeks

questions.explanation: Pausing the session and facilitating a conversation that surfaces the interests beneath each stated position is collaborative conflict resolution: it treats the disagreement as useful information, keeps ownership of the technical decision with the team, and repairs the psychological safety the silent mobbers just lost. Ruling in favor of the existing test conventions is forcing — it ends the noise but leaves the losing party uncommitted and teaches the team that the practitioner settles technical questions. Asking the principal architect for a binding call escalates a conflict the team is capable of resolving and outsources a decision that belongs to the people doing the work. Timeboxing a spike against the carrier sandbox is the strongest alternative, and evidence may well settle the stub-versus-integrate question later, but it answers the technical dispute while ignoring the interpersonal one: the mob went quiet over conduct, not over missing data.
questions.concept: Conflict management modes — collaborating versus forcing, escalating, and avoiding
questions.question: During a mob-programming session at a logistics startup, two senior developers begin arguing loudly about whether to stub or fully integrate a carrier's rate API in their tests. The other mobbers go quiet and start checking their phones. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Pause the session and facilitate a conversation in which each developer explains the interests behind their stated position
Settle it by applying the team's existing test conventions, so the session resumes at once on a defensible basis
Ask the principal architect for a binding call on stubbing versus live integration so the two developers can move on
Timebox a spike that tries both approaches against the carrier's sandbox and let the measured results settle the design question

questions.explanation: Pairing and mobbing on real pipeline stories transfers knowledge while the release work still gets done, converting a single point of failure into shared capability at the cost of a modest, visible slowdown — a trade the practitioner should help the product owner see as risk reduction rather than lost velocity. Ring-fencing her and deferring the handover to two weeks of documentation maximizes short-term output but bets the product on documents written under time pressure; deep tacit knowledge of a complex pipeline does not survive that compression, and any schedule slip erases the window entirely. Trying to block her transfer overrides her career choice, likely poisons her remaining engagement, and merely postpones the same problem. A contractor producing a reference manual creates a second temporary knowledge holder and a static artifact — the team that must live with the pipeline still learns nothing by doing.
questions.concept: Reducing single-person dependency through pairing and mobbing
questions.question: On a media-analytics team, one data engineer is the only person who understands the ingestion pipeline that feeds every customer dashboard. She is over-allocated, sits on the critical path of the current release, and has just announced she is transferring to another division in two months. The product owner wants her "ring-fenced" on delivery work until the release ships. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Agree to the ring-fencing for now, then reserve her final two weeks for written handover documentation so the release date holds and the pipeline knowledge is captured before she goes
Ask the division head to delay her transfer until a replacement has been recruited and trained by her, so the team is never left without pipeline expertise at all
Work with the product owner and the team to have her pair or mob with teammates on pipeline stories during the release, accepting some short-term slowdown to spread the knowledge
Bring in a contractor to shadow her through the release and produce a technical reference for the ingestion pipeline, so the knowledge survives her move next quarter

questions.explanation: A wide estimate spread is a signal of unresolved uncertainty, and refinement exists to reduce it: decomposing the item into a small investigation and a thin, independently valuable slice converts a guess into work the team can size and finish, while keeping a high-priority need moving. Averaging the high and low numbers hides the disagreement instead of resolving it and commits the team to work it does not yet understand. Recording the larger figure so the size itself covers the unknown is the most defensible alternative, since padding for genuine uncertainty is a recognized practice, but it prices the risk rather than removing it — nobody yet knows whether the tide feed can be polled or arrives as a daily file, and if it is a daily file the design of tide-aware allocation changes in a way no estimate absorbs. Moving the item to the bottom until the integration architecture is settled delays a high-value need and treats a days-long unknown as a blocker.
questions.concept: Decomposition and estimation of high-uncertainty backlog items
questions.question: During a backlog refinement conversation for a marine port berth-scheduling product, the team sizes the item "Tide-aware berth allocation." Three members estimate it as small; three estimate it as several times larger, saying nobody knows whether the harbour authority's tide feed can be polled in near real time or is published only as a daily file. The item is currently third from the top of the backlog and the product owner wants it in the next iteration. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Average the high and low estimates and let the team pull the item into the next iteration, on the view that the spread will even out and the team can adjust once work is underway
Record the larger estimate as the team's number so that the unknown tide feed is covered by the size itself, and keep the item where it sits in the backlog for the coming iteration planning session
Facilitate splitting the item — for example, a timeboxed investigation of the tide feed plus a first slice covering a single berth type — and have the team re-estimate the resulting pieces
Move the item to the bottom of the backlog until the integration architecture for external data feeds is decided, so that the team sizes the work only after that unknown has been settled

questions.explanation: The defect is not the arithmetic of the measure but its use as a comparative target, which is already distorting behavior; the effective move is to understand the decision the executive is trying to make, present the evidence of harm in terms he cares about — quality and avoided value-bearing work — and offer measures that answer that decision without inviting gaming. A joint retrospective agreeing shared reference stories and a no-splitting rule preserves the ranking and therefore the incentive to inflate; it only makes the comparison look credible while the distortion continues. Reporting completed story counts alongside escaped defects is the strongest rival, because the defect tally is a real improvement on points alone, but the monthly ranking survives, so teams shrink stories instead of growing them and risky work still costs a team its position. Adding a hardening step and a defect-containment item treats the escaped defects as the whole problem, buying late inspection while the incentive that produced them stands.
questions.concept: Metric misuse, gaming, and selecting outcome and flow measures
questions.question: Across a museum-ticketing program, a vice president has begun circulating a monthly slide ranking six teams by velocity, describing it as "friendly competition." Two iterations later the practitioner observes that reference stories have quietly grown in point value, teams are splitting cards into smaller pieces without changing scope, escaped defects reported by box-office staff have risen, and one team has declined to take on a risky payment-gateway migration this quarter. Several corrective actions are technically available. What is the BEST response?
choices: Bring the pattern to a joint retrospective with all six teams and agree a shared reference-story set plus a rule against splitting stories without a scope change, so the monthly ranking compares like with like and the point inflation disappears from the reported numbers.

Ask the six teams to report completed story counts and a running escaped-defect tally instead of points, so the vice president keeps the monthly comparison he asked for while the ranked measure can no longer be inflated by quietly growing reference stories.

Meet the vice president to learn what decision the ranking is meant to inform, show the observed side effects — point inflation, rising escaped defects, the avoided migration — and propose per-team trends of throughput, cycle time, escaped defects, and delivered outcomes instead.

Add a hardening step and a defect-containment item to each team's flow and report the resulting escaped-defect trend to the vice president each month, since the problems reaching box-office staff are the concrete customer harm the program has to stop before anything else.

questions.explanation: A voluntary community of practice with protected time creates the peer-to-peer channel where practitioners across the nine teams exchange approaches, and rotating facilitation keeps ownership with the members rather than with management. Making solved problems visible through demos, lightning talks, and a team-curated pattern library turns each team's solutions into discoverable assets, directly preventing the silent duplication of retry mechanisms described. A central board that must approve every integration design substitutes control for sharing — it creates a bottleneck and teaches teams to seek permission rather than to learn from each other. Monthly lessons-learned reports push documents up the hierarchy, where the engineers who need the knowledge will never read them. Consolidating integration work into one specialist team concentrates the knowledge into a silo and a queue — the opposite of spreading capability across nine teams.
questions.concept: Communities of practice and making knowledge visible across teams
questions.question: An organization has grown from three to nine agile teams in a year. Teams keep independently re-solving the same integration problems — three teams built near-identical retry mechanisms last quarter without knowing about each other's work. Which TWO actions would best promote knowledge sharing across the teams? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Charter a voluntary community of practice on integration engineering, with protected time to participate and a rotating facilitator
Stand up a central architecture board that must review and approve every team's integration design before build begins
Require each team to submit a monthly lessons-learned report to management for consolidation
Consolidate all integration work into a single specialist team so the knowledge lives in one place
Make solved problems visible through internal demos and lightning talks, backed by a searchable pattern library the teams curate themselves

questions.explanation: Bringing the operations chief, the team, and the account manager together to re-plan the remaining two iterations around the new highest-value need is the only option that welcomes late change, puts customer collaboration ahead of contract negotiation, and keeps the trade-offs transparent — the contract conversation can then follow a shared understanding rather than lead it. Invoking the change-control clause and issuing a costed impact assessment first is legitimate and genuinely defensible under a fixed-scope agreement; it loses on sequencing, because leading with contract mechanics freezes the relationship exactly when the customer's definition of value has moved. Absorbing the redirection through longer days hides the true cost of the change, breaks sustainable pace, and denies the client the information needed to choose. Delivering the contracted warehouse workflow and opening a follow-on engagement honors the letter of the agreement while knowingly shipping software the client has just told you is worth less.
questions.concept: Late-breaking change under contract; customer collaboration and transparency of trade-offs
questions.question: A distributed team spread across three time zones, using XP practices under a fixed-scope contract, is two iterations from a contractual release. The client's newly appointed operations chief demands that the workflow module be reoriented from warehouse staff to third-party delivery drivers. The team lead wants to invoke the contract's change-control clause first; the account manager suggests quietly absorbing the work through weekend overtime; some developers propose shipping the release as committed and treating the driver work as a follow-on project. What is the BEST response for the agile practitioner?
choices: Invoke the contract's change-control clause and complete a formal impact assessment with the account manager, so the operations chief receives a costed written change request before any re-slicing of the release scope is discussed

Absorb the redirection inside the two remaining iterations by having the team work longer days, so the committed release date holds and the newly appointed operations chief sees the delivery group as responsive

Convene the operations chief, the team, and the account manager to revisit the release goal, re-slice the remaining scope around the highest-value driver workflows, and make the cost and trade-offs of the change transparent

Deliver the committed warehouse workflow exactly as contracted and open a separate follow-on engagement for the driver work, since the fixed-scope agreement already defines what this release owes the client

questions.explanation: Shared vision comes from participation: when teams and stakeholders build the elevator statement together and explicitly connect each team's outcomes to it, they own the purpose and can use it daily to guide trade-offs. Emailing an approved statement is one-way broadcast — being informed of a vision is not the same as sharing it, and unread or unowned words change no behavior. Posting finalized objectives on dashboards adds visibility to decisions made elsewhere, which is transparency of output without the engagement that creates commitment. Walking team leads through the vision individually filters it through intermediaries, fragments the message across five retellings, and still leaves the people doing the work outside its creation.
questions.concept: Co-created vision artifacts and stakeholder alignment versus broadcast communication
questions.question: An agile practitioner wants a product group of five teams to genuinely share one vision and purpose, not merely be informed of it. Which action MOST effectively achieves this?
choices: Emailing the sponsor's approved vision statement to all five teams with a request that every member read it carefully before the next planning event begins
Publishing leadership's finalized quarterly objectives on each team's dashboard so the shared direction stays visible to everyone during their daily work
Facilitating a working session where teams and key stakeholders shape the product's elevator statement and agree how each team's outcomes ladder up to it
Meeting each team lead one-on-one to walk through the vision and answer their questions, so every lead can then brief their own team consistently

questions.explanation: Making decision authority explicit and handing over the branching decision with agreed guardrails is best: naming the decision and the authority level transfers ownership deliberately, matches the delegation to the team's current capability, and keeps coaching support in place so the team grows without being abandoned. Continuing to decide until the team "matures" is circular — a team cannot build decision-making capability while someone else makes its decisions. Abruptly refusing to answer swings from directing straight to abdication, a laissez-faire anti-pattern that creates anxiety and stalls work instead of building competence. Asking the manager to appoint a technical lead merely relocates the bottleneck to a new single decider and signals that the team still is not trusted to decide anything collectively.
questions.concept: Delegation levels and explicit decision boundaries
questions.question: A Scrum team formed eight months ago still brings nearly every technical choice — most recently its branching strategy — to the agile practitioner and waits for a ruling before proceeding. The practitioner realizes that by always answering, they have become the team's decision bottleneck. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Keep making the technical calls for now and step back gradually as the team demonstrates more maturity, so delivery quality holds steady while the team's judgment is still forming
Make decision authority explicit — for example, using delegation levels agreed with the team — and hand the branching decision to the team with clear guardrails, staying available to coach
Step back completely from technical questions so the team has no choice but to decide, and let it settle the branching strategy on its own without further input from the practitioner
Ask the engineering manager to appoint a technical lead who will own choices such as the branching strategy, so the practitioner is no longer the person every technical question reaches

questions.explanation: Pairing and mobbing on real tooling work transfers the tacit knowledge — judgment, workarounds, failure smells — that never makes it into a manual, and it validates the transfer immediately because teammates are doing the work with her while she can still correct them; lightweight notes then capture just enough explicit knowledge. Adding narrated video walkthroughs to the manual still transfers only what she can articulate, and none of it is tested until a crisis hits with her unreachable. A contractor with comparable tooling experience covers the four months but builds no internal capability, so the team is exactly as dependent when the contract ends. Finishing the manual and running a half-day handover workshop is the strongest alternative, since live questions do get answered — but a single session in her final week compresses years of judgment into hours, and people cannot ask the questions they do not yet know they have.
questions.concept: Tacit knowledge transfer through pairing and mobbing
questions.question: In a game studio's localization pipeline, only one engineer understands the custom string-extraction tooling, and she begins a four-month leave in three weeks. Her manager asks her to spend the remaining time writing a comprehensive operations manual. What should the agile practitioner recommend instead?
choices: Have her record narrated video walkthroughs of each tool alongside the manual, so teammates can replay the detail while she is away
Bring in a contractor with comparable localization tooling experience to cover the pipeline for the four months she is gone
Have her spend the remaining weeks pairing and mobbing with teammates on live tooling work, capturing lightweight notes as they go
Have her finish the manual and run a half-day handover workshop in her final week, so open questions get answered live

questions.explanation: The choice to surface the assumptions behind the extremes without attribution and then re-estimate anonymously is best because a 4-to-26-week spread is a signal of unshared information, not of irreducible risk. Two estimators almost certainly know something the others do not, such as segmentation testing or outage windows on a live control network. Wide band Delphi converges by circulating rationale while withholding identity, so a low estimator can revise upward without appearing to have been overruled. Averaging after trimming the extremes deletes exactly the data most likely to carry the new information, and produces a number whose reasoning no participant actually holds. Having the high estimators explain themselves by name and then talking to agreement in the room destroys the anonymity that keeps seniority, tenure, and talking volume out of the estimate; it yields stated agreement rather than independently held judgment. Publishing the raw round-one band treats information asymmetry as if it were uncertainty; ranges are a legitimate Delphi output, but after convergence rather than instead of it, and a band this wide gives the committee nothing to decide on.
questions.concept: Wide band Delphi: anonymous re-estimation after moderated discussion of outlier rationale
questions.question: At a regional water utility, a program team must size a SCADA control-system upgrade before the capital funding committee meets. An agile coach facilitates a wide band Delphi round with seven estimators: three field engineers, two integration developers, a cybersecurity specialist, and the operations lead. Round one returns anonymous estimates of 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 22, and 26 weeks. The coach has 90 minutes of the session left. What should the coach do next?
choices: Drop the highest and lowest estimates as outliers and average the remaining five, giving the committee a converged number within the session
Ask the two high estimators to present their reasoning by name, then keep discussing until everyone in the room agrees on a single number
Have the assumptions driving the extreme estimates presented and debated without attributing them to individuals, then collect a second anonymous round of estimates
Report round one as a 4-to-26-week three-point range to the committee, since the spread is itself an honest expression of the remaining uncertainty

questions.explanation: Coaching fits because her gap is not knowledge but clarity and commitment: coaching uses powerful questions to help someone generate their own answers, which is exactly what she asked for and what builds durable ownership of both the technical approach and her growth path. Additional training addresses a skill deficit she does not have — she already understands the techniques, so more instruction misdiagnoses the problem. Mentoring, which transfers the mentor's own experience as advice, contradicts her explicit request to think it through herself and risks fitting her situation to someone else's story. Handing her a step-by-step plan is directive management, which solves today's task while removing the reflective work that would let her handle the next ambiguous situation on her own.
questions.concept: Coaching versus mentoring versus training distinctions
questions.question: A developer on a Lean software team recently completed formal instruction in test automation and understands the techniques well. She tells the agile practitioner she feels stuck deciding how to apply automation in her team's legacy context and what her own growth path should be — and that she wants help thinking it through herself rather than being handed answers. Which development approach best fits this situation?
choices: Coaching — using open questions to help her surface her own options, choose her path, and commit to next steps
Additional training — enrolling her in an advanced automation course to close the remaining skill gap
Mentoring — sharing how the practitioner handled similar legacy-code and career decisions and advising her to follow the same route
Direction — giving her a concrete step-by-step plan for automating the legacy suite

questions.explanation: A team-owned information radiator makes the state of work continuously and passively visible, so stakeholders pull the information themselves whenever they need it — interruptions drop, trust rises, and no single person becomes the keeper of status. A daily consolidated email is push-based reporting: it goes stale between sends, adds overhead for the coordinator, and keeps the team dependent on a gatekeeper. A weekly status meeting delays information by up to a week and adds a ceremony where a glance at a radiator would do. Routing every inquiry through the coordinator protects developers from interruptions but deepens the bottleneck and hides information behind one person instead of opening it up.
questions.concept: Information radiators and pull-based status visibility
questions.question: A cross-functional team at a logistics company is building an internal shipment-tracking tool. Work status lives in a spreadsheet that only the team coordinator updates, and stakeholders regularly email individual developers asking where their requests stand. The interruptions are slowing the team down. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Have the coordinator publish a status summary each morning so stakeholders read it instead of writing
Help the team create a visible, team-maintained information radiator that anyone can view at any time
Hold a weekly status meeting where stakeholders can ask the team about their outstanding requests
Agree a working agreement that stakeholder questions go only to the coordinator, protecting focus time

questions.explanation: Facilitating the team to revisit its working agreements and adopt structured techniques treats the problem as a team-system issue and builds durable psychological safety: the team itself owns how it collaborates, and formats like silent writing neutralize the advantage of the loudest voice. Privately reprimanding the two engineers addresses symptoms through authority rather than helping the team improve its own interactions, and may create resentment without changing the meeting dynamics.
