Speaking on the specialist's behalf makes the practitioner a permanent intermediary, keeps her voiceless in the room, and signals that safety depends on a protector. Restricting spikes to senior engineers and adding a downstream review step institutionalizes the silo the team was formed to remove, delaying accessibility feedback to the most expensive point.
questions.concept: Psychological safety, working agreements, and inclusive facilitation in cross-functional teams
questions.question: A game studio team recently added an accessibility specialist so it could cover a new compliance goal without external handoffs. During fast-moving design spike discussions, two senior engineers repeatedly talk over her, and the agile practitioner notices she has stopped contributing entirely, though her review comments afterward keep catching significant issues. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Speak with the two senior engineers privately about the effect their interruptions are having, and ask them to leave room for the specialist in the next design discussion they join.
Facilitate a session where the team revisits its working agreements and adopts techniques such as silent writing and round-robin input so every specialty is heard during design.
Collect the specialist's concerns before each spike and raise them on her behalf in the discussion, so her findings reach the design while it can still be changed.
Move accessibility input to a formal review step after each spike, since her written comments already catch the significant issues, and keep the spikes to the engineers.

questions.explanation: Agreeing the acceptance tests with the requester before coding removes the ambiguity about intent that forces re-consultation later, and automating them on every build compresses the feedback loop from nine days to minutes while the developer still holds the context. A triage board and weekly defect review organize rework rather than prevent it, and a weekly cadence still leaves days of delay in the loop. A specialist code review before merge shifts inspection slightly earlier but preserves the hand-off and still checks code whose intent was interpreted alone. A coverage target verifies that code does what its author wrote, not what the requester meant, and publishing the percentage invites the number to be optimized instead of the outcome.
questions.concept: Acceptance test-driven development and shortening the intent-to-verification loop
questions.question: A hybrid team maintaining a museum ticketing engine writes acceptance tests only after a story is coded, then passes the story to a separate verification group that executes them as a gate. Defects found at that gate take an average of nine days to resolve because the developer has moved on and the original requester must be re-consulted about intent. Which change best embodies building quality in through early feedback?
choices: Introduce a weekly joint defect review with the verification group and a severity triage board, so rework from the gate is sequenced by business impact.
Have a verification specialist review each story's code before it is merged, so defects surface days earlier in the same pipeline that already finds them.
Write the acceptance tests collaboratively with the requester before coding begins, and run them automatically on every build so failures surface within minutes.
Raise automated unit-test coverage above ninety percent and report the figure at each iteration review, since untested code is what lets the gate find so many defects.

questions.explanation: The three items that complete an end-to-end transaction form a minimum viable increment: the smallest release that delivers real value and generates validated learning about whether renters and owners will transact at all. Facilitating that conversation reframes the disagreement from scope negotiation to learning value, and it keeps marketing as a partner rather than an obstacle. Ordering by effort optimizes for the appearance of progress; the cheapest items may be the referral program and saved searches, which are worthless if nobody can complete a rental. Building everything and hiding it behind a flag incurs the full cost and delay of a big-bang release while forgoing every early feedback signal, because the flag defers exposure, not investment. Splitting the eleven supporting items thinner is the strongest alternative and thinner slices are usually good practice, but it accepts that all fourteen must launch together and merely compresses them, so learning still waits behind ratings, saved searches and a referral program.
questions.concept: MVP definition and incremental release scope
questions.question: A team is preparing the first release of a peer-to-peer equipment rental marketplace. The backlog holds 14 items. The head of marketing insists all 14 must launch together to justify the campaign spend. During refinement, the team identifies that listing creation, search, and payment hold-and-release together let a renter complete one full transaction, while the remaining items are ratings, saved searches, a referral program, and similar enhancements. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Facilitate a conversation with the marketing lead and the team about releasing the smallest set that lets a real renter complete a transaction, and what would be learned from it
Sequence the 14 items by estimated effort so the cheapest complete first, protecting the launch date and giving marketing the largest possible count of finished capabilities
Build all 14 items and hold them behind a feature flag until the campaign date, so the team keeps delivering throughout while marketing still gets the single simultaneous reveal it wants
Ask the product owner to split the 11 supporting items into thinner slices so more of them fit before the campaign date without anything being dropped from the launch

questions.explanation: Several of these actions are technically possible, but the best first move is a private, data-informed coaching conversation with the manager: it assumes the good intent the manager actually has, uses objective flow evidence rather than accusation, protects team members who have explicitly signaled they do not feel safe being identified, and aims at the manager's behavior — the real system constraint — rather than at meeting logistics. Raising it in the retrospective sounds transparent, but with the manager present and members already masking their frustration, it risks a public blindside and suppressed candor rather than honest inspection. Barring the manager from the sync is directive, removes a symptom while leaving the command-and-control habit intact, and can damage a relationship the team depends on. Pushing the two members to confront the manager delegates the practitioner's coaching responsibility to the least-safe parties, who have just said they are not ready to do that.
questions.concept: Servant-leadership coaching of managers; micromanagement anti-pattern
questions.question: A line manager attends the daily sync of a flow-based team and routinely assigns the day's items to specific individuals. Throughput has been flat, the board shows aging items that nobody pulls, and two members privately tell the agile practitioner they feel like "ticket-takers" — but they ask the practitioner not to name them and continue telling the manager that everything is fine. The manager is well regarded and genuinely believes the assignments help. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Raise the assignment pattern in the next retrospective with the manager present, so the whole team can discuss its effect on flow and on the aging items that nobody is willing to pull
Ask the manager to step out of the daily sync so the team can pull its own work, offering a weekly flow summary in place of what the manager sees today
Coach the two members to take their concern to the manager directly, since the experience is theirs to describe and the practitioner would otherwise speak for colleagues who asked to stay anonymous
Meet the manager privately, share the flow data and its link to the assignment pattern, and explore how the manager could shift to setting outcomes while the team pulls its own work

questions.explanation: Coaching the team to pull its own work and helping members define their own pull policies builds the self-organization that Kanban depends on; the practitioner enables the behavior rather than becoming the replacement for the old supervisor. Assigning cards by strongest matching skill keeps the team dependent on an assigner, narrows cross-skilling, and simply substitutes one boss for another. Asking functional managers for daily assignment lists reintroduces external command-and-control and signals the team cannot be trusted to choose its own work. A fixed weekly rotation is push scheduling dressed up as fairness — it ignores actual flow and demand and still removes the team's ownership of how work gets done.
questions.concept: Self-organizing teams and pull systems
questions.question: A warehouse-automation team has just moved from supervisor-assigned work to a Kanban board. Every morning, team members line up at the facilitator's desk and ask which card each of them should take. The agile practitioner observes this pattern for the third day in a row. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Assign each card to the member whose skills match it most closely, so flow stays efficient while the team adjusts to the new board
Coach the team to pull work from the board themselves and facilitate a short session where they agree on simple pull policies together
Ask the functional managers to send a prioritized assignment list each morning until the team is ready to select its own work
Set up a fixed weekly rotation so every member knows in advance which cards are theirs and nobody needs to ask the facilitator

questions.explanation: Building a value case from measured benefits of increments already released, priced against actual cost per iteration, gives the sponsor a current, evidence-based comparison and treats funding as a recurring decision rather than a sunk commitment. Inviting the sponsor into the review adds direct observation of working functionality and a two-way conversation, which is far stronger evidence and better feedback than a curated summary. Deferring the decision until the whole roadmap ships denies the sponsor the very evidence that incremental delivery exists to produce, and asks for open-ended funding on faith. A detailed benefit forecast across all remaining roadmap items is speculation dressed as analysis; its precision will not survive the learning of the next quarter. Recomputing the original inception-era business case deliberately ignores everything the three releases have taught, anchoring the decision to assumptions that are now the least reliable information available.
questions.concept: Value-based decision-making and incremental funding using ROI evidence
questions.question: A team delivering a regional transit-fare platform has released three increments. The sponsor, who funds the work quarterly, asks for evidence that continued investment is justified before approving the next quarter, and notes that a competing internal project claims a stronger business case. The team has instrumentation on released increments and a rough cost-per-iteration figure. Which TWO actions best support value-based decision-making here? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Ask the sponsor to defer the funding decision until the full roadmap has been delivered and total benefits can be measured
Use the released increments' measured benefits and the known cost per iteration to build a transparent, current value case the sponsor can compare against the competing project
Have the product owner produce a detailed benefit forecast for all remaining roadmap items so the sponsor can see the full projected return
Invite the sponsor to the next review so they see working functionality and hear the team's evidence directly, rather than receiving a summary written for them
Recompute the original business case using the assumptions approved at project inception, since those were the basis for the funding commitment

questions.explanation: An information radiator broadcasts the current state of the work ambiently — large, always up to date, and understandable at a glance — so anyone can pull the answer to 'what is going on' the moment they wonder, which removes the need for status meetings. Tailored weekly emails are pushed snapshots that go stale within hours and create ongoing reporting work for the team. Logins plus filter training is an information refrigerator: the data exists, but stakeholders must expend effort to dig it out, so most never will. Circulating meeting recordings forces stakeholders to spend fifteen minutes listening for one fact and conveys nothing at a glance.
questions.concept: Information radiators versus pushed and refrigerated information
questions.question: Stakeholders of a Kanban maintenance team have requested twice-weekly status meetings because they 'never know what is going on.' Which response best applies the concept of an information radiator?
choices: Provide an always-current, prominently displayed board — physical or virtual — showing workflow states, blockers, and cycle-time trends that any stakeholder can glance at without asking anyone
Send each stakeholder a weekly status email tailored to the items they care about, so the information they want arrives on a predictable schedule without anyone calling a meeting
Give stakeholders accounts in the team's work-tracking tool, along with training on building the filtered views that will answer their own questions whenever a new one arises about the delivery work
Record the team's daily coordination session and circulate the link each morning, so that anyone wanting detail can watch exactly what the team discussed about the current work

questions.explanation: Little's Law relates average work in progress, average throughput, and average lead time: 24 items divided by 6 items per week is an average lead time of about 4 weeks, so at a steady 6 per week the work in progress consistent with a 3-week lead time is about 18 items, reached by capping starts and letting the system drain. Pushing throughput to 8 per week through extended hours would satisfy the arithmetic but breaks sustainable pace, and the gain evaporates or reverses through defects and burnout once the overtime stops. Re-slicing the same work into smaller reported units changes the counting, not the elapsed time a customer experiences, which is metric manipulation rather than system improvement. Starting more items raises work in progress, which by the same relationship lengthens lead time; high resource utilization and fast flow pull in opposite directions.
questions.concept: Applying Little's Law to WIP and lead time without gaming the metric
questions.question: A support-and-enhancement team runs a Kanban system. Over the last quarter it has averaged 24 items in progress and has finished an average of 6 items per week, and both figures have been stable. Stakeholders want average lead time reduced to roughly 3 weeks without adding people. Applying Little's Law, which action is most consistent with that goal?
choices: Ask the team to raise weekly throughput to 8 items by working extended hours until the in-progress work clears
Keep all 24 items in progress but re-estimate them in smaller units so that average item size, and therefore reported lead time, falls
Reduce and then hold the number of items in progress at about 18, protecting throughput while the system drains to that level
Start additional items so every specialist always has work in progress, raising utilization and therefore the number of items completed each week

questions.explanation: A radiator pushes current, honest information to anyone who walks by and provokes conversations without ceremony — the wall chart triggering an unprompted question about a two-day-old red build is exactly that mechanism working. A chart on the wall refreshed only when someone remembers before the weekly review has the right medium and the wrong currency; passers-by trust what they see, so stale data actively misinforms. The always-current dashboard is the strongest alternative, since it is truthful and managers do use it, but access granted on request is pull rather than push — an information refrigerator you must know about and ask to open — so incidental visibility is lost. The weekly emailed summary reaches only those who asked, arrives on a schedule rather than continuously, and its individual follow-up replies rebuild the very reporting burden a radiator exists to remove.
questions.concept: Information radiators versus pull-based and curated reporting
questions.question: Which of the following situations shows an information radiator functioning as intended?
choices: A build-health chart hangs on the team area wall but is refreshed only when someone remembers to do it before the weekly review, so passers-by are usually reading last week's state

An always-current build dashboard is available to anyone in the organization who requests viewer access from the tooling group, and several managers do open it on their own screens first thing most mornings
A hand-updated wall chart of build health prompts a passing product manager to ask the team about a failure that has been red for two days — without anyone preparing a report
A delivery lead emails a weekly build and flow summary to the stakeholders who asked for it, then answers each of their follow-up questions individually as the replies arrive over the week

questions.explanation: Explaining ideal time as a measure of size and then forecasting from the team's own four iterations of delivery history is best because it keeps the estimate and the schedule as two separate things joined by evidence. Ideal time strips out interruption so estimators can compare work honestly; the calendar answer then comes from what this team actually delivers, and a range communicates the confidence four data points genuinely support. Converting the 30 ideal days with a load factor drawn from the team's own interruption rate is the strongest rival and a widely used technique, but it substitutes a derived multiplier for throughput already measured, and one converted date presents an assumption as a promise. Re-estimating in calendar days that absorb meetings, on-call and production support embeds each person's disruption load into the size of the work, so items stop being comparable and the scale shifts whenever the environment does. Forecasting from the single strongest iteration cherry-picks the most favorable data point and hardens it into a firm commitment.
questions.concept: Ideal time as a sizing aid distinct from calendar duration and commitment
questions.question: At a wind-energy operator, a five-person analytics team sizes a turbine-telemetry migration at roughly 30 ideal days of work. The PMO director, encountering ideal time for the first time, asks whether that means the team will finish in six working days, and wants a date to put on the portfolio dashboard. The team has completed four iterations together and has records of what it delivered in each. How should the agile lead respond?
choices: Apply a load factor drawn from the team's own interruption rate to convert the 30 ideal days into elapsed working days, and give the director that single converted date so the portfolio dashboard carries one consistent number

Explain that ideal days describe size assuming uninterrupted focus, then forecast the finish date from the team's observed delivery rate over its four completed iterations, and give the director a date range rather than a point

Have the team re-estimate the migration in calendar days that already include meetings, on-call rotation, and production support, so the number reaching the portfolio dashboard needs no interpretation from the director or anyone reading it

Forecast from the strongest of the four completed iterations, since the migration is a single focused effort with no competing work, and give the director that date as the team's firm commitment on the portfolio dashboard

questions.explanation: Reframing around the value-stream map is best because 82% of elapsed time is non-value-adding wait, so cutting queue time delivers customer value far faster than squeezing more output from an already-stable team; it also uses transparency to redirect a well-meaning but harmful output target. Deflating estimates manufactures a bigger number without changing delivery at all — a textbook metric distortion that destroys the team's forecasting baseline. Adding a second team increases input into a system whose constraint is a shared environment and a monthly release window, so it grows the queue rather than the throughput. Stretch goals push more WIP into the same constrained system and turn the burndown into a pressure instrument instead of a feedback tool.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency and value-stream mapping versus velocity as an output target
questions.question: An agile team building a logistics pricing engine has been reporting velocity of 34, 36, and 35 points across three iterations. During a value-stream mapping workshop, the team discovers that a completed story waits an average of 11 days in a "ready for regression" queue before a shared test environment frees up, and another 4 days for a monthly release window. Total flow efficiency from commitment to production is 18%. A director praises the stable velocity and asks the practitioner to push for 40 points next iteration. What is the BEST response?
choices: Accept the director's target and have the team estimate stories more finely, so a larger number of points fits inside each iteration and the reported figure reaches 40 by next quarter
Show the director the value-stream map and flow efficiency, and reframe the improvement goal around shrinking the 15 days of queue and wait time rather than raising velocity
Add a second team working the same backlog in parallel, so combined velocity clears 40 points while the shared test environment continues operating as it does today
Set a stretch goal in each iteration and track completion of the stretch items on the burndown chart, so the team feels steady visible pressure to lift its delivery rate

questions.explanation: The manifesto value means working with the customer as a partner to maximize value as understanding evolves, rather than using the original agreement as a shield. Jointly re-prioritizing the remaining work treats the change as new information and keeps the customer inside the decision. Holding the business unit to the approved scope until a formal change order clears puts the contract mechanism ahead of the relationship and delays value without adding understanding. Delivering the agreed features first and funding the changes as a follow-on engagement is orderly and would be defensible with an external supplier, but with an internal business unit it manufactures a second funding cycle and knowingly builds features the customer has already said matter less. Recording the requests in a variation log for the next stage gate documents the conversation instead of having it, while the team keeps producing the old scope in the meantime.
questions.concept: Agile Manifesto values applied to scope change
questions.question: Midway through an initiative, an internal business unit wants to change several features that were agreed at the start. Which action best reflects the Agile Manifesto value of 'customer collaboration over contract negotiation'?
choices: Hold the business unit to the approved scope until a formal change order clears the governance process
Deliver the agreed features first and treat the requested changes as a separately funded follow-on engagement
Invite the business unit to jointly re-prioritize the remaining work around what now delivers the most value
Record the requested changes in a variation log and review them together at the initiative's next stage gate

questions.explanation: The interruptions are a symptom; the disease is that the board hides reality. A three-column board collapses several distinct stages into one bucket, so eleven simultaneous items and multi-week blockages look identical to healthy progress. Making the real stages, the blocked state, and a work-in-progress limit visible lets both the team and stakeholders see status without asking, and the limit attacks the aging that caused the questions in the first place. Producing a weekly spreadsheet adds a parallel reporting artifact that duplicates the board, ages between issues, and leaves the underlying flow problem untouched. Adding start dates and an aging counter is the strongest alternative and real flow practice — it would make the three-week items impossible to miss — but it measures aging without limiting the starting that causes it, and the supplier blockage and the missing stages stay invisible. Routing stakeholders to named developers keeps information in private conversations rather than on display, and makes each developer a bottleneck for their own status.
questions.concept: Board design: real workflow stages, explicit blocked state, WIP limits
questions.question: An agricultural equipment maker's firmware team uses a kanban board with columns To Do, In Progress, and Done. Stakeholders keep interrupting the team to ask when specific items will land. Reviewing the board, the practitioner sees eleven items in In Progress across six developers, several sitting untouched for over three weeks, and no visible marker for items blocked on a hardware supplier. The engineering manager suggests adding a weekly status spreadsheet distributed to stakeholders. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Build the weekly status spreadsheet the manager suggested and publish it every Friday, so stakeholders receive one predictable update rather than interrupting developers item by item
Facilitate a session where the team maps how work actually flows, splits In Progress into the real stages, marks blocked items explicitly, and agrees a work-in-progress limit
Add a start date and an aging counter to every card so the three-week-old items stand out, and review the oldest card first in each daily coordination meeting
Give each stakeholder a named developer as a standing contact for status questions, so the interruptions land with one person and the rest of the team keeps working

questions.explanation: Transparency is non-negotiable when leadership is deciding on distorted data, but how it is restored matters: visualizing all the work and partnering with the delivery manager on how it is framed gives the committee honest information while answering the manager's real fear, misinterpretation, with context rather than concealment. Making the rework visible on the team's board while leaving the committee's report untouched is the strongest distractor, since local visibility is a genuine gain and it respects the manager, but the committee keeps deciding on numbers the practitioner knows are wrong, for a period the manager alone controls. Presenting the data at the review without telling the delivery manager first is transparent, but it undercuts a colleague publicly before any attempt to solve the problem together, and invites the very micromanagement the manager fears. Working the queue down before widening the metrics leaves leadership knowingly misinformed while the picture is polished.
questions.concept: Courageous transparency when metrics hide bad news
questions.question: While preparing flow data for a steering-committee review, an agile practitioner on a Lean delivery team discovers that the lead-time metrics leadership sees exclude a steadily growing queue of defect rework. Customers are waiting longer, but the reported trend looks healthy. The delivery manager asks the practitioner to leave the metrics as they are, warning that showing the rework "will trigger micromanagement from above." What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Add the rework queue to the team's board so it is visible locally, and leave the committee's lead-time report as it stands until the delivery manager is ready to explain it
Make the rework visible on the board and in the flow metrics, and work with the delivery manager on presenting the fuller picture with context the committee can act on
Present the rework data at the steering-committee review without telling the delivery manager first, so the numbers reach the people whose decisions depend on them
Propose that the team work the rework queue down over the next two iterations and widen the reported metrics once the number is small enough to explain calmly

questions.explanation: Practical Little's Law gives average cycle time as work in process divided by throughput: 6 items divided by 3 items per week is roughly 2 weeks. Because the average already exceeds one week, and individual items vary around that average, a one-week commitment is indefensible without lowering work in process or raising throughput. Saying the promise holds if the item is expedited is the strongest rival, since an expedited class of service really can beat the average, but it keeps the promise by displacing other work and lengthening everyone else's wait, which is a policy exception rather than a statement about the current system. The half-week figure inverts the relationship by dividing throughput by work in process, which would absurdly imply that piling on more concurrent work makes items finish sooner. Quoting the fastest item from the ten weeks presents a best case as typical; the defensible answer is the average with its variability named.
questions.concept: Practical Little's Law applied to a delivery commitment
questions.question: A support-tooling team limits work in process to 6 items and completes an average of 3 items per week, measured consistently over 10 weeks with arrivals and departures roughly in balance. The product owner wants to promise a requester that a newly pulled item will be finished within one week. Using practical Little's Law against the team's current system, what is the most defensible statement the team can make?
choices: Average cycle time is about 2 weeks, so the promise holds only if this item is expedited ahead of everything already in process
Average cycle time is about 2 weeks, so a one-week promise is not supported unless work in process is reduced or throughput increases
Average cycle time is about half a week, because six items in process shared across three completions a week is roughly two days
These figures give an average, not a commitment, so the team should quote the fastest item it finished during the ten weeks it measured

questions.explanation: Situational leadership matches the leader's mix of direction and support to each team's current competence and commitment: a seasoned, self-managing team earns broad delegation, while an enthusiastic but inexperienced team needs more coaching and structure until its capability grows. Taking an identical hands-off stance with both effectively abandons the new team at exactly the stage it needs support — servant leadership means serving each team's actual needs, not treating them interchangeably. Directing both teams in detail micromanages the mature team, erodes the ownership it has built, and signals distrust. Rotating members between teams changes team composition to avoid adapting leadership style; it disrupts a well-functioning team and still leaves the practitioner without an answer for how to lead either group.
questions.concept: Situational leadership
questions.question: An agile practitioner supports two teams: a five-year-old platform team that reliably self-manages, and a team formed last month from recent hires that is enthusiastic but keeps stalling on unfamiliar technical decisions. Applying situational leadership, how should the practitioner adjust their approach?
choices: Hold the same hands-off servant-leader stance with both teams, so neither team feels singled out or judged
Give both teams detailed direction so that technical standards stay consistent across the program
Delegate broadly to the experienced team while giving the new team more coaching and structured guidance
Rotate experienced platform members into the new team so that a single leadership stance suits both

questions.explanation: A blameless review focused on systemic causes — missing safeguards, unclear procedures, gaps in automated checks — produces learning the whole organization can use, and sharing the findings openly satisfies the director's real need for accountability without punishing an individual. Listing everyone who touched the change spreads exposure rather than removing blame; the report still answers who instead of what allowed one change to interrupt a customer-facing service. Adding a peer-review gate for configuration changes is the strongest wrong answer, because such a control may well belong in the eventual fix, but naming it before the review has identified the real weakness is a solution in search of a cause and can leave the actual gap open. Having the junior engineer write the report herself sounds like ownership, yet it asks the most exposed person to document her own case under a blame frame, and one participant cannot see the whole system.
questions.concept: Blameless post-incident review
questions.question: At an energy utility, a junior engineer on a hybrid delivery team pushed a configuration change that briefly interrupted the customer-facing outage-reporting service. The operations director asks the agile practitioner to name the individual in the formal incident report "so accountability is clear." What is the BEST response?
choices: Propose a blameless post-incident review that examines how the system of work allowed one change to interrupt service, and share the findings openly with the director
Give the director a factual timeline naming everyone who touched the change, so accountability is shared across the whole team rather than resting on the newest engineer alone
Add a peer-review gate for configuration changes and report that control in the incident report, so the director can see a concrete corrective action was taken
Ask the junior engineer to write the incident report herself, since the person closest to the change can describe it best and will learn most from documenting it

questions.explanation: Facilitating a session in which the team drafts and commits to its own working agreements is best: norms the team authors are norms the team enforces, and the drafting conversation itself surfaces the cross-department assumptions causing the friction. Circulating the organization's handbook standards is faster but produces compliance without ownership, and a generic document cannot settle this team's arguments about cameras and response times. Asking each department's manager to brief their own staff fragments one team back into three reporting lines and signals that behavior is set outside the team. Meeting privately with the two members who have stopped responding is thoughtful and may be needed at some point, but it reads a week-old team's clash as a personal dispute when the disagreements are about agreements that do not yet exist.
questions.concept: Working agreements
questions.question: A payroll-migration program forms a new hybrid team drawing members from finance, development, and IT operations. Within the first week, members clash over which chat channel to use, whether cameras stay on, and how quickly messages deserve replies, and two members have stopped responding to each other. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Adopt the communication standards in the organization's project-management handbook and circulate them so everyone works from one published norm
Facilitate a session in which the team drafts and commits to its own working agreements covering channels, meetings, and response norms
Ask each department's manager to brief their own staff on the collaboration behavior expected on a hybrid team of this kind
Meet privately with the two members who have stopped responding first, and defer the wider norms conversation until that friction settles

questions.explanation: Co-creating outcome-based goals with both teams and the sponsor rebuilds the shared purpose that is actually missing: people commit to a vision they helped shape, and outcome goals let each team see how its backlog ladders up to the strategy. Asking the sponsor to issue one prioritized mandate is directive leadership that produces compliance rather than commitment, and it skips understanding why the teams diverged. Building an integrated dependency plan across both backlogs works at the output level — it coordinates activity without aligning intent, and the predictive detail decays as backlogs change. Merging the two backlogs under a single product owner is the most substantial alternative and would at least make one person accountable for ordering, but it dissolves a working Scrum and Kanban split to solve an alignment problem, and a single ordered list still does not tell either team why the sequence serves the strategy.
questions.concept: Co-creating outcome-based goals to align multiple teams to one vision
questions.question: A payments product is delivered by a Scrum feature team and a Kanban platform team. Each team optimizes its own backlog, and at the quarterly business review the sponsor observes that the combined results do not advance the product strategy, while the teams blame each other's priorities. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Facilitate a joint workshop where both teams and the sponsor co-create outcome-based goals traced to the product vision
Ask the sponsor to issue one prioritized mandate covering both backlogs so the teams stop optimizing their own plans
Build an integrated dependency plan across both backlogs for the quarter so the teams' work items line up in sequence
Merge the two backlogs under a single product owner who orders all the work so the product strategy shows in the sequence

questions.explanation: The problem is a long feedback loop, so the fix is to shorten it: frequent lightweight reviews with actual users surface problems while they are still cheap to correct and turn user insight into a steady input to prioritization — rotating the analyst group spreads engagement without burdening one person. Adding an upfront specification sign-off gate moves feedback earlier on paper but not on working software; documents approved before build routinely fail to predict how a feature behaves in use, and the gate adds process and delay. More detailed release notes rely on documentation over face-to-face interaction and still leave discovery to chance — analysts must notice, read, and self-report. Batching into a semi-annual release enlarges the batch and lengthens the loop, amplifying the very late-feedback problem the team is suffering from.
questions.concept: Shortening feedback loops; small batches over big releases
questions.question: A team using continuous-flow delivery for an internal budgeting tool releases features steadily behind a portal, but the finance analysts who use the tool only see what changed at a quarterly training session. By then their complaints arrive too late to fix cheaply, and rework is piling up. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Arrange short, frequent review sessions with a rotating group of analysts as features become available, feeding their observations directly into the backlog
Publish a detailed change log on the portal each week so that analysts can see exactly what shipped and raise any concerns through the existing service desk queue
Have the finance director approve each feature's specification before development starts, so the requirements are agreed before any code is written
Group the changes into a single semiannual release so one training session can cover every change while all of the analysts are together in the room

questions.explanation: Taking the adoption data and ride-along evidence to the people accountable for the benefits and proposing a re-prioritization keeps the focus on the outcome the money was approved for; a leaderboard and a manager report cannot produce fuel savings when 88 percent of drivers ignore the routes, and the practitioner's job is to make that dependency visible while the steering committee can still act on it next week. Completing the funded scope first honors a plan whose value assumption the evidence has already invalidated and delays the correction by a full cycle of burned savings. Adding the override to the backlog and leaving the choice to the team's iteration planning misplaces the decision — the team decides how to build, but a change of this magnitude to the release's value case belongs with the product owner and sponsor, and quietly queuing it also strands the evidence. Running an A/B test on the leaderboard spends weeks investigating a hypothesis the ride-alongs have already answered: drivers are not unmotivated, they are blocked by a route they cannot correct.
questions.concept: Outcomes over outputs and re-prioritizing a release against benefit evidence
questions.question: A waste-collection fleet operator funded a route-optimization module on a business case projecting $1.4M in annual fuel and overtime savings. Six weeks after the pilot depot went live, telemetry shows only 12 percent of drivers are following the optimized routes. Two items remain in the funded release: a driver leaderboard and a PDF report export for depot managers. Riding along with drivers, the product owner learns that routes go stale the moment a street is blocked or a bin is inaccessible, and drivers abandon the app for the whole shift because there is no way to override a stop; dispatchers have separately asked for exactly that override, which is not in the backlog. The sponsor's steering committee meets next week. What is the BEST response?
choices: Add the override capability to the backlog and let the team decide at the next planning session whether it outranks the leaderboard and the report export that depot managers were promised in this funded release

Finish the funded release scope exactly as approved, then raise the override request next planning cycle, so the commitments the team made to the steering group on the approved business case are honored first

Bring the adoption telemetry and the ride-along findings to the sponsor and product owner, and propose re-prioritizing the release around the override capability because the projected savings depend on drivers actually following the routes
Run an A/B test of the driver leaderboard across two depots to establish whether gamification alone lifts route adherence at the pilot depot, before any change is proposed to the funded release plan

questions.explanation: Sharing the validated learning directly with the sponsor and proposing a small, cheap next experiment respects both the funding relationship and the evidence: it turns a pivot-or-persevere question into a collaborative, data-driven decision instead of a confrontation, and keeps the cost of being wrong low. Simply continuing the roadmap treats an approved plan as more authoritative than observed customer behavior — the opposite of welcoming change and validated learning. Escalating to the portfolio board for a formal rebaseline before touching the backlog inserts a slow governance cycle where a direct sponsor conversation is available, and delays learning. Splitting capacity fifty-fifty is a technically possible compromise, but it dilutes both efforts, dodges the necessary conversation about where value actually is, and lets sunk-cost politics rather than evidence set the allocation.
questions.concept: Pivot-or-persevere decisions from validated learning versus sunk plans
questions.question: An agritech company released a minimum viable product for a soil-sensor subscription. Usage analytics show growers largely ignore the irrigation-forecast capability that anchors the funded roadmap, while a frost-alert feature built as a throwaway extra drives almost all daily engagement and word-of-mouth signups. The sponsor insists the team stay on the roadmap because the investment committee approved that business case. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Keep the funded roadmap as the team's commitment and gather three more months of usage data before raising the question, so the sponsor sees a durable trend rather than one quarter of analytics

Bring the usage evidence to the sponsor and propose a small next-cycle experiment that extends frost alerts while testing whether the roadmap's assumptions still hold, so the investment decision can be revisited with data

Split the team's capacity evenly between the funded roadmap and frost-alert enhancements so the sponsor's commitment is still honored and the growers who are actually engaged keep receiving more of the capability they already use

Ask the investment committee to rebaseline the business case before any backlog item changes, since the funding was approved against the irrigation forecast that still carries the organization's authorized intent for the coming year

questions.explanation: Visualization is a means, not an end: this board is simultaneously over-detailed where it adds no decision value and blind where the real risk lives, so the practitioner must first establish what decisions and risks the board needs to inform, then adapt it with the team who owns it — which is what finally makes the compliance dependency visible for the right reason rather than by coincidence. Making one member the board steward accepts the maintenance burden as a given and simply moves it onto one person; the day a week is still spent, and the board still fails to show the dependency that matters. Adding compliance to the swimlanes and the standup treats a missing dependency as a missing attendee: it enlarges an already over-detailed board and adds a daily meeting for a group whose constraint could be shown as a single visible item. Measuring column dwell time and retiring the idle columns is a genuine improvement and the strongest distractor, but it optimises the board that exists rather than asking what the board is for; it would trim the eleven columns while leaving the invisible compliance risk exactly as invisible.
questions.concept: Tailoring information radiators to decision needs and hidden dependencies
questions.question: An agile practitioner joins a team building a cross-border payments dashboard. The team maintains a highly detailed board: eleven columns, sub-swimlanes per stakeholder group, colored magnets for blockers, and a separate spreadsheet tracking readiness criteria for each item. Updating it consumes roughly a day of team effort per iteration, and the team says it "doesn't tell us anything we don't already know." Meanwhile, a data-residency compliance dependency that stalled two items for three weeks was never represented anywhere on the board. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Make one member the board steward each iteration, so maintaining the eleven columns, the swimlanes, and the readiness spreadsheet stops consuming a day of the whole team's effort every cycle
Add the compliance group to the board's stakeholder swimlanes and invite them to the daily standup, so their readiness constraints surface before any item is committed
Measure how long items sit in each of the eleven columns, then retire the columns where items barely wait at all, cutting the board's weekly update burden roughly in half
Facilitate the team in identifying the decisions and risks the board must inform, then adapt the visualization — including the invisible compliance dependency — to serve those needs

questions.explanation: Coaching the leaders addresses the root cause: the ranking has turned improvement signals into a competition, and leaders usually change course once they see they are paying for distorted data — flow metrics describe each team's unique system and were never comparable across teams. Working with the teams to keep radiators honest while adding goals, trends, and definitions restores transparency with enough context that the numbers explain themselves, protecting the teams without hiding anything. Withholding the metrics until leadership 'behaves' abandons transparency and treats leaders as adversaries rather than people to be coached. Standardizing story sizing chases fair comparison — but the premise is wrong: making teams comparable legitimizes the ranking that caused the dysfunction. Replacing radiators with a practitioner-curated narrative report makes one person the gatekeeper of truth, which is the opposite of transparency and reintroduces filtered status reporting.
questions.concept: Metrics misuse, gaming, and safeguarding transparency with psychological safety
questions.question: Portfolio leaders at a media company began pulling cycle-time and throughput figures from team information radiators into a monthly scorecard that ranks the twelve delivery teams. Within two quarters, two teams start splitting stories into tiny fragments to appear faster, and another quietly stops recording rework. An agile practitioner supporting the portfolio is asked to respond. What should the practitioner do? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Advise the teams to stop publishing flow metrics until leadership demonstrates it can use them responsibly.
Coach the portfolio leaders on what the metrics are for — signals for improving each team's own system — and show them the gaming behavior the ranking is now producing.
Standardize story sizing rules across all twelve teams so the cross-team comparisons become fair.
Replace the radiators with a monthly narrative status report curated by the practitioner to control how the numbers are interpreted.
Work with the teams to keep their radiators honest and add context — improvement goals, trend lines, and metric definitions — so the data informs rather than judges.

questions.explanation: Stopping the pull and swarming on the queue is best because in a pull system the constraint is verification, and every extra card started upstream lengthens lead time for everything already in flight; finishing what is closest to done releases value and shrinks the queue immediately, and it is an action the team can take today without permission. Raising the WIP limit to match the queue removes the very signal that exposed the problem — the limit is not a description of the mess, it is the tension that forces the team to deal with it, and lead time would keep climbing. Asking the manager for another verification engineer escalates before the team has tried the change within its own control, takes weeks to help, and treats a temporary rig outage as a permanent staffing gap. Splitting verification onto a downstream board makes Build look fast while hiding the real delay from the board and the customer, which is optimizing a part at the expense of end-to-end flow.
questions.concept: WIP limits and pull systems; stop starting, start finishing
questions.question: A firmware team runs a Kanban board with the columns Ready, Build, Verify (WIP limit 4), and Done. By Wednesday, Verify holds nine cards because the two engineers who run verification are tied up recovering a failed lab rig, yet developers keep pulling new cards into Build so they "stay busy." Average lead time has doubled over the last three weeks. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Move verification onto its own downstream board so Build flow is measured without the lab recovery skewing it.
Ask the team to stop pulling new cards and swarm on clearing the Verify queue before starting anything else.
Ask the functional manager for a third verification engineer so the queue drains without pausing Build.
Raise the Verify limit to nine so the board honestly reflects the way the team is working this week.

questions.explanation: Stating the riskiest assumption, releasing a minimal offer, and measuring real sign-ups against a threshold set in advance is the full build-measure-learn loop: a falsifiable hypothesis, the smallest product that can test it, and predefined evidence criteria that guard against rationalizing weak results. Building the complete platform does eventually produce real data, but only after spending the entire investment the experiment was meant to protect — it is the maximum, not minimum, viable product. Interviewing garage owners gathers opinions from intermediaries about what commuters might do, which is far weaker evidence than observing what commuters actually do when offered the service. Deferring the question to a later roadmap slot simply postpones learning and lets the unvalidated assumption keep steering investment.
questions.concept: Lean Startup build-measure-learn and MVP
questions.question: A product team believes urban commuters will pay a monthly fee to reserve parking spots near transit stations. Funding for a full build is available, but the team wants to apply Lean Startup thinking before committing it. Which action BEST applies hypothesis-driven development?
choices: Build the complete reservation platform across every transit station at once, since only revenue from the full network proves that commuters will pay
Interview parking-garage owners and transit planners about expected demand, then build the platform if their forecasts support the projected business case
State the riskiest assumption, release a minimal reservation offer in one station area, and measure actual sign-ups against a predefined success threshold
Put the reservation feature on the roadmap behind the current commitments and reassess commuter demand once the next major release has shipped

questions.explanation: A shared, always-visible board is an information radiator: it removes the need to ask because the answer is already on display, it is updated by the people doing the work, and it gives every stakeholder the same picture at the same moment. Publishing a weekly report keeps information locked in a push channel that is stale within a day and still leaves stakeholders guessing between issues. Routing every status question through the team lead spares the developers but makes one person the sole channel for information the whole team holds, adds a queue in front of a simple question, and still produces different answers on different days. A morning roundup at the operations desk is the strongest alternative, since it is same-day and everyone hears the same thing, but it is a push at a fixed moment: anyone who misses it or asks at noon is back to interrupting a developer, and nothing remains on display.
questions.concept: Information radiators and shared visual boards
questions.question: A port-terminal software team works in a shared office alongside operations staff. Because there is no single place to see the state of work, the yard supervisor, the customs liaison, and two account managers each message individual developers throughout the day asking whether their request has started. Developers are interrupted constantly, and stakeholders still receive conflicting answers. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Publish a formatted weekly status report to a stakeholder distribution list each Friday, so all three groups get the same answer at once
Ask stakeholders to route all status questions through the team lead rather than interrupting developers at their desks during the iteration
Set up with the team a shared, always-visible board showing every in-flight item and its current state, and point stakeholders to it.
Have the team lead give a status roundup at the operations desk each morning so all three groups hear the same picture

questions.explanation: Bringing team members face to face with clinicians and then mapping backlog items to clinician outcomes builds shared purpose experientially: people connect their daily work to real users, which is exactly what the survey shows is missing, and the mapping makes that connection concrete rather than abstract. Distributing the vision statement and collecting acknowledgments treats vision as a compliance artifact — reading a document does not create the understanding the survey found lacking. Adding an alignment section to status reports turns shared purpose into a monitoring metric for leadership instead of a lived understanding inside the teams. Cascading a roadmap briefing through team leads delivers the message secondhand and covers schedule and scope, not the customer "why" that is absent.
questions.concept: Connecting daily work to customer outcomes
questions.question: A hospital data-platform program runs several component teams in a hybrid model. A recent internal survey shows that fewer than a third of team members can describe how their component affects the clinicians who use the platform, and standup discussions focus entirely on interface contracts and ticket counts. Delivery is on schedule, but teams routinely optimize their own component at the expense of end-to-end outcomes. What is the BEST response?
choices: Facilitate a session where clinicians describe how they use the platform, then have teams map their backlog items to clinician outcomes
Circulate the approved product vision and ask every member to confirm in writing that they have read it, then track completion by team
Add an outcome column to each team's status report so program leadership can see which clinician need every backlog item serves
Ask each component lead to brief their own members on the roadmap, since the leads already understand how their component reaches clinicians

questions.explanation: Little's Law in its practical flow form gives average time in the system as average work in progress divided by average throughput: 12 items divided by 3 items per week is about 4 weeks, and because WIP here is counted from the commitment point, that figure is the lead time the stakeholder will experience. The second half matters just as much — the relationship is a proportion, so if WIP rises while throughput stays at 3 per week, average lead time rises with it, which is precisely the guidance the stakeholder needs before adding a request. The option claiming the 4-week figure holds regardless of additions misstates the law by treating lead time as a fixed property rather than a consequence of WIP and throughput. Multiplying 12 by 3 to reach 36 weeks inverts the relationship; the arithmetic direction is division, not multiplication, and no queuing argument produces that number. Claiming item size must be known first misunderstands the law's practical use — it operates on counts of items over a stable period, and averaging absorbs size variation, which is exactly why flow metrics forecast without estimation.
questions.concept: Practical Little's Law applied to WIP, throughput, and lead time
questions.question: A Kanban team has operated as a stable system for several months. On average, 12 work items are in progress at any time (counted from the moment an item is committed and pulled onto the board), and the team finishes an average of 3 items per week. The team wants to quote a realistic average lead time to a stakeholder who is deciding whether to add a request to the queue. Assuming the system remains stable, which statement is the most defensible application of these figures?
choices: Average lead time is roughly 4 weeks, and admitting more work without increasing throughput will lengthen it
Average lead time is roughly 4 weeks, and it will hold at that figure however many items the stakeholder adds
Average lead time is roughly 36 weeks, because a new request must wait behind all twelve items in progress
Average lead time cannot be quoted from throughput and work in progress until the items are sized consistently

questions.explanation: The consuming teams' need is forward-looking: they must plan their own work around when authentication capabilities become available and how firm those expectations are. A horizon-based roadmap with the near-term backlog slice and explicit confidence gives exactly that, and stating confidence keeps the roadmap honest rather than turning it into a commitment. A cumulative flow diagram is a flow-health instrument for the owning team; it reveals queues and work in progress but says nothing about which capability arrives when. A burndown of current iteration points is internal and short-horizon, and point totals mean little outside the team that produced them. The dependency register is the strongest alternative, since it names each request and an owner — but it reports activity rather than expected availability, ages badly, and never shows how firm any date is.
questions.concept: Selecting information radiators for external stakeholders
questions.question: A platform team has been asked to make its work visible to four dependent teams that consume its shared authentication service. The team already keeps a task board covering the current iteration's items. Which addition would MOST improve transparency for the consuming teams' planning?
choices: A cumulative flow diagram of the platform team's iteration tasks, refreshed daily so the four consuming teams can watch work move forward
A visible roadmap and near-term backlog slice showing which authentication capabilities are expected in which upcoming time horizons, with confidence indicated
A burndown chart of the points remaining in the platform team's current iteration, published where consuming teams can check it
A dependency register listing every request the four consuming teams have raised, with the engineer assigned and the date last updated

questions.explanation: Mode selection weighs the importance of the issue, the time pressure, and the relationships involved. A trivial issue at an emotionally hot, high-stakes moment is the textbook case for a deliberate, temporary withdrawal — paired with a genuine collaborative resolution through a team working agreement once the demo is over, so the conflict is deferred rather than ducked. Settling the rule by a quick team vote closes the noise but spends the team's last minutes before a customer on a formatting rule and manufactures a losing side. Leaving the two to work it out is the most principled-sounding option, since self-organizing teams do resolve their own disagreements, but the timing is what matters: withdrawing from a rising argument minutes before a demo abandons the group rather than trusting it. Proposing the linter's default may well be the eventual agreement, yet imposing it now is forcing on a minor issue.
questions.concept: Conflict-management mode selection under time pressure
questions.question: Fifteen minutes before a customer demo, two XP developers begin arguing loudly over a trivial code-formatting rule, and tempers are rising. Which response best applies the principle of matching a conflict-management mode to the situation?
choices: Step in and settle the rule by a quick team vote, so the disagreement is closed before the customer arrives
Leave the two to work it out, since a self-organizing team should resolve its own disagreements without a facilitator
Propose the pair adopt the linter's default rule, since an external standard ends debate without either developer conceding
Acknowledge the disagreement, deliberately set it aside until after the demo, then facilitate a working-agreement discussion to resolve it

questions.explanation: A minimum viable product exists to test the riskiest assumption with the least investment, so the disciplined move is to evaluate every candidate addition against the learning the release must produce and hold the line on scope that does not serve it. Endorsing the competitive-parity argument substitutes feature matching for evidence and inflates the release before anyone knows whether the core behavior happens. Compromising on the most foundational addition is scope negotiation by architecture preference rather than by learning value, and it still delays the feedback the team needs. Surveying prospective borrowers about stated preferences yields opinion about features rather than behavioral evidence about whether they will complete an application, and it postpones the release while adding little to the decision.
questions.concept: MVP scoping against the riskiest assumption
questions.question: A fintech team is preparing the first release of a small-business lending product. Analysis suggests the smallest offering that would let a business owner apply, receive a decision, and draw funds requires four capability areas. The team's chief architect argues for adding a partner-bank integration, a savings-rate comparison widget, and multi-currency support to the first release, reasoning that competitors already have them and a thin launch will embarrass the company. The product owner is uncertain and asks the practitioner for a view. The team has no evidence yet that owners will complete an online application at all. What is the BEST response?
choices: Support the architect, since a first release that visibly lags competitors on partner banking and currency coverage will be judged on those gaps rather than on what it does well
Include the partner-bank integration because it is the most architecturally foundational of the three, and defer the comparison widget and multi-currency support to a later release
Facilitate a session that tests each proposed addition against the riskiest assumption — that owners will apply and draw funds online — and hold the first release to what validates it
Survey prospective borrowers on how they rank the three proposed additions against the core application flow, then build the first release around whichever ordering comes back strongest

questions.explanation: Stating a measurable hypothesis and releasing a signup page with a manually operated scheduling service behind it is build-measure-learn in action: the smallest investment that generates validated learning from what customers actually do, compared against a target set in advance. Interviewing busy pet owners about their scheduling frustrations surfaces useful problem context, but funding the subscription on the strength of stated interest tests what people say rather than what they buy. Building a working integration with two clinics and measuring renewals is the strongest alternative, since renewal is hard behavioral evidence, yet it commits the build before any demand is shown and puts the answer a quarter away. Six months free measures appetite for a free service, which is not the willingness-to-pay assumption under test.
questions.concept: Lean Startup: hypothesis-driven development and minimum viable product
questions.question: A product team believes busy pet owners will pay for a subscription that auto-schedules veterinary visits, but the evidence is only anecdotal. Which action BEST applies the build-measure-learn loop to test this belief?
choices: Interview a sample of busy pet owners about their scheduling frustrations and use the strength of their stated interest to decide whether to fund the subscription
Build a working scheduling integration with two local clinics, then measure whether the owners who use it renew after a full quarter of service
State a measurable hypothesis, release a signup page with a manually operated scheduling service behind it, and compare actual signups against the target
Release the subscription free for six months and treat continued use at the end of the trial period as evidence that owners will pay for it

questions.explanation: Scripted password resets sit in the clear (obvious) domain: cause and effect are self-evident, so the right move is to categorize the request and apply the documented best practice. Database tuning that experts can analyze and predict is complicated: cause and effect are discoverable but require expertise, so the approach is sense-analyze-respond with good (not single best) practice. A novel product launch is complex: cause and effect are only visible in retrospect, so no amount of upfront analysis substitutes for safe-to-fail probes whose emergent results guide the response — this is the domain where agile experimentation pays most. A spreading outage under peak load is chaotic: acting first to stabilize precedes any sensing or analysis, because delay itself compounds the damage. The classic error this item tests is inverting the middle pair — applying expert analysis (a complicated-domain tool) to a complex situation where patterns must emerge from experiments, or running experiments where expert analysis would answer the question faster and cheaper.
questions.concept: Cynefin framework — matching decision approach to context
questions.question: Match each work situation (1-4) to the decision approach (A-D) that the Cynefin framework recommends for its context.
pairs: 1. Password-reset requests handled by a documented help-desk script
Sense the situation, categorize it, and apply established best practice
2. Tuning a database whose behavior experts can analyze and reliably predict
Sense the situation, analyze it with expertise, and apply good practice
3. Launching a novel product whose user behavior will only emerge after release
Probe with safe-to-fail experiments, sense the emerging patterns, then respond
4. A production outage spreading during a peak payment surge, with no time for analysis
Act immediately to stabilize, then sense the situation and respond

questions.explanation: Sharing personal experience, advising on stretch assignments, and opening one's professional network over a sustained period are the defining marks of mentoring: an experienced practitioner guiding a less experienced one's long-term development. It is not coaching, because a coach deliberately withholds his own answers and draws out the client's through questions — a one-on-one, career-focused format alone does not make a relationship coaching. It is not training, because training is the structured transfer of a defined skill against a curriculum with practice and assessment, not open-ended experience-based guidance. It is not facilitating, because facilitation is neutral stewardship of a group's process toward the group's own outcome — here the practitioner is neither neutral nor working with a group.
questions.concept: Coaching vs mentoring vs training vs facilitation distinctions
questions.question: A tester tells an agile practitioner she wants to grow into a product-owner role. The practitioner, who spent six years as a product owner, begins meeting with her monthly to share lessons from his own transition, suggest stretch assignments, and introduce her to contacts in his product network. Which development approach is the practitioner applying?
choices: Coaching, because the meetings are one-on-one and organized around the career goal she has set
Training, because he is transferring the skills of product ownership to her over time
Mentoring, because he draws on his own experience and network to guide her longer-term growth
Facilitating, because he stays neutral about which career path she settles on in the end

questions.explanation: Regulatory and privacy obligations are constraints on what can legitimately be called a shippable increment, not backlog items competing on value; the collaborative move is to bring the parties together and reshape the increment so it is releasable — either the controls become done criteria or the pilot uses data that does not trigger the obligation. Recording the three controls as ranked items with a remediation date knowingly exposes real claimant health data in the interim and misuses the debt concept for a compliance breach. Estimating them and pulling whichever fits remaining capacity treats a non-negotiable set as an a la carte menu. Having the data protection officer write the controls into the planned stories' acceptance criteria is the strongest alternative, but it freezes the increment's shape and replaces the conversation with a specification.
questions.concept: Regulatory and privacy constraints as increment release criteria
questions.question: An insurance carrier is replacing a claims intake portal. The team plans a first customer-facing increment for six weeks out. Late in release planning, the data protection officer states that any increment handling claimant health information must include consent capture, field-level encryption, and an access audit trail before real claimant data touches it — none of which appear in the release plan. The product owner argues these are non-differentiating and proposes shipping the increment to a small pilot group first and adding the controls in the following release. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Record the three controls as ranked backlog items with a fixed remediation date and launch the pilot on schedule with real claimant data, so the obligation stays visible while the customer-facing commitment is met
Ask the team to estimate consent capture, field-level encryption, and the audit trail, then pull whichever of the three fits the capacity left in the release and carry the remainder forward

Bring the product owner, data protection officer, and team together to reshape the increment — either fold the controls in as done criteria for handling real data, or scope the pilot to synthetic data
Have the data protection officer write consent, encryption, and the audit trail into the acceptance criteria of the stories already planned, so the increment keeps the shape it now has

questions.explanation: The usability sessions produced exactly the feedback short loops exist to surface, and its value depends on acting while there is still time to adapt — with two sprints left, the product owner and stakeholders can improve the screen, adjust the demo, or rescope, but only if they see the truth now. Suppressing it would trade transparency for comfort and convert a recoverable finding into a public failure. Parking the observation in a risk register for the post-release retrospective delays inspection until adaptation is most expensive and the trade-show damage is done. Adding an onboarding tutorial prescribes a fix before anyone understands why clinicians prefer the spreadsheet — the workaround is a signal about the design, not about user training. Disabling the spreadsheet import forces adoption by removing the users' coping mechanism, masking the signal and likely harming clinicians' work rather than learning from it.
questions.concept: Transparency and acting on short feedback loops
questions.question: Two sprints before a healthcare product's trade-show release, usability sessions reveal that clinicians avoid the new flagship scheduling screen and keep working through a legacy spreadsheet import instead. A teammate suggests keeping the finding quiet until after the release to protect the date and team morale. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Retire the legacy spreadsheet import during this sprint so clinicians have to use the new screen and the trade-show demo shows real usage
Record the finding in the project risk register and bring it to the post-release retrospective, when there is time to act on it properly
Share the sessions' findings openly with the product owner and stakeholders now and re-plan the remaining scope around what was learned
Add guided onboarding and tooltips to the scheduling screen so clinicians learn the new flow before the trade-show release

questions.explanation: Making blockers and aging explicit on the board, paired with a team agreement that stalled work signals a system problem rather than a personal failure, restores both the information radiator and the safety people need to use it honestly — the root cause here is fear, so transparency has to be rebuilt alongside safety. Tracking item aging privately and coaching each member whose cards stall treats a systemic fear problem as personal underperformance and confirms what the team already believes: stalled cards get you singled out. Adding the blocked marker and aging rule yourself is close, and the mechanism is right, but imposing it leaves the fear untouched, so members simply stop flagging cards and push their workarounds further off-board. A weekly written impediment report moves information off the team's own radiator into a management channel, adding overhead while keeping the audience people fear.
questions.concept: Information radiators and visualizing blocked work
questions.question: An insurance-claims platform team uses a Kanban board, but its cycle times have quietly doubled. The agile practitioner discovers that members leave blocked cards marked as ordinary in-progress work and chase workarounds off-board, because a previous manager publicly criticized anyone whose cards stalled. What is the BEST response?
choices: Track item aging privately and coach each member whose cards have stalled, so individual delivery habits improve before the slowdown becomes visible to leaders
Add a blocked marker and an aging rule to the board yourself so that stalled cards become visible from the next morning's coordination meeting onward
Introduce a weekly written impediment report to management so blockers are removed by leaders rather than chased informally by members off the board
Work with the team to make blockers and aging explicit on the board and agree together that stalled work signals a system problem, not an individual failure

questions.explanation: The real impediment is not build duration but a feedback signal the team no longer believes; once a red build carries no information, every downstream control degrades. Quarantining the unstable tests restores a trustworthy fast signal, visible build-health and escape data create the evidence for continuous improvement, and reserving capacity treats this technical debt as first-class work instead of something to do "when there's time." Faster agents make an unreliable answer arrive sooner — a one-in-three false failure rate at 30 minutes is still ignored. A manual regression checklist adds inspection at the end, lengthening lead time, enlarging batch size, and compensating for a defect source rather than removing it. Forbidding merges on red is the right rule applied to a broken instrument: with a third of runs failing spuriously, it stops the line for reasons that are not real and will be quietly abandoned or will strangle flow.
questions.concept: CI/CD reliability, flaky-test technical debt, and quality built in
questions.question: In a hybrid logistics program, one component team's continuous integration pipeline runs 95 minutes and fails on roughly one run in three, nearly always from a handful of timing-sensitive tests. Developers now merge on red "because it's probably just flaky," and three defects reached production last month that the suite had actually caught on earlier runs. The team lead has asked for budget for faster build agents; the release manager has proposed a manual regression checklist before every release. Both options are affordable and technically workable. What is the BEST response?
choices: Approve the faster build agents so the pipeline finishes in under thirty minutes, since a ninety-five minute wait for a verdict is what pushed developers into merging before the suite had finished telling them anything useful.
