Treat the untrustworthy pipeline as the team's top impediment: quarantine the flaky tests into a separate suite, make build health and defect-escape data visible, and reserve team capacity every iteration until the signal is trusted again.

Adopt the release manager's manual regression checklist as a release gate, so the defects that the suite already catches are caught by a human step before any customer ever sees them, while the timing-sensitive tests are repaired in the background.

Change the working agreement to forbid merging on a red build, review any violations at the daily standup, and have developers rerun a failing run until it passes, so the pipeline's verdict is treated as binding by the whole team again.

questions.explanation: Little's Law in its practical form relates work in progress, throughput and cycle time: 22 items divided by 4 items per week is about 5.5 weeks, which is precisely the cycle time the team observes. Anything added now therefore waits roughly 5.5 weeks behind what is already committed, no matter how small it is, so using that arithmetic makes the trade-off transparent and turns the conversation into a real prioritization decision. Asking the team to work extra hours violates sustainable pace, degrades quality, and disguises an overload problem as an effort problem; the underlying arithmetic does not change. Accepting the batch into the backlog and letting prioritization settle is the strongest rival, since nothing is truly started until it is pulled, but it defers the honest conversation and leaves the stakeholder believing urgent work is moving when it is merely queued. An expedite lane for ten items is not an exception but a second stream: it displaces everything already committed and lengthens every other item's wait.
questions.concept: Practical Little's Law applied to intake decisions
questions.question: A Kanban team supporting a logistics platform tracks flow data on its board: throughput averages 4 items per week, roughly 22 items are in progress across the board, and measured cycle time has settled at about 5.5 weeks per item. A stakeholder asks the team to accept an additional batch of 10 urgent items, promising they are all small. The team's coach reviews the flow data before the conversation. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Point out that with throughput at 4 items per week the 22 items already in progress represent roughly 5.5 weeks of queued work - exactly matching the measured cycle time - and use that to negotiate what will be stopped or deferred before anything new is started

Accept the batch of 10 and ask the team to put in extra hours over the next fortnight, since the stakeholder has described the items as small and the work already on the board should continue to flow at its usual rate while the urgent items are absorbed alongside it

Accept the 10 items into the backlog and let the team's own prioritization settle their order as capacity frees up, since nothing is truly started until someone pulls it and the limits already agreed on the board will govern how quickly any of the new batch enters flow

Set up an expedite lane for the 10 urgent items so they move ahead of what is already on the board, since the stakeholder has called them urgent and small items should clear the lane quickly without disturbing the sequence of everything else in progress

questions.explanation: Proposing a thin, working slice embraces empiricism: instead of pretending unstable requirements can be fixed up front, the team delivers something real quickly, learns from it, and lets evidence shape scope and dates. Estimating the whole forty-page specification in detail produces a precise-looking commitment resting on temperature thresholds the compliance group is still debating. Giving a date range that tightens as velocity becomes known is honest forecasting and clearly better than an invented single date, but it improves the accuracy of a forecast over a scope that is not yet stable, so the real uncertainty goes untested. Starting the settled parts is sensible as far as it goes, yet holding the threshold work until compliance finishes leaves the most contested area for last, when a thin slice through it would inform that very debate.
questions.concept: Empiricism vs. predictive up-front planning
questions.question: A team at a logistics startup is asked to build a route-optimization feature for refrigerated deliveries. The operations director hands the team a 40-page specification and asks them to commit to a delivery date before any code is written, even though the temperature-threshold requirements are still being debated by the compliance group. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Estimate the whole specification in detail with the team so the operations director gets the committed date she has asked for
Propose delivering a thin, working slice of the feature early so real feedback can shape the remaining scope and dates
Give the director a date range rather than a single date, and tighten it after each iteration as velocity becomes known
Have the team start on the settled parts and hold the thresholds until the compliance group finishes its debate

questions.explanation: Opening the teams' live boards and flow metrics to stakeholders turns stale, curated reporting into an always-current information radiator, removing both the three-week lag and the intermediary; inviting stakeholders to regular working-product demonstrations goes further still, because inspecting the actual product is the most honest progress signal agile offers and it creates a direct feedback loop. Producing a more detailed fortnightly written report merely shortens the cycle of the same push-based, curated channel — the information is still filtered, still aging, and still secondhand. Requiring project-office verification before stakeholders may see data reinstates a gatekeeper, adds delay, and signals that unpolished truth is unsafe to show. Restricting raw metrics to senior leadership is the opposite of transparency: it hoards information to prevent misinterpretation instead of radiating it and helping everyone read it well.
questions.concept: Information radiators and demonstrating working product to stakeholders
questions.question: An agile practitioner joins a manufacturing-analytics company where stakeholders learn about progress only through polished monthly slide decks assembled by a project office, and teams complain the decks are always three weeks out of date. Which TWO actions would MOST improve transparency? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Give stakeholders direct, always-on access to the teams' live boards and flow metrics
Replace the monthly deck with a more detailed written report produced every two weeks
Invite stakeholders to regular working-product demonstrations where they inspect outcomes and give feedback directly
Have the project office verify all team data before stakeholders are allowed to see it
Restrict raw metrics to senior leadership so other groups cannot misinterpret them

questions.explanation: The board is already telling the team the truth: a downstream queue is absorbing everything the team starts, and lead time is paying for it. Making the queue and the age of its cards visible, then limiting work in progress upstream so people move toward the constraint, attacks the actual cause and is a change the team can make itself today. Adding swimlanes and sub-columns raises the fidelity of the picture but changes no policy, so the queue keeps growing while the team redraws it. Requesting more testers escalates for budget before the team has tried the free improvement it controls, and it assumes capacity is the problem when unconstrained starting is. Parking waiting cards outside the main flow destroys the transparency the board exists to create, hiding the very delay the team needs to confront.
questions.concept: Reading a board for bottlenecks; WIP limits and swarming the constraint
questions.question: A vertical-farming company visualizes its firmware work on a board with the columns Ready, Firmware, Bench Test, Certification Lab, and Done. Over the past month the Certification Lab column has held between 9 and 12 cards while Firmware rarely holds more than 2, and average lead time has roughly doubled. In the retrospective, developers explain that they keep pulling new Firmware cards because there is nothing else for them to do. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Walk the board with the team, make the certification queue and the age of the cards in it visible, and agree work-in-progress limits upstream so people stop starting firmware and swarm the constraint instead.

Ask management to fund additional certification testers, since a queue of nine to twelve cards against a two-card firmware column points to a staffing shortage the team cannot solve from inside its own process.
Redesign the board with swimlanes and sub-columns so each certification step is captured in detail, on the reasoning that the team cannot manage a queue it cannot see the internal stages of.
Move the waiting cards into a separate on-hold area so the board shows only what the team can act on today, and review the parked certification cards together once a week until the queue clears.

questions.explanation: The board shows demand validated (11.4% versus an 8% threshold) but willingness to pay invalidated (12% versus 40%), with the interviews pointing to a specific cause: price versus perceived value. The evidence therefore supports a pivot on the offer, tested with another cheap experiment before further investment — exactly what a revised price-and-value probe does. Building the full platform reads only the first row and pours investment into a funnel that is proven not to convert. Spending more on marketing scales the top of that same unconverting funnel; more waitlist members declining at 12% just burns cash faster. Abandoning the product overreacts to one invalidated hypothesis and throws away the validated learning that real demand exists — the interviews suggest the value proposition, not the idea, is what needs to change.
questions.concept: Lean Startup validated learning and pivot-or-persevere decisions
questions.question: A Lean-Startup-style team reviews the hypothesis board shown in the exhibit. Based on this evidence, what should the team do next?
choices: Design a cheap follow-up experiment that tests a revised price-and-value offer before investing further in the product
Build the full subscription platform now, since waitlist signups cleared their threshold and demonstrate genuine demand for it
Increase marketing spend to enlarge the waitlist, so a bigger pool of trials offsets the weak conversion rate
Abandon the concept, since the paid-trial hypothesis missed its threshold and the evidence against it is decisive

questions.explanation: Both indices read 1.10, yet every flow signal points the other way, and the contradiction has one arithmetic source: roughly 40 percent of the credited earned value sits in unverified work. Recrediting to completed items only, then recalculating, is the first move because it determines whether there is any good news at all; removing that credit pulls earned value toward and probably below planned value, which reconciles the numbers with the doubled work in progress and cycle time rising from 6 to 14 days. Presenting the indices and pulling scope forward compounds the error, adding demand to a system whose queue is already the constraint, and it spends an inflated numerator as if it were free capacity. Keeping the figures and appending a narrative note is the strongest rival and is not wrong about method in general, since percent-complete crediting is a legitimate technique in other settings; it fails here because the team's completion criteria are this program's recognized measure of done, unverified diagnostic software carries real rework and regulatory exposure, and a footnote still leaves a materially overstated number on the sponsor's dashboard. Arguing that a six-week-old baseline cannot be stale answers a question nobody asked: baseline currency is not what is broken, the earned value credit is, and dismissing corroborating flow data because a formula looks healthy inverts the correct order of trust.
questions.concept: Crediting earned value strictly to items meeting completion criteria, and cross-checking EVM indices against work in progress and cycle time
questions.question: A clinical-diagnostics instrument program uses a rolling release baseline: the performance measurement baseline is re-authorized at the start of each quarterly release, and earned value is credited in the same story-point-derived cost unit as the baseline. Six weeks into the current release, the sponsor's dashboard shows PV $600,000, EV $660,000, AC $600,000. Over the same six weeks, work in progress on the team board has doubled, average cycle time has risen from 6 to 14 days, and the verification-and-validation column holds items representing about 40 percent of the credited earned value that are code-complete but have not cleared the team's completion criteria. What should you do first?
choices: Present the favorable indices as they stand and propose pulling scope forward from the next quarterly release, since an index above one on both cost and schedule means spare capacity is available to the team now

Recompute earned value crediting only items that have met the team's completion criteria, then re-derive the indices and read them against the work in progress and cycle time trends before anything goes to the sponsor

Leave the earned value figures unchanged, since percent-complete crediting of work in progress is an accepted measurement method, and add a narrative note flagging the rising work in progress and cycle time trends beside them
Accept the indices as valid because the baseline was re-authorized only six weeks ago so it cannot be stale, and treat the work in progress and cycle time movement as normal variation for now

questions.explanation: This is coaching: the practitioner deliberately withholds answers and uses powerful questions so the product owner discovers an approach she owns, leaving both the solution and the capability with the person being developed. It is not mentoring, because a mentor draws on personal experience and offers advice — 'here is how I have ordered backlogs like this' — and a seniority gap alone does not make an interaction mentoring. It is not training, because training transfers predefined content or skills against a curriculum, and no content is being transferred here. It is not facilitation, because a facilitator neutrally guides a group's process toward the group's own outcome, whereas this is a one-on-one developmental conversation aimed at growing one person's thinking.
questions.concept: Coaching vs. mentoring vs. training vs. facilitation; leaving ownership of the solution with the person being developed
questions.question: A new product owner asks an agile practitioner how to order a backlog that mixes regulatory deadlines with revenue features. Instead of proposing an ordering scheme, the practitioner asks questions — 'What would failure look like for each item? What does your sponsor lose if this one waits a quarter?' — until the product owner designs her own approach. Which development approach is the practitioner applying?
choices: Coaching, because the practitioner uses questions to help the product owner reach her own solution
Mentoring, because an experienced practitioner is passing on hard-won judgment to a newer colleague
Training, because the product owner is acquiring a new prioritization skill through practice
Facilitation, because the practitioner is steering a structured conversation toward a decision

questions.explanation: The exhibit shows an inflection exactly at Sprint 20, when the delivery manager arrived: decisions made by the team fall from 15 to 4, decisions referred upward climb from 1 to 13, and psychological safety slides from 4.5 to 2.9 — the classic disempowerment pattern. The first move is a private, curious conversation with the manager: show him the two converging trends, understand his intent, and coach him toward behaviors that push decisions back down. Raising the trends at the retrospective and asking the team to commit publicly to taking decisions back puts a team scoring 2.9 on safety into a confrontation with its manager before he has heard anything privately. Redesigning decision rights in a delegation workshop is a strong later step, but run before anyone understands why the referrals started it formalizes structure around an unexamined behavior. Coaching the team to reclaim each decision in the moment asks the least safe people to correct their manager repeatedly in public.
questions.concept: Diagnosing disempowerment from decision and team-health trends; coaching a command-style leader
questions.question: The agile practitioner reviews the exhibit for the museum ticketing platform team. Based on the data, what should the practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Meet the delivery manager privately, share the trend, explore what is driving the referrals, and coach him toward returning decisions to the team
Raise the referral trend and the safety scores at the next team retrospective, and ask the team to agree publicly on which decisions it will take back
Redesign the team's decision rights in a delegation workshop, so referral routes are formally defined before anyone's behavior is discussed
Coach the team to hand each decision back in the moment when the delivery manager takes it, so the pattern is corrected where it actually happens

questions.explanation: Coaching is question-driven: the coach helps the individual find their own answers and deliberately withholds advice, which is why it pairs with using powerful questions to surface the person's own goals and solutions. Mentoring is the advice-giving relationship: the mentor draws on personal experience to guide a less-experienced practitioner's growth over time — the element coaching explicitly avoids. Facilitating is content-neutral and group-focused: the facilitator owns the process of the conversation, not its outcome, so it matches guiding a group to its own decisions while staying neutral on content. Training is the only mode where a defined body of knowledge flows one way through structured instruction. The classic exam traps are treating coaching as advice-giving (that is mentoring) and treating facilitation as content delivery (that is training).
questions.concept: coaching vs. mentoring vs. facilitating vs. training
questions.question: Match each developmental approach on the left with the description on the right that BEST characterizes it.
pairs: Coaching
Uses powerful questions to help an individual surface their own goals and discover their own solutions, without supplying answers
Mentoring
Shares personal experience and advice over an extended relationship to support a less-experienced practitioner's longer-term growth
Facilitating
Guides a group's process and conversations so participants reach their own decisions, while remaining neutral on the content
Training
Transfers a specific skill or defined body of knowledge through structured instruction and practice

questions.explanation: Making the hidden wait state visible is the first move: the board should mirror the real workflow, so the queue where items actually stall becomes obvious to the team and to stakeholders, and the delay becomes a shared, measurable problem instead of an unexplained gap. Publishing a weekly status summary reports around the problem without exposing where work is stuck, and pushed information is a weaker substitute for a visible board anyone can read at any time. Escalating to procurement acts before the team even knows how much delay the handoff causes, and it reaches outside the team before collaborating within it — with no data, the request is unsupported. Appointing a coordinator to chase translations adds a person and a process to compensate for missing transparency, which buries the bottleneck behind individual effort rather than revealing it.
questions.concept: Workflow mapping and making queues/wait states explicit on the board
questions.question: A museum's digital ticketing team works from a board with three columns: To Do, Doing, Done. Every ticket-purchase screen must be translated by an external localization vendor before it can be tested, but that handoff is not shown anywhere on the board. Items sit in Doing for weeks, the team cannot explain the delays, and stakeholders interrupt members individually for status. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Publish a weekly written status summary so stakeholders stop interrupting individuals and the team can keep its attention on the items already in progress.
Facilitate the team in mapping how the work actually flows and adding an explicit 'awaiting translation' queue to the board with entry and exit policies.
Take the vendor's turnaround times to the procurement manager and negotiate a contract with a guaranteed translation service level, so the wait shortens.
Name one member as translation coordinator to chase the vendor daily and report where each screen sits, so the delays have a single clear owner.

questions.explanation: Twenty-seven of thirty-four days are queue time at a single hand-off, so the only change that materially shortens lead time is reducing that batch — and that requires collaborating directly with the compliance group rather than working around them. Standardizing intake and document assembly is real improvement work the team owns, which makes it the strongest alternative, but the entire seven days of hands-on effort is barely a fifth of the lead time; halving it still leaves a package waiting nearly a month. Deliberately sending one large batch every second Friday uses the reviewer's session efficiently at the team's expense, since larger batches lengthen average wait and raise the cost of any rejection. Folding the twenty-seven-day wait into every applicant estimate makes forecasts more honest while accepting the waste as permanent, and the team's own pair-programming proposal aims at touch time that the map shows barely matters.
questions.concept: Value stream mapping, queue time, and batch size at a hand-off
questions.question: A mortgage-origination team maps its value stream and finds an average lead time of 34 calendar days per application package. Roughly 7 days are hands-on work spread across intake, underwriting support, and document assembly; the remaining 27 days are spent waiting for a regulatory sign-off that an external compliance group performs in a batch every second Friday. At the next retrospective the team proposes adopting pair programming on the document-assembly tooling to "get faster." What is the BEST action for the agile practitioner?
choices: Reduce the seven days of hands-on work by standardizing intake and assembly, the part the team controls.
Send packages to compliance in one large batch every second Friday so that each review window is used fully.
Include the compliance wait in every package estimate so that forecasts given to applicants reflect the full thirty-four days.
Convene a joint working session with the compliance reviewers to shrink the sign-off batch and review more frequently.

questions.explanation: Backlog refinement is progressive: detail should increase as items approach implementation, so the nearest items get the most attention and distant items stay deliberately coarse until learning reduces their uncertainty. That directly fixes the reported symptom — top items arriving unclear — without adding time. Extending refinement to three hours doubles the cost of the same misallocation and elaborates items that may change or never be built. Having the product owner write acceptance criteria for the top items alone is the strongest alternative, because it at least aims attention at the right end of the backlog — but it removes the conversation that gives criteria their shared meaning, turning refinement into review of a handed-down specification. A three-minute timebox per item spreads attention evenly across 140 items, guaranteeing that the next ones pulled still arrive ambiguous.
questions.concept: Progressive elaboration and appropriate depth of refinement
questions.question: A cross-functional team maintaining a veterinary clinic scheduling product has a 140-item backlog. Refinement sessions run 90 minutes weekly, but the team spends most of that time debating the wording and estimates of items sitting 20 to 30 positions deep, and the top few items are still arriving at planning with unclear acceptance criteria. The product owner asks whether the team should extend refinement to three hours. What is the BEST response?
choices: Extend refinement to three hours each week so every backlog item gets discussed, keeping the wording and estimates of the distant items current
Have the product owner write acceptance criteria for the top items alone, so the team only reviews text she drafted beforehand
Refine depth-first: bring the nearest items to a ready state with clear acceptance criteria, and leave distant items coarse until they approach
Timebox every item to three minutes so the session covers more of the backlog and each item ends up carrying equal detail

questions.explanation: Little's Law relates average cycle time to average work in progress divided by average throughput. At 42 items in progress and 12 completed per week, average cycle time is about 3.5 weeks; holding throughput at 12 and capping work in progress at 24 gives about 2 weeks. The statement that cycle time rises to about 3.5 weeks inverts the relationship — it treats today's number as the improved state and claims that working on fewer items simultaneously makes each item slower. The claim that only adding people can shorten cycle time ignores the arithmetic entirely and reaches for capacity when the available lever is the size of the queue. The statement that throughput climbs to roughly 21 items per week contradicts the stem's stated condition of stable throughput and misreads Little's Law as a productivity multiplier; cutting work in progress often does help throughput indirectly by reducing context switching, but that is a second-order effect and not what the law asserts.
questions.concept: Interpreting flow metrics with Little's Law (WIP, throughput, cycle time)
questions.question: A support-and-enhancement team pulls all incoming work from a single queue. Over the past eight weeks it has completed an average of 12 items per week, and the board has held an average of 42 items between commitment and done. A stakeholder asks what to expect if the team enforces a policy capping items in progress at 24, with arrival rate and throughput otherwise stable. Which statement is the most defensible use of the team's flow data?
choices: Average cycle time would climb from about 2 weeks to 3.5 weeks, because a cap leaves fewer items moving at once.
Average cycle time is set by team size rather than work in progress, so only adding people shortens it.
Average throughput would rise in proportion to the cut in work in progress, reaching roughly 21 items per week instead.
Average cycle time should fall from about 3.5 weeks to about 2 weeks, provided throughput and arrival rate stay stable.

questions.explanation: Visualizing work is a diagnostic act, not a decorating act: the swollen Verifying column is a signal, and the team owns interpreting it. Walking the aged items together surfaces the real constraint (vendor slot scarcity, a skills bottleneck, oversized items, or rework) and lets the team choose the countermeasure — which may well include a new column or a limit, but chosen from evidence. Adding a column first makes the delay look normal and permanent; a board that renders a bottleneck as an accepted stage removes the very tension that drives improvement. Imposing a work-in-progress limit immediately is prescribing before understanding — the practitioner would be choosing the team's countermeasure for them, and an arbitrary limit set without knowing the cause simply pushes the queue upstream. Starting percent-complete reporting substitutes an output-flavored progress metric for flow transparency; it reports on stuck work rather than helping unstick it, and percent-complete on unfinished items is precisely the kind of illusory progress that flow measures such as cycle time and work item age replace.
questions.concept: Board design and bottleneck diagnosis vs. normalizing queues
questions.question: A distributed team maintaining a marine-freight tracking platform keeps their work visible on a shared electronic board with columns for Ready, Building, Verifying, and Done. Over the last six weeks the Verifying column has grown from three to eleven items while Building stays near two. Cycle time has more than doubled. In the team's improvement session, the tech lead proposes adding a new "Awaiting Vendor Test Slot" column so the board "reflects reality," and the sponsor separately asks the practitioner to start reporting a weekly percent-complete figure per item. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Add the new verification column so that the board mirrors what the team is actually doing, then re-measure cycle time a month later
Ask the team to walk the aging items in Verifying together and identify what is actually blocking flow before changing the board
Introduce a work-in-progress limit on Verifying immediately, since capping that column stops the queue from growing while the cause is found
Begin the weekly percent-complete reporting the sponsor asked for, since leadership visibility into the growing verification queue is what will bring help

questions.explanation: Little's Law in its practical flow form gives average cycle time as work in progress divided by throughput, and the stable, unchanged conditions described are exactly what makes the law applicable here: 24 items divided by 6 items per week equals 4 weeks. The same relationship identifies the fastest lever a team actually controls — cutting the number of items in progress lowers cycle time proportionally when throughput holds, so 12 items at 6 per week yields roughly 2 weeks. Adding two people to double weekly completions is the strongest wrong answer because its arithmetic works, but it is the slower and costlier lever: hiring takes weeks, throughput dips while newcomers ramp up, and limiting work in progress can be agreed today. Dividing throughput by work in progress inverts the formula and yields no meaningful duration. Quoting the single slowest item is cautious but wasteful; the disciplined version of that instinct is a percentile from the distribution, not the worst case seen.
questions.concept: Little's Law applied to cycle time and WIP
questions.question: A support-tooling team pulls work from a single queue. Over a stable eight-week period they averaged 24 items in progress and completed an average of 6 items per week; arrival rate and staffing were unchanged throughout. The team wants a defensible figure to quote customers for how long a newly pulled item takes to finish, and wants to know which lever would shorten that figure fastest. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Average cycle time is about 4 weeks, so halving items in progress to 12 while holding throughput would bring it to about 2 weeks
Average cycle time is about 4 weeks, and the fastest lever is adding two people so weekly completions rise from six items to twelve
Average cycle time is about 0.25 weeks, because dividing the six items finished each week by the 24 in progress gives the time per item
Average cycle time is about 4 weeks, but the only defensible quote is the slowest item the team finished in the eight weeks

questions.explanation: Vertical slicing keeps each piece independently valuable, testable and small enough to finish, which is exactly what INVEST asks for; shipping card payment for a single booking first also answers the product owner's real concern, because that slice genuinely serves a customer end to end and generates feedback on the riskiest part of the flow. Keeping the item whole with separate acceptance criteria per payment type creates the appearance of progress while nothing is releasable until the entire bundle lands. Splitting into card integration, invoicing rules, refunds and audit logging is the strongest alternative, since each part would fit an iteration — but these are component pieces nobody can demonstrate or release alone, and integration risk waits until the end. A spike into the provider may help later, yet it spends an iteration producing knowledge rather than a finishable item.
questions.concept: Vertical slicing and INVEST-based decomposition of oversized backlog items
questions.question: During refinement for a marine-freight booking platform, the team sizes the item "Customers can pay for a booking" and agrees it is larger than anything they have ever finished in a single iteration. It bundles card payment, invoicing for contract shippers, refunds, and a payment audit log. The product owner resists breaking it up, saying "half a payment feature is useless to a customer." What is the BEST response?
choices: Keep the item whole but write separate acceptance criteria for each payment type, so the team can show progress against those criteria while delivering the feature in one release.
Split the work by the parts it contains — card integration, invoicing rules, refund handling, and audit logging — so each piece is small enough to finish inside a single iteration.
Facilitate splitting it into independently valuable vertical slices — for example, card payment for a single booking first — and sequence them so each slice can be released and validated on its own.

Run a spike in the next iteration to explore what the payment provider actually supports, then re-estimate the item once the team understands what building each of the four payment capabilities involves.

questions.explanation: The recurring impediments show the retrospective is not producing real learning because one voice dominates. Changing the facilitation format — silent idea generation and structured turns before open discussion — equalizes airtime immediately, while private coaching helps the architect see the unintended silencing effect; together these address both the mechanism and the behavior. Inviting the engineering manager typically reduces candor further, since members are even less likely to raise problems in front of authority. Replacing the retrospective with an anonymous survey abandons the conversation entirely — anonymity may collect complaints but removes the dialogue and shared ownership that turn feedback into improvement, and it institutionalizes the assumption that open speech is unsafe. Splitting by location fragments the team, entrenches the divide between co-located and remote members, and leaves the dominance dynamic unaddressed whenever the whole team does meet.
questions.concept: Facilitation techniques for equal voice in distributed retrospectives
questions.question: A hybrid team split across three time zones holds its retrospectives on video. The co-located lead architect answers most questions first, remote members have contributed almost nothing for months, and the same impediments keep recurring even though delivery metrics look acceptable. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Invite the engineering manager to the next retrospective to draw out the quieter remote members, since a senior voice asking directly for their input will make room for them to speak
Redesign the retrospective to include silent writing and round-robin input so every member contributes before open discussion, and privately coach the architect on the effect of always speaking first

Replace the retrospective discussion with an anonymous survey each iteration, so remote members can report the recurring impediments honestly without having to interrupt the lead architect on the call
Run separate retrospectives for each location and carry the themes between them, so remote members can raise impediments without the architect answering every question ahead of them

questions.explanation: Diagnostic intuition is tacit knowledge — held in experience and hard to articulate — and tacit knowledge moves person-to-person through shared work, observation, and conversation, exactly what pairing during real incidents provides. Runbooks capture only the explicit fraction she can verbalize, which she has already said is small. A recorded lecture is one-way explicit transfer with no interaction with real situations. An external certification teaches generic industry practice, not the context-specific judgment the team actually wants to spread.
questions.concept: Tacit versus explicit knowledge transfer
questions.question: A platform team wants to spread the incident-diagnosis intuition of its most experienced reliability engineer, who says she 'can't really write down how she knows where to look.' Which knowledge-sharing approach best matches the nature of what the team is trying to transfer?
choices: Have her write her diagnostic heuristics into detailed runbooks the team can follow signal by signal
Record her narrating past incidents in a lecture series that new joiners watch on demand at their own pace
Enroll the team in an external incident-management certification so everyone shares a common diagnostic vocabulary
Pair teammates with her during live incident response so they absorb her approach by working alongside her

questions.explanation: New regulatory reality is exactly the kind of change agile teams harness rather than resist: reprioritizing the backlog to redesign the affected features now delivers a compliant, valuable release, and keeping governance informed respects the hybrid program's controls without freezing adaptation. Finishing the release as planned knowingly ships non-compliant features — protecting a date at the expense of value and legal exposure. Halting all development for a complete legal impact analysis is big-bang analysis; the team can keep delivering unaffected work while compliance questions are answered incrementally. Filing a change request while continuing to build the features as originally designed manufactures known waste — every additional hour on a non-compliant design must be redone.
questions.concept: Welcoming late-breaking regulatory change (responding to change over following a plan)
questions.question: A hybrid program is midway through a release when a data-privacy regulator publishes guidance that makes two approved features non-compliant as designed. Several team leads argue the program should finish the release as committed and address compliance in a follow-up project. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Deliver the release on the committed date and open a follow-on compliance project immediately afterward, recording the regulatory exposure in the program risk register
Pause work on the two affected features until the legal department completes a full impact analysis of the guidance and issues formal written direction to the program
Raise a change request through program governance and keep building the two features as designed until the change board rules on how the regulator's new guidance applies to them
Work with the product owner to reprioritize the backlog so the affected features are redesigned for compliance within the current release, keeping program governance informed

questions.explanation: The team is optimizing outputs — stories completed and demos applauded — while the outcome the product exists to produce is flat, so the corrective move is to make the outcome the iteration goal and put the evidence in front of the review. Rebuilding the business case around carousel click-through swaps the outcome for a proxy the enhancements are likelier to move, which flatters the chart while quietly lowering the bar the investment was justified against. A retrospective on why six enhancements failed is the strongest alternative, and that reflection is worth having — but it looks inward at process when the missing mechanism is outward: no goal has ever named an outcome and no review has inspected the data. Pausing delivery for two iterations of controlled experiments buys clean attribution at the cost of all value.
questions.concept: Outcome-based goals and value measurement versus output-based delivery
questions.question: A media streaming team has delivered eleven iterations of a personalized recommendations feature. Every iteration review is well attended, demos run smoothly, and stakeholders applaud. The product manager, however, reports to the team that the business case metric — the share of viewing sessions that start from a recommended title — has not moved since iteration three, even though six recommendation enhancements shipped. The team's iteration goals have all been phrased as lists of stories to complete. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Coach the team and product manager to frame the next iteration goal as a measurable change in recommendation-driven session starts, and instrument the increment so the review examines that evidence
Have the product manager rebuild the business case around a metric the enhancements are more likely to move, such as click-through on the recommendation carousel, so progress becomes visible
Hold a retrospective on why six enhancements failed to shift the metric and add the resulting improvement actions to the team's backlog before any further recommendation work is planned
Pause new recommendation work and spend the next two iterations running controlled experiments on what has already shipped, so the effect of the six enhancements can be isolated before building more

questions.explanation: Flow efficiency is the only measure among these that splits an item's elapsed time into active work and waiting, so it answers the first question directly. The cumulative flow diagram plots cumulative arrivals and departures per state over time, so the vertical thickness of each band shows exactly how each queue grew or shrank across the quarter — it is a history of the system, not a forecast. A probabilistic forecast built on the team's throughput history is what produces a date range with an attached confidence level; a cumulative flow diagram can suggest a trend but cannot express likelihood, and single-point velocity extrapolation yields a date with no confidence statement at all. The risk burndown chart plots the sum of residual risk exposure over successive iterations, so a falling line is the evidence that risk responses are working — no flow metric shows this, because risk exposure is not work sitting in a workflow state. The two most tempting confusions are pressing the cumulative flow diagram into forecasting, which mistakes a descriptive chart for a predictive one, and reading a burndown of remaining work as if it showed risk, which conflates scope with exposure.
questions.concept: Selecting the right flow and risk metric
questions.question: Match each question a team or stakeholder is asking (1-4) with the metric or chart that most directly answers it (A-D).
pairs: The team wants to know what proportion of an item's elapsed time was spent being actively worked on versus sitting in queues.
Flow efficiency (active time divided by total lead time)
A stakeholder asks how the size of the queue in each workflow state has changed over the past quarter, given arrival and completion rates.
Cumulative flow diagram
The product owner wants a delivery date range for a 30-item scope, expressed with a confidence level and derived from historical completion data.
Throughput-based probabilistic forecast (for example, Monte Carlo simulation)
The team wants evidence that the residual exposure from its identified threats is actually shrinking iteration over iteration.
Risk burndown chart

questions.explanation: The failure is a feedback delay: the team learns it built the wrong thing only at review, weeks after the misunderstanding occurred. Shortening that loop with brief, regular customer contact — arranged collaboratively with the product owner rather than around them — engages the actual customer and catches misinterpretation while it is still cheap to correct. A formal sign-off gate on written requirements adds process and pushes the team further toward treating documents as truth; signed requirements can still be misread. A dedicated clarification phase is big-bang analysis that assumes ambiguity can be talked away in advance, when the evidence shows finance recognizes the gap only on seeing something concrete. Having the product owner walk finance through each completed story at the review is the strongest rival and does structure the objections, but it leaves the loop at its current length, so a third of the work is still built before anyone learns it is wrong.
questions.concept: Shortening customer feedback loops to reduce rework
questions.question: A team building a self-service tax-filing feature has a product owner who forwards written requirements from the finance department but discourages direct contact with them, saying "they are busy during filing season." At the last two reviews, the finance staff who finally attended rejected roughly a third of the completed stories as "not what we meant." The team's velocity looks stable, but rework consumes about 30 percent of each iteration. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Introduce a sign-off gate where finance approves each written requirement before development starts, so the team builds only what the department has confirmed
Add a requirements-clarification phase before the next iteration so ambiguity in the forwarded documents is resolved before any story is pulled
Work with the product owner to arrange short, regular working sessions with finance representatives so the team can validate slices as they are built
Have the product owner walk finance through each completed story at the review, so objections are raised in one structured session every iteration

questions.explanation: Pairing and mobbing on real interface work transfers tacit knowledge — the judgment calls, quirks, and debugging instincts that never make it into documents — and starts reducing the bus factor immediately while the expert is still available to correct misunderstandings. Having her document the mainframe interface thoroughly captures explicit knowledge only, is untested by real use before she leaves, and spends her scarce remaining time writing rather than transferring skill. Bringing in a mainframe contractor imports generic skill, not knowledge of this specific interface, and recreates the single-expert dependency in someone who also leaves. Pulling the interface stories forward so she finishes them before her leave is the strongest alternative — it does clear the queue — but it concentrates even more of the work in one pair of hands, and any interface story arriving during those twelve weeks still has nobody who can take it.
questions.concept: Tacit knowledge transfer and reducing single-point-of-knowledge risk
questions.question: On a hybrid payroll-modernization program, one engineer is the only person who understands the batch interface to the legacy mainframe, and every story touching it queues behind her. She has just announced twelve weeks of parental leave starting in two months. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Have her document the mainframe interface thoroughly, since twelve weeks away is long enough for the details to fade
Bring in a mainframe contractor for the twelve-week leave, so interface stories keep flowing while she is away
Pull the interface stories forward so she finishes them before the leave, clearing the queue behind her
Set up pairing and mobbing sessions immediately so other engineers work the interface alongside her before she leaves

questions.explanation: Regulatory and privacy requirements are quality attributes of the increment rather than optional features, so bringing the team, product owner, and a compliance voice together to assess the exposure and decide whether the control belongs in the Definition of Done keeps the decision transparent and with the people accountable for it. Having the team simply add encryption inside the current story is the strongest alternative, because it does fix the plain-text storage quickly and treats protection as engineering quality — but it settles a compliance question without the compliance voice and hides the cost from the product owner. Ranking encryption first for the iteration after launch accepts a known compliance defect as shippable. Dropping the settlement report may prove right, but choosing it first is a unilateral scope cut made before anyone has assessed the exposure.
questions.concept: Definition of Done carrying regulatory and privacy quality attributes of the increment
questions.question: A payments team is two weeks from a release that opens a new merchant category. In refinement, a developer mentions that the settlement report will store merchant tax identifiers in plain text, which conflicts with the data-protection standard the company must meet in the target market. The product owner responds that the compliance item can be logged as technical debt because no regulator will look at the product for at least a year, and the launch date is committed. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Ask the team to add the encryption inside the current story as ordinary technical work, since protecting stored identifiers is an engineering quality concern rather than a scope decision
Bring the team, product owner, and a compliance representative together to assess the exposure and decide whether the protection belongs in the Definition of Done for this release
Add encryption of the tax identifiers to the backlog as the top-ranked item for the iteration after launch, so the release date holds and the gap closes within weeks
Drop the settlement report from the release so that no tax identifiers are stored in plain text anywhere, and the new merchant category still opens on the planned date

questions.explanation: Making delegation explicit — jointly classifying decisions, agreeing which ones the team owns now, and deliberately widening that boundary over time — respects the lead's quality concern, gives the team real authority, and gives the lead a safe, incremental path to letting go. Telling the team to decide and inform him afterward undermines the lead, invites a trust rupture, and teaches the team to work around leadership instead of with it. Escalating to the lead's manager to strip out the approvals forces change on the lead before any direct collaborative attempt, which usually produces resentment and covert re-imposition of control. Taking over the approvals personally swaps one bottleneck for another and moves the team no closer to owning its own decisions.
questions.concept: Delegation levels and decision boundaries
questions.question: A Lean delivery team at a power utility has a team lead who was previously the group's supervisor. Every design decision — large or small — waits in his review queue for sign-off, some for a week. Members have stopped proposing ideas, saying "he'll change it anyway." The lead tells the agile practitioner he is "protecting quality." What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Advise the team to make routine design decisions and inform the lead afterward, so work stops waiting a week in his review queue for a sign-off
Ask the lead's manager to take the sign-off step out of the workflow, so decisions stop queuing while the lead settles into his new role on the team
Work with the lead and the team to classify decision types and agree explicitly which decisions the team owns outright, widening that set as confidence grows
Offer to review the smaller design decisions yourself so nothing sits for a week, leaving the lead free to concentrate on the quality he says he is protecting

questions.explanation: The diagram has already located the constraint; the useful next act is to share that evidence with the group that owns it and agree how work will be pulled through it. Data-led collaboration across the boundary is what changes system throughput, and it treats the security group as a partner rather than an obstacle. An expedite lane only reshuffles the order of items after the wait and does nothing about the wait itself, while eroding the pull policy for everyone else. Starting more items to keep people busy raises WIP, lengthens lead time further, and mistakes resource utilization for flow. Deleting the column erases the single most important fact on the board — where value stops moving — and makes the metrics flattering rather than true.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagrams, queues, and cross-boundary WIP policy
questions.question: A claims platform team pulls work across a board with WIP limits. Over eight weeks the cumulative flow diagram shows the band for "awaiting external security review" widening steadily while every other band stays stable; average lead time has nearly doubled. The security review group is a separate department with its own queue and its own priorities. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Create an expedite lane so that items coming back from the security group are pulled ahead of everything else, protecting lead time for work that has already waited its turn in a queue outside the team's control.

Have the team start additional items whenever work is waiting on security review, so that capacity is never idle and the board keeps showing steady progress through the columns the team controls while the external step clears in parallel.

Take the flow data to a joint working session with the team and the security group, make the queue visible to both, and agree a pull policy — earlier engagement, a review WIP limit, or reserved review capacity.

Remove the security review column from the board and track that step outside the team's metrics, since the delay belongs to another department and its queue distorts the team's cycle-time data and the improvement targets the team owns.

questions.explanation: The team already has evidence pointing at one specific cause, so the highest-value first move is to understand it fully with the people who do the work and let them design the countermeasure — typically building quality in by making environment configuration automated and identical across environments, so the defect class becomes impossible rather than merely reviewed for. An architecture review board plus a signed checklist adds a queue and a handoff to every change, lengthening lead time while doing nothing about configuration drift that no architect would catch in a design review. A manual regression pass adds inspection after the fact, is unlikely to detect environment-specific values, and pushes the team toward slower, larger batches. Naming a single accountable release owner converts a systemic problem into an individual one; it invites blame, suppresses the honest reporting that produced the incident notes, and leaves the drift in place.
questions.concept: Blameless root-cause analysis versus added process controls
questions.question: A logistics routing service has been rolled back three times in six weeks. The delivery manager proposes a mandatory architecture review board for every change plus a signed release checklist. The team's own incident notes show that all three rollbacks traced to configuration values that differ between the staging and production environments. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Support the review board and the signed checklist, since three rollbacks in six weeks show changes are reaching production with too little scrutiny.
Have the team add a manual regression pass against production settings before each release, so configuration mismatches are caught before customers see them.
Name a senior engineer as release owner accountable for approving every deployment, so someone checks the environment values before each change ships.
Facilitate a blameless root-cause session on the environment configuration differences and let the team propose the smallest change that removes the cause.

questions.explanation: A recurring defect class is a system signal, so understanding the cause with the people who do the work and the person feeling the pain, then letting the team build the check into the pipeline, both removes the defect source and gives the operations director better evidence than a manual pass ever would. Accepting the reconciliation sign-off for three releases while investigating in parallel is the strongest rival, since it does restore the director's confidence immediately, but it adds two days of inspection to every release and temporary gates are rarely removed once the calendar depends on them. Adding a rounding item to the definition of done with a second developer verifying every tax calculation institutionalizes manual double-checking, scales badly, and still rests on human vigilance over the rounding paths nobody has thought of. A hardening iteration to sweep the tax engine pauses normal delivery and treats a permanent capability as a one-off cleanup that the next change can quietly undo.
questions.concept: Root-cause analysis versus inspection gates; quality built in
questions.question: For the third release in a row, a payroll tax engine has leaked a currency-rounding defect into production. The operations director, visibly frustrated, proposes a mandatory manual reconciliation sign-off before every release, which would add two days to each release cycle. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Accept the reconciliation sign-off for the next three releases while the team investigates the failures in parallel, since the operations director's confidence has to be restored before any change that lengthens the release cycle can reasonably be negotiated away.

Ask the team to add a rounding item to the definition of done and have a second developer independently verify every tax calculation before a story is called complete, so the defect class is caught inside the team.

Propose a hardening iteration before the next payroll release so the team can sweep the rounding logic across the whole tax engine, add the missing calculation tests, and clear the defect class entirely before normal delivery resumes.

Facilitate a blameless root-cause analysis with the team and the operations director, then have the team build the countermeasure into the pipeline, such as automated characterization tests for the rounding rules whose results are visible on every release.

questions.explanation: The board is hiding the real constraint: a single-person dependency. Making blockers explicit turns an invisible queue into visible data the team can act on, whether by pairing to spread database skills, swarming to finish started items, or pulling work that does not need the specialist. That treats the work-in-progress limit as a signal rather than a nuisance and keeps the improvement decision with the team. Raising the limit to nine removes the very signal that surfaced the problem and will push cycle time higher, since more parallel work means longer queues. Telling developers to stop pulling until work in progress falls back to four is the strongest alternative and restores an agreement the team made for itself, but it is a directive rather than a diagnosis: the specialist dependency stays unnamed and the nine started items still have no route to finishing. Requesting a second specialist spends money before anyone has tested whether skill-sharing would resolve it, and hiring will not shorten today's cycle time.
questions.concept: WIP limits, blocked-work visualization, and cycle time
questions.question: A Kanban team maintaining a hospital bed-management platform has agreed WIP limits, but the board shows nine items in "In Development" against a limit of four. The team lead explains that items sit there because the single database specialist is on leave, so developers pull new work rather than idle. Cycle time has climbed from 6 days to 19 days over two months. What is the BEST response?
choices: Raise the development limit to nine so the board honestly reflects the way the team is working while its only database specialist is away on leave
Bring the team together to make the blocked-on-specialist dependency explicit on the board and decide together how to unblock or reduce it
Have developers stop pulling new items until work in progress falls back inside the agreed limit of four, restoring the policy the team set for itself
Ask the department head to fund a second database specialist so the constraint is removed before cycle time climbs beyond nineteen days

questions.explanation: Getting a small number of practicing adjusters in front of a working increment, exercising a real claim, closes the loop where the rework is actually generated — the gap between what the proxy approves and how the work is really done. Involving the analyst and sponsor in arranging it keeps the relationship intact and treats her as an ally rather than an obstacle. A user acceptance gate with adjuster sign-off is the strongest rival, since it does put adjusters in front of the software and gives their judgment formal weight, but it leaves the feedback at the end of the quarter, so the same rework arrives on the same schedule with more ceremony attached. Writing far more detailed acceptance criteria up front is big-bang analysis: screen sequence and terminology problems surface when people use software, not when they read a specification. Circulating a recorded walkthrough for written comments is one-way and low fidelity — adjusters react to a video rather than driving a real claim.
questions.concept: Customer proxies versus direct end-user involvement
questions.question: On a claims-modernization program the insurer supplies a single business analyst as the team's point of contact. She attends every review and approves each increment. Practicing claims adjusters have never seen the software; each quarter, when a release finally reaches them, they raise dozens of change requests about screen sequence and terminology. The analyst maintains that her approval should be sufficient. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Work with the analyst and the sponsor to bring two or three practicing adjusters into the next review and walk a real claim through the increment with them.

Introduce a user acceptance test gate with adjuster sign-off before each quarterly release, so terminology and sequence problems are caught before the software reaches adjusters doing real claim work.
Ask the analyst to write far richer acceptance criteria covering screen sequence, terminology, and decision points, so the team builds what adjusters expect the very first time.
Record a walkthrough of each increment and circulate it to the adjuster group for written comments, so their input reaches the team without pulling adjusters off live claims.

questions.explanation: The Stacey Matrix positions work by uncertainty on two axes: how far stakeholders are from agreement on requirements, and how far the team is from certainty about technology. The wearable coaching feature is far from both — no one knows whether users want it and the sensor technology is unstable — placing it in the complex zone where short cycles, experiments, and frequent feedback pay off most. The repeat payroll migration has known requirements and proven technology; it sits near the simple corner, where a predictive plan is efficient and iteration adds little. The statutory filing has requirements fixed by law and a well-understood production process — low uncertainty on both axes. The vendor system installation may be complicated, but a proven playbook exists, so the uncertainty that agile is designed to burn down is largely absent. Agile is not wrong for those three, but they are the cases where it adds least; the question asks where it adds most.
questions.concept: Stacey Matrix and agile suitability — matching approach to uncertainty
questions.question: Applying the Stacey Matrix, which of the following initiatives would gain the MOST from an adaptive (agile) approach rather than a predictive one?
choices: Rolling out a vendor's warehouse scanning system by following the standard implementation playbook the vendor has run at forty comparable sites
Repeating a payroll data migration that this same team delivered for a sister company last year on tooling they already know well
Creating a wearable-device coaching feature where user desirability is unproven and the underlying sensor technology is still maturing
Producing the annual regulatory filing whose format and required content are fixed by statute and unchanged for three years

questions.explanation: Proposing an early, working slice of the highest-value rider journey and letting real rider feedback shape what comes next embodies the agile mindset: working software over comprehensive documentation, welcoming change, and a short loop between assumption and evidence. Running workshops to document and freeze a full year of scope invests heavily in predictions that will be wrong precisely where uncertainty is highest, and it delays all value delivery. Telling the sponsor that software differs from construction and asking her to trust the team until the first release is directionally right about the difference, but it asks for faith instead of offering evidence; a sponsor who has always managed risk through documents will not trade that for a promise, and she is given nothing concrete to hold. Accepting the sign-off and adding change control treats change as an exception to be administered rather than an expected source of learning, adding process instead of adapting the approach.
questions.concept: Agile Manifesto values and iterative value delivery vs. big up-front requirements
questions.question: A city transit authority has hired an agile practitioner to help deliver a new trip-planning app. The sponsor, who has only run infrastructure construction projects, insists that development cannot begin until she has signed off on a complete requirements document covering every feature for the next year. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Run a series of requirements workshops so that the full year of scope is documented and signed off before any development work begins.
Explain that software work differs from construction, and ask the sponsor to trust the team's approach until the first release has proved that it works.
Propose delivering a small working slice of the highest-value rider journey early, then using real rider feedback to shape what gets built next.
Accept the sign-off requirement and add a formal change-control process, so that requirements can be revised as rider needs become clearer.

questions.explanation: A blameless joint root-cause workshop brings both teams to the same table, replaces blame with a shared examination of the system, and produces causes the group actually owns — the necessary first step before any structural change is chosen. Supporting the change-approval board as an interim control adds an approval gate before anyone understands the causes; it slows flow and typically increases batch size and risk rather than reducing escapes. Publishing defect-origin data by pipeline stage is the strongest alternative, because the measure is systemic rather than personal and the workshop will want exactly this data — but posted to two teams already blaming each other, the chart becomes ammunition each side reads as proof about the other. Embedding a release engineer to own the handoff papers over the wall instead of dismantling it, and creates a new single point of failure.
questions.concept: Blameless root-cause analysis across team boundaries
questions.question: In a Lean flow-based delivery group, a defect escapes to production every few weeks. The operations team blames developers for "throwing code over the wall"; developers blame operations for configuration drift. A director, tired of the finger-pointing, wants to institute a change-approval board for all releases. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Support the change-approval board as an interim control while the teams rebuild trust and escapes are watched
Facilitate a blameless joint root-cause workshop tracing the last three escaped defects to their systemic causes
Publish defect-origin data by pipeline stage so both teams can see objectively where the escapes enter
Embed a release engineer between the teams to own the handoff and absorb configuration drift

questions.explanation: In its practical flow form, average cycle time equals average work in progress divided by average throughput: 24 items divided by 6 items per week is 4 weeks. Because throughput is pinned by fixed staffing, the only remaining lever in the relationship is work in progress, so halving it to about 12 items drives average cycle time toward 2 weeks — exactly what stakeholders asked for, achieved by starting less and finishing more. The 6-week answer reports a figure the data does not produce (6 is the weekly throughput, not a duration) and then prescribes the one lever the scenario has explicitly ruled out. The suggestion to pull more items onto the board inverts the law: adding work in progress at fixed throughput lengthens cycle time, and the extra context switching usually reduces throughput as well. Demanding story points confuses relative sizing with flow measurement; Little's Law works on item counts and elapsed time, and the stated stability of arrivals, departures, and item size is precisely the condition under which the heuristic holds.
questions.concept: Practical application of Little's Law to shorten cycle time
questions.question: A support-and-enhancement team measures its board across a stable ten-week window: average work in progress is 24 items and average throughput is 6 items per week, with arrivals and departures roughly balanced and item sizes fairly consistent. Stakeholders want faster turnaround, but staffing is fixed and throughput is not expected to rise. Using Little's Law as a practical planning heuristic, which statement is MOST defensible?
choices: Average cycle time is about 6 weeks, so halving it would mean lifting throughput to roughly 12 items per week, which fixed staffing rules out entirely
Average cycle time is about 4 weeks, and pulling more items onto the board would keep everyone fully busy, lifting throughput and shortening cycle time along with it
Average cycle time cannot be projected from these figures until every item on the board is sized in story points and converted into a velocity forecast
Average cycle time is about 4 weeks, and with throughput fixed, reducing average work in progress to about 12 items should move average cycle time toward 2 weeks

questions.explanation: Pairing or mobbing on the constrained work attacks both problems at once: the queue moves faster now, and every session grows generalizing specialists so the single point of failure shrinks permanently — collective ownership is the durable fix. Requesting an additional expert from a functional manager outsources the team's problem, adds cost and onboarding delay, and leaves knowledge siloed in two heads instead of one. Deferring payments work in the backlog sequences around the constraint rather than addressing it, likely delaying customer value. An intake template merely organizes the queue feeding the bottleneck — it formalizes the silo and the side-channel emailing instead of dissolving them.
questions.concept: Generalizing specialists and collective ownership over queue management
questions.question: On an XP-influenced product team, only one developer understands the payments module. Her personal queue keeps growing while teammates sit partially idle, and members have started emailing her work requests directly instead of raising them at the board. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Encourage teammates to pair or mob with the payments developer on her queued items so the knowledge spreads while the bottleneck drains
Ask the functional manager to add a second developer with payments experience so the module no longer runs through one person's queue
Re-sequence the backlog so payments items wait until her queue drains, smoothing flow while teammates take up work they can already do
Introduce a standard intake form so requests reach her through the board instead of email, making the payments queue visible to everyone

questions.explanation: The data localizes the constraint precisely: 19 of 23 days sit in a queue in front of a shared resource the team does not own. Making that constraint visible to the parties who actually control it, the three consuming teams and the rig owner, is the only move that can change the system, and it collaborates before prescribing. Hiring contract testers adds capacity downstream of the bottleneck rather than at it; testers without rig access cannot shorten a rig-access queue, and the spend is committed before anyone has confirmed the constraint. Capping Awaiting Rig at three is a plausible Kanban action, but a limit on a queue whose supply the team does not control simply pushes the wait upstream into To Do, where it becomes invisible, so it belongs after the constraint conversation rather than before it. Smaller stories may help at the margin but do not touch booking contention: more, smaller items still queue for the same rig, and the practitioner would be tuning local team behavior while the systemic constraint stays hidden.
questions.concept: Bottleneck identification and queue wait time in a Kanban system with a shared external resource
questions.question: A hardware-firmware team runs a Kanban board with columns To Do, Dev, Awaiting Rig, Integration Test, Done. Awaiting Rig has no work-in-process limit and holds 14 items; the shared test rig is booked by three teams and is owned by a separate lab group. Firmware cycle time has grown from 6 days to 23 days, and 19 of those 23 days are spent in Awaiting Rig. At the flow review, the engineering manager proposes hiring two contract testers to "work down the queue faster." What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Back the hiring proposal, because two additional testers would move the fourteen queued items through integration test faster and bring the twenty-three day cycle time back toward the six days it used to be
Make the rig contention visible as the constraint by putting the queue data in front of the three consuming teams and the rig owner, and agreeing a shared scheduling or capacity decision with them
Put a work-in-process limit of three on Awaiting Rig at once, so the queue stops growing and developers can see the constraint before they pull anything new out of the To Do column
Have the team slice firmware stories thinner so more of them fit inside its existing rig bookings, raising the number of items verified per booked window without asking the lab group

questions.explanation: Putting the two working permit types in front of a small group of real applicants now converts assumptions into evidence while two iterations of rework are still affordable; a rough but working slice is exactly what early feedback is for, and the two most common permit types are the highest-traffic part of the journey. Recording a walkthrough for the product owner keeps the end-of-iteration-three date intact and gathers comment from the person already closest to the team, which is the least new information available to it. Asking the permit clerks to try the two types is the strongest rival — they know the journey and are easy to reach — but insiders cannot reproduce the confusions a first-time applicant hits, which is where the risk actually lives. Putting the slice on a public beta site and reading analytics at the end of iteration three exposes the rough version widely, defers the learning to the same late point, and shows what applicants did without ever explaining why.
questions.concept: Validating a thin end-to-end slice with real users
questions.question: A cross-functional team is rebuilding the permit-application journey for a municipal water utility. The product owner has scheduled the first citizen-facing demonstration for the end of the third iteration, "once the whole journey works end to end." After iteration one the team already has a rough but working version of the two most common permit types. What is the BEST response?
choices: Hold to the schedule but record a walkthrough of the two working permit types and ask the product owner for comments before the next iteration
Ask the permit clerks who process the applications to try the two working permit types this week, since they know the journey well
Arrange for a small group of real applicants to use the two working permit types this week and feed what is learned into the next iteration
Put the two working permit types on a public beta site and review the usage analytics with the product owner at the end of the third iteration

questions.explanation: Story mapping's distinctive contribution is the two-dimensional arrangement of items along the user's activity sequence, which exposes gaps in the journey and lets a team slice a release horizontally across the whole flow rather than building one area deep. Kano analysis is specifically about the non-linear relationship between a feature's presence and customer satisfaction, separating must-have basics — whose absence causes dissatisfaction but whose presence delights no one — from performance features and delighters. A definition of ready is the team's own shared guideline about the information an item typically needs before work starts; it is useful as a conversation aid and harmful when enforced as a rigid gate that blocks collaboration. A minimum marketable feature is defined by releasability and recognizable benefit, which is precisely what distinguishes it from a journey arrangement, a satisfaction model, or a start-readiness guideline.
questions.concept: Distinguishing story mapping, Kano, definition of ready, and MMF
questions.question: A team is preparing its backlog for an upcoming quarter and uses several distinct product techniques. Match each technique on the left to the description that best captures its distinctive purpose.
pairs: Story mapping
D: Arranges backlog items along the sequence of user activities so the team can see the whole journey and slice releases across it
Kano analysis
A: Classifies candidate features by how customer satisfaction responds to their presence or absence, separating expected basics from delighters
Definition of Ready (used as a team guideline)
C: A shared, adaptable understanding of the information a backlog item generally needs before the team can start it confidently
Minimum Marketable Feature
B: The smallest coherent piece of functionality that can be released and produce recognizable benefit for a customer or the business

questions.explanation: The board shows Testing holding seven items against a limit of three while upstream columns are at or under their limits — Testing is the bottleneck starving Done.
