The fastest flow improvement is to subordinate the rest of the system to the bottleneck: pause new pulls into Development and swarm existing capacity onto the testing queue. Raising the Testing limit to seven removes the very signal that exposed the problem and lets even more inventory pile up in front of the constraint. Requesting two additional testers adds cost and takes weeks before anyone has even tried to exploit existing capacity — team members outside Testing can often verify, automate, or pair right now. Splitting Testing into two columns adds board structure without moving a single item; the queue is already painfully visible at more than double its limit.
questions.concept: bottlenecks
questions.question: A team's throughput has fallen for two consecutive weeks. Based on the exhibit, what should the team do FIRST to improve flow?
choices: Raise the Testing limit to seven so the board matches the real workload the team carries
Stop pulling new items into Development and swarm to clear the items stuck in Testing
Add two testers so Testing can keep pace with what Development is finishing daily
Split Testing into a waiting column and an active column to make the queue visible

questions.explanation: The team has sliced horizontally by technical layer, which violates the independent, valuable, and testable qualities of INVEST: nothing is demonstrable, feedback is deferred to the end, and risk piles up in the final integration. Re-slicing vertically — a complete but narrow path through screen, service, and data for one fare type — gives a working slice each iteration and real feedback while it is cheap to act on. Pulling all four layered items into one iteration is the strongest alternative, since the flow would at least be shown working, but it keeps the layer as the unit of work and turns the whole refund capability into one all-or-nothing commitment that fails together if any layer slips. Writing acceptance criteria for each layer makes the layers checkable rather than valuable: a database table can pass its criteria while no customer can request a refund. Merging the four back into a single estimate hides the slicing problem inside a large number and makes forecasting and flow worse.
questions.concept: INVEST and vertical story slicing
questions.question: During refinement for an airline's refund platform, a team breaks the epic "self-service refund request" into four backlog items: build the refund screen, build the refund service endpoint, add the refund tables to the database, and wire the pieces together. The product owner points out that none of the first three can be demonstrated or validated on its own. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Keep the four layered items but pull all of them into the same iteration, so the epic is joined up and demonstrated as one working refund flow at the iteration review.
Have the product owner write acceptance criteria for each of the four items, so the refund screen, the service endpoint, and the database tables can each be validated as they are finished.
Facilitate re-slicing the epic into thin end-to-end items — for example, a refund request for a single fare type — each of which can be built, tested, and shown independently.
Merge the four items back into the original epic and estimate it as a single number, since the pieces only produce value for a customer once the whole flow is finished.

questions.explanation: Keeping the radiator honest while preparing explanatory context turns transparency into an asset: executives who see real blockers are exactly the people who can remove organizational impediments, and reframing the manager's discomfort as a chance to get help coaches him rather than fights him. Swapping the Blocked column for a summary slide during the walk-through converts an information radiator into a marketing display and teaches the organization that inconvenient data is negotiable. Letting the team decide is genuinely respectful of self-management and is the closest call here, but it leaves the team to absorb their own manager's pressure alone and skips the coaching conversation the practitioner is best placed to have. Moving anything blocked more than two weeks into a holding area hides precisely the items that most need executive attention — the oldest blocks are the signal, not the noise.
questions.concept: Transparency and information radiators
questions.question: An engineering manager at a medical-device firm asks the agile practitioner to remove the 'Blocked' column from the team's wall board before the quarterly executive walk-through, saying the number of blocked items 'will invite uncomfortable questions.' What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Replace the Blocked column with a summary slide for the walk-through and restore the board afterward, so executives get a clear picture without facing a wall of red cards
Ask the team to decide together whether the column stays, since the board belongs to them and the manager's request is theirs to answer rather than the practitioner's
Explain that visible blockers are what enable leaders to help, and offer to prepare context so executives understand what the column shows and what support is needed
Keep the column but move anything blocked more than two weeks into a separate holding area, so the board shows current work and the older blocks sit elsewhere

questions.explanation: Privacy and regulatory controls for identifiable health data are quality attributes of a releasable increment, not optional scope, so folding them into Done and reslicing to a narrower compliant scope preserves both the constraint and the flow of value, and it brings the specialist into the team's conversation rather than into an approval gate. Logging them as technical debt for later prioritization treats a non-negotiable obligation as a tradeable backlog item and produces an increment that cannot lawfully be used. Flagging the feature on for real patients while the controls are missing still processes identifiable data without consent or retention limits; a feature flag limits blast radius, not legal exposure. Halting all work pending complete written legal guidance stops value entirely, converts a collaboration into a handoff, and asks for exhaustive up-front certainty when a targeted conversation about this slice would unblock the team in hours.
questions.concept: Compliance and privacy constraints embedded in the Definition of Done
questions.question: A health-tech team is one day from the iteration review of a symptom-tracking feature that stores identifiable patient records. During a walkthrough, a developer mentions that consent capture, data-retention limits and the privacy impact assessment were parked as "hardening work for later" so the feature could be demonstrated on time. The feature works, and the product owner is keen to switch a small group of real patients onto it straight after the review. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Let the review go ahead with the working feature and record the consent capture, retention limits and privacy assessment as technical debt for the product owner to weigh against other items competing for space in the next iteration, since the feature already works

Switch a small group of real patients on behind a flag so the team gets genuine usage feedback on the tracker, and run the consent, retention and assessment work in parallel so that no schedule time is lost before the launch

Work with the team and the privacy specialist to treat the consent and retention controls as part of Done for this feature, keep real patient data out of it until they exist, and reslice so a narrower but compliant version can ship

Halt all work on the symptom tracker until the legal department issues written guidance covering the whole product area, so that nobody on the team is left interpreting patient privacy obligations without a documented legal position from counsel standing behind those decisions

questions.explanation: The map shows 15.0 of 19.5 days is waiting and only 4.5 days is work — roughly 23% flow efficiency — and the two release-and-review queues alone account for 10.5 days, more than half the lead time. Attacking those queues with the people who own them, through smaller and more frequent releases and a review turnaround agreement, targets where the time actually goes. Starting with the 3.0-day integration-test wait is the strongest alternative because it is a real queue the team owns outright, but it is under a third of the delay, and the idea that other groups must be earned before they can be approached is a self-imposed limit rather than a fact about them. Pair programming would trim about 1.25 days from 19.5 while consuming two people per item, optimizing the longest touch time rather than the longest delay. Batching items into one monthly release cuts trips through the board but enlarges the batch, so the average item waits longer and a rejection costs more.
questions.concept: Value stream mapping, flow efficiency, and queue-driven lead time
questions.question: The claims portal team, alarmed by a 19.5-day average lead time, has proposed adopting pair programming to cut development time roughly in half. Based on the value stream map, what should the agile practitioner recommend the team do FIRST?
choices: Attack the 3.0-day integration-test wait first, since it is the one delay the team owns outright, and leave the approval board and peer review queues alone until the team has proved to those other groups that it can improve its own flow.

Proceed with pair programming and measure the effect on lead time after two iterations, since halving the longest single work activity on the map is the change with the clearest and most easily measurable payback for everyone on the team.

Take the two largest queues — the 6.0-day wait for the release approval board and the 4.5-day wait for peer review — to the team and the approval group, and experiment with smaller, more frequent releases and a same-day review agreement.

Invite the release approval board into the team's iteration reviews and batch several items into each larger release, so the board has to look at the queue only once a month rather than holding each individual item for six days.

questions.explanation: Inviting the newcomer's perspective on topics where she has expertise, and visibly appreciating what she offers, builds the psychological safety that makes voluntary contribution feel low-risk — the practitioner changes the environment rather than the person. Telling her privately that participation is expected applies directive pressure and treats silence as a compliance problem instead of a safety problem. Involving her functional manager escalates outside the team and could embarrass her, further reducing safety. Mandating that everyone speak forces performative participation; working agreements should be co-created by the team, and compelled speech is not the same as feeling safe to speak.
questions.concept: Inclusive facilitation to build psychological safety for new members
questions.question: A Scrum team building interactive exhibits for a museum's digital-experience program has just added a data analyst, the team's first non-developer hire. During the last three refinement sessions she has not spoken, even when stories touch visitor-analytics work she knows well. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Tell the analyst privately that speaking up in refinement is expected of everyone here, so she knows what the team wants
Ask the analyst's functional manager to encourage her to contribute in refinement, since he has standing with her
Model inclusive behaviors in refinement by inviting her perspective on analytics stories and visibly valuing her input
Add a working agreement that every member speaks at least once in each refinement session, so no voice goes unheard

questions.explanation: The question leadership is asking is behavioral - does drop-off fall - and only real customers making real onboarding decisions can answer it. A small toggled release of a thin slice produces that evidence within weeks at low blast radius, which is early feedback on the outcome rather than on the artifact. A usability walkthrough with internal staff gives valuable feedback on usability, but experienced internal processors are not the population whose drop-off is in question and their behavior does not predict a prospect's abandonment. Demonstrating the finished redesign in month three is feedback after the investment is fully sunk - it validates nothing early and leaves no room to change course. Instrumenting the existing flow builds a useful baseline and is worth doing, but measurement infrastructure alone tests no hypothesis; it postpones the actual learning until the redesign ships in full.
questions.concept: Thin-slice release to real users to validate an outcome hypothesis
questions.question: A product team is midway through a three-month effort to replace a customer onboarding flow. Leadership wants an early read on whether the redesigned flow actually reduces drop-off, and the team debates how to get it. Which approach most directly embodies seeking early feedback on the intended outcome?
choices: Run a usability walkthrough of the high-fidelity mockups with eight internal staff who process onboarding applications daily, noting where they hesitate
Demonstrate the finished redesign to leadership and the customer advisory group at the end of the three-month effort and gather their reactions
Instrument the existing onboarding flow now so a rich drop-off baseline is already in place by the time the redesigned flow finally ships
Release the redesigned first two steps to 5 percent of real customers behind a feature toggle and compare their drop-off against the existing flow

questions.explanation: The team defers not because it lacks formal authority but because it lacks a shared basis for judging tradeoffs. Turning the vision into concrete decision filters — what this product optimizes for and what it deliberately sacrifices — gives the team the intent it needs to decide at the point of information, which is what genuine empowerment requires. A daily office hour makes deferral faster without reducing it; the product manager remains the gate, and refinement still stalls whenever she is away. Granting the team authority over tradeoffs worth less than a day, reviewed weekly, is a defensible delegation move that would relieve some waiting, yet permission is not the missing ingredient — without shared criteria the team still cannot judge speed against configurability, and the threshold itself becomes the new argument. Sitting in on customer interviews builds real empathy, but two members once a month works slowly and leaves the rest of the team without the intent.
questions.concept: Translating shared vision into decision filters for decentralized decision-making
questions.question: During refinement, a team routinely defers every tradeoff question — 'speed versus configurability,' 'polish versus scope' — to the product manager, even on small items, stalling work whenever she is unavailable. Which leadership action would MOST reduce this dependency?
choices: Ask the product manager to hold a short daily office hour for refinement questions so the team's tradeoffs are answered without a long wait
Hold a working session that translates the product vision into a few explicit decision filters the team applies to tradeoffs itself
Agree that the team decides any tradeoff worth less than a day of work and reviews the choices it made with her once a week
Invite two team members to sit in on customer interviews each month so they build a firsthand feel for what users value most

questions.explanation: Coaching assumes the capability or knowledge already exists and only needs to be surfaced through questions; here there is a genuine knowledge gap, which is precisely what training exists for — teach the mechanics, then return to coaching as competence develops. Persisting with open-ended questions for another two weeks cannot draw out knowledge the team does not yet possess, which is exactly why the first two weeks changed nothing. Switching to mentoring and sharing how earlier teams held their limits offers useful context and is the most tempting alternative, but mentoring passes on personal experience one-to-one and still does not teach a whole team the mechanics it is missing. Configuring the board to block any card that breaches the limit enforces the policy without building understanding; people route around a tool that stops them for reasons they cannot explain, and the team never learns to relieve the bottleneck the limit exposes.
questions.concept: Coaching vs mentoring vs training: selecting by type of gap
questions.question: A team new to pull systems keeps violating its WIP limits because members genuinely do not understand how the mechanics of a pull system work. For two weeks the agile practitioner has responded only with open-ended coaching questions, and nothing has changed. Which adjustment best applies the distinction between coaching, mentoring, and training?
choices: Keep to open-ended questions for another two weeks, since learning the team discovers itself holds better than instruction
Deliver direct training on pull-system mechanics first, then shift back to coaching as the team's competence grows
Switch to mentoring and share how earlier teams the practitioner worked with held their limits under delivery pressure
Have the board configured to block any card that breaches the limit, so the system enforces what the team cannot

questions.explanation: Delivering a thin slice of working functionality early and refining the remaining requirements through frequent feedback embodies the agile mindset: when regulations and vendor APIs change frequently, working software and short feedback loops reduce the risk of building to stale specifications. Timeboxing the analysis to a few weeks and documenting only the stable regulatory requirements is the strongest alternative, a sensible tailoring move that does target the volatility — but it still front-loads a documentation phase before anything is built, and it assumes the team can tell in advance which rules will hold still. Converting the analyst's requirements into user stories with acceptance criteria changes the format of the upfront specification without changing its size or its timing. Prototyping the vendor integrations first is useful risk reduction, yet it is paired here with finishing the full requirements document afterward, which preserves the big upfront analysis this environment cannot support.
questions.concept: Agile vs predictive thinking; welcoming change through iterative delivery
questions.question: An agile practitioner joins an insurance claims-processing modernization effort. A business analyst proposes spending the first four months documenting every requirement in detail so that "nothing is missed," even though the regulations and third-party vendor APIs the system depends on change frequently. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Timebox the analysis to a few weeks and document in detail only the requirements tied to regulations that are known to be stable
Ask the analyst to capture the requirements as user stories with acceptance criteria so they are easier to revise across the four months
Suggest delivering a thin slice of working functionality early and refining the remaining requirements through frequent feedback
Prototype the vendor API integrations first to retire the technical risk, then finish the full requirements document as planned

questions.explanation: She has a goal but has not yet diagnosed her own obstacle, which is precisely the situation coaching serves: through questions and reflection she discovers what blocks her and owns the actions that follow, building durable capability. Training transfers a defined skill efficiently — but no skill gap has been identified yet, so a course would be prescribing a cure before the diagnosis and might target the wrong thing entirely. Mentoring shares the mentor's experience and pathway, which can be valuable later, but leading with 'do what I did' substitutes someone else's answer for her self-discovery and may not fit her context or strengths. Handing her talking points solves one meeting while creating dependence and teaching her nothing about the underlying pattern.
questions.concept: Coaching versus training versus mentoring — selecting the right knowledge-transfer intervention
questions.question: A data engineer tells the agile practitioner she wants to become more influential in the team's design discussions, but she cannot pinpoint what is holding her back. Which developmental approach is MOST appropriate for the practitioner to apply first?
choices: Coaching — ask open, powerful questions that help her surface her own obstacles and define the growth actions she will own
Training — enroll her in a structured facilitation and technical-communication course to close the capability gap efficiently
Mentoring — describe how the practitioner personally became influential in design forums and advise her to follow a similar path
Directing — give her prepared talking points and a reserved speaking slot to use in the next design discussion

questions.explanation: The team has two broken loops — a six-week technical loop (code to defect discovery) and a one-year product loop (release to customer reaction) — and the two correct actions attack one loop each. Continuous integration with automated tests on every change collapses defect discovery from six weeks to minutes, while the mistake is still fresh in the developer's mind. Demonstrating working increments to customers every iteration collapses the value-feedback loop from annually to every few weeks, so the team learns whether it is building the right thing long before the annual release. More thorough design documentation is predictive effort that adds no feedback at all — it attempts to prevent error rather than accelerate learning. A hardening phase at the end of each release actually institutionalizes late feedback by batching all quality discovery at the end. A monthly leadership dashboard reports lagging aggregate data to people who do not do the work; it informs governance but gives the team no faster signal about its code or its product.
questions.concept: Technical and product feedback loops (continuous integration and iteration reviews)
questions.question: A payroll-software team receives defect reports from a separate QA group roughly six weeks after code is written, and hears customer reactions only after each annual release. Which TWO changes would MOST directly shorten this team's feedback loops? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Require developers to produce more thorough design documentation before coding begins
Move QA sign-off into a dedicated hardening phase at the end of each release
Build a continuous integration pipeline that runs automated tests on every change within minutes
Publish a monthly dashboard summarizing defect counts for senior leadership
Demonstrate working increments to a representative group of customers at the end of every iteration

questions.explanation: Deliberately routing pricing stories through rotating pairs and mob sessions is best because hands-on collaboration transfers the tacit, judgment-heavy knowledge to several people while real product value is still being delivered, closing the single-point-of-failure risk inside the six weeks actually available. Having her spend those weeks writing comprehensive documentation produces a static artifact that captures far less than working knowledge, delivers no customer value during the window, and leaves no one who has actually exercised the code. Bringing in a contractor works around the gap instead of closing it — the knowledge still walks out the door when she leaves, and ramping up an outsider consumes her scarce remaining time. Deferring all pricing work until she returns stalls customer value for six months and squanders the one window in which knowledge transfer is still possible.
questions.concept: Bus-factor risk and knowledge diffusion through pairing and mobbing
questions.question: On an XP team, only one developer deeply understands the pricing engine, and she begins six months of leave in six weeks. The product owner is worried that pricing work will stall while she is away. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Ask her to spend the remaining weeks writing thorough design notes on the pricing engine so the team has a reference while she is away
Bring in a contractor with pricing-domain experience before she leaves so the team still has a specialist on the module during the leave
Have the product owner sequence pricing stories out of the plan until she returns, so the team avoids work nobody else can safely deliver
Work with the team to schedule pricing-engine stories now so she pairs with rotating partners, using mob sessions on the trickiest areas

questions.explanation: Average cycle time equals average work in progress divided by average throughput, so 12 items at 3 per day gives about 4 days today; holding throughput near 3 and reducing work in progress to roughly 7 or 8 items yields about 2.5 days, achieved by finishing before starting rather than by hiring. Adding contractors to lift completions to about 4 a day gives 12 divided by 4, or 3 days — closer, but still short of the target, and bought with cost and onboarding drag instead of the lever already in the team's hands. Splitting each escalation into two cards is the strongest rival, because smaller items genuinely do flow faster in most systems, but as described it doubles both terms and 24 divided by 6 is still 4 days, while the requester now waits for two cards rather than one. Measuring from first touch instead of intake reports a smaller number while hiding exactly the queue time leadership is asking about.
questions.concept: Practical Little's Law applied to WIP limits and cycle time
questions.question: A support-escalation team pulls work across a Kanban board that averages 12 items in progress and completes an average of 3 items per working day, and both figures have been stable for two months. Leadership asks the team to bring average cycle time down to about 2.5 days. Applying Little's Law, which action is most consistent with that goal?
choices: Keep average items in progress at 12 and add contractors to lift daily completions to about 4, since throughput is the only lever
Split each escalation into two smaller cards so items finish faster, leaving about 24 in progress and 6 completions a day
Measure cycle time from when an analyst actually starts a card rather than from intake, so the reported average nears 2.5 days
Tighten the board's WIP limits so average items in progress falls to roughly 7 or 8 while daily completions hold at about 3

questions.explanation: Two problems are entangled and both are addressed by the same conversation: the team is optimizing a proxy for value rather than the outcome the customer bought, and the rising throughput is being purchased with evening work that cannot last -- joining sponsor and team to define an observable outcome measure reorients the work toward value, restores the customer's confidence through shared evidence rather than reassurance, and puts the pace question where the trade-off can honestly be made. Reassuring the sponsor with flow metrics answers a value question with a speed answer and confirms exactly the anxiety she expressed. Adding a drop-off metric to the dashboard points in the right direction but done unilaterally it produces a number nobody has agreed how to interpret or act on, and it leaves the unsustainable pace untouched. Fixing the pace and re-forecasting before speaking to the sponsor keeps the team's real capacity hidden from the person funding the work, trading transparency for internal tidiness at the moment transparency matters most.
questions.concept: Outcome measures versus flow proxies, with sustainable pace
questions.question: A team is midway through a twelve-week engagement rebuilding a university admissions portal. Flow metrics look healthy -- lead time is stable and throughput is rising -- yet the sponsor tells the agile practitioner privately that she is uneasy: she sees polished demonstrations but cannot tell whether applicant drop-off is actually improving, which was the reason she funded the work. The team's board has no measure tied to that outcome. Two developers separately mention they are working evenings to keep throughput climbing. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Reassure the sponsor with the lead-time and throughput trends, which objectively show the team delivering faster than at the start of the engagement, and offer her a written flow summary at the end of every month
Add an applicant drop-off metric to the team's board and wire it to the live analytics feed so the sponsor can watch the number move between demonstrations without interrupting the team's work

Bring the sponsor and the team together to define what a measurable improvement in applicant drop-off looks like, agree how it will be observed on real users, and examine whether the current pace is sustainable
Ask the two developers to stop working evenings, then re-forecast the remaining scope at the team's true sustainable capacity before raising the applicant drop-off question with the sponsor

questions.explanation: The deciding factor is not the headline figure but the risk attached to it: the group-booking epic starts returning benefit after one iteration and its first release tests the assumption behind the forecast before the rest of the money is spent, so the observatory keeps the option to stop, change, or invest further. Choosing dynamic pricing on the larger net present value alone accepts a number wholly contingent on a four-iteration plan and an untested price-sensitivity assumption; discounting prices time, not the chance that the model is wrong. Building dynamic pricing while demoing the model to the commercial team each iteration is the strongest alternative, since it creates a real inspection cadence — but it tests internal opinion, and price sensitivity is only settled when visitors face real prices. Starting a slice of each raises work in progress and delays both tests.
questions.concept: Value-based prioritization using NPV alongside earlier benefit realization and preserved optionality
questions.question: A product owner for an observatory's visitor-ticketing platform must choose which of two epics to start. Dynamic pricing has a modeled net present value of about $180,000 over three years; it needs four iterations, returns nothing until the whole capability is live, and its model rests on an assumption about visitor price sensitivity that cannot be tested until then. Group-booking self-service has a modeled net present value of about $150,000, can be delivered in two slices, and its first slice — releasable after one iteration — is expected to capture roughly 60 percent of the benefit and to show quickly whether its booking-volume assumption holds. Both models use the same discount rate. Which reasoning BEST supports the prioritization decision?
choices: Choose dynamic pricing, because its net present value is the larger figure and net present value already reflects the timing of every cash flow in the comparison
Choose group-booking self-service first, because benefit begins several iterations sooner and the release after the first slice tests the forecast before the remaining investment is committed
Choose dynamic pricing but demo the pricing model to the commercial team each iteration, so the price-sensitivity assumption gets checked repeatedly while the build proceeds
Start a slice of each epic in parallel, so some benefit begins immediately and neither the price-sensitivity assumption nor the group-booking forecast waits to be tested

questions.explanation: Value ranking that ignores how work assembles into a usable customer outcome produces increments no one can actually use, and mapping the journey against the backlog lets the team and product owner see together which combination forms the smallest genuinely valuable slice. Promoting the shared data-import capability to the top is the strongest alternative, because the dependency is real and the sequence does have to change — but it repairs one dependency while leaving the ranking method that created it intact. Building the import capability as enabling work ahead of the release hides infrastructure outside the visible backlog and separates it from the customer value it serves. Re-scoring all forty items with the sales director and the team improves the inputs to an instrument that still scores items one by one, which can never reveal which combination completes a usable task.
questions.concept: Story mapping to find a coherent, usable slice across a value-ranked backlog
questions.question: A product team at a seed-lab company is preparing the first release of a germination-tracking tool. The product owner has ranked 40 backlog items by "business value points" supplied by the sales director. During refinement, two developers note that six of the highest-ranked items all depend on a shared data-import capability sitting near the bottom of the ranking, and that shipping any one of the six alone would not let a customer complete a single end-to-end task. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask the product owner to move the shared data-import capability to the top of the ranking, since none of the six highest-ranked items can be delivered without it
Facilitate a session where the team and product owner map the customer's end-to-end journey against the backlog to identify the smallest slice that delivers a usable outcome
Have the developers build the data-import capability as enabling work ahead of the release, so the ranked items afterward flow through without stalling partway to done
Ask the sales director to re-score all 40 items with the team present, so the business value points reflect delivery reality as well as raw market appeal

questions.explanation: Pausing the session, restating the team's agreement that retrospectives examine how the system of work allowed a failure rather than who touched it last, and redirecting to contributing process causes is the only action that protects psychological safety while the damage is occurring: the team sees the norm is real, the analyst is defended publicly where she was blamed publicly, and the analysis can still produce learning about labeling. Letting the discussion run and giving the senior engineer candid feedback immediately afterward is a legitimate follow-up and the strongest alternative, but as the primary response it arrives too late, once the analyst has gone quiet and the group has learned that blaming is tolerated in session. Ending the retrospective and rebooking with an external facilitator abandons learning that is needed now. Pulling up the shipment records to identify the handoff wins the argument on the accuser's terms, keeping the hunt for a culprit at the center.
questions.concept: Psychological safety and blameless retrospectives
questions.question: During a retrospective after a mislabeled-shipment incident, a Kanban team that routes blood products between hospitals watches a senior engineer repeatedly interrupt to insist the newest analyst 'obviously caused this.' The analyst stops speaking, and other members drift into side conversations. As facilitator, what should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Pause the session, remind the team of its agreement that retrospectives examine how the system of work allowed the failure rather than who touched it last, and redirect the analysis toward contributing process causes

Let the discussion run its course so the session is not derailed further, then give the senior engineer candid one-on-one feedback immediately afterward about the effect his public accusations had on the analyst

End the retrospective early and rebook the session with a neutral external facilitator, on the grounds that the practitioner's own working relationships with this team make an impartial intervention hard to attempt in the moment

Pull up the shipment records in the session and establish exactly which handoff introduced the mislabeling, so the accusation collapses on the evidence and the analyst is cleared in front of everyone still present

questions.explanation: The distinctions turn on scope and mode. A community of practice is voluntary and crosses team boundaries — its glue is a shared discipline rather than a shared work item, which separates it from every within-team mechanism. Mob programming is the whole team collaborating on a single item at one workstation, so knowledge transfer happens as a live by-product of delivery — distinguishing it from pairing, which involves only two people at a time. Pair rotation is the deliberate re-shuffling of partners inside a team so component knowledge keeps moving; its purpose is coverage, not a single collaboration. An information radiator is passive and pull-based: it shares the state of the work continuously with anyone who looks, unlike the other three, which all require people actively working or meeting together. The common traps are confusing mobs with pairs (whole team vs two people), communities of practice with team meetings (cross-boundary and voluntary vs within-team and scheduled), and radiators with reports (information pulled by the viewer vs pushed by an author).
questions.concept: Knowledge-sharing mechanisms: CoP, mobbing, radiators, pair rotation
questions.question: Match each knowledge-sharing mechanism (1-4) with the description (A-D) that best distinguishes it from the others.
pairs: Community of practice
A voluntary group spanning team boundaries that gathers around a shared discipline to exchange practices and lessons
Mob programming
The whole team works the same item at one workstation, spreading tacit knowledge in real time while the work is being produced
Information radiator
A large, always-current visual display that lets anyone learn the state of the work by looking, without asking or attending a meeting
Pair rotation
Team members regularly change partners across work items so that no component's knowledge resides with only one person

questions.explanation: Facilitating a guardrail-setting session honors both legitimate needs at once: the director's need for risk control after a real outage and the mature team's need to keep decision authority. Rooting the guardrails in the outage's root causes makes the boundaries evidence-based, and explicit decision boundaries are exactly how a leader sustains empowerment for a high-maturity team. Asking the director to approve only a defined high-risk category is the closest alternative and would unblock most releases, but the categories get drawn without the outage evidence and without the team, so the boundary stays the director's rather than something the team owns. Taking the approval role for a trial period, even with published lead times, concedes that centralized approval is the right control and installs the practitioner as the bottleneck. Adding automated verification and one-step rollback is valuable engineering work, yet on its own it changes the pipeline while the approval mandate and the demoralization remain.
questions.concept: Delegation levels and decision boundaries after an incident
questions.question: After a painful production outage, the operations director instructs the agile practitioner to personally approve every deployment decision for a mature cross-functional team that has released continuously for two years. Team members say this will demoralize them and slow delivery to a crawl. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Ask the director to approve only a defined category of high-risk deployments, letting the team release everything outside that category without waiting for a decision
Facilitate a session where the team and the director use the outage's root causes to define deployment guardrails and decision boundaries that the team will own
Take on the approval role for a fixed trial period while publishing approval and deployment lead times, then use that data to renegotiate the arrangement
Have the team add automated deployment verification and one-step rollback, then show the director the class of outage the pipeline now catches by itself

questions.explanation: Cycle time is a distribution, not a single number, and a one-to-27-day spread is exactly what stakeholders experience as unpredictability. Sharing the spread with a percentile that can actually be used for commitments makes the variation transparent, and examining what the long-tail items shared points at the external data-quality dependency that is the real cause. Reporting the six-day average more often reinforces a figure that already fails to describe most items and will erode trust further when the next 27-day item lands. Swapping to velocity trades a flow measure stakeholders care about for a team-internal capacity measure that says nothing about how long a request takes. Opening a service-level agreement with the data-quality team is the strongest rival and aims at the right dependency, but it commits to a negotiated remedy before the team has shown from its own data which items stretch the tail — and that evidence is what would make the conversation succeed.
questions.concept: cycle-time distribution and percentile-based forecasting
questions.question: Over the past quarter a hybrid delivery team's average cycle time has held steady at six days, yet stakeholders keep describing delivery as unpredictable. Examining the raw data, the practitioner sees completed items finishing anywhere between one and 27 days, with a long tail of items that were blocked on an external data-quality team. What should the practitioner do next?
choices: Report the six-day average in every stakeholder update and add a confidence range once a quarter, so the number becomes familiar and trust in the team's predictability is rebuilt.
Replace cycle time with velocity in stakeholder reporting, since it varies far less from iteration to iteration and gives a steadier basis for the forecasts stakeholders ask for.
Open a service-level agreement with the external data-quality team so that blocked items are answered inside a fixed window, since those items are what stretched the tail of the distribution.
Show the team and stakeholders the full spread of completed items, quote an 85th-percentile figure alongside the average, and facilitate a look at what the long-tail items had in common.

questions.explanation: The transparency did not fail on its own; it collapsed because the data was weaponized, so the root cause is how leadership used the metrics. Resetting expectations with the director restores the conditions under which the team can safely radiate information again, and it does so through direct collaboration rather than avoidance. Coaching the team to put the board and cumulative flow diagram back up is right about the stakes, since hidden work is the larger risk, but it asks the team to re-expose itself to the same misuse with nothing changed. A work-in-process limit on the review step is sound flow practice and would stop the queue growing, yet it treats a trust failure as a flow problem. Giving the director a detailed weekly narrative substitutes a curated account for the data, keeps the team in the reporting business, and leaves him free to rank teams from whatever figures he can still obtain.
questions.concept: Metric misuse and the safety preconditions of transparency
questions.question: After a director began quoting team throughput figures in leadership meetings to rank teams against one another, one Kanban team took down its wall board and stopped publishing its cumulative flow diagram. The practitioner notices that work is now quietly piling up in a 'waiting for review' state that stakeholders can no longer see. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Coach the team to put the board and cumulative flow diagram back up, since hidden work risks the program more than an unfavorable ranking does
Add a work-in-process limit on the review step so the queue stops growing while the team decides what it is willing to publish
Meet with the director to reset expectations about how flow metrics will be used, so the team can safely make its work visible again
Give the director a detailed written narrative of the team's progress each week, so his leadership updates no longer depend on raw throughput figures

questions.explanation: Agile teams welcome changing requirements even late in development when the change protects the customer's advantage, and a compliance module that is non-compliant on the day it ships has lost most of its value. Working with the customer to reorder the remaining backlog trades lower-value planned items for the newly critical work, harnessing the change instead of resisting it. Adding the amended rule as extra scope while deferring the planned refactoring holds the date by quietly borrowing from quality, and it hides the prioritization decision from the customer who should be making it. Supporting the freeze puts the release plan above the product's fitness for use, which inverts agile priorities. Shipping on plan and releasing the amendment as a patch two weeks later is the strongest alternative, since the gap is short and the commitment holds — but it knowingly puts incorrect payroll withholding into production, which is not a defect customers can absorb for two weeks.
questions.concept: Welcoming changing requirements for customer advantage
questions.question: An XP team is two iterations from releasing a payroll-compliance module when the national tax authority publishes an amended withholding rule that invalidates part of the remaining backlog. The operations lead proposes freezing scope, shipping as planned, and handling the amendment in a "phase 2" six months later, noting the team has already committed to the release plan. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Add the amended rule to the release as extra scope and protect the committed date by having the team defer its planned refactoring work
Support the freeze, since a compliance module delivered on the committed date is worth more to the customer than a late one
Plan the amended rule as a patch released two weeks after the module ships, so the current release plan stays intact
Work with the customer to reorder the remaining backlog so the release delivers the amended rule in place of lower-value items

questions.explanation: Co-creating a customer-outcome vision with representatives of every team builds ownership — people commit to what they help create — and it works regardless of whether a team runs Scrum, Kanban, or a hybrid. Mapping backlog items to those outcome goals on each team's own board makes the link between daily work and strategy visible at the moment work is chosen, which is what turns a statement into lived purpose. A mandated sponsor video is one-way broadcast: it may raise awareness briefly but creates no ownership, and compulsory viewing often breeds cynicism. Tying purpose alignment to performance appraisals converts an intrinsic motivator into an extrinsic control, encouraging people to game the measure rather than internalize the mission. Publishing the strategy on the wiki with links in meeting invitations is passive documentation — the survey already shows the strategy exists but is not connecting, and another distribution channel does not change that.
questions.concept: Co-created vision and visible work-to-strategy linkage in distributed teams
questions.question: An insurance platform's five feature teams work from three countries; two use Scrum, two use Kanban, and one runs a hybrid. A recent internal survey shows fewer than 30 percent of team members can explain how their work supports the platform strategy. Which TWO actions by the agile practitioner would most effectively rebuild shared purpose? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Ask the sponsor to record a video restating the strategy and require every member to watch it
Facilitate a workshop where representatives of all five teams and product leadership co-create a vision statement tied to customer outcomes
Introduce a purpose-alignment KPI into each team member's annual performance appraisal
Publish the strategy document on the wiki and link it in every planning-meeting invitation
Map backlog items to the strategy's outcome goals visibly on each team's board or information radiator

questions.explanation: The failure here is follow-through, not idea generation, so the fix is to reduce the improvement batch to one experiment that is owned, capacity-protected on the iteration backlog, and measured, which restores the team's belief that retrospectives change something. A full-day session generates more discussion about a backlog the team has already proven it cannot execute, adding cost without changing the underlying capacity problem. Having a manager assign owners and due dates removes the self-organization that makes improvement stick and turns learning into compliance reporting. Swapping to an anonymous survey addresses participation, not execution, and removes the collaborative space where the team would design and commit to a change.
questions.concept: Retrospective follow-through as limited improvement experiments
questions.question: A museum ticketing team's retrospective board carries 14 unfinished improvement actions accumulated over five retrospectives. Attendance is falling and two members propose dropping retrospectives altogether because "nothing ever changes." What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Facilitate the team in picking one improvement to run as an experiment next iteration, with an owner, a slot on the iteration backlog beside delivery work, and a measure inspected at the following retrospective.
Book a full-day retrospective so the team can work through all 14 open actions in one sitting, clear the board, and enter the next iteration with a freshly ordered improvement backlog behind it.

Ask the delivery manager to assign every open action to a named owner with a due date and to track completion in the weekly status report, so improvements finally receive the attention that delivery work receives.

Replace the retrospective with a monthly anonymous survey feeding a ranked improvement list, so quieter members contribute and the team spends less time in a meeting that it has visibly stopped valuing.

questions.explanation: A blameless session with both groups in the room shifts attention from "who failed" to "how the system allowed this," which is where recurring incidents live — here, most likely in the seam between configuration practice and tooling feedback that neither group can see alone. Keeping the change-approval board as an interim control adds a heavyweight gate before the cause is understood, slows flow, and reviews intent rather than system behavior. Instrumenting the deployment tooling so swallowed errors surface is genuinely strong and will probably be one of the countermeasures, but adopting it now accepts one side's account of the failure and treats a fix as a substitute for diagnosis. Having each group analyze the outages separately and then meet sounds well prepared, yet both sides arrive with a defended conclusion, which reproduces the talking-past-each-other outcome of the last review.
questions.concept: Blameless root-cause analysis and systems thinking
questions.question: At an online retailer using Lean and DevOps practices, three similar checkout outages have occurred in six weeks. The platform group insists application teams are shipping untested configuration changes; application teams say the platform's deployment tooling swallows errors. The last incident review ended with both sides talking past each other, and a director is now proposing a change-approval board. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Keep the change-approval board in place as a temporary control while the outage pattern is studied, since a shared gate catches bad changes before they ship
Have the deployment tooling instrumented so swallowed errors surface loudly, since the argument cannot be settled while the evidence about each failure is still disputed
Ask each group to review the three outages separately and bring conclusions to a joint meeting, so both sides arrive prepared rather than improvising
Facilitate a blameless root-cause session with people from both groups, walking through the actual sequence of events in the system rather than each side's conduct

questions.explanation: Working agreements the team writes and owns create shared norms, mutual accountability, and a foundation of trust from day one, and overlapping core hours with a persistent virtual team room give distributed members the closest substitute for co-location — space for spontaneous, direct conversation. Assigning detailed individual task lists fragments collective ownership and signals that members work in parallel silos rather than collaborating on shared goals. Routing questions through the project manager inserts a communication bottleneck and contradicts the preference for direct interaction between the people who need to talk. Publishing individual output rankings pits teammates against one another, undermining both collaboration and the safety needed to ask for help.
questions.concept: Working agreements and distributed-team communication
questions.question: An agile practitioner is helping a newly formed, partially distributed cross-functional team begin working together. Which TWO actions will best promote a collaborative team environment? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Facilitate the team in creating and owning its working agreements
Assign each member a detailed individual task list to prevent duplicated effort
Establish overlapping core hours and a persistent virtual team room for the distributed members
Route cross-team questions through the project manager to keep communication consistent
Publish a monthly ranking of members by individual output to encourage effort

questions.explanation: Bringing the teams together to map their dependencies and design their own lightweight working agreement attacks the actual problem — slow, low-bandwidth interaction across time zones — with more collaboration rather than more contract; overlapping hours, shared demos, and pairing on high-dependency changes shrink the feedback loops a ticket queue would lengthen. Having each team stub the other's service is a genuinely strong technical answer that probably belongs in the eventual solution, but stubs decouple development, not integration: the mismatches would still appear when real changes land, and nothing about the friction between the teams changes. Putting dependent work on a shared quarterly plan with fixed handoff dates hardens the handoff into a schedule and assumes the sequence holds for a quarter. Introducing the intake system with a five-day service level, even at both leads' request, codifies a customer-supplier contract in which five days becomes the norm rather than the ceiling.
questions.concept: Cross-team coordination and working agreements for distributed teams
questions.question: A mobile experience team in Lisbon and a payments platform team in Singapore block each other several times per release: each waits days for the other's changes, and frustration is rising. Both team leads separately ask the agile practitioner to institute a formal intake ticket system with a five-day service-level agreement so 'expectations are documented.' What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Facilitate a joint session where both teams map their dependencies and create a lightweight cross-team working agreement — overlapping hours, shared demos, and pairing on high-dependency changes.
Ask each team to stub the other's service so that neither has to wait for real changes to land, removing the technical dependency that produces the waiting and the frustration in every release.
Have both teams place their dependent work on a shared quarterly plan with fixed handoff dates, so each knows when the other's changes land and can sequence its own work around them.

Introduce the intake ticket system the two leads asked for, with the five-day service level and a weekly adherence report, so each team has documented expectations it can hold the other to on every request.

questions.explanation: A board that collapses several real steps into one column hides where work actually waits; making the true workflow visible is the prerequisite for any improvement and lets the team give stakeholders a truthful answer. Due dates add schedule pressure without revealing where the delay comes from, so late cards stay just as opaque. Moving long-running cards into a blocked lane makes the board look tidier while concealing the very signal the team needs, and most of those cards are not blocked at all — they are queued between steps. Publishing averages substitutes a summary metric for transparency and treats a legitimate request for visibility as noise to be suppressed.
questions.concept: Workflow visualization and revealing hidden queues
questions.question: A Kanban team building a freight-tracking portal reviews its board with the agile practitioner. Every card sits in a single column called "In Progress," which spans design, build, and carrier-integration testing. Cards routinely sit there nine to fourteen days, and when stakeholders ask what is happening, the team can only say "still in progress." What is the BEST response?
choices: Add a due date to every card so the team can see which ones are running late and stakeholders know when each item finishes
Move the long-running cards into a separate blocked swimlane so the main board stays readable and attention goes to the items still moving
Work with the team to break the single column into the actual steps their work passes through, then observe where items are waiting
Report weekly cycle-time and throughput averages to stakeholders so they have a progress measure and stop asking the team about individual cards

questions.explanation: Read together, the numbers tell a specific story: members still speak up (steady near 3.8-3.9) and delivery is fine (4.0 rising to 4.2), but debate has shifted from ideas to people (4.3 down to 2.1) and decisions keep getting relitigated (4.1 down to 2.4). That combination is conflict escalating from healthy task-focused disagreement toward personal antagonism, with eroding commitment to outcomes — a dysfunction that delivery metrics mask until it is severe. Making the trend transparent and facilitating the team to diagnose it and renew its own norms addresses the system while the team still talks openly. Waiting for delivery to suffer ignores that lagging output indicators are the last thing to fall; the leading indicators have already collapsed by half. A decision log with re-approval gates treats reopened decisions as a process defect when the data shows they are a symptom of unresolved interpersonal conflict — adding bureaucracy will not make decisions stick. Hunting for individual culprits assumes a few bad actors cause a team-level pattern, keeps the diagnosis in private one-to-ones, and bypasses the transparent, whole-team conversation the trend calls for.
questions.concept: Interpreting team health signals of escalating conflict
questions.question: An agile practitioner reviews the team's quarterly health-check trend shown in the exhibit. Delivery commitments are being met and stakeholders have raised no concerns. Based on the exhibit, what should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Hold off while completion scores keep rising, and revisit the health-check trend next quarter if delivery commitments or stakeholder satisfaction actually begin to slip
Introduce a decision log with a formal re-approval step before any settled decision may be reopened, so agreed decisions stop being relitigated in later conversations
Observe the next several working sessions to identify which individuals are making the personal remarks, then coach each of them privately so the behavior stops without public exposure
Share the trend openly with the team and facilitate a session on why debates turned personal and decisions stopped sticking, then help them renew their conflict and decision norms

questions.explanation: A timeboxed spike in the actual noisy environment converts an argument about opinions into evidence within days, which is the cheapest way to retire a technical unknown before it is built into the product. Asking the designer to write detailed acceptance criteria covering engine noise, accented speech and background chatter is the strongest rival, since it makes the concern testable and is good practice in general, but criteria cannot be written well for behavior nobody has measured, and verification then lands at the story review, after the phrasing has already been built in. Adopting whichever phrasing won the vendor's published benchmarks borrows evidence gathered under the vendor's conditions rather than this chain's lanes, accents and microphones, which is the exact variable in dispute. Pulling the wake-word work out and settling it once customers are ordering from their cars makes production the first real test, at the point where a wrong choice is most expensive to unwind.
questions.concept: Spikes to validate assumptions empirically
questions.question: Five days into a two-week iteration, a team is building voice ordering for a drive-through restaurant chain. A designer raises a concern that the chosen wake-word phrasing may fail with engine noise and accented speech; nobody on the team knows whether it will. The team has spent an hour debating phrasing options in a design session with no resolution. What is the BEST response?
choices: Timebox a spike this week: record a rough test of the phrasing with a handful of staff in a live, noisy lane and bring the results back to the team.

Ask the designer to write detailed acceptance criteria covering engine noise, accented speech, and background chatter, so the concern is captured as testable behavior and verified when the story is reviewed.
Have the team adopt whichever wake-word phrasing performed best in the vendor's published benchmarks, since that evidence already exists, costs the team nothing, and keeps the iteration on track.
Pull the wake-word work out of this iteration so the ordering flow can be finished, and settle the phrasing later once real customers are using the system in their cars.

questions.explanation: Putting actual associates in front of working software every iteration attacks the real cause: the feedback loop is eight weeks long and runs through a proxy, so misunderstandings surface only after weeks of build. Shortening the loop and going to the real users converts rework into course correction. More detailed, signed-off requirements from district managers doubles down on the proxy and on up-front documentation, which is what produced the rework in the first place. A change control step slows the arrival of the feedback the team needs and treats learning as a deviation to be governed. A satisfaction survey collects opinions about features already built, long after the cost of the misunderstanding has been incurred, and is far weaker evidence than watching a real user attempt a real task.
questions.concept: Shortening customer feedback loops and avoiding proxy stakeholders
questions.question: A team is building a shift-swap application for store associates at a regional grocery chain. The product owner collects requirements from district managers and relays them to the team; the associates who will actually use the app see the software only at an eight-week stakeholder showcase. The last two showcases each produced several weeks of rework. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Ask the product owner to write fuller requirements and have the district managers formally sign them off before each iteration starts, so the team builds from a baseline everyone agreed.
Introduce a change control step so rework raised at the showcase is assessed and approved before it enters the backlog, keeping the eight-week delivery plan from being disrupted.
Survey a sample of store associates every month, asking them to rate the features delivered so far and describe what makes swapping a shift difficult in their own store.
Arrange for a few store associates to work through real tasks on the running increment with the team at the end of every iteration, feeding what they observe straight into the backlog.

questions.explanation: Facilitating a session that surfaces the interests and quality criteria underneath each position moves the pair from defending positions to solving a shared problem — the collaborating mode of conflict management — and keeps ownership of the technical decision with the people closest to the code. Asking the architect for a binding ruling ends the argument but not the conflict: it escalates before the team has tried to resolve it, and the developer who loses inherits a design he never bought into. Separating the developers onto different stories is avoidance dressed as scheduling; the disagreement concerns a shared service, so it resurfaces at the next integration point, now with added resentment and a team still steering around the topic. Adding a standing design-review gate imposes permanent process to settle a single unresolved conversation — prescribing structure before understanding the problem, and taxing every future design with ceremony the team never asked for.
questions.concept: Collaborative problem solving in technical conflict
questions.question: Two developers on an XP team have argued for three days over whether a shared service should expose a coarse-grained or a fine-grained API. Pairing sessions that include either developer have turned tense, and the rest of the team has started steering around the topic entirely. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Bring the two developers together and facilitate a conversation that surfaces the interests and quality criteria behind each position
Ask the software architect to issue a binding ruling on the API granularity question so the team can stop debating and resume delivery
Schedule the two developers onto separate stories and pairs until the disagreement over the shared service design has had time to cool down
Introduce an API design-review gate so that this dispute and future design disagreements are settled by a formal process

questions.explanation: Every option here is technically possible, which is what makes this hard. Understanding each engineer's underlying interests privately, then reframing the dispute as a joint, evidence-generating experiment, is the only choice that resolves the conflict at the level of interests: it converts adversaries into co-investigators, produces data the team can trust, and models constructive disagreement for the juniors who are watching. A behavior-focused retrospective in front of the whole team risks publicly shaming two seniors and asks juniors who already feel unsafe to participate in confronting them — safety must be rebuilt before that forum can work. Moving an engineer removes a person instead of resolving anything: the technical question remains undecided, the team loses a senior, and everyone learns that hard conflict gets solved by transfers. Ordering deference to the current definition of done is forcing plus delay — the sarcasm will continue underground through the release, and the postponed debate will return sharper.
questions.concept: Interest-based resolution of hardened technical conflict
questions.question: Two senior engineers on an XP team disagree about whether contract tests or end-to-end tests should gate the deployment pipeline. The dispute has hardened: mob programming sessions now feature sarcastic remarks, and two junior members have privately admitted they hold back ideas whenever both seniors are present. The product owner, anxious about an approaching release, asks the agile practitioner to move one of the engineers to a sister team. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask both engineers to work under the team's existing definition of done until the release ships, then schedule a dedicated session on pipeline gating criteria early in the next quarter's planning cycle
Meet each engineer separately to understand the interests beneath their positions, then bring them together to design a time-boxed experiment testing both gating approaches against agreed criteria
Run a full-team retrospective focused on the mob-session behavior, so the whole team can name the sarcasm pattern openly and the junior members' withheld ideas finally surface in the room
Agree to move one of the engineers to another team, since the approaching release date and the junior members' reluctance to contribute justify separating the two seniors right away

questions.explanation: Taking the dispute out of the public channel de-escalates it, and a facilitated conversation built on active listening surfaces each person's underlying interests and moves the group from positions — whose fault the escapes are — to their shared interest in product quality, which is the collaborating approach to conflict. Posting the defect-ownership section of the quality management plan uses a document as positional authority: it may decide ownership, but it repairs none of the damage now silencing the rest of the channel. Asking the three to settle it between themselves is the strongest alternative, since conflict is best resolved at the lowest level, but they have already shown they cannot de-escalate unaided, and sending them back unassisted risks hardening the positions. Routing escaped defects automatically to the next available member is a process fix applied before the conflict is understood, and the resentment behind it will surface elsewhere.
questions.concept: Conflict management modes; collaborating versus forcing, avoiding, and delegating the conflict away
questions.question: During a hybrid firmware release, two testers and a developer clash openly in the team chat channel over who should own escaped defects, and the messages are becoming personal. Other team members have gone quiet in the channel. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Post the defect-ownership section of the quality management plan in the channel, so the team has an authoritative answer and the personal exchanges stop straight away
Move the discussion out of the channel and facilitate a conversation in which each person is fully heard and the group reframes the issue around their shared goal of product quality
Ask the two testers and the developer to settle the ownership question directly between themselves, and bring whatever agreement they reach back to the whole team at the next daily coordination
Add a defect-triage policy to the team's board so escaped defects route automatically to the next available member, removing the ownership question the three are arguing over

questions.explanation: Having the whole team design its own working agreements attacks the root cause: three role-based silos operating as a relay race instead of one cross-functional team. Overlap windows and pairing across specialties replace ticket handoffs with real interaction, and self-created norms carry far more commitment than imposed ones. Appointing coordinators through the managers adds an intermediary layer that institutionalizes the handoffs rather than removing them, and pulls ownership away from the team. A richer handoff template is a process-and-tools answer to an individuals-and-interactions problem — better documentation of a handoff still leaves the handoff, and the delay and misunderstanding that come with it. Waiting for a quarterly review postpones action on an actively deteriorating team dynamic when feedback loops should be short.
questions.concept: Working agreements and cross-functional collaboration in distributed teams
questions.question: A product team is distributed across three locations: UX designers in Lisbon, developers in Bengaluru, and testers in Toronto. Work moves between the groups only through tool tickets, rework is climbing, and group chats have turned into blame threads about incomplete handoffs. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask each location's manager to nominate a coordinator who owns the handoffs into and out of that group, so incomplete work stops crossing the sites unannounced and rework falls
Introduce a detailed handoff template so every group records complete context before passing work on, and the rework caused by missing information falls away
Raise the collaboration breakdown at the next quarterly delivery review, where all three sites are present and can agree together on a single remedy for the handoffs
Facilitate a whole-team session to create working agreements — overlap windows, pairing designers, developers, and testers on the same items, and a shared definition of done

questions.explanation: With 6 of 34 days spent working, roughly 18 percent of the elapsed time is value-adding, so the leverage is overwhelmingly in the waiting. Attacking the largest queue first — collaboratively, with the group that owns it, and by making the review smaller and earlier rather than simply demanding it be faster — is exactly the Lean move a value stream map is drawn to support. Speeding up the hands-on work optimizes the smallest component: eliminating half of it saves three days out of thirty-four. Raising utilization targets makes matters worse, because queues lengthen sharply as utilization approaches capacity and the pressure simply pushes more work in progress into the system. Naming queue owners and reporting weekly adds an administrative layer that measures the delay more precisely without changing any of the conditions that cause it.
questions.concept: Value stream mapping; wait time versus touch time
questions.question: A value stream mapping workshop for a seed-genetics laboratory information system produces this picture: a typical change takes 34 calendar days from request to production, of which 6 days are hands-on work. The rest sits in three queues — 11 days waiting for regulatory sign-off, 9 days waiting for a shared test environment, and 8 days waiting for release batching. The workshop group now debates where to improve. What is the BEST response?
choices: Invest in faster build tooling and pair programming so that the six days of hands-on work compress by half, since that is the only part of the stream the laboratory team fully controls itself.
Focus the first improvement experiment on the largest queue — the regulatory sign-off wait — and work with that group to find what evidence would let them review in smaller, earlier slices.
Raise each specialist's utilization target so that less capacity sits idle between steps, on the reasoning that a busier stream will push more changes through in the same period.
Give each of the three queues a named owner who reports its length weekly, so the group can watch the waits move and decide later which one deserves the first improvement effort.

questions.explanation: The rework is caused by decisions being made far from the people who dispatch outage crews and by a proxy with no authority; bringing real dispatchers into the feedback loop and equipping the liaison to decide inside an agreed scope attacks both causes and shortens the decision cycle. Logging the delays as a program risk and padding each iteration accepts a twelve-day decision latency as permanent and hides the waste inside a buffer rather than removing it. Asking the liaison to obtain a signed requirements baseline trades a fast feedback loop for a document that will be wrong the moment the districts see working software. Recording assumptions in place of the missing decisions and confirming them at the quarterly review is the strongest rival, since writing an assumption down beats guessing silently and it keeps work moving, but it formalizes what the team already does badly and pushes confirmation months out, making the rework batch larger and later than the nine-to-twelve-day wait it replaces.
questions.concept: Customer proxies versus real users; decision latency
questions.question: On a hybrid program modernizing a utility's outage-reporting system, the customer organization has appointed a single business liaison. She attends every iteration review but answers most questions with "I'll have to check with the districts." Answers come back in nine to twelve days, and the team's rework rate has climbed for three iterations because they build against her interim guesses. What is the BEST response?
choices: Bring actual district dispatchers into review sessions and agree a decision mandate for the liaison within a defined scope.
Log the decision delays as a program risk with an owner, and add buffer so each iteration absorbs the wait.
Ask the liaison to obtain a signed requirements baseline, so district questions are asked and answered once, up front.
Record assumptions in place of the missing decisions so work continues, and confirm them at the quarterly review.

questions.explanation: Facilitating joint story-level working sessions replaces the document handoff with direct collaboration: designers and developers discover constraints and intent together before work begins, which removes the root cause of the rework rather than managing its symptoms. Having developers review and approve each mockup before it enters the backlog is the strongest alternative and does surface technical objections earlier, but it preserves the design-then-review sequence, so developers still react to a finished artifact instead of shaping it, and the approval step adds a queue between the two groups. A technical-constraints checklist documents the handoff more thoroughly rather than replacing it, and the constraints that cause rework are usually the ones nobody thought to list. Asking the leads to agree clearer ownership boundaries hardens the wall between specialties when the wall is the problem.
questions.concept: Replacing sequential handoffs with cross-discipline collaboration
questions.question: On a distributed product team using two-week iterations, UX designers finish mockups and attach them to tickets, and developers pick the tickets up a few days later. Both groups blame each other for rework: designers say the builds ignore the designs, while developers say the mockups ignore technical constraints. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Have developers review and approve each mockup before it enters the iteration backlog, so technical objections surface earlier
Facilitate joint story-level working sessions where designers and developers shape the solution together before work begins
Add a technical-constraints checklist that designers complete on every ticket, so builds match what was designed
Ask the design and development leads to agree clearer ownership boundaries so the rework blame stops circulating

questions.explanation: Collaborating with the product owner to pull a scalability spike forward creates a risk-adjusted backlog: a small, time-boxed investment buys down the release's biggest uncertainty while there is still time to change course cheaply.
