Recording the concern on the risk register with a named owner and a standing review keeps it visible but leaves it unexplored while more work is built on the assumption — documenting a risk is not reducing it. Having the architect design a fallback to a second mapping provider commits substantial effort to a solution before anyone has evidence the current service fails at the projected volume, which is speculative work that may be thrown away entirely. Adding a load test to the definition of done for the scaling stories is the strongest rival and is good practice in itself, but those stories sit near the end of the release, so the answer still arrives at the point where a bad result leaves no room to respond.
questions.concept: risk-adjusted backlog and spikes
questions.question: During backlog refinement, a developer on a hybrid team warns that the third-party mapping service the product depends on may not handle the projected transaction volume — but the stories that would exercise it at scale are scheduled near the end of the release. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Record the scalability concern on the risk register with a named owner so it is reviewed at every checkpoint until it closes
Ask the lead architect to design a fallback to a second mapping provider now, so the release is protected whatever the volume proves to be
Add a load-test task to the definition of done for the scaling stories so the volume question is answered before the release ships
Work with the product owner to reorder the backlog so a time-boxed spike tests the service's scalability in the next iteration

questions.explanation: Facilitating a session that moves both developers from stated positions ("refactor now" versus "refactor later") to underlying interests and assumptions lets the team own a technical decision that is theirs to make, and it repairs the collaboration that the conflict is eroding. Asking the lead architect for a binding ruling hands the decision to outside authority — one developer "loses," neither owns the outcome, and the resentment that stopped their pairing remains untouched. Re-pairing the two with other teammates is avoidance: it manages the symptom while the disagreement festers and the team loses a productive pairing. Parking the debate until after the milestone defers a conflict that is already damaging daily collaboration, guaranteeing it resurfaces later with higher stakes and more accumulated friction.
questions.concept: Conflict management — surfacing interests behind hardened positions
questions.question: On an XP team at a game studio, two senior developers have spent two iterations arguing over whether to refactor the rendering pipeline now or after the next content milestone. They have quietly stopped pairing with each other, and their exchanges during daily coordination have turned sarcastic, visibly draining the rest of the team. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Ask the studio's lead architect for a binding ruling on the rendering pipeline, so the team has an authoritative decision and the argument stops consuming iterations.
Re-pair each developer with other teammates for the next few iterations so the sarcasm stops draining the team while the pipeline question waits for a calmer moment.
Park the refactoring question until the content milestone ships, so delivery is protected and the decision is made when schedule pressure has come off the team.
Facilitate a session where both developers surface the interests and assumptions behind their positions and the team weighs the options against the milestone goal.

questions.explanation: A blameless root-cause analysis moves the team from behavioral exhortation to the actual conditions in the automation that let the failures through, and encoding those conditions as automated pipeline checks builds quality in so the defect class cannot recur — analysis paired with a durable countermeasure is what makes an improvement stick. Making one engineer approve every deployment creates both a hero and a bottleneck, and human vigilance is the weakest available control against a systemic automation defect. A change advisory board gate adds an external approval queue that lengthens lead time while leaving the underlying cause untouched. Extending the manual regression cycle delays feedback and inflates batch size, which historically raises release risk rather than reducing it.
questions.concept: Root-cause analysis paired with built-in quality
questions.question: After a semiconductor-fab tooling team changed its release-automation scripts, production incidents rose from about one per month to seven per month. The retrospective produced two actions: "be more careful" and "add a pre-release checklist." The agile practitioner judges that neither will change the outcome. Which TWO actions best advance continuous improvement here? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Have the release engineer personally review and approve every deployment before it is allowed to run.
Facilitate a blameless root-cause analysis on two representative incidents, using Five Whys or a cause-and-effect diagram to reach the conditions that allowed the failures rather than who erred.
Require change advisory board sign-off on every deployment until the incident rate falls back to its earlier level.
Extend the manual regression cycle by two days before each release so that more testing can be completed.
Add automated checks to the deployment pipeline that reproduce the failure conditions the analysis identifies, so that class of defect is caught before release.

questions.explanation: The defining problem here is not the size of the threat but the width of the estimate — two days to three weeks is uncertainty, and the agile response to uncertainty is to buy information cheaply and early. A timeboxed spike converts the guess into evidence within one iteration, and ranking the resulting work on the risk-adjusted backlog lets the product owner trade risk reduction against features with real numbers while four iterations of runway remain. Having the product owner press the vendor for a late cutover date is worth doing in parallel and is the strongest alternative, but it rests the plan on a commitment the vendor owes nobody and teaches the team nothing about the rework. Scoring the risk and revisiting it each iteration review keeps it visible without narrowing it; four reviews of an unchanged rating leave the estimate as wide as it started. Spending a whole iteration on a vendor-neutral abstraction burns a fifth of the runway on speculative design.
questions.concept: Spikes and the risk-adjusted backlog
questions.question: An agritech team delivering a drone-imagery platform has five iterations left before a release tied to a fixed regulatory reporting deadline. The third-party geospatial service the platform depends on has just announced a breaking change to its authentication and tiling endpoints, with no firm cutover date beyond 'this year.' The team's estimate of the rework ranges from two days to three weeks and nobody can narrow it. The product owner, the architect and the sponsor each propose a different course of action. What is the BEST response?
choices: Run a timeboxed spike this iteration to build a thin adapter against the vendor's new endpoints, then size the resulting rework with the product owner and rank it on the risk-adjusted backlog so the exposure burns down before the deadline.

Ask the product owner to open a conversation with the vendor about a cutover date falling after the regulatory deadline, and keep the team on the planned backlog until a firm date is published rather than spending capacity on speculative rework.

Record the vendor change in the risk register with probability and impact ratings and revisit it at each iteration review, so the exposure stays visible to everyone while the team protects the committed feature scope for the fixed regulatory deadline.

Dedicate the next iteration to abstracting every geospatial call behind a vendor-neutral integration layer, so this breaking change and any later vendor change can be absorbed in one place without disturbing the release scope already committed for the deadline.

questions.explanation: Communities of practice live on voluntary participation and member-generated value; attendance collapsed as the format drifted from peer exchange to one-way broadcast. Running a short retrospective with the members and shifting toward member-driven topics and formats applies two core agile behaviors — seek feedback early and empower the people closest to the problem — and restores the pull that made the community work. Having the lead survey members on tooling topics is the strongest alternative because it does seek input, but it asks only what to broadcast next; the lead still owns the agenda, and format rather than topic choice is what emptied the room. Recruiting a second lead so presenting rotates widens the perspectives while keeping the community in broadcast mode. Dropping to a monthly cadence improves attendance per session and gives the lead more preparation time, treating the symptom while the one-way format survives.
questions.concept: Communities of practice; voluntary participation and member ownership
questions.question: Eight months ago an agile practitioner helped launch a quality-engineering community of practice that drew volunteers from every delivery team. Attendance has since fallen by half, and the last three sessions consisted entirely of the community lead presenting tooling updates to a quiet room. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask the community lead to survey the members on which tooling topics they want covered, then build the next quarter's schedule from the results
Run a short retrospective with the members on what they want from the community, and shift sessions toward member-driven topics and formats
Recruit a second lead from another delivery team so presenting duty rotates and members hear a wider range of technical perspectives
Reduce the community to a monthly cadence so the sessions that do run are better attended and the lead has more time to prepare content

questions.explanation: Empiricism pairs with deciding from observed evidence through repeated inspection and adaptation — it is the general stance of trusting what you observe over what a fixed plan predicted. Systems thinking pairs with optimizing the whole value flow rather than parts, because its defining insight is that locally rational improvements (a faster silo, a busier specialist) can worsen end-to-end outcomes. The Cynefin complex domain pairs with cause and effect being knowable only in retrospect, which is why its prescribed response is probing with safe-to-fail experiments before committing. Hypothesis-driven development pairs with stating a measurable expected outcome before building and validating it with data — the meaningful distinction from empiricism is that empiricism is the broad inspect-and-adapt posture, while hypothesis-driven development is a specific discipline of committing to a falsifiable prediction up front so that learning is deliberate rather than incidental.
questions.concept: Empirical, systems, and complexity thinking distinctions
questions.question: Match each way of thinking (1-4) with the description (A-D) that best characterizes it.
pairs: Empiricism
Making decisions from observed evidence and adapting through repeated inspection rather than following a fixed upfront plan
Systems thinking
Optimizing the whole flow of value rather than individual parts, recognizing that local improvements can degrade overall outcomes
Cynefin complex domain
Cause and effect are visible only in retrospect, so teams probe with safe-to-fail experiments before committing to a direction
Hypothesis-driven development
Stating an expected, measurable outcome before building, then using real data to validate or invalidate it

questions.explanation: Reading the diagram honestly and reducing open work before forecasting is best: the widening bands with a flat completion line say the system is choked by work in progress, and cutting that is the one lever that shortens cycle time without inventing capacity, after which a range based on the observed four-per-week rate can be offered. Committing to double the observed rate with weekend coverage promises a throughput the system has never produced and sacrifices sustainable pace, which degrades the rate further. Splitting the remaining items purely so the weekly count reaches eight changes the unit of measure rather than the system's capability, and it destroys the comparability of the historical throughput any forecast depends on. Daily percent-complete reporting adds surveillance overhead and reports on started work, while the diagram already shows that starting work is not the problem.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation and empirical forecasting
questions.question: A cumulative flow diagram for a data-migration team shows the Analysis and In-Progress bands widening steadily for eight weeks while the Done band's slope stays flat. Measured over that period the team averages 22 items in progress and completes about 4 items per week. Thirty items remain. In a stakeholder meeting the sales vice-president asks the team to "commit to eight items a week" so a customer date can be confirmed. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Accept the eight-per-week rate and arrange weekend coverage, since the customer date is already in play and the team can reassess its own throughput after the first two weeks of the push.
Show that with throughput steady near four items a week the widening bands mean too much work is open, and work with the team to cut items in progress before offering a forecast range.
Split the remaining thirty items into smaller pieces so the weekly item count reaches eight, and report that count to the vice-president as the team's new throughput.
Ask each specialist to report daily percent-complete on their open items, so the forecast rests on detailed progress data from every workstream rather than on an average of past weekly output.

questions.explanation: Proposing a blameless review of how the pipeline, safeguards, and workload allowed the failure reframes the incident from who failed to how the system permitted it, which is systems thinking in action: punishing an individual does not fix a pipeline that let a bad change reach production, and sharing the resulting improvements gives the department head something more valuable than a name. Handing over the deployment timeline without names and promising to report back is close to right and the most defensible alternative, but it answers on the department head's terms and commits to nothing blameless, so the search for a culprit survives the conversation. Adding a mandatory second approver prescribes a control before the cause is understood and slows every future deployment on the evidence of one outage. Running the review but keeping the findings inside the team protects safety at the cost of transparency and leaves leadership with nothing but the name it asked for.
questions.concept: Blameless post-incident reviews and systems thinking
questions.question: After a failed deployment takes an online service down for an hour, a department head asks the agile practitioner supporting the Lean delivery team to 'find out who pushed the change and make sure it goes on their record.' What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Give the department head the deployment timeline without names and offer to report back once the team has worked out what let the failing change reach production
Add a mandatory second approver to the deployment pipeline and tell the department head that no one person can now take the service down on their own
Ask the team to run its own review of the outage and keep the findings internal, since an honest improvement conversation depends on people feeling safe
Propose a blameless review of how the pipeline, safeguards, and workload allowed the failure, and share the resulting improvements with the department head

questions.explanation: The log shows five of six recent decisions — including everyday technical calls such as pairing assignments, story splitting, and the automation framework — made by the agile lead, while the performance data shows a team plainly capable of owning them and the top retrospective note shows the team wants that ownership. The right first move is a structured delegation conversation in which the lead and the team explicitly renegotiate which decision types shift and to what level. Having the lead explain his reasoning at the retrospective is a reasonable, low-friction step that shares criteria, but it still leaves him deciding, which is what the team is asking to change. Setting and publicly tracking a target share of decisions measures the outcome without negotiating the boundary, and it invites gaming by pushing trivial choices down. Rotating a single technical decision-maker each iteration swaps one central decider for a series of them.
questions.concept: Delegation levels and reading team maturity signals from decision data
questions.question: An agile practitioner reviews the exhibit for a mobile app team. Based on this information, what should the practitioner recommend first?
choices: Have the agile lead explain the reasoning behind each of his decisions at the retrospective, so members absorb the criteria and gradually begin deciding more on their own
Set a target for the share of technical decisions the team makes without the lead next quarter, and track that number publicly at every iteration review
Facilitate a delegation dialogue (for example, delegation poker) in which the agile lead and the team explicitly agree which decision types the team will own going forward
Rotate a different member into the technical decision-maker role each iteration, so the responsibility spreads across the whole team instead of resting with the agile lead alone

questions.explanation: Situational leadership matches the mix of direction and support to the team's maturity, which is how a leader calibrates how much autonomy a team can absorb. Directing (high direction, low support) fits a team that is enthusiastic but not yet competent — it needs to be shown what to do and how. Coaching (high direction, high support) fits a team whose skills are developing while confidence dips — the leader still guides closely but now explains the reasoning and invites input to rebuild commitment. Supporting (low direction, high support) fits a capable team whose motivation wavers — the leader steps back from task direction and instead facilitates and shares decisions to restore ownership. Delegating (low direction, low support) fits a mature, self-organizing team — the leader entrusts the work entirely and shifts energy to clearing organizational obstacles. The common error is treating one style as universally 'most agile': delegating to a novice team abandons it and produces failure that damages confidence, while directing a mature team smothers the self-organization it has already earned. The style must move as the team's maturity moves.
questions.concept: Situational leadership styles mapped to team maturity and degree of delegated autonomy
questions.question: Match each situational-leadership style (left) with the team situation where it fits best (right).
pairs: Directing
The team is new to the practice and needs specific instruction on what to do and how to do it
Coaching
The team's skills are growing but confidence is flagging; the leader explains decisions, invites input, and still guides the work closely
Supporting
The team is capable but its commitment fluctuates; the leader facilitates, shares decision-making, and provides little task direction
Delegating
The team is highly competent and committed; the leader entrusts outcomes to the team and focuses on removing organizational impediments

questions.explanation: The recurring item is a symptom of a broken improvement loop, so the highest-value use of the session is examining why improvement work never gets pulled, then converting the outcome into a single change that has an owner and a place in the iteration's capacity — which is what makes people believe attending is worth their time. Taking the flaky suite to the engineering manager and asking for dedicated capacity is the strongest alternative and might well get the repair funded, but it hands away the team's ownership of its own quality practice and treats a commitment problem as an external blocker. A fresh format with an outside facilitator addresses boredom rather than the complaint, which is that outcomes never materialize. Quarantining the failing tests turns the suite green while removing coverage of precisely the area that keeps breaking, and repair work scheduled for a later iteration is the same promise that has already failed three times.
questions.concept: Retrospective effectiveness and follow-through on improvement actions
questions.question: A distributed team building a payments reconciliation engine has run the same retrospective format for eleven iterations. The last three retrospectives produced the same top item: "nightly regression suite is flaky, so we ignore red builds." Each time the team wrote an action item, no one picked it up, and the suite is now red most mornings. Today's retrospective is about to start and two engineers have privately said they plan to skip it because "nothing changes." What is the BEST response?
choices: Take the flaky suite to the engineering manager as an impediment the team has repeatedly failed to clear, and ask for dedicated capacity in the next iteration to repair it properly
Run the retrospective on the recurrence itself — why the same action item keeps failing to get done — and leave with one owned, sized change pulled into the next iteration
Switch to a fresh retrospective format with an outside facilitator, so participation recovers before the team takes on the flaky regression suite one more time
Have the team quarantine the failing tests so the nightly suite runs green again, and schedule the repair work for a later iteration once the release pressure has eased

questions.explanation: Running a blameless root-cause analysis with the delivery and operations groups together attacks the systemic conditions that let incidents recur - three months of repetition signals a system problem, not a people problem - and sharing the findings and countermeasures openly answers the director's accountability concern with something far more useful than a list of names. Handing over logs that identify individuals invites blame, destroys the psychological safety the team needs to surface problems early, and changes nothing about why the system keeps producing incidents. A mandatory review board adds a control gate before anyone understands the causes, prescribing process ahead of diagnosis and slowing all delivery for an unexamined problem. Coaching the team privately to write fuller reports delays the response, reads as defensive, and leaves both the recurring causes and the director's request unaddressed.
questions.concept: Blameless root-cause analysis and systemic problem solving
questions.question: Production incidents traced to one delivery team have recurred for three months, and the operations director asks the agile practitioner to identify which individuals keep causing them so that 'accountability can be enforced.' What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Facilitate a blameless root-cause analysis with both groups and share the systemic findings openly with the director
Provide the deployment records naming who approved each release, since the director has asked for accountability
Introduce a change-approval board ahead of every production release so that no untested change can reach customers again
Have the team tighten its own incident write-ups first, then answer the director once those reports look thorough enough

questions.explanation: Kano treats must-be attributes asymmetrically: their presence is barely noticed but their absence produces sharp dissatisfaction, so they act as an entry condition rather than a satisfaction lever, while attractive attributes deliver disproportionate delight once the baseline is met. Ordering the upgrade offer first ignores that a delayed confirmation undermines the whole booking experience regardless of how delightful the upgrade is. Deprioritizing the confirmation because guests do not mention it inverts the model — silence about a must-be is exactly what the category predicts when it is working. Claiming the categories cannot inform sequencing misreads the model, which is specifically about how different attribute types translate into satisfaction and therefore into ordering decisions.
questions.concept: Kano model interpretation for release ordering
questions.question: A team building a hotel-booking mobile app scores candidate features with the Kano model using guest research. "Booking confirmation arrives within 60 seconds" scores as a must-be attribute. "Room upgrade offered at check-in based on stay history" scores as an attractive attribute. The product owner asks how the two scores should influence the ordering of the next release. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: Order the attractive attribute first, because it produces the largest measurable gain in guest satisfaction per unit of development effort while the must-be attribute produces almost none
Deliver the must-be attribute first, because its absence causes dissatisfaction that no amount of the attractive attribute offsets; the attractive attribute differentiates once that baseline holds
Treat the must-be attribute as an infrastructure quality target rather than a backlog item and let the attractive attribute carry the release, since confirmation speed is an operational concern

Order the two by expected revenue contribution, since Kano categories describe how guests feel rather than what the booking business earns, and sentiment alone cannot settle sequence for a commercial product

questions.explanation: The disagreement has moved from a technical debate to personal friction that is now suppressing the whole team's review flow, so the practitioner's first move is to resolve it at the lowest possible level with the people who own it. Bringing the two developers together, naming the disagreement without blame, and facilitating agreement on shared criteria (consistency for existing clients, migration cost, industry interoperability) settles both the convention and the relationship, and leaves the pair with a method for the next design dispute. Asking the architect to rule escalates a team-level decision to an authority outside the team; the pair gets a verdict they had no part in, the sarcasm remains, and the friction resurfaces on the next contested design. Imposing a mandatory standards document substitutes process for a relationship fix, slows every future pull request, and still does not decide which convention is right. Rebalancing the board to separate the two is avoidance: it hides the symptom, leaves the withdrawn reviewers and the sarcasm unaddressed, and shrinks shared ownership of the codebase.
questions.concept: Collaborative conflict resolution at the lowest level
questions.question: Two developers on a Kanban team maintaining a payments API have clashed for two weeks over whether error responses should follow the team's legacy convention or a newer industry standard. Their code-review comments have turned sarcastic, and other members have quietly stopped reviewing either developer's pull requests. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Ask the software architect to rule on which error-response convention is correct, so that the team has an authoritative answer and can move forward together
Introduce a mandatory coding-standards document that every pull request is checked against, so the convention question is settled once
Bring the two developers together, name the disagreement openly, and facilitate a conversation in which they agree on shared decision criteria
Rebalance the board so the two developers pull work in separate service areas until the tension between them has had time to cool

questions.explanation: Cause and effect that is visible only in retrospect, plus repeated surprises from small releases, are the signature of the complex domain, where the fitting response is probe–sense–respond: run safe-to-fail experiments, read the system's reaction, and amplify successful patterns. Treating it as complicated work assumes experts can analyze their way to the right answer up front, but expertise cannot predict emergent user behavior that is only explainable afterward. The chaotic response of acting first to impose stability applies when there is an active crisis with no discernible cause-effect at all — not a market that rewards deliberate experimentation. Applying an adjacent market's best practice assumes a clear domain with known, repeatable cause and effect, precisely what this unprecedented segment lacks.
questions.concept: Cynefin domain recognition and response
questions.question: A product group is entering a market segment where user behavior is unprecedented, the outcome of any feature can only be explained in hindsight, and small pilot releases keep producing surprising results. According to the Cynefin framework, how should the group treat this work?
choices: As complicated work — engage domain experts to analyze the market and design the right solution before building
As chaotic work — act immediately to impose stability, then reassess once order returns
As clear work — identify the established best practice from adjacent markets and apply it
As complex work — run safe-to-fail probes, sense the results, and respond by amplifying what works

questions.explanation: Discounting is precisely a statement about timing: a dollar realized in year one is worth more than the same dollar in year three, so front-loading benefit raises net present value even when the undiscounted totals match, and early delivery also buys early learning about whether the remaining scope is worth building. Calling the sequences equivalent because the totals match ignores the time value of money; handoff efficiency is a delivery concern, not the tie-breaker between two benefit schedules. Preferring the even three-year spread because it smooths the revenue line is the strongest alternative, and smoothing does feel safer — but a longer horizon gives the forecast more time to be wrong and delays the feedback that would test it. Saying the earlier sequence wins only above the hurdle rate misreads discounting: any positive rate favors earlier benefit.
questions.concept: NPV and the timing of benefit realization
questions.question: A product owner for a veterinary-clinic scheduling service compares two release sequences for the same scope at the same total cost. Sequence 1 delivers about 70 percent of the expected financial benefit in year one; Sequence 2 spreads the benefit evenly across years one through three. Undiscounted, the two produce identical total benefit. Applying value-based decision making, which conclusion is correct?
choices: Sequence 1 has the higher net present value, because benefits arriving sooner are discounted less — and earlier delivery also surfaces feedback that can correct the scope still to come.
The two sequences are financially equivalent, because total benefit and total cost match; the choice should rest on which sequence the delivery team can build with the fewest handoffs.
Sequence 2 is preferable, because spreading the benefit evenly across three years smooths the revenue line and reduces the chance that any single year's forecast turns out to be wrong.
Sequence 1 wins only when the discount rate sits above the organization's hurdle rate; below that threshold the two sequences carry the same present value and should be ranked as equal candidates.

questions.explanation: Communities of practice survive only on voluntary, member-perceived value, so the first step is to learn why people stopped attending — especially the lapsed members, who hold the diagnosis — and then let the members reshape the community around what they actually need; the drift from peer exchange to a slide monologue is a symptom to investigate, not to paper over. Booking a well-known external speaker treats the problem as one of attraction when the evidence points to lost value, so any attendance bump decays once the guest leaves. Asking the senior tester to trim his slides and leave room for questions is sensible and probably part of the eventual answer, but it is a remedy the practitioner picks without asking the members who walked away what they needed. Closing the community moves cross-team learning into team-bounded retrospectives, which cannot connect testers across the XP teams.
questions.concept: Communities of practice: voluntary participation and member-driven value
questions.question: Eighteen months ago an agile practitioner helped testers from several XP teams launch a community of practice. Attendance has slid from about thirty to five, and sessions have drifted into one senior tester presenting slides. Leadership asks the practitioner whether the community should be shut down. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Invite a well-known external speaker for the next few sessions so testers have a reason to start attending again
Ask current and lapsed members what value they need from the community and let them reshape its format and topics
Ask the senior tester to cut the slides down and leave time for questions so sessions feel less like a lecture
Recommend closing the community and moving its topics into each team's retrospective, where improvements get acted on

questions.explanation: Surfacing the underlying interests behind each position and guiding the whole team to a shared standard is collaborating - the conflict mode that produces a durable, jointly owned resolution and converts the disagreement into a better team norm before it splits the team further. Rearranging the pairing schedule is avoiding: the tension remains, keeps leaking into stand-ups, and the team loses a productive pair. Applying the organization's published threshold by direction is forcing through policy; it ends the argument without resolving it, strips the team of ownership of its technical standards, and invites one or both developers to disengage. Alternating the two standards each iteration is compromising - both sides lose half the time, the codebase gets an inconsistent quality bar, and the root disagreement is never examined.
questions.concept: Conflict management modes (collaborating vs. avoiding, forcing, compromising)
questions.question: On an XP team, two developers who usually pair have stopped pairing after a sharp disagreement over how much unit-test coverage is 'enough.' Their debate now resurfaces in every stand-up, and other team members have started taking sides. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Facilitate a session where the pair surface the interests behind their positions and the team agrees a shared testing standard
Rearrange the pairing schedule so the two work apart, ending the friction that is pulling other members into taking sides
Apply the organization's published coverage threshold and ask both developers to treat that number as settled for this codebase
Alternate the two coverage standards by iteration so each approach gets a fair trial and neither developer feels dismissed by the team

questions.explanation: Little's Law for a stable system gives average cycle time as work in progress divided by throughput: 25 items divided by 5 items per week is about 5 weeks. Because throughput is fixed by the system's capability in the short term, the lever the team controls immediately is WIP, so cutting the number of concurrent items shortens cycle time. The variant that recommends increasing the items in progress inverts the relationship: more concurrent work with unchanged throughput lengthens the wait. Multiplying WIP by throughput to reach 125 weeks misapplies the formula, which divides rather than multiplies. Requiring story-point sizes first confuses estimation with flow measurement; Little's Law works on counts of items and observed throughput, which is one reason flow metrics can forecast where estimates are unavailable.
questions.concept: Practical application of Little's Law to forecast cycle time
questions.question: A support-tooling team pulls work through a single-queue Kanban system. Over the last quarter it has averaged 25 items in progress and completes an average of 5 items per week. The product owner asks how long a newly pulled item should be expected to take from pull to done, assuming the system stays stable. Applying Little's Law, what is the most defensible answer?
choices: About 5 weeks, and the team can shorten it most directly by reducing the number of items in progress
About 5 weeks, and the team can shorten it most directly by increasing the number of items in progress
About 125 weeks, because average cycle time is the product of WIP and throughput
It cannot be estimated without first knowing each item's story-point size

questions.explanation: At 12 percent flow efficiency, roughly six of every seven elapsed days are queue and wait time outside the team, so speeding up or expanding the doing part of the process addresses the small remainder while the dominant delay is untouched. Using the value-stream map to redirect the improvement investment toward the approval waits — embedding the database skill, moving to a continuous security review, or granting the team delegated authority — is the transparent, data-driven move. Adding two developers increases the arrival rate into the same constrained approval queues, which by Little's Law lengthens cycle time rather than shortening it. Overtime on the active day attacks under one-seventh of the elapsed time, erodes sustainable pace, and buys almost nothing. Tightening the definition of ready is a plausible-sounding local optimization, but the delay described is waiting for the approver's availability and a weekly meeting cadence, not incomplete inputs.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency and value-stream mapping to target wait states
questions.question: A team supporting a subscription billing service measures flow efficiency by comparing active work time to total elapsed time per item. The current figure is 12 percent. Value-stream mapping shows items wait an average of four days for a shared database administrator to approve schema changes and another two days for a security review board that meets weekly. Active work averages under a day. Management has asked the team to improve delivery speed and has offered to fund two more developers. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Accept the two additional developers and pair them with the team, since more capacity will shorten the queue of waiting items
Present the value-stream map and flow-efficiency data to management and propose targeting the approval wait states rather than adding developers
Ask the team to work extra hours on the active portion of each item so more items finish every week
Introduce a stricter definition of ready so items reach the database administrator complete and schema approval passes first time

questions.explanation: Incrementally automating the riskiest regression checks into the pipeline is best because it builds quality in and shortens the feedback loop from ten days to minutes, which is exactly what stops week-one defects from being discovered in week two; doing the automation inside each iteration also keeps the improvement sustainable rather than turning it into a one-off project that never gets funded. Moving the regression pass into the first two days of the next iteration ends the late nights, a real gain, but it lengthens the gap between writing a defect and finding it and lets items be called done before they are verified. Chartering a separate quarter-long automation project removes two developers from the people who feel the pain and defers every benefit while the manual pass continues. Testing each item as soon as it is coded is genuinely good practice and the closest alternative, yet on its own it leaves regression manual and growing, so the same crunch returns as the product gets larger.
questions.concept: Building quality in through continuous integration and incremental regression-test automation
questions.question: A mobile banking team performs a four-hour manual regression pass during the final two days of every two-week iteration. About a third of the defects it uncovers trace back to work completed in the first week, unfinished items are routinely carried over, and testers work late at the end of each iteration. The team asks the agile practitioner for help. What is the BEST course of action?
choices: Move the regression pass into the first two days of the following iteration so that testers no longer work late, and let the product owner order any defects it finds alongside the new feature work.

Help the team make automation of the highest-risk regression checks part of the work of every iteration, starting with the paths that fail most often, so that those checks run in the pipeline on every change.

Charter a separate automation project staffed by two of the team's developers who will build a complete regression suite over the coming quarter, so that its own iterations can stay focused on delivering new features to customers.
Have the team test each item as soon as it is coded, so the manual pass at the iteration's end covers only the most recent work and finishes comfortably inside the final two days without overtime.

questions.explanation: A widening band on a cumulative flow diagram is by definition a growing queue at that stage: work arrives faster than it leaves, and the horizontal distance across the chart — approximate cycle time — stretches for everything entering behind it, which is why the fix is a work-in-progress limit or help at that stage rather than more input. A risk burndown that flattens shows responses that have exhausted their effect; continuing to monitor the same responses will not move the line, so the remaining exposure needs fresh mitigation, avoidance or acceptance decisions. On a burnup, a steady completion slope paired with a rising scope line separates two things a burndown would blur together: capability is fine, and the conversation belongs with whoever keeps adding scope. Points far outside the control limits on a cycle-time chart are special-cause signals attributable to specific events — a long approval wait, an environment outage — so they should be examined case by case; folding them into the average would slow every forecast to account for conditions that are not normal.
questions.concept: Interpreting cumulative flow, risk burndown, burnup and cycle-time control charts
questions.question: During a quarterly improvement review, an agile practitioner walks a delivery group through four charts drawn from the same program. Match each chart pattern (1-4) to what it most directly signals (A-D).
pairs: A cumulative flow diagram in which the "Ready for Test" band grows steadily thicker week after week while the other bands hold roughly constant width
Arrivals into that stage exceed departures from it, so a queue is building and items entering it will take progressively longer to finish
A release risk burndown chart whose total exposure fell sharply for six weeks and has then run almost flat for the last four
The current risk responses have stopped reducing exposure, so the remaining threats need new or different response strategies rather than continued monitoring of the existing ones
A release burnup chart in which the completed-work line rises at a steady, consistent slope while the total-scope line above it keeps climbing
The team's delivery rate is stable and the schedule pressure comes from growth in what is being asked for, not from any slowdown in the team
A cycle-time control chart in which most items cluster tightly but four items sit far above the upper control limit
Those few items experienced special-cause variation and should be investigated individually for what blocked them, rather than being averaged into a slower process-wide expectation

questions.explanation: The entire four-month investment rests on one untested assumption: that drivers will comply with suggested routes. Hypothesis-driven thinking says to test the riskiest assumption first with the cheapest experiment that produces real behavioral evidence — a small pilot with actual drivers does exactly that, and its result should shape whether and how the module gets built. A comprehensive upfront analysis is big-bang learning: it produces documents and projections, not evidence of behavior, and delays the moment of truth by months. Adding developers to ship the full module faster just accelerates spending on an unvalidated bet — building the wrong thing sooner is not learning sooner. A survey measures what drivers say they would do, and declared intent notoriously diverges from revealed behavior; it is cheaper than the pilot but produces far weaker evidence on the very question that matters.
questions.concept: Lean Startup — riskiest-assumption testing and validated learning before full investment
questions.question: A logistics company's product director asks a team to spend four months building a complete route-optimization module, based on her belief that delivery drivers will follow system-suggested routes. No one has any evidence about how drivers will actually behave. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Propose a small, inexpensive test of the riskiest assumption — for example, offering basic suggested routes to a handful of drivers for two weeks and measuring whether they actually follow them
Commission a full driver-workflow and market analysis so the module's requirements rest on solid research before any of the four months of development that the product director has requested is spent
Add developers so the complete module ships in two months rather than four, halving the wait before drivers are using it and the team can see whether the suggested routes get followed
Survey drivers across the whole organization about whether they would follow a system-suggested route, and size the first release around how many of them answer that they would use it

questions.explanation: Pruning with the team restores the log's signal, since obsolete and duplicate entries are exactly what made it unreadable, and a named owner plus a concrete next action is what turns an entry from a complaint into work. Pairing that with visible aging on the board and a recurring review of the oldest items builds the feedback loop that keeps the log honest, because impediment age is the measure that shows whether removal is actually happening. Assigning all 34 to the agile practitioner creates a single-point bottleneck and strips the team of ownership over obstacles it is frequently best placed to remove itself. Batch-escalating everything older than two iterations pushes unfiltered noise upward, burns credibility with the steering committee, and skips the team-level collaboration that resolves most impediments faster than management can. A three-day logging threshold suppresses early signals and delays feedback at exactly the moment a blocker is cheapest to clear — it shrinks the log by hiding problems rather than solving them.
questions.concept: Impediment log hygiene, ownership, and aging visibility
questions.question: A team building a national parks reservation service has an impediment log that has grown to 34 open entries over six iterations. Some are five iterations old with no owner; several duplicate one another; two entries block work that has since been canceled. The team has stopped reading the log, and blockers are raised verbally in daily coordination and then forgotten. The agile practitioner wants to make impediment management effective again. Which TWO actions best serve that goal? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Prune the log with the team — close resolved and obsolete entries, merge duplicates, and give each survivor a named owner and a next action
Assign all 34 impediments to the agile practitioner so the team is freed to focus purely on delivery
Escalate every impediment older than two iterations to the steering committee as a batch for management resolution
Make the remaining impediments visible on the team board with an aging indicator, and review the oldest ones in the flow review or retrospective
Require that impediments be logged only after they have blocked an item for at least three full working days, to keep the log small

questions.explanation: Framing the adoption belief as an explicit hypothesis and shipping the smallest version that can test it — a basic percentage set-aside for one courier segment, with the adoption signal defined in advance — applies build-measure-learn: the riskiest assumption, that couriers want automated withholding at all, is tested in weeks for a fraction of the funding. Starting with the three tax-agency integrations attacks the largest technical risk, which is the right instinct aimed at the wrong risk; the integrations will probably work, the demand may not, so this spends months proving the part nobody doubts. Building the funded feature in thin increments with sponsor demos is the strongest distractor, and incremental delivery does beat a four-month reveal — but a sponsor demo tests the sponsor's conviction, not courier behavior, so the adoption risk survives untouched. A market-research study substitutes stated preference for real behavior on exactly the question that matters.
questions.concept: Lean Startup: hypothesis-driven development and MVP
questions.question: A payments startup believes gig-economy couriers will adopt a feature that automatically sets aside estimated taxes from each payout. The sponsor has approved four months of funding to build the complete feature: tax projections, integrations with three tax agencies, and an analytics dashboard. What should the agile practitioner recommend first?
choices: State the belief as a testable hypothesis and release a minimal version—such as a simple percentage set-aside for one courier segment—defining in advance the adoption signal that would justify further investment
Start with the three tax-agency integrations because they carry the most technical risk, then add the projections and the dashboard once the hardest part is proven to work end to end
Build the funded feature in thin increments and demo each one to the sponsor as it lands, since the four months are approved and staged delivery surfaces problems early enough to correct
Commission a market-research study of how couriers handle tax set-asides today, so the team designs against evidence about real behavior before any of the four months of funding is spent

questions.explanation: An information radiator matches the highly visible, continuously updated display: its defining trait is passive broadcast — status flows to anyone who walks by, with no meeting or request needed. A working agreement matches the team-created explicit norms: unlike a radiator, it governs how people behave rather than displaying what is happening, and it only works because the team authored it. Psychological safety matches the shared belief about raising risks without fear: it is an interpersonal climate, not a document or a display — a team can have beautiful radiators and signed agreements and still be unsafe. A generalizing specialist matches the deep expert who deliberately broadens: this enabler is about the shape of an individual's skills and its effect on flow and handoffs, not about norms, climate, or transparency. The distinctions matter on the exam because each enabler solves a different collaboration failure: opacity (radiator), unspoken expectations (working agreement), fear of speaking up (safety), and skill bottlenecks (generalizing specialist).
questions.concept: Collaboration enablers — radiators, agreements, safety, generalizing specialists
questions.question: A coach is helping a newly formed cross-functional team understand four distinct enablers of a collaborative team environment. Match each enabler (1-4) with the description (A-D) that defines it.
pairs: Information radiator
A highly visible, continuously updated display that lets anyone absorb the team's current state without having to ask
Working agreement
Team-created norms that make expectations about behavior, communication, and collaboration explicit
Psychological safety
A shared belief that team members can raise questions, risks, and mistakes without fear of embarrassment or punishment
Generalizing specialist
A team member with deep expertise in one discipline who deliberately broadens into adjacent skills, reducing bottlenecks and handoffs

questions.explanation: Pairing the engineer with an experienced teammate on a small story plus a genuine listening conversation is best: mindset shifts come from directly experiencing the practices succeed, and active listening surfaces the underlying concerns — usually about rigor, quality evidence, or personal accountability — so the practitioner understands before prescribing. Having the team walk him through its reasoning at the retrospective is open and team-owned, and it is the closest call, but it stages a frustrated group against one newcomer and asks him to defend a career's worth of belief in public; argument rarely does what direct experience does. Sending him to a certification course while holding back stories sidelines a senior engineer and relies on classroom instruction to overturn long-held convictions. Restating the norm and asking the functional manager to reinforce it is command and control, buying compliance while pushing the resistance somewhere teammates can no longer engage it.
questions.concept: Coaching mindset change through experiential learning and active listening
questions.question: A senior engineer who recently joined an XP team from a plan-driven defense contractor keeps asking for a complete requirements specification before writing any code and describes test-driven development as "rework in disguise." Teammates are becoming frustrated. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Ask the team to walk the engineer through its reasoning for test-driven development at the next retrospective, so the objection is answered openly and the agreements reaffirmed
Enroll the engineer in a certification course covering agile engineering practices and hold back story assignments until it finishes, so the fundamentals are in place first
Pair the engineer with an experienced teammate on a small story, and separately hold a one-on-one conversation to genuinely explore the engineer's concerns about incremental work
Restate test-driven development as a team norm the engineer accepted on joining, and ask the functional manager to reinforce that expectation at their next one-on-one

questions.explanation: Regulation constrains what can be released to production; it does not constrain who may use a working increment in a controlled environment. Moderated task-based sessions in the validated test environment give observed behavior from actual clinicians every iteration, which is the point of early feedback, and they carry no compliance risk. Relying on requirement reviews with a single subject-matter expert substitutes one person's opinion about a description for many users' behavior with the product. Seeking a regulatory exception pushes against a control that exists for patient safety when a compliant path to the same learning is readily available. Toggling the screen on for everyone at release still defers all learning until after release and additionally exposes every clinician at once to an unvalidated interaction design.
questions.concept: Obtaining early user feedback under regulatory or release constraints
questions.question: A team building a portal for an infusion-pump servicing business works under regulated change control: production releases require a validation cycle that runs only once a quarter. Clinicians will therefore not touch the new medication-reconciliation screen for about four months. The product owner treats this as an unavoidable fact of regulated life and plans a single review with a clinical subject-matter expert before release. What is the BEST response?
choices: Keep the quarterly cadence and rely on structured requirement walkthroughs with the clinical subject-matter expert, since one informed reviewer can represent clinicians until validation runs.
Ask the regulatory group for a documented exception so that a small group of clinicians can use the new reconciliation screen in production ahead of the next validation cycle.
Release the screen behind a toggle at the next validation cycle, enable it for every clinician on release day, and gather reconciliation feedback from live use afterwards.
Run moderated sessions in the validated test environment where clinicians complete real reconciliation tasks on each working increment, and feed what is observed into the next iteration.

questions.explanation: Psychological safety was damaged by a specific behavior, so the practitioner addresses the behavior directly — privately, preserving the senior developer's dignity — and then helps the whole team make its norms explicit so failed experiments are treated as learning rather than ammunition. An anonymous idea-submission channel treats the symptom: it institutionalizes the assumption that speaking openly is unsafe instead of restoring safety, and the ridicule goes unaddressed. Reserving the next spikes for senior members punishes the people who were hurt, blocks skill growth, and signals that experimentation belongs to a few. Opening the next walkthrough by drawing out what the failed spike taught is genuinely good practice and belongs in the repair — but as the first move it addresses the audience rather than the cause, and celebrating learning in public while the behavior that punished it goes unmentioned reads as hollow, which is why the private conversation comes first.
questions.concept: Psychological safety and working agreements
questions.question: During a walkthrough of a failed technical spike, a senior developer ridicules a newer teammate's approach in front of stakeholders. In the weeks since, the team's newer members have stopped proposing ideas or volunteering for experimental work. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Discuss the behavior's impact privately with the senior developer and then have the team revisit its working agreements on how experiments and failure are treated
Introduce an anonymous idea-submission channel so quieter members can put experimental proposals forward without exposing themselves to criticism in front of the whole team
Assign the next few spikes to the senior members, since experimental work carries reputational risk that newer teammates should not have to absorb this early on
Open the next walkthrough by drawing out what the failed spike taught the team, so newer members see that experiments which miss are still valued

questions.explanation: The team has jumped from symptoms straight to a countermeasure, and a failure repeating across three iterations is exactly the signal that the real cause sits below anything anyone has named — the practitioner's job is to slow the group down long enough to understand before it prescribes. A manual checklist owned as a release gate adds after-the-fact inspection and a bottleneck person; it is the opposite of building quality in and will not survive contact with the underlying cause, whether that is environment drift or an unreliable test suite. Adding regression cases for the three specific features protects against yesterday's defects only and leaves the mechanism that produced them untouched. Reporting the trend upward and requesting an audit takes the improvement away from the team that owns the work, delays action, and reframes a learning opportunity as a compliance problem.
questions.concept: Root-cause analysis (Five Whys / fishbone) preceding countermeasure selection
questions.question: For the third iteration running, a feature the team had called done was rolled back within a day of release. In the retrospective the team lists what it noticed — "tests were flaky," "the release went out late in the day," "the config was different in production" — and within ten minutes votes to adopt a manual pre-release checklist. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Accept the checklist as the team's countermeasure and have a senior engineer own it as a release gate, since the team converged quickly and the fastest way to learn is trying their own idea.

Facilitate a structured root-cause pass — walking one specific rollback back through successive "why" questions, or laying the candidate causes out on a cause-and-effect diagram — before the team commits to a countermeasure.

Ask the tester to build regression coverage for the three rolled-back features first, so the team's flaky tests are stabilized before the group spends more time debating which candidate cause matters most.

Take the three observations to the release manager and request a review of the deployment process, since the same failure recurring across three iterations points beyond what a single team can see alone.

questions.explanation: Managing value delivery means steering by outcomes rather than by counts of output. Nine accepted, released items that failed to move the target metric is strong evidence that the underlying value hypothesis is wrong, and the honest agile move is to surface that disconfirming data transparently and re-plan collaboratively around hypotheses that can be tested cheaply, stopping investment where the assumed value has already been disproven. Accepting a higher item-count target and deferring the metric check compounds the error — it converts a disproven hypothesis into a larger batch and delays feedback that is already available today. Standing up a separate analytics workstream while the team keeps building offloads learning to another group, delays the decision, and adds process instead of putting the existing evidence in front of the people who set priority. Requiring a measured abandonment drop inside each item's acceptance criteria conflates a done condition with an outcome the team cannot control within an iteration; it makes items unfinishable and buries the real conversation about whether the roadmap bet is sound.
questions.concept: Outcomes over outputs and validating value hypotheses
questions.question: A subscription grocery service has a product goal of reducing first-order abandonment. Over the last four iterations the team delivered nine backlog items tied to that goal, all accepted and released. At the review, the marketing director praises the throughput and asks the team to commit to fifteen items next quarter. The practitioner pulls the analytics: first-order abandonment has moved from 31% to 30.6%, within noise. The product owner says the roadmap for the next quarter already lists twelve more checkout features. What is the BEST response?
choices: Accept the fifteen-item target since the delivered throughput plainly supports it, and revisit abandonment once the whole roadmap set has shipped and first-time customers have had several weeks to change their checkout habits

Bring the abandonment data into the next roadmap conversation and work with the product owner and stakeholders to reframe upcoming items around testable outcome hypotheses, pausing items whose value assumption is unsupported

Ask the marketing director to fund a separate analytics workstream that determines why the nine released items did not move abandonment, while the team keeps delivering the roadmap it has already agreed to

Add an acceptance criterion to every remaining checkout item requiring a measurable drop in abandonment before that item can be called done, so that value is enforced item by item at each iteration review

questions.explanation: A new team carrying habits from a directive environment needs to experience ownership, not be told about it: explaining the intent and then facilitating the members as they pull and negotiate work themselves builds the self-organizing muscle while the practitioner stays close enough to support. Continuing to assign tasks 'for now' feels safe but reinforces exactly the dependency the team needs to unlearn, and there is never a convenient moment to stop. Handing assignment authority to functional managers moves the team further from self-management and fragments it along reporting lines. A rotating roster is still an externally imposed allocation mechanism — it swaps a human dispatcher for a schedule and removes the daily conversation in which members weigh skills, dependencies, and learning opportunities.
questions.concept: Growing self-organization in a newly formed team
questions.question: A newly formed delivery team in its second week keeps waiting each morning for the agile practitioner to hand out individual tasks, explaining that this is how their previous project worked. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask each member's functional manager to set the individual assignments for now, so specialist work is matched to skills while the new team builds its shared knowledge
Explain the intent behind self-organization, then facilitate the team in pulling and negotiating work among themselves at the board while remaining available to support
Post a rotating assignment roster beside the board so the work is spread evenly and nobody waits for direction, and review how the rotation is working each retrospective
Keep handing out the daily tasks until the team reaches its third or fourth iteration so early delivery is protected, then introduce self-organization once the group has settled

questions.explanation: Velocity is a team-local capacity heuristic denominated in a unit the team defines, so it is trivially inflatable and meaningless across teams; showing the director the inflation already occurring and offering measures that are far harder to game, such as throughput, cycle time, and value actually released, addresses the real need for portfolio visibility while protecting the integrity of the data. Normalizing points against a reference story preserves the false premise that estimate units are comparable across different teams, domains, and technologies, and it invites the same inflation once the target returns. Complying while keeping a private set of real numbers creates two truths, erodes transparency, and leaves the flawed league table driving investment decisions. Blocking the team's reporting and funneling questions through the practitioner reduces transparency and positions the practitioner as a gatekeeper rather than resolving the measurement problem.
questions.concept: Misuse of velocity as a comparative productivity target
questions.question: A newly appointed portfolio director has begun circulating a league table comparing the velocity of six delivery teams and has asked every team to raise velocity by 15% next quarter. Within two iterations, the practitioner's team has quietly started sizing items more generously, and a developer jokes that the team "can hit any number they like." What is the BEST response?
choices: Meet the portfolio director with evidence of how estimate inflation distorts the league table, and propose throughput, cycle time, and released-value measures for cross-team visibility
Normalize story points across the six teams against a shared reference story, so the league table compares like with like and a 15 percent rise carries the same meaning everywhere it appears
Meet the 15 percent target for one quarter while privately tracking the team's real cycle time, so the team keeps the director's confidence and the practitioner keeps an honest measure
Ask the team to stop reporting velocity upward and route portfolio questions through the practitioner, so estimates stay a planning tool and the pressure to inflate them disappears

questions.explanation: Explaining that visible blockers attract help and proposing to discuss the impediment during the visit preserves transparency and turns the information radiator into what it is for: an honest signal that lets leaders remove obstacles, such as pressuring the payment vendor. Taking the column down for the day and restoring it afterward makes the radiator dishonest and teaches the team that truth is negotiable whenever leadership is watching. Relabeling the blocked items as awaiting external input so the wall reads as work in motion is cosmetic reclassification — the items are still stalled, and dressing a queue up as flow misinforms the very people who could clear it. Offering to brief the executives afterward and simplifying the wall for the tour is the most defensible alternative, since the practitioner does intend to tell them, but it loses on timing: the moment decision-makers are in the room is exactly when an external impediment should be raised.
questions.concept: Information radiators and honest visualization of impediments
questions.question: A Kanban team maintaining a museum ticketing platform keeps a large wall board showing all work, including a column of blocked items awaiting a payment-vendor fix. The operations director asks the agile practitioner to take down the blocked column before an executive site visit because "it makes us look like we can't manage our work." What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Take the column down for the day of the visit and put it back afterward, so the operations director's concern is respected in full
Move the blocked items into a lane labeled awaiting external input so that the wall reads as work in motion rather than stalled work
Offer to brief the executives on the vendor issue after the visit and simplify the wall so that the tour stays focused on delivered value
Explain that visible blockers invite executive help with the vendor issue, and suggest using the visit to discuss the impediment openly

questions.explanation: Bringing both parties into one session where the real costs and the real stakes become transparent, then letting the group shape the option together, applies every relevant agile decision rule at once: make the invisible visible, collaborate before escalating, and let value data rather than authority or tension drive the trade-off; blending thin slices also avoids a big-bang bet in either direction. Backing the product lead and deferring the whole stabilization effort until after the show is the strongest alternative, because the trade-show commitment is real — but a suite already masking defects puts the demonstrated build itself at risk. Absorbing the flaky tests quietly inside the definition of done hides the capacity it consumes, so forecasts drift and the lead's distrust of estimates grows. An even capacity split is compromise without analysis, and silencing the lead's questions suppresses a legitimate concern instead of addressing it.
questions.concept: Collaborating conflict mode in a quality-versus-commitment trade-off
questions.question: A product team wants to spend the next two weeks stabilizing a flaky automated test suite that has begun masking real defects. The product lead insists that all capacity go to features already promised for an industry trade show, and daily standups have turned tense, with the lead openly questioning the team's estimates. Several responses are defensible, but what is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Support the product lead, since the trade-show dates are already committed to customers and define near-term value, and schedule the full stabilization effort for the first iteration after the show so the suite is repaired without putting the promised demonstration at risk

Facilitate a joint session where the team quantifies the flaky suite's cost in escaped defects and rework, the lead states what the trade show actually requires, and the group shapes a blended option such as thin stabilization slices alongside the highest-value features

Have the team absorb the flaky tests inside its own definition of done without renegotiating scope, so quality work proceeds quietly alongside the promised features and the lead has no reason to keep questioning estimates in front of the whole team each morning

Split the team's capacity evenly between stabilization and feature work so both positions are honored equally, and ask the product lead to hold questions about estimates until after the trade show so the standups return to a calmer working rhythm

questions.explanation: A private conversation built on active listening is the right first move because the behavior — withdrawal after being outvoted — is a recognizable conflict response, and the practitioner does not yet know what is driving it: the poll mechanism, feeling disrespected, or something entirely outside work. Understanding must precede any prescription. Waiting another iteration because delivery metrics look fine mistakes lagging output for team health; disengagement compounds quietly and the cost of lost design feedback grows. Asking the product manager to mandate designer sign-off imposes a process remedy for a relational problem and restores her influence by decree rather than by genuine collaboration — it may even breed resentment in the rest of the team. Raising the pattern at a retrospective before speaking with her puts a withdrawn person under a public spotlight without consent, which typically deepens withdrawal; a retrospective conversation may follow later, but only after she has been heard and agrees to it.
questions.concept: Recognizing withdrawal/avoidance and active listening
questions.question: A senior UX designer on a cross-functional product team has stopped contributing during refinement since two of her design proposals were voted down in quick team polls. She now delivers exactly what tickets specify, declines design-review invitations, and keeps her camera off. Delivery metrics remain healthy. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Raise the pattern at the next retrospective so the whole team can examine how design proposals are being decided
Ask the product owner to require design sign-off on each story, so her expertise carries formal weight again
Since delivery metrics stay healthy, observe one more iteration so the pattern is confirmed before any action
Meet with the designer privately and use active listening to understand her perspective before deciding on any action

questions.explanation: The best first move is a direct, collaborative conversation with the manager that connects observable evidence (members no longer pulling work) to the manager's own goal, and coaches toward pull-based self-assignment — this addresses the root behavior while preserving the relationship and restoring the team's ownership of its workflow. Asking the team to raise the change itself at the retrospective is defensible, since self-organization includes speaking up, but it puts the people with the least positional safety in front of a new manager and delays feedback to a forum he may not even attend. Proposing a published rotation for the daily assignments only makes command-and-control assignment feel more polite; the team still does not choose its own work. Reserving one day a week for self-selected items grants token autonomy while legitimizing assignment on the other four days, so the anti-pattern is bargained with rather than corrected.
questions.concept: Pull-based self-organization vs. task assignment; coaching leaders out of command-and-control anti-patterns
questions.question: A Kanban team that handles infrastructure requests has always pulled its own work from the board. A newly hired engineering manager, wanting to "optimize utilization," begins assigning every incoming request to a named individual each morning. Within two weeks, team members have stopped volunteering for anything they were not assigned. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the team to raise the change themselves at the next retrospective, since a self-organizing team should be able to push back on its own manager
Propose a published rotation for the daily assignments so the work at least feels evenly shared while people settle in under the new manager
Meet with the manager, share what has changed on the board, and explore how pull-based self-assignment creates the ownership the manager is seeking
Ask the manager to keep assigning most of the work but reserve one day a week for self-selected items, so utilization holds up and volunteering returns

questions.explanation: The untested auto-save assumption is the single largest risk to the nine-month investment, so the best move is to convert it from opinion into validated learning while most of the budget is still uncommitted — a thin slice used by real gig workers measures what they actually do, not what a report says they might do, and each alternative fails on exactly that point. Continuing the funded plan defers the moment of truth nine months and risks delivering a polished product nobody funds their savings through; deference to leadership confidence is not evidence. A three-month ethnographic study gathers what people say rather than what they do, delays contact with real behavior by a quarter, and still puts nothing of value in users' hands. Building everything behind feature flags spends the entire build cost before any learning occurs — flags manage rollout and operational risk, not demand risk, and switching a feature off after launch is learning at the most expensive possible moment.
questions.concept: Riskiest-assumption testing with an MVP (Lean Startup)
questions.question: Leadership at an insurtech has funded a nine-month build of a full-featured micro-savings product for gig workers, based on an extensive purchased market-research report. Reviewing the plan, the agile practitioner notices the core assumption — that gig workers will let the app automatically divert a percentage of each payout into savings — has never been tested with actual users. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Proceed with the funded nine-month plan, since the purchased research already covers this market and reopening the business case now would stall the initiative
Commission a three-month ethnographic study of gig workers' money habits so the automatic-diversion assumption rests on solid evidence before any code is written
Build the full product behind feature flags and release automatic diversion to a slice of users at launch, so whatever fails to land with them can simply be switched off later
Reframe the first release around the riskiest assumption and put a thin working slice in the hands of a small group of real gig workers to measure actual saving behavior

questions.explanation: The director has a legitimate need — spotting teams that need help — served by the wrong instrument, so the strongest move is to address the need with measures that genuinely compare across teams and reflect flow and outcomes, while naming why point totals cannot. Recalibrating points to a common scale manufactures false comparability, since points encode each team's own reference stories, and it rewards the gaming already underway.
