Telling the team to absorb the criticism quietly leaves a measurement system that is actively corrupting estimates and demoralizing people, and it is not honest with the director. Withholding velocity and sending only a burnup reduces transparency, looks evasive, and still leaves the director without the diagnostic information requested, so the dysfunction simply reappears in another form.
questions.concept: Velocity as a team-local metric; countering cross-team comparison and metric gaming
questions.question: A newly appointed portfolio director publishes a dashboard ranking six delivery teams by velocity and asks each team's agile practitioner to explain in writing why their team sits below the top performer. Within a fortnight, two teams have visibly inflated their estimates and one has stopped splitting stories. The director's stated goal is to know which teams need help. What is the BEST response?
choices: Help the team recalibrate its story points against the leading team's reference stories, so the dashboard compares like with like and the director can see which teams genuinely need help rather than which ones simply size their work most conservatively.

Meet the director, explain that story points are a team-local unit that cannot be compared across teams, and offer a comparable set instead — cycle time, throughput trend, defect escape rate and delivered outcomes — presented with each team's context.

Coach the team to keep estimating honestly and answer the written request plainly, since the practitioner's job is to protect the team's integrity and let leadership draw its own conclusions from numbers the team knows to be sound.

Stop supplying velocity to the dashboard and share the release burnup instead, since a burnup shows leadership real progress toward a release date while keeping an internal planning unit out of a ranking it was never built for.

questions.explanation: Average time in process is a function of how much work is in the system divided by how fast it leaves — 24 divided by 6 is about four weeks — so the honest explanation and the remedy are the same thing: start less, finish more. Overtime attacks a queueing problem with unsustainable effort, and the queue refills as soon as intake resumes. Story-point estimation makes the label on each item more precise without changing the queue that actually determines delivery time. Quoting four weeks and changing nothing is transparent but stops one step short: it reports the symptom instead of removing the cause the team can control this week.
questions.concept: Practical Little's Law: WIP, throughput, cycle time
questions.question: A claims-automation team pulls all work from one queue. Over the last quarter they have averaged 24 items in progress and have finished an average of 6 items per week. Stakeholders complain that requests they were told would take "about two weeks" routinely take a month, and they want a firmer commitment process. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask the team to work extra hours until the in-progress queue is cleared, then reset stakeholder expectations from a clean board.
Introduce story-point estimation for every incoming request so that per-item forecasts given to stakeholders become more accurate.
Tell stakeholders the honest figure is about four weeks per request, and keep the current way of working since the data now supports the longer quote.
Show that 24 items in progress at 6 finished per week implies about four weeks per item, then cut how much work the team starts.

questions.explanation: An ignored red build means the team has lost its fastest feedback signal, and the escaped defects are the price already being paid. Framing the debt in the sponsor's terms — defects reaching customers and the rework they cause — turns a technical argument into a value conversation, and reserving a small, continuous slice each iteration for the highest-risk tests repays the debt incrementally while features keep shipping. Deferring everything to a hardening iteration after the feature set keeps the feedback loop broken throughout, lets more defects escape, and stacks the riskiest work where the least time remains. Splitting the suite so a fast subset runs nightly is the strongest rival, since a green result the team will actually read is worth something — but moving the remainder to monthly widens the gap on the very paths where defects are escaping, buying the green by testing less rather than by fixing what is broken. Handing repair to the test specialists separates quality from the people writing the code and weakens shared ownership.
questions.concept: Technical debt, trustworthy build feedback, and quality built in
questions.question: A team building firmware for smart irrigation controllers runs a nine-hour automated regression suite overnight. It has been red on eleven of the last fourteen nights, and the team has stopped reading the result; three defects have escaped to customers this quarter. The sponsor, who is funding a new scheduling feature set, wants every remaining iteration spent on those features. What is the BEST response?
choices: Make the cost visible to the sponsor using escaped-defect and rework data, and reserve a slice of each iteration for stabilizing and speeding the tests that cover the highest-risk paths first.

Plan a dedicated hardening iteration once the scheduling features are delivered, so feature flow is not interrupted while the sponsor's funding is committed, and clear the escaped defects in one pass.
Split the suite so that a fast subset runs nightly and the remainder runs monthly, restoring a green result the team will actually read without spending any of the sponsor's feature capacity.
Hand repair of the regression suite to the test specialists so the developers stay entirely on the scheduling features, and report the suite's health at each iteration review.

questions.explanation: The initiative was funded to produce an outcome — better routing performance for depots — and the evidence says the chosen outputs are not producing it while an unplanned capability is. Taking that evidence to the sponsor at the review is transparent, keeps the funding decision with the person accountable for it, and reframes success as outcomes achieved rather than scope completed; it also uses the review for its actual purpose, inspecting real usage and adapting the plan. Continuing to deliver the listed scope treats an approved document as more authoritative than measured reality, spending four weeks of remaining funding to produce features that 6% of depots have shown any appetite for. Commissioning a market study consumes runway the initiative does not have and substitutes industry averages for direct evidence from this company's own depots, which is the stronger data. Reprioritizing quietly reaches a defensible destination by an indefensible route: it withholds material information from the person accountable for the money, and the moment the concealment surfaces it costs the team the trust that makes every future adaptation possible.
questions.concept: Outcomes over outputs: evidence-based re-planning of remaining investment
questions.question: A waste-management software company funds initiatives quarterly. Eight weeks into a twelve-week initiative for a 'route optimization suite,' telemetry shows the two released features are being used by 6% of depots against a business case that assumed 40% adoption within a month. Meanwhile, a small capability the team prototyped from support tickets — automatic re-scheduling of missed collections — is used daily by every depot that has it, and dispatchers have asked for it by name. Four weeks of funding remain, and the approved business case lists three more optimization features. Several courses of action are technically feasible. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Commission a market study of route-optimization adoption at comparable waste operators before proposing any change of direction to the sponsor, so that the recommendation rests on wider industry evidence rather than on eight weeks of internal telemetry drawn from a single quarter of early access

Continue delivering the three remaining optimization features, because the sponsor personally approved the business case on that scope and reopening the commitment eight weeks into a twelve-week initiative would cost the team credibility that it will need at the next quarterly funding round

Bring the adoption telemetry and the missed-collection usage data to the sponsor at the next review and jointly re-decide what the remaining four weeks should buy, framing the discussion around the outcome the initiative was funded to produce rather than the scope it listed.

Reprioritize the backlog toward the missed-collection capability now and explain the change to the sponsor at the end of the quarter, once the usage results are strong enough to make the case on their own without a difficult mid-initiative conversation about the funded scope

questions.explanation: The director's demand is a solution to an unstated problem: being blindsided. Listening first to surface the real need — early, trustworthy visibility — and then offering transparency the team already generates through reviews, a visible board, and empirical forecast data satisfies her legitimate concern while protecting the team's self-organization. Setting up a weekly forecast review is the strongest alternative and may well be part of the eventual answer, but it prescribes a mechanism before anyone has asked what visibility she actually lost, and it commits the team to individual reports in the meantime. Complying for a quarter while costing the reports installs a control practice that becomes hard to remove and signals that one missed commitment justifies abandoning agile ways of working. Publishing a commitment-reliability trend beside the board is cheap transparency, but it answers a question about accuracy when her stated concern is about being told early.
questions.concept: Responding to command-and-control anti-patterns with active listening and transparency
questions.question: After a missed release commitment, a delivery director tells an agile practitioner that, effective immediately, every developer will send her a weekly individual status report and the practitioner must personally approve the team's forecasts before they are shared. The team calls this a return to command-and-control; the director says she "cannot be blindsided again." What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Set up a weekly forecast review where the team walks the director through its board and confidence range, then drop the individual reports once she has sat through two sessions
Meet the director to learn what visibility she actually lost, then propose alternatives that meet that need — attending reviews, seeing the team's board, and using its forecast data
Implement the individual reports for one quarter while tracking the hours they cost the team, then use that evidence to propose a return to team-level forecasting and reporting
Have the team publish its own commitment-reliability trend beside the board each week, so the director can judge forecast accuracy for herself without collecting a report from each developer

questions.explanation: A timeboxed split test replaces three weeks of opinion with a few days of evidence: where experts disagree and debate has stopped producing new information, only real player behavior can reveal which tutorial flow works, and small cohorts keep the cost of being wrong low. Handing the decision to the creative director restarts work but settles it by authority rather than evidence, and if the weaker flow is chosen the studio finds out only after release. Commissioning a comparative analysis against usability heuristics extends the same analytical stalemate, because heuristics are the past experience both factions are already citing. A moderated usability session with a handful of players is the strongest alternative — cheap, fast, and it does put real users in front of both flows — but it observes short-term confusion in an artificial setting, while the question that matters for a mobile title is retention, which only in-product behavior over time can answer.
questions.concept: Split testing and empiricism over debate
questions.question: For three weeks, a game studio's cross-functional team has argued in design reviews over two competing tutorial flows for a mobile title. Each faction cites its own past successes, no new information is emerging, and the release plan is slipping. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask the creative director to choose between the flows so the release plan recovers and the team can start building
Commission a comparative analysis of both flows against usability heuristics and adopt whichever one scores higher overall
Run a moderated usability session with a handful of players and let observed confusion decide which flow ships
Propose a timeboxed split test that ships both flows to small player cohorts and lets retention data settle the question

questions.explanation: Pairing on the real, aging work items transfers tacit knowledge hands-on, removes the single point of failure while the expert is still present, and keeps customer value flowing — the strongest first move a servant leader can make. Spending her remaining time writing comprehensive documentation captures only explicit knowledge, goes stale quickly, and still leaves no one able to actually work the module. Escalating for a contractor with equivalent settlement experience outsources the problem before the team has tried to solve it, adds onboarding delay, and often just creates a second silo. Blocking reconciliation work from entering the board halts customer value and closes no knowledge gap at all — the risk simply reappears when she returns.
questions.concept: Reducing single points of failure through pairing
questions.question: A Kanban team supporting a payments platform relies on one engineer who is the only person who understands the settlement-reconciliation module. She is about to begin three months of leave, and work items touching that module are already aging on the board. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Ask her to spend her remaining time writing comprehensive documentation of the reconciliation module
Pair the engineer with other team members on the aging reconciliation items before she leaves
Escalate the staffing risk to the functional manager and request a contractor with equivalent settlement experience
Add a board policy that blocks new reconciliation work from entering the board until she returns

questions.explanation: Bringing the functions together to map and optimize the end-to-end flow is the systems-thinking response: every part locally efficient while the whole degrades is the classic signature of local optimization, and it can only be resolved by examining the interactions, queues, and handoffs between functions as one system, accepting that global flow sometimes requires a part to run below its own peak efficiency. Adding capacity to whichever function has the longest queue treats the visible queue as the constraint without knowing where delay actually accumulates, and it can simply push work faster into the next bottleneck. Measuring the wait between functions and giving each handoff its own reduction target is the strongest distractor, because measuring those waits is exactly right — it then fragments the system again by making each gap a separate owner's number. Having every function report cycle time so leaders can identify who is holding the others back keeps the part-by-part comparison and adds blame to it.
questions.concept: Systems thinking versus local optimization
questions.question: Every function in a medical-device firm — design, verification, and regulatory review — has met its individual efficiency targets for four consecutive quarters, yet the total time from concept to market clearance keeps lengthening. Which action best applies systems thinking to this situation?
choices: Add capacity to whichever function has the longest queue of waiting work, since relieving the busiest step will shorten the total time to clearance
Measure how long work waits between the functions and give each handoff its own reduction target, so delays are attacked where they are actually occurring
Have every function report cycle time alongside efficiency, so leaders can compare the functions and identify which one is holding the others back
Bring the functions together to map the end-to-end flow and optimize the whole path, even if some individual functions become less locally efficient

questions.explanation: A voluntary community of practice with protected time gives the knowledge a living, self-sustaining home where the practitioners who actually face the customs problems converge on shared patterns, and short-term member exchanges with cross-team pairing move tacit knowledge the way it genuinely travels — through people working side by side on real problems. Mandated weekly lessons-learned reports produce compliance artifacts that pile up unread; push-style documentation with no community consuming it does not change what teams do. A single appointed knowledge manager creates a bottleneck and an owner for knowledge that should be collectively held — the interviews capture snapshots while the real learning keeps happening elsewhere. Routing reuse through an architecture-review approval step adds a gate that actively discourages the borrowing this program needs more of, punishing exactly the behavior it should amplify.
questions.concept: Communities of practice and tacit knowledge transfer through shared work
questions.question: A Lean logistics program spread across six time zones keeps re-solving the same customs-integration problems because hard-won lessons stay trapped inside individual teams. Which TWO actions would BEST build durable knowledge sharing across the program? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Require every team to file a weekly lessons-learned report into a central repository
Sponsor a voluntary customs-integration community of practice with protected time to meet and publish shared patterns
Appoint a single knowledge manager responsible for interviewing teams and maintaining all program documentation
Route any reuse of another team's solution through an architecture-review approval step
Arrange short-term member exchanges and cross-team pairing on shared integration problems

questions.explanation: The two response patterns describe different categories of customer need. Something whose absence causes severe dissatisfaction but whose presence earns no praise is an expected, taken-for-granted quality — offline reliability is table stakes, and failing it damages the product no matter how appealing the rest is. Something whose presence delights but whose absence goes unnoticed is a differentiator that pays off only after the basics are secure. Leading with auto-resequencing because it scored highest on satisfaction misreads the asymmetry: delight features cannot compensate for a broken baseline, and calling reliability a purely technical concern hides a first-class customer need from the backlog where value decisions get made. Dropping auto-resequencing because nobody misses it inverts the logic — going unmissed when absent is the defining signature of a delighter, not evidence that it is worthless. Weighting both equally throws away the sequencing information the survey gives you; the whole point of reading needs by category is that it tells you what must come first, not merely what matters.
questions.concept: Kano-style need categories: expected qualities versus delighters
questions.question: A team building a hotel housekeeping scheduling app surveys staff about a proposed feature that automatically re-sequences a housekeeper's room list when a guest checks out early. Respondents report high satisfaction when they imagine having it, and no dissatisfaction when they imagine not having it. The same survey shows staff report severe dissatisfaction when the app is unavailable on the floor's weak Wi-Fi, but no extra satisfaction when it works — they simply expect it to. How should the team apply this reading?
choices: Treat offline reliability as a baseline the product must meet regardless, and treat auto-resequencing as a differentiator to invest in once that baseline holds
Prioritize auto-resequencing first because it produces the highest measured satisfaction, and treat offline reliability as a technical concern outside the product backlog
Drop auto-resequencing from consideration because a feature nobody misses when it is absent has not been validated as a real user need
Treat both as equally weighted backlog items, since each of them scored strongly on one half of the survey

questions.explanation: Pairing and mobbing on real reconciliation work spreads the tacit knowledge — the judgment, quirks, and failure modes that never make it into a document — across several people while the expert is still available, and the notes captured during those sessions preserve the explicit parts too. A comprehensive wiki page written in the final week transfers only what she remembers to write down, arrives too late for anyone to ask follow-up questions, and captures none of the hands-on judgment. Delaying her rotation until a replacement is hired and trained avoids the transfer problem rather than solving it, and simply recreates a single point of failure in the next person. A recorded handover presentation is one-directional and passive; viewers cannot probe it when the scripts behave unexpectedly at 2 a.m.
questions.concept: Tacit knowledge transfer through pairing and mobbing (reducing key-person risk)
questions.question: In a payments organization, only one engineer truly understands the nightly settlement-reconciliation scripts, and she is scheduled to rotate onto another initiative in six weeks. Her manager has asked her to "write everything up on the wiki during her final week." What should the agile practitioner recommend instead?
choices: Have her pair and mob with teammates on live reconciliation work over the remaining weeks, capturing notes as they go
Require a comprehensive wiki page, reviewed and signed off by the manager, before she is released to the new initiative
Delay her rotation until a replacement engineer is hired and fully trained on the scripts
Ask her to record a single detailed handover presentation that the team can replay whenever questions arise

questions.explanation: In its practical form, average cycle time equals average work in progress divided by average throughput. With throughput steady at about seven items per week, cutting work in progress from 21 to about 7 brings cycle time from roughly three weeks to roughly one — and it requires no extra people and no overtime. Raising the commitment to 21 items per week confuses a target with a capability; asking for more output without changing the system simply inflates work in progress and makes cycle time worse. Splitting items is often genuinely helpful for flow, but the reasoning offered is wrong: splitting does not automatically triple throughput, and if all three pieces are started at once, work in progress rises in step with item count and cycle time per item is unchanged. Re-estimating in story points changes the unit of conversation, not the physics of the queue; no amount of estimation moves items through the system faster.
questions.concept: Practical Little's Law applied to cycle time reduction
questions.question: A service delivery team measures an average of 21 work items in progress and completes an average of 7 items per week; measured average cycle time is close to 3 weeks. Leadership asks the team to bring average cycle time down to roughly one week without adding people and without overtime. Applying Little's Law, which action is most consistent with that goal?
choices: Reduce average work in progress to about seven items by tightening column limits and finishing items before starting new ones.
Raise the weekly commitment from seven items to twenty-one so more work finishes each week and the queue drains three times faster.
Split every item into three smaller pieces, tripling the item count so that average cycle time per item falls to about a third.
Report cycle time per story point rather than per item, so variation in item size stops distorting the three-week average.

questions.explanation: A band that widens over time on a cumulative flow diagram means items are entering that state faster than they leave it — a queue is forming, work is aging, and lead time is stretching even though completions continue. The practitioner's job is to make that visible to the people doing the work and let them diagnose the cause, because the right countermeasure (swarming on reviews, a review WIP limit, pairing, smaller items) depends on what is actually happening. Reporting a reviewer shortage to the portfolio office asserts a capacity cause before anyone has examined the data and routes the problem away from the team closest to it. Concluding that a rising "Done" line means all is well confuses throughput with flow health: steady throughput alongside a growing queue guarantees longer waits and older work in progress. Imposing a mandatory two-reviews-before-pull rule prescribes a remedy without diagnosis and adds process the team did not choose; the team may well arrive at a similar working agreement, but it should be their experiment, owned and inspected by them.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation and queue detection
questions.question: A media-streaming platform team pulls work across a Kanban board. During the weekly flow review, the cumulative flow diagram for the last six weeks shows the "Ready for Review" band widening steadily, while the "Done" line continues to rise at a constant but modest slope. Nobody has raised a concern. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Report the widening band to the portfolio office as evidence of a reviewer shortage and request an additional person
Take no action, because the "Done" line is still climbing at its usual rate, which shows delivery remains on track
Show the diagram to the team and facilitate a conversation about why work is piling up before review
Introduce a rule that no developer may pull new work until they have personally reviewed two other items

questions.explanation: Framing the two designs as testable hypotheses and putting low-fidelity versions of each in front of a small merchant segment converts an opinion battle into cheap, fast, empirical learning — the essence of hypothesis-driven development. Building both onboarding paths to production quality and split-testing across the entire new-merchant population would produce statistically solid evidence, but it maximizes the cost of learning; an experiment should be the smallest investment that answers the question, not two finished products exposed to every merchant. Commissioning one rigorous combined study prolongs the analysis and still measures what merchants say rather than what they do. Having the product owner run a structured decision session and commit is the strongest alternative, since prioritization is genuinely the product owner's call and refinement is blocked — but weighing two sets of dueling memos produces a decision without new evidence, when the product itself could supply the answer in days.
questions.concept: Hypothesis-driven development (Lean Startup validated learning)
questions.question: Two product managers on a payments team have argued for three sprints about whether new merchants prefer a guided setup wizard or a single-page "quick start" form. Each has commissioned market-research memos supporting their own view, and the standoff is now stalling backlog refinement. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Help the team frame each option as a testable hypothesis and release a low-fidelity version of each to a small merchant segment, letting real usage data settle the question
Build both onboarding paths to production quality and run a full split test across the entire new-merchant population, so the winner is settled by statistically solid usage data
Commission one rigorous combined study of what new merchants actually prefer during setup, so backlog refinement rests on a single evidence base rather than two dueling memos
Have the product owner run a structured decision session, weigh both memos against the product goals, and commit to one onboarding flow so refinement can resume

questions.explanation: The decision here is an allocation problem: demand is three times supply, capacity is fixed, and the distortion is that seniority and airtime, not value, have been setting the order. Pricing the features and issuing purses that cannot cover a group's own wish list makes scarcity a property of the game rather than a claim someone has to argue against a senior voice; requiring groups to pool money for the expensive items forces the negotiation into the open, and every group spends the same currency, which gives the compliance analysts a channel equal to the finance director's without requiring them to out-talk him. The speed boat option is a genuine collaboration game, but it elicits impediments and drags on today's users; it produces a list of problems, not an allocation against fixed capacity, and nothing in it caps total demand or stops the loudest voice from interpreting which anchors matter. Writing an independent picture of a successful launch is also a real game and does give quiet participants a private channel, but it converges on shared goals and success criteria rather than on which two-thirds of the nominations get cut this quarter; the three-to-one over-subscription survives it untouched. Placing nominations on a tree to keep growth balanced is a legitimate shaping and prioritization game, but it optimizes the product's shape rather than imposing a budget, and the stated tiebreak — build the branches with the most leaves — rewards whichever group posts the most cards, reproducing exactly the dominance problem the agile lead is trying to break.
questions.concept: Matching a collaboration game to the decision type — constrained trade-off allocation versus scope shaping or impediment discovery
questions.question: A regional water utility is replacing its customer billing portal. Delivery capacity for the next quarter is fixed and cannot be increased. Four stakeholder groups — field operations, the call center, finance, and regulatory compliance — have each nominated features they describe as essential, and the combined list is roughly three times what the team can build. In the two prior workshops the finance director, the most senior person present and the one who talked most, effectively set the order; the compliance analysts said almost nothing in the room and afterward emailed the agile lead that two of their items are non-negotiable. The agile lead has one 90-minute session with all four groups and needs an ordering the groups will stand behind afterward. Which facilitation approach best fits this decision?
choices: Run a speed boat exercise so the groups surface the anchors slowing billing portal users today, then order the nominated features by how many anchors each one removes and how heavy those anchors are for users

Run remember the future, asking each group to write independently what the portal looks like six months after a successful launch, then derive the ordering of the nominated features from the description the four groups end up sharing

Run buy a feature: price every nominated feature by relative cost, hand each group a purse worth far less than its own nominations, and set the expensive items above any single purse so groups must pool money to buy them

Run prune the product tree, having every group post its nominations onto the tree so the portal's growth stays balanced across every branch, then build out the branches that end up carrying the most leaves

questions.explanation: A voluntary, member-led community of practice creates a durable network where practitioners exchange tacit integration knowledge because they want to, and cross-team demos and brown-bag sessions move working solutions between teams quickly through direct, interactive show-and-tell - both spread knowledge without imposing process. Mandated weekly reports to a PMO repository generate compliance artifacts that few read and capture little of the tacit 'how,' adding exactly the heavy process leadership wants to avoid. Funneling all integration designs through one approving architect creates a bottleneck and a gatekeeper rather than a knowledge flow, and it disempowers the teams. Restricting chat channels to force everything into an official repository shuts down the informal, high-bandwidth exchanges through which most real knowledge sharing actually happens.
questions.concept: Communities of practice and lightweight cross-team knowledge exchange
questions.question: An agile practitioner supports several teams whose engineers keep independently solving the same integration problems, each unaware of the others' work. Leadership wants knowledge to flow across teams without adding heavy process. Which TWO actions should the practitioner take? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Require every team to submit a weekly lessons-learned report to the PMO knowledge repository
Sponsor a voluntary community of practice around integration, letting its members set the agenda and cadence
Appoint a single architect as the mandatory approver of all integration designs across the teams
Restrict cross-team chat channels so that information is captured only in the official repository
Encourage short cross-team demos and brown-bag sessions where teams show how they solved recent integration problems

questions.explanation: A blameless review is best because it treats the outage as a system failure — the change passed whatever tests, reviews, and pipeline gates existed, so those are what must improve — and it preserves the safety that makes engineers report the next near-miss early instead of hiding it. Giving the director the two names privately still individualizes blame and adds secrecy, so it corrodes trust in both directions while fixing nothing. Naming the pair and adding senior sign-off on future refactorings pairs punishment with a gate that slows every later change and leaves the detection gap untouched. Having the pair walk the director through what they changed is the most defensible alternative, since first-hand context is valuable, but staged in front of someone already seeking individuals to hold accountable it becomes an interrogation, and it centers the review on two people's reasoning rather than on the system that let the failure reach customers.
questions.concept: Blameless incident reviews and systems thinking about failure
questions.question: During a hardening effort, an XP pair pushes a refactoring that takes a customer-facing service down for an hour. The operations director asks the agile practitioner to identify who wrote the change so the individuals can be "held accountable" in the incident review. What is the BEST response?
choices: Give the director the two names privately while keeping them out of the written incident report, so the request for accountability is met without a permanent record
Facilitate a blameless review that examines how the tests, pipeline, and practices allowed the failure to reach production, with the whole team owning the follow-up actions
Name the pair this once and add a senior sign-off on all future refactorings, so the director sees both the accountability he asked for and a concrete control against recurrence
Ask the pair to walk the director through what they changed and why, so the reasoning is heard first-hand and the review can then move on to remediation work

questions.explanation: The root problem is loop length, not testing effort: defects discovered a quarter after the code was written are expensive precisely because the feedback arrives long after the context is gone. Integrating and testing small slices continuously moves discovery to within days of the change, when defects are cheapest to fix. Adding testers to the quarterly window finds more defects at the same late, expensive point. Documenting and jointly reviewing interface contracts before coding is genuinely useful in a multi-team program and would prevent some mismatches at the source, but agreed documents drift from running code, so it belongs alongside continuous integration rather than instead of it. Moving the pass to monthly is a step in the right direction, yet integration remains a separate group's batch event and defects still queue behind a calendar.
questions.concept: Continuous integration as a feedback-loop shortener in hybrid programs
questions.question: A hybrid program spans component teams in three time zones. The teams build in two-week cycles, but a separate quality group performs integration testing only once a quarter, as inherited from the program's predictive phase. Integration defects are now surfacing months after the code was written, and each one is expensive to trace and fix. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Add testers to the quarterly integration window so defects are found faster once the code from three time zones has been assembled
Work with the teams to integrate and test smaller slices of the product continuously so integration defects surface within days of being introduced
Require interface contracts to be documented and jointly reviewed before coding starts, so the component teams stop introducing the mismatches at the source
Ask the quality group to run the integration test pass monthly rather than quarterly, and give each team a fixed window for the fixes

questions.explanation: The recurring debates are a symptom: each person is optimizing for a different, privately held definition of success. Co-creating a vision and shared success measures with the customer and the whole team gives every future trade-off a common yardstick, and co-creation — not receipt of a document — is what produces genuine commitment. Publishing the sponsor's business case is one-way broadcast; people rarely align around a document they had no hand in shaping, and it will not settle story-level trade-offs. Routing every disagreement to the customer for a ruling resolves individual disputes but keeps the team dependent on arbitration and never builds alignment. Hard-coding a refactoring allowance into the definition of done patches one argument with process while leaving the underlying misalignment — and every future trade-off — untouched.
questions.concept: Co-created vision and success measures as a decision filter
questions.question: On an XP team building a claims platform, pairs repeatedly clash over refactoring depth versus shipping speed. Asked what success looks like, the tester says "zero defects," a developer says "fastest delivery in the portfolio," and the onsite customer says "lower call-center volume." The same trade-off debate restarts with almost every story. What is the BEST response?
choices: Publish the sponsor's original business case on the team wiki and refer the pair to it whenever a refactoring trade-off starts another debate
Ask the onsite customer to make the final call whenever a pair cannot agree on depth, since the customer represents the business value that the team delivers
Add a clause to the definition of done fixing how much refactoring each story may carry, so the trade-off is settled before a pair starts work
Facilitate a working session in which the customer and the whole team co-create a product vision and the success measures they will use to steer trade-offs

questions.explanation: Each mechanism closes a different loop at a different timescale, and the distinctions matter. Pair programming is the tightest loop of all: a second set of eyes reacts to each design and coding decision as it happens, in seconds — before the code even exists as a commit. Continuous integration operates at the next timescale: every merge triggers an automated build and test run, exposing integration and regression problems within minutes rather than at a painful end-of-project integration phase. The iteration review or demo closes the stakeholder loop once per timebox: working functionality is inspected against expectations, catching direction errors within weeks. An MVP release closes the longest and most consequential loop — the market loop — replacing internal opinion with real customer behavior about whether the product idea has value. A common trap is conflating the demo (stakeholder acceptance of an increment) with the MVP (market validation of the value hypothesis), or treating CI as code-quality feedback when its distinctive contribution is integration feedback; pairing, not CI, is the mechanism that shortens the design-decision loop to seconds.
questions.concept: Nested feedback loops across engineering, iteration, and market levels
questions.question: Match each feedback mechanism (left) to the loop it shortens (right). Each description is used exactly once.
pairs: Pair programming
Gives second-by-second feedback on design and coding decisions as they are being made
Continuous integration
Reveals within minutes whether newly merged code works with the rest of the system
Iteration review / demo
Confirms at the end of every timebox whether the increment meets stakeholder expectations
MVP release to the market
Provides real behavioral evidence of whether customers value the product idea at all

questions.explanation: A cumulative flow diagram is a conversation starter, not a verdict. A band that widens while the upstream bands hold steady says only that work is arriving at Verification faster than it leaves; it does not say why. The cause could be an approval queue, a shared test environment, unclear entry criteria, or rework arriving from upstream. Taking the picture to the team so they can diagnose the accumulation together honors transparency and keeps the improvement with the people who own the work. Asking the two specialists to work extra hours attacks the people rather than the constraint, is unsustainable, and suppresses the very signal the diagram is giving. Requesting funding for another specialist commits money to a solution before anyone has confirmed that capacity is the problem; if the delay is a waiting approval, an extra person simply enlarges the queue. Removing Verification as its own band destroys the transparency that surfaced the issue and makes the growing queue invisible.
questions.concept: Reading a cumulative flow diagram to detect a growing queue
questions.question: A Kanban team that processes municipal permit applications reviews its cumulative flow diagram at the weekly flow review. The band representing the Verification stage has widened for six consecutive weeks, the bands for the earlier stages have stayed roughly constant, and the delivered line is rising more slowly than it did a quarter ago. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Ask the two verification specialists to work extra hours until the Verification band narrows back to its earlier width
Bring the diagram to the whole team and facilitate a conversation about why work is accumulating in Verification
Report the widening trend to the department head and request funding for an additional verification specialist
Stop plotting Verification as its own band so the diagram is simpler for stakeholders to read

questions.explanation: Regulatory and compliance needs are not simply another value score to compare against features; without the affordability check the product cannot legally originate loans, so its absence sets the realizable value of everything else to zero — making that dependency explicit lets the product owner make a genuinely informed ranking, which is the practitioner's contribution here. Shipping the customer features and deferring compliance knowingly launches into penalty exposure and a product that becomes unlawful to operate a week later. Asking the sponsor to authorize a short delay is the strongest alternative and may end up being the right call, but it escalates for a schedule concession before the prioritization conversation has happened, and the delay may prove unnecessary once the constraint reframes the ranking. Scoring the check high on customer value reaches the right order by corrupting the measure: a legal precondition is recorded as customer demand, so the method still cannot tell a constraint from a preference, and the next one gets the same fudge.
questions.concept: Regulatory constraints in value-based prioritization
questions.question: A fintech team is two iterations from the launch of a lending app MVP. A regulator publishes updated affordability-check rules that take effect one week after the planned launch date; non-compliance carries per-application penalties and the product cannot legally originate loans without the check. The product owner has ranked the remaining backlog by customer-value score and the compliance work scores low because "no customer asks for it." The team's capacity leaves room for either the compliance work or the two highest-scoring customer features, not both. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Deliver the two highest-scoring customer features as ranked, then take the affordability check in the first iteration after launch, before penalties apply
Help the product owner reframe the compliance item as a launch constraint whose absence blocks all value, then re-prioritize with that reality visible
Ask the sponsor to authorize a short launch delay so the affordability check and the two ranked customer features can all ship in the same release
Score the affordability check high enough on customer value to lift it to the top of the ranked backlog, so the existing prioritization method still sets the order

questions.explanation: With only 2 of 12 days spent working, the lead time lives in the waits, and the largest wait is the queue in front of a single security specialist; cross-training targets exactly that constraint, and running it as a bounded experiment with a stated hypothesis, a measure, and the specialist's own involvement respects the regulatory risk while letting the team learn cheaply before committing. Automating a deployment step that already takes 20 minutes optimizes a stage that is not the constraint and cannot move a 12-day lead time meaningfully. Adding two contractors raises work in progress against an unchanged bottleneck and consumes still more of the specialist's time in onboarding. Asking the specialist to put this team's queue ahead of other requests is the strongest rival, since it would cut the 4.5 days immediately and costs nothing to try, but it buys this team's flow by pushing other teams' work back rather than adding review capacity, and the single-person dependency survives untouched.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency, bottleneck targeting, and hypothesis-driven improvement experiments
questions.question: A regulated payments team maps its value stream: average lead time is 12 working days, of which roughly 2 days is hands-on work, giving a flow efficiency near 17 percent. The single largest wait is a 4.5-day queue for a security review performed by one specialist. Leadership has just asked for "30 percent more output next quarter." In an hour-long session the group floats four ideas: automate the deployment pipeline (deployments already take 20 minutes), bring in two contractors, drop exploratory testing, and cross-train two developers to perform a first-pass security review. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Automate the deployment pipeline first, since continuous delivery is the widely accepted route to shorter lead time, it is the least disruptive of the four proposals on the table, and the team can build it without asking the security specialist to change anything.

Bring in the two contractors, since leadership has asked for thirty percent more output next quarter and added hands are the most direct way to raise the amount of work the team can finish inside a quarter no longer than the one just measured.

Run the cross-training idea as a time-boxed experiment with an explicit hypothesis and measure — halving the security-review queue within four weeks with no rise in escaped defects — and review the flow data with the team and the security specialist before scaling it.

Ask the security specialist to work the team's review queue ahead of other requests, since the 4.5-day queue is the largest delay in the value stream and clearing it first would cut lead time without asking anyone on the team to change how they work.

questions.explanation: Eighteen percent flow efficiency with a nine-day wait at a shared specialist says the constraint sits outside the team's own board, which is why two rounds of WIP reduction changed nothing; mapping the stream with the people who own that step makes the queue undeniable to everyone and opens the highest-leverage move — growing capability at the constraint through cross-training while keeping the engineer's oversight and the regulatory trail intact. Weekly batching enlarges batch size and adds up to a week of waiting for anything that misses the window, which is the opposite of flow. Funding a second engineer may eventually be right, but it commits budget and hiring lead time before the constraint has been examined with its owners and before cheaper experiments have run. Dropping validation on self-assessed low-risk items buys speed by removing built-in quality in a regulated product, trading a flow problem for a compliance and safety problem.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency, shared-resource bottlenecks, value stream mapping
questions.question: A regulated medical-device software team measures flow efficiency at 18 percent for the last quarter: items sit an average of nine days waiting for a single validation engineer who is shared with two other teams. The team has already cut its WIP limits twice and lead time has barely moved. The delivery manager lays out three choices: fund part of a second validation engineer, batch validations into one weekly session, or skip validation for items the team judges low risk. Iteration reviews are well attended and the backlog is in good shape. What is the BEST response?
choices: Batch validation into one scheduled weekly session, so the shared engineer meets predictable consolidated demand and can plan the work across all three teams that depend on the role.
Map the value stream with the team and the validation engineer's manager, then run an agreed experiment such as cross-training two team members under the engineer's review.
Request funding for a second validation engineer, since WIP has already been cut twice with no effect and a nine-day wait points to a plain shortfall of validation capacity.
Drop the validation step for items the team assesses as low risk, keeping full validation only for the changes the team judges capable of affecting patient safety.

questions.explanation: With 3.5 days of work inside 21 days of lead time, flow efficiency is about 17 percent, so roughly 83 percent of elapsed time is pure waiting waste sitting in queues the team does not control; showing that redirects effort from squeezing the working sliver toward removing the waiting that dominates delivery time. Keeping daily status calls without individual targets still spends the team's attention on reporting the touch time rather than dissolving the wait states, and adds a meeting that shortens no queue. Re-estimating stories more accurately would improve a forecast of a broken system without removing a single day of waiting, and estimation error appears nowhere in the evidence. Splitting the team into two does nothing about a shared environment, a sign-off queue, or a monthly release train — the same three queues would simply serve two teams and would most likely lengthen, not shrink.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency, value-stream mapping, and waiting waste
questions.question: A team maintaining a freight-tracking service measures lead time from the moment a request enters the backlog to release. Median lead time is 21 days. When the team maps the value stream they find the actual hands-on work totals about 3.5 days; the rest is waiting for a shared integration environment, waiting for a security sign-off queue, and waiting for the monthly release train. A manager sees the 21-day figure and proposes a productivity push: daily status calls and individual throughput targets per developer. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Accept the daily status calls but drop the individual targets, as that preserves the visibility asked for without measuring people
Present the value-stream map showing roughly 17% flow efficiency and steer the conversation toward the three wait states
Ask the team to size incoming requests more carefully so that the manager's 21-day lead-time figure becomes dependable
Split the team into two so that each half works a smaller batch and the shared environment queue drains faster

questions.explanation: Psychological safety collapsed because admitting a mistake was met with a blame signal, so the practitioner must address the source — helping the manager understand the impact of name-collecting on candor — and then rebuild explicit blameless norms with the team. Announcing that the report was a one-time event and instructing the team to be open decrees safety rather than demonstrating it; people re-test safety through experience, not announcements. Making the retrospective a permanent anonymous survey treats the symptom, institutionalizes the fear, and sacrifices the rich dialogue that makes retrospectives valuable. Unilaterally barring all managers is a directive workaround that damages the relationship with management and never resolves the blaming behavior, which will resurface in other forums.
questions.concept: Psychological safety and blameless retrospectives
questions.question: During a retrospective, a member of an XP team openly admitted that a refactoring shortcut they took caused a production outage. A senior manager who attends the retrospectives responded by asking for individual names to include in an incident report. In the two retrospectives since, team members have offered only vague, positive comments. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Meet privately with the manager to explain how the request affected candor, and work with the team to re-establish a blameless working agreement for retrospectives
Announce at the next retrospective that the incident report was a one-off, and ask the team to resume the open discussion it once had
Replace the retrospective discussion with a standing anonymous survey, so that members can raise problems in depth without any risk of being named or quoted afterward
Ask the senior manager to stop attending retrospectives so the team can speak freely, and send him a written summary of the improvement actions afterward

questions.explanation: An unreliable test suite has destroyed the signal the team depends on and is now letting real defects through; making its repair prioritized, visible work is impediment management applied to the constraint that most threatens quality built in. Configuring the pipeline to retry failing tests automatically makes the red disappear without making the code correct — it automates the rerun habit that already let two production defects escape, and a test that passes on the second attempt is precisely the evidence being discarded. Adding a manager approval step for merges on red neither restores the signal nor removes the flakiness; it slows flow while asking a person to adjudicate results nobody trusts. Running a fast subset on every merge with the full suite overnight is the strongest rival and is sound practice once tests are reliable, but here it confuses duration with trustworthiness: the nondeterminism travels with whichever tests land in each set, and coverage that has already caught real defects moves further from the change that broke it.
questions.concept: Treating unreliable CI signal as a prioritized impediment rather than adding approval gates
questions.question: An insurance claims team's automated regression suite takes 90 minutes and fails intermittently about one run in four for reasons unrelated to the change under test. Developers have begun rerunning the pipeline until it passes and, when in a hurry, merging on a green rerun without investigating. Two production defects last month were later traced to failures the suite had actually caught. The delivery manager asks the agile practitioner to require manager approval for any merge with a failed build. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Configure the pipeline to retry failing tests twice automatically, so the intermittent noise disappears while a genuine, repeatable failure still stops the merge from landing
Have the team treat the flaky suite as a top impediment: quarantine and fix unreliable tests as prioritized, visible work before adding new features
Add the manager approval step, so no merge reaches production until a person has reviewed the failed runs sitting behind each green rerun
Run a fast subset on every merge and the full suite overnight, so developers get a signal they can trust without waiting ninety minutes

questions.explanation: Private, specific feedback addresses the behavior at its source while preserving the technical lead's dignity, and revisiting the working agreements lets the whole team own the norm that dissent is welcome — repairing safety rather than routing around it. Switching to an anonymous online format is genuinely tempting and would surface the estimation concerns, but it treats the symptom: it makes fear a permanent design feature, does nothing about sarcasm in code reviews or daily conversation, and concedes that open disagreement is impossible here. Splitting retrospectives by company of origin avoids the conflict and hardens the very divide a merged team must bridge. Thanking the two developers and promising to reopen the estimation topic with the lead present is the strongest alternative, and reopening it is right — but it puts the same people back into the same room under the same norms, with nobody having spoken to the lead about the remark that closed the conversation.
questions.concept: Working agreements and repairing interpersonal risk after a safety breach
questions.question: During a retrospective on a team recently merged from two acquired companies, a contractor questions the technical lead's estimation approach. The lead answers with a sarcastic remark, the room goes silent, and the topic is dropped. Afterward, two developers separately tell the agile practitioner they will no longer raise concerns in retrospectives. Which action is BEST?
choices: Switch future retrospectives to an anonymous online format so members can raise concerns about estimates without exposing themselves to ridicule in the room
Split retrospectives into smaller groups drawn from each original company until enough trust has built between the two sides for one combined conversation
Give the technical lead private feedback on the impact of the remark, then facilitate the team in revisiting its working agreements on how disagreement is handled
Thank the two developers for their candor and assure them the estimation topic will be reopened with the technical lead present, so their concerns still reach the team

questions.explanation: Four recurrences of the same failure category mean the team has been treating symptoms; the disciplined Kaizen move is to understand before prescribing, using a technique such as Five Whys or a fishbone diagram to find whether the cause is a missing shared rounding utility, an ambiguous acceptance criterion, a gap in test data, or an unstated assumption about precision. Adopting the peer-review checklist is the strongest rival — it targets the right defect category at a real control point — but it prescribes a fix before diagnosis and adds permanent process cost that depends on human vigilance, the least reliable form of defense. Adding currency-rounding cases to the regression suite catches the failures already known and does nothing about whatever systemic gap keeps producing new variants, so the pattern recurs in a fifth form. Having the tech lead pair on all currency code spreads one person's knowledge but makes that person the control, consumes lead capacity indefinitely, and still leaves the cause unnamed.
questions.concept: Root cause analysis (Five Whys, fishbone) on recurring defect patterns
questions.question: A payments team's defect data shows the same category of failure — incorrect currency rounding — recurring in four separate releases. Each time, the team patched the specific calculation and closed the ticket. The tech lead now proposes adding a mandatory peer-review checklist item for currency handling on every pull request. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Adopt the checklist item, since it targets the recurring defect category at the point where changes are reviewed
Facilitate a root cause analysis with the team on the recurring pattern before selecting a countermeasure
Add currency-rounding cases to the regression suite so the next occurrence is caught before release
Have the tech lead pair with each developer on currency code until the pattern stops recurring in releases

questions.explanation: The arithmetic shows a real and actionable gap: 46 points of Must-have work leaves roughly 38 points in the low case and 62 points in the high case for 58 points of Should-have work, so Should-have delivery is genuinely uncertain, and the 41 points of Could-have work cannot fit under any scenario -- surfacing this while three iterations remain gives stakeholders time to re-order or trim scope. Reporting the release as on track is true only of the Must-have layer and conceals that most of the remaining backlog will not ship. Asking for roughly 48 points per iteration demands a sustained 50 percent lift over a stable six-iteration average; that is a wish rather than a plan, and it pressures the team instead of adjusting scope. Deleting the Could-have items unilaterally makes a scope decision that belongs to the product owner and stakeholders and discards the contingency those lower-priority items provide if the team runs at the high end of its range.
questions.concept: Release forecasting with MoSCoW and velocity range
questions.question: Refer to the exhibit. Three iterations remain before the Release 4 date, which is fixed by a regulator's reporting deadline. The product owner has seen the numbers but has not yet discussed them with stakeholders. Based on the exhibit, what should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Tell the sponsor that Release 4 is on track, since the 46 points of Must-have work fit comfortably inside even the low end of the velocity range, and describe the Should-have and Could-have items as stretch scope the team will pick up if the current pace holds.

Ask the team to commit to roughly 48 points per iteration, the rate needed to finish all 145 remaining points by the regulator's date, and track progress against that rate daily so any shortfall becomes visible early enough for the team to recover the ground before the deadline.

Take the forecast to the product owner and stakeholders now, showing that all Must-have work fits, that Should-have work is at risk at the low end of the velocity range, and that almost none of the Could-have work will fit, so scope can be re-ordered while three iterations remain.

Remove all nine Could-have items from the release backlog now so the forecast is clean and nobody is distracted by work that cannot possibly fit, then take the reduced plan to the stakeholders once the next two iterations have confirmed that the Should-have work sits safely inside the range.

questions.explanation: This starts regulatory work immediately without violating the readiness agreement, because the item pulled is genuinely understood and its output is precisely the information the build items need — urgency and readiness are reconciled rather than traded against each other. Pulling the whole item with unknown record scope and unknown consent mechanics invites rework and defects in exactly the area under regulatory scrutiny. Holding the item for a full requirements workshop with legal and the district is the strongest alternative, since those parties genuinely hold the answers — but running it as one big up-front batch burns weeks of an eleven-week window before the team can inspect anything. Planning all eleven weeks with the consent flow in the final three iterations puts the least understood, most scrutinized work at the point of least remaining schedule and depends on legal answering by an unagreed date.
questions.concept: Readiness agreements under regulatory pressure
questions.question: A team maintaining a school-district attendance system has a working agreement that an item is ready to pull only when its acceptance criteria and data-privacy handling are agreed. A regulator has just published guidance requiring a new parental-consent flow in eleven weeks. The product owner wants the item pulled into the current iteration immediately, but nobody yet knows which student records are in scope or how consent will be recorded. What is the BEST response?
choices: Pull the whole item now and let the team settle record scope and consent capture as it builds, since the regulatory clock is already running and the team can adapt later
Hold the item out of the iteration and run a full requirements workshop with legal and the district first, so the team starts only once scope is fully known
Propose the team pull a small, well-understood slice now — a time-boxed spike to determine record scope and consent capture — and refine the build items from what it learns
Plan all eleven weeks now with the consent flow scheduled into the final three iterations, once legal has answered the outstanding questions about which student records actually fall in scope

questions.explanation: Making the definition of done explicit, visible, and inclusive of privacy and data-handling checks gives everyone one shared standard for "finished" and prevents the audit failures that come from quality criteria living in individual heads. Extending the board to reflect the real states — including waiting queues and external approval blockers — makes delay and dependency visible so stakeholders can see why items sit and where the constraint actually is. Private sign-off before reviews removes the disagreement from the room but also removes the feedback, leaving the underlying quality standard undefined. A hardening iteration defers privacy work into a batch at the end, which is precisely the pattern that let non-compliant features be called done, and it separates quality from the increment that creates it. Naming a single privacy owner concentrates a whole-team responsibility in one person, creating a hand-off and bottleneck that weakens collective ownership of quality.
questions.concept: Definition of done and workflow visualization for quality transparency
questions.question: A distributed team building a clinical-trial data portal has increasingly contentious reviews: stakeholders question whether items shown are truly finished, several "complete" features later failed a privacy audit, and the team's board shows only Doing and Done with no indication of items waiting on external data-sharing approvals. The agile practitioner is asked to improve confidence in what the team delivers. Which TWO actions should the agile practitioner take? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Make the team's definition of done explicit and visible — including the privacy and data-handling checks — and hold reviews against it
Extend the board to show the states work actually passes through, including a visible queue and marker for items waiting on external approvals
Ask the product owner to sign off each item privately before it appears in the review so disputes do not occur in front of stakeholders
Introduce a hardening iteration before each release to complete privacy checks on everything the team has built
Assign one team member as privacy owner to review all completed items and approve them on the team's behalf

questions.explanation: A voluntary community of practice spreads capability laterally while leaving the cross-functional teams intact: practitioners pull the knowledge they need, pair across boundaries, and carry improvements straight back into their own teams, which builds durable distributed skill. A central automation team creates a hand-off dependency and a silo — the product teams stop learning automation because someone else owns it, reintroducing exactly the bottleneck cross-functional teams exist to remove. Certifying one member per team and naming them the testing owner concentrates the skill in a single point of failure and contradicts collective ownership; classroom training alone also transfers content without the ongoing practice that changes behavior. A quarterly auditing standards group is compliance-driven governance that inspects output after the fact rather than growing capability, and it frames knowledge as enforcement instead of sharing.
questions.concept: Communities of practice versus centralized specialist teams and compliance bodies
questions.question: An organization wants to raise test-automation capability across eight stable, cross-functional product teams without restructuring them. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
choices: Sponsor a voluntary community of practice where members from all eight teams share techniques, work real problems together, and pair across team boundaries
Stand up a central automation team that writes and maintains the regression suites for all eight product teams, so the scarce specialist skill sits where it is deepest
Send one member of each team to an external certification course and make that person their team's testing owner, so capability enters all eight teams at once
Charter a standards group to publish an automation rulebook and audit each team's test code quarterly, so practice converges on one agreed level

questions.explanation: The exhibit isolates the constraint: the development band is flat at six or seven items and the test band is shrinking from three to one, while review swells from 2 to 19 and weekly completions fall from 5 to 2. Total work in progress has climbed from 11 to 26, so by Little's Law average cycle time has gone from roughly two weeks to about thirteen — the developers are busy manufacturing inventory the system cannot absorb, and downstream testing is being starved. Agreeing a WIP limit on the review state, pausing new development while the queue drains, and pairing developers with the architect attacks the queue and the single-person dependency at the same time, building shared review capability rather than protecting a bottleneck. Asking the architect to work evenings breaks sustainable pace, degrades the quality of the very reviews that gate release, and leaves the system just as dependent on one person next month. Pulling more development work feeds the queue that is already starving delivery, widening the review band and lengthening cycle time further. Reporting the trend and requesting funding for a second architect is a slow escalation in place of an action the team can take this week, and adding capacity without limiting WIP merely raises the level at which the queue settles.
questions.concept: Interpreting a cumulative flow diagram to find and relieve a bottleneck
questions.question: The team's board data for the last six weeks is shown in the exhibit. New work has arrived steadily at about five items per week throughout. At the review, the sponsor asks why fewer items are delivered every week even though the developers are as busy as ever. What is the BEST action for the team to take next?
choices: Ask the solution architect to review in the evenings until the sign-off queue is cleared, and then return to the normal review pattern once weekly completions have recovered to their earlier level.
Pull more development work each week so a larger supply of reviewed-ready items is always waiting whenever the architect frees up, keeping developer utilization at its current level.
Agree a WIP limit on the review state with the team, stop starting new development while the queue is drained, and pair developers with the architect so sign-off no longer depends on one person.
Show the sponsor the falling completion rate alongside the board data and request funding for a second solution architect so that review capacity finally matches the arrival rate.

questions.explanation: Seeking first to understand the intent behind the mandate — usually visibility, alignment, or predictability across teams — and then offering transparent evidence of the team's outcomes turns a compliance conflict into a collaborative, empirical conversation, and models the mindset the transformation claims to want: principles and outcomes over uniform ceremony. Adopting the mandated cadence for a quarter and returning with before-and-after data is the strongest distractor, because it is empirical and respectful; it loses because it spends a quarter degrading practices that already work, and the experiment is unnecessary when the team can share its existing flow metrics today. Keeping the current practices and letting delivery results answer the criticism forfeits the conversation entirely and leaves the team labeled not agile by people it never spoke to. Mapping existing practices onto the mandated ceremony names for reporting buys peace with a false picture, a transparency failure that costs far more trust when discovered.
questions.concept: Principles over practices in organizational agile adoption
questions.question: A newly hired transformation VP mandates that all forty product teams adopt an identical two-week sprint cadence, one prescribed toolset, and a standard ceremony template. A long-standing team that uses continuous flow with WIP limits, pair programming, and test-driven development is told it is "not agile" because it holds no sprint events. What should the agile practitioner on that team do?
choices: Meet with the VP to understand the outcomes the mandate is meant to achieve, then share the team's flow metrics and delivery results and propose aligning on those outcomes while tailoring practices
Adopt the mandated cadence and ceremony template for one quarter to demonstrate good faith, then bring the before-and-after flow data back to the VP if delivery and quality have measurably degraded
Keep the team's flow practices exactly as they are today and let the delivery results answer the criticism, since a mandate that overrides what demonstrably works will lose credibility on its own

Map the team's existing flow practices onto the mandated ceremony names so transformation reporting shows the team as compliant while the way of working the team relies on is left untouched in practice

questions.explanation: Each situation names a distinct failure with a distinct remedy. Different mental pictures of the customer is an audience problem, and research-grounded personas give the team one concrete, shared user to design for instead of an abstraction each person fills in privately. Inability to see how items connect to the journey is a structure problem, and a story map's horizontal spine of activities with detail beneath makes the whole path visible so release slices can be drawn across it rather than argued item by item. Items stalling mid-increment on missing dependencies and test data is a readiness problem, and agreed contextual entry conditions catch those gaps before work is pulled, at the moment they are still cheap to fix. Ninety requirements against a fixed deadline with no agreement on obligation is a prioritization problem under a hard constraint, and classifying them together with the requesting parties forces the distinction between what must be there for compliance and what merely should or could be. Swapping any pair fails: personas will not sequence a journey, a story map will not adjudicate what a regulator actually mandates, entry conditions do not tell you which of 90 requirements matters most, and a priority classification does nothing about missing test data at the moment work starts.
questions.concept: Selecting among personas, story mapping, readiness criteria and MoSCoW by the problem each solves
questions.question: A product team preparing a two-quarter release is choosing which artifact or technique fits each situation it faces. Match each situation on the left to the technique on the right that most directly addresses it.
pairs: The team keeps building features that satisfy no identifiable user, because everyone pictures a different customer when they discuss needs
C: A set of research-grounded personas that give the team a concrete, shared picture of who the product serves
Stakeholders cannot see how individual backlog items connect to the end-to-end user journey, so slicing debates keep circling
A: A story map that arranges activities and steps horizontally with supporting detail below, so release slices can be drawn across the journey
Items reach the increment with unanswered dependencies and no test data, stalling mid-increment while the team hunts for missing inputs
D: An agreed set of contextual entry conditions items should satisfy before the team pulls them into an increment
A regulator and three business units have submitted a combined 90 requirements for a fixed compliance deadline, with no agreement on what is truly obligatory
B: A MoSCoW classification agreed with the requesting parties to separate the genuinely obligatory from the desirable within a fixed date

questions.explanation: Running timeboxed spikes on both candidates converts an unwinnable opinion debate into a cheap, evidence-based decision in the team's own context — other companies' published benchmarks cannot predict this product's latency behavior. Backing the thirty-page comparative evaluation is big-bang analysis: it halts development, still rests on borrowed data, and produces predictions where a few days of code would produce measurements. Prototyping only the event-driven design because it carries the greater unknown is the strongest distractor and is genuinely empirical, but it measures one option against the target with no baseline, so a pass says nothing about whether the simpler polling design would have met the target at lower cost. Starting with polling and migrating later if production misses is a legitimate simplest-thing-that-could-work strategy, yet it defers a strict latency risk to production, which is the one place this team cannot afford to learn it was wrong.
questions.concept: Architectural spikes and set-based decision making
questions.question: An XP team has spent two weeks debating whether an event-driven architecture or a simpler polling design will meet a new product's strict latency target. Each side cites benchmarks published by other companies, and the tech lead now wants to pause development to write a 30-page comparative evaluation before any code is written. What is the BEST response?
