choices: Timebox short spikes that implement a thin slice of each design against the real latency target, then decide based on the measured results
Back the tech lead's evaluation, since a documented comparison lets the team commit to one architecture before spending any build effort
Build a proof of concept of the event-driven design alone, since it carries the greater unknown, and adopt it if it meets the latency target
Start with the simpler polling design and plan to move to events later if production measurements show the latency target being missed

questions.explanation: The sponsor's demand comes from a mental model in which change signals planning failure. Seeking first to understand the concern and then walking through how recent experiment results redirected investment away from features the market rejected reframes change as deliberate risk control, addressing the root of the objection rather than its symptom. Publishing a twelve-month roadmap of outcome themes while weekly experiments continue underneath resembles good practice, but as framed it satisfies a governance expectation with a surface the sponsor is meant to accept instead of changing what the sponsor believes, and a commitment read one way by governance and another by the teams will eventually break. Inviting the sponsor to sit in on the weekly reprioritization sessions is the strongest alternative and worth doing later; alone it shows the ritual before the reasoning, so an unconvinced sponsor is likely to see the suspicion confirmed. Fixing two quarters of features freezes scope exactly where experiments are already producing results.
questions.concept: Validated learning reframes change as risk management
questions.question: At an insurance startup using a Lean Startup approach, teams reprioritize the backlog weekly based on the results of pricing experiments. A newly assigned sponsor with a long predictive-delivery background demands that the product group commit to a fixed twelve-month feature list, arguing that frequent changes are evidence of poor planning. What is the agile practitioner's BEST response?
choices: Meet with the sponsor to understand the underlying concern, then walk through how recent experiment results redirected investment away from features the market rejected, framing change as risk control rather than poor planning

Publish a twelve-month roadmap of outcome themes and funded bets for the sponsor to treat as the commitment, while weekly experiments continue underneath it, so the governance expectation is met without disturbing how the teams work

Invite the sponsor to sit in on the next few weekly reprioritization sessions so the discipline behind each change becomes visible to him, and revisit his fixed feature list once he has watched the process work

Offer to fix the feature list for the first two quarters and leave the rest open to experiment results, so the sponsor gets the predictability he is asking for while later investment still follows what the market shows

questions.explanation: A direct, private conversation with the architect about the impact of the remark, tied back to the team's agreed norms, addresses the safety-damaging behavior at its source while preserving the architect's dignity — the practitioner collaborates before escalating and repairs the environment so the tester can speak up again. Putting the exchange on the next retrospective agenda is the strongest alternative, and the team may well need that conversation, but taking it to the group first exposes the tester publicly a second time and puts the architect on the defensive in front of everyone, which usually hardens the behavior. Meeting the tester to acknowledge how the remark landed is supportive and worth doing, yet co-presenting her idea makes her voice depend on the practitioner instead of restoring it. Adding the test-suite rebuild to the improvement backlog validates the idea while ignoring the behavior, so the next newcomer meets the same reception.
questions.concept: Responding to safety-damaging behavior in real time
questions.question: During a mob programming session at a freight-logistics company, a recently hired tester suggests deleting a chronically flaky test suite and rebuilding it around the riskiest routing rules. The lead architect laughs and remarks that this is "exactly why testers shouldn't touch the pipeline." For the rest of the week the tester says nothing during mobbing. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Speak privately with the architect about the impact of the remark and re-anchor the team's agreed norms for how ideas are treated
Put the exchange on the next retrospective agenda so the whole team can examine how ideas from newer members are received in mobbing
Meet the tester, acknowledge how the remark landed, and offer to co-present her test-suite idea so it gets a fair hearing
Add the flaky test suite rebuild to the improvement backlog, showing the tester that her suggestion was taken seriously

questions.explanation: A team-maintained information radiator gives the stakeholder continuous, unfiltered, self-service visibility — transparency by design rather than by request — and removes the staleness problem entirely. Scheduling a mid-week status meeting doubles the reporting overhead while still producing point-in-time snapshots that are stale again by the next day. Asking the program office for a richer standard report template adds documentation ceremony and still delivers curated, lagging information on the same weekly rhythm that caused the complaint. Inviting the stakeholder to the daily standup is the strongest alternative, and direct contact with the team beats reading a spreadsheet; it loses because it makes her visibility depend on attending a session held for the team's own coordination, risks turning that session into a status report for an observer, and still shows her nothing on the days she cannot attend.
questions.concept: Information radiators versus push-based status reporting
questions.question: A payroll-migration program runs as a hybrid: predictive data-conversion workstreams alongside an agile configuration team. A steering-committee member complains she never knows the real state of the agile work because the only source is a spreadsheet the team lead updates every Friday, and by Monday it is stale. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Schedule a mid-week status meeting so the steering-committee member gets a second update each week and can ask her questions directly
Work with the team to put current work, progress, and blockers on an always-available information radiator the stakeholder can view at any time
Ask the program office to issue a richer standard report template that the team lead completes each week alongside the predictive workstream reports
Invite the stakeholder to the team's daily standup so she hears progress and blockers directly from the people doing the configuration work

questions.explanation: A regulatory effective date is a constraint on the sequence, not another candidate to be ranked by return: ten weeks contain five two-week iterations, the reporting work needs about four of them, and missing the date suspends the license — which forfeits the settlement feature's net present value and every future return with it. Keeping the ranking by net present value applies a financial rule to an item whose downside the calculation never priced in. Splitting the team into parallel sub-teams raises work in progress and delivery risk precisely when a hard date must be met. Asking compliance for the smallest subset an auditor would accept is the strongest alternative, and that scoping work is genuinely useful — but using an unconfirmed reduction as the reason to keep the settlement feature first bets the license on it.
questions.concept: Value-based prioritization under regulatory and compliance constraints
questions.question: A payments team maintains a merchant settlement product. The product owner has ranked a new instant-settlement feature first because its three-year net present value is by far the highest in the backlog; it is estimated at about three iterations. Separately, a payment-services regulation takes legal effect in ten weeks, and the mandatory reporting changes it requires are estimated at about four iterations. Operating without the reporting changes after the effective date would suspend the company's license to process merchant payments. The team runs two-week iterations. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Keep the ranking by net present value intact, since ordering the backlog by modeled financial return is what maximizes value across the three-year horizon, and treat the mandatory reporting changes as the theme the team pulls immediately after the settlement feature ships

Split the team into two sub-teams so the reporting changes and the instant-settlement feature progress at the same time, staffing both from the members already on the team so neither the effective date nor the ordering the product owner set has to move

Ask the compliance stakeholder for the smallest reporting subset an auditor would accept at the effective date, then keep the settlement feature first on the expectation that the reduced regulatory scope will fit into the weeks that remain afterward

Facilitate a re-sequencing conversation with the product owner and the compliance stakeholder that treats the effective date as a hard delivery constraint, schedules the reporting changes to finish before it, and re-checks what capacity remains for the settlement feature

questions.explanation: Flow metrics measure the behavior of the system — queues, blockers, interruptions, dependencies — not the diligence of individuals, and most delay lives in wait states no single person controls. Steering the director toward systemic causes both diagnoses the real problem and enlists leadership where it has genuine leverage: removing organizational impediments. Naming the individuals privately after the review still frames the deterioration as personal failure and quietly teaches the team that metrics are used against people, so next month the data will be shaped rather than reported. Publishing per-person cycle-time dashboards turns a system measure into individual surveillance and destroys the safety that makes transparency possible. Agreeing a cycle-time service-level expectation is the strongest alternative and a sound Kanban practice, but it is a target rather than a diagnosis; committing to a number now would put a goal on the scatterplot before anyone has established why it deteriorated.
questions.concept: Systems thinking applied to flow metrics
questions.question: During a monthly flow review, a Kanban team's cycle-time scatterplot shows a sharp deterioration. The operations director, attending for the first time, asks the agile practitioner to identify which team members worked the slowest items so those individuals can be "coached." What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Give the director the slowest items along with the members who worked them privately after the review, so accountability is addressed without anyone being named in front of their teammates
Redirect the analysis toward systemic causes — such as aging blocked items, expedite interruptions, and shared-specialist wait time — and invite the director to help remove them
Publish per-person cycle-time dashboards so each member can see where their own items slow down and take personal responsibility for the numbers they own from month to month
Agree a cycle-time service-level expectation with the team and track it monthly, so the deterioration is corrected against a clear target the director can follow

questions.explanation: Demonstrating the finished print-driver slice this week is best: working software already exists, the users are available at no cost, and any correction they trigger is cheap while the other two parts are still unbuilt. Recording a screen capture with a written summary is convenient for busy supervisors and better than nothing, but it shows them the software instead of letting them drive it on real hardware, and asynchronous comments arrive later and thinner than reactions watched in the room. Waiting for the template editor delays feedback three weeks for the sake of narrative tidiness; the print driver is a complete, usable capability on its own, and coherence is not a precondition for learning. Spending the slot walking through the remaining backlog and confirming acceptance criteria substitutes discussion of intent for observation of behavior — the supervisors would approve descriptions of software while working software sits unused next door.
questions.concept: Incremental demonstration of working software to real users
questions.question: A five-person team is building a warehouse label-printing capability made of three parts: a print driver, a template editor, and a reprint queue. The print driver now works end to end on real hardware, but the team has decided to show nothing to the warehouse supervisors until all three parts are finished in about three weeks. The supervisors work in the building next door and have a standing 30-minute slot free each week. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Ask the team to demonstrate the working print driver to the supervisors in this week's open slot and capture how they react to it on real hardware.
Record a short screen capture of the print driver and send it to the supervisors with a written summary, so they can respond whenever it suits them.
Wait until the template editor is finished as well, so the supervisors see a coherent slice of their workflow rather than one isolated component.
Use this week's open slot to walk the supervisors through the remaining backlog and confirm the acceptance criteria for all three parts of the capability.

questions.explanation: The business case is a stack of untested assumptions, however persuasive; the empirical move is to convert its core claim into a hypothesis and buy real customer evidence with the smallest possible release, so the four-month investment is steered, or stopped, by validated learning. Starting the build because the funding window is closing treats an approved document as evidence and puts the whole budget at risk before any customer signal exists. Breaking the four months into two-week iterations with internal demos is a real improvement on a single large batch and lets the money be stopped early, but internal demos test the business case against colleagues' opinions, and the assumption at risk is whether customers want the calculator. Building everything and surveying at launch collects feedback when the ability to change course is gone.
questions.concept: Hypothesis-driven development and MVP validation
questions.question: A product group at an insurance company has secured budget for a four-month build of a premium-calculator feature, based on a persuasive internal business case. No customer has seen any version of the idea. The delivery team is assembled and ready to begin. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Start the four-month build as planned, since the business case is approved and the funding window closes if the assembled team is left waiting on it
Reframe the business case as a testable hypothesis and release a minimal version to a subset of customers to validate demand before committing to the full build
Break the four-month build into two-week iterations with internal demos, so the business case can be revisited at each one before more money is committed
Build the complete calculator, then run a customer satisfaction survey at launch, so the business case is measured against how real customers respond to the feature

questions.explanation: Three teams solving the same message-bus problem in isolation is a knowledge-flow failure, not a discipline failure, so the fix must connect the engineers rather than police them. A community of practice puts the people who own the code in direct contact, lets them converge on conventions they helped write and will therefore actually follow, and leaves a standing channel so the next shared concern is solved once instead of three times — alignment emerging from collaboration. Endorsing a mandatory review board installs a stage gate that queues work at a scarce group, shifts design authority away from the people closest to the problem, and converts a learning gap into a compliance ritual that teams route around. Declaring the senior team's design the standard is directive, throws away what the other two teams learned in their own implementations, and buys grudging refactoring rather than commitment. Leaving all three implementations alone misreads autonomy: agile autonomy is bounded by alignment to the whole, and three divergent solutions to one shared integration problem is waste that is already showing up as undiagnosable field defects.
questions.concept: Communities of practice for cross-team alignment
questions.question: In a scaled Lean environment building an industrial-IoT platform, three product teams have each written their own retry and error-handling logic for the shared message bus. The implementations behave differently, and field defects are getting harder to diagnose. The architecture group proposes a central design review board that must approve every team's integration design before coding starts. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Encourage engineers from the three teams to form a community of practice that converges on shared conventions and keeps learning flowing between teams
Back the review board, since one approval point produces consistent integration behavior across the platform and makes field defects far easier to diagnose
Have the most experienced team's retry implementation declared the platform standard and ask the other two teams to refactor their message-bus code to match
Leave each team's implementation alone, since teams own their technical decisions and the differences have not stopped any of the three delivering

questions.explanation: Private coaching with open questions is best: the lead is a capable engineer repeating the behavior that earned the promotion, and self-discovered insight about delegation — paired with explicit decision boundaries — produces durable change while preserving trust. Having the team map its own decision boundaries and then present them to the lead for agreement makes a decision about the lead without her, which predictably triggers resistance rather than growth. Showing her the engagement scores beside the healthy delivery metrics is the strongest alternative, because the data is real and the conversation is with the right person, but leading with numbers that indict her invites defense of the record instead of reflection; that evidence works better once she is already examining her own pattern. Asking the team to raise the bottleneck at the retrospective puts the people being overridden in front of the person overriding them, and the survey already shows they are not speaking up.
questions.concept: Delegation levels and coaching a directive leader
questions.question: At a medical-device software firm using a lean, flow-based approach, a senior developer recently promoted to team lead reviews and frequently overrides the team's design decisions. Delivery metrics look healthy, but the latest engagement survey has dropped sharply, and the agile practitioner observes team members postponing decisions until the lead is available. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Facilitate a workshop where the team maps which design decisions it can make alone, then present the resulting boundaries to the lead for agreement
Coach the lead privately, using open questions to help them recognize the pattern and identify which decisions they could delegate within clear boundaries
Show the lead the engagement scores next to the healthy delivery metrics, so the data makes clear that the current review approach is costing the team
Ask the team to raise the decision bottleneck themselves in the next retrospective, since feedback from the people affected carries more weight than coaching

questions.explanation: The root cause is local optimization in the absence of a shared purpose, so the leadership move is to bring both teams together, revisit the product vision, and let them co-create outcome measures that both sub-goals serve; alignment the teams build themselves holds when the practitioner is not in the room. Asking the sponsor to rank booking speed above documentation escalates before collaborating and yields a decree the losing team will quietly resist. Merging the scheduling and clinical teams into one backlog is a heavy structural intervention that disrupts two functioning teams to solve an alignment problem a conversation can solve. A shared integration suite with a release gate is the most defensible alternative — the integration defects are real and the suite is worth building — but a blocking gate arbitrates the symptom late, adds queueing, and leaves both teams still optimizing metrics that pull apart.
questions.concept: Realigning sub-teams from local metrics to shared product outcomes
questions.question: Two feature teams contribute to the same telehealth product. The scheduling team keeps optimizing appointment-booking speed while the clinical team optimizes visit documentation, and their releases now collide — each team insists its metric matters most, and integration defects are rising. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Facilitate a joint session where both teams reconnect their local metrics to the overarching product vision and agree on shared outcome measures
Have the product sponsor rank booking speed above documentation quality and cascade that order so both teams optimize against a single stated priority
Merge the scheduling and clinical teams into one team with one backlog so a single product owner is forced to settle the metric argument
Introduce a shared integration suite and a release gate that blocks either team from shipping until the combined build passes cleanly

questions.explanation: Naming the constraint as acceptance criteria and pulling the privacy reviewer into refinement makes a genuine product requirement visible on the item and sets the slow three-to-four-week review running in parallel with the team's remaining two iterations, so the storage design is settled before anyone writes code that would have to be undone. Stripping identifying detail inside the upload pipeline is the strongest alternative and may well form part of the eventual design, but redaction of prescription names from photographs is unreliable, and a team deciding on its own that its mitigation makes protected health information safe for an uncovered third party is making exactly the judgment it is not qualified to make. Accepting the item now and booking the move off that network as technical debt knowingly ships protected health information under an agreement that does not cover it. Sending a design document for written approval hands the question to specialists in the slowest available form, spending the lead time on a document exchange.
questions.concept: Compliance and privacy constraints as explicit acceptance criteria in refinement
questions.question: During refinement for a health-savings-account mobile app, the team discusses an item that lets members attach a photo of a pharmacy receipt to a reimbursement request. A developer points out that receipt images routinely show prescription names, so the images are protected health information, and the team's default image pipeline pushes uploads to a third-party content delivery network whose agreement does not cover such data. The organization's privacy office typically needs three to four weeks to assess a new data flow. The product owner wants an estimate today; the item is currently scheduled two iterations out. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Capture the privacy constraint as explicit acceptance criteria and a visible risk on the backlog item, and invite the privacy reviewer into refinement now so the constraint shapes the design before the team pulls the work

Ask the developer to strip identifying detail from receipt images inside the upload pipeline, so the existing content delivery network can still be used and the privacy concern is solved in code without reopening refinement

Have the product owner accept the item as written now and add a later backlog item to move receipt images off the third-party network, treating the exposure as technical debt paid down once volumes justify it

Have the team produce a design document covering the data flow and retention rules for receipt images and send it to the privacy office for written approval before the item is refined further, so specialists settle it

questions.explanation: A band that widens over time on a cumulative flow diagram means arrivals into that state are outpacing departures from it: review is where the queue is forming, so that is where the team should investigate and run a cheap experiment together. Splitting review into separate waiting and active columns is the strongest rival, because distinguishing queue time from touch time genuinely sharpens the diagnosis, but it is a measurement refinement that buys several more weeks of data when the chart already shows where work is piling up. Closing intake for two weeks would drain the queue, yet it halts service to permit applicants unilaterally and explains nothing about why review slowed, so the band regrows as soon as intake reopens. Working oldest-first with a weekly aging report improves fairness and visibility but changes neither the arrival rate nor review capacity; the queue simply grows while being documented more precisely.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation and constraint relief
questions.question: A municipal permitting team runs a kanban system with five workflow states. Over the last five weeks their cumulative flow diagram shows the 'In Review' band growing steadily thicker, the arrival rate into the system essentially unchanged, and the 'Done' line rising at a slower slope than it did in the previous quarter. Team members say review 'just takes a while now.' What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Split review into two columns, one for waiting and one for active work, so the diagram separates queueing from reviewing and the team can see how long a review truly takes once it starts.
Ask the team to stop pulling new permits and keep intake closed for two weeks, so the review queue that has built up over the last five weeks has a chance to clear.
Bring the diagram to the team and explore review as the constraint — for example, setting a work-in-progress limit on review, pairing on reviews, or swarming to drain the queue.
Have reviewers take the oldest permits first and publish a weekly aging report for the review state, so the items that have waited longest leave the system and the Done line steepens again.

questions.explanation: Co-created working agreements that explicitly define how disagreement and mistakes will be treated give the team a shared, self-owned norm that makes interpersonal risk predictable — the structural foundation of safety. Responding to a failed experiment by publicly asking what was learned, and spreading the lesson, models that intelligent failure is valued information rather than a mark against anyone, which is exactly the behavior fearful members need to witness. Celebrating zero-defect performers does the opposite: it rewards not-failing, so people avoid stretch work and hide errors. Having account managers reassure contractors addresses contractual anxiety through hierarchy outside the team and does nothing to change how the team itself treats candor. Permanent anonymity treats the symptom while conceding that attributable honesty is impossible; it blocks follow-up dialogue and prevents the team from ever practicing safe, open disagreement.
questions.concept: Practices that build psychological safety
questions.question: An agile practitioner wants to strengthen psychological safety on a newly formed cross-functional team that includes several contractors who admit they are afraid of 'looking bad.' Which TWO actions are most likely to help? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Publicly celebrate the members who complete their work with zero defects each iteration
Facilitate the team in creating working agreements that spell out how disagreement and mistakes will be handled
Ask the contractors' account managers to reassure them that their contracts are secure
When a team experiment fails, ask 'What did we learn?' in front of the whole team and share the lesson openly
Make all retrospective input permanently anonymous so no comment can ever be traced to a person

questions.explanation: Bringing the sponsor into a data-driven root-cause review wins on three counts: it diagnoses before prescribing, it keeps the team owning its own process, and it builds stakeholder alignment through shared evidence rather than quiet resistance. Running the analysis with the team alone and returning later with a recommendation is genuinely defensible and gets the sequence right, but it leaves the sponsor outside the evidence, so a well-founded conclusion arrives as the team's opinion against hers. Trialing the sign-off on high-risk items looks empirical, yet it tests an undiagnosed countermeasure that adds a queue and a handoff, and four weeks of data pass while cycle time keeps climbing. Recording a defect cause on every completed item presumes the slowdown is a quality problem, taxes every item with administration, and still postpones the conversation the sponsor needs to be part of.
questions.concept: Root-cause analysis with flow data before process intervention; stakeholder alignment through transparency
questions.question: The cycle time of a Lean back-office service team has doubled over six weeks, and the business sponsor tells the agile practitioner to install a supervisor sign-off step "so mistakes get caught earlier." What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Run root-cause analysis with the team alone and bring the sponsor a recommendation once the cause of the slowdown is understood
Trial the sign-off on high-risk items only and review its effect on cycle time with the sponsor after four weeks of data
Invite the sponsor to join the team in reviewing its flow data and running root-cause analysis before any process change is made
Ask the team to record a defect cause on every completed item so quality evidence exists before the sponsor's concern is discussed

questions.explanation: A community of practice is the natural vehicle here: it carries the technique across team boundaries practitioner-to-practitioner, lets other teams question and adapt it to their own pipelines, and grows the developer by giving her visible credit for her work. Documenting the fix only in the team's own wiki leaves the knowledge siloed where the struggling teams will never think to look. Pushing it to the PMO to be mandated as a standard turns a helpful option into imposed process and skips the peer learning that makes a practice actually stick. Waiting for the quarterly all-hands delays help that other teams need now and trades a hands-on demonstration for a one-way broadcast.
questions.concept: Communities of practice as cross-team knowledge channels
questions.question: A developer on a data-pipeline team discovers a technique that cuts the team's flaky end-to-end test failures in half. The agile practitioner knows several other teams in the organization struggle with the same problem. What should the practitioner do?
choices: Document the technique on the team's wiki and link it from the shared engineering index so other teams can find it
Propose to the PMO that the technique be adopted as a mandated standard for every team's end-to-end test suites
Hold the insight until the quarterly engineering all-hands so the demonstration reaches every team at the same time
Encourage the developer to demonstrate the technique at the organization's test-automation community of practice

questions.explanation: Every option is defensible on its surface, which is what makes this hard: the contract is real, the sponsor's concern is real, and the evidence is real. The best agile response brings the people who own those concerns into one conversation around the data — customer collaboration over contract negotiation means exploring, with the customer, how to deliver the most value the evidence supports while respecting what was agreed. Simply backing the contractual position discards validated learning and knowingly delivers what users do not use; a contract clause is a poor reason to spend three iterations on low-value work if the customer would happily rebalance. Directing an even capacity split is a unilateral compromise that dilutes focus, decides for the team, and satisfies neither the evidence nor the agreement — splitting the difference is not the same as making a value-based decision. Going to the sponsor to renegotiate the contract before any joint replanning skips the collaborative step, delays action, and treats a value conversation as a legal one from the outset.
questions.concept: Pivot-or-persevere decision under contractual constraints
questions.question: Three iterations before a contractual delivery date, usage analytics from a limited beta show customers largely ignore the product's flagship workflow but heavily use a minor utility the team built as a stopgap. The product owner wants to stay the course because the flagship workflow is named in the contract; the sponsor is questioning the low beta engagement; the team believes investing the remaining iterations in the utility could triple engagement. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Support the product owner and complete the contractually named flagship workflow first, since honoring the signed commitment protects the organization and the stopgap utility can be expanded in a follow-on release after the contract closes

Facilitate a conversation among the product owner, sponsor, and customer to examine the beta evidence together and explore rebalancing the remaining iterations toward the higher-value utility within the contract's constraints

Direct the team to split its remaining capacity evenly between the flagship workflow and the utility, so the contract commitment and the beta usage signal are both partly satisfied before the delivery date

Take the analytics to the sponsor and recommend renegotiating the contract's scope clause before any replanning begins, so the team is protected from a commercial claim about the workflow the contract names

questions.explanation: A thin vertical slice exercised by actual technicians in their real working conditions converts assumptions into evidence in weeks rather than months, and it is the only choice that produces feedback from use rather than from opinion. Moving wireframe review to iteration 4 still leaves four iterations of unvalidated back-end work built on a document, and reviewing pictures is far weaker evidence than watching someone try to dispatch a real job. Lengthening user acceptance testing budgets for rework instead of preventing it: the cost of a wrong assumption grows the longer it stays undiscovered, so a bigger late feedback window is the expensive option. Re-confirming the document with a supervisor gathers a proxy opinion from someone who does not do the work, and a second signature on the same 40 pages adds no new information about whether the screen actually works on a shift.
questions.concept: Thin vertical slices validated by real users in real conditions
questions.question: A hybrid delivery team is rebuilding the dispatch screen used daily by 400 field technicians. The current plan is three iterations of back-end services, then two iterations of user interface work, then a two-week user acceptance test with technicians immediately before the release. The product owner is comfortable, because a group of technicians signed off on a 40-page requirements document during discovery. In iteration 1 planning, what should the agile practitioner propose?
choices: Pull one complete dispatch scenario — a thin back-end path plus a rough interface — into iteration 1 and have technicians use it on a real shift.
Keep the planned sequence but bring two technicians in to review the interface wireframes at the end of iteration four, before any screens are built.
Extend the user acceptance test from two weeks to four so there is room to absorb the rework the technicians' feedback is likely to generate.
Ask the product owner to re-confirm the signed requirements with the technicians' supervisor, since the document may no longer match daily practice.

questions.explanation: The debate is stuck because both positions rest on unverified claims; the fastest way out is to generate evidence. Time-boxed spikes that run a thin slice of each approach against real devices convert speculation into observed behavior at low cost, and the decision then rests on data the whole team can see. Co-authoring a decision record and voting documents the disagreement carefully but resolves it by preference — the unrefuted risks survive the vote unchanged. Adopting the vendor's reference architecture borrows real field experience and may even prove right, yet it settles by analogy rather than by testing against these controllers and this network. Choosing whichever architecture is cheaper to reverse and starting to deliver is the strongest alternative, since biasing toward reversible decisions is sound practice, but firmware already shipped to field devices is expensive to unwind, and a short spike buys the same evidence first.
questions.concept: Spikes and set-based exploration to resolve design uncertainty
questions.question: An XP team building over-the-air firmware updates for smart irrigation controllers has spent three weeks in recurring design debates between two candidate update architectures. Each camp cites risks the other cannot disprove, no code has been written, and the debates are getting sharper. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask both camps to co-author a decision record listing each option's risks and assumptions, then have the team vote between them
Adopt the vendor's reference update architecture, since it reflects proven field experience with controllers much like the ones deployed here
Pick whichever architecture is cheaper to reverse and start delivering, refactoring toward the other if field data later disagrees
Propose time-boxed spikes that implement a thin slice of each approach against real devices, then decide from the observed results

questions.explanation: Declaring a measurable success criterion up front and running the smallest real experiment produces validated learning: actual user behavior either supports or refutes the hypothesis before significant investment, and the decision rule is set before the data arrives. Surveying users measures stated intent, which routinely diverges from real behavior, so it tests opinions rather than the hypothesis. Building the complete feature first maximizes investment before any evidence exists and delays learning until the most expensive possible moment, even if a toggle controls exposure. Analyzing comparable products yields second-hand, context-mismatched insight — big-bang analysis in place of direct empirical feedback from this product's own users.
questions.concept: Hypothesis-driven development and validated learning (Lean Startup)
questions.question: A product team is uncertain whether a proposed in-app referral feature will actually increase new-user signups. Which approach BEST applies hypothesis-driven development to this uncertainty?
choices: Survey a representative sample of existing users about whether they would refer friends if the feature existed, and build it when the reported intent is strong enough
Build the complete referral feature behind a toggle and switch it on for everyone once every other planned capability has been finished, so the signup effect is measured on the finished product
Commission an analysis of the referral programs running in comparable products and use its conclusions to decide how the feature should be designed and where it belongs in the backlog
State a measurable signup target, release the smallest instrumented version of the feature to a subset of users, and decide from the observed data whether to expand, adjust, or drop it

questions.explanation: Each team is behaving rationally against its own local metric, so the blame cycle is a system problem, not a people problem. Co-creating a shared product goal with end-to-end success measures — integrated, working product in customers' hands — realigns the incentives at their source, and because both teams help create it, they commit to it. Drafting a vision statement and circulating it may produce awareness but rarely commitment; people support what they help create, and a document alone changes neither team's success measures. An integration control board arbitrates the symptoms of misalignment at each milestone while leaving the conflicting incentives fully intact, and it adds process plus a dependency on outside authority. Merging the teams under one manager is a heavyweight structural change made before the simpler, faster alignment intervention has even been attempted, and shared reporting lines do not by themselves create shared purpose.
questions.concept: Aligning teams through shared goals and end-to-end success measures
questions.question: In a hybrid program building a connected thermostat, the firmware team measures success by defect counts while the mobile-app team measures success by feature throughput. Each team hits its own targets, yet integration milestones keep slipping and each team blames the other in status reports. The sponsor asks the agile practitioner to 'get these teams pulling in the same direction.' What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Facilitate a joint workshop where both teams and product leadership co-create a shared product goal and agree on end-to-end measures of success
Write a program-level vision statement yourself and circulate it to both teams so everyone has one common reference for what the product is for
Stand up an integration control board that arbitrates cross-team disputes at each milestone, so slips get resolved before they reach the sponsor's report
Recommend merging the firmware and mobile teams under one manager so the boundary disappears and a single leader owns both sets of targets

questions.explanation: Coaching the team lead on why pull systems outperform push assignment, and then helping the team co-create explicit pull policies, addresses the root behavior while preserving the relationship and transferring real decision authority to the team — the essence of empowerment in Kanban. Adding a skills matrix and a weekly rotation layers more process onto the board while someone other than the team is still handing out work, and it treats a coverage problem the scenario never reports. Walking the board yourself to model how members should select work replaces one directive leader with another and teaches the team to wait for a different boss. Raising the habit at the retrospective is genuinely defensible, since process belongs to the team — but taking it there before the lead understands pull turns coaching into a public confrontation and exposes the two members who spoke privately.
questions.concept: self-organizing teams and pull systems
questions.question: A software support team recently adopted Kanban. During the daily walk-the-board session, the team lead still assigns every ticket to a specific person, and members wait to be told what to work on next. Throughput has stalled, and two members privately tell the agile practitioner they feel like "ticket takers." What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Introduce a skills matrix and a weekly rotation so ticket assignments spread evenly and nobody is stuck with the same work
Walk the board yourself for the next several days and model how members should be selecting their own next ticket
Coach the team lead privately on pull-based flow, then help the team define its own explicit pull policies for the board
Ask the team to raise the assignment habit at its next retrospective so the lead hears it from everyone at once

questions.explanation: The dysfunction is that refinement effort is spread evenly across a list where value is not evenly distributed: items nobody will pull consume the session while the items about to be worked stay ambiguous. Ordering the backlog against near-term product goals, refining deeply only near the top, and letting unpulled items age out or be archived restores the emergent, just-enough nature of a backlog and directly fixes the thin-top problem that has twice damaged iteration starts. A two-day workshop refining 240 items to uniform detail is big-bang analysis producing detail that decays before it is used, at a large cost in team time. A mandatory readiness checklist enforced at planning adds a gate and may be a useful tailored aid later, but imposing it now treats a symptom while the ordering problem remains. Parcelling the backlog out for parallel solo refinement removes the shared conversation that gives refinement its value and would still polish items that will never be pulled.
questions.concept: Progressive elaboration and backlog hygiene in a large inherited backlog
questions.question: A team modernizing an insurance claims intake system has a 240-item backlog inherited from a canceled program. Refinement sessions run 90 minutes weekly and consistently cover four or five items, most of which are old and never get pulled. Meanwhile the top of the backlog is thin, and the team twice started an iteration with items that had unresolved questions about which claim types were in scope. The product owner insists every item must be refined because "someone asked for it at some point." What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Coach the product owner to treat the backlog as a living, ordered list — refining depth-first at the top against near-term product goals and letting stale items age out or be archived
Book a two-day workshop with the product owner and the team to bring the whole backlog to a consistent level of detail, so that iteration planning is never again blocked by unclear items
Adopt a readiness checklist that every item must satisfy before it can enter an iteration, and hold the line at planning so unresolved scope questions stop reaching the team
Split the backlog by claim type and have each team member refine one subset between sessions, so all 240 items are covered without extending the weekly ninety minutes

questions.explanation: A vertical slice is defined by cutting through every layer required to produce working, observable value, which is what distinguishes it from a layer-by-layer split. A spike delivers no product value at all; its output is knowledge, timeboxed deliberately so that learning does not become open-ended, and it is used when uncertainty blocks sizing or sequencing. Acceptance criteria are item-specific and testable — they describe what one particular story must do for the customer to accept it. The Definition of Done is item-independent and applies to every increment the team produces, covering the quality, integration and compliance conditions that make work releasable. The pair most often confused is acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done: criteria vary per item and describe behavior, while the Definition of Done is stable across items and describes completeness.
questions.concept: Distinguishing refinement artifacts: slice, spike, acceptance criteria, Definition of Done
questions.question: Match each backlog refinement artifact or technique on the left to the description on the right that best captures its distinct purpose.
pairs: Vertical slice
A thin piece of functionality that touches every layer needed to work and delivers observable user value on its own
Spike
A timeboxed investigation undertaken to reduce uncertainty so that an item can be sized, sequenced or designed with confidence
Acceptance criteria
The specific, testable conditions describing the behavior the customer expects from one particular backlog item
Definition of Done
The team-wide quality bar every increment must satisfy before it can be considered potentially releasable, independent of any single item

questions.explanation: Showing the real data with its full forecast range is best because transparency is what lets the sponsor inspect and adapt: with honest information now, the sponsor can trade scope, move the date, or adjust funding while those options are still cheap. Presenting only the optimistic line with a spoken caveat is curated data — the chart anchors the sponsor to a number the evidence does not support, and a verbal disclaimer does not undo a misleading picture. Declining and asking the program manager to give the news personally avoids complicity but abandons the practitioner's own duty to make the state of delivery visible, and the filtered message still reaches the sponsor. Presenting the most likely forecast with recovery options is the closest call, since the options are genuinely useful, but dropping the pessimistic case still trims the range the sponsor needs to weigh the downside.
questions.concept: Transparency of unfavorable forecasts
questions.question: A hybrid program's burn-up chart shows the release trending six weeks past the contractual date. The program manager asks the agile practitioner to present only the most optimistic trend line at next week's sponsor review "so the sponsor doesn't panic," arguing the teams can catch up later. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Present the optimistic trend line as asked, while noting verbally that the forecast carries a range and the date could still move
Decline to present the forecast and ask the program manager to give the sponsor the schedule news personally at the review
Present the most likely forecast without the pessimistic case, and bring the recovery options the teams believe could still close the gap
Show the full range of forecasts with the actual data, and use the review to explore scope, date, and staffing options with the sponsor

questions.explanation: Splitting by claim type against real volume data produces small items that each stand alone and deliver usable value, and it puts the slice that touches 58 percent of claimants into customers' hands first, where it can be validated before the remaining types are built — and possibly before some are built at all. A full analysis iteration across all seven types is big-bang analysis that consumes a third of the available capacity, produces no working software, and still assumes every type is worth building. Splitting by wizard screen creates items that cannot be released on their own — a claimant cannot file anything with only screen one — so value arrives only when the last layer lands. Building marine cargo first gets the slicing right and rests on a real argument, since retiring the hardest type early is legitimate risk-first sequencing, but it spends the release on under 2 percent of volume while the type most claimants need waits.
questions.concept: Vertical slicing of oversized backlog items using demand data
questions.question: A regional insurer's team is building a new claims-intake wizard. The backlog holds one item, "Support all claim types in the new intake wizard," which the team estimates at roughly three iterations of capacity. The product owner wants it in the release that begins in two iterations. The insurer handles seven claim types; internal data shows auto glass accounts for 58 percent of annual claim volume, while marine cargo accounts for under 2 percent. During refinement, the team is unsure how to proceed. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Spend the coming iteration on a detailed analysis of all seven claim types with the product owner, so that the item can then be split on solid ground
Split the item by wizard screen so each smaller item covers one screen of the intake flow end to end for every claim type, keeping the design consistent
Facilitate a split by claim type using the claim-volume data, so the highest-volume type can be built, released and validated with real claimants first
Split by claim type but build marine cargo first, since retiring the hardest type early removes the most technical uncertainty from the release

questions.explanation: The benefit named in the "so that" clause, interface consistency, is a property the delivery organization wants; nothing changes in what the receptionist can accomplish, so the item describes an output with no articulated customer outcome. The estimability objection is contradicted by the scenario itself — the team knows the library and sized the item inside one iteration. The independence objection overstates coupling: a single screen can usually be migrated on its own, and nothing in the item indicates a required ordering. The testability objection is wrong as a general claim and as a fact here, since the item already carries acceptance criteria for the screen's behavior; the defect is the missing user-meaningful reason, not any impossibility of verification.
questions.concept: Applying INVEST — Valuable and outcome-framed benefit
questions.question: A team writes the following backlog item for a veterinary clinic scheduling product: "As a clinic receptionist, I want the booking screen rebuilt in the new component library so that the interface is consistent." The team has used the component library before and sizes the item comfortably inside one iteration, and the item already carries acceptance criteria describing the screen's expected behavior. Applying INVEST, which characteristic is MOST clearly violated, and why?
choices: Valuable — the stated benefit is internal consistency rather than an outcome the receptionist or the clinic experiences
Estimable — an item touching a shared component library cannot be sized confidently until the migration is under way
Independent — a rebuilt screen always depends on every other screen in the shared library migrating first
Testable — visual and interface work can only be judged by subjective review, never verified against acceptance criteria

questions.explanation: Arranging the items along the resident's end-to-end journey converts an argument about departmental turf into a shared conversation about the user's flow of work; the map exposes which slices actually complete a usable journey and which items are orphans, so sequencing becomes value-driven rather than political, and it surfaces the gaps a flat list of 340 items hides. Asking the sponsor to rank the three departments escalates a decision the stakeholders can make collaboratively once they share context, and a ruling entrenches turf rather than dissolving it. Splitting into three department backlogs destroys the single ordered view of value, guarantees local optimization, and makes cross-journey dependencies invisible — the queue-jumping would simply move inside each list. Having the practitioner score all 340 items alone is a big-batch analysis exercise that substitutes one person's judgment for stakeholder collaboration and produces a stale ranking before it is even finished.
questions.concept: Story mapping to resolve competing stakeholder priorities
questions.question: A hybrid team building a municipal permit-renewal portal keeps a single flat backlog of 340 items. Stakeholders from three city departments each claim their items are urgent, and the team spends most of each refinement session arguing about which department goes next rather than clarifying items. The team's flow metrics show items sitting in "ready" for weeks while newly arrived items jump the queue. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Facilitate a story mapping session with the three departments so items are arranged along the resident's end-to-end permit journey, making sequence and gaps visible
Ask the program's steering group to rank the three city departments against each other, so that refinement has a clear tie-breaker whenever their items compete
Give each department its own backlog to refine and order, then serve the three in rotation so every department gets an equal turn
Introduce a weighted scoring model, score all 340 items against it, and use the resulting ranking to settle which department's work is served next

questions.explanation: A jointly created product vision with shared success measures addresses the root cause: the merged group has no common definition of what winning looks like, so every prioritization debate collapses back into legacy loyalties. Co-creating the vision with both factions and the stakeholders builds the alignment and ownership that no imposed decision can produce. Scoring the combined backlog on expected revenue from each legacy base only looks objective: without an agreed vision the factions argue over the weights and the revenue assumptions instead of the features. A joint story map is the strongest alternative and is genuinely collaborative work that would expose overlaps and duplication, but mapping a product whose definition of success is still contested turns the map into the next battleground; it is the right second step, not the first. Interviewing customers from both bases gathers useful evidence yet answers whose customers matter, and each faction will read the findings as vindication.
questions.concept: Co-creating a shared product vision after reorganization
questions.question: After an acquisition, two product teams that previously built competing field-service applications are merged into one group to deliver a single unified product. Three iterations in, each faction still lobbies to prioritize features for its own legacy customer base, and refinement sessions stall in arguments about whose customers matter more. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Have the product owner score the combined backlog against expected revenue from each legacy customer base, so refinement decisions rest on numbers rather than loyalty
Take both factions through a joint story map of the unified product so the overlaps, gaps, and duplicated features across the two legacy backlogs become visible
Facilitate a joint visioning session with both factions and key stakeholders to define one shared product vision and the success measures for the unified product
Interview customers from both legacy bases and bring the findings back to the group, so the argument about whose customers matter is settled by evidence

questions.explanation: A private conversation that shares specific observations — ideas drying up, members waiting for direction — helps the director see the unintended impact of expert-turned-leader behavior and opens a coaching path toward servant leadership, such as jointly agreeing which decisions belong to the team. Raising the pattern at the retrospective so the team describes the impact itself is genuinely defensible and keeps things transparent, but it asks a team that has already gone quiet to give critical feedback to a newly promoted leader in a group setting, before he has had any private signal. Asking the director to skip planning treats a symptom, damages the relationship, and loses the technical insight he genuinely offers. Coaching members to hold their estimates and object when tasks are reassigned delegates a leadership conflict to the people with the least positional safety.
questions.concept: Servant leadership and the expert-manager anti-pattern
questions.question: At a game studio, a newly promoted development director — formerly the team's strongest engineer — now joins the team's planning sessions, revises their estimates, and reassigns tasks mid-iteration. The agile practitioner notices team members have stopped volunteering ideas and wait to be told what to do. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Raise the pattern at the next retrospective so the team can describe its ownership impact to the director
Ask the director to skip planning sessions until the team's confidence in its own estimates recovers
Meet the director privately, describe the observed impact on team ownership, and coach toward agreed decision boundaries
Coach the team members to hold their own estimates and speak up when tasks are reassigned mid-iteration

questions.explanation: Roughly four weeks is correct because average cycle time equals average WIP divided by average throughput: 12 items divided by 3 items per week is about 4 weeks. The honest options are to quote that figure or to lower WIP so cycle time actually shrinks. Reading throughput of 3 per week as "items finish in a week" confuses completion rate with elapsed time per item — throughput on its own says nothing about how long any individual item waits. Dismissing Little's Law as manufacturing-only is wrong; in its practical knowledge-work form it holds for any reasonably stable queue over a sensible observation window, which is exactly how Kanban teams forecast. Pulling in more parallel items raises WIP against the same capacity, which by the same relationship lengthens cycle time rather than shortening it.
questions.concept: Practical Little's Law applied to a delivery forecast
questions.question: A Kanban team's board shows an average of 12 work items in progress across all active columns, and the team completes an average of 3 items per week. The team promises a stakeholder that a newly requested item, pulled in under the same policies with no expediting, will be "done in about a week." Applying Little's Law to the team's current system, how should the practitioner assess that promise?
choices: The promise is reasonable, because a throughput of 3 items per week means that any single item takes only about two days of elapsed time once it is started
The promise is unrealistic; average cycle time is roughly four weeks at current WIP and throughput, so the team should either quote about four weeks or reduce WIP
The promise cannot be assessed this way, because Little's Law holds only for a stable manufacturing system in which each item is of a broadly similar size and type
The promise is reasonable if the new item is pulled ahead of the 12 already underway, since a single item moving on its own through the board will clear in days

questions.explanation: The review failed as a feedback mechanism because attendees inspected a description rather than a working increment; nodding at slides is not evidence of fit. Having stakeholders operate the increment against their own real permit cases turns the review into genuine inspection and surfaces mismatches during the session instead of a week later as rework. Simply converting the change requests into backlog items treats the symptom while the same broken review format keeps generating late change requests every iteration. Requiring written acceptance-criteria approval before stories start pushes verification upstream into documents, adds a gate, and still asks people to predict behavior they have not seen. Inviting more attendees widens the audience for the same ineffective format; ten people nodding at slides yield no more signal than two.
questions.concept: Effective reviews and demonstrations as real inspection
questions.question: A team delivering a municipal permit-application service holds an iteration review. The product owner walks through slides describing the four completed stories, and the two attending planning-department staff nod and say it looks fine. The following week those same staff file three change requests describing behavior that does not match how they process permits. The team's next review is in two weeks. What is the BEST response?
choices: Convert the three change requests into backlog items and let the planning staff rank them against other work at the next refinement session
Restructure the review so attendees operate the working increment against their own permit cases and capture observations directly
Have the two attendees approve written acceptance criteria before each story starts, so mismatches are caught before any code is built
Invite more planning-department staff to the next walkthrough so the team hears from a broader sample of permit processors

questions.explanation: The review is the natural forum for inspecting outcomes and adapting the backlog, and putting real usage data in front of the sponsor turns an opinion-driven investment decision into an evidence-driven one without stripping the sponsor of authority. Replacing the sponsor with a household panel swaps one narrow audience for another and cuts out a legitimate stakeholder instead of widening the feedback loop. Continuing and revisiting at release end delays adaptation until the investment is already sunk, which is exactly the feedback delay agile approaches exist to prevent. Adding prompts to drive adoption assumes the features are valuable and merely undiscovered, prescribing a fix before the low-usage signal has been understood.
questions.concept: Outcomes over outputs; validated usage data driving value decisions
questions.question: A team building a home-solar monitoring app has demonstrated four increments to the internal sponsor, who approves each one enthusiastically. Telemetry from the two thousand pilot households shows the newest features are opened by under three percent of users, while a modest export-my-data feature added in the first increment is used weekly by nearly half. The sponsor wants the next increment to continue the current feature line. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Suggest the team stop demonstrating to the sponsor and demonstrate to a panel of pilot households instead, so approval comes from the people who use the product
Bring the usage evidence into the next review so the sponsor and team can weigh continuing the current line against investing where households show value
Continue as the sponsor directs and revisit the usage data at the end of the release, when a larger sample of household behavior will make the comparison more reliable
Ask the team to add in-app prompts encouraging households to try the newer features, then re-check the telemetry before changing any investment decision

questions.explanation: Deployment is a technical event; feedback requires that real customers use the capability and reveal whether it delivers value. Turning capability on for adjusters once a quarter means the team can be wrong about value for three months no matter how often code reaches production, so the loop that matters — build, expose, learn — is unchanged. Framing the issue as wasted pipeline capacity and infrastructure cost mistakes a minor efficiency point for the central problem, and frequent deployment is genuinely valuable anyway for shrinking batch size and integration risk. Toggle-driven code complexity and eventual velocity drag are a real maintenance concern, but they are a secondary consequence and say nothing about the customer-feedback question the situation raises. Claiming the regression cycle distorts the cycle time metric redirects attention to how a number is presented when the substantive issue is that adjusters cannot influence a capability until a quarter after it was built.
questions.concept: Distinguishing deployment cadence from validated customer learning
questions.question: A team supporting an insurance claims portal deploys behind a feature toggle every few days but only turns new capability on for real adjusters once per quarter, after a full regression cycle. Leadership is pleased that deployment frequency is high. From a customer-feedback standpoint, what is the most significant problem with this arrangement?
choices: Deploying far more often than capability is actually released consumes pipeline capacity and inflates infrastructure cost without returning anything to the adjusters or to the business that pays for it
Frequent deployment without exposure to real users means validated learning still arrives only quarterly, so the feedback loop on whether the capability is valuable has not actually shortened
Long-lived feature toggles accumulate branching throughout the code, and that complexity will slow the team down further with every quarter the toggles are left switched off in production
A quarterly regression cycle stretches the measured cycle time far beyond the team's real working time, making the portal's flow metrics look worse than the delivery actually is

questions.explanation: Running automated acceptance checks on every merge is the only option that moves the moment of feedback from months after coding to minutes after coding, while the author still has full context — a direct application of shortening the loop between action and learning. Adding testers makes the late phase finish faster but the feedback still arrives a quarter after the work was done. More detailed upfront specifications attempt to prevent defects through prediction rather than shorten any loop, and in complex work the specification itself is a source of late-discovered error. A triage board speeds the handling of feedback that is already late; it optimizes the downstream of a loop instead of shortening the loop itself.
questions.concept: Continuous integration as feedback-loop compression versus late-phase optimization
questions.question: A payments team discovers most of its defects during a quarterly user-acceptance phase, weeks or months after the code was written, by which time the authors have moved to other work. Applying the principle that the cost and difficulty of acting on feedback grow with the delay in receiving it, which change most directly shortens this feedback loop?
choices: Add more testers to the acceptance phase so that it finishes in half the time
Automate acceptance checks so they run in the continuous integration pipeline on every merge
Require more detailed upfront specifications so that fewer defects reach the acceptance phase
Create a triage board so acceptance-phase defects are prioritized and dispatched to owners faster

questions.explanation: The problem is not which items sit at the top; it is that the ordering rule ignores value. Replacing seniority with agreed, explicit value criteria in a session the stakeholders themselves attend changes the decision rule, gives the product owner cover to order the backlog on evidence, and makes the reasoning transparent so future disagreements are about criteria rather than status. Reordering the backlog unilaterally on churn data usurps the product owner's accountability, acts on a single signal, and leaves the department heads ambushed — the seniority convention would quietly return. Classifying all three hundred items before touching the ordering is a big-batch analysis of a backlog whose lower reaches will change or expire before anyone builds them; refinement effort belongs near the top. Analysing the quote value stream is genuinely useful work and the strongest alternative, but it studies how the process performs while leaving the seniority rule that decides what gets built untouched, and its answer arrives long after the next items are pulled.
questions.concept: Value-based prioritization replacing authority-based ordering
questions.question: On a marine freight-booking platform, the backlog of roughly three hundred items is ordered by the seniority of whoever requested each item, a convention inherited from the previous manager. Two mid-sized shippers have canceled their contracts this quarter, both citing slow quote turnaround, and support data shows quote requests take an average of nineteen hours to answer. The product owner tells the practitioner she is uncomfortable with the ordering but does not want to offend the department heads. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Facilitate a working session in which the product owner and the department heads agree explicit value criteria — including the quote-turnaround outcome and the churn evidence — and reorder the top of the backlog against them, with the rationale left visible to everyone.

Move every quote-related item to the top of the backlog now, since two canceled contracts and a nineteen-hour response time are harder evidence than any requester's seniority, and show the reordered backlog to the department heads at the next stakeholder review.

Run a classification workshop across all three hundred backlog items so that every request carries an agreed priority label before anything is reordered, then work down the resulting list starting with whatever the department heads have marked as must-have for this quarter.

Start a value-stream analysis of the quote process with the support and sales teams to find where the nineteen hours are actually spent, so the backlog can be reordered later around the specific delays that the analysis exposes as the cause of the churn.

questions.explanation: Routing real engine work through pairing and mob sessions transfers tacit knowledge in context, tests it immediately while the expert is still present to correct misunderstandings, and permanently raises the team's bus factor. Commissioning a comprehensive reference manual is a big-bang documentation effort: it captures only explicit knowledge, stays unverified until its author is gone, and pulls her out of the flow of delivery for the very weeks the team could be learning from her. Bringing in a contractor with similar legacy experience substitutes one single point of failure for another, adds onboarding cost, and moves no knowledge into the team. Setting the WIP limit for engine items to zero protects nothing: it defers customer value and leaves the knowledge gap exactly as wide on the day she returns.
questions.concept: Reducing single-person dependency through pairing and mobbing (tacit vs. explicit knowledge transfer)
questions.question: A Kanban team maintaining a freight-routing platform depends on one senior developer who is the only person who understands the legacy rate-calculation engine. She has just announced she will begin an extended leave in eight weeks, and work items touching the engine already sit in the blocked column whenever she is out for a single day. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Ask her to spend her remaining eight weeks writing a comprehensive reference manual for the rate-calculation engine before she leaves
Bring in a contractor with legacy rate-engine experience to cover engine work items while she is away on leave
Route the upcoming engine work items through pairing and mob sessions with her, so the knowledge transfers on real work
Set the WIP limit for engine-related items to zero until she returns, so no at-risk work enters the system

questions.explanation: Every option is technically possible, but only one is empirical, fast, and team-owned. A time-boxed spike building thin slices of both strategies produces real performance data in days — it is set-based thinking applied at experiment cost, and in a complex domain observed behavior beats predicted behavior. The four-week design study is the most seductive distractor because it is framed as "evidence-based," yet it produces analysis, not evidence: documents about how each cache should behave under load, at a cost of a month, when running code could show how each actually behaves in days. Referring the choice to the enterprise architecture board escalates a decision the team can settle itself with data, adds queue time, and yields a verdict based on position rather than measurement. Adopting the architect's preference to protect the date is authority-based deciding that defers learning until production — the most expensive possible place to discover the wrong failure characteristics.
questions.concept: Time-boxed spikes and set-based decisions vs. big-bang analysis
questions.question: A team modernizing a freight-booking platform is deadlocked between two caching strategies with very different failure characteristics under load. The senior architect proposes a four-week comparative design study to make an evidence-based choice. The operations lead wants the enterprise architecture board to decide, since the choice is strategic. The product owner, worried about the release date, suggests simply adopting the architect's preferred option to save time. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Support the full four-week comparative design study, since a caching choice that is expensive to reverse deserves the depth of evidence only a thorough comparison produces
Refer the caching decision to the enterprise architecture board, since a strategic platform choice needs alignment beyond the team and the board already owns those technical standards
Adopt the architect's preferred strategy now to protect the release date, and add a backlog item to revisit the caching choice once real production load data becomes available
Facilitate agreement on a short time-boxed spike: implement a thin slice with each strategy, run both against production-like load, and let the measured results decide within days

questions.explanation: Slicing along thin end-to-end journeys — one currency, one limit band, one payer type — produces items that are independently valuable, testable and small enough to finish, which is exactly what INVEST asks for, and each slice can be released and learned from while the competitor threat is live. Splitting by interface, integration and data layers lets specialists start in parallel but creates pieces that are neither valuable nor testable alone, hiding integration risk until the join. Taking the item in as a spike is the strongest alternative, since a new national rail genuinely carries protocol unknowns — but it spends an iteration producing knowledge when a thin slice that moves real money would produce knowledge and a payment. Commissioning a full specification first is big-bang analysis that delays feedback and produces detail slicing will invalidate.
questions.concept: Vertical slicing and INVEST-based decomposition
questions.question: A payments squad's highest-value backlog item is "Support the new national instant-transfer rail." The team's rough estimate is roughly four times the largest item it has ever completed in a two-week iteration, and refinement is tomorrow. The product owner wants the capability started next iteration because a competitor has just launched something similar. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Split the item by component into an interface story, an integration story, and a data story so each specialist starts in parallel and the parts join at the end
Facilitate refinement so the team and product owner slice the item into thin end-to-end journeys that each move real money for a narrow case, then re-estimate the slices
Take the item into the next iteration as a spike so the team can learn the rail's protocol first and size the remaining work once the unknowns are resolved
Have a business analyst write a complete specification of the transfer rail before refinement, so the decomposition rests on confirmed requirements rather than the team's guesses

questions.explanation: Little's Law states average cycle time equals average WIP divided by average throughput: today that is 24 ÷ 8 = 3 weeks.
