Holding throughput at 8 items per week, cutting average WIP to about 12 yields 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 weeks — achieved purely by finishing before starting, with no new staff. Increasing WIP to 36 moves the math the wrong way, pushing cycle time toward 4.5 weeks. Changing the unit of measure to story points alters the reporting, not the flow — the same work still ages in the same queues. Starting every committed item at once is a disguised WIP increase: items pulled early simply age in progress instead of waiting in Ready, so measured cycle time gets worse, not better.
questions.concept: Little's Law and cycle time
questions.question: A Kanban team averages 24 items in progress and completes 8 items per week. A stakeholder asks the team to bring average cycle time under 1.5 weeks without adding people. Applying Little's Law, which change is MOST likely to achieve this?
choices: Increase WIP to 36 items so more work is moving through the system at once
Switch from counting items to tracking velocity in story points for finer-grained measurement
Tighten WIP limits so average work in progress falls to about 12 items
Start all committed items at the beginning of the week so nothing sits in the Ready queue

questions.explanation: The response pattern is the classic Kano signature: high satisfaction when present combined with indifference when absent marks an excitement (delighter) attribute, while strong dissatisfaction when absent combined with neutrality when present marks a must-have (basic) attribute — so the battery is a threshold that has to be satisfied for the release to be viable, and the voice alert is the differentiator layered on top. Ranking by satisfaction gain alone inverts the model, because a delighter shipped on a product missing a basic need still leaves users dissatisfied. Calling both performance attributes ignores the asymmetry in the data, since a performance attribute moves satisfaction in both directions as its level changes. Deferring both pending willingness-to-pay interviews discards data the team already has and delays a threshold need users will punish the product for missing.
questions.concept: Kano model attribute classification applied to release scope
questions.question: A product team scoring candidate features for a warehouse-safety wearable applies the Kano model. Survey results show that when a hands-free voice alert is present, users report high satisfaction, and when it is absent they report indifference. Battery life lasting a full shift produces strong dissatisfaction when absent but only neutral feelings when present. How should the team use this pattern when shaping the next release?
choices: Prioritize the voice alert ahead of the shift-long battery, because the survey shows that it delivers by far the larger measured gain in reported user satisfaction
Treat both of them as performance attributes and invest in each in proportion to the effort it takes, since more of either one steadily raises satisfaction for the wearer in the field
Treat the voice alert as an excitement attribute worth including to differentiate the product, and the shift-long battery as a must-have that has to be met before the release ships
Defer both features until willingness-to-pay interviews establish which of the two attributes warehouse safety customers would actually be prepared to pay the most for

questions.explanation: Running a blameless review first grounds the response in the actual root cause rather than the director's assumption about it, and returning with team-designed safeguards plus explicit guardrails answers the director's legitimate risk concern while keeping decision authority with the people closest to the work — empowerment survives by making its boundaries visible, not by resisting oversight. Taking the approval role even temporarily inserts a bottleneck, signals to the team that it is not trusted, and controls imposed after an incident are rarely given back. Escalating over the director's head converts a solvable risk conversation into a political conflict and skips collaboration with the person who owns the concern. A change advisory board multiplies the bottleneck across several calendars, adding delay and ceremony without touching the configuration weakness that caused the outage.
questions.concept: Delegation and empowerment within explicit guardrails
questions.question: Two days after a faulty configuration change caused a customer-facing outage, a director tells the agile practitioner that, effective immediately, the practitioner must personally approve every change the platform team releases. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Accept the personal approval role for one quarter to rebuild the director's confidence, then negotiate returning release authority to the team once the change failure rate has settled
Facilitate a blameless post-incident review, then bring the director the team's own proposed safeguards and the explicit guardrails under which release authority stays with the team
Ask the vice president to overturn the mandate, since requiring personal sign-off on every release contradicts the delegation model the organization has publicly adopted for its delivery teams
Establish a weekly change advisory board so that release approvals are shared among several senior stakeholders instead of resting on one person's individual judgment

questions.explanation: Several of these actions are defensible in the long run, which is what makes the item hard; the discriminator is what comes first. Restructuring the retrospective with equal-voice techniques changes the system rather than blaming a person: it rebalances participation immediately, honors the confidence the quieter members extended, singles out no one, and generates first-hand evidence about whether the dynamic was a facilitation artifact. Coaching the quieter members to state and hold a position shifts the burden onto the people who already feel least safe and exposes them in the very forum where they have been overridden. Meeting the principal engineer privately is a genuinely reasonable later step, but doing it first means relaying concerns given in confidence that he can easily trace back, and it frames a facilitation-design problem as a personal fault in someone acting in good faith. Rotating facilitation spreads ownership, yet it changes who runs the session rather than how ideas are surfaced and weighted.
questions.concept: Facilitation techniques for balancing participation and psychological safety
questions.question: On a Lean software team, retrospectives consistently end by adopting whatever improvement the principal engineer proposes. Three quieter members separately tell the agile practitioner in confidence that they have stopped raising concerns because 'there's no point arguing with him,' and the team's improvement actions have stalled at treating symptoms. The principal engineer is well-intentioned and unaware of the effect. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Coach the three quieter members on techniques for stating a position and holding it under challenge, then encourage each of them to raise their own concerns openly at the next few retrospectives
Redesign the next retrospective around structured techniques — silent writing, affinity grouping, and dot voting — so every voice carries equal weight, then observe whether the pattern shifts
Meet the principal engineer privately, share what the quieter members reported, and ask him to hold his proposals back until the others have spoken so that the room opens up
Have the team rotate retrospective facilitation so a different member runs each session, giving the group shared ownership of how its improvement actions get chosen each time

questions.explanation: Refinement should be progressive: detail is added as items approach delivery, because analysis done a year early is likely to be wasted when the need or the market shifts. Limiting detailed refinement to the near-term horizon and holding the rest coarsely ordered by value reclaims the team's time without losing the option value of the backlog. Pushing refinement into an asynchronous document sacrifices the shared conversation that gives items their meaning and typically produces specifications rather than understanding. Freezing new submissions blocks emerging customer needs and treats a healthy inflow of ideas as the problem. Splitting the team into parallel refinement subgroups fragments shared understanding and still spends effort detailing work that may never be built.
questions.concept: Progressive elaboration and appropriate backlog depth
questions.question: A university is building a self-service course-registration replacement. The backlog holds 340 items and grows faster than it shrinks; refinement sessions have become two-hour marathons where the team discusses items unlikely to be built for a year, and developers have started skipping them. The vice-provost sponsoring the work has begun asking why delivery has slowed. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Move all refinement into an asynchronous document so the team's meeting time is protected and only the unresolved questions are brought to a short live session each week
Ask the product owner to pause new submissions until every one of the existing items has been estimated and placed into a single fully ordered list
Propose that the team refine only the depth of backlog it can plausibly start soon, ordering the rest coarsely by value and revisiting as items approach delivery
Break the largest items into epics and hand each one to a subgroup that refines it in parallel, so the whole backlog reaches a ready state quickly

questions.explanation: Reprioritizing with the customer and then updating the agreement treats the contract as a boundary and the working relationship as the vehicle for value decisions: the customer helps choose the trade, obsolete scope is dropped rather than dutifully built, and the paperwork follows the collaboration rather than leading it. Requiring a formal change order before any conversation puts negotiation mechanics ahead of the relationship — exactly the ordering the Manifesto value warns against. Quietly absorbing the change is not collaboration either: it hides the cost and schedule trade-offs, violates transparency, and sets up a later, larger conflict. Sending the matter to legal first treats the customer as a counterparty to be defended against rather than a partner in maximizing value. Note that the correct response still respects the contract — the value says collaboration is valued more, not that agreements don't matter.
questions.concept: Agile Manifesto value — customer collaboration over contract negotiation
questions.question: Midway through a fixed-price engagement, a regulator announces a rule change that makes part of the contracted scope obsolete and demands a new capability. Four possible responses are on the table. Which one BEST reflects the Agile Manifesto value of customer collaboration over contract negotiation?
choices: Ask the customer to raise a formal change request so the obsolete items and the new capability can be priced and approved before the delivery plan is changed
Absorb the new capability into the current plan without reopening the agreement, since responsiveness to the customer matters more than the paperwork and the team can still deliver on time
Meet with the customer to reprioritize remaining scope together — trading the now-obsolete items for the new capability — and then update the agreement to reflect what was decided
Have the contract manager draft an amendment striking the obsolete scope and adding the new capability, then present the finished amendment to the customer for their review and signature

questions.explanation: Three days of work inside 22 days of elapsed time is roughly 14 percent flow efficiency, which means almost all of the lead time is waiting. Directing the improvement at the dominant wait — shrinking the review batch, increasing review frequency, or bringing the reviewer into the team's rhythm — is the change that actually moves lead time, and using the team's own map to redirect the team's own proposal keeps ownership of the improvement with the team. Pair programming has real benefits, but even halving the three days of touch time takes 22 days to about 20, and remeasuring a month later would only confirm the queue was untouched. Holding changes back to fill each fortnightly window enlarges the batch, lengthening average wait and multiplying the damage when a batch returns rejected. Asking the reviewer's manager for a five-day service level is the strongest alternative, since a published turnaround makes planning honest, but it negotiates the wait instead of removing it and a fortnightly batch cannot honor five days anyway.
questions.concept: Value stream mapping, flow efficiency, and waiting waste
questions.question: A medical-device firmware team maps the value stream for a typical change and finds 3 days of hands-on work spread over 22 calendar days, with 14 of those days spent waiting in an external regulatory reviewer's queue that is cleared once a fortnight. At the improvement session, the team's proposal is to adopt pair programming so the coding goes faster. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Show the team what its own map says — the queue, not the touch time, controls elapsed time — and target the review wait with smaller, more frequent review batches or a reviewer who joins the team's cadence.

Endorse the pair-programming proposal and remeasure flow efficiency in a month, since raising the share of elapsed time that is value-adding is the point of value stream work and touch time is what the team owns.
Have the team hold changes back so a fuller batch is waiting each time the reviewer clears the queue, making better use of the fortnightly window and cutting the number of trips through it.
Ask the regulatory reviewer's manager for a five-day service level on each change and track adherence on the team's board, so the wait becomes an agreed and predictable input to planning.

questions.explanation: Co-creating a unified vision with the whole group and its stakeholders builds ownership — people commit to a purpose they helped shape — and anchoring that vision to customer outcomes gives both legacy camps a reason larger than either old product. Making the shared objectives visible and reviewing them together at every cadence keeps the purpose alive day to day: information radiators plus joint review turn a one-time event into a shared habit. A management-issued mission enforced through performance reviews produces compliance rather than commitment, and imposed purpose is precisely what fails to displace legacy identities. Keeping the backlogs separate for several quarters institutionalizes the "their stuff versus our stuff" split the practitioner is trying to dissolve. Tracking individual utilization measures busyness rather than alignment, and comparing contribution between the two legacy groups feeds the rivalry instead of the shared goal.
questions.concept: Co-created vision and visible shared goals
questions.question: After an acquisition, two formerly competing product teams are merged into a single Lean value stream. Months later, members still introduce themselves by their old product names, quietly prioritize work that favors their legacy codebase, and treat the combined roadmap as "their stuff versus our stuff." Which TWO actions would most effectively build shared purpose across the merged group? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Facilitate a session where the whole group and key stakeholders co-create a unified product vision explicitly tied to customer outcomes
Have senior management publish the new mission statement and tie adherence to it to individual performance reviews
Keep the two legacy backlogs separate for several quarters so the groups integrate gradually with less friction
Track individual utilization across the value stream to demonstrate that both legacy groups contribute equally
Make the shared objectives visible in the team space and review progress against them together at every cadence event

questions.explanation: A facilitated chartering session lets the merged team and the customer co-create their understanding of purpose and success measures, which builds genuine ownership and reconnects story selection to customer value — shared vision is built together, not handed down. Having the customer representative circulate the vision, roadmap, and success measures in writing is one-way communication: read once, debated never, and rarely enough to change how people choose work. Having the product owner rank the backlog strictly and requiring pull from the top is the strongest alternative, since it would stop interest-driven selection immediately and is ordinary good practice — but it enforces alignment mechanically without creating it, and reviewers would keep asking why features were built. Onboarding sessions for the four newer members produce four private understandings instead of one shared purpose, and exclude the original members, whose alignment also needs refreshing after the merge.
questions.concept: Team chartering after a change in team composition
questions.question: Midway through a release, an XP team that recently absorbed four members from a dissolved team is producing technically sound increments, yet reviewers keep asking why certain features were built at all. The newer members admit they pick stories based on what looks interesting to work on. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Facilitate a chartering workshop where the whole team and the customer representative reconnect the backlog to the product vision and success measures
Ask the customer representative to circulate the product vision, roadmap, and success measures in writing so every member can check story choices against them
Have the product owner rank the backlog strictly and require the team to pull from the top only, so story selection stops depending on individual interest
Run onboarding sessions with the four newer members covering the vision and the success measures, so they catch up without slowing the team

questions.explanation: Explaining why self-organization matters and then helping the team craft its own working agreement for pulling and swarming on work builds genuine ownership: the team designs its own way of working with the practitioner's support, which is the essence of servant leadership. Assigning the items herself, even for the first two iterations, reinforces the very dependency the team needs to outgrow and makes her the daily decision bottleneck, and there is rarely a convenient moment to stop. Asking the product owner for a finer ranking is the most useful-sounding alternative, and a clearly ordered backlog is a genuine precondition for pull, but ordering answers what to work on rather than who takes it or how members coordinate — the team would still be waiting to be told. A skills matrix routing each type of work to the best-qualified person is task assignment automated into a process: it removes the team's daily judgment and blocks swarming.
questions.concept: Self-organizing teams and servant leadership
questions.question: A newly formed data-engineering team joining a hybrid analytics program tells the agile practitioner they would prefer that she assign work items to each person every morning, because their previous manager always did. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Assign the items each morning for the first two iterations so delivery holds, then hand selection back to the team
Ask the product owner to rank the backlog more finely so the team can take the top item without being told
Explain the intent of self-organization and facilitate a team working agreement for pulling and swarming on work
Build a skills matrix that routes each type of work to the best-qualified person so throughput stays high

questions.explanation: Getting real contractors onto the working increment inside the iteration, and reading actual usage and support data with the sponsor in order to reprioritize, are the two best actions: together they replace a proxy sign-off with direct evidence from the people who use the product - one loop qualitative and inside the iteration, the other quantitative and drawn from live behavior - and both feed the backlog so that value is reprioritized rather than merely reported. A usability checklist signed off by an analyst adds process and yet another proxy; the criteria already pass, which is precisely the problem. A market research study that gates the next release replaces fast empirical feedback with slow big-bang analysis and stops delivery while learning could be happening. A quarterly ticket summary to the product owner delays feedback by up to three months and leaves it as a report rather than a conversation with users, so the same defects in understanding recur across several releases.
questions.concept: Validating value with real end users through qualitative and quantitative feedback loops
questions.question: A team delivers a public permitting portal in three-week iterations. The funding sponsor attends every iteration review and signs off on the increment; the small contractors who actually file permits have never seen the product before release. Acceptance criteria pass consistently, yet after each release support calls climb and roughly a third of started applications are abandoned. The sponsor has begun questioning the team's quality. Which TWO actions should the agile practitioner take FIRST? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Recruit a small rotating panel of contractors to work through real permit tasks on the increment with the team during each iteration, and turn what is observed into backlog items.
Expand the acceptance criteria template to include a usability checklist that the business analyst signs off before a story can be accepted.
Commission a market research study of contractor needs and hold the next release until the findings are available.
Instrument the live portal and review abandonment and support-call data with the sponsor and users, then reorder the backlog around where real users are actually struggling.
Ask the support desk to send the product owner a quarterly summary of ticket themes.

questions.explanation: Little's Law in its practical flow form gives average cycle time = average work in progress divided by average throughput, so 24 items divided by 6 items per week is about 4 weeks — but it holds only under the stated conditions: reasonably stable WIP, arrivals matching departures, items that are actually finished rather than abandoned, and roughly first-in-first-out pull. Stating the average with those conditions attached is honest and useful. Dividing throughput by work in progress inverts the ratio and produces a nonsensical quarter-week answer. Calling it exactly four weeks and a committed date misuses an average of a variable distribution as a promise; individual items will land above and below it. Refusing to forecast without story points and velocity ignores that the flow data already in hand supports a forecast — sizing is not a precondition for a Little's Law estimate, and demanding it delays the answer the stakeholder needs.
questions.concept: Practical application of Little's Law to forecasting
questions.question: An internal tooling team pulls work through a Kanban system. Over the last quarter the board has held an average of 24 items in progress, the team has completed an average of 6 items per week, and arrival and departure rates have been roughly equal. A stakeholder asks how long a new request placed at the back of the queue is likely to take. Applying Little's Law, which response is MOST defensible?
choices: About a quarter of a week, dividing the six items completed each week by the twenty-four items in progress to get the time each one spends.
Around four weeks on average, provided work in progress and throughput stay near current levels and items are pulled in roughly the order they arrive.
Around four weeks, and since Little's Law is an arithmetic identity the team can commit to that date whatever happens to arrivals from here.
No forecast is defensible until the request is sized in story points and run against velocity, since Little's Law assumes items of roughly comparable size.

questions.explanation: Bringing testing into the team's daily flow — testers collaborating as stories are built, backed by automated checks that run as each story lands — shortens the loop between writing code and learning whether it works from weeks to hours, which is the actual problem. Embedding one tester in the team while the department keeps its three-week validation is the strongest alternative and a real gain in collaboration, but the three-week gate survives, so most defects still surface long after the code was written: it shortens one loop and leaves the dominant one intact. Asking the QA group to order its validation queue by risk finds the most exposed defects sooner inside the window, yet the window itself is the delay. Writing more detailed acceptance criteria before coding is predictive effort on the wrong problem; better criteria help, but they cannot substitute for feedback or shorten a three-week wait.
questions.concept: Integrating testing into flow versus phase-gate QA
questions.question: An XP-influenced team building an insurance claims product finishes stories continuously, but every increment is handed to a separate QA department that validates for three weeks in a staging environment before anything reaches users. Most defects are discovered near the end of that window, long after the code was written. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Embed one tester from the QA department in the team while the department keeps its three-week validation of every increment before release
Collaborate with the QA group to move testing into the team's daily flow, with automated checks running as each story is built
Ask the QA group to order its validation queue by risk, so the most exposed parts of each increment are tested first
Write more detailed acceptance criteria before coding so fewer defects reach the validation window in the first place

questions.explanation: Testing as the bottleneck is best supported: work arrives at about 9 items per week while Done grows at only 3-4, and the test band widens from 4 items in week 1 to 22 in week 8 — larger than the analysis band, the development band, or the untouched backlog, and growing far faster than any of them. That is the classic signature of a downstream constraint, and the correct response is to stop feeding it and swarm to drain it. Calling development the constraint misreads the chart: that band is stable, and moving a tester into development while raising its limit strips capacity from the constrained stage and feeds it faster. Throttling intake and rebuilding the forecast is the strongest rival, since arrivals really do exceed delivery, but Done rises by a steady 3 or 4 every week rather than flattening, and producing a new number before acting leaves the queue growing. Blaming a shared environment assumes a cause the exhibit never shows.
questions.concept: Reading a cumulative flow diagram to locate a bottleneck and diagnose growing WIP
questions.question: The practitioner reviews the cumulative flow diagram above with the team at a flow review. Which interpretation is BEST supported by the exhibit, and what should the team do next?
choices: Arrival rate exceeds delivery rate and the widest, fastest-growing band is the test stage, so the team should treat testing as the bottleneck, stop starting new development, and swarm to drain the test queue

The development band is the widest on the diagram, so the team should treat coding capacity as the constraint, move a tester across into development work, and raise the development limit to keep items flowing

Arrival rate exceeds delivery rate, so the team should ask the product owner to stop feeding new items into the backlog and rebuild the release forecast from the flattening Done line before changing anything else

The test band is widening because testers are waiting on a shared environment, so the team should book more environment time and keep pulling new development at the current rate while that is arranged

questions.explanation: Running automated tests on every change collapses the technical feedback loop from weeks to minutes — developers learn about a defect while the code is still fresh — and reviewing working product with stakeholders frequently collapses the customer feedback loop, so misunderstandings are caught mid-cycle instead of at release. Lengthening the release cycle for a bigger end-phase testing effort moves in the opposite direction, delaying all feedback further. A detailed upfront sign-off phase is predictive thinking that lengthens the loop before work begins and cannot substitute for feedback on the working product. A polished monthly status report is push communication about the work rather than feedback on the work — stakeholders reading a report still have not seen or steered the product any sooner.
questions.concept: Technical and stakeholder feedback loops (CI and frequent reviews)
questions.question: A newly formed cross-functional team releases a benefits-enrollment product monthly. Stakeholders complain they only discover what was built at release time, and defects surface weeks after the code that caused them was written. Which TWO actions would most effectively shorten this team's feedback loops? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Lengthen the release cycle to allow a more thorough end-of-cycle testing phase
Adopt continuous integration so automated tests run against every change as it is made
Add a detailed requirements sign-off phase before development starts to reduce downstream defects
Assign a liaison to compile a polished monthly status report for stakeholders
Hold short working-product review sessions with stakeholders on a frequent cadence rather than waiting for release

questions.explanation: The regulator's announcement is new information that may change what is most valuable, so the agile response is to make it visible and let the people who own value re-evaluate priorities together. A working session with the product owner, the compliance lead, and the team welcomes the change even mid-effort and lets the customer decide whether the privacy rule outranks the previously committed scope. Waiting for a full written interpretation of the rule first is reasonable — compliance expertise is genuinely needed — but it makes analysis a gate, when the compliance lead is more useful in the room while that interpretation matures. Routing the rule through the quarterly change-control board treats change as an exception to be managed and delays a time-critical decision. Finishing the promised billing scope first honors the commitment, but it burns runway against a fixed four-month legal date and risks rework in what is being built right now.
questions.concept: Welcoming changing requirements (Agile Manifesto Principle 2)
questions.question: A Kanban team at a municipal utility is midway through integrating smart-meter data into the billing platform when the state regulator announces a new interval-data privacy rule taking effect in four months. A senior operations stakeholder insists the team "deliver what was promised this quarter" before looking at the rule. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the compliance lead to produce a full written interpretation of the interval-data rule before the team reconsiders the ordering of any of its remaining work
Facilitate a session with the product owner, the compliance lead, and the team to reassess the value and ordering of the remaining work against the new rule
Route the new rule through the quarterly change-control board so that this quarter's commitment stays protected until the next planning cycle opens
Have the team finish the promised billing scope first and then take up the privacy rule as a separate stream once this quarter's committed items are delivered

questions.explanation: Making the certification wait its own visible queue with item aging turns an invisible delay into shared information the team and product owner can reason about, which is the core purpose of visualizing work: expose the real flow, including waiting states, before changing anything. Asking for daily written status updates adds reporting overhead that duplicates the board, keeps knowledge in individual inboxes, and still leaves the systemic queue invisible. Contacting the lab manager for priority escalates outside the team before the size and pattern of the delay have even been made visible, and it treats a symptom in one direction only. Imposing a rule that items cannot start without a booked slot prescribes a policy before the team has any data on how long the queue actually is; a pull policy may well be the right eventual experiment, but it should emerge from the team once the wait is visible.
questions.concept: Making hidden queues and wait states explicit on the board
questions.question: A firmware team maintaining smart-meter devices runs a kanban board with three columns: To Do, In Progress, Done. Items regularly sit in In Progress for six or seven days because they are queued for an external certification lab, but nothing on the board shows this. In the daily coordination meeting, people repeatedly say "still in progress," and the product owner has started asking why simple items take two weeks. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Facilitate a short session where the team makes the certification wait explicit on the board as its own queue, with an item-age indicator, so the delay becomes visible to everyone
Ask each member to post a short written status on their in-progress items each day, so the product owner can see where the time is going without waiting for the coordination meeting
Approach the certification lab manager and ask that this team's submissions move up the lab's queue, since that wait is the largest single component of the item's cycle time
Introduce a policy that no item may be pulled into In Progress until a certification slot has been booked, so work never starts ahead of the capacity that finishes it

questions.explanation: Helping the team see its own flow data and choose to swarm or pair across specialties attacks the root cause: a siloed, handoff-driven structure in which no one owns a whole item. It lets the team locate the bottleneck empirically and decide collectively how to collaborate, which builds shared ownership of quality. Adding a test automation engineer puts capacity into the queue while leaving the silos and the handoff that create it untouched. Blocking new pulls until Waiting for Test is empty is the strongest alternative and is close to a work-in-process limit, but imposed as a rule rather than chosen by the team it invites gaming and makes people wait rather than help. A pre-handoff checklist formalizes the very boundary that lets defects be called the testers' problem.
questions.concept: Swarming and shared ownership across specialties
questions.question: A Kanban team responsible for a payments platform is organized so that database specialists, application developers, and testers each pull only work items matching their own specialty. Items routinely sit in the 'Waiting for Test' column for days, and several team members describe defects as 'the testers' problem.' What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Add a test automation engineer so the waiting column clears faster while each specialty keeps pulling the work that matches it
Introduce a rule that no new item is pulled until everything in Waiting for Test is finished, forcing the queue down each week
Facilitate a session where the team examines its own flow data and explores swarming or pairing across specialties to finish items together
Ask the testers to write a pre-handoff checklist developers must complete before passing work over, so fewer items come back as defects

questions.explanation: The 9-day validation wait and the 40-page document are the strongest candidates. The wait is pure delay — the single largest non-value-adding block in the flow — and it also delays defect discovery, making rework more expensive when validation finally happens. The document is overproduction and partially done work: roughly 38 pages of effort that is never consumed, plus inventory that goes stale as understanding changes. The daily 15-minute coordination meeting is a small, high-value feedback and impediment-surfacing loop; cutting it removes coordination, not waste. The build-to-deployment hand-off ticket is a genuine hand-off cost, but at about ten minutes with same-day action it is trivial in magnitude beside a nine-day queue and 38 unread pages, and removing it requires changing an organizational boundary — a candidate for later systemic improvement rather than the strongest immediate target. The customer demonstration is the team's primary source of external feedback and directly creates value; removing it would blind the team to whether it is building the right thing.
questions.concept: Identifying Lean waste types (delay, overproduction, partially done work) and sizing them in a mapped value stream
questions.question: A Lean-oriented team building an insurance underwriting portal maps its delivery process and finds: (1) a completed story waits an average of 9 days before a business analyst validates it; (2) a 40-page solution design document is produced upfront for every epic, of which stakeholders read roughly the first two pages; (3) a daily 15-minute team coordination meeting; (4) work items are handed from the build team to a separate deployment team, each hand-off requiring a written ticket that takes about ten minutes to raise and is normally actioned the same day; (5) a per-iteration demonstration of working software to customers. Which TWO of these are the strongest candidates for waste elimination? (Choose TWO.)
choices: The 9-day wait before business analyst validation
The 40-page upfront design document that stakeholders largely do not read
The daily 15-minute coordination meeting
The hand-off ticket between the build and deployment teams
The per-iteration demonstration of working software to customers

questions.explanation: The widening band identifies a single accumulation point in the flow, and the wait is caused by how client data is requested rather than by anything the team lacks internally; bringing the data to the team and the client stakeholders and jointly redesigning the request-and-response process attacks the actual constraint and keeps the customer engaged in solving it. Accepting two more developers so more items can be started in parallel injects capacity upstream of the constraint, which only inflates work in progress and lengthens lead time without releasing a single parked item. Returning the eleven parked items to the backlog cosmetically shrinks the queue but destroys the very transparency that made the constraint visible, and the customer commitments do not disappear. Having the delivery manager chase every request daily after three days is the strongest rival, since persistent follow-up does shake loose some replies — but it is manual expediting that grows with volume and never asks why eleven different client contacts find these requests hard to answer.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation and constraint identification
questions.question: A hybrid team maintaining a payroll integration platform pulls work through a five-column Kanban board. Over the last quarter the board's cumulative flow diagram shows the "Awaiting Client Data" band widening steadily while every other band stays thin. The team's delivery manager proposes adding two more developers so more items can be started in parallel. The agile practitioner reviews the board and sees eleven items parked in that column, each waiting on a different client contact for file specifications. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Accept the two additional developers so the team can start more items in parallel while the eleven parked cards wait for their client data to arrive
Surface the widening band to the team and client stakeholders, and work with them to redesign how client data requests are made and answered
Return the eleven parked items to the backlog so the board shows only active work and cycle time reflects what the team controls
Require the delivery manager to chase every client data request daily once it has gone three days without an answer from the client

questions.explanation: The root problem is not the reporting interval but the distance between the team and the people using the product: feedback is second-hand and arrives two months after the increment shipped. Putting real users and frontline staff in front of the working kiosk every iteration shortens the feedback loop to days, gives the team observed behavior rather than filtered summaries, and lets the payment problem be diagnosed now. Moving the summary to weekly still leaves the team relying on a proxy's interpretation of complaints and only trims the delay. A sign-off gate adds process and front-loads documentation, which slows delivery without producing any empirical evidence about usability. Logging a defect and scheduling it treats the symptom for one flow and leaves the same blind spot in place for everything the team builds next.
questions.concept: Direct, early feedback on a working increment versus delayed proxy reporting
questions.question: A hybrid team is delivering self-service ticketing kiosks for a chain of regional museums. Customer feedback reaches the team only through a business analyst who summarizes call-center complaints in a monthly report. This month's report shows visitors abandoning the payment step — a flow the team finished and shipped two months ago. What is the BEST response?
choices: Ask the business analyst to publish the complaint summary weekly instead of monthly, so the team hears about kiosk problems while the flow is still fresh in mind.
Arrange for a small group of visitors and front-desk staff to try the working kiosk with the team each iteration, starting with the payment flow this week.
Add a business sign-off on payment requirements before any coding begins, so future kiosk changes are approved by the people who know visitor behavior best.
Raise a defect for the abandoned payment step and schedule it into the next iteration, since repairing a flow visitors leave is the most urgent work.

questions.explanation: A community of practice creates a voluntary, ongoing channel where practitioners across team boundaries surface problems and solutions to each other — exactly the missing connection that let three teams solve the same problem in isolation — and it does so without adding gatekeepers or overhead. Appointing a chief engineer to pre-review every design centralizes knowledge in one bottleneck rather than spreading it, and slows all teams to prevent occasional duplication. A mandated, audited wiki produces compliance behavior rather than knowledge flow: entries get written to pass the audit, and nobody reads them. Having the three teams compare approaches at the next joint review and standardize on the strongest is the closest contender and worth doing, but it settles one calibration problem at one meeting; nothing carries learning forward, so the next shared problem is solved three times over, and declaring a winner in a single session can bury the reasons the approaches differ.
questions.concept: Communities of practice
questions.question: At a joint review, an agile practitioner at an agricultural-drone company learns that three product teams each spent weeks independently solving the same geofencing-calibration problem, unaware of one another's work. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Help interested engineers start a community of practice that meets regularly to share solutions across teams
Ask leadership to appoint a chief engineer who reviews every team's technical design before build work begins
Require every team to record its solutions in a central wiki that is audited for completeness each month
Have the three teams compare approaches at the next joint review and standardize on the strongest one

questions.explanation: Releasing a small working slice — the two screens dispatchers use most — to a pilot group now creates validated learning while most of the budget is still unspent, so the remaining three months are steered by evidence instead of assumptions. Keeping the twelve-screen plan and demonstrating finished screens to the sponsor every two weeks improves visibility but collects reactions from a proxy rather than the dispatchers who will live in the tool, and the scope itself goes unchallenged. Testing clickable mockups of all twelve screens with dispatchers is the strongest alternative, since cheap prototypes with real users are legitimate discovery, yet it still elaborates the whole scope before anything ships and captures opinions about a design rather than behavior under real workload. Interviewing dispatchers about their current routine informs design but confirms nothing about the proposed screens; asking is weaker evidence than shipping.
questions.concept: MVP and early validated learning from real users
questions.question: A team building a field-service scheduling app plans to collect its first user feedback after all twelve planned screens are complete, about three months from now. The sponsor asks the agile practitioner whether this approach is sound. What should the practitioner recommend?
choices: Keep the twelve-screen plan but demonstrate the finished screens to the sponsor every two weeks, so problems surface well before the three months are up
Build all twelve screens as clickable mockups and test those with dispatchers first, so no development effort is spent on screens that turn out to be wrong
Interview a sample of dispatchers about their current scheduling routine now, and use what they say to confirm the twelve screens before any are built
Release a small working slice — such as the two screens dispatchers use most — to a pilot group now, and let their feedback shape the remaining screens

questions.explanation: Every option could technically produce some transfer, but only the one-on-one conversation addresses the cause. Her refusal to pair likely has a reason — fear of losing status, worry that others will degrade a validated component, or discomfort teaching — and active listening surfaces it so a transfer approach can be designed that she genuinely supports, which is what makes the knowledge actually move. Mandated documentation captures only explicit knowledge, poorly and resentfully, while the tacit judgment inside a calibration engine transfers through interaction. Forcing pairing through the working agreement weaponizes a team artifact against one member and invites passive compliance. Routing the issue through her manager's performance objectives converts a collaboration problem into a coercion problem and damages trust just when her engagement matters most.
questions.concept: Emotional intelligence and active listening in knowledge transfer
questions.question: On a biotech lab-software team, only one scientist-developer understands the instrument calibration engine. She declines pairing invitations, works apart from the team, and her extended leave begins six weeks before a regulatory submission that depends on that component. The team has proposed several fixes. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Add mandatory pairing on calibration work to the team's working agreement, so the transfer starts before her leave
Have her document the calibration engine fully, since the regulatory submission needs that evidence anyway
Ask her manager to make knowledge transfer an explicit performance objective before the leave is approved
Meet her one-on-one, listen for what is driving the reluctance, and co-design a transfer approach she supports

questions.explanation: The team is measuring output completion while the funded goal is an outcome, so the fix is to reframe goals as testable hypotheses about the target metric and build measurement into the increments, which turns each iteration into a real experiment. Adding a second team accelerates production of features that have already been shown not to move the metric, scaling the wrong thing. Displaying repeat-order rate on a dashboard adds visibility but changes nothing about how work is chosen or what each increment is expected to prove. Commissioning a market study is a large upfront analysis effort that delays feedback the team could gather directly from its own users within an iteration.
questions.concept: Outcomes versus outputs; outcome-based iteration goals
questions.question: A team delivering a subscription meal-kit ordering app has produced four increments over eight weeks. Every review has been accepted, and the burnup shows 100% of planned scope complete. At a quarterly business review, the sponsor points out that repeat-order rate — the reason the initiative was funded — has not moved, and asks the team to "go faster." The team's iteration goals have all been phrased as lists of features to complete. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Propose funding a second team so the remaining roadmap items reach customers sooner, since the sponsor's stated concern is that the initiative is not delivering results quickly enough
Work with the product owner and sponsor to restate upcoming iteration goals as measurable outcome hypotheses tied to repeat-order rate, and instrument the increments to test them
Add repeat-order rate to the team's existing velocity dashboard so the business measure sits beside completed scope and stays visible to everyone at every review
Commission a study of competing meal-kit apps and use what it finds to reshape the ordering backlog before the team commits its capacity to another iteration of work

questions.explanation: A high discount rate penalizes distant cash flows heavily, so a larger year-three benefit can easily be worth less today than a smaller stream beginning next quarter — that is precisely what net present value is designed to expose. The agile consideration reinforces the same choice: earlier returns mean earlier validation of the value hypothesis and earlier opportunity to change course. Choosing on the larger undiscounted total ignores the time value of money, which is the entire reason the organization discounts at all. Starting both in parallel splits capacity, raises work in progress, and delays both — it avoids the prioritization decision rather than making it. Waiting on internal rate of return because net present value depends on a chosen discount rate inverts the logic: the discount rate encodes the organization's cost of capital and risk appetite, which is what makes NPV decision-relevant, and IRR — the rate at which net present value reaches zero — is a supplementary lens, not a precondition for ranking.
questions.concept: NPV, discount rate, and time value in prioritization
questions.question: A retail-analytics team is choosing between two candidate initiatives with roughly equal build cost. Initiative A returns modest cash benefits starting next quarter and continuing steadily. Initiative B returns a larger total cash benefit, but nearly all of it lands in year three. Leadership evaluates initiatives on net present value at a high discount rate and also wants the team to keep delivering incrementally. Applying these considerations, which reasoning is MOST sound?
choices: Initiative B should be selected because its total undiscounted benefit is larger than Initiative A's, and equal costs make the raw total return the deciding factor
Initiative A is favored because a high discount rate reduces the present value of B's distant benefits, and its earlier returns also generate feedback sooner
Both initiatives should be started in parallel, since their costs are equal and neither near-term learning nor long-term value would have to be sacrificed
Ranking should wait until internal rate of return is calculated, because net present value depends on a chosen discount rate and is therefore not comparable

questions.explanation: The conflict has escalated past a task disagreement into a personal one, and it is chilling the wider team's psychological safety — so the practitioner should first understand each engineer's perspective through private, active-listening conversations, then facilitate a direct dialogue where the two rebuild a working relationship. Diagnosis before intervention, and direct facilitation between the parties, is the strongest conflict response at this stage. Raising the behavior in the retrospective is tempting because retros exist for team issues, but publicly dissecting a personal conflict is likely to humiliate both engineers, harden positions, and make the quiet members even more guarded. Going to the functional manager escalates while a facilitated resolution is still very much available, and hands the team's relational problem to hierarchy at the cost of the practitioner's credibility as a facilitator. A stricter working agreement addresses symptoms with process: it may suppress the sarcasm in meetings while the underlying resentment continues to leak into design decisions and reviews.
questions.concept: Conflict escalation levels, active listening, and psychological safety
questions.question: On a fintech platform team, a long-running technical disagreement between two senior engineers has turned personal: retrospectives now feature sarcastic exchanges between them, and quieter team members have stopped raising issues at all. The team's manager is aware and expects the agile practitioner to handle it. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Name the sarcastic exchanges at the next retrospective, so the whole team can agree how it wants disagreements handled from now on
Hand the pattern to the engineers' manager now, since a conflict that has turned personal is past what team-level facilitation can settle
Meet privately with each engineer to listen and understand their perspective, then facilitate a direct conversation between the two
Have the team adopt a working agreement on respectful communication and review how well it is being honored each retrospective

questions.explanation: The developers are responding rationally to an environment where visible defects damage individuals, so it is the measurement system generating the fear — not the people reacting to it — that must change; working with the manager to replace individual rankings with team-level quality measures removes the incentive to hide problems and restores honest data. Mandating logging backed by audits layers surveillance on top of fear, which deepens concealment and turns the relationship adversarial. Hiding the rankings from the team while the manager still judges individuals by them leaves the underlying threat intact and reduces transparency even further. Publicly surfacing who has been quietly fixing bugs would expose individuals to precisely the blame the dashboard created, destroying whatever safety remains.
questions.concept: Individual-blame metrics corrode transparency and honest data
questions.question: A distributed team spanning three time zones supports a city's 311 service-request platform using a Kanban system. A well-intentioned engineering manager recently added a public dashboard ranking individual developers by defect count. Since then, the practitioner has noticed developers quietly fixing bugs without logging them, and the defect data trending misleadingly toward zero. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Remind the team that every defect must be logged and add periodic audits of the commit history, so the dashboard's numbers become dependable for everyone reading them
Meet with the manager to explain how individually ranked defect metrics are driving the data underground, and propose team-level quality measures instead
Ask the manager to restrict the ranking so only he can see individual numbers, while the team keeps a public view of overall defect trends
Raise the unlogged fixes at the next team meeting and ask the developers to explain why the recorded data stopped matching what is actually happening

questions.explanation: Naming the systemic risk transparently and spreading the knowledge through pairing and rotation converts a hero dependency into collective team capability — it addresses both the fragile bus factor and the learned helplessness already visible in a team that waits for her before acting. Accepting the approver role while pairing a second engineer on every approval buys some coverage but still installs her as a mandatory gate on every production change, deepening the waiting behavior. Having her write runbooks first captures the explicit fraction of late-night firefighting knowledge and leaves the proposed approver role unchallenged. Investigating why releases keep breaking at the same points is genuinely strong — the rescues are a symptom and that analysis should follow — but it does not answer the decision on the table, and leadership is about to formalize the dependency while the practitioner studies causes.
questions.concept: Leadership anti-patterns — hero culture and single points of failure
questions.question: At a payments company running a hybrid delivery model, one engineer routinely rescues releases with late-night fixes that only she understands. Leadership, impressed, proposes making her the mandatory approver of every production change. The agile practitioner has noticed the rest of the team increasingly waiting on her before acting. What is the BEST response?
choices: Accept the approver role but pair a second engineer with her on every approval, so the team gains coverage while release quality stays protected
Surface the single-point-of-failure risk to leadership and facilitate pairing and rotation so the whole team learns the areas she keeps rescuing
Have her write runbooks for the systems she keeps rescuing before the approver role starts, so the knowledge stops living in one person's head
Investigate why releases keep breaking at the same points, so the late-night rescues stop being needed and the approval question becomes unnecessary

questions.explanation: Communities of practice run on voluntary energy and member ownership, so the decline signals that the sessions stopped serving the people they exist for. Exploring what current and lapsed members actually value — and handing them the redesign — applies understand-before-prescribing and restores the ownership that sustains a community. Making attendance a managerial expectation converts a community into a compulsory meeting and destroys the intrinsic motivation that defines it. Rotating facilitation is the most tempting alternative because it does break up the one-way lecture, but it is a fix the practitioner selects for a visible symptom without ever asking why five teams' worth of members stopped attending; it belongs inside a member-led redesign, not ahead of one. Bringing in an external expert for a lecture series doubles down on the broadcast format that caused the disengagement.
questions.concept: Communities of practice: voluntary participation and member ownership
questions.question: A testing community of practice that once drew members from six teams has shrunk to a handful of attendees, and recent sessions have become one senior tester lecturing to a silent room. The agile practitioner wants the community to recover. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Bring in an external testing expert to deliver a polished monthly lecture series that will draw lapsed members back from all six teams
Meet with the remaining and lapsed members to explore what they would find valuable and let the community redesign its own format
Ask the functional managers to make attendance a standing expectation so the community regains the critical mass it needs
Rotate facilitation among the remaining members each session so that no single voice keeps dominating the conversation

questions.explanation: The duplicated work, the growing cycle time, and the missed dependency all trace back to no one being able to see the whole flow; a shared visualization the teams design themselves restores that view at the source, addresses all three symptoms, and is run as a time-boxed experiment so it can be inspected and adapted. A dependency spreadsheet maintained by leads adds a parallel artifact that duplicates the boards, decays between updates, and covers only one of the three symptoms. Producing the consolidated slide more often keeps information flowing through an intermediary on a delay instead of making the flow directly visible to the people doing the work. Merging the sub-teams is a heavy structural intervention imposed to solve a visualization problem, and it overturns a team-design decision that may have been made for sound reasons.
questions.concept: Visualizing cross-team flow and dependencies
questions.question: A team supporting a rail-freight booking product has used a shared kanban wall for two years. Recently the team split into two sub-teams working from separate boards in different tools, and the product owner now assembles a weekly consolidated slide of both. Cycle time has grown, duplicate work has appeared twice, and a dependency between the sub-teams surfaced only after one had built the wrong integration. In the retrospective, one sub-team proposes a shared spreadsheet of cross-team dependencies, updated daily by each lead. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Adopt the daily-updated dependency spreadsheet, since it targets the missed dependency directly and asks neither sub-team to change the tool it uses
Have the product owner assemble the consolidated slide twice a week rather than weekly, so cross-team problems surface while there is still time to act on them
Facilitate the two sub-teams in designing a single shared visualization of the end-to-end flow, including cross-team handoffs, and try it for a few iterations
Merge the two sub-teams back into one team so a single board covers everything again and the duplicated work disappears along with the split that produced it

questions.explanation: Evolving regulation plus unproven models places this work in the high-uncertainty zone (in Stacey Matrix terms, far from simple), where a detailed long-range task plan is fiction dressed as certainty. The agile response meets the director's legitimate need — predictability for leadership — with the mechanism that actually works under uncertainty: an outcome-level roadmap, near-term detail, and empirical forecasting refreshed each cycle. Converting the backlog into fourteen months of dated milestones is the strongest wrong answer, because velocity-based forecasting really is empirical; it fails on scope, since the extrapolation is only as good as the backlog beneath it, and here the requirements themselves will move. Producing the task-level plan and reforecasting on every variance adopts predictive thinking where its core assumption of stable, knowable requirements is false, so the variance updates never stop. Front-loading a discovery phase assumes regulatory and actuarial unknowns can be settled by study rather than by delivering and observing.
questions.concept: Agile vs predictive thinking; planning under uncertainty (Stacey Matrix)
questions.question: An insurance company is creating a usage-based pricing product in a market where regulations are still evolving and the actuarial models are unproven. The program director asks the agile practitioner for a task-level plan covering the next 14 months "so leadership knows exactly what it is getting and when." What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Explain that with this degree of requirements and technical uncertainty, short delivery cycles with frequent inspection give leadership more reliable predictability, and propose an outcome-based roadmap with detail planned in rolling waves

Convert the current backlog into dated milestones spanning all fourteen months using the team's measured velocity, so the forecast leadership receives rests on real delivery data rather than on estimates written before any of the work began

Produce the fourteen-month task-level plan leadership asked for and commit to reforecasting it whenever a variance appears, so the organization keeps the certainty it expects while reality is tracked against the baseline

Propose a discovery phase that resolves the regulatory and actuarial unknowns first, so the fourteen-month plan can then be built on settled assumptions rather than on guesses about a market that nobody has tested yet

questions.explanation: Working directly with the stakeholder to understand the outcome behind the request, and then splitting it into small, clearly defined items, lets the team estimate, prioritize by value, and start delivering the most urgent slice quickly — the essence of backlog refinement. Sizing the request against a similar past portal item manufactures a date from an analogy to work nobody has yet defined, and quoting it commits the team to scope it never agreed. Using the expedite class of service is the most defensible alternative, since classes of service are the proper way to handle urgency claims, but expedite is designed for small, well-understood work; an item too large to size would occupy the lane indefinitely and displace everything else. Pulling the request onto the board as one card and refining it in flight destroys flow: it ages in the system, consumes work-in-progress capacity, and leaves nobody able to say what done means.
questions.concept: Backlog refinement and story splitting
questions.question: A support-services team using Kanban receives a request from a key stakeholder to "modernize the customer portal." The stakeholder insists it is urgent, and the service request manager wants it pulled into the workflow immediately. The item is far too large and vague for the team to size or start. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Have the team size the request against a similar portal item so the service manager can quote a date
Collaborate with the stakeholder to clarify the intended outcome and split the request into smaller, clearly defined items
Apply the team's expedite class of service so the stakeholder's urgency claim is tested against work already running
Pull the request onto the board as one card and let the team refine details in flight

questions.explanation: Two things actually change whether people speak: the structures the team agrees to and the behavior leaders model. Co-created working agreements with equalizing techniques such as silent writing and round-robins give quieter, remote voices a structural path into the conversation that they helped design — ownership of the norm is what makes it stick. Modeling vulnerability and answering every concern with curiosity demonstrates, repeatedly, that candor is rewarded rather than punished, which is the behavioral foundation of psychological safety. Distributing recordings improves passive information flow but gives silent members no additional voice — they can watch a conversation they still were not part of. Mandating two minutes of speaking per person compels performance, not candor; forced airtime under pressure typically produces safe filler while real concerns stay hidden. Relaying concerns anonymously through the practitioner institutionalizes the workaround: it confirms that speaking directly is unsafe, creates dependency on an intermediary, and leaves the underlying fear untouched.
questions.concept: Psychological safety in distributed teams
questions.question: A distributed platform team spans four time zones. In remote retrospectives, only the three co-located members speak; two remote members regularly message the agile practitioner afterward with concerns they never raise live, and one recently stayed silent about a risky shortcut that later caused a production outage. Which TWO actions would most improve the team's psychological safety? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Record every retrospective and distribute the recording so remote members can review the discussion afterward
Facilitate a session where the team co-creates working agreements for raising concerns, including silent-writing and round-robin techniques that equalize participation across locations
Require each member to speak for at least two minutes in every retrospective so participation is guaranteed
Offer to relay the remote members' concerns anonymously in team meetings so their issues are heard without exposure
Model vulnerability by openly acknowledging one's own mistakes in team forums and responding to every raised concern with curiosity rather than judgment

questions.explanation: Visualizing work means making the real workflow — including waiting and hand-off states — visible so delays become discussable facts rather than invisible friction. Splitting out the fare-rules review queue exposes where time is actually lost and gives the team and stakeholders shared data to act on. Capping days in a column imposes a policy without changing the underlying constraint; the external review still takes as long as it takes, and the rule just generates violations and pressure. Moving waiting items back to To Do erases the evidence of the bottleneck and misrepresents work already started, reducing rather than increasing transparency. A weekly written report is a reporting workaround layered on top of an opaque board — it adds effort, delays information, and still does not reveal that waiting, not working, consumes most of the cycle time.
questions.concept: Making hand-off and queue states explicit on the workflow board
questions.question: A Kanban team supporting a regional transit fare system uses a board with columns To Do, In Progress, and Done. Stakeholders repeatedly ask "where is the fare-cap change?" and the team keeps answering "in progress." Items sit in In Progress for eight to eleven days, and the team discovers most of that time is spent waiting on an external fare-rules review. What is the BEST response?
choices: Agree a policy that no item may sit in In Progress longer than three days, so that stakeholders always get a predictable answer
Move items waiting on the fare-rules review back to To Do, so the board shows only the work the team is actively touching today
Make the waiting state visible as its own column with an explicit queue, then review the flow data with the team and stakeholders
Send stakeholders a weekly written note giving each item's current stage and expected date, so that they no longer need to keep asking

questions.explanation: Open, upward challenge followed by a merit-based debate is the defining behavioral signature of psychological safety: a lower-status member takes an interpersonal risk against a higher-status expert, and the team's response is engagement rather than punishment or dismissal. Consistent harmony with rare disagreement is more often evidence of the opposite — safety produces more voiced conflict about ideas, not less, because people stop self-censoring; smooth silence frequently means people are withholding. Very few reported impediments or near-misses is a classic warning sign, not a health sign: safe teams surface more problems because reporting carries no penalty, so a quiet channel usually means suppression. Deferring to the most senior voice before speaking is anchoring and status-based self-censorship — the exact pattern psychological safety removes. Psychological safety is not comfort or politeness; it is the license to dissent, question, and admit error without fear.
questions.concept: Behavioral indicators of psychological safety vs. artificial harmony
questions.question: An enterprise coach is assessing psychological safety across several product teams. Which observation is the STRONGEST evidence that a team is psychologically safe?
choices: A mid-level developer openly challenges the architect's design during refinement, and the team debates the trade-offs on their merits
Retrospectives finish early with a short, agreeable action list, and the team reports that open disagreement is rare because trust is high
The team raises very few impediments to management and has reported the lowest defect count of any team in the division this year
Members wait for the most senior engineer to state a position before commenting, which the team says keeps discussion efficient

questions.explanation: The consumers' complaint and the cycle-time drift point at the same gap: one lumped column hides where work actually sits. Mapping the real stages — including queues such as awaiting review or awaiting security scan — makes the bottleneck visible to the platform team and its consumers at the same time and produces evidence before any policy changes. A reporting add-on generates charts on top of an unmodeled process, so the burnups would render the same opaque "in progress" bucket in prettier form. Setting a limit of six prescribes a number before anyone knows where the constraint is; work may simply pile up in an invisible waiting state, and the limit is imposed on the team rather than adopted by it. Adding six representatives to a daily meeting substitutes verbal status reporting for a visualization that would answer the question continuously, burdening the meeting without shortening the delay.
questions.concept: Workflow mapping and queue visibility for a shared-service team
questions.question: A platform team supplies internal APIs to six product teams. Its board shows a single "In Progress" column that has held between 14 and 22 cards for months. Cycle time has drifted from 6 days to 23 days. Consuming teams complain they cannot tell whether their request is being coded, reviewed, or waiting on a security scan. The platform team's lead proposes buying a reporting add-on that generates a weekly burnup for each consuming team. What is the BEST response?
choices: Support buying the reporting add-on, since a weekly burnup sent to all six consuming teams would answer the visibility complaint without disturbing the team's work
Propose splitting "In Progress" into the actual stages work passes through, including its waiting states, and observing where items accumulate before changing anything else
Set a work-in-progress limit of six on In Progress now, since capping the queue is the fastest way to bring cycle time down
Have each consuming team send a representative to the platform team's daily coordination call, so every requester hears the state of their items firsthand

questions.explanation: Co-creating a customer-outcome release goal with all three teams and product leadership attacks the root cause: the trade-off fights exist because each team is optimizing a local measure with no shared definition of success, and involving the teams in creating the goal builds genuine commitment rather than compliance. Linking each radiator to that goal keeps the shared purpose visible where daily decisions actually get made. A dashboard that ranks teams by component metrics intensifies local optimization and adds competition on exactly the wrong measures. Escalating trade-offs to the sponsor outsources decisions the teams could make themselves once they share a goal, and it must be repeated for every future dispute. Cross-team technical training builds useful knowledge but addresses capability, not purpose — teams that understand each other's components can still pull in different directions.
questions.concept: Aligning local team metrics to a shared customer-outcome vision
questions.question: A hybrid program building a connected-thermostat product has three component teams. The agile practitioner notices that each team's information radiator celebrates local measures — API uptime, firmware defect counts, mobile-app store rating — yet nobody interviewed can say how the current release helps a customer. Trade-off arguments between the teams' backlogs are increasing. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Build a program dashboard that rolls the three component measures into a single weighted health score reviewed by leadership each week
Ask product leadership to publish a ranked order across the three backlogs each week, so trade-off arguments have an authoritative tie-breaker
Run cross-team technical sessions so each team understands the others' components and can settle trade-offs with better information
Bring the teams and product leadership together to co-create a release goal expressed in customer outcomes, and connect each radiator to it

questions.explanation: Turning the funded belief into an explicit hypothesis and testing it with a minimal cohort release produces behavioral evidence about the riskiest assumption — that the feature changes retention — at a fraction of the two-quarter cost, and the existing feature flags make this experiment cheap and safe. A large survey measures what subscribers say, not what they do; stated intent is a notoriously weak predictor of retention behavior. Monthly increments with sponsor demonstrations look iterative but validate against the wrong audience — the sponsor already believes in the feature — so two quarters of funding could be spent without ever testing the churn claim with subscribers. A design thinking workshop can sharpen the concept but still yields no evidence about the value hypothesis, and with mixed interview signals the priority is real behavioral data, not more refinement of an unvalidated idea.
questions.concept: Hypothesis-driven development and MVP validated learning
questions.question: A sponsor at a streaming-media company is convinced that a social "watch party" feature will reduce subscriber churn and has secured funding to build it over two quarters. Early user interviews are mixed, and the delivery group works in a Lean flow model with feature flags already in place. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Commission a large-scale subscriber survey and a churn-driver analysis to confirm the demand before any development spending begins, so that two quarters of funding are not committed on a mixed signal
Restate the churn belief as a testable hypothesis and release a minimal version of the feature to a small cohort behind a feature flag, measuring retention against a pre-agreed threshold
Deliver the watch-party feature in monthly increments and review the sponsor's feedback at each demonstration, adjusting the scope as her understanding of the market develops
Facilitate a design thinking workshop with the interviewed subscribers to sharpen the concept, then build the refined version of it across the two quarters already funded

questions.explanation: Flow efficiency here is about 3.5 of 18 days, so roughly 80 percent of lead time is pure waiting — the waste is in the queues, not in the work. Securing scheduled windows or another performance-test instance attacks the single largest wait the map identified, and making queue time explicit on the board with item aging converts invisible waiting into managed, discussable delay the team can keep attacking.
