Pushing developers to compress the 3.5 days of active work targets the smallest component of lead time; eliminating it entirely would still leave more than 14 days of waiting. Raising the WIP limit adds inventory in front of an already-queued constraint, lengthening lead time rather than shortening it. Swapping the value-stream map for a burnup chart trades diagnostic detail about where time is lost for a progress-reporting view that says nothing about queues.
questions.concept: Value-stream mapping, flow efficiency, and queue waste
questions.question: A team has mapped its value stream from "request accepted" to "in production" and found total lead time of 18 days, of which 3.5 days is hands-on work; the largest single wait is a 6-day queue in front of a shared performance-test environment. The team wants to improve flow efficiency. Which TWO actions most directly address what the value-stream map reveals? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Negotiate scheduled access windows or an additional instance of the shared performance-test environment to shrink the 6-day queue
Make the queue times visible on the board as explicit wait columns with item aging, so waits are managed rather than invisible
Ask developers to increase their hands-on hours per item to compress the 3.5 days of active work
Raise the team's WIP limit so more items are in the system while the waits are being addressed
Replace the value-stream map with a burnup chart so leadership can see scope and progress in one view

questions.explanation: The response pattern is the Kano signature: delight when present and indifference when absent marks an excitement (attractive) attribute, while dissatisfaction when degraded and no enthusiasm when adequate marks a basic (must-be) attribute. That implies protecting the basic — no amount of offline capability compensates for scans that misread — and taking a small, early slice of the exciting one to learn whether the delight is real. Calling offline picking a basic expectation misreads delight as an obligation and would over-invest in it while treating a must-be as merely proportional. Flattening both into performance attributes and choosing by estimate ignores the categories entirely and lets the cheaper item win regardless of the dissatisfaction risk. Labeling offline picking indifferent confuses "no pain when absent" with "no value when present," which is precisely how excitement attributes are lost.
questions.concept: Kano model applied to prioritization decisions
questions.question: A product team surveys users of a warehouse picking app. For a proposed "offline picking mode," most respondents say they would be delighted if it were available but report no dissatisfaction when told it is absent. For barcode scan accuracy, respondents report strong dissatisfaction when it degrades and little enthusiasm when it simply works. Applying the Kano model, how should the team treat these two items in the next release?
choices: Treat offline picking as an excitement attribute worth a small early slice for differentiation, while protecting scan accuracy as a basic expectation that is never traded away.
Treat offline picking as a basic expectation because delight signals real demand, and manage scan accuracy as a performance attribute improved in proportion to what is invested
Treat both as performance attributes and build whichever carries the smaller estimate first, because Kano categories converge toward performance as a product and its market mature
Classify offline picking as indifferent since no dissatisfaction was reported when it was absent, and spend the release protecting and improving barcode scan accuracy alone

questions.explanation: Surfacing the team's own defect and overtime data links the unsustainable pace to the escaping defects and gives the product owner an evidence-based basis for a different scope decision rather than an opinion to argue with. Building automated coverage into the definition of done and planning against a capacity people can hold indefinitely stops new technical debt at its source and treats quality as something built in rather than added later. Freezing all feature requests until defects fall is a blunt unilateral constraint that removes the product owner's ability to steer value and changes none of the practices producing the defects. Adding a quality-assurance reviewer at the end inspects quality in after the fact, introduces a handoff and a queue just before a pilot, and leaves both the missing automation and the overtime untouched. Extending the iteration by a week bends the cadence to absorb the overload, hides the real capacity signal that team and product owner both need before the pilot, and does nothing to stop the same shortfall recurring next iteration.
questions.concept: Technical debt, sustainable pace, and quality built in
questions.question: A team on a marine-navigation product is three iterations from a customer pilot. Over the last month, defects found after release have tripled, the team has worked late four nights a week to hit iteration commitments, and the automated test suite has not been extended since the pace increased because "there is no time." The product owner has already added two features to the next iteration. Which TWO actions should the agile practitioner take? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Make the connection between the increased pace, the frozen test suite, and the rising escaped defects visible to the team and product owner using the team's own defect and overtime data
Facilitate the team in agreeing an explicit definition of done that includes automated coverage for new work, and plan the next iteration against a sustainable capacity
Ask the product owner to freeze all new feature requests until the escaped-defect count returns to its previous level
Add a dedicated quality-assurance reviewer to inspect each story before it is marked complete
Extend the next iteration by one week so the team can catch up on the missing tests before the pilot

questions.explanation: The failure is not that decisions go unrecorded in a document; it is that the reasoning happens on a one-to-one channel nobody else can overhear or retrieve. Making open, named, searchable channels the place work is actually discussed rebuilds for a distributed team what a shared room gives a co-located one, and the record becomes a by-product of the conversation itself — in the participants' own words, at the moment of the decision, still findable a year later. Restating direct-message outcomes in the channel closes the residual leak without banning a channel that has legitimate uses. A curated decision log kept by the team lead is the strongest alternative and does create traceability, but it is a secondhand account written after the fact, it bottlenecks on one person, it captures conclusions far better than arguments, and the deciding conversation still happens where nobody can see it. Widening the overlap for a synchronous design call buys visibility with synchrony that is expensive across three time zones, and spoken decisions are neither persistent nor searchable. A monthly architecture review re-confirms settled calls on a slow cycle while the next decision disappears into another direct message.
questions.concept: Persistent searchable many-to-many channels as distributed osmotic communication, versus curated decision logs or synchronous meetings
questions.question: A satellite-imagery analytics company runs a single product team split across Bengaluru, Warsaw, and Denver, with about two hours of daily overlap. When the team went fully distributed, most working conversation moved onto a chat platform. Six months on, two recently hired engineers keep re-opening questions the team considers settled: why the tile cache expires at 90 days, why the ingest retry limit is three. Tracing each one, the agile lead finds it was decided in a direct message between two engineers, and neither the decision nor the reasoning behind it exists anywhere the rest of the team can find. Standups are well attended, the backlog is current, and delivery trends are healthy. What best addresses the underlying problem?
choices: Ask the team lead to keep a curated decision log recording the context and rationale behind each call once it is made, and have new joiners work through it during onboarding so every settled question has one authoritative source

Establish that working conversations happen in open, named team channels any member can read and search, with an explicit norm that anything settled in a direct message is restated in the relevant channel before it counts as decided

Negotiate a wider daily overlap window and hold a synchronous design call inside it where every cross-cutting technical decision is made with all three sites present, so that nobody at any site misses the reasoning behind a call

Run a monthly architecture review in which the newer engineers bring their open questions and the whole team re-confirms each standing decision, so that questions settled long ago stop being reopened again and again during ordinary day-to-day work

questions.explanation: Getting agreement on shared evaluation criteria and then running time-boxed spikes converts an opinion battle into an evidence-based decision the team itself owns, and it gives the silent teammates a safe, factual way back into the conversation. Handing the call to an architect outside the team ends the argument but disempowers the team and teaches it to escalate every hard technical decision. Splitting the architecture so that some modules use events and others use synchronous calls optimizes for ending the disagreement rather than for the best outcome, and it saddles the product with inconsistent integration patterns nobody chose on merit. Deferring to a quarterly review leaves work blocked now and hands the decision to people further from the problem than the two developers arguing about it.
questions.concept: Collaborative problem solving through spikes and shared decision criteria
questions.question: On an XP team building a logistics API, two developers have been deadlocked for three days over whether the new inventory service should integrate through asynchronous events or synchronous calls. Daily standups have grown tense, and the rest of the team has begun avoiding the topic entirely. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Ask the platform architect, who sits outside the team, to make the final call so work can resume
Suggest the developers compromise by using events in some modules and synchronous calls in others
Have the developers agree on evaluation criteria, then run short time-boxed spikes to test both approaches
Park the decision until the organization's next quarterly technical review, when senior engineers will be present

questions.explanation: Putting the finished, highest-volume screens in front of real adjusters now converts assumptions into evidence while the remaining five screens are still cheap to change; the feedback arrives when it can still influence design rather than after the money is spent. Holding the demonstrations and writing detailed acceptance criteria for the remaining five keeps the product owner's coherent picture but specifies five screens against assumptions the three built screens could already test, concentrating every discovery into one late, high-stakes event. Surveying adjusters about all eight screens asks them to imagine a system instead of using one, and yields opinions about stated requirements rather than reactions to working software. Asking the claims supervisors to review on the team's behalf is the most practical alternative, since they are easy to schedule and know the domain — but supervisors do not process claims all day, so the friction that slows an adjuster is exactly what a supervisor is least likely to notice.
questions.concept: Incremental feedback loops on working software
questions.question: A claims-intake redesign has three of eight screens built and demonstrable. The product owner suggests holding all demonstrations until the eighth screen is finished, saying the adjusters "should see a coherent picture rather than half a system." The three finished screens cover the highest-volume claim type. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Agree to hold demonstrations, and use the time to write detailed acceptance criteria for the remaining five screens with the product owner.
Propose putting the three finished screens in front of a few adjusters this week and using what they learn to shape the remaining five.
Survey the adjusters about all eight screens now, so the remaining five are built to stated needs rather than to the team's guesses.
Ask the claims supervisors to review the three finished screens on the team's behalf, since they can be scheduled far more easily than adjusters.

questions.explanation: The constraint is on releasing to production, not on getting the increment in front of users. Standing up a mirrored environment and having supervisors exercise it every two weeks converts a three-month feedback gap into a two-week one, so misunderstandings are corrected while the work is cheap to change and the quarterly release carries far less rework risk. Lengthening iterations makes the feedback loop worse, not better, and does nothing about the queue of unvalidated work. A readiness checklist raises quality conditions but cannot tell the team that supervisors wanted a different workflow — no checklist substitutes for a user touching the software. Escalating to compliance treats the regulatory cadence as the first thing to attack, when the team can act inside its own control today; if a faster validation cadence is genuinely needed, that conversation is far more persuasive after the team can show validated, user-approved increments waiting to ship.
questions.concept: Shortening feedback loops when the release cadence is externally constrained
questions.question: A team builds cold-chain telemetry software for a pharmaceutical distributor. It produces a working, tested increment every two weeks, but the regulated production environment accepts only one validated release per quarter, so increments queue up for months. After last quarter's release went live, warehouse supervisors raised forty change requests in three weeks, most of them about screens the team had built in the first iteration of the quarter. What is the BEST response?
choices: Lengthen the team's iterations from two weeks to a month, so fewer increments queue up and the cost of integrating them between releases falls
Add validation-readiness checks to the team's definition of done so each increment is already release-ready and fewer change requests appear after go-live
Deploy every increment to a non-production environment that mirrors warehouse conditions, and have supervisors work real scenarios on it at each increment review
Ask the compliance group to open a second validation window each quarter, so that finished increments reach the warehouse supervisors twice as often

questions.explanation: The notes show three distinct conflict levels demanding three distinct responses. Blue's language is problem-focused and specific ("let's list where our readings differ") — a level-one problem to solve, healthy debate the practitioner should leave with the team, offering light help only if asked. Red's language has shifted from the problem to the person ("you always protect your side") with camps forming — contest-level conflict, where the practitioner should actively facilitate the parties back from personal positions to underlying interests. Green shows withdrawal and exit behavior, with transfer requests already filed — fight-or-flight escalation beyond what ordinary facilitation resolves, calling for separate conversations with each party and likely help from leadership or an outside facilitator. Running a single joint workshop for everyone treats three different levels with one blunt instrument and wrongly labels Blue's constructive disagreement as unhealthy. Prioritizing Blue because its conflict appeared first inverts the diagnosis: Blue's conflict is the productive kind that improves decisions and needs no rescue, while Red and Green are the items actually deteriorating. Reading Green's silence as a conflict burning itself out confuses disengagement with resolution — at this stage withdrawal is the most severe signal in the exhibit, not recovery.
questions.concept: Leas' levels of conflict and matching interventions
questions.question: An agile practitioner supporting the program reviews the observation notes in the exhibit and applies a levels-of-conflict model (such as Leas') to decide where and how to intervene. Which interpretation should guide the practitioner's response?
choices: All three teams are showing conflict that has turned unhealthy, so one joint resolution workshop covering the whole program reaches Blue, Red, and Green at once with one consistent and efficient intervention
Blue needs the most urgent attention because conflict is cheapest to resolve at its first appearance, and Red's personal remarks and Green's withdrawal can be handled once Blue's dispute is settled

Blue's disagreement is healthy problem solving to leave with the team; Red's personal attacks call for active facilitation back to interests; Green's withdrawal signals escalation past light facilitation
Green's withdrawal shows the conflict burning itself out and needs no action, so facilitation belongs with Blue's specification dispute and Red's estimate dispute, where people are still engaged

questions.explanation: The reaction pattern identifies a basic expectation and a delighter. A capability whose absence angers customers but whose presence goes unremarked is an expected baseline: it must be present and reliable in the earliest release, and effort beyond 'good enough' buys almost no additional satisfaction. The capability that excites customers when present but is not missed when absent is a differentiator, best sequenced once the baseline holds and before it decays into a mere expectation. Leading with the exciting capability leaves the baseline missing, so early customers are dissatisfied no matter how impressive the differentiator is. Reading the strong negative reaction as a quality complaint about the existing reminders is the most plausible alternative and does put the right capability first, but owners were reacting to reminders being absent rather than working badly, so it risks polishing something that only needs to be reliably present. Treating both equally ignores that the two produce completely different satisfaction curves.
questions.concept: Kano analysis applied to prioritization and release sequencing
questions.question: A team building a veterinary practice platform surveys clinic owners about two candidate capabilities. Owners react enthusiastically to an AI-generated visit-summary feature when shown it, but are untroubled when told it does not exist. Owners barely comment on automated appointment reminders when they are present, yet react strongly negatively when told reminders would be absent. How should the team apply this information during backlog refinement?
choices: Deliver the enthusiastically received capability first, since the strong positive reaction is the clearest available signal of what clinic owners will pay a premium for.
Treat the strong negative reaction as a quality complaint about the existing reminders and improve those before either candidate capability is scheduled.
Give both capabilities equal weight in the next release, since each drew a strong reaction and the research does not say which of the two matters more.
Build the barely-noticed capability to a solid 'good enough' level in the earliest release, and position the enthusiastically received one later as a differentiator.

questions.explanation: Demonstrating a running increment instead of a signed-off specification privileges working software over comprehensive documentation — the increment, not the document, is the measure of progress. Working through the ambiguous licensing clause with the customer's own representative, rather than trading formal change requests, is customer collaboration over contract negotiation; although two individuals are interacting, the defining feature is resolving a contractual ambiguity through partnership with the customer rather than through the contract mechanism. Replanning the iteration when telemetry contradicts the roadmap is responding to change over following a plan — new evidence outranks the original plan. Dropping the ticket-routing workflow that blocked direct conversation is individuals and interactions over processes and tools; it could be mistaken for customer collaboration, but the parties are testers and developers inside the team, and the obstacle removed is a process, not a contract.
questions.concept: Four Agile Manifesto values
questions.question: Match each team behavior (1-4) to the Agile Manifesto value (A-D) it most directly demonstrates.
pairs: Instead of circulating a 40-page design specification for sign-off, the team demonstrates a running increment to stakeholders every two weeks
Working software over comprehensive documentation
When a licensing clause proves ambiguous, a developer and the customer's operations lead work through concrete examples together rather than exchanging formal change requests
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
After production telemetry contradicts the assumptions behind the release roadmap, the team replans the next iteration around the new data
Responding to change over following a plan
The team abandons a mandated ticket-routing workflow that was preventing testers and developers from talking directly, and agrees to face-to-face refinement instead
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools

questions.explanation: Meeting the two developers privately and facilitating an interest-based conversation addresses the conflict at its source while it is still workable: beneath the positions ("refactor first" versus "ship first") lie legitimate interests — code health and delivery speed — that a shared working norm, such as agreed refactoring conditions in the definition of done, can reconcile. Adjusting the pairing rotation so the two no longer work together is avoidance: it hides the friction without resolving the standards disagreement, which will resurface with other pairs. Waiting for the retrospective airs an interpersonal issue in front of the whole team before the individuals have had a chance to resolve it, hardening the sides already forming. Posting a respectful-communication reminder and sending the debate back to the workstation is reasonable on tone and venue, but it leaves the two arguing privately about a standard they cannot settle alone.
questions.concept: Interest-based conflict resolution
questions.question: On an XP team, two developers who often pair have started clashing: one insists on refactoring aggressively before adding features, while the other pushes to ship and clean up later. Their disagreement has moved from the workstation into the team chat channel, where sarcastic remarks are appearing. Other pairs are starting to take sides. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Adjust the pairing rotation so the two no longer work together, which removes the friction point and keeps other pairs out of the disagreement
Wait for the next retrospective and raise the chat remarks with the whole team present, so norms for written debate are set by everyone at once
Post a reminder about respectful communication in the chat channel and ask both developers to take the refactoring debate back to the workstation instead
Speak with the two developers privately, surface the interests behind each position, and guide them to a shared norm for when refactoring happens

questions.explanation: Matching the amount of delegated authority to the team's current maturity — clear boundaries now, widening deliberately as capability grows — applies situational leadership and builds genuine empowerment without abandoning a forming team. Settling branch strategy, environments, and story splitting in a workshop with the two vendor leads is the strongest alternative, since it removes ambiguity quickly and the leads carry real authority, but it decides on the team's behalf, excludes the people who must live with the choices, and moves the approval bottleneck up rather than removing it. Funneling the same approvals through one rotating representative reduces interruptions while leaving the practitioner as the decision-maker, which is a routing change rather than a growth in capability. Granting full authority immediately ignores the team's low maturity and unclear expectations, and a floundering team usually triggers a swing back to command and control.
questions.concept: Situational leadership and progressive delegation
questions.question: An agile practitioner joins a hybrid program where a newly formed team blending employees and two vendor groups routes every decision to her for approval - branch strategy, environment choices, even how to split stories. The team has never worked together, and its members are unsure of program expectations. What is the BEST response?
choices: Hold a decision workshop with the two vendor leads and settle branch strategy, environments, and story splitting with them before the team starts any building
Agree explicit decision boundaries with the team, delegate the decisions it is ready to own today, and widen its authority as capability and confidence grow
Route the recurring approvals through one rotating team representative who brings them to her, so the requests stop interrupting everyone else's work
Give the team full authority over these technical decisions immediately, since a group trusted from day one develops confidence faster than one held back

questions.explanation: The retrospective has failed at its only real test — it is not producing change — so the practitioner should turn the improvement lens on the practice itself and restore the feedback loop by limiting WIP on improvements: one item, actually finished, rebuilds the team's belief that the session changes something. Replacing the session with an anonymous survey removes the team's collaborative sense-making and routes feedback upward rather than into team-owned action, guaranteeing that even less changes. Assigning owners and due dates to all 31 items applies process pressure to a backlog the team already cannot absorb; the problem is not missing names, it is too many improvements in flight with no capacity reserved for any of them. Inviting the delivery manager to enforce follow-through introduces management surveillance into what must be a psychologically safe space, which typically suppresses the candor that makes retrospectives valuable in the first place.
questions.concept: Retrospective effectiveness and limiting WIP on improvement actions
questions.question: Six months into a program, a component team has held retrospectives every iteration. The action list has accumulated 31 items; 6 were completed, and the rest carry forward. Attendance is dropping and one engineer says openly that the session is "a ritual where we write things nobody does." The delivery manager suggests replacing retrospectives with an anonymous monthly survey to save time. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Adopt the anonymous monthly survey so improvement feedback still reaches leadership without spending team time on a ritual nobody values
Give the 31 open action items named owners and due dates, so follow-through becomes visible and the stalled list finally moves
Facilitate the next retrospective on the retrospective itself, and have the team pick one improvement to complete before the next session
Invite the delivery manager to the next session so the team's improvement commitments are made in front of someone who tracks them

questions.explanation: Little's Law makes the trade-off explicit and testable: average cycle time equals average work in progress divided by average throughput, so with throughput steady the team halves cycle time by roughly halving the work it holds open — about 13 items at 1.5 per day is close to nine days. That is a policy change the team can make this week, at no cost, and reverse if the data disagrees. Adding contractors assumes throughput scales linearly with headcount, ignores ramp-up and the extra coordination load, and in practice first increases work in progress, pushing cycle time the wrong way before it helps. Re-baselining onto a percentile that makes today's number look acceptable games the measurement instead of improving the system and destroys the metric's credibility with the director. Daily percent-complete reporting manufactures status effort, measures individuals rather than the system, and produces no information the flow data does not already carry.
questions.concept: Little's Law applied to work in progress and cycle time
questions.question: A semiconductor test-tooling team works in a hybrid cadence and measures flow. Over the last quarter the system holds an average of 27 items in progress and completes an average of 1.5 items per day, giving an average cycle time of about 18 days. The engineering director asks the team to get cycle time down to about 9 days by the end of next quarter and offers to fund two contractors. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Accept the two contractors and target three completed items per day, since holding average work in progress steady while doubling throughput is what halves cycle time, and revisit the board's work-in-progress limits only if the added capacity fails to move the cycle-time number next quarter.

Re-baseline the target on the 85th percentile of the team's historical cycle time, so the commitment reflects what the system actually delivers rather than an aspiration nobody can meet, and report the team's performance against that revised service-level expectation at each monthly engineering review with the director.

Walk the team and the director through Little's Law — with throughput held steady, cutting average work in progress from about 27 to about 13 halves cycle time — and agree a lower work-in-progress limit plus a rule to finish started items before pulling new ones.

Ask each engineer to report daily percent-complete on their open items and review the slowest of them at every standup, so delays surface early enough for the team to intervene and keep individual items from stretching the quarterly cycle-time average any further before the next review.

questions.explanation: The described approach — drawing out the individual's own thinking through open-ended questions while deliberately holding back one's own answers, on the premise that the person is resourceful and grows most by finding his own path — is coaching. Sharing one's own product-ownership experience, war stories, and recommended moves would be the alternative approach the practitioner is explicitly withholding, in which a more experienced person guides a less experienced one from personal history. Structured transfer of defined knowledge or skills against a curriculum or competency target is a different approach again, and nothing here describes a syllabus or a skills gap being taught. Guiding a group through a discussion or decision without steering its content is a group-process skill, not a developmental one-on-one relationship, so it does not fit the setting described.
questions.concept: Coaching vs. mentoring vs. training vs. facilitation distinctions
questions.question: An agile practitioner is supporting a business analyst who wants to grow into a product ownership role. In their one-on-one sessions the practitioner deliberately withholds advice drawn from her own product experience and instead asks open-ended questions that help the analyst examine his assumptions and choose his own next development step. Which approach is the practitioner applying?
choices: Coaching
Mentoring
Training
Facilitation

questions.explanation: The exhibit shows five of six decisions made unilaterally by the lead — including working-agreement matters such as code-review rules and defect triage order that belong to the team — with broad input sought exactly once, while the team's reported sense of influence fell from 71% to 38% over the same six weeks. The fitting response is coaching the lead toward progressive, explicit delegation: classify upcoming decisions and hand agreed categories to the team first where its knowledge is strongest. Having the lead keep deciding but explain his reasoning in stand-ups improves transparency, yet authority stays exactly where it is. Adding decision cycle time to the flow metrics measures speed, which was never the problem — the speed is being purchased with ownership. Handing over every category at once swings from autocracy to abdication and teaches the lead nothing about delegating deliberately.
questions.concept: Delegation levels and centralized-decision anti-pattern
questions.question: The agile practitioner reviews the exhibit with the team's agile lead, who says, "Decisions get made fast — what exactly is the problem?" Based on the exhibit, what should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Ask the lead to keep deciding but explain his reasoning in each stand-up, so the team understands the thinking behind those calls
Add decision cycle time to the team's flow metrics, so the log can show whether centralized decisions actually slow delivery
Coach the lead to classify upcoming decisions and progressively delegate agreed categories to the team, starting where team knowledge is highest
Hand the team authority over every decision category at once, since autonomy is exactly what the engagement scores show is missing

questions.explanation: A flat risk burndown says the program is consuming time without retiring uncertainty. Pairing that transparency with a concrete, cheap proposal — a timeboxed spike that buys real information about the integration — respects the sponsor's authority over ordering while giving them what they actually need before a contractual decision. Unilaterally re-sequencing the backlog and informing the sponsor afterwards may produce the right technical outcome but destroys the trust and transparency the relationship depends on, and invites the sponsor to police the backlog thereafter. Adding a mitigation plan and contingency reserve documents the exposure without reducing it; the burndown would stay flat at the next review because nothing was learned. Referring the question to an architecture review board substitutes an opinion for evidence, inserts a hand-off delay into the last two iterations, and still leaves the team not knowing whether the integration actually works.
questions.concept: Risk burndown, risk-adjusted backlog sequencing and spikes
questions.question: A hybrid program delivering a hospital scheduling system maintains a risk-adjusted backlog and reviews a risk burndown chart every second iteration. The chart has been essentially flat for three consecutive reviews. Investigation shows the single largest remaining exposure — an unproven integration with the regional patient index — sits near the bottom of the backlog because the sponsor has insisted that visible front-end features come first. Two iterations remain before a contractual go/no-go decision. What is the BEST response?
choices: Reorder the backlog so the patient-index integration is built next, since unproven technical exposure outranks feature visibility, and brief the sponsor once the first results are available
Keep the sponsor's ordering and strengthen the risk register with a detailed mitigation plan and a contingency reserve, reviewing the exposure at every risk burndown checkpoint
Show the sponsor the flat risk burndown against the go/no-go date and propose a short timeboxed spike on the patient-index integration next iteration, so the decision rests on evidence
Ask the architecture review group to assess the interface specifications and issue a written feasibility opinion, then set the backlog order once their assessment arrives

questions.explanation: The forecasts slip because the unit of forecasting has been inflated: a point now measures compliance with an incentive rather than relative size, so any projection built on points drifts. Naming that mechanism for the sponsor, evidenced by the gap between a 40% velocity rise and flat feature delivery and defect escape, and moving the program onto measures that cannot be inflated without actually delivering — completed items per period, the spread of cycle times, escaped defects, value released — restores forecastability and points the program at outcomes instead of activity. The calibration workshop is the most tempting alternative and is technically achievable, but it legitimizes cross-team comparison of a team-internal aid and leaves the growth-linked bonus untouched, so the drift resumes in calibrated units. Withdrawing metrics from the teams trades one dysfunction for another: it destroys the transparency teams need to inspect their own delivery and leaves the sponsor holding private numbers nobody trusts. Switching to ideal hours changes only the units — hours are just as inflatable under a growth-linked bonus — and it drags the program further toward measuring effort rather than delivered value.
questions.concept: Measurement dysfunction when velocity becomes a comparative target
questions.question: In a program of five teams building a hospital scheduling suite, the program management office publishes a monthly league table of velocity by team and has tied part of each team's discretionary bonus to velocity growth. Across two quarters, reported velocity has risen roughly 40% while released features and the defect-escape rate are unchanged; two teams now routinely split stories to raise their counts, and release forecasts have become unreliable. The sponsor asks the agile practitioner why forecasts keep slipping. What is the BEST response?
choices: Run a cross-team calibration workshop around common reference stories so that a story point carries the same meaning on all five teams, then keep the monthly league table and the bonus link in place, since the comparison between teams is finally made on a consistent and defensible basis

Show the sponsor the divergence between rising velocity and flat delivery, explain that velocity stops measuring anything once it is rewarded, and propose replacing the league table with outcome and flow measures — throughput, cycle-time distributions, escaped defects, and released value — used to produce forecast ranges

Recommend that the program management office stop publishing the league table to the teams and track velocity privately for forecasting, while leaving the bonus tied to velocity growth, so the incentive to improve survives but the teams can no longer tune their splitting to the ranking

Convert all five teams from story points to ideal hours so the unit is objective and directly comparable, publish the same monthly ranking in hours, and let the bonus keep rewarding the teams whose measured output grows fastest, since hours cannot be inflated simply by splitting stories

questions.explanation: Meeting the department head to uncover the underlying need — usually visibility and predictability — and then demonstrating how the existing flow metrics, board, and reviews already satisfy it applies two core agile decision rules: understand before prescribing, and collaborate before escalating. It also creates the opening to explain why assigning tasks to named individuals undermines a self-managing pull system. Coaching the team to comply quietly while running the real work from the board sacrifices transparency and creates two versions of the truth. Producing utilization reports alongside the flow metrics each week institutionalizes utilization thinking that conflicts with flow and adds pure waste rather than resolving the mismatch. Arranging Lean training for her is the most constructive alternative and may help later, but prescribing a class before anyone has asked what she actually needs is slow, impersonal, and easily read as a rebuke by a senior stakeholder whose support the team depends on.
questions.concept: Servant leadership, self-managing teams, and influencing traditional managers
questions.question: A department head with a traditional PMO background is newly assigned to oversee a Lean software team. Within a week she begins requesting individual utilization reports from each member and assigning specific tasks to named developers mid-flow. Team members are frustrated but keep pulling work from the board. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Meet with the department head to understand what she needs from the reports and show how the team's flow metrics and reviews can provide it
Coach the team to comply quietly with the utilization requests while continuing to manage their real work from the board, so flow is undisturbed
Produce the utilization reports alongside the team's flow metrics each week so that she can compare the two views at her own pace
Arrange Lean training for the department head so she can learn how flow-based teams operate before her next round of reporting

questions.explanation: Four incidents with four different proximate causes point to systemic contributing conditions — most likely gaps in what the pipeline verifies and in environment and configuration management — and a fishbone across all four surfaces those shared categories, which is also the evidence the team needs to answer leadership with something stronger than a preference for autonomy. Five Whys on the single most recent incident drills deep into one causal chain and would explain the feature flag while leaving the certificate, the schema change, and the sandbox mismatch unexplained, so it cannot reveal what the four have in common. Accepting a 48-hour review board, even temporarily, inserts a manual queue into a continuous pipeline: batch sizes grow, feedback slows, and the board reviews stated intent rather than executing the checks that would actually have caught any of these four failures — and controls adopted under incident pressure rarely come back off. Adding smoke tests immediately is a plausible eventual control prescribed before anyone understands the pattern; it would probably have caught the expired certificate and perhaps the sandbox mismatch while missing the schema and flag failures, and jumping to a partial fix forfeits the analysis that would justify the right set of automated gates to leadership.
questions.concept: Root-cause analysis technique selection and CI/CD pipeline controls
questions.question: A team on a national logistics platform has a continuous delivery pipeline that deploys on every merge. Over the past five weeks, four production incidents have followed deploys, each traced to a different cause: an expired certificate, a schema change without a migration, a third-party sandbox mismatch, and a misconfigured feature flag. Leadership wants a change advisory board with a 48-hour review before any production deploy. The team is convinced the board would make things worse but cannot articulate why beyond preferring autonomy. Two engineers want to run Five Whys on the most recent incident; another wants a fishbone across all four; the platform lead wants to add pre-deploy smoke tests immediately. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Run Five Whys on the most recent incident, since it is freshest in the team's memory and depth on one cause beats breadth
Accept the 48-hour review board as an interim control while the team investigates, then propose removing it once deploys stop failing
Facilitate a fishbone across all four incidents to find shared contributing conditions, then take the evidence to leadership with proposed pipeline controls
Have the platform lead add pre-deploy smoke tests this week, since faster feedback inside the pipeline is the agile response to failures

questions.explanation: The board is hiding the very things that explain the rising cycle time: handoffs, queues and external waits. Mapping the real workflow with the team and making those states and queues explicit — with limits the team sets itself — turns the board into an honest model of the work, and walking it right to left shifts the daily meeting from personal status to finishing the oldest items. Agreeing a Definition of Done and finishing before starting is the strongest alternative and is sound in general, but none of the three vendor waits, the two sign-offs, or the three-week item are the team's to finish, so a stricter rule on an invisible queue simply parks people. Timeboxes and a burndown change cadence and reporting, not the hidden queues. Per-person swimlanes organize the board around who holds work rather than what it waits on.
questions.concept: Explicit workflow states, queues and WIP limits on a board
questions.question: A municipal water-billing team works in a continuous-flow manner with a three-column board: To Do, In Progress, Done. Fourteen items sit in In Progress across six people. The daily coordination meeting has become a round-robin of "still on mine." Average cycle time has risen from four days to eleven. When the practitioner asks about specific items, she learns three are waiting on a vendor meter-reading API, two are waiting on a compliance officer's sign-off, and one has been "nearly done" for three weeks — none of which the board shows. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Agree a definition of done with the team and require every item to satisfy it before anyone starts another, so work stops bouncing back and the In Progress column begins to drain.
Map the real workflow with the team, making states such as analysis, build, verify and external wait explicit with visible queues and team-agreed limits, and walk the board right to left each day.
Introduce two-week timeboxed iterations with a burndown chart, so the team commits to a smaller batch of work and both the team and its stakeholders can see each day how much of that batch remains.
Split the In Progress column into a swimlane for each person and track how long items sit in each one, so the daily meeting can concentrate on whoever is carrying the heaviest load.

questions.explanation: The disagreement is about how crews will behave, and the crews are downstairs — a timeboxed spike buys that information in days for the price of deliberately throwaway code, and settles the debate with observed behavior rather than persuasion. Two weeks of comparative analysis delays a decision that real users could resolve this week and still yields documented opinion rather than evidence. Asking the product owner to choose ends the argument by authority, ignores the cheapest available source of truth, and leaves the losing camp unconvinced and half-committed. Building both approaches in parallel doubles the cost, creates half-finished inventory, and hardens each group's advocacy through sunk cost — which is precisely why a spike is kept small and disposable.
questions.concept: Timeboxed spikes to resolve design uncertainty with user evidence
questions.question: An e-scooter operator's team has spent three days in design workshops deadlocked between two approaches for a rebalancing tool that tells street crews which scooters to move: a rules engine the crews can edit themselves, or a demand-prediction model. Neither camp will concede, and the architect proposes a two-week comparative analysis ending in a decision paper. Depot crews start every shift in the same building as the team. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Back the architect's two-week comparative analysis, since a documented evaluation gives a defensible written basis for settling a question the team has already argued over for three whole days.
Ask the product owner to decide between the rules engine and the demand-prediction model, since ordering value is her call, so the deadlock ends and the team can start building the rebalancing tool.
Split the team so that each group builds its preferred approach for a full iteration, then compare the two working versions, since real code settles an argument that discussion alone has not.
Propose a short timeboxed spike that puts a rough version of each approach in front of depot crews on their next shift, and decide from what the crews actually do with them.

questions.explanation: Facilitating the team to examine its own feedback patterns and reshape its working agreements treats psychological safety as what it is — a property of the whole team's interaction system — and produces norms every member, including the principal engineer, helped author and will therefore uphold; the withdrawal of three engineers shows the damage is already collective, not a one-person issue. Privately coaching the principal engineer is a reasonable supplementary step, but alone it addresses only the sender of the feedback: the colleagues who have gone silent hear nothing that rebuilds their confidence to contribute, and the team gains no shared agreement to prevent recurrence. Routing proposals through the practitioner for anonymized discussion makes the practitioner a permanent intermediary, hides the problem instead of healing it, and undermines the direct collaboration agile depends on. Escalating to the engineering manager hands the team's interpersonal dynamics to the hierarchy before the team has attempted to self-correct, eroding self-management and likely deepening the fear of speaking openly.
questions.concept: Psychological safety in distributed teams
questions.question: A platform team is distributed across Berlin, Bangalore, and Sao Paulo and does most design work in asynchronous threads. A principal engineer repeatedly dismisses colleagues' proposals with curt one-line verdicts. Two mid-level engineers have stopped posting alternatives, and a third now books private calls to get his approval before sharing anything publicly. Delivery remains on track, and the principal engineer's technical judgments are usually sound. What is the BEST response?
choices: Guide the team to examine together how design feedback is exchanged — for example in a retrospective — and to reshape its working agreements
Speak privately with the principal engineer about the tone of his written replies, then watch whether the two engineers begin posting alternatives again
Route design proposals through you so options can be discussed without the author's name attached until the team has settled on one
Raise the pattern with the engineering manager, since a principal engineer's influence is beyond what the team can reasonably correct itself

questions.explanation: Jointly crafting the vision with the team, the current sponsor, and the three competing departments creates alignment through participation — people commit to what they help build, and getting transit, permits, and parks to negotiate one vision is precisely the stakeholder-alignment work this situation demands. Keeping that vision visible and linking each backlog item to its outcomes during refinement then makes purpose operational, so 'closing tickets' becomes 'advancing outcomes' in the team's own daily conversation. Publishing the original charter fails because that document predates three sponsor changes and was never shaped by the current team or stakeholders; pointing at a stale artifact creates no ownership and no agreement between the three departments. A mandatory recitation ritual produces compliance theater rather than understanding — repeating words nobody helped write breeds cynicism, especially in a team that has already disengaged. Bonus incentives tied to vision items rely on extrinsic motivation, which crowds out the intrinsic sense of purpose the practitioner is trying to rebuild and invites gaming of how items get classified.
questions.concept: Co-created vision, intrinsic motivation, and connecting daily work to purpose
questions.question: A municipal-services portal effort has cycled through three executive sponsors in twelve months. The blended team of contractors and city staff now describes its work as 'closing tickets,' and the transit, permits, and parks departments each pull the backlog in a different direction. Which TWO actions should the agile practitioner take to rebuild shared purpose? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Publish the original project charter on the team wiki and reference it during stand-ups
Facilitate a workshop where the team, the current sponsor, and the three departments jointly craft a concise product vision and agree on how each release advances it
Add a recitation of the vision statement to the opening of every stand-up as a required practice
Tie individual performance bonuses to delivery of vision-aligned backlog items
Make the agreed vision visible in the team space and, during refinement, connect each backlog item to the outcomes it names so daily work traces to purpose

questions.explanation: The failures are a symptom; the cause is a feedback loop so slow that rational developers batch their work, and large batches integrated at the same moment make attribution of any failure nearly impossible. A fast commit stage that answers within minutes restores the economics of pushing small changes often, and each failure then points at one small change, which collapses the morning archaeology. Funding a contractor to repair builds institutionalizes the waste, creates a role whose existence depends on the broken loop continuing, and changes neither the batch size nor the delay that produced it. Requiring the full suites locally pushes a 95-minute wait onto every workstation, which makes batching worse rather than better and still produces no shared integration signal. Running the pipeline at midday as well as overnight halves the interval but leaves the batch size and the multi-hour feedback delay essentially intact, so failures continue to arrive tangled together.
questions.concept: Continuous integration feedback-loop duration driving batch size
questions.question: A data-platform team runs a single pipeline that compiles, executes 4,200 unit tests, provisions containers, and runs a full regression suite — about 95 minutes end to end. Because the wait is long, developers accumulate changes locally and push once at the end of the day; roughly a third of the nightly runs fail, and untangling whose change broke what consumes the first hours of the next morning. In the retrospective the team proposes asking for a contractor to fix broken builds. What is the BEST response?
choices: Support the contractor request, since a third of the nightly runs fail and the first hours of those mornings are lost to untangling them, and the team has itself identified the true cost of those failures and the remedy it wants to try first

Ask developers to run the full unit and regression suites locally before every push, so that most failures are caught on the developer's own machine, and keep the shared pipeline running overnight as the final safety check that nothing was missed

Schedule the full pipeline to run at midday as well as overnight so failures surface twice a day and less work accumulates between runs, and rotate a build marshal each week whose job is to untangle whichever changes broke the run

Treat the 95-minute wait as the impediment itself: split the pipeline so a fast commit stage of unit tests and critical checks returns in minutes on every push, run the long regression suite behind it, and agree to integrate small changes frequently

questions.explanation: The defining feature of the exchange is that the practitioner offers no advice and no expertise, only powerful questions that help the tester surface her own goals and next steps, which is coaching. Mentoring would have the practitioner share personal experience and advice drawn from having walked a similar path, and no such experience is offered here. Training would mean structured instruction aimed at closing a defined skill gap, yet no automation content is taught at all. Facilitation describes guiding a group's process toward the group's own outcome, typically in a meeting or workshop; this is a one-on-one developmental conversation, and the label misses the developmental intent behind the questions even though it correctly notes that the practitioner supplies no content.
questions.concept: Coaching versus mentoring, training, and facilitation
questions.question: A tester tells an agile practitioner she wants to move into a test-automation role but feels stuck. Rather than recommending a path, the practitioner asks open questions — "What does success look like for you? What have you already tried? What is one experiment you could run this iteration?" — and lets the tester define her own next steps. Which approach is the practitioner using?
choices: Coaching, because the practitioner uses questions to help the tester discover her own path rather than supplying answers
Mentoring, because the practitioner draws on the route she walked herself so the tester can model a proven path
Training, because the conversation is designed to transfer the specific test-automation skills the tester says she lacks
Facilitation, because the practitioner is running the structure of the conversation while staying out of its actual content

questions.explanation: Falling attendance is a symptom, so the agile response is to diagnose the cause with the people affected and then let the community redesign itself around real practitioner problems — communities of practice live or die on voluntary, member-driven value. Making attendance a performance objective fills the room with bodies rather than engagement and converts a learning community into a compliance ritual that breeds resentment. Shutting the community down and relying on team retrospectives abandons the cross-team learning channel entirely; a retrospective improves one team's way of working and has no mechanism for spreading techniques between teams. Imposing a rotating presentation schedule is the same compliance instinct in different clothing — content pushed by obligation instead of pulled by interest, which is precisely what emptied the sessions.
questions.concept: Communities of practice; voluntary participation and root-cause analysis
questions.question: A quality-engineering community of practice that once drew members from every team now attracts only three regulars, and its sessions have drifted into status updates. A department head offers to make attendance mandatory so the investment is not wasted. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Accept the department head's offer and add community attendance to members' performance objectives, so participation recovers and the earlier investment is protected
Close the community and move quality topics into each team's retrospective, where the people closest to the testing work already meet and can act on it
Bring current and former members together to surface why the sessions lost value, then let practitioners reshape the format around problems they actually face
Keep the sessions running by having each team present its testing approach on a rotating schedule, so every meeting has prepared content and a reason to attend

questions.explanation: Raising an impediment inside the team's own standup is not the same as raising it with the group that can remove it, and no conversation has happened yet; carrying the wait-time data to the platform group frames their queue as a shared flow problem rather than an accusation, and it usually surfaces causes the team can help fix, such as demand spikes, poor request quality, or a constraint inside the platform group itself. Reordering the backlog keeps people busy but hides the impediment, defers the highest-value work, and quietly normalizes a three-week wait. Escalating to the delivery office may eventually be justified, but going there before speaking to the platform group damages a relationship the team depends on every iteration and asks a third party to arbitrate a discussion that has never taken place. Standing up an unofficial environment in a personal cloud account creates unsanctioned infrastructure with security, cost, and data exposure, adds technical debt, and removes the visible pain that would otherwise drive a systemic fix.
questions.concept: Cross-team impediment removal and escalation timing
questions.question: A team needs test environments provisioned by a central platform group. Requests are taking about three weeks against a published target of two days. The team has raised this in its own daily standup for two iterations and the impediment is aging on its board. The organization's formal escalation route is the delivery office. A senior developer offers to stand up an unofficial environment in a personal cloud account over the weekend, and the product owner suggests reordering the backlog to only stories that need no environment. Nobody from the team has yet spoken with the platform group. What is the BEST response?
choices: Reorder the backlog toward stories that need no test environment, keeping the team productive and its velocity steady while the platform group's provisioning queue clears on its own over the coming iterations
Take the team's aging-impediment and wait-time data directly to the platform group and ask to work together on where their queue is congested and what a faster path could look like
Hand the impediment to the delivery office through the formal route with two iterations of standup evidence, asking it to move this team's provisioning requests up the platform group's queue
Accept the developer's offer so the team is unblocked this week, and tell the platform group about the unofficial environment after the fact, once its published provisioning target is met again

questions.explanation: With stale market research, the biggest risk is building the wrong product; shaping a minimum viable product releases real value early and replaces year-old assumptions with evidence from actual customers, which then steers the remaining investment. Sequencing all forty features by business value improves the order but keeps the single nine-month release, so the ranking is still built on year-old research and no customer sees anything until the end. Testing a clickable prototype with a customer panel is the strongest alternative, because it does attack the stale-research risk early and cheaply — but a panel reacting to a prototype gives opinions about intentions, while a release gives evidence from people who use and pay for the product. Monthly internal releases improve stakeholder visibility while leaving the customers whose behavior would validate the list outside the loop.
questions.concept: MVP and incremental value delivery
questions.question: An agile practitioner joins a hybrid program in which stakeholders insist that all 40 planned features must be complete before anything is released in nine months, because "customers expect a finished product." The market research behind the feature list is more than a year old. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Sequence all 40 features by business value so the most valuable ones are built first inside the same nine-month release window
Test a clickable prototype with a customer panel to confirm the feature list is still the right one before development starts
Propose an internal release each month so stakeholders can inspect real progress and adjust the plan well ahead of the public launch
Work with stakeholders to identify a minimum viable product that can be released early to validate assumptions with real customers

questions.explanation: A pre-mortem is designed to surface exactly what routine ceremonies miss: by assuming failure has already happened, it gives people permission to name concerns that feel impolite or speculative while there is still time to act on them. Putting the resulting risk responses into the backlog and tracking a risk burndown turns those concerns into real, ordered, pulled work and makes falling risk exposure visible each iteration. Collecting private emails destroys the collective sense-making that makes risk identification work, leaves the practitioner as a single filtering point, and hides risks from the people best placed to act on them. An independent PMO assessment adds weeks of external review, arrives as a report rather than as work the team can pull, and disempowers the team that actually understands the system. Freezing the backlog removes the team's ability to respond to what it learns in the final iterations and gives only an illusion of safety — the largest risks in a clinical go-live are already present in what has been built.
questions.concept: Pre-mortem facilitation and risk burndown through backlog-managed risk responses
questions.question: A team is three iterations from the go-live of a medication-reconciliation module in a hospital network. The agile practitioner is concerned that daily coordination and iteration reviews are surfacing only day-to-day obstacles, and that longer-range go-live risks are going unnamed and unworked. Which TWO actions best address this? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Facilitate a pre-mortem in which the team imagines it is six months past a failed go-live and works backward to name the plausible causes
Ask each team member to email the practitioner their top three concerns privately so a consolidated risk register can be produced without anyone feeling exposed
Ask the sponsor to commission an independent pre-go-live risk assessment from the PMO
Add the highest-exposure risk responses to the product backlog so they are sized, ordered and pulled like any other work, and track a risk burndown each iteration
Freeze the backlog for the remaining three iterations so that no new change can introduce additional risk

questions.explanation: The exhibit shows Validate holding six items against a limit of two, with its oldest item at 11 days — beyond last month's entire 8-day average cycle time — so the board is signaling a bottleneck the team has been ignoring, which is why stakeholders are surprised despite having board access. Swarming to finish Validate items and re-honoring the limit acts on the signal: stop starting, start finishing. Pulling more work into Build feeds additional WIP toward the bottleneck and worsens flow. Raising the limit to six legitimizes the overload and silences the very signal the limit exists to give. Requesting a specialist escalates for resources before the team has tried swarming and cross-skilling to clear the constraint itself — possibly a later step, but not the first.
questions.concept: Acting on information-radiator signals: WIP limits and aging work
questions.question: An insurance-claims modernization team shares its Kanban board link with stakeholders, yet stakeholders report being surprised by delays. The agile practitioner reviews the morning snapshot in the exhibit with the team. Based on the exhibit, what should the team do first?
choices: Swarm on the items in Validate to bring that stage back within its WIP limit before pulling any new work
Raise the Validate limit to match the queue that has formed so the board reflects the demand the team faces
Pull the next ready items into Build so developers keep moving while Validate works through its queue
Add a validation specialist to the team so the stage gains the capacity its growing queue demands

questions.explanation: Five Whys produces a hypothesis, not a verdict, and the correct next move is to check that hypothesis against other evidence before changing the system. If split staffing genuinely drives late criteria, the smallest useful experiment targets it — earlier example-based collaboration between analyst, developer and tester, or protecting the analyst's time — and the team inspects the result at the next retrospective. A two-person sign-off reacts to the presenting symptom of ambiguity rather than the absent analyst; approval gates add delay, diffuse responsibility, and generate no shared understanding of the requirement. Handing the item to management abandons the team's own influence, since how and when acceptance criteria get elaborated is largely within its control. A definition of ready demanding complete criteria up front sounds disciplined but would simply have blocked the story with no plan for who elaborates it, pushing the same problem upstream while front-loading analysis.
questions.concept: Five Whys, kaizen experiments, and avoiding process gates as root-cause responses
questions.question: During a retrospective at a marine-logistics software firm, a team examines why a customs-declaration feature reached production with a defect that halted two shipments. A tester says "the requirement was ambiguous." The facilitator runs Five Whys and the chain converges on: acceptance criteria were written the night before the iteration ended because the analyst had been pulled to a different product for three weeks. Two developers immediately propose a mandatory two-person sign-off on every acceptance criterion before coding begins. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Adopt the two-person sign-off on acceptance criteria, since a lightweight control is a proportionate response to an ambiguity that halted two customer shipments this month
Conclude that the chain ends in a staffing decision outside the team's control, and ask management to guarantee the analyst's availability before any countermeasure is attempted
Test the cause first — check whether the analyst's split assignment explains other late criteria, then design a small experiment aimed at that cause rather than adding an approval gate
Add a definition of ready requiring complete acceptance criteria before any item enters the iteration, so ambiguous requirements are caught at the boundary rather than at the end of the work

questions.explanation: The action recurs for two reasons: nobody has diagnosed why the build fails, and the improvement work has no place on the board where capacity is actually allocated. Tracing one concrete failure back through its causes turns a vague wish into a specific, changeable defect, and putting the resulting fix into the iteration backlog makes it compete for capacity honestly instead of depending on goodwill. A working agreement to stop starting while the suite is red is the strongest rival, since it would end the rerun habit outright, but adopted before any diagnosis it halts the whole team two or three nights a week for a cause nobody understands, and an agreement that costly is quietly abandoned under delivery pressure. Quarantining the intermittent tests makes the suite green by deleting the signal, and revisiting after the release is the same deferral that has already failed four times. Folding stabilization into the definition of done spreads undiagnosed, unbounded repair across every story, so nobody owns or sizes it.
questions.concept: Five Whys root-cause analysis and making improvement work visible in the backlog
questions.question: For four iterations running, a mixed Scrum/XP team's retrospective has produced the same action: "stabilize the build." The nightly suite still fails two or three nights a week, developers rerun it until it passes, and nobody has ever picked the action up during an iteration. Every other retrospective outcome gets acted on; this one keeps reappearing. What is the BEST response?
choices: Facilitate a Five Whys on a specific recent build failure, then pull the resulting fixes into the iteration backlog as visible, owned work held to the same acceptance criteria as any other item.
Add a working agreement that nobody on the team starts new work while the nightly suite is red, so failures can no longer be absorbed by developers rerunning the build until it passes.

Quarantine the tests that fail intermittently so the nightly suite reports green again and the team stops losing time to repeated reruns, then revisit the quarantined tests after the current release ships.
Make build stabilization part of the definition of done so every story carries a small share of the fix and the repair work is spread evenly across the whole team rather than sitting unowned.

questions.explanation: Mentoring fits because the request combines a long-term development horizon with an explicit ask to draw on the practitioner's own experience in the target role — the two defining features of a mentoring relationship. Using powerful questions to help her find her own answers describes coaching, which deliberately withholds the senior person's experience; that is not what she asked for and is poorly suited to transferring role wisdom she does not yet possess. Delivering a structured curriculum on backlog management describes training, which transfers defined skills in discrete sessions and is too narrow and episodic for a year-long career transition. Remaining content-neutral while guiding process describes facilitation, which serves group process rather than one person's development and is not a developmental relationship at all.
questions.concept: Coaching vs. mentoring vs. training vs. facilitation as knowledge-transfer modes
questions.question: A tester tells the agile practitioner she wants to grow into a product-owner role over the next year and asks for regular guidance drawing on the practitioner's own years in that role. Which developmental approach fits this request, and why?
choices: Coaching, because the practitioner should use powerful questions to help her discover her own answers
Training, because she needs a structured curriculum covering backlog management and prioritization techniques
Mentoring, because the practitioner shares personal experience to guide her longer-term professional growth
Facilitation, because the practitioner should remain neutral on content while guiding her process

questions.explanation: The root cause is a missing shared picture of the whole product: each team is rationally optimizing what it can see. Bringing the teams and product leadership together to co-create the vision and shared outcome measures re-aligns local metrics beneath a common purpose, and doing it jointly means every team owns the result rather than complying with it. Circulating an integration charter for sign-off documents today's conflicting assumptions but creates alignment only on paper — sign-off is not shared understanding, and the document will drift the moment assumptions change. A design authority that approves assumptions adds a control gate that slows flow and substitutes policing for purpose; teams that share a vision do not need permission to align. Asking sponsors to reset targets escalates the symptom while skipping the collaborative step: even perfectly recalibrated targets handed down from above will not give the teams the shared 'why' that lets them make consistent daily decisions.
questions.concept: Aligning multi-team metrics to a co-created product vision
questions.question: Three teams building a hybrid logistics platform have each begun optimizing their own component metric: one chases API response time, another warehouse-scan accuracy, and the third a mobile-app store rating. At the latest integration demo it emerged that the components make conflicting assumptions about who the primary user even is. Sponsors remain satisfied because every team is hitting its local targets. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Facilitate a joint session where the three teams and product leadership co-create the overall product vision and derive shared outcome measures their local metrics must ladder up to
Draft an integration charter documenting each component's primary-user definition and interface assumptions, and circulate it to the three teams for formal sign-off before the next demo
Establish a cross-team design authority that reviews and approves interface contracts and user assumptions before any team proceeds with dependent development work
Ask the sponsors to reset each team's local targets, since they own the incentive structure that is driving the component-level optimization in the first place

questions.explanation: A regulatory change is new information that changes where value lies; agile teams welcome it and reorder the backlog immediately so the next iteration delivers what matters most, while keeping governance informed transparently rather than blocked on it. Waiting for the monthly board trades several weeks of a six-week runway for procedural comfort and treats the process as more important than responding to change. Finishing planned scope to protect velocity optimizes a team metric over customer and compliance value — exactly backwards. Freezing work for a comprehensive impact analysis of everything remaining is big-bang predictive analysis; agile thinking analyzes just enough to reprioritize now and refines the rest progressively as more is learned.
questions.concept: Welcoming changing requirements within hybrid governance
questions.question: Mid-iteration, a regulator announces a rule change taking effect in six weeks that invalidates several backlog items for an insurance-claims product. The product operates within a hybrid program whose change control board meets monthly. The product owner asks the team's agile practitioner for advice. What is the BEST response?
choices: Wait for the monthly change control board to authorize the change, so the reprioritization is formally approved before the team moves any work at all
Finish the currently planned iteration scope first so the commitment holds, then bring the compliance items into planning for the following iteration
Stop new work while the team runs a full impact analysis of every remaining backlog item against the new rule, so nothing invalidated gets built by mistake
Help the product owner reprioritize the backlog now so the highest-value compliance items enter the very next iteration, and inform the board in parallel

questions.explanation: Practical Little's Law gives average cycle time as work in progress divided by throughput: 30 tickets divided by 20 tickets per week is 1.5 weeks. The essential caveat is that the relationship holds only for a stable system — arrivals roughly matching departures and WIP not trending — which is why practitioners use it as a planning heuristic rather than a guarantee. Calling 1.5 weeks a firm commitment misuses the law: it describes an average across a stable period and says nothing about the variability any single ticket will experience, so individual tickets routinely finish far outside it. Dividing throughput by WIP inverts the formula and produces a number with no meaning as a duration. The 30-week figure assumes strict sequential single-piece processing, which contradicts the premise that 30 items sit in the system concurrently while 20 finish every week.
questions.concept: Applying practical Little's Law and recognizing its stability assumption
questions.question: A support-and-maintenance team pulls tickets through a Kanban system. Over a stable eight-week period the team completed an average of 20 tickets per week and consistently had about 30 tickets in the system between intake and done. The product owner asks how long a newly arriving ticket will typically take to reach done, assuming the system stays stable. Using practical Little's Law, what is the best answer and its most important caveat?
