choices: About 1.5 weeks, valid only while arrival and departure rates stay roughly balanced and WIP remains stable
About 1.5 weeks, and it holds as a firm commitment because it is derived from eight weeks of the team's actual data
About 0.67 weeks, since dividing throughput by work in progress gives the average time each item spends in the system
About 30 weeks, because each of the 30 items in progress must be completed before the newly arrived ticket is started

questions.explanation: The group has adopted agile mechanics without the mindset — ceremonies run on schedule while command-and-control behaviors continue, which is exactly why the adjuster experiences the events as overhead. Using an existing inspect-and-adapt forum to surface the values gap puts supervisors and team in the same conversation as participants rather than as accuser and accused, and committing to one small behavioral experiment is how mindset actually shifts: through changed daily behavior that people chose. Cutting or shortening ceremonies treats the complaint as a calendar problem, removes the feedback loops that could expose the real issue, and leaves the controlling behaviors fully intact. Sending supervisors to certification training defers the conversation for months and assumes the gap is missing knowledge, when supervisors who assign tasks and rewrite estimates are usually acting from accountability pressure and habit, which a class does not touch. Requesting a top-down policy banning supervisors from assigning work uses mandate to install empowerment — a contradiction that buys surface compliance and resentment instead of genuine self-organization.
questions.concept: Agile mindset versus mechanical practice adoption
questions.question: An insurance claims-processing group adopted agile six months ago. Daily standups, reviews, and retrospectives all happen on schedule, yet supervisors still assign work items to named individuals each morning and adjust the team's estimates before they are recorded. In a hallway conversation, an adjuster tells the agile practitioner, 'Agile here just means more meetings.' What is the BEST response?
choices: Arrange certification training for the supervisors, since they are applying familiar management habits and a shared vocabulary would show them what self-organization actually asks of them day to day
Bring supervisors and the team together in a retrospective to examine how current behaviors conflict with agile values such as self-organization, and agree on one concrete behavior to change
Ask the transformation office to publish a standard stating that teams pull their own work and own their estimates, giving supervisors an unambiguous rule they must follow
Reduce the number of ceremonies, since the practices are already running on schedule and the complaint the adjuster raised is squarely about the meeting load that they create

questions.explanation: The basic listing-and-booking flow with manual payment handling is a true MVP: it is the smallest release that tests the riskiest business assumption — will farmers rent equipment through a marketplace at all — with real users, and the concierge-style manual back end is a legitimate way to avoid building unvalidated infrastructure. Launching the largest feature set a deadline allows is scope-driven, not learning-driven; nothing about it tests an assumption. An internal prototype shown only to executives generates approval, not market evidence — no real user behavior is observed. Thinning out every planned feature spreads effort across the whole vision without decisively testing any single hypothesis; an MVP is defined by the learning it produces, not by being a miniature of the complete product.
questions.concept: Minimum viable product and validated learning
questions.question: A team is applying minimum viable product (MVP) thinking to a new farm-equipment rental marketplace. Which action MOST accurately reflects the intent of an MVP?
choices: Building the largest feature set the team can finish before the industry trade show, so the new marketplace makes the strongest possible first impression on the farmers and dealers who attend
Releasing a polished internal prototype to company executives and equipment dealers for their approval, so the direction is agreed before any code reaches paying customers
Shipping a thin version of every planned feature at once, so that early users experience the whole product vision and can tell the team which parts of it matter most to them
Offering a basic listing-and-booking flow to a small group of farmers — with staff manually processing payments behind the scenes — to test whether they will actually rent equipment this way

questions.explanation: Detail is perishable. Refining only what is about to be worked, and leaving distant items as coarse placeholders, matches the level of detail to the level of certainty and stops the team paying to specify work that feedback will change. Freezing the backlog protects the paperwork by blocking learning, which is precisely backwards: the clinician feedback that invalidated those items is the most valuable thing happening. Splitting sessions by specialty removes the cross-functional conversation that builds shared understanding, creates handoffs, and does nothing about the wasted effort. Shortening the session or moving it to asynchronous review treats the symptom (meeting length) while the team keeps producing detail on work that may never start, and it strips out the discussion where ambiguity actually gets resolved.
questions.concept: Progressive elaboration and refinement depth
questions.question: A telehealth platform team maintains a backlog of roughly 380 items. Twice a week the team spends two hours in refinement, and most of that time goes to writing detailed acceptance criteria for items the product owner expects to start in six to nine months. Over the last quarter, the team estimates that a third of the items it detailed were later dropped or substantially rewritten after clinician feedback. Team members now describe refinement as "paperwork night." What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Ask the product owner to hold the roadmap steady for two quarters, so the detail written in refinement is not invalidated by clinician feedback arriving later.
Facilitate the team and product owner in detailing only items likely to start in the next one or two iterations, keeping the rest coarse until they approach.
Split refinement into separate sessions by specialty so each member attends only the portion that touches their own skill set and spends fewer hours.
Move refinement to an asynchronous written review that members comment on between iterations, so the same detail is produced without the long twice-weekly sessions.

questions.explanation: The map shows the constraint is a large-batch queue, so the highest-leverage move is to work with the constraint's owner to shrink batch size and review continuously, which directly attacks the waiting waste that dominates the lead time. Pulling extra items so a fuller batch waits for each monthly review feeds that queue and inflates work in progress, making the average wait longer rather than shorter. Automating the airworthiness evidence package is useful work the team owns, but it shortens the reviewer's handling time inside a review that still happens once a month, and a nine-day queue created by cadence does not shrink because each submission is tidier. Asking the compliance group to publish its review criteria is the strongest alternative, since fewer first-pass failures would cut rework, yet an item that passes first time still waits for the next monthly batch — the interval between reviews, not the pass rate, is what sets the nine days.
questions.concept: Value stream mapping and batch-size reduction at the constraint
questions.question: An agricultural-drone firmware team maps its value stream and finds a 22-calendar-day average lead time against roughly 3 days of actual work. The single largest wait is a 9-day queue in front of an airworthiness-compliance review that the compliance group performs in one batch once a month. The team's improvement time for the next iteration is uncommitted. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Have the team pull extra items into each iteration so a fuller batch is waiting whenever the monthly compliance review runs, making better use of every review window.
Use the improvement time to automate the airworthiness evidence package, so the compliance group receives a complete submission and spends less time on each item.
Ask the compliance group to publish its review criteria so the team can self-check items and submit only work that is certain to pass on the first attempt.
Invite the compliance reviewer to collaborate with the team on a small, frequent cadence, reviewing each item as it completes rather than in one monthly batch.

questions.explanation: Bringing two adjusters into the review and observing them work a live claim is best: the reported problem is a mismatch between the software and real field behavior, and only direct contact with the people doing that work exposes the actual sequence they follow. Reporting an adoption metric monthly measures the symptom more precisely without creating any customer contact, so the team keeps building on the same second-hand understanding. Commissioning personas and journey maps from the analyst produces polished artifacts derived from the very proxy whose model has already proved wrong, and it delays contact further. Funding training and job aids assumes the software is correct and the users are the defect, which inverts the feedback the adjusters actually gave.
questions.concept: Customer proxies versus direct user engagement and observation
questions.question: A regional insurer is rebuilding the tool its claims adjusters use in the field. A business analyst attends every iteration review and answers questions "on behalf of the adjusters," who are described as too busy to attend. Adoption of the last two releases has been low; when asked, adjusters said the new screens do not match the order in which they actually work a claim on site. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Add an adoption measure to the release dashboard and report the trend to the sponsors monthly, so the shortfall stays visible to them.
Ask the business analyst to build detailed personas and a journey map of a claim so the team can plan the next iteration from them.
Fund targeted training and job aids so the adjusters can work the new screens confidently before the next release reaches them.
Arrange for two adjusters to join the next review and to be observed working a live claim with the current release in the field.

questions.explanation: Active listening comes first: her requests for signed-off specifications are almost certainly a bid for the predictability and protection her old environment provided, and no technique will stick until that underlying concern is heard. Pairing then lets her experience — rather than be told — how conversation, tests, and short feedback loops produce the clarity she is seeking, which is how mindsets actually shift. Explaining the rules and asking her to comply with the working agreements dismisses her concern and may harden her resistance; correct information rarely changes a belief that is rooted in discomfort. Sending her to a fundamentals course delays the issue, outsources a coaching responsibility that sits with the practitioner and the team, and signals that she is a problem to be fixed elsewhere. Asking the customer to write detailed criteria just for her stories accommodates the old pattern, creates a two-track process, and quietly undermines conversation-based collaboration for the entire team.
questions.concept: Active listening and experiential coaching for mindset change
questions.question: A developer who spent a decade in a plan-driven PMO joins an XP team. In her second week she blocks two stories as 'requirements incomplete,' asks the on-site customer for signed-off specifications, and tells the agile practitioner the team's way of working feels chaotic. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask open-ended questions to understand what feels unsafe about the approach, then pair her with an experienced teammate so she experiences how the team gains clarity through conversation and tests
Explain that XP deliberately replaces signed specifications with conversations and tests, and ask her to follow the team's working agreements until she has seen a full iteration play out

Ask the on-site customer to write fuller acceptance criteria for every story she picks up, so she has the written detail she is accustomed to and can start coding without waiting on another conversation
Enroll her in a formal agile fundamentals class for newcomers and hold her story assignments until she finishes it, so the team is not slowed by questions its own practices already answer

questions.explanation: Moving the customer's look at working software earlier — the moment a screen is usable rather than at the end of the iteration — shortens the feedback loop and lets the change be made while the work is still in progress, which is the direct cure for late-discovered rework. Adding a design sign-off gate before coding pushes decisions to the point where the least is known and creates a documentation handoff instead of a conversation; it delays learning rather than accelerating it. Lengthening the iteration to three weeks makes each feedback loop longer, so misunderstandings live longer and rework grows rather than shrinks. Richer acceptance criteria help, but written criteria still encode a guess about layout and alerting that only the user's reaction to a live screen can validate; that substitutes more up-front specification for actual feedback.
questions.concept: Shortening the customer feedback loop with mid-iteration demonstration of working slices
questions.question: A distributed team building a warehouse robotics dashboard works in two-week iterations. The team demonstrates completed work only at the iteration review, where the operations manager who will use the dashboard consistently asks for layout and alerting changes that force rework in the following iteration. The team's rework rate has climbed to roughly 30 percent of capacity. The team lead suggests adding a formal design sign-off gate before development starts. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Propose that the operations manager review working slices mid-iteration, as soon as a screen is functional, rather than waiting for the review
Add the design sign-off gate the team lead proposes, so the operations manager approves layout and alerting before any screen is coded
Extend iterations to three weeks so feedback and the rework it triggers land inside a single iteration rather than spilling into the next
Ask the product owner to write the operations manager's layout and alerting expectations into acceptance criteria before items enter an iteration

questions.explanation: A minimum viable product is distinguished by actual release to real customers with the explicit purpose of testing a value hypothesis — it is Lean Startup's engine of validated learning, not merely a small first version. An A/B test is defined by concurrent comparison: two live variants measured against the same metric to let user behavior pick the winner, which is different from releasing one minimal offering to see whether it has value at all. A spike is the one technique on the list that faces inward rather than toward customers — a time-boxed investigation that buys technical knowledge (can we do it, and how) before the team commits, producing learning rather than product. A low-fidelity prototype belongs to design thinking's explore phase: cheap and disposable, it exists to sharpen understanding of user needs before build investment, and unlike an MVP it is never released as the product. The common trap is treating MVP, prototype, and spike as interchangeable "small first steps" — they differ in audience (customers vs. team), timing (pre-build vs. released), and the hypothesis each one tests (value, need, or feasibility).
questions.concept: Experimentation techniques — MVP, A/B test, spike, prototype distinctions
questions.question: Match each experimentation technique (1-4) with the description (A-D) that best characterizes it.
pairs: Minimum viable product
The smallest releasable version of an offering, put in front of real customers to test a value hypothesis and generate validated learning
A/B test
Two variants run concurrently with live users to compare their performance against a defined metric
Spike
A time-boxed technical investigation carried out to reduce uncertainty about feasibility or approach before committing to build
Low-fidelity prototype
An inexpensive, often disposable mock-up used early to explore and refine understanding of user needs before anything is built

questions.explanation: The past spikes failed because they had no discipline around learning, so the two fixes are structural to the experiment itself: a timebox tied to an explicit question keeps the probe cheap and focused, and transparent sharing of all outcomes — failures included — turns every experiment into team learning while reinforcing that failed experiments are safe; likewise, writing the hypothesis and its confirming or refuting signal before starting is what separates an experiment from tinkering, because the team knows in advance what evidence would count. Showing stakeholders only the successes destroys transparency and teaches the team to hide failure, which suffocates safe-to-fail experimentation. Requiring a business case and steering-committee approval adds a heavyweight gate that makes small, fast, cheap probes slower and more expensive than the learning they produce — most will simply never happen. Outsourcing experimentation to a separate innovation squad removes learning from the people who need it: the delivery team stops experimenting at all, and insights generated elsewhere rarely transfer.
questions.concept: Designing safe-to-fail experiments: hypotheses, timeboxes, and transparent learning
questions.question: A telecom platform team wants a stronger culture of early experimentation, but past 'innovation time' produced unfocused spikes with nothing to show for them. Which TWO actions would MOST improve the quality of the team's experiments? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Timebox each experiment or spike and state up front what question it must answer, then share the results — including failures — openly with the whole team
Present only the successful experiments at reviews so stakeholders keep confidence in the team
Require a formal business case and steering-committee approval before any experiment begins
Define the hypothesis and the measurable signal that will confirm or refute it before the experiment starts
Move all experimentation to a separate innovation squad so the delivery team's throughput is unaffected

questions.explanation: INVEST asks each story to be independently valuable and testable; a vertical slice through the stack that lets a member add and see one beneficiary can be demonstrated, accepted, and if needed released on its own. The schema layer is a horizontal slice, necessary work but producing nothing a user or stakeholder can evaluate, so no meaningful acceptance test exists for it. Estimability alone does not make a story good: a technical task can be highly estimable and still deliver zero value, and INVEST weighs several attributes together rather than optimizing one. Independence from the user interface is not what the I in INVEST means; it refers to independence from other stories in ordering, and the schema story is in fact a prerequisite that creates dependency. Relative size is incidental, because a vertical slice is not automatically smaller than an infrastructure task, and small does not imply valuable or testable.
questions.concept: INVEST criteria and vertical versus horizontal story splitting
questions.question: A team is splitting a large item, "Members can manage their beneficiaries," for a life insurance portal. One proposed split is "Build the beneficiary database schema," and another is "A member can add a single beneficiary and see it listed on their policy." Applying INVEST, which statement BEST explains the difference between these two candidate stories?
choices: The schema story is stronger because it is far more estimable and retires the technical uncertainty of the data model before any member-facing behavior is committed to an iteration
The add-a-beneficiary story is stronger because it is valuable and testable on its own, while the schema story delivers no observable outcome until later work is completed
The schema story is stronger because it is independent of the interface and can be built while beneficiary screen designs are still being settled with the business
The add-a-beneficiary story is stronger because it is smaller in effort than building the schema and can therefore be finished comfortably inside a single iteration

questions.explanation: Bringing the engineers together to surface underlying concerns and agree on objective criteria is best: it converts a positional standoff into collaborative problem solving, uses evidence rather than authority, and repairs the working relationship at its source. Planning to raise the testing question at the next retrospective delays feedback while the sarcasm keeps poisoning code reviews and chilling other pairs away from the gateway code. Adopting the standard the other payments teams already use is genuinely attractive — it settles the question with organizational precedent and costs nothing in delay — but it imports a decision without checking that those teams face the same third-party gateway risks, and it ends the argument by convention rather than evidence, leaving both engineers' concerns unexamined. A code-review etiquette agreement attacks the tone, a symptom, while the technical disagreement fueling the conflict remains unresolved.
questions.concept: Interest-based facilitation and objective criteria in technical conflict
questions.question: On an XP team building a payments integration, two engineers have argued for a week about whether contract tests or full end-to-end tests should guard the third-party gateway. The disagreement has spilled into sarcastic code-review comments, and other pairs are starting to avoid touching that area of the code. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Note the tension privately and plan to raise the testing question as a discussion topic at the team's next retrospective, when the whole team can weigh both approaches calmly and decide the standard together

Adopt the gateway testing standard already used by the other payments teams, so the question is settled by existing organizational convention rather than by another week of argument between the two engineers

Bring the two engineers together to surface the concerns behind each position and agree on an objective test, such as a time-boxed spike of both approaches measured against real defect and runtime data
Introduce a code-review etiquette agreement that rules out sarcastic comments, and ask the team to adopt it so reviews in that part of the code turn civil enough for other pairs to rejoin

questions.explanation: The unused staging link has already proved that access is not the constraint — nobody has a reason to visit a rehearsal environment during a working day. Releasing behind a feature flag to consenting pilot operators puts the increment into real work, and the combination of usage telemetry and a short weekly debrief produces both behavioral evidence and conversation, with the operations director engaged as a partner rather than left as a bottleneck. Naming two operators who commit to reviewing each build within three days is the strongest alternative because it fixes responsibility and a deadline, but it still asks busy people to visit a rehearsal environment out of obligation, and chasing missed reviews turns feedback into compliance. One-week iterations simply double the number of staging emails nobody opens. A guided script tells the director where to look yet still seeks a reaction to a demonstration rather than evidence from real work, and leaves the quarterly pile-up of assumptions intact.
questions.concept: Limited real-user (canary) release with telemetry as a customer feedback loop
questions.question: A compliance-reporting product for agricultural drone operators has been in development for five months. The team deploys a working increment to a staging environment every two weeks and emails the link to the customer's operations director, but audit logs show almost no staging usage. The operations director gives substantive feedback only at the quarterly steering meeting, where two increments' worth of assumptions get questioned at once. The organization has a group of pilot operators who have agreed to try new tooling, a compliance officer available for reviews, and a feature-flag mechanism that supports limited releases. What is the BEST response?
choices: Ask the operations director to nominate two experienced operators who will commit to reviewing each staging build within three days, and follow up with them directly whenever one of those reviews is missed or arrives late.

Partner with the operations director to release the next increment behind a feature flag to a small group of consenting pilot operators, instrument real usage, and hold a short weekly debrief on what the data and the operators show.

Shorten the iteration to one week so that increments reach the staging environment twice as often, on the reasoning that a smaller change is easier for the operations director to absorb and respond to between the quarterly steering meetings.

Write a short guided script for each staging build describing what to try and which questions the team needs answered, and send it along with the link so the operations director knows exactly where to look and what to comment on.

questions.explanation: Shortening the distance between the team and the people who do the work is what fixes the problem: real users at the review, plus observation of actual use, replaces relayed opinion with first-hand evidence and cuts the feedback delay from weeks to days, while the analyst stays engaged as a collaborator rather than being cut out. More detailed acceptance criteria signed by the proxy only make the proxy's assumptions more precise, and turning her signature into a baseline reframes later dispatcher feedback as a scope dispute rather than as learning. Moving to four-week iterations is the strongest rival, because it really would bring the regional calls inside the cycle — but it lengthens every feedback loop the team has and still routes dispatcher reactions through a monthly meeting. Surveying all 200 dispatchers after each review gathers breadth without depth: it counts stated preferences from people who have not used the increment, and majority ranking buries the minority whose work the tool actually breaks.
questions.concept: Shortening the feedback loop to real users instead of relying on a proxy stakeholder
questions.question: A hybrid team building a field-service scheduling tool demonstrates every two weeks to a business analyst who represents 200 dispatchers. What the dispatchers actually think reaches the team three to five weeks later, after the analyst's monthly regional calls, and roughly a third of that feedback contradicts what was accepted at the review. What is the BEST response?
choices: Ask the analyst to write richer acceptance criteria in advance and to sign each story at the review, so the feedback that arrives weeks later has an agreed baseline it can be reconciled against.
Invite two or three working dispatchers to each review and arrange short sessions observing them use the increment in their own work, keeping the analyst as a partner rather than as a filter.
Move the team to four-week iterations so that the analyst's regional calls fall inside the cycle and dispatcher reactions arrive before the increment is accepted at the review.
Survey all 200 dispatchers after each review and prioritize the changes that the largest number of respondents ask for, so the team spends its capacity on what most users want.

questions.explanation: The skilled but hesitant team pairs with low direction and high support: they need no task instruction, they need encouragement and shared decision-making to close a confidence gap. The brand-new enthusiastic team pairs with high direction and low support: with no competence yet in flow practices, explicit instruction on how to run the replenishment meeting is what moves them, and their morale is not the constraint. The long-standing, confident team pairs with low direction and low support — delegation — because anything more directive would undercut the self-organization they have already earned. The discouraged post-failure team pairs with high direction and high support: their skills are still developing and their commitment has dipped, so they need continued guidance on the work and active rebuilding of belief at the same time. The common trap is reversing the two middle cases — giving a skilled but hesitant team more instruction, which insults their competence and misses the real gap, or giving a discouraged, still-developing team pure encouragement with no guidance, which leaves them unable to succeed and deepens the discouragement.
questions.concept: Situational leadership styles mapped to team competence and commitment
questions.question: A servant leader adapts their style to each team's maturity. Match each team situation (1-4) to the leadership behavior (A-D) that situational leadership recommends.
pairs: A skilled team hesitates to commit to an ambitious quarterly objective and keeps seeking the leader's reassurance before deciding
Low direction, high support: share decision-making, listen, and encourage — the capability exists but confidence is wavering
A newly formed team, enthusiastic but with no experience of flow practices, is unable to run its first replenishment meeting
High direction, low support: give explicit step-by-step instruction and closely monitor execution while competence is built
A long-standing team with strong skills and high confidence is ready to own its release decisions end to end
Low direction, low support: hand over ownership of decisions and outcomes, staying available but stepping back
A team has learned the mechanics of its practices but is discouraged and losing commitment after a failed release
High direction, high support: continue guiding the work while explaining decisions, inviting questions, and actively rebuilding confidence

questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria are item-specific and behavioral: they define what "works as intended" means for that single piece of functionality, and they are how the customer or product owner judges that item. The Definition of Done is universal rather than item-specific — one quality bar every item must clear (testing, documentation, security scanning, deployability) for the increment to be genuinely releasable. A Definition of Ready is a team working agreement about readiness to pull, and its value depends on holding it lightly; applied rigidly it becomes a gate that pushes the team back toward up-front specification and stalls flow. The iteration goal is an outcome statement that gives the timebox a purpose and coherence, so the team can renegotiate specific items with the product owner and still deliver the intended result. Confusing the item-level criteria with the universal quality bar is the classic error: acceptance criteria vary per story, the Definition of Done does not, and neither can substitute for the other.
questions.concept: Distinguishing acceptance criteria, Definition of Done, readiness agreements, and iteration goals
questions.question: A team preparing a subscription-billing increment uses several distinct product artifacts and agreements. Match each item on the left to the description that best captures its purpose.
pairs: Acceptance criteria
C: The item-specific conditions that determine whether that particular piece of functionality behaves as the customer expects
Definition of Done
A: A shared quality bar applied to every item, describing the conditions the increment must satisfy before it is considered complete and potentially releasable
Definition of Ready
D: A team's working agreement about how much shared understanding an item needs before it is pulled, used as a guide rather than a gate
Iteration goal
B: A concise statement of the outcome the team intends to achieve during the timebox, giving coherence to the selected items and room to adapt the details

questions.explanation: The team is trying to resolve an empirical question through opinion, which is why three weeks of debate have produced nothing. Running short, time-boxed spikes converts the argument into an experiment: real code against a realistic workload produces evidence, the time-box caps the cost of learning, and the team owns the decision. Handing the choice to an architecture board removes the decision from the people closest to the work and adds delay without adding data. Deferring to the most senior engineer substitutes authority for evidence and can entrench exactly the untested assumption that caused the stalemate. A detailed written comparison is still analysis without contact with reality — it extends the paralysis and produces predictions where a spike would produce facts.
questions.concept: Spikes as time-boxed experiments to replace opinion with evidence
questions.question: A hybrid delivery team modernizing a warehouse-management system has spent three weeks in meetings debating whether to adopt an event-streaming platform or nightly batch integration, and design work has stalled while both camps argue from experience on past projects. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask the enterprise architecture board to rule on the integration approach so the team's design work can restart this week
Adopt the option the most experienced engineer recommends, since past project results are the evidence at hand
Have both camps produce a weighted written comparison and adopt whichever of the two options scores higher
Facilitate a time-boxed spike of each option against a realistic workload and decide based on the observed results

questions.explanation: The unknown that threatens the pilot is concentrated in a few screens, above all evidence upload. Testing those with actual claimants within days, then building and re-testing thin slices, shrinks both the batch of learning and the batch of build, and it validates the real journey rather than a simulation of it. The full six-week lab program consumes more than a third of the remaining runway before a single line of working software exists, and still tests a prototype rather than the product. Building everything and waiting for the pilot pushes feedback past the point where change is cheap and makes a public pilot with real claimants the first genuine test — exactly the wrong place to discover that the upload step fails. Halving the study while building in parallel looks like a compromise but preserves the same big-batch structure: feedback still lands after most of the build is committed, and nothing directs attention to the riskiest screens first.
questions.concept: Batch size of learning and risk-first slicing of feedback
questions.question: An insurer is rebuilding its claims-intake journey. The design group has produced a fully clickable prototype of all 14 screens and wants a six-week usability lab program before any code is written; the delivery team wants to start building immediately. The program has publicly committed to a pilot with real claimants in four months, and nobody yet knows whether claimants can complete the evidence-upload step unaided. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Compress the lab program to three weeks across all fourteen screens while the team builds in parallel, so full coverage is preserved and the four-month pilot date is still comfortably met
Run the full six-week lab program as designed, since usability defects discovered once code exists cost far more to correct and the pilot is still four months away
Have the team start building all fourteen screens now and gather claimant feedback from the pilot itself, since real usage teaches far more than any lab session ever can
Facilitate agreement to test the two or three highest-risk screens with real claimants within days, then build and re-test those thin slices while the rest of the learning continues

questions.explanation: Systems thinking points at the real constraint: a six-week delay combined with large batches means every defect is discovered when it is most expensive to fix. Collaborating with the lab to test smaller slices earlier, against emulated hardware or a rotating subset of rigs, attacks the delay itself, so learning arrives while context is fresh and rework cost collapses. Lengthening the team's iterations to match the lab's six-week cycle institutionalizes the slow loop instead of shrinking it; the feedback would be just as late, merely tidier on the calendar. Appointing a defect coordinator manages the symptom of big late batches without making feedback arrive a day sooner, and adds coordination cost. Reserving a third of every iteration as a standing rework allowance is the most pragmatic-sounding option and would genuinely stabilize forecasts, but planning capacity around the waste makes it permanent — an accommodation of the broken loop rather than a repair.
questions.concept: Systems thinking — batch size, handoff delay, and the decaying value of late feedback
questions.question: In a hybrid program building smart irrigation controllers, an agile firmware team receives defect reports from a downstream hardware-integration lab roughly six weeks after each code drop, delivered in large batches long after the team has moved on to other work. Rework on stale code now consumes a third of the team's capacity. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Lengthen the team's iterations to match the lab's six-week cycle so each code drop and the defects it generates land inside the same iteration and rework becomes planned work
Appoint a defect coordinator to triage each incoming batch and schedule the fixes into upcoming iterations, so rework on stale code becomes planned work rather than an interruption to the team's flow
Work with the lab to test smaller slices of firmware earlier — for example, against emulated hardware or a rotating subset of physical rigs — so defects surface while the work is still fresh
Reserve a third of every iteration's capacity as a standing rework allowance so the arriving batches no longer disrupt committed work and the team's forecasts become dependable again

questions.explanation: The pairing of a falling SPI with a steady completed-scope slope, a faster-rising total-scope line, and flat throughput is the signature of a denominator problem: planned value is still spread over a scope definition that three approved changes have superseded, so earned value can never catch a planned value curve that now describes different work. Naming that cause, keeping the agreed rebaseline cadence, and showing the index next to the burn-up and flow data gives the committee a defensible read without destroying trend comparability. Re-authorizing the baseline this month is the closest rival, since it does make the index arithmetically current, but it resets the very trend that evidences scope growth, breaks month-to-month comparison, and abandons the change-control cadence the program agreed to. Reporting 0.86 unqualified and opening a recovery plan treats a measurement artifact as a performance failure, and CPI 1.03 with stable throughput already argues against an execution breakdown. Asking the finance office to accept the burn-up and throughput in place of earned value discards a reporting obligation unilaterally and reads as avoiding an unflattering number rather than explaining it.
questions.concept: Diagnosing SPI decline caused by a stale scope baseline, and honoring release-boundary rebaselining instead of mid-cycle resets
questions.question: You manage a smart-meter firmware program for a regional utility. The finance office requires monthly earned value reporting against the performance measurement baseline authorized at program start. Since then, three approved change requests have added regulatory scope; the team absorbed the new work into the backlog, and by agreement the baseline is re-authorized only at release boundaries, with the release 3 boundary six weeks away. This month's report shows SPI 0.86 (down from 0.94, then 0.90) and CPI 1.03. The release burn-up shows the completed-scope line climbing at a steady slope while the total-scope line climbs faster, and eight weeks of flow data show stable throughput and flat cycle time. The steering committee asks whether the program is falling behind. What is your most appropriate response?
choices: Re-authorize the performance measurement baseline this month so that planned value covers the three approved regulatory changes, on the grounds that an index computed against superseded scope misleads the finance office more than an off-cycle rebaseline would; then report the corrected schedule index and note the timing exception in the monthly narrative sent to the utility

Report the 0.86 as it stands, since baseline integrity is what makes variance analysis meaningful in the first place, and open a schedule recovery plan that adds temporary capacity and defers lower-priority backlog items until the index climbs back up toward 1.0 well before the release 3 boundary arrives and the baseline is re-authorized

Explain that planned value is still spread over a scope definition the approved changes have superseded, so the declining SPI is measuring scope growth rather than a drop in delivery performance; hold the baseline until the scheduled release 3 rebaseline and, until then, present SPI beside the burn-up's rising total-scope line and the stable throughput

Ask the finance office to accept the burn-up chart and the throughput trend in place of earned value reporting for the remainder of the release, since flow measures describe the team's actual delivery rate month by month, while a schedule index built on fixed firmware scope adds little that the program can actually act on

questions.explanation: Facilitating co-creation of the quarter's goals and success measures is best because people commit to a purpose they helped shape, and a jointly owned goal lets each group make aligned local decisions without ongoing arbitration. Drafting the goals yourself from the roadmap and walking all three groups through them is faster and does produce one consistent statement, but the practitioner is not the value authority for the product, and goals people have explained to them are not goals they own — the joint retrospective already showed the groups disagree about intent. Asking the sponsor to rank onboarding speed above fraud prevention and stability escalates before collaborating and yields imposed priorities each group will quietly reinterpret. Adding an architecture review step treats the symptom with a control gate: it catches conflicts late and expensively, slows flow, and leaves intent unaligned at the moment decisions are made.
questions.concept: Co-created vision and success measures for stakeholder alignment
questions.question: In a hybrid program, two feature teams and an operations group keep making conflicting local decisions: one team is streamlining customer onboarding for speed while another is adding verification friction to cut fraud, and operations is optimizing for stability. A joint retrospective reveals that no one can state what the product is trying to achieve this quarter. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Draft the quarter's product goals yourself from the current roadmap and walk all three groups through them, so everyone works from one consistent statement of intent
Ask the executive sponsor to publish a ranking that puts onboarding speed above fraud prevention and stability, so every group knows which way to decide whenever the three collide
Introduce an architecture review step where a senior reviewer checks each group's decisions against the others, so conflicting choices are caught before customers meet them
Facilitate a working session where the sponsor, product owner, and representatives of all three groups co-create the quarter's goals and agree on how success will be measured

questions.explanation: A widening band on a cumulative flow diagram identifies exactly where the queue is growing; verification is the constraint, and the practitioner's job is to make that visible and let the team diagnose the cause before anything about the system is changed. Raising the WIP limit to six treats the symptom of idle people by pushing more work into a system that already cannot finish what it has, which lengthens lead time and grows the verification queue further. Reducing story size may help eventually but is a guess made before anyone understands why verification is starved or overloaded, and it hands the decision to the product owner rather than the team that owns its own flow. Assigning two developers full time to verification is a directive fix imposed from outside the team; it skips the shared diagnosis that would reveal whether the constraint is capacity, environment availability, or a handoff delay, and it may simply move the bottleneck upstream.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation, bottlenecks, and WIP limits
questions.question: A hybrid team building a warehouse robotics scheduler works in two-week iterations but pulls work through a Kanban board with a WIP limit of four in "In Progress." For three iterations the board has sat at the WIP limit nearly every day, yet throughput has fallen from nine items per iteration to five. The team's cumulative flow diagram shows the "Ready for Verification" band widening steadily while all other bands stay flat. The team lead proposes raising the WIP limit to six so people stop being blocked. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Support raising the work-in-progress limit to six so nobody waits for a free slot while items queue ahead of verification
Point the team to the widening verification band and facilitate a working session on why items accumulate before verification
Ask the product owner to split stories smaller so items clear verification faster and the widening band starts to drain
Move two developers onto verification full time until the band flattens and throughput returns to the earlier nine items an iteration

questions.explanation: The remote members clearly have things to say — the private messages prove it — so the barrier is the format and the perceived risk of speaking, not apathy. Gathering input anonymously and asynchronously, with silent writing and a board open across time zones before the session, lowers the cost of contributing without exposing anyone, which is how a facilitator changes the environment rather than the people. Bringing the privately messaged concerns into the next session unattributed betrays a confidence; once members learn their quiet words get relayed, the last open channel closes. Asking the co-located lead and developers to hold their comments until the remote members have spoken is a reasonable technique that might help at the margins, but it constrains the confident speakers without giving the silent ones a safer way in. Rotating the meeting time helps only if inconvenient hours are the cause, and these members are already contributing candidly outside the session.
questions.concept: Facilitation techniques that create safe participation in distributed retrospectives
questions.question: A facilitator runs retrospectives for a product team split across three time zones. In live sessions only the co-located lead and two on-site developers speak; afterward, remote members privately message the facilitator with candid concerns they never raise in the meeting. What should the facilitator do FIRST?
choices: Bring the privately messaged concerns into the next session unattributed, so the issues remote members raise off-line finally reach the whole team
Ask the co-located lead and the two on-site developers to hold their comments until the remote members have spoken, so airtime is shared evenly
Restructure the retrospective to gather input anonymously and asynchronously, such as silent writing and a board open across time zones before the session
Rotate the retrospective time zone by zone each iteration, so the meeting stops landing at the end of the remote members' working day

questions.explanation: She has explicitly asked the practitioner to draw on a career transition the practitioner personally made, and support built on sharing lived experience and judgment inside an ongoing relationship is precisely what distinguishes mentoring. Asking open questions while deliberately withholding personal opinion describes coaching; it is powerful when someone must surface their own answer, but here it withholds the very experience she asked for. Structured instruction to close an identified skill gap describes training, and she has named no skill gap — she says she knows her framework inside out and is wrestling with direction, not competence. Designing and running a group process so participants own the outcome describes facilitation, which does not fit a one-on-one question about one person's career path.
questions.concept: Coaching vs mentoring vs training vs facilitation distinctions
questions.question: In a one-on-one, a test engineer tells the agile practitioner: "I know our automation framework inside out. What I can't figure out is whether to stay on the quality-engineering path or move toward product management — you made a switch like that once; how did you think it through?" Which form of developmental support is she requesting?
choices: Mentoring — a more experienced person shares personal experience and judgment about a path they have traveled, within an ongoing relationship
Coaching — a practitioner asks open questions and deliberately withholds personal opinion so the person reaches a conclusion that is entirely her own
Training — structured instruction delivered against a defined curriculum to close a specific, identified gap in skill or knowledge
Facilitation — a neutral party designs and runs a group process so the participants themselves own the discussion and its outcome

questions.explanation: The visible symptoms — divergent purpose statements, churning priorities, conflicting feedback — all trace to the absence of a shared vision, and a vision people help create is one they actually align behind; a facilitated workshop that produces a common product goal and success measures gives the product owner a stable basis for ordering the backlog and gives reviews a focus. Asking the sponsor to publish a vision produces a directive statement nobody internalized, so behavior is unlikely to change. Freezing backlog priorities imposes stability by rule while leaving the underlying disagreement about purpose untouched — and it blocks legitimate reprioritization based on learning. Reposting the original charter re-communicates a document that predates the team's learning and was never a shared understanding, which is precisely the problem.
questions.concept: shared vision and chartering
questions.question: Three sprints into a new product, each developer on a Scrum team describes the product's purpose differently, and the product owner reprioritizes the backlog after every stakeholder meeting. Sprint reviews feel unfocused, and stakeholders give conflicting feedback. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the sponsor to write and publish an authoritative product vision statement so every developer and stakeholder works from one description of purpose
Facilitate a product visioning workshop where the product owner, the team, and key stakeholders co-create the product goal and its success measures
Recommend the product owner freeze backlog priorities for the next three sprints, giving the team the stability it needs to deliver a coherent increment
Post the original project charter in the team space and walk through it at the start of every sprint planning so the purpose stays in view

questions.explanation: Frequent increment reviews with real users shrink the gap between doing the work and learning whether it is right, which is exactly what the quarterly gate failed to do; issues found within weeks are cheap to fix. Extending upfront requirements and prototyping sign-off is big-bang analysis that assumes usability can be fully predicted before build, which this program has already disproved. Adding a second QA team inspects quality in at the end rather than learning earlier, and internal testers cannot substitute for real user feedback on usability. Locking requirements with sign-off so changes become chargeable protects the contract, not the customer, and pushes discovery of problems even later.
questions.concept: Frequent customer validation versus stage-gate batch feedback
questions.question: In a hybrid program, an agile build team hands completed functionality to the business for validation only at quarterly stage-gate reviews. At the most recent gate, users uncovered major usability problems in work finished two months earlier, forcing expensive rework. The sponsor asks the agile practitioner how to prevent this from happening again. What is the BEST response?
choices: Extend discovery so interactive prototypes are usability-tested and signed off before build starts, removing surprises from the quarterly gate
Fund a second quality assurance team to test each build against the specification more thoroughly, so problems are caught well before the gate
Have users formally sign off the requirements up front so usability findings raised at the gate are handled as funded change requests rather than rework
Arrange short, frequent increment reviews with real users throughout the quarter so usability issues surface within weeks of the work being done

questions.explanation: The joint facilitated session is best: every option here is technically possible, but only this one treats the conflict as a signal of a system problem — unclear ownership and unmet needs on both sides — and produces a solution both teams shape and will sustain. Accepting the director's ruling on ownership ends the ambiguity fastest, but an imposed answer disempowers both teams and teaches everyone that escalation beats collaboration. Having each team bring its proposed fix to a joint review is the closest alternative to collaboration and does get both positions on the table, yet the practitioner selecting the stronger option is forcing dressed as facilitation: one team leaves defeated and neither side's underlying need is examined. Provisioning a separate sandbox pipeline removes the friction point yet doubles maintenance, forfeits shared standards, and dodges the collaboration problem entirely.
questions.concept: Collaborative problem solving and root-cause analysis in inter-team conflict
questions.question: At a streaming-media company, a platform team and a feature team share a build pipeline. The platform team keeps hardening it with restrictions; the feature team keeps working around them. Members now snipe at each other in public chat channels, and both teams have separately complained to the agile practitioner, each proposing its own fix. The engineering director has offered to 'just decide ownership' if asked. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Accept the director's offer so that pipeline ownership sits with one team, since a single accountable owner ends the ambiguity that both groups keep working around
Ask each team to bring its proposed fix to a joint review and select the stronger option as the practitioner, so a decision lands before the public sniping does further damage
Provision a separate sandbox pipeline for the feature team so it can bypass the hardening safely, which removes the daily friction that is driving the exchanges in the chat channels
Facilitate a joint session where both teams articulate their underlying needs, examine why the workarounds keep happening, and co-create a working agreement for the shared pipeline

questions.explanation: Three days of work inside 26 days of elapsed time is about 12 percent flow efficiency: even eliminating every minute of coding effort would cut lead time by less than a fifth, while the wait states hold the other 23 days. Bringing the map to leadership and to the people who own those queues makes that visible and reframes the request as a system problem the team cannot solve alone, and proposing bounded experiments keeps the conversation improvement-oriented. Moving the approval board to twice weekly is the closest alternative and a genuine gain, but it writes off the shared environment and the security questionnaire as unchallengeable without ever asking their owners, and reporting a shorter approval wait as developer productivity misdescribes what changed. Per-developer throughput dashboards optimize the smallest component of delay while inviting local gaming. Pair programming is sound practice aimed at the three days of touch time, not at the waiting.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency and value-stream mapping to locate the real constraint
questions.question: A value-stream mapping workshop for a payments team shows an average of 26 days from request to production, of which roughly 3 days is hands-on work. The remainder is spent waiting for a shared test environment, for a security questionnaire to be returned, and for a weekly change-approval board. Leadership's reaction to the map is to ask the team to "raise developer productivity by 20 percent." What is the BEST response?
choices: Ask the change-approval board to convene twice a week instead of weekly, treating the shared environment and the security questionnaire as fixed constraints the payments team has no standing to renegotiate, and report the shortened approval wait to leadership as the productivity gain they asked for.

Introduce per-developer throughput dashboards so leadership can see who contributes what and slower contributors can be coached toward the twenty percent target, since the request was framed around developer productivity and that data is already collected in the tracking tool the team uses daily.

Take the map back to leadership together with the queue owners, show that roughly 12 percent flow efficiency means the dominant delay is waiting rather than working, and propose targeted experiments such as on-demand test environments and folding the security review into the work as it is built.

Adopt pair programming across the team so each item spends less time being coded and the three days of hands-on work shrink further, showing leadership that the team answered the productivity request with a concrete engineering practice rather than a debate about the map.

questions.explanation: A roadmap is a forecast, not a contract, and a confirmed regulatory date is a hard constraint that changes the value calculus for everything queued behind it. Surfacing it in a transparent re-sequencing conversation lets the product owner and stakeholders — the people accountable for value — make an informed trade-off with full information. Folding the disclosure into the proposal-comparison work as a technical task buries a scope change inside an existing item: the capacity it consumes is real but invisible, stakeholders never see the trade-off they are making, and a legal obligation becomes dependent on an unrelated feature's fate. Releasing the comparison capability a month early protects both commitments on paper while assuming the same scope fits in less time, converting a prioritization problem into schedule pressure. Confirming with compliance which quotes the disclosure covers is the strongest alternative and genuinely useful, but it is detail the re-sequencing conversation can gather, and continuing the committed work meanwhile burns the quarter before anything is decided.
questions.concept: Compliance-driven prioritization and roadmap re-sequencing
questions.question: A cross-functional team building a solar-installation quoting tool plans releases quarterly. Midway through the quarter, a new energy-efficiency regulation is confirmed that requires disclosure language on every generated quote by a date one month before the planned release. The team's roadmap for the quarter is fully allocated to a customer-requested proposal-comparison capability. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Bring the regulatory constraint into a roadmap and backlog conversation with the product owner and stakeholders to re-sequence work against the new date
Have the team fold the disclosure language into the current proposal-comparison work as a technical task, so the committed roadmap is met without renegotiation
Ask the product owner to release the proposal-comparison capability a month early, so the committed work and the disclosure both land before the regulatory date
Confirm with the compliance group which generated quotes the disclosure applies to before anything changes, continuing the committed work meanwhile

questions.explanation: Running a blameless post-incident review is best because it treats the failure as a property of the system (test coverage, merge practices, pipeline checks) rather than of a person, produces concrete improvements, and gives the director something more valuable than a name: evidence the team is learning. It also protects psychological safety — engineers who fear being reported to HR stop surfacing mistakes early, which makes the next incident worse. Handing over the engineer's name, even with a plea for leniency, converts an honest error into a punishable offense and teaches the whole team to hide problems. Adding a mandatory senior approval gate prescribes process before understanding the cause, slows flow, and signals distrust of the team. Deferring the discussion to a quarterly review delays feedback until context is lost and leaves the director's blame-seeking request unaddressed in the meantime.
questions.concept: Blameless post-incident review
questions.question: A firmware team at a warehouse-robotics company practices Extreme Programming with continuous integration. A mis-merged change halts the client's pick line for two hours. The operations director asks the agile practitioner to name the engineer responsible so HR can "document the error." What is the BEST response?
choices: Give the operations director the engineer's name privately and ask that any documented consequence stay proportionate to one mis-merged change
Offer the director a written timeline of the two-hour stoppage and the fix, and work the underlying causes quietly into the next quarterly review
Propose a blameless post-incident review that examines how the pipeline let the fault through, then share the improvement actions with the director
Propose a mandatory senior-engineer approval on every merge, so no change can reach the pipeline without a second engineer looking at the merge itself

questions.explanation: The delivery record is being financed by unpaid debt — overtime, attrition, and eroding automation — and none of that appears in the on-time metric leadership is celebrating. Making the true cost visible and reforecasting from demonstrated sustainable capacity is the agile response: it gives leadership real information for a real decision and treats scope or date, rather than the people, as the adjustable variable. Adding a manual regression sign-off accepts the accelerated date and layers more manual effort onto the exact activity already consuming the team, deepening the problem while creating an illusion of control. Cutting the velocity target unilaterally acts on the team's behalf without either the team's or leadership's involvement, hides the reasoning, and adjusts a symptom number rather than the commitment that produced it. Bringing in contract testers scales the manual regression that automation should be replacing, adds onboarding load onto exhausted engineers, and leaves both the quality-built-in gap and the unsustainable pace intact.
questions.concept: Using trend data to expose unsustainable pace and reforecast from demonstrated capacity
questions.question: A team supporting a hospital scheduling product has hit its release date four quarters running, but the last two releases each required three consecutive weekends of work, two senior engineers have resigned citing exhaustion, and the automated test suite has not been extended in five months while manual regression checking has grown. Leadership, pleased with the delivery record, has just committed the team to an accelerated date for the next release. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Support the accelerated date and protect quality with a manual regression checklist signed off before release, so the growing gap in automated coverage is at least covered by a documented manual pass

Show leadership the trend data — weekend work, attrition, growing manual regression, stalled test automation — and facilitate a conversation that reforecasts scope or date based on the team's demonstrated sustainable capacity
Reduce the team's velocity target on its behalf so the new commitment lands where the remaining engineers can sustain it, and hand leadership the revised number as the plan for the accelerated date
Bring in contract testers to absorb the manual regression load so the accelerated date is met without further weekend work, and revisit the stalled test automation after that release has shipped

questions.explanation: Little's Law relates work in progress, throughput, and cycle time only for a roughly stable system. Here arrivals exceed departures, work in progress has nearly tripled, and cycle time is climbing, so any number derived from this history will be optimistic and will keep drifting. Showing the sponsor the arrival-versus-departure gap turns a demand for a date into a shared problem, and capping work in progress so the team finishes before it starts is the fastest route to both a shorter cycle time and a forecast worth quoting. Dividing 40 by 5 applies the law precisely where its assumptions are violated and converts a deteriorating trend into a commitment the team will miss. Switching to points does not help, because velocity is measured over the same unstable flow and re-estimating changes nothing about how much is started; it merely repackages the problem in units the sponsor cannot inspect. Extra hours buy a brief spike at the cost of sustainable pace and defect rates, and the unchanged inflow refills the queue as soon as the overtime ends.
questions.concept: Practical Little's Law, system stability, and throughput-based forecasting
questions.question: A Kanban-based data platform team is asked when the 40 remaining migration items will be finished. Over the last eight weeks the team has completed an average of 5 items per week, but its cumulative flow diagram shows items entering the board at about 8 per week; work in progress has grown from 14 to 39 items, and average cycle time has stretched from 2.6 weeks to 7.1 weeks. A sponsor presses for a date in the meeting. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Show the team and the sponsor the widening gap between arrivals and completions, agree to cap work in progress and finish what is already started, and then offer a throughput-based forecast range.
Divide the 40 remaining items by the eight-week average of 5 completions per week and commit to a date eight weeks out, since that average already reflects how the team has been performing.
Re-estimate the 40 items in story points and forecast from velocity instead, since points describe the size of the work rather than a count and are less sensitive to work in progress.
Ask the team to work extra hours until work in progress is back near 14 items, then give the sponsor a date once average cycle time returns to roughly 2.6 weeks.

questions.explanation: One metric praised in isolation has become a target, and the balancing measures show exactly what it is costing: escaped defects up more than fivefold and 85th-percentile cycle time more than doubled. Presenting the three trends side by side restores transparency, moves the conversation from protecting a number to asking what the number is costing, and leaves the choice of improvement with the team that owns the work. Showing those trends but asking that velocity be dropped from town-hall reporting is the strongest rival and its diagnosis is right, yet removing a number leadership already watches looks evasive and forfeits the contrast that makes the argument land. Holding accepted work at the earlier level and pulling in rework items treats a symptom, invites point inflation, and is a prescription the team did not choose. Running a retrospective on the defect rise alone repeats the single-metric error in a new place, and a peer-review step added to the definition of done inspects quality in rather than building it in.
questions.concept: Balanced metric sets and the distortion caused by treating a measure as a target
questions.question: Across five iterations a mobile banking team's velocity has risen from 32 to 51 points. Over the same five iterations, defects reported by customers after release rose from 2 to 11 per iteration, and the 85th-percentile cycle time grew from 6 days to 14 days. At a town hall the delivery manager praises the velocity trend and asks the team to "protect that number." What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Show the delivery manager the cycle-time and escaped-defect trends and ask that velocity be dropped from town-hall reporting, so the number the team is now being asked to protect stops shaping how it works.
Have the team hold its accepted work at the earlier level and pull explicit rework items into the backlog, so the growing defect and cycle-time trends have somewhere visible to be worked down.

Bring velocity, escaped defects and cycle time into a single view for the next review and retrospective, so the team and the delivery manager can see the trade-off and choose an improvement experiment together.

Run a retrospective on the defect rise alone and extend the definition of done with a peer-review step before a story is counted, since undetected quality gaps are what customers actually feel after each release.

questions.explanation: On a cumulative flow diagram, the vertical width of a band is the work in progress in that state and the slope of the done band is throughput. A steady done slope with a widening in-progress band therefore means throughput is roughly constant while WIP climbs; by Little's Law — average cycle time equals WIP divided by throughput — a rising numerator over a flat denominator drives average cycle time up, which is exactly the quiet degradation the steady completion line conceals. Reading rising throughput from the widening band looks in the wrong place: a band widens when items enter faster than they leave, which counts started work, not finished work. Concluding that arrivals have slowed confuses a constant-width ready band with reduced demand; equal entry and exit rates there are consistent with unchanged arrivals. The claim that cycle time is unchanged is the strongest wrong answer because its premise is right — throughput really is constant — but a ratio does not hold still when its WIP term climbs.
questions.concept: Reading cumulative flow diagrams through Little's Law
questions.question: A support-portal team's cumulative flow diagram for the past two months shows the "Done" band rising at a steady slope, the "In Progress" band widening progressively from left to right, and the "Ready" band roughly constant in width. Applying Little's Law to what this picture shows, which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Throughput is rising, because a widening in-progress band shows the team pulling more work than it did in the first week
WIP is growing while throughput holds steady, so average cycle time is increasing even though delivery looks healthy
Arrivals have slowed, because the ready band holds a constant width while items keep moving out of it into progress
Cycle time is unchanged, because the steady slope of the done band shows constant throughput, which fixes time per item

questions.explanation: Structured facilitation changes the dynamic immediately: silent writing lets every idea exist before anyone can dismiss it, round-robin guarantees airtime, and working agreements the team writes itself make respectful listening a shared norm rather than the facilitator's rule. Urging quiet members to push back harder asks the people with the least safety to absorb the most risk, without changing the conditions that silence them. Going to the lead's manager escalates before any direct, collaborative attempt to change the pattern and can convert a facilitation problem into a political one. Pausing retrospectives removes the team's primary inspect-and-adapt loop precisely when it is needed most — trust is built by practicing safe interaction, not by waiting for it to appear socially.
questions.concept: Retrospective facilitation techniques and working agreements
questions.question: A practitioner newly assigned to a data-platform team reviews its last four retrospectives and finds that the technical lead produced nearly every improvement item while others stayed silent. An anonymous survey reveals members hold back because their ideas 'get dismissed in the first thirty seconds.' What should the practitioner do next?
choices: Meet privately with each of the quieter members and encourage them to push back on the technical lead's first reaction, so that their ideas survive the opening minute
Facilitate the next retrospective using silent writing and round-robin sharing, then co-create working agreements on how ideas get heard before being judged
Ask the technical lead's manager to coach him on how quickly he dismisses ideas, so the behavior is corrected by the person who writes his performance review
Pause retrospectives for a few iterations and run informal team-building sessions instead, so trust recovers before the group tries to improve anything

questions.explanation: Bringing the flow data to the team and encouraging pairing and mobbing is best because it grows generalizing specialists: teammates gain enough 3-D skill to handle routine work, the bottleneck dissolves from inside the team, and the team owns the solution to a problem its own data revealed. Requesting a new hire escalates for external resources before the team has tried to solve the constraint itself, takes months, and merely widens the silo from one person to two. A prioritized intake queue with service targets adds process that manages the queue rather than shrinking it — the wait itself remains. Scheduling everything around the specialist's estimated availability is predictive planning around the constraint; it institutionalizes the bottleneck and adds up-front estimation overhead instead of improving flow.
questions.concept: Generalizing specialists
questions.question: A museum's digital-exhibits team uses Kanban with lead-time tracking. Flow data shows nearly every card spends most of its life queued for the team's only 3-D graphics specialist, whose column drives the bulk of overall lead time. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Facilitate a team review of the flow data and encourage pairing and mobbing with the specialist so the 3-D capability spreads across the team
Ask for a second 3-D graphics specialist to be hired into the team, doubling capacity at the step that drives most of the current lead time
Give the specialist a prioritized intake queue with agreed service-level targets, so the highest-value cards clear his column before the others
Batch the 3-D work into a dedicated iteration and schedule every other card around the specialist's availability so the queueing stops

questions.explanation: Material new knowledge arriving late is exactly what agile teams treat as an asset rather than a threat: put the evidence in front of the customer and product leadership, quantify the impact, and reshape the remaining two weeks together — descope, correct partially, or move the date — so the trade-off is made by the people who bear its consequences. Shipping the contracted workflow with a fast-follow release is the strongest alternative, since a few weeks is a short wait and the commitment holds, but it knowingly hands front-desk staff a workflow that does not match how they work, and it makes that call without the customer in the room. Rebuilding the sequence inside two weeks by deferring automation and hardening decides the trade-off unilaterally and pays for it in quality on a near-complete release. Running wider usability sessions before raising anything spends scarce runway confirming a finding the customer could be weighing now.
questions.concept: Harnessing late change for the customer's advantage
questions.question: Two weeks before the contracted delivery of a booking integration for a hotel chain, a hybrid program team's usability probe reveals that front-desk staff process group reservations in a fundamentally different sequence than the near-complete workflow assumes. Correcting it would invalidate a significant slice of the release. The sponsor is pressing to ship on schedule, the architect proposes shipping now and reworking the flow next quarter, and a business analyst wants a full impact analysis of every requirement before anything is decided. What is the agile practitioner's BEST response?
choices: Ship the contracted workflow on schedule and open a fast-follow release for the corrected sequence, so the commitment holds and front-desk staff still get the fix within a few weeks

Have the team rebuild the group-reservation sequence inside the remaining two weeks by deferring the automation and hardening work, so that the release still ships on the contracted date and behaves correctly
Run a wider round of usability sessions with more front-desk staff across several properties before raising anything, so that the customer is not alarmed by a conclusion drawn from one small probe

Present the usability findings transparently to the customer and product leadership, quantify the impact, and collaboratively reshape the remaining two weeks of scope around the highest-value response

questions.explanation: Five days a week of capacity is going into reformatting information that already exists, which is classic over-processing, but the cure has to preserve the visibility leadership legitimately needs. Tracing each report section to a real decision separates what matters from what is habit, and serving that need from the teams' own live data removes the transcription entirely while increasing, not reducing, transparency. Timeboxing preparation to two hours keeps the same waste at a smaller size and degrades the reporting for whichever decisions genuinely depend on it.
