Moving compilation to a program analyst relocates the waste rather than eliminating it and inserts another transcription layer between the data and its consumers. Asking the sponsor to cancel reporting goes over the PMO's head before anyone understands what the reports are for, trading a collaboration problem for a political one and risking the removal of something leadership actually relies on.
questions.concept: Over-processing waste in reporting; information radiators at the source
questions.question: In a hybrid program, each of five feature teams produces a weekly six-page status deck plus a separately formatted metrics workbook for the PMO. The teams estimate this consumes roughly a day of capacity per team per week. The PMO's stated reason is that "leadership needs visibility," and the delivery numbers being retyped into the workbook already exist on each team's board. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask each team to timebox report preparation to two hours a week and submit whatever detail fits in that window, so the reporting cost is capped without renegotiating anything.
Have a program analyst assemble all five decks and the metrics workbook centrally, so that the five teams recover their capacity while leadership keeps exactly the reporting format it expects.
Ask the sponsor to cancel the weekly deck and workbook outright as non-value-adding work, so that all five of the teams get back a full day of delivery capacity each and every week.
Work with the PMO to identify which decisions the reports actually inform, serve those decisions from live flow metrics on the teams' own boards, and retire whatever no decision depends on.

questions.explanation: Refinement should produce small, independently valuable, testable slices, and progressive elaboration means only near-term work needs detail. Slicing vertically so turbine-access logging is auditable end to end lets the team meet the regulatory date early, get real feedback from auditors, and defer detail on log types that may still change. A timeboxed spike is the strongest alternative, since the directive is new, but its stated purpose here is to size all eight iterations of work before committing — precisely the up-front detail progressive elaboration exists to avoid, and the ten-week clock runs while nothing auditable ships. Splitting by schema, services and interface produces pieces that deliver nothing usable until the last one lands, hides integration risk to the end, and cannot satisfy the directive on its own. Handing decomposition to an architect working alone produces a specification instead of shared understanding and wastes the design and estimating knowledge of the people who will build it.
questions.concept: Vertical slicing of a large regulatory backlog item
questions.question: An offshore wind maintenance-planning product carries a backlog item for "regulatory inspection logging" that the team sizes at roughly eight iterations of work. A new safety directive requires only turbine-access logs to be auditable within ten weeks; the remaining log types have no fixed date. The team says the item is too big to pull, and refinement has stalled on it for two sessions. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Keep the item whole and pull a timeboxed spike into the next iteration, so the team can learn enough about the new safety directive to size all eight iterations of logging work before committing

Split it along technical layers, building the database schema first, then the services, then the interface, so every specialist can start at once and the three parts integrate once each layer is finished
Ask the solution architect to decompose the item offline into a fully specified task list covering every log type, then have the team pull those tasks once the breakdown has been reviewed
Work with the product owner and team to split it into vertical slices that each deliver usable logging end to end, sequencing the turbine-access slice first and leaving the later log types coarse.

questions.explanation: Providing more directive support now and progressively releasing control is best because leadership style must match team maturity: a newly formed team lacks the shared norms and mutual trust that make full autonomy workable, and it is explicitly asking for structure. Empowerment is grown in stages, not declared on day one. Holding the hands-off stance confuses self-organization with abandonment — self-organization emerges within clear boundaries and support, and withholding both is a recognized servant-leadership anti-pattern. Asking management to insert a team lead outsources the practitioner's own responsibility and adds a hierarchy layer the team will later have to unwind. Producing a detailed process manual substitutes heavyweight documentation for the lightweight, evolving working agreements a young team actually needs, and freezes practices before the team has learned what works.
questions.concept: Situational leadership and team maturity stages
questions.question: An agile practitioner who previously served a long-standing, highly autonomous team is assigned to a team formed three weeks ago from members of four dissolved projects. Applying the same hands-off style that worked before, the practitioner lets the team define its own working agreements, estimation approach, and priorities. The team misses its first two commitments, arguments about basics keep recurring, and two members privately ask for "someone to just tell us how this is supposed to work." What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Provide more structure and direction now — clear boundaries, concrete starting practices, frequent check-ins — and deliberately hand decisions back to the team as its capability grows
Hold the hands-off stance and let the team work through its own storming, since stepping in with direction now would undercut the self-organization that this team has to develop for itself
Ask management to add an experienced team lead who can supply the direction the team is asking for, leaving the practitioner free to stay in a purely facilitative role
Have the team write a detailed process manual covering estimation, priorities, and working agreements, so the same basics stop being argued about at the start of every iteration

questions.explanation: Silence spreading through the team is a system problem in how the team treats dissent, so the first move is to make the norm explicit and team-owned: facilitating a working agreement on how challenges are raised and received addresses the root cause, keeps the resolution inside the team, and rebuilds the expectation that every voice is welcome. Coaching the analyst to bring claims data next time puts the burden on the person with the least power and implies her challenge failed for want of evidence, when it was actually waved away by appeal to tradition. Asking the engineer to document the rationale behind the routing rule is genuinely useful, since unexamined habit becomes an explicit claim others can test, but it addresses one rule rather than the norm. Round-robin input in replenishment is the closest call and would help immediately, though it is a facilitator's device for one meeting rather than an agreement the team maintains.
questions.concept: Working agreements as a repair mechanism for eroded psychological safety
questions.question: During a replenishment meeting, a junior business analyst on a Kanban team at an insurance firm questions a senior engineer's approach to a claims-routing rule. The engineer replies, "That is how we have always routed claims," and moves on. Over the next two replenishment meetings the analyst says nothing, and two other junior members have also gone quiet. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Facilitate a team conversation to create a working agreement on how the team invites and responds to challenges and dissenting views
Coach the junior analyst to bring claims data with her next time so a challenge to a routing rule is harder to wave away
Ask the senior engineer to write up the rationale behind the current claims-routing rule so that future challenges start from a shared basis
Use round-robin input in replenishment so every member is asked in turn and quieter voices are heard without having to interrupt

questions.explanation: New information has invalidated the plan: a service that fails for forty percent of applicants is not delivered value, so the right move is to make the evidence and its cost transparent and re-plan collaboratively, protecting the legally mandated items while trading discretionary ones. Deferring the fix to a later release satisfies a Definition of Done that plainly does not cover the real customer context and knowingly ships an unusable service to a large share of residents. Reducing testing depth hides the cost as quality debt in a public service carrying legal obligations and quietly lowers the standard the team agreed to. A workaround that pushes residents to in-person application preserves the announced list while abandoning the outcome the service exists to produce, and it burdens exactly the population already disadvantaged.
questions.concept: Adapting release scope to customer feedback under fixed-date and compliance constraints
questions.question: A team is four iterations into a nine-iteration release for a municipal permit-application service. At the review, a resident-advocacy participant demonstrates that the document-upload step fails for the roughly forty percent of applicants using older phones, making the whole service unusable for them. Fixing it well would consume the equivalent of two iterations. The department's release date is fixed by a council commitment, the current increments meet the Definition of Done, three remaining backlog items are legally mandated, and the sponsor has already announced the feature list publicly. What is the BEST response?
choices: Add the upload fix to the next release, since the current increments meet the Definition of Done and the announced list is committed
Ask the team to absorb the fix by reducing testing depth on items not legally mandated, keeping the announced scope intact
Bring the evidence and the two-iteration cost to the sponsor and product owner, and facilitate a re-plan of the remaining release scope
Have the team spend the next iteration building a workaround page telling affected residents to apply in person, preserving the announced scope

questions.explanation: Training transfers a defined body of knowledge or procedure, so it fits the analyst who must perform a regulated process exactly as specified. Mentoring is guidance from someone who has already walked the path the learner wants to walk, so it fits the developer seeking a staff engineer's lived experience. Coaching draws out the learner's own thinking through questions rather than supplying answers, so it fits the product owner who partly sees her own solution already. The combination that pairs coaching with the developer and mentoring with the product owner reverses those two needs — the developer explicitly asked for someone else's lived experience, not questions, and the product owner needs her own reasoning unlocked, not a career story. The two combinations that hand the analyst mentoring or coaching fail for the same reason: a fixed regulated procedure leaves nothing to discover or adapt — it must simply be learned accurately, which is training's job.
questions.concept: Coaching versus mentoring versus training distinctions
questions.question: An agile practitioner is planning how to support three colleagues: a compliance analyst who must execute a regulated evidence-collection procedure exactly as specified, a developer who wants guidance from someone who has already grown into the staff-engineer role he aspires to, and a product owner who wants help thinking through a prioritization dilemma she already partly understands. Which combination of development approaches correctly matches each need?
choices: Training for the analyst; coaching for the developer; mentoring for the product owner
Training for the analyst; mentoring for the developer; coaching for the product owner
Mentoring for the analyst; training for the developer; coaching for the product owner
Coaching for the analyst; mentoring for the developer; training for the product owner

questions.explanation: A flat risk burndown over four iterations is the signal that risk-reduction work is being crowded out; making that transparent to the people who set priority — team and product owner together — lets them weigh a cheap spike now against a very expensive discovery later, which is a value decision they own. Asking the architecture group to benchmark the vendor separately is the strongest rival, since it buys the measurement without spending team capacity, but it moves the learning away from the team that will build the integration, adds a handoff and a wait, and leaves the prioritization pattern untouched. A contractual warranty transfers liability rather than latency: the platform still misses 200ms at production volume and the team still rebuilds. Attaching a latency acceptance criterion to the intake stories sounds disciplined but tests the wrong work, since intake does not exercise the fraud-scoring vendor, and it defers verification to the integration work that keeps losing priority.
questions.concept: Risk burndown and risk-adjusted backlog prioritization
questions.question: An insurance claims platform team has kept a risk-adjusted backlog for two quarters. At the last review, the top item was "third-party fraud-scoring vendor may not meet 200ms latency at production volume," scored at high probability and high impact. The team has since delivered four iterations of claims-intake features and the risk burndown chart has been flat across all four. In today's iteration planning the team again ranks intake features above the vendor spike, because intake is what the sponsor asks about weekly. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Ask the architecture group to benchmark the vendor separately, so intake delivery keeps its current pace while the latency risk is investigated
Have the vendor warrant the 200ms latency in a contract amendment, so the exposure sits with them and intake delivery continues
Show the team and product owner the flat risk burndown alongside the vendor risk score, and facilitate a decision on scheduling the spike now
Add a latency acceptance criterion to the intake stories, so the 200ms target gets verified naturally when the integration work finally arrives

questions.explanation: The retrospective has become theatre because nothing changes as a result of it; converting one recurring theme into a small, owned experiment that is carried in the iteration's work restores the inspect-and-adapt loop and makes improvement visible. Varying the format also re-engages the team and surfaces issues the fixed two-question script never reaches. Swapping in a timeline exercise is the strongest rival, since it would genuinely surface richer detail than the went-well round, but it preserves the log-and-file habit that is the real failure — better material still lands in a document nobody acts on. Making attendance optional and cutting the session to fifteen minutes shrinks a meeting that already produces nothing, and self-selection loses exactly the people whose issues keep recurring. Handing facilitation to the senior developer may lift energy briefly, but he is the one calling it a ritual, and a new facilitator over an unchanged follow-through habit yields the same filed list.
questions.concept: Retrospective effectiveness and improvement experiments
questions.question: A claims-processing team has held the same retrospective format for eleven iterations: each person names one thing that went well and one that went poorly, the practitioner logs them, and the list is filed. Attendance is drifting, and one senior developer says the sessions are "a ritual we perform." Reviewing the logs, the practitioner notices the same three items appear repeatedly and none has an owner or a follow-up. What is the BEST response?
choices: Rotate the retrospective format and have the team select one recurring item to turn into a concrete improvement experiment with an owner, tracked in the next iteration's work
Replace the went-well and went-poorly rounds with a timeline exercise so the team surfaces far richer detail about each iteration, and keep logging whatever the session produces
Make attendance optional and cut the session to fifteen minutes, so only the people who have something substantive to raise spend their time in the retrospective
Ask the senior developer to facilitate the next few sessions, since a respected voice leading the discussion will restore the team's confidence in the practice

questions.explanation: Running a cheap concierge-style experiment with defined success criteria attacks the riskiest assumption, paying demand, with the least investment, which is the essence of Lean Startup and minimum viable product thinking: buy validated learning before buying features. Funding a shorter first phase to build the diagnostics engine is the strongest alternative and is real risk reduction, but it still constructs the product before testing whether anyone pays, and a demonstration collects reactions rather than purchase decisions. Interviewing gym owners about subscribing at the planned price is fast and cheap, yet stated willingness to pay routinely overstates real buying, so it firms up the business case with the same kind of evidence that made it persuasive. Proceeding with monthly benefits reviews checks against sales results that cannot exist for nine months.
questions.concept: Lean Startup / MVP and validated learning
questions.question: A product team at a fitness-equipment manufacturer believes gym owners will pay for a remote diagnostics subscription. The sponsor is ready to fund nine months of development on the strength of a persuasive internal business case. The agile practitioner notices that the core demand assumption — that owners will actually pay — has never been tested with a real customer. What is the BEST response?
choices: Ask the sponsor to fund a shorter first phase that builds the diagnostics engine, then confirm willingness to pay once the subscription can be demonstrated to a group of gym owners in working form

Have the product owner interview a representative sample of gym owners about whether they would subscribe at the planned price, and use their stated intentions to firm up the business case before the build is funded
Recommend proceeding on the approved business case while adding a monthly benefits review, so the demand assumption is checked against sales results as the nine months of development progress

Propose a time-boxed experiment — such as a manually delivered "concierge" diagnostics service for a handful of gyms — with explicit success criteria to test willingness to pay before scaling the investment

questions.explanation: A work-in-progress limit on the constrained column, paired with an agreed response when the limit is hit, is the direct lever on the queue that is inflating cycle time, and it prompts the team to swarm on verification rather than start more work. Making card aging visible turns the board back into a radiator that shows where flow is degrading, so stalling items get discussed rather than silently aging. Adding a Blocked column to relocate stalled cards makes the queue look shorter while the same work sits idle, reducing rather than increasing transparency. Pulling more cards into Build feeds the bottleneck and will lengthen cycle time further. Replacing the board with a status email removes the shared visual signal entirely and substitutes a push report for a pull-based flow tool.
questions.concept: WIP limits and card aging to diagnose flow bottlenecks
questions.question: A team maintaining a warehouse inventory system uses a kanban board with columns for Ready, Build, Verify, and Deployed. Over the last month, cards have piled up in Verify while Build stays busy, cycle time has roughly doubled, and stakeholders have begun asking for status updates by email because the board no longer tells them when anything will be delivered. The practitioner wants to restore the board's usefulness as an information radiator and improve flow. Which TWO actions best serve those goals? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Set an explicit work-in-progress limit on the Verify column and make the team's response to hitting that limit an agreed working agreement
Add a Blocked column so that stalled cards are removed from Verify and the queue appears shorter
Make aging visible on the board — for example, marking each card with days in its current column — so the team can see and discuss the items that are stalling
Increase the number of cards pulled into Build each week so that throughput into Verify keeps rising
Replace the board with a weekly status email to stakeholders summarizing what is in progress and what shipped

questions.explanation: An information radiator pushes current, truthful information into the environment passively and continuously — its value lies in being ambient, honest, and available to everyone without a request or a meeting. Using it to track individual productivity converts a transparency tool into surveillance, which distorts the data people are willing to display and damages safety. Archiving history for auditors describes a record-keeping system; a radiator is deliberately about the present state, not reconstruction of the past. Delivering status in scheduled formal meetings is periodic, gated communication — precisely the pattern radiators exist to replace with always-on visibility.
questions.concept: Information radiators
questions.question: Which statement BEST captures the purpose of an information radiator in an agile workspace?
choices: It continuously displays the team's current, honest state of work — problems included — so anyone passing by can understand progress without having to ask
It gives leaders a continuously updated view of each member's completed work so individual contribution can be compared fairly in performance conversations
It preserves a full history of the team's delivery metrics so later audits and estimates can be grounded in what the team actually experienced
It presents a polished summary of progress at scheduled reviews so every stakeholder group hears a consistent message about where the program stands

questions.explanation: Agile teams welcome changing requirements, even late in development, because responding to a real shift in the environment delivers more value than conformance to an outdated plan — and a regulatory change is the clearest possible case. Collaborating with the sponsor and product leadership to re-order the backlog addresses both the sponsor's credibility concern, by making the reasoning transparent, and the customer's actual need. Continuing to deliver the locked roadmap spends capacity on a partially obsolete capability while an urgent compliance gap widens. Submitting the requirement to the change control board is the strongest alternative, since documented authorization has genuine value in regulated telehealth, but building the obsolete item while the decision is pending turns a value question into a permission queue and funds known waste. Starting the work quietly in slack capacity produces the capability at the cost of transparency, and unfunded scope discovered later destroys the practitioner's credibility.
questions.concept: Welcoming changing requirements late in development (Agile Manifesto principle) versus plan conformance
questions.question: Midway through a release, a new national telehealth regulation is announced that makes one planned capability partially obsolete and creates an urgent need for consent-tracking that was never on the roadmap. The sponsor reminds everyone that the roadmap was 'locked' at the funding review and warns that changing it now would look undisciplined to the executive board. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Continue delivering the locked roadmap through the end of the release, since honoring a funded commitment is what protects the team's standing with executives, and carry the consent-tracking requirement into the next planning cycle

Submit the consent-tracking requirement to the change control board and keep building the partially obsolete capability until a formal decision is issued, so that any roadmap change carries documented authorization

Have the team begin the consent-tracking work quietly inside the current release using slack capacity, so the capability exists by launch without having to reopen the roadmap question with the sponsor or the executive board

Facilitate a working session with the sponsor and product leadership to re-order the backlog around the new regulation, framing the ability to absorb this change as protection for the organization rather than a lapse in discipline

questions.explanation: The dysfunction comes from two groups still operating as two systems, so the remedy is to have the people who do the work jointly build one system: co-created working agreements, a single visible workflow, a shared definition of done, and deliberate overlap hours rebuild direct collaboration and shared ownership of defects. Merging the two defect lists into one backlog with a named integration owner is the strongest alternative and would stop items bouncing, but it repairs an artifact while the separate boards, channels, and quality standards that produced the bouncing remain, and the named owner can become the new intermediary. Supporting the coordinator for a quarter routes every cross-site conversation through one person, and bridging roles tend to institutionalize the divide. Running a retrospective at each site and combining the findings lets each group analyze the other in its absence and then negotiate through documents, when what the merged team needs is one conversation.
questions.concept: Working agreements and transparency in distributed teams
questions.question: After an acquisition, development groups in Lisbon and Singapore were merged into a single product team, but each site still maintains its own board, its own defect list, and its own chat channels. Integration defects bounce between the sites for days while each side blames the other's 'process.' A manager proposes appointing a full-time coordinator through whom all cross-site communication will flow. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Merge the two defect lists into one shared backlog with a named owner for integration work, so defects stop bouncing between the sites and each has a visible next step
Support the coordinator appointment for a quarter while the sites build familiarity, then retire the role once integration defects fall and people are talking to each other directly
Facilitate a joint session where members from both sites co-create shared working agreements — one visible workflow for all work, a shared definition of done, and overlapping collaboration hours
Run a retrospective at each site on the integration defects, then combine the two sets of findings into one improvement plan for the merged team to work through together

questions.explanation: When cause and effect can only be understood in retrospect and expert opinion conflicts, the work sits in Cynefin's complex domain, where the correct pattern is probe–sense–respond: run safe-to-fail experiments, observe emergent results, and amplify what succeeds while dampening what fails. Engaging specialists to analyze and then apply good practice is the sense–analyze–respond pattern for the complicated domain, where cause and effect are discoverable by expertise—not the case here. Reusing proven patterns from earlier products assumes the clear domain, where best practice applies to well-understood, repeatable problems. Acting first to impose stability is the act–sense–respond pattern reserved for the chaotic domain, where there is a crisis and no time to probe; nothing in this situation is a crisis.
questions.concept: Cynefin complex domain: probe–sense–respond
questions.question: A product team is exploring a wellness feature built on a novel behavioral-science idea. No competitor offers anything similar, credible experts disagree about what will drive engagement, and the team expects to understand cause and effect only in hindsight. According to the Cynefin framework, which approach fits this situation?
choices: Run several small safe-to-fail experiments, observe which user behaviors emerge, and amplify what works
Engage recognized specialists to analyze the problem thoroughly, then implement the good practice they recommend
Apply the proven engagement patterns that worked on the company's previous products
Act immediately to impose stability, then reassess options once order is restored

questions.explanation: Discounting $110,000 arriving in year one at 10 percent gives roughly $100,000, while four annual instalments of $30,000 discounted over years one through four give roughly $27,300, $24,800, $22,500 and $20,500 — about $95,000 in total. The nearer money is worth more, and the earlier feedback on the pricing assumption is additional value the spreadsheet does not capture. Comparing the raw totals of $120,000 and $110,000 ignores when the money arrives, which is precisely what net present value corrects. Calling the two equivalent and deciding on staffing is the strongest alternative, since roughly $5,000 is a thin margin — but it is a real margin running the same way as the learning advantage. Arguing that a four-year stream spreads forecasting risk inverts the logic: a longer horizon gives the forecast more time to be wrong.
questions.concept: Applying net present value and time-to-feedback to backlog ordering
questions.question: A product owner must choose between two epics of roughly equal cost and effort; only one can be funded this year. "Route Optimizer" is forecast to return about $120,000 in evenly spread annual amounts over four years. "Instant Quote" is forecast to return about $110,000, essentially all of it within the first year, and it would also put a pricing assumption in front of real customers within a quarter. The organization discounts future cash flows at 10 percent. Applying value-based prioritization, which conclusion is most defensible?
choices: Route Optimizer wins, because its four-year total of $120,000 exceeds $110,000, and with the two epics costing about the same amount the larger overall return is clearly the better use of this year's single funding slot.
The two are effectively equivalent once discounting is applied, so the decision should rest on which epic the organization can staff this year without pulling people off commitments already made.
Route Optimizer wins, because a benefit stream that runs for four years is worth more than one concentrated in a single year, and the longer horizon also spreads the forecasting risk across periods.

Instant Quote is the stronger candidate, because money arriving sooner is discounted far less — its present value is roughly $100,000 against about $95,000 — and it also returns market learning within a quarter.

questions.explanation: This is a systems-thinking failure: leadership optimized a local measure — each specialist's utilization — and degraded the global outcome, end-to-end cycle time. Queueing dynamics make the effect nonlinear, because wait time in front of a resource climbs steeply as it approaches full utilization, which is exactly why lean methods manage flow and limit work in process instead of maximizing busyness. Goodhart's Law is the strongest alternative and is genuinely at work here, since utilization became a target and stopped informing anyone, but it explains why the measure went bad rather than the mechanism that tripled cycle time. Brooks's Law concerns the coordination cost of adding people to late work, and nobody was added. Parkinson's Law describes tasks stretching to fill generous time; these requests are not padded, they are queueing between specialists who are all fully busy.
questions.concept: Systems thinking: local optimization versus end-to-end flow
questions.question: An analytics department at a manufacturing firm drives every specialist to 100% utilization. Within a quarter, the average cycle time for completed requests has tripled, and work items now queue for weeks between specialists. Which concept BEST explains what leadership overlooked?
choices: Goodhart's Law — once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure of performance at all
Brooks's Law — adding people to work that is already late raises the cost of coordinating it
Parkinson's Law — work expands so as to fill up the time that is available for its completion
Systems thinking — optimizing each part of a system in isolation degrades the flow of the whole

questions.explanation: Redesigning how input is gathered with the whole team treats the real problem — the current format makes disagreement feel risky for half the team — and does it in a way that builds safety: asynchronous written channels lower the cost of dissent across language, culture, and time-zone barriers, and norms co-created by the people affected make speaking up an expected behavior rather than an act of courage. Nominating a spokesperson through the site lead inserts hierarchy into a peer conversation and lets individual concerns die before reaching the group. Rotating meeting times addresses schedule fairness, which is worthwhile, but a fairer time slot does not make it safe to contradict a design in front of the whole team — the silence pattern would survive the rotation. Privately collecting concerns and relaying them makes the practitioner a permanent intermediary and implicitly confirms that raising issues directly is unsafe, which is the opposite of the goal.
questions.concept: Psychological safety in distributed teams
questions.question: A product team split between Berlin and Manila holds backlog refinement on video calls scheduled at 9 a.m. Berlin time. The Manila members rarely speak and agree with every estimate, yet later rework reveals they had unvoiced concerns about the designs. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask the Manila site lead to nominate a spokesperson who voices the group's concerns during refinement, so the quieter members are represented without having to speak on the call themselves
Work with the whole team to redesign how input is gathered — for example, asynchronous written feedback before sessions and co-created norms that make dissent an expected contribution
Rotate the schedule so Berlin takes the early slot every other week, since sharing the inconvenient hour equally will make the Manila members readier to challenge estimates
Collect the Manila members' concerns privately after each session and carry them into the team's next discussion yourself, so design issues reach the group before rework is created

questions.explanation: Visualizing work only pays off when the information radiator actually radiates to everyone who needs it; the team owns its own board design, so inviting them to rework the visualization for a distributed context restores shared transparency at the source and removes the need for the side conversation. Photographing the wall each afternoon delivers stale, one-way, non-interactive information and still leaves the remote pair unable to update anything themselves. Adding a second daily sync where the board is read aloud compensates for a broken radiator with more meeting time, increasing process overhead while the transparency gap remains. Routing remote blockers through chat so an on-site member updates the wall preserves the asymmetry — the remote pair still cannot see the system or change it — and creates a handoff plus a second, partial source of truth.
questions.concept: Information radiators for distributed teams
questions.question: A hybrid team building a hospital pharmacy restocking tool keeps its work on a physical wall: sticky notes move from "Ready" to "Building" to "Verifying" to "Released." Since two members started working remotely, the remote pair say they never know what is blocked, and the on-site members have started holding a separate side conversation each morning to catch them up. The board is accurate, but only for people standing in front of it. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the team to redesign how work is made visible so the same information is available to everyone, wherever they are
Assign one on-site member to photograph the wall each afternoon and email it out, so the remote developers see the day's state
Schedule a second daily sync for the remote pair where on-site members walk through every column of the physical wall
Ask the remote pair to post their blockers in team chat so an on-site member can update the wall for them

questions.explanation: The root problem is not this defect — it is that fear of ridicule is suppressing honest information, which corrupts transparency and slows the whole system. Addressing the behavior directly with the senior engineer and then resetting team working agreements tackles the cause and rebuilds the conditions in which anyone can raise bad news safely. Logging the defect anonymously on the tester's behalf treats one symptom while leaving the fear in place, and makes the practitioner a permanent intermediary. Escalating to the engineering manager hands the problem up the hierarchy before any direct, collaborative conversation has been attempted, which itself signals that problems are handled through authority rather than openness. Creating a defect-triage committee adds process to route around a human-behavior problem; agile teams fix interactions before adding structure.
questions.concept: Blameless defect reporting and working agreements
questions.question: A tester on an embedded-firmware team discovers a serious defect in code written by the team's most senior engineer. Instead of logging it, the tester spends three days quietly trying to work around it, telling the agile practitioner, "The last person who flagged his code was humiliated in front of the whole team." What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Log the defect yourself so the fix starts moving while the tester's name stays out of it and the team avoids another public confrontation
Take the senior engineer's conduct to the engineering manager and ask that it be handled through the organization's normal performance process
Address the humiliating behavior directly with the senior engineer and work with the team to reset working agreements on how defects are raised
Introduce a defect-triage group that reviews every finding, so that no individual has to raise a defect against another person's code in the open

questions.explanation: A widening band means arrivals into that state exceed departures from it, so the review stage is accumulating work and is the constraint — that is exactly what the growing "In Review" band shows. The flattening "Done" slope means the delivery rate is flat or declining while total work in process grows, and by Little's Law a larger WIP divided by an equal-or-smaller throughput yields a longer average cycle time. The claim that throughput has increased contradicts the flattening "Done" slope, which is the visual representation of throughput. Estimate accuracy is unrelated: a cumulative flow diagram plots item counts moving through states, and re-estimating changes no arrival or departure rate. Work entering the system too slowly would show narrowing "Ready" and "In Progress" bands, but those bands are described as constant.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation and bottleneck identification
questions.question: A cumulative flow diagram for the last eight weeks shows the "In Review" band widening steadily week over week, while the slope of the "Done" band has flattened. The "Ready" and "In Progress" bands are roughly constant in width. Which TWO statements are best supported by this diagram? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Work is entering review faster than it is leaving it, making review the current constraint on flow
The team's throughput has increased over the period, which is why more items are visible in review
Average cycle time is rising, because work in process is growing while the delivery rate is flat or falling
The team's story point estimates have been too low, and re-estimating the backlog would correct the trend
Work is being pulled into the system too slowly, starving the upstream stages of the board

questions.explanation: Publishing an always-visible board is the agile answer because it turns status from something people must request into something anyone can see. It removes the lead as a bottleneck, gives stakeholders real-time truth, and lets team members see priority changes the moment they happen. A consolidated Friday email is push reporting: it is stale the moment it is sent, keeps the lead as a middleman, and adds recurring overhead. A weekly walkthrough of the tool has the same staleness problem and spends a meeting where a glance would do. Buying extra licenses for the most frequent askers is the closest alternative and would genuinely help those few, but it solves the problem one paid seat at a time, leaves everyone else emailing, and still does nothing for team members who learn about priority changes secondhand.
questions.concept: Information radiators vs. push reporting
questions.question: A team using Kanban tracks all of its work in a licensed tool that only the team lead and the delivery manager can log into. Business stakeholders send the lead several status-request emails each week, and team members often learn about priority changes secondhand. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Have the team lead send a consolidated status email to all stakeholders each Friday so requests stop arriving one at a time
Hold a weekly status meeting where the team lead walks the stakeholders through the tool and the current priorities
Work with the team to publish a board visible to everyone that shows work items, blockers, and current priorities in real time
Buy extra tool licenses for the stakeholders who ask most often, so they can log in and run the reports they need for themselves

questions.explanation: A blameless root-cause session that puts all three parties in front of the actual failure data replaces competing blame narratives with a shared understanding of cause, and any control added afterward will target the real problem. Adopting the PMO's sign-off checklist first prescribes a control before anyone understands the cause — if the defect originates in the vendor's extracts, a signature will not catch it, and the process weight is permanent. A stabilization iteration before each release institutionalizes late defect detection and lengthens feedback loops instead of preventing the errors. Asking the vendor to validate its extracts before delivery is the strongest of the wrong answers, because every failure did begin with legacy data and source validation is a reasonable countermeasure — but it adopts one party's account of the cause before the evidence is examined, leaving the rushed-testing claim untested.
questions.concept: Blameless root-cause analysis
questions.question: A hybrid data-migration program has shipped reconciliation errors to production in three consecutive releases. Developers blame the legacy vendor's extract files; the operations group blames rushed testing; the PMO proposes a mandatory sign-off checklist before the next release. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Support the PMO's sign-off checklist, since a gate ahead of the next release protects production while the groups' tempers cool
Facilitate a blameless root-cause session with developers, operations, and the vendor, examining data from all three failures
Add a stabilization iteration before each release so reconciliation errors surface internally rather than at the customer
Ask the vendor to validate its extract files before delivery, since all three failures began with data arriving from the legacy system

questions.explanation: The board has stopped being an honest information radiator because Done means three different things, so transparency is the defect to repair. Convening the teams to agree on a shared definition of done and common column semantics both restores the board's signal and keeps ownership of the working agreement with the people doing the work. Rolled-up percentage reporting layers a second, derived artifact over an untrustworthy source and hides rather than fixes the ambiguity. An integration checklist run by a coordinator treats a symptom — late defects — while leaving the misleading board and the inconsistent completion rules intact. Imposing the strictest team's process removes team autonomy and invites compliance without shared understanding; the agreement matters more than which template wins.
questions.concept: Shared definition of done and board semantics across multiple teams
questions.question: A three-team program building a patient-scheduling platform releases to production every two weeks. The teams use a shared kanban board, but each team has quietly adopted its own column names and its own rule for when a card counts as complete — one team moves cards to Done at code merge, another after staging validation, the third only after a clinician sign-off. Stakeholders reviewing the board at the program level believe far more is finished than has actually shipped, and the last two releases slipped when integration defects surfaced. What is the BEST response?
choices: Have each team report a weekly completion percentage so the program manager can reconcile the differences into a single rolled-up status view for the stakeholders
Introduce an integration checklist that a release coordinator runs before every release so that mismatched completion states surface before they reach production
Bring representatives from all three teams together to agree on a shared definition of done and a common board vocabulary, then make the board reflect it
Standardize on the strictest team's columns and completion rule and require the other two teams to adopt them from the next release onward

questions.explanation: The symptom — a team executing tickets with no curiosity about the pharmacists who will use the product — is a shared-purpose gap, and purpose is rebuilt through involvement rather than announcement. A facilitated session in which the sponsor and real pharmacy users describe the problems, and everyone including the vendor members co-creates the vision and connects live epics to it, gives every member a visible line of sight from today's work to patient-facing outcomes. A sponsor-circulated vision walked through at planning reaches both staff groups at once, which beats an email, but it is purpose delivered rather than built, and nobody in the room has met a pharmacist. A monthly traceability report adds compliance paperwork; teams learn to fill it in rather than to care. Co-locating vendor and internal staff may genuinely help cohesion, yet a well-blended team can burn down a backlog just as incuriously.
questions.concept: Co-creating product vision to restore intrinsic motivation
questions.question: A hybrid program is building a hospital-pharmacy inventory product with a team split between internal staff and a vendor. In the latest retrospective someone writes, "We just burn down whatever appears at the top of the backlog." Engagement is falling, and team members have stopped asking questions about the pharmacists who will use the system. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Ask the sponsor to circulate a refreshed vision statement and the program objectives, then walk through it at the next iteration planning so internal and vendor staff hear the same message
Introduce a monthly traceability report in which each team confirms that its items map to program objectives, and review the exceptions with the vendor's delivery lead
Arrange for the vendor staff to sit with the internal team for the next two iterations, since the split between the two groups is what is draining engagement and curiosity
Facilitate a session where the sponsor and pharmacists describe the problems to be solved, and the whole team including vendor staff co-creates the vision and maps current epics to it

questions.explanation: The live corrupting fault is chaotic: no time exists for analysis, so the right move is to act immediately to stop the damage, then sense and respond once stability returns. The statutory overtime formula is clear (obvious): the rule is published and unambiguous, so the team senses, categorizes, and applies the best practice. The wearable launch is complex: market behavior emerges only after contact with real users, so safe-to-fail probes and amplify-or-dampen decisions are the fit — this is where agile experimentation earns its keep. The database tuning is complicated: expert analysis can reliably reach one of several good practices, which distinguishes it from the complex case where no amount of up-front analysis can predict the outcome. The exam's favorite trap is precisely that complicated/complex boundary — analyzable-by-experts versus knowable-only-through-experiment.
questions.concept: Cynefin framework domain recognition
questions.question: Match each work situation (left) to the Cynefin-based response that best fits it (right).
pairs: A live payment-processing fault is corrupting transactions right now, and losses grow by the minute
Act, sense, respond — stabilize the situation first, then work out what happened
Calculating statutory overtime pay using a published, unambiguous government formula
Sense, categorize, respond — apply the established best practice; cause and effect are obvious to everyone
Launching a wearable device for a market whose response cannot be known until real customers use it
Probe, sense, respond — run safe-to-fail experiments because cause and effect are visible only in hindsight
Tuning a slow database where several sound solutions exist and specialists can determine a good one through analysis
Sense, analyze, respond — engage experts to evaluate the options and select a good practice

questions.explanation: Explaining that needs emerge in this kind of work, so the team builds small slices of working software and uses stakeholder feedback on each to steer what is defined next, teaches the empirical foundation of agile and helps a colleague from a predictive background understand the mindset rather than just the rules. Producing the full specification once to smooth her transition abandons the team's approach on work where needs are still moving, and postponing the lesson makes it harder to teach later. Telling her the team keeps documentation light because the Manifesto values working software over comprehensive documentation is the most tempting wrong answer, since it quotes a real value — but the Manifesto ranks documentation lower rather than rejecting what adds value, and citing a value explains nothing about how the team manages risk. Pointing her to the roadmap and release plan as her old specification's equivalent misrepresents both, since neither fixes scope in advance.
questions.concept: Empiricism and emergent requirements vs. predictive specification
questions.question: A biomedical technician joining a team that delivers software in two-week iterations for tracking hospital lab equipment asks the agile practitioner why the team refuses to sign off a complete requirements specification before development begins, the way her previous projects did. What should the practitioner do?
choices: Explain that when needs emerge and change, the team deliberately builds small slices of working software and uses stakeholder feedback on each slice to steer what is defined next
Agree to produce the full upfront specification this one time so that her transition is smooth, then introduce iterative practice on the piece of work after this one

Explain that the team keeps documentation light because the Manifesto values working software over comprehensive documentation, so writing a full specification would be effort spent away from delivering the product
Point her to the product roadmap and release plan as the equivalent of her old specification, since between them they already set out what the team intends to build

questions.explanation: Building the compliance requirement into the definition of done stops the defect from recurring, and pulling the officer into refinement and reviews closes the feedback loop that was missing — the root cause was an absent voice, not a lack of diligence. Deferring remediation until after the release ships a product that violates a legal obligation and lets the same defect accumulate in every item built meanwhile. Asking for a checklist to apply in a hardening iteration batches quality work into a separate phase — precisely the pattern that produced six items of rework — and leaves the completed items nominally closed while they are not actually done. Reworking only the screens the authority audits is the most tempting alternative because it is the cheapest way to pass inspection, but it optimizes for the audit rather than the requirement: anyone using a screen reader is failed on every skipped screen, and the definition of done still says nothing about accessibility.
questions.concept: Compliance criteria embedded in definition of done
questions.question: A team delivering a public-transit fare-capping feature runs two-week iterations. In the last review, they demonstrated a working fare calculator, but the transit authority's accessibility officer — who had not attended any prior review — pointed out that the fare display fails the contrast and screen-reader requirements the authority is legally bound to meet. Reworking six completed items will consume most of the next iteration. The team's definition of done does not mention accessibility. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Create a separate accessibility remediation item, size it with the officer, and schedule it after the fare-capping release so the launch date and the team's current momentum are preserved
Ask the accessibility officer for a written checklist the team can apply during a hardening iteration before launch, keeping the completed items closed and the review cadence intact
Have the product owner rank the six items so only the screens the authority actually audits are reworked now, and treat the remaining contrast fixes as follow-on work after launch
Work with the team and the accessibility officer to add the accessibility criteria to the definition of done, invite the officer into refinement and reviews, and replan the rework openly

questions.explanation: Making the hidden wait explicit turns an invisible constraint into shared data — the board now tells the truth about where time goes, the director can see status without asking, and the team has evidence to take to the environment owners. A weekly status email builds a reporting channel around the opacity rather than removing it, and pushes information through one person instead of creating a self-service signal. Tightening the work-in-progress limit may be useful later, but applied now it treats a symptom while the actual delay driver remains unmeasured, and it could simply idle the team without shortening the queue. Demanding a guarantee from the platform group escalates to another group before the team can quantify the impact, which weakens the case and skips the transparency step that would support the conversation.
questions.concept: Explicit workflow states and queue visibility
questions.question: A five-person team maintains a hospital scheduling product using a flow-based approach with work-in-progress limits. Their board shows columns for Ready, Build, Verify, and Done. A department director complains that she can never tell whether her requested change is progressing, because items sit in Build for eight to twelve days and nothing visible changes. The team confirms that most of that time is actually spent waiting on a shared test environment they do not control. What is the BEST response?
choices: Send the director a weekly written update on each of her items, giving the date it entered Build and when it should reach Done
Split the Build column into explicit in-progress and waiting-for-environment sub-states so the wait becomes visible on the board, then review the resulting data with stakeholders
Lower the work-in-progress limit on Build so fewer items sit in the column at once, and tell the director that her change will therefore move faster
Ask the platform group to commit to a guaranteed turnaround on test environments, and hold new items in Ready until that commitment is in place

questions.explanation: Observing the discussions firsthand and then introducing balancing structures such as silent writing and round-robin input verifies the pattern with the practitioner's own data, immediately gives quieter members a structurally protected voice, honors the confidence, and leaves room to coach the senior engineer later from direct observation. Taking the feedback to the senior engineer straight away acts on secondhand information the practitioner has not yet witnessed and risks exposing the analyst, destroying the fragile safety that produced the disclosure. Pushing the analyst to raise it in the retrospective transfers the interpersonal risk onto the least powerful person in the dynamic before any safety has been built. Requiring a documented vote on every significant decision adds ceremony that treats the symptom — dominated decisions can still be rubber-stamped by disengaged voters — while leaving the participation imbalance untouched.
questions.concept: Psychological safety and facilitation techniques for balanced participation
questions.question: A soft-spoken analyst privately tells the agile practitioner that a senior engineer dominates every design discussion, and that several teammates have quietly stopped contributing — though in team sessions the decisions still look like consensus. The analyst asks the practitioner not to reveal the conversation. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Meet the senior engineer privately and share the feedback so the dominating behavior can be corrected before the next design discussion takes place
Encourage the analyst to raise it herself at the next retrospective, since the team owns its dynamics and the concern lands better first-hand
Observe the next few design discussions firsthand, then introduce balancing facilitation structures such as silent writing and round-robin input
Propose a working agreement that every significant design decision is settled by an anonymous written vote taken before discussion closes

questions.explanation: Little's Law in its practical flow form gives average cycle time as average work in progress divided by average throughput: 24 items divided by 6 items per week is about 4 weeks, and because throughput is comparatively hard to move quickly, cutting WIP is the lever most immediately available to the team. The variant claiming only more people can help ignores that lowering WIP reduces multitasking and queueing and shortens cycle time without any staffing change — and that new people initially reduce throughput. Multiplying 24 by 6 to reach 144 weeks misapplies the relationship, which divides WIP by throughput rather than multiplying. Claiming the data is insufficient without story points misunderstands the law, which relies on item counts and completion rates, and that independence from sizing is precisely why flow metrics work for teams that have abandoned estimation.
questions.concept: Practical application of Little's Law to cycle time
questions.question: A support-and-enhancement team works from a single Kanban queue with no iteration boundaries. Over a stable four-week period the board holds an average of 24 items in progress and the team completes an average of 6 items per week. A stakeholder asks how long a new item is likely to take from the moment work on it starts to the moment it is done. Applying Little's Law to these figures, the most defensible answer is:
choices: About 4 weeks, and the team can shorten it most directly by reducing the number of items in progress
About 4 weeks, and the only way to shorten it is to increase the number of people on the team
About 144 weeks, because average work in progress multiplied by throughput gives average cycle time
The figures are insufficient, because average cycle time cannot be estimated without story point sizes

questions.explanation: Running acceptance tests on every commit collapses the interval between writing a defect and seeing it from days to minutes, and it does so for every change rather than for a sampled few. A tester exploring alongside the developer catches what automation cannot express — confusing behavior, missing edge cases, wrong assumptions — at the moment the code is still in working memory, which is why both actions attack the eleven-day gap at its source. A quarterly regression cycle enlarges the batch enormously and pushes discovery even further from the moment of creation. A triage coordinator speeds the routing of a defect after it has finally been found, shortening a small tail of the delay while leaving the eleven days untouched, and adds a hand-off. Batching stories into larger test packages optimizes environment setup at the direct expense of feedback speed, trading away the very thing the team is trying to improve.
questions.concept: CI-based acceptance testing and paired exploratory testing to shrink defect feedback latency
questions.question: On an online-ordering platform, the team measures that defects are typically found eleven days after the code that caused them was written; each discovery pulls someone off current work and forces them to reconstruct forgotten context. The team wants to shorten the distance between making a mistake and learning about it. Which TWO actions most directly shorten that feedback loop? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Schedule a full regression cycle in the week before each quarterly release.
Add automated acceptance tests to the delivery pipeline so they execute against every commit.
Appoint a defect-triage coordinator to route each finding to the right developer more quickly.
Have a tester work alongside the developer while the story is still in progress, exploring the behavior as it is being built.
Batch stories into larger test packages so the shared test environment has to be provisioned less often.

questions.explanation: Making all work items and blockers visible on a shared board creates a single, always-current source of truth, an information radiator, which removes the need for private spreadsheets and one-off status emails and lets the whole system see and swarm on blockers. A shared spreadsheet the operations director can open himself is the closest alternative and would end the weekly round of emails, but a hand-maintained file is only as current as the last person who remembered, and it shows blocked items detached from the flow they are blocking. Inviting the director to the daily standup gives him direct contact while turning the team's coordination event into a status report for one stakeholder. A weekly blocker review adds a meeting and leaves impediments waiting for the next session.
questions.concept: Information radiators and visualizing work in Kanban
questions.question: An agile practitioner joins a warehouse-automation team that uses Kanban. Team members track their blocked work items in personal spreadsheets, and the operations director emails each member separately every week asking for individual status updates. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask each member to log blocked items in a shared spreadsheet the operations director can open himself, replacing the weekly round of emails he sends
Work with the team to visualize all work items and blockers on a shared board that the team and the director can see at any time
Invite the operations director to attend the team's daily standup so he hears blockers directly from the people holding them rather than collecting updates member by member
Start a weekly blocker review where the team walks the operations director through each open impediment and agrees who clears it before the next review session

questions.explanation: Delivering a small working increment to real users now generates validated learning while most of the budget is still unspent; if the first reports miss the mark, only a fraction of the work must change. Reconfirming the requirements document tests words, not working software — users routinely approve documents and then reject the product built from them. Showing clickable mockups of all twelve reports is the strongest alternative and genuinely worth doing, since layout and comprehension problems surface in days, but a mockup cannot reveal whether the numbers are right, whether the underlying data supports the report, or whether anyone uses it to make a decision — and keeping the four-month plan untouched means nothing learned changes what gets built. Finishing all twelve and then running a two-week acceptance test maximizes both the feedback delay and the potential rework, which is precisely the risk incremental delivery exists to remove.
questions.concept: incremental delivery and early feedback
questions.question: A team building an internal reporting tool plans to spend four months completing all twelve requested reports before showing anything to the finance users who asked for them. What should the agile practitioner recommend?
choices: Release one or two finished reports to the finance users now and use their feedback to shape the remaining ones
Have the finance users reconfirm the requirements document so all twelve reports are built to a validated specification
Show finance users clickable mockups of the twelve reports now and keep the four-month build plan as it is
Build all twelve reports, then run a two-week acceptance test with the finance users before releasing the tool

questions.explanation: The root cause is damaged psychological safety, so the best response works at that level: private coaching addresses the behavior that broke trust without publicly shaming the lead in turn, and refreshing working agreements lets both teams collectively re-own the norms for raising concerns — restoring safety rather than routing around its absence. An anonymous reporting tool adds mechanism instead of trust; it institutionalizes the fear and signals that open conversation is no longer expected. Handing the matter to a functional manager and HR escalates before any direct, collaborative attempt to resolve it, and is likely to deepen defensiveness across the teams. Waiting two more iterations to confirm the trend delays action on a problem already evidenced by late defects and members' own admissions — the cost of silence compounds while the practitioner watches.
questions.concept: Psychological safety and working agreements
questions.question: Two cross-functional teams are building interactive exhibits for a science museum. Since a joint review in which one team's technical lead publicly ridiculed a colleague's estimate miss, retrospective comments from both teams have turned vague, defects are increasingly discovered late by the museum's staff rather than raised early by developers, and members have privately admitted they no longer flag risks in shared meetings. Delivery pace itself looks normal. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Introduce an anonymous defect-and-risk reporting channel for both teams, so that members are able to raise concerns early without attaching their own names to what they choose to report
Ask the technical lead's functional manager to address the conduct through the organization's formal performance process, so the behavior is handled by the proper authority
Track the defect and retrospective trends across two more iterations to confirm the pattern is real before intervening in how the two teams work with one another day to day
Privately coach the technical lead on the impact of the public criticism and facilitate both teams in refreshing their working agreements about how concerns and mistakes are raised

questions.explanation: Releasing small increments behind feature toggles to a subset of live customers turns every release into an experiment and yields behavioral data — what customers actually do — within days rather than a quarter. Inviting real customers to exercise working software at each iteration review adds direct, high-bandwidth feedback every cycle from the people the product serves. Both actions connect the team to genuine customers quickly and repeatedly. A monthly steering-committee review shortens nothing that matters here: it is internal stakeholders discussing progress, not customers using the product, and it is still slower than an iteration. Lengthening iterations so demonstrations look more complete moves in exactly the wrong direction — bigger batches mean rarer feedback and more work built on unvalidated assumptions. Negotiating a detailed upfront sign-off tries to eliminate the need for feedback instead of accelerating it, which assumes requirements can be fully known in advance — the very assumption the team's quarterly-survey pain disproves.
questions.concept: Small-batch releases, feature toggles, and direct customer feedback
questions.question: A meal-kit subscription team currently learns about customer reactions only through a quarterly satisfaction survey run by the marketing department. The team wants much faster insight into how customers actually use new features. Which TWO actions would most directly shorten the team's feedback loop with real customers? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Release small increments behind feature toggles to a subset of live customers and observe usage data within days
Add a monthly progress review with the internal steering committee
Invite a rotating panel of actual customers to try the working software at every iteration review
Lengthen iterations so each demonstration contains more finished functionality
Negotiate a detailed upfront requirements sign-off so less customer feedback is needed later

questions.explanation: The control has outlived the cause that justified it and is now suppressing improvement ideas — the empowerment loss, not the three-day queue, is the real damage. Bringing the director and the team together to agree guardrails, such as risk thresholds under which the team decides autonomously, restores decision authority collaboratively, respects the director's legitimate ownership of the control, and uses the fixed root cause as the evidence for change. Committing to a same-day turnaround optimizes the bottleneck instead of removing it; the team still learns that every improvement waits on one person's attention. Showing the director that the root cause is fixed and asking him to lift the requirement is a strong, evidence-based alternative, but it asks him to surrender a control rather than replace it with something he can trust, leaves the team out of the conversation, and sets no boundary for the next incident. Moving approval to the senior engineer relocates the bottleneck inside the team.
questions.concept: Delegation and decision guardrails
questions.question: After a costly production incident, a director required the agile practitioner to personally approve every database schema change a Lean software team makes. Four months later the incident's root cause has been fixed, approvals now average three days in queue, and team members have stopped proposing schema improvements, saying "it'll just sit waiting anyway." What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Keep approving each change but commit to a same-day turnaround, so the queue stops discouraging the team from proposing improvements
Meet with the director and the team to agree on decision guardrails that return schema changes to the team within defined risk limits
Show the director that the incident's root cause is now fixed and ask that the approval requirement be lifted as no longer needed
Move the approval to the team's most senior engineer so decisions sit closer to the work while a named reviewer still signs each change off

questions.explanation: The same item recurring four times shows the team has named a symptom it has never traced to a cause, and has never given the improvement any capacity to compete with feature work. Walking recent interruptions back through successive "why" layers usually turns a vague complaint into something specific and actionable, such as one integration's known defect generating most of the tickets, and converting one countermeasure into an owned, estimated backlog item is what turns retrospective talk into delivered change. Measuring every interruption for an iteration is the strongest rival and would produce genuinely useful data, but it defers any action by a full iteration when concrete recent examples are already in hand. Capping the unplanned support work the team accepts protects planned capacity while leaving the interruptions themselves untouched, which manages the symptom by queueing it somewhere else. Skipping the retrospective for a stakeholder workshop concedes the premise that the cause is already known, and it removes the team's own inspection point exactly when its improvement loop is failing.
questions.concept: Retrospective follow-through and root-cause analysis
questions.question: For four consecutive iterations a marketing-technology team's retrospective has produced the same improvement item: "too many unplanned support interruptions." It is written on a wall chart that never changes, nothing has improved, and this iteration a team member proposes skipping the retrospective because "we already know what is wrong." What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask the team to track every interruption for one iteration and size the total, so the next retrospective can open with real data on how much capacity the support work consumes each iteration

Facilitate a root-cause exploration of the interruptions using recent concrete examples, then help the team turn one specific countermeasure into an owned, sized item that enters the next iteration alongside feature work
Agree a limit on how much unplanned support work the team accepts each iteration and hold the remainder in a visible queue, so planned work is protected while the interruptions continue

Accept the proposal to skip the session and spend the time in a facilitated problem-solving workshop with the stakeholders who raise the support requests, since the team already understands the issue well

questions.explanation: Slicing vertically — a thin path through data, services and interface that lets a real grower irrigate one pivot with two zones — produces items that satisfy INVEST: each is independent, valuable, and testable on its own, and each returns real agronomic feedback after the first slice rather than after the whole capability converges. Splitting by architectural layer produces pieces that are not independently valuable: no grower can use a database schema, nothing is demonstrable until the last layer lands, and the deferred integration item concentrates technical risk at the point in the release where there is least time to absorb it. Leaving the item whole across three iterations gives up exactly the transparency and feedback that decomposition exists to create, and percent-complete on an unfinished capability is a progress illusion rather than working software. Commissioning a full up-front design before splitting is big-bang analysis: it delays the first usable slice, spends effort on decisions the first slice would have informed, and moves understanding out of the team that has to build it.
questions.concept: Vertical slicing and INVEST-compliant decomposition of large backlog items
questions.question: An agri-tech team builds an irrigation platform for commercial growers. The backlog item 'Support variable-rate irrigation for center-pivot systems' is sized far larger than anything the team has completed inside a two-week iteration. The product owner wants it broken down before the next iteration planning. In refinement, the developers propose splitting it into three items: database schema changes, service-layer changes, and grower-facing screens. What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Accept the developers' three-layer split, since it lets the database, service, and interface specialists all work in parallel on their own areas, and schedule a dedicated integration item near the end of the release to bring the three pieces back together

Coach the team to slice the work end to end instead — for example, a single pivot with two prescription zones first, then multiple zones, then imported prescription maps — so each slice is independently usable and testable by a grower.

Keep the backlog item whole for now and let it run across three iterations, tracking it with a percentage-complete measure reported weekly, so the product owner sees steady progress and the team avoids spending refinement time on splitting it up

Ask a solution architect to produce a detailed design of the full capability first, so the team has a complete technical picture of the pivot hardware and the prescription formats before it attempts any decomposition of the item into thinner, usable slices

questions.explanation: Acknowledging the analyst for raising the problem promptly, then steering the team toward examining how the error became possible, reinforces psychological safety in the exact moment it is being threatened — people keep reporting problems early only when doing so is visibly rewarded, not punished. Moving the sync along and coaching her privately afterward frames the incident as an individual failing, and it leaves the senior engineer's sigh as the last thing the team witnessed, which teaches everyone watching that admitting a mistake invites quiet correction. Proposing a peer check on every configuration change imposes process before the team has understood the problem: it adds a permanent control step in response to a single incident, signals distrust, and never surfaces how the misconfiguration became possible. Correcting and reissuing the report immediately is necessary work and the most tempting distractor, but choosing it over tracing the cause explicitly trades the learning for the fix, and the same filter error remains available to the next person.
questions.concept: Reinforcing psychological safety when errors are admitted publicly
questions.question: During a daily sync, a junior analyst on a Kanban team supporting a logistics dashboard admits she misconfigured a data filter, which caused an inaccurate report to reach an internal customer. A senior engineer sighs loudly and mutters that this keeps happening, and the rest of the team falls silent. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Move the sync along and coach the analyst privately afterward on checking her filter settings, sparing her from being singled out in front of the team
Propose a peer check on every dashboard configuration change, so a second pair of eyes catches filter errors before any report reaches internal customers
