Thank the analyst for surfacing the issue quickly, and guide the team to treat the error as shared learning about how the mistake became possible
Ask the team to correct and reissue the inaccurate report immediately, since restoring the internal customer's confidence matters more than tracing how the error happened

questions.explanation: Rework caused by delayed, written-only feedback is cured by putting real users in front of working software early and by removing the friction that keeps them away — meeting them on their site, in their hours, with the people who do dunning daily rather than only their manager. A thin working slice makes the feedback concrete and cheap to act on, which is what actively engaging customers looks like in practice. Getting advance sign-off on acceptance criteria and reclassifying later feedback as change requests is a contractual defense that protects the team's schedule while guaranteeing the wrong product; it treats customer learning as a scope violation. Recording a short walkthrough is the most reasonable of the rejected options because it respects the manager's stated constraint, but it still routes everything through the one person whose comments have already produced three rounds of rework. Building the full slice and then running extended acceptance testing keeps the loop at its current length while enlarging the batch.
questions.concept: Engaging hands-on users directly instead of proxy sign-off
questions.question: A subscription-billing team releases to production twice a week. The product owner represents a regional operations group that will use a new dunning workflow, but that group's manager has declined to attend reviews, saying, "Send me a summary and I'll comment." Written summaries have produced three rounds of rework so far, each discovered two weeks after release. The team is about to start the largest slice of the workflow. What is the BEST response?
choices: Ask the product owner to sign off the acceptance criteria in advance so the operations manager's later comments can be handled as change requests instead of rework the team absorbs
Offer to record a short walkthrough of the dunning workflow for the manager to review on their own schedule, since they have already said they cannot attend the reviews
Propose a 30-minute working session where two operations users who do dunning daily walk through a thin working slice, and offer to hold it at their site during their shift
Build the full slice to the written summary, then run an extended acceptance testing cycle with the operations group so defects surface before the change reaches production

questions.explanation: A risk burndown plots aggregate exposure -- probability times impact summed across the register -- so the line is a net figure. A flat net line beside real closures means new or re-scored exposure is arriving at about the same rate it is being retired, and that is a genuine signal worth chasing with a root-cause technique such as Five Whys or a fishbone at the next retrospective. Declaring the chart miscalculated assumes closures can only subtract, which ignores the additions side of the ledger and would discard the most informative reading on the chart. Re-scoring risks downward because nothing has happened yet mistakes the absence of a trigger for a lower probability; for a migration whose cutover is still ahead, exposure has not changed at all, and lowering scores would simply make the chart look better. Pausing risk-reduction work to catch up on features inverts the purpose of a risk-adjusted backlog, where risk-reduction items earn their place alongside features precisely because avoided cost is value -- and on a migration, deferring that work concentrates the exposure at the worst possible moment.
questions.concept: Risk burndown interpretation and the risk-adjusted backlog
questions.question: A data-migration team maintains a risk-adjusted backlog and reviews a risk burndown chart each iteration. Over the last four iterations the chart shows total risk exposure essentially flat, even though the team completed risk-reduction work every iteration and formally closed two risks. Which interpretation and follow-up is most appropriate?
choices: The chart must be miscalculated, since formally closing two risks should lower total exposure; the team should rebuild the curve from the risk register before showing it at the next review.

The remaining risks should be re-scored downward, since four iterations without an incident suggest the original probability estimates were pessimistic, and the lower exposure figure should then be reported to stakeholders.
Risk-reduction work is crowding out feature delivery; it should be paused for one iteration so the team can restore throughput before it returns to working the risk-adjusted backlog again.
New exposure is being identified at roughly the rate old exposure is being burned down; the team should investigate what keeps generating risk rather than reading the closures as progress.

questions.explanation: A joint working session applies responding to change over following a plan at the multi-team level: the people closest to the dependency examine the real impact and adapt the shared design collaboratively, preserving decentralized decision-making while keeping the system-level view coherent. Handing re-sequencing to a program manager centralizes a decision the teams have the best knowledge to make and weakens their ownership of the outcome. Waiting for the next quarterly workshop honors a stale plan while every team builds toward an integration that no longer exists — the cost of delayed adaptation compounds each week. Adding a formal dependency gate is a process response to a single event; it grows governance overhead before anyone has even examined the change at hand.
questions.concept: Cross-team coordination and adapting shared plans
questions.question: Three teams — one using Scrum, one using Kanban, and one using a hybrid approach — are building a shared payments platform. Midway through the quarter, the external banking gateway they all integrate with announces a mandatory API overhaul, invalidating the integration design agreed at the quarterly planning workshop. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the program manager to re-sequence each team's milestones around the API overhaul and publish the revised integration plan to all three teams
Have the teams finish the work they committed to this quarter and take the API overhaul into the next quarterly planning workshop for redesign
Institute a formal impact-assessment gate for every external dependency, so a change like this gateway overhaul is caught before it invalidates a plan
Facilitate a joint session where representatives of the three teams inspect the new API's impact and adapt the shared integration plan together

questions.explanation: An impediment the team cannot remove on its own must be escalated, but escalated well: with evidence of its cost, through the person who actually owns the interface, and aimed at removing the constraint permanently rather than punishing anyone. Quantified blocked days turn a complaint into a business case, and the product owner is the natural partner because the delay is eroding delivered value. Planning less work each iteration is accommodation rather than removal — the team absorbs the waste quietly and the organization never learns it exists. Requiring confirmed credentials before integration work is pulled is a sensible readiness rule, yet it writes a four-iteration-old delay permanently into the team's own process and still leaves delivery hostage to an unmanaged external queue. Building a stubbed laboratory interface is the strongest alternative and legitimate engineering, but it postpones the integration risk rather than removing it and hides the impediment just as its cost was about to become visible.
questions.concept: Impediment escalation path; making blocked time visible and quantified
questions.question: On a veterinary telehealth product, every iteration stalls for three to five days while the team waits for a partner laboratory to issue sandbox credentials for the integration test environment. "Waiting for lab credentials" has sat on the team's impediment board for four iterations running and nothing has changed. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Have the team plan less work each iteration so the recurring credential wait no longer threatens the iteration goal, and treat the lost days as known capacity in forecasts.
Add a definition-of-ready condition requiring that sandbox credentials be requested and confirmed a full iteration before the related integration work is pulled onto the board.
Quantify the blocked days and their effect on cycle time, then go with the product owner to the manager who owns the laboratory relationship and negotiate a standing credential arrangement.
Have the team build a stubbed laboratory interface so integration stories can proceed without sandbox credentials, then verify against the real sandbox whenever the partner access finally arrives.

questions.explanation: A widening band on a cumulative flow diagram means items are entering that stage faster than they leave it: work in progress, and therefore cycle time, is increasing even though the team's completion volume looks stable. Taking the diagram into the team's next improvement conversation turns a stakeholder complaint into shared, transparent data and lets the people doing the work diagnose the constraint before anyone prescribes a fix. Presenting the six-iteration velocity trend as proof of health mistakes an internal capacity measure for a delivery-speed measure; velocity says nothing about how long a customer waits, which is exactly what the stakeholders are describing. Lowering the iteration commitment until the integration-test band drains is the strongest rival, because reducing arrivals really would stop the band widening — but it is a remedy chosen before diagnosis and throttles the whole team for a constraint sitting in one stage. A hardening iteration clears the queue once and leaves the imbalance that created it, so the band starts widening again immediately.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram interpretation and cycle time versus velocity
questions.question: A payments team reviews a cumulative flow diagram covering the last ten weeks. Work arrives at a steady rate, the deployed line rises at a steady but noticeably shallower slope, and the band labeled "Awaiting Integration Test" grows wider every single week. At the iteration review the team reports that velocity has held steady at about 32 points for six iterations and concludes that delivery is healthy. Business stakeholders push back, saying features "take forever to actually show up." What is the BEST next step for the agile practitioner?
choices: Present the six-iteration velocity trend to the stakeholders as evidence that the team's delivery rate has been stable, then ask them which specific releases are behind their concern.
Ask the team to lower its iteration commitment until the integration-test band drains, so that arrivals match the deployed rate and the diagram flattens out again.
Bring the cumulative flow diagram into the team's next improvement conversation and explore the widening integration-test band as a growing queue that is stretching cycle time.
Add a hardening iteration dedicated to clearing everything waiting in integration test, then return to the normal cadence with the same velocity target as before.

questions.explanation: Helping the manager understand pull-based flow and restoring the team's ability to select its own work within WIP limits addresses the root behavior — push assignment — through direct, collaborative education, and it rebuilds the self-selection that was driving skill spread and flow. Routing assignments through the practitioner merely swaps one assigner for another; the team still is not pulling its own work, and the practitioner becomes a new bottleneck. Escalating to the manager's supervisor jumps past a direct, good-faith conversation with a new manager and damages trust before collaboration has even been attempted. A fixed rotation schedule makes push assignment tidier but leaves the anti-pattern intact: individuals are still handed work rather than pulling it, and the learning benefit of choosing unfamiliar ticket types is lost.
questions.concept: Self-organizing teams and pull-based work assignment
questions.question: A newly appointed delivery manager for a Kanban-based customer support team has started assigning incoming tickets to specific individuals every morning "to balance the workload fairly." Within two weeks, cycle times have lengthened and team members have stopped volunteering for unfamiliar ticket types. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the manager to route the daily assignments through the practitioner, who knows each member's strengths better
Coach the manager on pull-based flow and have team members select their own work within the agreed WIP limits
Escalate the concern to the manager's supervisor before the behavior becomes established
Create a fixed rotation schedule so that ticket assignments are at least distributed evenly

questions.explanation: An information radiator has three defining properties working together: the team owns and maintains it, it is current and honest (blockers included), and it broadcasts passively — anyone can pull the information just by looking, with no request, no meeting, and no intermediary. The wall display with daily team updates exhibits all three. The access-gated dashboard is current but not radiating: information you must ask permission to see behaves like an information refrigerator, however fresh its contents. The Friday email is honest but is pushed, curated by one person, and stale for six days out of seven — a report, not a radiator. Reviewing a cumulative flow diagram inside the retrospective is a valuable inspection practice, but it is periodic and internal to the team; nothing is being continuously broadcast to the surrounding organization.
questions.concept: Defining properties of information radiators vs. push reporting
questions.question: Which situation best reflects the intent behind an information radiator?
choices: A team plots its burn-up and current blockers on a wall display in its work area, updates it daily, and visiting stakeholders absorb it without asking anyone
A coach keeps an always-current online dashboard of the same charts, and stakeholders open it themselves once the tooling group grants them viewer access
A project manager compiles the team's metrics into a candid status email every Friday and sends it to all stakeholders so nobody has to hunt for the numbers
A team pulls up its cumulative flow diagram at the start of every retrospective and studies it together to find the bottleneck that formed during the iteration

questions.explanation: A community of practice is the enduring, voluntary cross-team group organized around a shared discipline; its defining trait is sustained learning over time, which separates it from any single event. An information radiator is the passive mechanism — a large visible display that pushes current status to anyone nearby without their having to ask, sharing knowledge with no meeting at all. Mob programming is the real-time working mechanism: the whole team on one item at one workstation, so skills transfer while the work itself gets done. An open space session is the event whose distinguishing feature is an emergent, participant-driven agenda, with attendees convening the topics they care about. The common traps are confusing the ongoing community with the open space format for a single gathering, and treating the radiator as a facilitated activity when it is deliberately passive.
questions.concept: Knowledge-sharing mechanisms: communities of practice, radiators, mobbing, open space
questions.question: Match each knowledge-sharing mechanism (1-4) to the description (A-D) that best distinguishes it.
pairs: Community of practice
A voluntary group spanning teams that sustains learning in a shared discipline over the long term
Information radiator
A large, always-visible display that broadcasts current status to anyone passing by, without being asked
Mob programming
The whole team works the same item at one workstation, transferring skills in real time as roles rotate
Open space session
Participants propose and self-select the discussion topics, so the agenda emerges from whoever attends

questions.explanation: She already holds the skill; what she needs is help unlocking her own thinking for one specific, sensitive context — that is coaching, which uses open questions to draw out her options and leaves ownership of the approach with her. Enrolling her in an advanced facilitation workshop addresses a skills gap she does not have, cannot be tailored to this particular session, and will not arrive in time. Recounting how the practitioner once handled a similar retrospective is mentoring — occasionally useful, but it transfers his answer instead of developing hers, and his team's dynamics may differ sharply from this one's. Designing the agenda for her is directing: it solves tonight's problem while taking away her ownership and growing nothing, the opposite of what a capable person asking to "think it through" is requesting.
questions.concept: Coaching versus mentoring versus training as modes of capability transfer
questions.question: An experienced facilitator on a hybrid team must run a retrospective that will examine a sensitive quality failure. She has facilitated many retrospectives, but tells the agile practitioner she is "stuck on how to approach this one" and wants help thinking it through. Which form of support best fits this situation?
choices: Training — enroll her in an advanced facilitation workshop before the retrospective
Mentoring — walk her through exactly how the practitioner handled a similar retrospective earlier in his career
Coaching — ask open questions that help her surface options and choose her own approach
Directing — design the retrospective agenda for her and ask her to follow it

questions.explanation: Every option here is technically possible, so the deciding factor is which one protects the customer, preserves trust, and keeps the decision with the person accountable for value. Toggling off the affected household type stops the damage within minutes without discarding a working increment, posting the finding and the decision on the board keeps the team and the early-access group honestly informed, and a same-day call gets the product owner's ordering decision at the speed the situation demands. Switching the whole capability off for all ninety adjusters is the safest-sounding alternative, but it is disproportionate to a fault already isolated to one household type and withdraws working capability from eighty-eight people it never touched. Leaving the toggle on with written instructions to re-sort claims by hand pushes the defect's cost onto the users and leaves wrong priorities in front of them. Canvassing the other eighty-eight first sounds like evidence gathering, but the reports are specific and reproducible, and the faulty ranking stays live meanwhile.
questions.concept: Responding to early-access feedback within a live increment
questions.question: An insurance claims platform team delivers continuously behind feature toggles. Four days into a two-week increment, the automated claim-triage capability is switched on for an early-access group of ninety adjusters. Two of them report that for multi-policy households the triage priority comes out inverted, so low-urgency claims are being worked first. No claimant is at risk of harm, but one adjuster has already told a broker that the new tool "cannot be trusted." The product owner is traveling and reachable by phone; the iteration review is in two days. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Prompt the team to switch the whole triage capability off for all ninety early-access adjusters until the priority logic has been reviewed across every claim segment, and tell the early-access group that it will return once the team is confident that nothing else in the queue is ranked wrongly

Prompt the team to switch the toggle off for the affected household type, make the finding and that decision visible on the board and to the early-access group, and get the product owner on a call the same day to decide whether the fix belongs in this increment.

Leave the toggle on and give the early-access group written guidance for reordering multi-policy household claims by hand each morning, so that no adjuster is blocked during the pilot while the corrected priority logic is ranked against the rest of the increment at the next planning session

Ask the team to gather more evidence from the remaining eighty-eight adjusters before changing anything, since two reports out of ninety may reflect local practice in two branch offices rather than a defect in the ranking, and bring the fuller picture to the product owner later this week

questions.explanation: Stopping the start of new work and swarming the over-limit column is the standard Kanban response to a breached WIP limit: the limit exists precisely to trigger this conversation, and pulling the queue down restores flow and shortens cycle time immediately without inventing any new process. Raising the limit to five is the opposite move — it silences the signal the system is sending and legitimizes the queue that caused the cycle-time increase. Asking a manager to assign a dedicated reviewer escalates outside the team before the team has attempted the simplest self-organized fix, and it treats a flow problem as a staffing problem. Adding a waiting column only relabels the queue; the delay is already plainly visible, and another column reduces neither the queue nor the cycle time.
questions.concept: WIP limits and stop-starting/start-finishing behavior
questions.question: A port-documentation team at a marine logistics firm works from a Kanban board with the columns Ready, Build, Peer Review, Verify, and Done. Peer Review carries a WIP limit of 3, but it currently holds five cards and two of them have been sitting untouched for six days. Developers keep pulling new items into Build, explaining that they "shouldn't sit idle while waiting on a review." Average cycle time has climbed from four days to nine over the last month. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Ask the team to stop starting new items and swarm on the review queue until Peer Review is back within its limit.
Raise the Peer Review limit to five, so the board reflects the way the team is genuinely working today.
Ask the functional manager to assign the team a dedicated reviewer, so that review work never forms a queue again.
Add a Waiting for Review queue column so the two cards that have sat six days become visible to the whole team.

questions.explanation: Coaching the lead toward pull-based work selection addresses the root cause: push-style assignment strips the team of ownership and of the option to swarm, which is exactly what the falling throughput and the silence signal. A servant leader grows the lead's understanding rather than working around the behavior. Studying throughput trends before saying anything is the most defensible alternative — evidence usually beats assertion with a newly appointed lead — but throughput has already declined, the behavioral signals are unambiguous, and a trend line cannot isolate the spreadsheet as the cause while the habit hardens. Keeping the spreadsheet and sizing assignments to each person's capacity polishes a push system and leaves ownership and flow broken. Limiting work in process is sound Kanban practice, yet it governs how much work is in flight rather than who chooses it; a limited board still has one person dealing out tickets every Monday.
questions.concept: Self-organizing teams and pull-based work selection
questions.question: An agile practitioner joins a Kanban team at a payroll services company. The newly appointed team lead prepares a spreadsheet every Monday assigning each ticket on the board to a named person for the week. Team members comply without comment, but throughput has declined and daily conversations have gone quiet. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Analyze throughput trends first to confirm the weekly spreadsheet is really the cause before raising the practice with a newly appointed lead
Suggest the lead keep the spreadsheet but size each person's assignments to their capacity, so the declining throughput recovers
Coach the team lead on letting members pull their own work from the board, explaining how pull-based selection builds ownership and flow
Introduce WIP limits on the board so work stops piling up, since limiting flow restores throughput without disturbing how tickets get assigned

questions.explanation: A backlog is a living, ordered list of what the product still needs, not an archive of every request ever made. Bringing the accountable product owner and stakeholders together to test aged items against the current product goal removes waste at its source, keeps the decision with the people who own value, and gives the team a reason for anything that remains. Reordering by value score leaves 190 dead items in the list, where they still consume attention and still appear in searches and reports; the canceled-initiative items would score poorly yet linger indefinitely. Auto-deleting on an age rule strips the product owner of a value judgment and could discard something genuinely valuable that simply has not been scheduled, replacing the conversation with a mechanical trigger. Doubling refinement frequency spends more of the team's capacity discussing work that should not exist, treating an unmaintained backlog as though it were a capacity shortage.
questions.concept: Backlog hygiene — pruning aged items against the current product goal
questions.question: A team maintaining a municipal permit portal holds a weekly refinement session. The backlog contains 340 items; the oldest 190 have not been touched in more than a year and include feature requests from a council initiative that was canceled. Refinement regularly runs long because the team debates whether to keep or reword these old items. A new team member asks why they are being discussed at all. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Reorder the whole backlog by business value score so the stale items settle to the bottom and remain available if the canceled council initiative is ever revived
Agree a rule that any item untouched for six months is removed automatically, so refinement time is never spent debating aged requests again
Facilitate a session where the product owner and stakeholders decide which of the aged items still serve the current product goal, and remove the rest
Split refinement into two shorter sessions each week so there is enough time for both the near-term items and the aged ones the team keeps rewording

questions.explanation: A lightweight, team-owned set of readiness signals gives refinement an explicit target — the conversation ends when the item is clear enough to start, not when the clock runs out — and it exposes exactly which information (retention rules, sample payloads, demonstration approach) is repeatedly missing. Bringing a data-retention specialist to every session is the strongest alternative and would answer one of the three recurring gaps at source, but it commits a scarce expert to a weekly meeting while the sample payloads and the demonstration approach stay unresolved, and it treats one symptom rather than the missing shared standard. Setting a target of two iterations' worth of refined items measures how much has been refined, not whether any of it is clear; with no agreed meaning for refined, the target is met by items that still collapse on the first day. Pulling unclear items in and resolving them mid-iteration pushes discovery after commitment, which inflates rework and makes the iteration goal unreliable.
questions.concept: Backlog refinement effectiveness and contextual readiness criteria
questions.question: An insurance claims platform team holds a 90-minute refinement session each week. The same items are re-debated in consecutive sessions, and on the first day of each iteration the team still discovers that top-ranked items lack data-retention rules, sample claim payloads, or an agreed way to demonstrate them. The product owner is frustrated that refinement "never sticks." What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Invite a data-retention specialist to every refinement session, so the rules that keep going missing are answered on the spot instead of being rediscovered on the first day of the iteration
Set a target of two iterations' worth of refined items in the backlog and track it at every planning session, so the team always starts an iteration with prepared work waiting
Facilitate the team and product owner in agreeing a short, shared set of readiness signals that an item should meet before it is pulled into an iteration, then refine against those signals
Have the team pull the top-ranked items anyway and settle the open questions with the product owner during the iteration, since answers come faster once the work is actually under way

questions.explanation: The log tells one consistent story: the dispute settled by decree reopened three weeks later and produced retrospective tension, the parked issue festered into multiplying workarounds, and the split-the-difference coverage threshold is followed by no one — while the single facilitated, team-built agreement is the only outcome still holding. That evidence points to coaching the team toward collaborative resolution and digging into why the API dispute keeps returning. Reading the record as conflict avoidance is the strongest rival interpretation, since one issue was parked, but these disputes are being raised and settled badly rather than dodged, so a safety-building program would treat a problem the log does not show. Blaming thin working agreements and writing detailed decision rules treats reopening as a documentation gap, when the coverage threshold nobody follows shows that written rules without agreement do not hold. Coaching the lead to rule sooner confuses speed of closure with durability; his ruling is the outcome that reopened.
questions.concept: Conflict management modes and durability of resolution
questions.question: An agile practitioner reviews the conflict log shown in the exhibit. Based on this record, what should the practitioner conclude?
choices: The pattern shows a team that avoids conflict rather than one that manages it poorly, so the practitioner should build the psychological safety that lets real disagreements surface at all

Items keep reopening because the team's working agreements lack detail, so the practitioner should have the team write explicit decision rules covering each of the topics that keeps returning to the log
The lead closes disputes faster than the team manages on its own, so the practitioner should coach him to rule sooner on any disagreement that stays open longer than a couple of days
Outcomes reached by ruling, parking, and splitting the difference are not holding; the team needs help reaching genuinely collaborative resolutions, starting with the root cause of the API dispute

questions.explanation: The flat, non-negotiable language marks the one-click attachment as a basic or must-be need: its absence causes strong dissatisfaction, its presence earns almost no credit, so it should be satisfied adequately and no further. The unprompted excitement about the anomaly overlay is the signature of an attractive need, where discretionary investment buys differentiation. Calling the overlay a performance attribute and polishing both until they beat every competitor misreads the curve: performance attributes scale with how much you deliver, and nobody had imagined the overlay at all. Treating both as basic because they came up in the same interviews ignores the language staff used, which is where the categories are read. Refining the attachment until staff describe it enthusiastically, while holding the overlay until clinics ask for it by name, labels the attachment correctly and is the strongest wrong answer — but gold-plating a must-be need earns nothing, and delighters are by definition never requested by name.
questions.concept: Kano model applied to backlog investment decisions
questions.question: During discovery interviews for a veterinary imaging product, clinic staff describe attaching a scan to the patient record in one click in flat, unenthusiastic terms — "obviously it has to do that; if it didn't I'd throw the software out" — while they become animated about an automatic anomaly-highlighting overlay that none of them had previously imagined. Applying the Kano model to shape the backlog, what is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: The anomaly overlay is a performance attribute whose value rises in proportion to how well it works, so the team should keep investing in both it and the one-click attachment until each one outperforms every competing product.

Both capabilities are basic expectations because clinic staff raised them in the same interviews, so each should be delivered to the same high standard and further discovery deferred until the release has shipped.

The one-click attachment is a basic expectation: build it to a good-enough standard and direct the surplus effort into the anomaly overlay, whose absence would not be missed but whose presence could differentiate the product.

The one-click attachment is a basic expectation, so the team should keep refining it until staff describe it enthusiastically, and hold the anomaly overlay until several clinics have asked for that capability by name.

questions.explanation: Convening the team and the stakeholder to assess value and urgency, then reordering the work, treats the external change as new information to harness for the customer's advantage — the essence of welcoming change even late in delivery. Finishing all committed work first honors a commitment made before the carrier changed the rules; agile teams re-plan when reality moves rather than protecting a plan that is now partly obsolete. Producing the written impact report before anything is reordered is the strongest distractor, because the stakeholder's request is reasonable and analysis has real value — but it puts a document ahead of the conversation that would produce the same understanding faster, and a Kanban team can reorder at its next replenishment without a formal study. Asking the vendor relationship manager to press the carrier for a delay resists the change instead of adapting to it, and stakes the release on a third party the team does not control.
questions.concept: Responding to change over following a plan
questions.question: A Kanban team maintaining a logistics platform learns that a major shipping carrier has unexpectedly changed its API authentication scheme, which will break a customer-facing feature scheduled to ship in three weeks. Two developers argue the team should finish the currently committed work first because the carrier change "was not in the plan," while a key stakeholder demands an immediate written impact report. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Have the team finish its committed work first and pull the carrier change at the next replenishment, honoring the commitments it has already made
Produce the written impact report the stakeholder is asking for before anything is reordered, so the decision rests on a documented analysis
Bring the team and the stakeholder together to assess the value and urgency of responding to the carrier change, and reorder the upcoming work accordingly
Ask the vendor relationship manager to press the carrier for a delay to its authentication rollout so the current feature can still ship on its committed date

questions.explanation: The exhibit shows the reported-complete line rising (30→36) while points meeting the full definition of done fall (28→16) and carried-forward defects grow tenfold (2→22): the gap between claimed and true progress widens every iteration, meaning the celebrated velocity is inflated by hidden undone work. The genuinely-improving reading looks only at the first column and calls a tenfold defect increase 'variation,' which the steady four-iteration trend contradicts. Relaxing the definition of done would make the columns converge by redefining reality — it hides the gap rather than closing it, the opposite of transparency. Blaming testers and inserting a QA sign-off gate adds a control step before diagnosing the cause, and undone work is a whole-team quality problem, not one role's failure.
questions.concept: Hidden undone work — interpreting radiator data against the definition of done
questions.question: At a hybrid program's quarterly review, a sponsor congratulates a team because 'reported velocity has climbed four iterations in a row.' The agile practitioner shows the data above from the team's radiator. Based on the exhibit, what is the MOST accurate interpretation?
choices: Testing capacity has not kept pace with development, so adding a separate quality sign-off gate before items are reported complete would restore the accuracy of the reported numbers
Throughput is genuinely improving and the rising defect count is ordinary variation that the team will absorb once the current run of high-value features is finished
The definition of done has become too demanding for this team's context and should be relaxed so that the reported and the truly finished figures converge once again
Reported progress is increasingly overstated — truly finished work is falling while undone work and defects accumulate, and the team should surface this gap and address its causes

questions.explanation: The telemetry says this product's dominant risk is building features nobody uses, and the customer relationship is the asset worth protecting. Turning the request into an outcome hypothesis, shipping a thin slice to that account plus comparable accounts, and steering on observed adoption engages the customer as a partner, delivers value quickly, keeps options open for a team at its capacity ceiling, and generates the evidence that the debt-versus-features conversation needs. Accepting the full funded module ignores the eight-in-eleven adoption record and commits scarce capacity on the strength of revenue weight rather than demonstrated value. Re-scoring the entire backlog is big-bang analysis that stalls the customer conversation for weeks and produces stakeholder opinions rather than usage data. Refusing until the debt is repaid is a technically defensible instinct but withholds all value, treats debt repayment as a prerequisite rather than something interleaved with a thin slice, and takes the prioritization decision away from the product owner and customer.
questions.concept: Outcome hypotheses and validated demand with a major customer
questions.question: A subscription analytics product has one account representing 28 percent of revenue. That customer asks for a bespoke workflow module and offers to co-fund it. Product telemetry shows only 3 of the last 11 shipped features are used by more than 10 percent of the customer base. The product owner is inclined to accept immediately, the team is already at a sustainable-pace ceiling, and known technical debt in the reporting engine is slowing every change. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Support accepting the co-funded request and placing it at the top of the backlog, since a paying customer's stated need is the clearest value signal the team has and the funding covers the extra work

Convene a stakeholder prioritization workshop and re-score the whole backlog on value, risk and effort before any commitment is made to the customer, so the decision rests on a complete comparison of everything waiting

Have the product owner and customer restate the request as a measurable outcome, release the thinnest usable slice to that account and two similar accounts, and let observed usage decide what is built next
Advise the product owner to decline until the reporting-engine debt is repaid, since the team is already at its sustainable ceiling and throughput will fall further under a new stream of bespoke work

questions.explanation: Asking what the goal looks like to the analyst and inviting a self-chosen first step is coaching: the coach uses open questions to help the person define success and generate their own path, working from the belief that the answers already live with the individual. Sharing how the practitioner personally built the same expertise and directing the analyst to repeat it is mentoring — valuable, but it transfers the mentor's experience instead of drawing out the analyst's own thinking. Enrolling the analyst in a vendor course is training: transferring a defined body of knowledge through instruction, appropriate for a skill gap but not a coaching interaction. Writing the growth plan and inspecting progress monthly is directive management — the practitioner owns both the plan and the accountability, leaving the analyst executing someone else's roadmap, which is the opposite of a coaching stance.
questions.concept: Coaching versus mentoring versus training stances in growing expertise
questions.question: A data analyst tells the agile practitioner, "I want to become the team's go-to person for pipeline reliability, but I don't know where to start." The practitioner wants to respond from a purely COACHING stance. Which response reflects that stance?
choices: "What would being the go-to person look like for you, and what is one small step you could take this iteration to move toward it?"
"When I ran pipeline reliability, I began by reading a year of incident history, so start there and bring me whatever patterns you find next week."
"I'll book you onto the vendor's three-day reliability engineering course next month, and we can talk the role over once you have finished it."
"Here is the path I would follow: shadow the on-call rotation for a month, then own one alert yourself, and I'll review your progress monthly."

questions.explanation: Cause and effect knowable only in hindsight is the signature of the complex domain, where the fitting response is probe–sense–respond: run cheap, safe-to-fail probes, read the customer signal, and amplify what works — exactly what short experimental feedback loops provide. Thorough expert analysis before building fits the complicated domain, where cause and effect can be discovered through analysis; here there is nothing yet to analyze, because the relationships do not exist until customers interact with something real. Adopting a competitor's template assumes an obvious-domain best practice exists, but the scenario states there are no comparable offerings to copy. Detailed upfront decomposition with conformance tracking is predictive thinking suited to stable, well-understood work; in a complex context it measures obedience to a plan that was guesswork the day it was written.
questions.concept: Cynefin complex domain: probe–sense–respond via safe-to-fail experiments
questions.question: A team is asked to build a recommendation capability for a product category the company has never sold, in a market with no comparable offerings. Cause-and-effect relationships between features and customer behavior will be knowable only in hindsight. Given this context, which approach is MOST appropriate?
choices: Engage domain experts to analyze the problem thoroughly and design the correct solution before building
Adopt the practices behind a competitor's successful recommendation system as a proven template
Run a series of small, safe-to-fail experiments and amplify whatever shows a positive customer response
Decompose the work into detailed tasks up front and manage delivery by tracking conformance to the plan

questions.explanation: Regulatory and privacy requirements are value to the customer and the organization, and deferring unfamiliar work into a single terminal release concentrates every unknown at the point of least remaining schedule. Slicing consent, export, and deletion into thin increments and having the privacy advisor validate each one converts a compliance cliff into a series of small, checkable deliveries. Moving the hardening release to month three adds contingency around a plan whose real defect is its shape; a buffer on a big batch is not a managed risk. Spiking the three areas now is the strongest alternative, since it attacks the team's inexperience early — but it buys a better estimate for a deferred batch instead of validated slices. Having the advisor write detailed acceptance criteria up front turns collaboration into a handoff and freezes an interpretation before anything tests it.
questions.concept: Slicing and sequencing increments to validate obligations early
questions.question: A companion app for an implantable cardiac monitor must comply with a new data-privacy regulation that takes legal effect in five months. The regulation requires granular consent management, patient data export, and verified deletion. The product owner has placed all three at the bottom of the backlog, reasoning that they generate no revenue, and has scheduled a four-week "compliance hardening" release in month four. The team has never built consent or deletion flows in this product. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Accept the sequencing but ask the product owner to move the four-week hardening release into month three, so there is a full month of contingency before the regulation takes legal effect.
Ask the team to spike the consent, export, and deletion work now so that the four-week hardening release can be estimated accurately and defended with evidence when the release plan is next reviewed.
Facilitate a session with the product owner, a privacy advisor, and the team to treat the regulatory needs as customer value, slice them into thin releasable increments, and validate each one early.
Have a privacy advisor write detailed acceptance criteria for the three regulatory items now, so the team can build them correctly and quickly once the hardening release begins in month four.

questions.explanation: The defining symptom is that the item spans roughly three iterations with no way to show progress partway, which is the small characteristic failing; the remedy is vertical splitting into thin slices, each demonstrable and each carrying some value, so feedback arrives every iteration instead of once a quarter. The valuable characteristic is not the clearest failure here — the item does state a business outcome, and adding a numeric target would not make it deliverable. Sizing is not the problem either: the team produced an estimate of roughly three iterations, so a spike would delay work the team already understands well enough to plan. The presence of named components is a secondary concern at best — they read as scope rather than imposed design, and simply deleting the detail would leave an item that is still far too large to demonstrate.
questions.concept: INVEST applied to decomposition
questions.question: A team refining a warehouse robotics backlog is looking at the item: "As a floor supervisor, I want the full pick-path optimization engine, including multi-zone routing, battery-aware scheduling, congestion avoidance, and the new operator dashboard, so that throughput improves." The team estimates it at roughly three iterations of work and cannot describe how they would demonstrate it partway. Applying INVEST, which characteristic is MOST clearly violated, and what follows from that?
choices: Valuable — the item names no measurable throughput target, so a numeric goal belongs in the story text before the team accepts the item into an iteration
Estimable — the team cannot size the work at all, so a research spike should replace the item on the board until an estimate becomes possible for the routing work
Small — the item exceeds what can be completed and demonstrated within a single iteration, so it should be split along thin slices that each deliver observable behavior
Negotiable — the item fixes specific solution components up front, so the technical detail should be stripped out and left for the team to settle while the work is under way

questions.explanation: Rework after release combined with high proxy confidence points to a feedback loop that never reaches the actual users; putting supervisors in front of the working increment produces direct, evidence-based reactions while keeping the analyst engaged as a partner rather than displacing her. Adding a satisfaction question to the analyst's acceptance checklist measures the same falling signal one step earlier without explaining it, and it still asks the proxy to judge on the supervisors' behalf. Running a root-cause review of the two reworked features is the strongest rival — the rework is real evidence and the review would probably surface the missing user contact — but it studies two past items while the loop that produced them keeps running. Sending the analyst to observe supervisors on the warehouse floor genuinely improves her information, yet what reaches the team is still her summary of what she saw, a week later, rather than a supervisor reacting to working software in front of the people who built it.
questions.concept: Direct user feedback versus proxy customer representation
questions.question: A logistics team demonstrates its increment every two weeks to a business analyst who represents warehouse supervisors. Satisfaction scores from the supervisors themselves have fallen for two releases, and two recently accepted features were substantially reworked after go-live. The analyst is well liked and says she is confident she knows what the supervisors need. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Add a satisfaction question to the analyst's acceptance checklist so falling scores surface before a feature is accepted
Run a root-cause review of the two features reworked after go-live so the acceptance criteria that missed can be tightened
Have the analyst spend a week observing supervisors on the warehouse floor and report back at the next review
Invite one or two warehouse supervisors to the review, alongside the analyst, to operate the increment themselves

questions.explanation: Little's Law gives average cycle time = average WIP / average throughput, so today the team runs 18 / 6 = 3 weeks. Holding throughput at 6 per week and targeting 2 weeks requires an average WIP of 2 x 6 = 12 items, which the team can steer directly by lowering its WIP limits. Pushing for 9 completions per week through extended hours satisfies the arithmetic but does so by burning people rather than improving the system; it is unsustainable and typically reduces throughput once defects and turnover appear. Raising WIP to 24 moves cycle time the wrong way — at 6 per week it would stretch average cycle time to 4 weeks. Reducing WIP to 3 items misapplies the formula by substituting the current cycle time for the target throughput; 3 items at 6 per week implies a half-week cycle time and would leave most of the team idle.
questions.concept: Practical application of Little's Law to set WIP limits
questions.question: A platform support team's Kanban metrics for the last quarter show an average of 18 items in progress and an average throughput of 6 items completed per week, with a stable arrival rate and no major process changes. Stakeholders have asked whether average cycle time can be brought down to roughly two weeks. Applying Little's Law to the team's own data, which action follows most directly?
choices: Keep WIP at 18 items and lift throughput to 9 per week instead.
Increase average WIP to about 24 items to start more requests.
Reduce average WIP to about 12 items while protecting the current throughput.
Reduce average WIP to about 3 items, matching the three-week cycle time.

questions.explanation: Impediment removal starts at the lowest level that can actually solve it, and it starts with data: the aging of the eleven blocked cards and the delayed customer release make the cost visible, and the other program is the only party that can change the booking pattern. Requesting funding for a second chamber may eventually prove to be the right capital decision, but it takes months, makes a case nobody has evidenced yet, and leaves eleven aging cards waiting in the meantime. Starting the next feature keeps people busy while raising work in progress, lengthening cycle time and burying the impediment under fresh inventory instead of resolving it. Asking the customer to accept the cards on bench-test evidence with chamber verification deferred until after release trades away the definition of done on a product whose entire value is temperature accuracy, and it puts unverified firmware in the field to solve what is really a scheduling problem.
questions.concept: Blocked-item aging and collaborative impediment removal on a shared constraint
questions.question: A firmware team building cold-chain temperature sensors shares an environmental test chamber with a hardware program in the same company. For nine straight days the chamber has been booked solid by that program. Eleven cards now sit in the team's "Ready for Chamber Test" column, the oldest aging twelve days, and none of them can be released to the customer until verified. The team lead suggests simply starting the next feature while they wait. What is the BEST response?
choices: Take the blocked-card ages and the resulting delivery impact to the other program's team and work out a shared chamber schedule with them.
Request funding for a second environmental chamber so the two teams stop competing for a single rig, and hold the eleven waiting cards until it arrives.
Start the next feature so the team keeps moving, and verify the eleven waiting cards in one batch once the chamber is free again.
Ask the customer to accept the aged cards on bench-test evidence, with full chamber verification completed after the release ships.

questions.explanation: A risk-adjusted backlog sequences high-value, high-uncertainty work early so that learning arrives while there is still time and money to respond; a time-boxed spike on the actual target hardware converts speculation into evidence within days, and a risk burndown keeps the shrinking — or stubborn — exposure visible between monthly meetings. A pre-mortem is a legitimate technique, but it generates more hypotheses rather than evidence and leaves the risky work sitting in the final iteration, where a surprise has nowhere to go. A contingency buffer conceals the risk inside the schedule instead of reducing it, and it will be consumed by whatever problem arrives first. Assigning one engineer to research the library off to the side delays feedback until the next monthly meeting, isolates the learning in a single person's head, and produces an opinion rather than a measurement on the hardware that matters.
questions.concept: Risk-adjusted backlog, spikes, risk burndown
questions.question: A satellite ground-station firmware team has committed to a high-value feature that depends on an unproven open-source compression library. No one on the team has used it, and the vendor's published benchmarks were run on different hardware. The team's risk register is reviewed at a monthly program meeting, and the feature is currently sequenced for the last iteration before the release. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Facilitate a pre-mortem for the release so the team surfaces plausible failure modes, record each one in the risk register with a named mitigation owner, and review the compression risk at the next programme meeting.
Keep the current sequence and size a contingency buffer into the release forecast that covers the compression work, so the committed date still holds if the library underperforms on target hardware.

Propose reordering the backlog so the risky work is attempted early, beginning with a time-boxed spike that exercises the library on the target hardware, and show the remaining uncertainty on a risk burndown.
Ask the most experienced engineer to evaluate the library between iterations and bring a recommendation to the monthly programme meeting, so the team's iteration capacity is not spent on exploration.

questions.explanation: This is a systems-thinking situation: the churn is a symptom, and the best first move is to understand the system producing it. Exploring the drivers with the product director may reveal genuinely volatile market conditions, in which case the team tailors its cadence or moves toward a flow-based approach so change becomes an input rather than a disruption. Holding the sprint boundary firm is defensible Scrum mechanics and would restore some stability, but it treats change as the enemy and can leave real value waiting while the volatility goes unexamined. Reserving unplanned capacity every sprint absorbs the shocks and may suit the team later, though applied now it normalizes the churn and quietly shrinks planned capacity. Shortening sprints to one week prescribes before diagnosing; priorities moving every few days will break weekly plans too.
questions.concept: Systems thinking and process tailoring in response to high-volatility stakeholder demand
questions.question: At a logistics firm, a product director reprioritizes the backlog every few days, and a Scrum team's sprint plans rarely survive until the review; throughput and morale are both falling. The delivery lead asks the agile practitioner to "fix the stakeholder." Several responses are technically possible. Which is the BEST?
choices: Hold the sprint boundary firm and agree with the product director that new priorities can enter only at the next planning session, so the team is able to finish what it starts
Coach the team to hold a slice of unplanned capacity in every sprint so that the director's frequent changes can be absorbed without disturbing committed work
Explore with the product director what is driving the frequent shifts, then adapt the team's planning cadence or move toward a flow-based approach that can absorb them
Shorten the sprints from two weeks to one so that no newly raised priority waits more than a few days for an entry point and each plan survives to its review

questions.explanation: The cost of every defect here is amplified by the three-month gap between building and validating. Bringing the controller into an end-of-iteration review of a small set of finished calculations against real sales data shrinks that loop so errors surface while the change that caused them is still fresh — frequent inspection of working software with the person who knows what correct means. An automated regression suite over historical commission data is the strongest alternative and worth building, but it can only protect behavior the team has already encoded correctly; it cannot reveal that the team misunderstood a commission rule in the first place, which is what quarter-end keeps exposing. Asking the controller to document every rule in full detail is predictive thinking, since the edge cases emerge in real data. Tagging each merged change with the rule it affects improves the archaeology after the fact while leaving the three-month delay untouched.
questions.concept: Iteration-cadence stakeholder validation of working software
questions.question: An XP team automates commission calculations for a sales organization. The finance controller validates the calculations only during quarter-end close, and every error found there takes weeks to trace back through dozens of merged changes. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Work with the controller to validate a small set of finished calculations against real sales data at the end of every iteration
Build an automated regression suite over historical commission data so calculation errors are caught long before the quarter-end close
Ask the controller to document the commission rules in full detail so the team can verify its own calculations without waiting
Tag every merged change with the commission rule it affects so errors found at quarter-end can be traced back within hours

questions.explanation: The team has outgrown a directive style, but approval-seeking habits persist because delegation was never made explicit; naming the decision types, agreeing ownership visibly through delegation levels or a delegation board, and coaching through the first real decisions transfers authority deliberately and safely — the situational-leadership move for a team at this maturity. Pointing to the working agreement and simply declining further approval requests is defensible, since the authority is already theirs on paper, but it swings from directing to withdrawal and removes support at the moment new decision habits are forming. Continuing to approve while praising the team's judgment publicly rewards the dependence and blocks growth exactly when the team is ready. Rewriting the agreement with detailed release and tooling criteria adds a rulebook rather than authority: the team already has a written agreement it does not act on, and criteria the practitioner authors still say she defines a correct decision.
questions.concept: Situational leadership and explicit delegation as team maturity grows
questions.question: An agile practitioner has spent six months with a warehouse-automation team that was new to Lean delivery. Early on she was deliberately directive — teaching flow concepts and making several process calls herself. The team is now technically strong, meets its commitments, and its working agreement says the team owns release scheduling and tooling choices — yet members still bring those decisions to her for approval. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Point the team to the working agreement, remind members it already grants them release and tooling authority, and decline further approval requests from now on
Review decision types with the team, agree explicitly which ones the team now owns (for example with a delegation board), and coach them through the first few
Keep approving the release and tooling calls while praising the team's judgment publicly, since visible endorsement builds the confidence members still lack
Rewrite the working agreement with detailed criteria for release scheduling and tooling choices, so members can check their own decisions against it before acting

questions.explanation: The unreliable tests are the root impediment, and every visible symptom traces back to them: re-running until green teaches the team to ignore red, the 68-minute wait drives batching, and larger batches guarded by a distrusted safety net explain the doubled escape rate. Because the fix costs capacity, the decision belongs with the product owner — surfacing the escape-rate evidence and time-boxing a diagnosis effort produces an informed value trade-off rather than a unilateral technical detour, while leaving room to fix the worst offenders first. Quarantining the failures into a nightly job restores a green pipeline by deleting the signal: the same unreliability persists, feedback on it slides hours later, and the escape rate is likely to worsen; the parallel plea for frequent commits also ignores that it was the wait, not developer willingness, that caused the batching. Splitting into a fast gate plus a full post-merge suite is a genuinely sound practice and the most tempting alternative, but applied now it spreads 6% unreliability across both tiers — a flaky fast gate still cannot be trusted, so reliability has to be fixed before tiering buys anything. Shipping on a manual regression pass and deferring the fix trades an automated safety net for a slower manual one at the precise moment defects are escaping, and next-iteration promises to fix pipelines rarely survive the next feature request.
questions.concept: Test unreliability as a systemic impediment; CI feedback trust and batch size
questions.question: A payments team runs a continuous-delivery pipeline. Over three months the suite has grown to 4,100 automated tests taking 68 minutes, and roughly 6% fail intermittently without any code change. Developers now re-run failed builds until green — averaging 2.4 runs per commit — and two developers have started batching a day's work into a single large commit to avoid the wait. The production defect escape rate has doubled this quarter. In the retrospective, the technical lead proposes quarantining all intermittently failing tests into a nightly job so the main pipeline goes green again, and separately asks the team to commit more frequently. Several developers agree; the product owner wants the two blocked customer stories released this week. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Support quarantining the intermittent tests and reinforce the practice of small, frequent commits, so the pipeline reports green again within days and the two customer stories still reach production on the cadence the product owner already expects

Treat the unreliable tests as the impediment with the largest downstream cost and facilitate the team in ranking a time-boxed effort to diagnose and fix them ahead of new feature work, with the product owner in the conversation

Split the suite so a fast subset gates every commit while the full sixty-eight-minute run happens nightly after merge, restoring rapid feedback on every commit without asking the product owner to give up any feature capacity this iteration

Ship the two customer stories behind a manual regression pass this week, then put pipeline reliability at the very top of the next iteration's backlog, so the commitment already made to the customer is honored on the agreed schedule

questions.explanation: The purpose of arranging a map as a backbone of activities with options ranked beneath is to let releases be sliced horizontally: a thin cut across every activity gives a walking skeleton in which a real patient can enroll, submit a prescription, get it verified, scheduled, tracked and reordered — exactly what a pilot must exercise. Building the two leftmost activities to full depth produces polished enrolment for patients who then cannot receive anything; depth without breadth leaves the journey broken. Cherry-picking the highest individually scored stories ignores the sequential dependency of the journey and typically leaves gaps that make the release unusable, since value in a journey is realized only when the user can finish it. Filling the release with whatever fits under a capacity line optimizes for volume of stories rather than a completable experience, and it lets capacity, rather than the user's journey, decide what the product does.
questions.concept: Story map release slicing and the walking skeleton
questions.question: A team working on a pharmacy home-delivery service has built a story map: across the top, the user activities in sequence — enroll, upload prescription, verify insurance, schedule delivery, track shipment, reorder — and beneath each activity, candidate stories arranged from most essential down to most elaborate. The product owner wants a first release for a 200-patient pilot. Applying story mapping correctly, how should that release be sliced?
choices: Build the two leftmost activities, enroll and upload prescription, to their full depth and release those first, because a pilot patient meets them earliest and they must feel complete from day one.

Cut a thin horizontal slice across the whole backbone — the most essential story beneath every activity — so a pilot patient can complete the journey end to end, then deepen the slices in later releases.

Select the stories carrying the highest individual value scores, wherever they happen to sit on the map, and release exactly that set, so the pilot returns the greatest value for the effort the team spends.

Take whatever stories fit beneath the team's estimated capacity line for the release, whichever activity they sit under, so the pilot ships on its planned date with the greatest number of stories the team can finish.

questions.explanation: Flow efficiency is value-adding time divided by total lead time: 2.5 divided by 14 is about 18%, meaning roughly four-fifths of elapsed time is waiting. When waiting dominates, attacking queues, handoffs, and work-in-progress limits yields far more than optimizing the already small touch time. Declaring 18% healthy and responding by starting more items in parallel raises work in progress, which lengthens queues and makes lead time worse. Reading the gap as an estimating problem misinterprets a flow measurement as a forecasting error; smaller items may help flow, but re-estimating removes no waiting. Concluding that more people are needed ignores that capacity sits idle relative to elapsed time, so the constraint is queueing and handoff delay rather than headcount.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency calculation and value-stream waiting time
questions.question: A Kanban team's board shows an average lead time of 14 days per item. When the team maps the value stream, they find that the total hands-on work across all steps is about 2.5 days; the remainder is items sitting in queues between steps. Which conclusion best supports the team's next improvement decision?
choices: Flow efficiency is roughly 18%, so the largest gains will come from reducing queues and handoffs rather than from making work steps faster
Flow efficiency is roughly 18%, which is healthy for knowledge work, so the team should raise throughput by starting more items in parallel
The gap indicates that the team's estimates are inaccurate, so re-estimating the backlog in smaller units should be the first step
Lead time cannot be improved without adding people, because the hands-on work already consumes the available capacity

questions.explanation: Kano analysis describes the shape of the satisfaction response, distinguishing basic expectations whose absence causes dissatisfaction from performance attributes and delighters, which matches the classification of how satisfaction responds to a feature. MoSCoW is a commitment-tier technique used to protect a fixed date by separating what must ship from what is allowed to flex, which matches the commitment-tier description. Dividing cost of delay by duration is an economic sequencing rule that balances the value lost while waiting against the size of the item, which matches the ranking description that favors urgent short items. Story mapping is a spatial visualization of the user's journey with supporting depth stacked beneath each step, which matches the journey-and-slices description; note that it organizes and exposes scope rather than scoring or ranking it, and that is what separates it from the other three.
questions.concept: Distinguishing prioritization, economic sequencing, and visualization techniques
questions.question: A product team is choosing among several backlog techniques for an upcoming refinement workshop. Match each technique (1-4) to the description that best captures what it does (A-D).
pairs: Kano analysis
Classifies features by how customer satisfaction responds to them, separating expected basics from more-is-better attributes and unexpected delighters
MoSCoW
Sorts candidate scope into commitment tiers against a fixed delivery date, so everyone knows what must ship and what is allowed to flex
Cost of delay divided by duration
Ranks items by weighing the value lost for each unit of time an item waits against the effort it takes, so urgent short items are sequenced first
Story mapping
Arranges the backlog as the user's journey across time with supporting detail stacked beneath each step, exposing gaps and coherent release slices

questions.explanation: Splitting by vendor makes each piece independent of the others, small enough to estimate, and — most importantly — valuable and demonstrable on its own, because dispatchers see real vehicles as soon as the first vendor is connected. Adding an all-four regression criterion does make the item testable but leaves it large, coupled to every vendor, and unable to deliver anything until the last one is done. Converting it into technical tasks slices the work horizontally, so no slice is independently valuable to a dispatcher, and assigning tasks to individuals erodes the negotiability and shared ownership the item needs. Giving it the largest size and spreading it over three iterations plans around the problem rather than fixing it: the item is still not small, still not demonstrable early, and the estimate remains a guess.
questions.concept: INVEST characteristics and vertical story splitting
questions.question: During refinement, a fleet-logistics team is looking at this item: "As a dispatcher, I want the system to work with all of our telematics vendors so that I can see every vehicle." Four vendors expose different APIs, the team cannot agree on an estimate, and nothing can be shown to a dispatcher until all four connections exist. Which change would most improve this item against the INVEST characteristics?
choices: Add the acceptance criterion that all four vendor integrations pass regression testing, so the item becomes clearly testable as written
Split it into one item per vendor, each delivering dispatcher-visible vehicle positions for that vendor's portion of the fleet.
Break it into four technical tasks: adapter, schema mapping, polling, and error handling, then give each to a developer
Estimate it at the team's largest size and spread it across three iterations to fit the release plan

questions.explanation: Acknowledging the disagreement and then facilitating both members in examining the flow data and the original intent of the criteria turns a personal clash into collaborative problem solving: the real question is whether an explicit policy still serves flow, and the team, not any individual, should answer it from evidence. Asking the service delivery manager to rule converts a solvable team conflict into an escalation and teaches the team that disputes get settled above them. Redrafting the criteria after the meeting and circulating them has the practitioner prescribing a fix before anyone knows whether the criteria are genuinely outdated, and it sidelines the two people who care most. Reinforcing the current criteria and booking the disagreement for the retrospective is the most defensible alternative — policies should not bend mid-meeting — but it quietly rules against one member and leaves a personalized conflict hanging in front of a now-silent team.
questions.concept: Collaborative problem solving over explicit workflow policies
questions.question: During a Kanban replenishment meeting, a quality analyst openly accuses a developer of repeatedly pulling items into In Progress before the entry criteria are met. The developer snaps back that the criteria are outdated and are slowing the whole board down. The exchange grows tense and the rest of the team goes quiet. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Ask the service delivery manager to rule on whether the entry criteria still apply, since an explicit policy needs a single accountable owner if the board is to stay consistent
Redraft the entry criteria after the meeting so they are unambiguous, then circulate that version for comment, removing the ambiguity that set the two members against each other
Acknowledge the disagreement, then facilitate both members in examining the flow data and the original intent of the criteria so the team can decide whether the policy should change
Reinforce the current criteria for now and put the disagreement on the next retrospective agenda, so replenishment finishes on time and the policy still gets a proper review later

questions.explanation: This conflict has escalated past a technical disagreement into personal antagonism that is already changing how others pair, so the best move is a facilitated conversation in which both developers surface the intent behind their testing approaches and co-create working agreements — the collaborating mode, which resolves the underlying disagreement and repairs the working relationship. Asking each of them privately to stop rewriting the other's tests and to keep commit messages neutral is the most reasonable alternative and would improve the tone quickly, but it polices behavior without ever examining the disagreement driving it, so the substance stays unresolved and the avoidance continues. Having the technical coach pick a standard and enforce it through the pipeline may settle the artifact but not the animosity, and it teaches the team that its conflicts get decided for it. Moving them onto different feature areas is the avoiding mode: the friction leaves view while the tension keeps shaping behavior.
questions.concept: Conflict management modes — collaborating versus avoiding and forcing
questions.question: On an XP team building fare-calculation software for a ferry operator, developer Mira keeps deleting and rewriting Jonah's characterization tests, calling them "brittle noise" in her commit messages. Jonah has begun reverting her changes, their pull-request comments have turned sarcastic, and other pairs are quietly avoiding working with either of them. The agile practitioner notices the pattern during a code-review session. What should the practitioner do next?
choices: Ask each of them privately to stop rewriting the other's tests and to keep their commit messages neutral, so their code-review exchanges improve straight away
Invite Mira and Jonah to a facilitated conversation where each explains the intent behind their testing approach and they agree on shared working agreements
Ask the technical coach to choose which testing style becomes the team standard and to enforce it through the continuous integration pipeline
Move Mira and Jonah onto different feature areas so their commits no longer overlap and the other pairs are willing to work with either of them

questions.explanation: Exploring the program manager's underlying concern while defending the honest radiator is best: it treats him as a collaborator rather than an adversary, and it reframes the blocked items as evidence — executives who see six items stalled on a vendor are exactly the people who can act on that dependency. Building a simplified executive view alongside the real wall creates two versions of the truth, and trust in everything the team reports collapses the moment the gap is noticed. Relabeling the six items as awaiting vendor input is the most tempting move because the wording is literally accurate, yet it dresses work that cannot finish as work in motion and quietly removes the pressure to resolve the dependency. Taking the lane down and circulating a written summary does disclose the problem, but it substitutes a curated note for live evidence and concedes that the board may be edited for an audience.
questions.concept: Protecting information radiator integrity under stakeholder pressure
questions.question: A Kanban team at an insurance firm maintains a wall-sized board showing all work, including a Blocked lane that currently holds six items stuck on a third-party data provider.
