Two weeks before a funding review, a program manager asks the team to remove the Blocked lane because visiting executives "will get the wrong impression." What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Build a simplified executive view of the board without the Blocked lane and keep the full wall for the team, so that the team's own transparency is preserved intact
Keep the lane in place but relabel the six items as awaiting vendor input, so the board reads as work in motion rather than as six items the team cannot finish
Explore the program manager's underlying concern, and explain that the visible blockers give executives exactly the evidence they need to act on the vendor dependency
Agree to take the lane down and instead brief the visiting executives on the data-provider dependency in a short written summary circulated ahead of the funding review

questions.explanation: Taking the increment to the actual users closes the feedback loop that matters. The assumptions the team is making are about ward staffing conventions, and charge nurses — not the sponsor — are the people who can confirm or destroy them; meeting them where they work removes the attendance barrier while keeping the sponsor involved. Asking the sponsor to name a nurse manager who signs off each iteration is the strongest alternative, since it creates a named, accountable voice — but sign-off approves a description rather than use of the increment, and one manager is exactly the single source that produced these assumptions. Listing assumptions on the board and confirming by email is one-way reporting nobody tests against working software. An in-app feedback control gathers reports only after release, four iterations of scheduling rules too late.
questions.concept: Increment review and early feedback from actual users
questions.question: A team delivering a hospital shift-swapping app has a running increment after three iterations. The clinical sponsor has repeatedly canceled the iteration review, saying "just send me the release notes, I trust you." The team has now built four iterations of scheduling rules with no direct nurse feedback, and the practitioner notices developers making assumptions about ward staffing conventions during daily coordination. What is the BEST response?
choices: Offer to run a short review on the ward with two or three charge nurses actually using the increment, and invite the sponsor to attend or delegate
Ask the sponsor to name a nurse manager who can sign off the scheduling rules each iteration, so the team has one accountable source of truth
Have the developers list every ward staffing assumption on the board and confirm the list by email each iteration, since the sponsor prefers written updates
Add an in-app feedback control to the increment so nurses can report scheduling problems after release, and review what comes in each iteration

questions.explanation: The strongest response combines emotional intelligence with systems thinking: it honors the vice president's genuine intent, preserves the relationship, uses transparent data to reframe the heroic save as a symptom of work-in-progress overload and late integration, and enlists him as sponsor of the systemic fix. Recruiting more engineers with the same weekend commitment takes the request literally and scales the dysfunction, since adding people to an overloaded, late-integrating system multiplies the overload rather than relieving it. Correcting the record during the review may be accurate but embarrasses a senior leader in front of peers, signals low emotional intelligence, and closes the door to the influence needed to change anything. Capping work in progress and integrating daily is the right underlying work and the closest alternative, yet it leaves the executive's mental model unchallenged for a full release while the department is told to copy the hero, and it declines the sponsorship on offer now.
questions.concept: Hero-culture anti-pattern; emotional intelligence and systems thinking with executives
questions.question: At a quarterly business review, a senior vice president publicly celebrates a developer who spent the entire weekend rescuing a failed release, calls him the model for the department, and asks the agile practitioner to 'find more people like him.' The practitioner knows the emergency was caused by chronic work-in-progress overload and late integration, and that the team is nearing burnout. What is the BEST response?
choices: Take the request at face value and start recruiting engineers with the same commitment, since more hands on the release path is the fastest way to relieve the overload the team feels
Thank the VP for the recognition, then share flow and defect-escape data showing how overload and late integration forced the weekend save, and invite the VP to sponsor fixing those causes
Correct the record during the review by explaining that the weekend rescue came from overload and late integration, so the department does not adopt an avoidable failure as its model
Work with the team to cap work in progress and integrate daily, then show the VP the result once the next release ships without a rescue, so evidence makes the argument

questions.explanation: Delivering a thin, high-value slice and letting real user feedback shape the remaining requirements embodies empiricism: knowledge comes from doing and observing rather than from predicting everything up front, and it speaks directly to the analyst's fear of rework, because misunderstandings surface while they are still cheap to fix. Accepting the sign-off and relying on the existing change-request process keeps the heavyweight gate and turns every discovery into a negotiation, which is contract thinking where collaboration is needed. Having the analyst document the whole enhancement in parallel while the team builds is the strongest alternative, since delivery is not blocked and the organization still gets its record — but it commits the analyst to specifying scope that feedback is about to change, so document and product drift apart and the feared rework returns as documentation churn. Scheduling a two-week requirements workshop simply recreates big design up front on a shorter timescale.
questions.concept: Empiricism vs. predictive up-front analysis
questions.question: An insurance company has just moved its claims-portal team to iterative delivery. A senior business analyst insists that development must not begin on a portal enhancement until every requirement is documented and formally signed off, "the way we've always avoided rework." What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Accept the sign-off, and reassure the analyst that anything the team learns later can still be handled through the organization's existing change-request process
Have the analyst document the whole enhancement in parallel while the team builds, so a complete signed record exists without delivery waiting for it
Suggest the team start with the highest-value slice of the enhancement, deliver it quickly, and use real user feedback to shape the remaining requirements
Schedule a two-week requirements workshop so the analyst can document and sign off the full portal enhancement before the first iteration starts

questions.explanation: Waiting is by far the dominant waste here: items are idle roughly four times longer than they are worked, so the fastest lead-time gain comes from attacking the queue itself. Putting the measured wait time in front of the people who own the work, and then partnering with the hardware lab on a scheduling or policy change, treats the delay as a shared system problem and keeps the improvement with the team. Continuing to pull new cards whenever the bench queue is full feels productive but raises work in progress, which at unchanged throughput lengthens cycle time and converts waiting into more partly done inventory. Asking the lab to reserve weekly slots is the strongest alternative and may well end up part of the answer, but it prescribes one solution before the two groups have looked at the data together, and fixed reservations create idle slots as easily as they remove queues. Adding wait time to the weekly report improves visibility for leadership and removes no wait.
questions.concept: Waiting waste and queue time in a Kanban system
questions.question: A Kanban team building firmware for irrigation controllers records how long each card spends in every column. On average a card is actively worked for 1.4 days and then sits for 6 days in a "Waiting for hardware bench slot" queue between development and verification. The queue column is visible on the board, but no one has ever discussed it; developers simply start new cards so they are never idle. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Have developers keep pulling new cards whenever the bench queue is full, so no development capacity sits idle waiting on verification.
Ask the hardware lab to reserve dedicated bench slots for the team each week so verification stops waiting on shared scheduling.
Bring the touch-time-versus-wait-time data to the team's next flow review and work with the hardware lab on a way to shrink the queue.
Add wait time to the weekly report so that leadership can see the size of the delay and decide whether to fund more bench capacity.

questions.explanation: The disagreement persists because both sides argue from anecdote, so the highest-value move is to replace opinion with evidence — frame each flow as a testable hypothesis, release a minimal version of each to a small user segment, and let measured onboarding completion decide. Running a structured decision workshop where the product owner commits is a reasonable facilitation move and would restart the idle team fastest, but the decision would still rest on the same anecdotes: it resolves the argument without resolving the uncertainty. Building both flows completely behind a feature toggle defers learning until maximum cost has been spent, the opposite of minimizing work to maximize validated learning. Analyzing the existing funnel and prior interviews is the strongest alternative, because existing data is nearly free and should inform the hypotheses — yet neither flow has ever run, so historical data cannot say which of two unbuilt experiences performs better.
questions.concept: Hypothesis-driven development to resolve stakeholder disagreement
questions.question: Two senior stakeholders at a fintech company have argued for six weeks over which of two competing onboarding flows the product should adopt; each cites persuasive customer anecdotes, and the delivery team is partially idle waiting for the decision. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Run a structured decision workshop where both stakeholders present their evidence and the product owner then commits to one flow so the idle delivery team can resume
Build both onboarding flows completely behind a feature toggle so that leadership can compare the two finished experiences before committing the product to either one
Help the team frame each flow as a testable hypothesis and release a minimal version of each to a small user segment, letting measured onboarding completion decide
Analyze the existing onboarding funnel and prior customer interviews to determine which set of anecdotes the current data actually supports before building

questions.explanation: The sponsor is asking for outcomes, so the correct move is to co-define the rider outcome measures that matter, instrument releases to capture them, and report value alongside delivery pace. Adding defect density and code coverage substitutes one set of internal output metrics for another and still answers a question the sponsor did not ask. Replacing the delivery charts with the quarterly rider satisfaction survey is the strongest alternative, because it does speak about riders — but a quarterly attitudinal survey is slow and disconnected from what actually shipped, and dropping delivery data entirely leaves the steering group unable to weigh cost against benefit. Releasing more often and reporting release counts raises the throughput of output with no evidence that any of it changes rider behavior; shipping unmeasured functionality faster simply produces waste faster.
questions.concept: Outcomes versus outputs and value measurement
questions.question: A regional transit authority's fare-payment app team reports to a monthly steering group using velocity trends, story counts completed, and a burn-up of remaining backlog items. After the third such report, the sponsor says, "You keep telling me how fast you are moving. Tell me what any of this has done for a rider." What is the BEST response?
choices: Add defect-density and code-coverage charts to the monthly pack, so the steering group can see the quality of what has been delivered alongside the pace at which it arrived.
Replace the delivery charts with a summary of the quarterly rider satisfaction survey, so the pack speaks only to how riders feel about the fare-payment app.
Increase release frequency so more finished functionality reaches riders every month, and report the count of releases in place of the velocity trend.
Agree a small set of rider outcome measures with the sponsor and product owner, instrument the product to capture them, and report them alongside the delivery data.

questions.explanation: The riskiest assumption is 'commuters will pay,' and validated learning requires observing real behavior against that assumption with the least buildable thing. A purchase-attempt test on a simple descriptive page is a classic minimum viable experiment: days of effort, real users, real payment intent — the loop closes almost immediately. Building the full algorithm first is the longest possible route to the same answer and maximizes waste if the hypothesis is false. A survey is fast but yields opinions, not behavior — stated willingness to pay is notoriously unreliable, so it is not validated learning. A three-month beta produces rich behavioral data but deliberately delays learning by a quarter and limits it to corporate clients, who may not represent individual commuters.
questions.concept: Lean Startup build-measure-learn and minimum viable experiments
questions.question: A product team believes commuters will pay for a premium carpool-matching feature. Applying build-measure-learn thinking, which action provides validated learning about the belief with the SHORTEST feedback loop?
choices: Build the full matching algorithm and release it to every user with analytics enabled so real purchase behavior is observed
Survey a large sample of commuters about how much they would pay for premium matching before any code is written
Show a simple in-app page describing the premium feature to a subset of users and measure how many attempt to purchase it
Run a three-month beta with a set of corporate clients and interview the participants once the beta period concludes

questions.explanation: The riskiest assumption is adoption, and the cheapest reliable way to test it is a thin, usable slice released to a small pilot group of growers, whose observed behavior rather than stated opinion produces validated learning before two quarters of spend are committed. Supporting the full build while adding monthly demonstrations to growers is the strongest alternative, because regular contact with real users is genuine feedback; it loses because a demonstration is not adoption, and six months of growers nodding along at demos still leaves the team without evidence that anyone will use the product in the field. Negotiating the build down to one quarter is a smaller version of the same big-bang bet on the same untested assumption. Commissioning a structured demand study delays delivery and yields stated preferences, which are far weaker evidence than watching a pilot group work with something real.
questions.concept: MVP and validated learning (Lean Startup)
questions.question: Product leadership at an agritech startup wants the team to spend two full quarters building a complete sensor-analytics suite before any release, arguing that "farmers will never adopt a partial product." Early customer interviews were mixed, and actual demand is unproven. The agile practitioner is asked for a recommendation. What is the BEST response?
choices: Support the two-quarter build but add monthly demonstrations with growers, so their feedback is gathered steadily while the complete suite is finished
Negotiate the build down to a single quarter so the bet is halved, then release the finished suite to every grower at the end of that quarter
Commission a structured demand study across the grower segment and start development once its findings confirm both the size and shape of the demand
Propose releasing a thin slice of the suite to a small pilot group of growers to test the adoption assumption before committing the full investment

questions.explanation: Putting the adoption and abandonment evidence on the table with the sponsor present keeps ordering collaborative and transparent, respects the sponsor's stake, and lets a value and cost-of-delay comparison rather than volume of voice decide the sequence, while the product owner retains the decision. Promoting the theming item on the strength of the account's revenue substitutes stakeholder power for value and leaves the abandonment problem that drives the platform's revenue untouched. Sizing both and shipping the cheaper theming item first is the strongest alternative, since small items that please an important customer are often worth doing, but ordering on cost alone ignores the cost of delay on a flow that 40 percent of users abandon. Telling the sponsor his request is deferred because backlog order follows the analytics is a unilateral rejection dressed as evidence: it takes the decision away from the product owner and overstates the case, since satisfaction attributes can carry real value once they are weighed against the alternatives.
questions.concept: Value-based prioritization using outcome evidence and cost of delay
questions.question: A fleet-maintenance platform team meets for backlog refinement. The sponsor at the largest customer has been pressing for a customizable color theme on the analytics dashboard and wants it at the top of the backlog. The team's product analytics show that the dashboard is opened by 3 percent of licensed users each month, while 40 percent of users who begin the parts-reorder flow abandon it before submitting, and reorder volume is the platform's main revenue driver. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Place the dashboard theming item at the top of the backlog, since the request comes from the account that contributes the most revenue and that customer relationship needs protecting through the renewal negotiation next quarter

Bring the adoption and abandonment data into the refinement conversation with the sponsor and product owner, and compare the expected customer outcome and cost of delay of each option before the backlog order is set.
Ask the team to size both items first, then order the backlog so the cheaper theming item ships this iteration and the reorder work begins once capacity frees up in the iteration that follows

Take the abandonment finding straight to the sponsor as the reason his request is being deferred, and explain that backlog order in this product follows the product analytics rather than requests coming in from individual accounts

questions.explanation: Value-based ordering weighs not only whether a return clears the hurdle but how soon and how certainly it arrives; the higher IRR, nine-month payback, and unconditional benefits deliver value now, while benefits that cannot be realized for three years lose almost nothing by waiting a quarter and gain better information in the meantime. Treating regulation-linked work as automatically first confuses eventual obligation with present urgency: a rule that takes effect in 36 months does not need to be built this quarter. Accepting the 14% initiative purely because it exceeds the 12% hurdle ignores the time value of the return and the risk that the regulation shifts, which is exactly what payback period and benefit contingency are there to surface. Splitting capacity between the two raises work in progress, slows both initiatives, and delays every dollar of benefit rather than accelerating any of it.
questions.concept: Applying IRR, payback period and benefit contingency to backlog ordering
questions.question: A product team compares two backlog investments against the organization's 12% hurdle rate. Initiative X has an IRR of 14% with a 30-month payback, and its benefits depend on a regulation that only takes effect in 36 months. Initiative Y has an IRR of 22% with a 9-month payback, and its benefits begin as soon as it is released. Only one can be started this quarter. Which reasoning is MOST consistent with value-based prioritization?
choices: Start Y: its return is both larger and sooner and its benefits are not contingent, so deferring X until nearer the rule's effective date costs little and preserves the option to re-evaluate it.
Start X: work whose benefits are tied to a coming regulation carries greater strategic weight, so securing readiness now outranks a discretionary return the team could pursue in a later quarter.
Start X: it clears the 12% hurdle rate and that is the decisive test, since payback period describes only the timing of cash rather than the true profitability of an investment.
Split the quarter's capacity between X and Y so that neither slips: both clear the hurdle rate, and running them together keeps the regulatory option open while returns begin arriving.

questions.explanation: Psychological safety is defended in the moment it is threatened. Redirecting from 'who' to 'what allowed this' models blameless analysis, tells the silent juniors the session is still safe, and keeps the learning conversation alive — defects reaching production are almost always a system problem (test coverage, review practice, deployment safeguards) rather than an individual one. Reading the author's name out of the commit log and then pivoting confuses transparency about work with exposure of people; the naming lands first and confirms the blame frame. Asking the two juniors what they observed is the strongest wrong answer, since restoring their voice is sound facilitation, but it questions them while the accusation still hangs in the room, so they speak under suspicion. Closing the session for written timelines gathers evidence at the cost of abandoning the room, and invites defensive self-justification instead of shared learning.
questions.concept: Blameless postmortems and facilitator intervention
questions.question: An XP team is holding a postmortem after a pricing defect reached production. Midway through, a senior architect scrolls through the commit history and asks, 'Whose change was this?' Two junior developers immediately stop contributing and the room goes quiet. The agile practitioner is facilitating the session. What is the BEST response?
choices: Answer the question from the commit log as asked, then steer the group back to contributing conditions, since withholding facts would weaken the review
Ask the two junior developers directly what they observed while the pricing change was made, so their perspective returns to the discussion
Close the session and collect a written timeline from each participant instead, so the findings rest on evidence rather than recollection
Redirect the discussion in the moment toward what conditions allowed the defect to reach production, restating the session's blameless purpose

questions.explanation: Pulling integration and the applicable regulatory checks inside the Definition of Done is what collapses the six-week feedback gap: defects surface hours after they are created, are found by the people who created them, and "done" starts meaning releasable. Toggled deployment to a pilot fleet converts finished work into actual learning about value and behavior in real vehicles, which is the other half of incremental delivery — validated, not merely built. Lengthening iterations from two weeks to four moves in exactly the wrong direction, increasing batch size and delaying discovery further. A dedicated hardening iteration institutionalizes late defect discovery as a permanent budgeted cost instead of removing its cause. A defect-triage owner processes the symptoms more efficiently while leaving the batch, and the delay that manufactures the defects, completely untouched.
questions.concept: Definition of Done expansion and early validated deployment to reduce integration batch risk
questions.question: A hybrid team building an in-vehicle telematics feature has produced four increments over eight two-week iterations' worth of work, none of which has reached a vehicle. Integration and regulatory type-approval checks are deliberately batched for a single go-live at the end of the quarter. The most recent integration attempt surfaced a cluster of defects that trace back to work the team considered finished six weeks earlier. Which TWO actions best help the team deliver value incrementally and reduce this risk? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Extend the Definition of Done so no item is complete until it is integrated into the release candidate and has passed the regulatory checks that apply to it.
Lengthen iterations from two weeks to four so that more complete work is available at each integration point.
Deploy validated increments to a small fleet of pilot vehicles behind a feature toggle to obtain real usage feedback well before the quarterly go-live.
Schedule a dedicated hardening iteration before go-live so there is capacity to fix the defects that batch integration exposes.
Appoint a defect-triage owner who reviews all integration defects weekly and assigns owners for the fixes.

questions.explanation: Sharing techniques drawn from the practitioner's own experience, giving advice about what fits this context, and offering ongoing review of the member's work is mentoring — an experience-based relationship in which the more experienced person transfers know-how and guidance. Coaching would instead use questions to help the member discover their own approach, with the coach deliberately withholding answers from personal experience. Training is the structured transfer of a defined skill or curriculum, typically prepared content delivered to a group of learners rather than an advice conversation prompted by one person's request. Guiding a group's process neutrally toward the group's own outcome — facilitation — does not describe a one-on-one exchange of advice at all.
questions.concept: Coaching versus mentoring versus training distinctions in knowledge transfer
questions.question: A team member tells the agile practitioner, "I struggle to split large stories — how did you handle this on your last program?" The practitioner describes specific splitting techniques that worked in a similar context, explains why they fit, and offers to review the member's next few story splits. Which competency-development approach is the practitioner using?
choices: Coaching
Mentoring
Training
Facilitation

questions.explanation: The practitioner's first job is to reinforce that surfacing problems is welcomed, then help the analyst raise the observation herself in a blameless way — this builds durable psychological safety and treats the recurring error as a team learning opportunity rather than a personal accusation. Adding an automated configuration check to the pipeline is the strongest distractor and probably belongs in the eventual fix, since automation prevents a class of error without depending on anyone's courage; it fails as the first move because it silently routes around the real issue, which is that a new joiner does not believe she can speak, and the team never learns what she saw. Raising the error with the experienced engineer on her behalf fixes one defect while confirming that speaking up requires an intermediary. Deferring it to the next retrospective as an anonymous observation delays the feedback and signals that candor is safe only in disguise.
questions.concept: Blameless problem-raising and modeling candor
questions.question: A newly hired analyst on a Kanban-based service team privately tells the agile practitioner that she has noticed a recurring configuration error in deployments handled by the team's most experienced engineer, but she does not want to "cause trouble" by mentioning it. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Add an automated configuration check to the deployment pipeline so the recurring error is caught before anyone has to raise it with the team
Raise the configuration error with the experienced engineer privately on her behalf, so the problem gets fixed without putting a new joiner at risk
Thank the analyst for speaking up and work with her on how to raise the observation openly with the team as a blameless learning opportunity
Bring the deployment error to the next retrospective as an anonymous observation so the team can address the pattern with nobody named

questions.explanation: She has just admitted the current style is unsustainable — that self-assessment is the ideal coaching moment. Situational leadership holds that the leader's style should shift toward delegating as the team demonstrates competence and commitment, and this team is technically strong; coaching her to hand over named decisions explicitly rebuilds team ownership while relieving her load, and keeps her as the author of the change. Encouraging the team to decide behind her back and present decisions as done manufactures a trust conflict and undermines her authority instead of resolving a style problem. Going to her manager to strip her technical authority escalates before any direct coaching has been attempted and would likely destroy both the relationship and her confidence. A formal decision-approval matrix adds bureaucracy that codifies the bottleneck rather than growing delegation — documented approvers are still gatekeepers, and self-organization needs fewer gates, not better-documented ones.
questions.concept: Situational leadership and delegation matched to team maturity
questions.question: A team lead at a medical-device firm, promoted six months ago from senior engineer, still makes every technical decision, down to variable naming in code reviews. The team is technically strong, yet members now wait for her direction even on trivial choices, and work visibly stalls whenever she is pulled into regulatory audits. She confides to the agile practitioner that she is exhausted and "can't be everywhere." What should the practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Advise the team to start taking routine technical decisions without waiting for her and to walk her through the outcomes afterward, so she experiences that delegation is safe
Use the opening she has created to coach her on matching her level of delegation to the team's demonstrated maturity, and help her identify specific decisions to hand over explicitly
Recommend that her manager redefine the team-lead role so that technical decision authority sits with the engineers, removing the bottleneck that stalls the work during regulatory audits
Introduce a decision matrix naming an approver for each decision type, so the team knows exactly what it may decide on its own while she is pulled into regulatory audits

questions.explanation: Once facilitation of opinions has deadlocked, the strongest move is to shift the conflict from positions to evidence: agreeing on objective fitness criteria first depersonalizes the dispute, and short time-boxed spikes produce data the whole team can accept — the decision is settled by learning, ownership stays with the team, and a month of tension is converted into shared knowledge. Accepting the sponsor's ruling is fast but decides a technical question by hierarchy, guaranteeing a disengaged "loser" and teaching the team that its deadlocks are resolved above it. Commissioning an external architect is the same authority move outsourced — the team still does not own the outcome, and the losing engineer can dismiss the verdict as uninformed by the team's context. Partitioning the capability so both approaches ship avoids the conflict rather than resolving it, permanently embedding two inconsistent architectures and their ongoing maintenance cost in the product.
questions.concept: Resolving positional technical conflict through agreed criteria and set-based experiments rather than authority or avoidance
questions.question: Two senior engineers on a hybrid product team have argued for a month over whether a new billing capability should be split into services or built inside the existing modular monolith. Velocity is slipping, teammates are taking sides, and a joint design session the practitioner facilitated ended without agreement. The sponsor now offers to end the dispute by ruling in favor of one option. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Partition the billing capability so each engineer builds the style they favor, letting the codebase itself show over time which structure serves the product better
Guide the engineers and the team to agree on objective fitness criteria, then run short time-boxed spikes of both options and let the results drive the decision
Bring in an external architect to weigh both options against the organization's reference architecture and issue an independent recommendation to follow
Accept the sponsor's offer to rule, since a month of debate has already cost velocity and a decision from outside restores the team's flow immediately

questions.explanation: Each practice closes a different loop at a different speed, and each answers a different risk question. Pair programming is the tightest loop of all — a second set of eyes catches design and defect issues in seconds, as keystrokes happen. Continuous integration operates at the minutes scale: every commit is merged and exercised by the automated build, so integration and regression problems surface almost immediately rather than at a late merge. The iteration review closes a weeks-scale loop with stakeholders, confirming the increment is the right product before more is built on top of it. The MVP release closes the slowest and riskiest loop — the market itself — testing whether real customers behave as the value hypothesis predicts before major investment. Confusing these (for example, expecting a demo to validate market demand, or expecting CI to confirm stakeholder fit) leads teams to trust the wrong evidence.
questions.concept: Feedback-loop granularity across engineering, product, and market levels
questions.question: Match each practice (1-4) to the feedback loop it primarily shortens (A-D).
pairs: Pair programming
Provides second-by-second feedback on design choices and defects while the code is being written
Continuous integration
Confirms within minutes whether newly committed code integrates cleanly and passes the automated build
Iteration review (demo)
Verifies with stakeholders at the end of each timebox that the increment actually meets their needs
Minimum viable product release
Tests a value hypothesis against real market behavior before further investment is made

questions.explanation: A blameless retrospective that looks for systemic causes and ends with a small number of improvement experiments converts the failure into organizational learning while preserving the psychological safety people need to speak honestly about what happened. Radiating release-health indicators where everyone can see them builds the transparency that lets the next emerging problem surface early instead of overnight. Individual sign-off logs aimed at identifying who caused each defect create a blame culture that drives problems underground and makes future incidents harder to detect. A mandatory two-week stabilization gate adds process and delays feedback for every release while doing nothing about the underlying causes of this one. Restricting incident discussion to managers until a root cause is confirmed is the opposite of transparency—it slows learning and signals that failure is something to hide.
questions.concept: Psychological safety, blameless retrospectives, and information radiators
questions.question: After a failed overnight release disrupts appointment booking across a network of dental clinics, senior leaders ask an agile practitioner how the organization should respond so the failure leads to lasting improvement. Which TWO actions best reflect an agile mindset? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Introduce individual sign-off logs so the person responsible for each defect can be identified after future releases
Facilitate a blameless retrospective that examines systemic causes and commits the group to one or two concrete improvement experiments
Add a mandatory two-week stabilization and approval gate before every future release
Limit discussion of the incident to managers until a root cause has been formally confirmed
Publish release-health indicators on an information radiator visible to teams and stakeholders

questions.explanation: Facilitating a suitability assessment with the team and tailoring a hybrid fits the situation: compliance documentation and a fixed audit date are constraints, not a verdict against agility, and short build-and-test cycles can produce verified firmware increments whose outputs roll up into the mandated deliverables. Starting iterations while leaving the checklist until the audit approaches treats regulatory evidence as an end-of-project documentation exercise, and reconstructed records rarely survive an audit. Mapping the checklist onto signed phase exits with retrospectives added is the strongest alternative and is a real hybrid, but phase exits batch feedback to the boundary, so the team inspects its process while working firmware stays unavailable until late. Asking the quality function to rule on iterative development first stalls the team and hands the choice to a group that will not live with it.
questions.concept: Agile suitability assessment and hybrid tailoring in regulated environments
questions.question: A medical-device company must deliver firmware that satisfies a regulator's fixed documentation checklist and an immovable audit date. The newly formed team asks the agile practitioner whether an agile approach is even possible under these constraints. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Reassure the team that agile suits any domain and start two-week iterations now, treating the checklist as documentation to be produced near the audit date
Map the regulator's checklist onto a plan with signed phase exits, and add retrospectives so the team still gains some of the benefits of agile
Ask the quality function to confirm that the regulator permits iterative development before the team considers any approach, and hold the current plan until it answers
Facilitate a suitability assessment with the team and tailor a hybrid approach — short build-and-test cycles feeding the mandated compliance deliverables

questions.explanation: The snapshot shows a classic downstream blockage: Build holds six items against a limit of four and Verify holds five against a limit of two, with individual items aged 11 and 9 days inside a 10-day iteration. Work is being started faster than it is being finished, which is exactly how a fully busy team produces falling throughput — so the first move is to stop starting, pull from the right, and finish the aged items in Verify before anything new enters Build. The nine items waiting in Ready are a queue, not the constraint; adding refinement effort upstream feeds a system that already cannot drain. Filling Analysis to its limit optimizes analyst utilization at the cost of pushing yet more unfinished inventory into an already overloaded downstream. Extending the iteration by three days hides the flow problem behind a longer timebox and further delays the feedback the aged items were meant to generate.
questions.concept: Reading WIP limits and item age on a board to diagnose flow constraints
questions.question: A team's throughput has declined for three consecutive iterations, yet every member reports being fully occupied and no one is idle. Based on the board snapshot in the exhibit, what should the agile practitioner raise with the team FIRST?
choices: The Ready queue holds nine items with the oldest aged fourteen days, so the team should put more of the iteration into refinement and keep that upstream queue healthy enough that it never starves the developers.
Analysis is sitting below its agreed limit while everyone reports being busy, so the team should pull more items into Analysis and bring that column up to the limit the team agreed to work within.

Build and Verify are both over their agreed limits with items aging past the length of the iteration itself; the team should stop starting new work and swarm right-to-left to finish what is sitting in Verify.
Only one item has reached done by day six, so the team should extend this iteration three days and let the work already in flight finish, so it still closes with a credible amount of work completed.

questions.explanation: The item fails on smallness, on a clear negotiable scope, and above all on testability: "fast" and "good experience" cannot be verified by anyone. Slicing it into specific valuable pieces makes each one deliverable and independently useful, and adding acceptance criteria with observable conditions and thresholds makes each piece verifiable and the shared understanding explicit. Assigning a story-point estimate does not resolve the ambiguity; sizing something nobody can define produces a meaningless number and the item still could not be called complete. Moving it to the top of the backlog forces the team to pull work that remains untestable and too large, which is precisely why it has stalled for five iterations. Having the product owner rewrite it alone removes the collaborative conversation that produces shared understanding and realistic criteria, reducing the story to a handoff specification.
questions.concept: INVEST and testable acceptance criteria for readiness
questions.question: A team building a peer-to-peer equipment rental marketplace is refining an item written as: "As a renter, I want the system to be fast so I have a good experience." The item has been carried across five iterations without being pulled. The team wants to make it ready for delivery. Which TWO actions would MOST improve this item? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Split it into specific, independently valuable slices such as search results for a renter's chosen category returning within a stated time
Add testable acceptance criteria that state the observable condition and threshold the team will verify
Assign the item a story-point estimate so it can be scheduled into an iteration
Move it to the top of the backlog so its age forces the team to address it
Ask the product owner to rewrite the item alone and present the finished version at the next refinement session

questions.explanation: Coaching draws the answer out of the person: through open, powerful questions the coach helps the individual surface her own obstacles, options, and plan, on the premise that she is resourceful and owns her growth. Enrolling her in a certification course is training — transferring a defined skill set through structured instruction — useful, but the direction comes from the course, not from her own reflection. Recounting one's own transition and recommending the same path is mentoring: guidance based on the mentor's experience, which supplies answers rather than eliciting hers, and may not fit her situation. Assigning automation stories with senior review is delegation with support — a legitimate development tactic, but it is the manager choosing the growth path for her rather than helping her discover it.
questions.concept: Coaching vs. mentoring vs. training vs. delegation
questions.question: A tester tells the agile practitioner she wants to move toward test automation but feels stuck and does not know where to begin. If the practitioner intends to respond as a COACH — rather than as a mentor, trainer, or delegating manager — which response fits that intent?
choices: Enroll her in a vendor's automation certification course and check on her progress monthly
Ask open questions that help her articulate what is blocking her and shape her own development plan
Describe how the practitioner personally made the same career transition and recommend she follow similar steps
Assign her the team's next automation stories with a senior engineer reviewing her work

questions.explanation: A risk-adjusted backlog is ordered by the combination of value delivered and risk retired: a 40 percent chance of $300,000 in rework is roughly $120,000 of exposure, far larger than one iteration's delay of a feature worth $50,000 a year, and two days of investigation buys that information while the data layer is still cheap to change. Choosing the reporting feature first mistakes certainty of value for optimal sequence, because the feature's value is merely delayed, whereas the rework cost grows with every iteration the wrong library stays embedded. Splitting the team into parallel sub-teams spreads scarce skills, raises work in progress, and typically delays both items, and a two-day investigation is far too small to justify fracturing the team. Waiting for the pre-launch compliance review is the classic late-discovery trap: it moves the finding to the point where rework is most expensive and least recoverable.
questions.concept: Risk-adjusted backlog and expected exposure in sequencing
questions.question: A product owner maintains a risk-adjusted backlog. Two candidates compete for the top of the next iteration. The first is a reporting feature customers have requested, worth an estimated $50,000 per year and buildable entirely from proven components. The second is a two-day investigation into whether the chosen encryption library is approved for the regulated market the product launches into; the architect judges roughly a 40 percent chance it is not, in which case reworking the data layer would cost about $300,000. Which sequencing decision best reflects a risk-adjusted backlog?
choices: Run the encryption investigation first, because its expected exposure of roughly $120,000 outweighs delaying one iteration of a $50,000-per-year feature
Build the reporting feature first, because it carries certain customer value while the investigation may prove the concern groundless and deliver nothing
Split the team into two parallel sub-teams for the whole iteration so that neither customer value nor risk reduction is delayed
Defer the encryption investigation to the compliance review already scheduled before launch and spend the whole iteration on customer-visible value

questions.explanation: The largest risk is not polish; it is spending nine months building on an unvalidated assumption. A minimal offering released to a small, controlled segment converts that assumption into an early, cheap test while honoring the vice president's legitimate concern, because exposure is deliberately limited. Accepting the directive and strengthening quality assurance polishes a product without ever testing whether anyone will switch to it; execution quality cannot rescue a wrong bet. A market-research survey on switching intent respects the brand concern and produces something, but stated intent from customers of an entrenched competitor is notoriously weak evidence. Building the switching-related features first is the strongest alternative and is genuine risk-first sequencing, yet proving them internally shows the features work, not that customers will move, so the real assumption survives to launch.
questions.concept: MVP and validated learning (Lean Startup)
questions.question: A product group practicing hypothesis-driven development is told by the marketing vice president that nothing may reach customers until the full nine-month feature set is complete, because "a half-finished product would damage the brand." The initiative's riskiest assumption — that customers will switch from an entrenched competitor — remains completely untested. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Accept the directive and strengthen quality assurance across the nine months, so the eventual launch is polished enough to win customers over
Commission a market-research survey on switching intent, so the riskiest assumption is examined without putting an unfinished product in front of customers
Sequence the nine months so the switching-related features are built first, since the riskiest part of the product is then finished and proven internally
Propose releasing a minimal offering to a small, controlled customer segment to test the switching assumption early while limiting brand exposure

questions.explanation: Changing the facilitation structure equalizes participation immediately, without exposing the confider or acting on a single secondhand account: silent writing and anonymous voting let all ideas surface on merit, and facilitating it firsthand gives the practitioner direct observation of the dynamic before any individual intervention. Asking the tech lead to facilitate the next sessions hands the loudest voice the facilitator's authority as well, and someone unaware that he talks over people is unlikely to notice it while running the room. Reviewing the last four sets of actions with the whole team uses evidence everyone can see, which is appealing, but that conversation would itself be governed by the dynamic in question, and the quieter members will not contradict the lead in front of him. A rotating facilitator with a round-robin check-in guarantees everyone speaks yet leaves ideas and votes in the open, so the steering continues.
questions.concept: Facilitation techniques and psychological safety when a dominant voice skews team decisions
questions.question: After a retrospective on a wind-farm monitoring software team, a quiet developer approaches the agile practitioner privately: the tech lead, she says, talks over others, dismisses ideas he did not originate, and the team's votes always land where he steers them — this retrospective's actions, like the last three, reflect one voice. She asks the practitioner not to reveal that she said anything. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Ask the tech lead to facilitate the next two retrospectives, so he notices how much space his own input takes
Redesign the next retrospective around silent idea writing, affinity grouping, and anonymous dot voting, and observe the dynamics firsthand
Review the actions from the last four retrospectives with the whole team and ask whether they reflect everybody's priorities
Introduce a rotating facilitator and a round-robin check-in so every member speaks at least once in each session

questions.explanation: Collecting silent, anonymous input from every member before open discussion begins equalizes voices structurally: ideas land on their own merit before status and anchoring take hold, and remote members get the same channel as everyone else, which changes the facilitation system rather than blaming an individual. Asking the principal engineer to hold his proposals until everyone else has spoken is the strongest alternative and a real facilitation technique, but it singles out one person for a dynamic the whole group is producing, and it does little for the remote members, who would still be entering an open discussion where speaking first carries the most risk. Closing each session with a vote legitimizes whatever is already on the table, ratifying the anchoring rather than preventing it. Replacing the live retrospective with an asynchronous survey removes the conversation and shared commitment that make retrospectives produce real improvement.
questions.concept: Facilitation techniques that counter anchoring and status effects in distributed retrospectives
questions.question: A product team distributed across two countries used to hold lively retrospectives. Since a well-known principal engineer joined, the sessions have gone quiet: whatever he proposes first is quickly agreed to, and the facilitator notices that the last three improvement actions were all his ideas. Remote members contribute almost nothing. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask the principal engineer to hold his proposals until everyone else has spoken so his view stops setting the agenda
Close each retrospective with a team vote on the candidate actions so the improvements chosen carry everyone's support
Restructure the retrospective so input is gathered silently and anonymously from everyone before any open discussion begins
Replace the live retrospective with an asynchronous survey the facilitator summarizes, so time zones stop shaping who contributes

questions.explanation: A joint root-cause session puts the people closest to the problem — both teams — in front of the actual incident evidence, converts blame into shared understanding, and produces countermeasures the teams themselves will trial and inspect, which is how Lean problems get solved. Going to the vice president first skips collaboration entirely: even if leadership compels a change, the upstream team gains no understanding of the failure modes, and the two teams are now positioned as adversaries. An intake checklist is a unilateral control gate that slows flow and treats the symptom — it inspects for defects rather than removing their cause, and it was designed without the team that would live under it. Waiting another quarter to build an undeniable trend delays action while the harm recurs every month; a collaborative conversation does not require a courtroom-grade evidence file to begin.
questions.concept: Cross-team root-cause analysis and countermeasure trials
questions.question: A platform-operations team at a streaming-media company works in a Lean flow. After each monthly release from the upstream metadata team, incidents spike. Several operations engineers want the agile practitioner to take the incident data straight to the vice president; others want an approval gate placed on all upstream changes before they reach production. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Bring the two teams together to analyze the recent incidents to root cause and agree on countermeasures they will trial jointly.
Take the incident data to the vice president, since leadership can compel the upstream team to change how it releases.
Help the team define an intake checklist that every upstream change must clear before it reaches the operations team's production platform.
Gather one more quarter of incident data first, so that the conversation with the upstream team opens from a trend nobody can dispute.

questions.explanation: The team is building the wrong thing efficiently: excellent delivery metrics alongside 18% adoption means the feedback loop reaches the sponsor but never the users whose behavior defines value. Observing technicians at work turns adoption from a guess into evidence and lets the team re-order the backlog around real barriers before spending 40 features' worth of capacity — early, direct feedback at the point where change is cheapest. Continuing to deliver the sponsor's list mistakes acceptance authority for validated value; accepting an increment confirms it matches expectations, not that anyone uses it. Training and an adoption campaign presume the product is right and the users are deficient, which pushes cost onto the customer and leaves an unvalidated backlog intact. A mass anonymous survey delays action, yields self-reported opinions rather than observed behavior, and stops delivery while waiting — slower and weaker than watching a handful of technicians work this week.
questions.concept: Validating delivered value with real users versus sponsor sign-off
questions.question: Six weeks after the first release of a field-service scheduling application, usage telemetry shows that only 18% of the 400 technicians open it more than once a week; most still schedule jobs by phone. The VP of Operations who sponsored the work attended every iteration review, accepted every increment, and has now prioritized 40 further features. The team's quality metrics are strong: no escaped defects, automated pipeline, two-day cycle time. What is the BEST response?
choices: Continue delivering the sponsor's prioritized backlog, since the accountable decision maker has reviewed and accepted every increment the team has produced.
Pause new feature development, spend shifts alongside a small group of technicians, and re-order the backlog around what direct observation and the usage data reveal.
Commission training and a structured adoption campaign so technicians learn the features already delivered, then revisit the usage numbers once the rollout is complete.
Survey all 400 technicians about the application and pause new backlog work until the responses are analyzed and the reasons for the low usage are properly understood.

questions.explanation: A joint root-cause analysis replaces blame with shared evidence: mapping the breakages together surfaces the systemic cause — missing environment-reset automation, undocumented data dependencies, conflicting configuration assumptions — and whatever remedy follows is then aimed at a verified cause and co-owned by both teams. Dividing access into time slots treats the symptom, throttles both teams' flow, and leaves the corruption mechanism waiting for whoever deploys next. Asking leadership to assign responsibility from the logs turns a solvable technical-collaboration problem into a verdict, hardening the adversarial dynamic the practitioner needs to dissolve. Cloning environments may eventually be justified, but prescribing an expensive structural change before anyone understands the failure mode duplicates cost while the real cause travels into both copies.
questions.concept: Collaborative root-cause analysis across teams
questions.question: Two Kanban teams share one integration test environment. For six consecutive weeks, blocked cards have accumulated while each team blames the other's deployments for corrupting the environment, and the weekly cross-team sync has become an exchange of accusations. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Broker a shared calendar that divides environment access into dedicated deployment slots for each team, so their changes stop colliding at all
Ask program leadership to review the deployment logs from both teams and determine whose changes are corrupting the shared integration environment
Have both teams build separate cloned environments so their deployments no longer interfere and the blocked cards can start moving again
Bring both teams together to map the recent breakages on a timeline and run a joint root-cause analysis before considering any structural fix

questions.explanation: The rework is caused by distance between the team and the people who do the work, so the fix is to shorten that distance: real users in the review plus hands-on access to the increment produce concrete, observed feedback within days instead of months. More detailed criteria signed off by the proxy only hardens second-hand assumptions and adds up-front documentation waste without ever testing them against real use. A two-week acceptance phase before each quarterly release still delays discovery by up to three months and turns feedback into a late gate, when the cost of change is already high. A post-release questionnaire arrives after the money is spent and yields stated opinions rather than observed workflow, which is exactly the kind of second-hand information that caused the rework.
questions.concept: Customer proxy risk and shortening the feedback loop
questions.question: A team building regulatory reporting software demonstrates every three weeks to an internal business analyst who acts as the customer proxy. The twelve branch controllers who actually use the reports see the software only at the quarterly release. Two of the last three features required significant rework in the weeks after go-live because the controllers' real workflow differed from what the proxy described. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Have the business analyst write far more detailed acceptance criteria and sign each story off before development starts on it
Insert a two-week acceptance test with the controllers ahead of every quarterly release so workflow mismatches surface before go-live
Send all twelve controllers a structured questionnaire after each release and feed the biggest reported gaps into the backlog
Invite a rotating pair of branch controllers to each review and give them hands-on access to the working increment between reviews

questions.explanation: The heart of the problem is that daily assignment has replaced the team's pull-based self-organization, and members are already becoming passive. The best move is a direct, collaborative one: help the coordinator see the effect of prescriptive assignment, and coach the team to own an explicit work-selection policy, which can address the legitimate cherry-picking concern without central assignment. Putting a work-in-process limit on the ready column is reasonable flow hygiene but a mechanical tweak that shortens the queue while the command-and-assign behavior continues. Posting the morning assignments on the board only makes the disempowerment transparent; it does not return the decision to the team. Agreeing that the oldest ready ticket is always pulled first is the strongest alternative — it is an explicit team policy and it does answer cherry-picking — yet it substitutes one rigid rule for the team's judgment about skills, capacity, and swarming, and it leaves the coordinator's habit unaddressed.
questions.concept: Self-organizing teams and pull systems
questions.question: A warehouse-robotics company uses Kanban for its fleet-software team. A senior engineer recently given the title of technical coordinator has begun deciding each morning which team member will pull each ticket from the ready column, saying this prevents people from cherry-picking easy work. Team members have started waiting for their daily assignments instead of pulling work themselves. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Put a work-in-process limit on the ready column so the coordinator has fewer tickets to hand out each morning and the queue in front of the team stops growing
Ask the coordinator to post each morning's assignments on the board so the allocation is at least transparent and the team can see how work is being shared
Discuss with the coordinator how prescriptive assignment undermines the pull system, and coach the team to re-establish its own policy for selecting work
Facilitate a team agreement that the oldest ready ticket is always pulled first, which answers the cherry-picking concern without a daily allocation

questions.explanation: A queue that grows while throughput holds steady is the signature of a bottleneck downstream of the team's own control. Optimizing flow starts with making the constraint visible and collaborating with the people who own it to set an explicit work-in-progress limit and service expectation — that attacks the actual delay and builds a shared agreement rather than a workaround. Adding a second daily standup piles coordination overhead onto the team that is not the constraint; the reviewers' capacity is unchanged, so the queue keeps growing. Reporting the sign-off wait as its own metric at the iteration review is the strongest rival, since making the constraint visible is half of the right answer, but it stops at reporting and frames the delay as someone else's fault, with no limit or service expectation ever agreed with the reviewers themselves. Splitting sign-off into a separate downstream item hides the wait rather than removing it, taking the delay off the board that surfaced it.
questions.concept: Bottleneck identification via queue growth and WIP limits at handoff points
questions.question: A hybrid team maintaining a hospital scheduling platform pulls work through a five-column Kanban board. Over the last eight weeks the "Awaiting Clinical Sign-off" column has grown from two cards to fourteen, while every other column stays near its WIP limit. Average lead time has doubled, but the team's throughput of completed cards per week is unchanged. The team lead proposes adding a second daily standup so the team can chase the clinical reviewers more often. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Make the queue growth visible and take the constraint to the clinical reviewers and the team together to agree on a WIP limit and service expectation for that column
Add the second daily standup as proposed, since a queue this visible is a coordination gap and meeting again each afternoon keeps clinical reviewers aware of waiting cards
Report the sign-off wait as its own metric at the iteration review, so stakeholders can see that lead time is driven by a step the delivery team does not perform
Split each card so clinical sign-off becomes a separate downstream item owned by the reviewers, keeping the team's board free of work it cannot finish itself

questions.explanation: The value of showing working functionality early lies in the timing of the feedback: what the customer-service leads learn from the two finished stories can still reshape the three not yet built, when changing them costs almost nothing. Framing the session as accountability for the commitment makes it a status report to prove the team is on track, which converts a feedback event into a progress review. Treating it as a mandatory ceremony obeys a rule without naming any benefit, and rule-compliance is not why the practice exists. Supplying velocity evidence to a sponsor spends the customer's time on an internal reporting need and pushes the team toward measuring output rather than validated value.
questions.concept: Timing of customer feedback on partial working increments
questions.question: A team building a self-service returns portal for a retailer has finished two of five planned stories partway through the iteration. The product owner suggests waiting until all five are done before showing anything to the retailer's customer-service leads, so the demonstration tells a complete story. What is the strongest reason to show the two completed stories to those leads now?
choices: It keeps the team accountable to its iteration commitment by making visible progress evident to stakeholders
It satisfies the rule that every iteration must end in a demonstration regardless of what is finished
It gives the product owner evidence to justify the team's velocity to the sponsor
Feedback on working functionality arrives while the three remaining stories can still be changed cheaply

questions.explanation: The dysfunction is that work state flows through a private intermediary and reaches the shared radiator a week late — useless for coordination across time zones. A team-owned working agreement to keep the board current at the moment work changes state gives every member, in every zone, an always-fresh asynchronous view, and because the team co-creates the agreement, they own keeping it alive. A daily status email keeps the lead as the bottleneck and merely changes the broadcast frequency of second-hand information. Adding another synchronous meeting imposes meeting load on a distributed team to compensate for a stale artifact, when the artifact itself should carry the information. An hours-logging spreadsheet makes effort visible rather than work state visible — it serves monitoring, not coordination, and adds administrative burden without reducing surprises.
questions.concept: Information radiators and working agreements for distributed teams
questions.question: A product team is distributed across three time zones. Members report progress privately to the team lead by direct message, and the lead updates the shared board once a week before the stakeholder review. Team members frequently duplicate work and say they are 'always surprised' by what colleagues are doing. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask the team lead to consolidate private updates into a daily status email so that everyone starts the day with the same picture of progress
Add a second synchronized daily meeting, timed so members in all three zones can all join the same live conversation every working day
Facilitate a working agreement in which each member updates the shared board as work changes state, making it the single current source of truth
Introduce a tracking spreadsheet where each member logs hours against assigned tasks, so that individual effort becomes visible to everyone across the whole team

questions.explanation: The exhibit shows authority eroding on exactly two decisions — technical stack (agreed Inquire, observed Sell) and deployment timing (agreed Agree, observed Sell) — while iteration scope and working hours are unchanged. That selective pattern suggests something specific changed for those decisions (an incident, an architectural mandate, cost pressure), so the practitioner should first seek to understand the director's reasons, then bring director and team together to consciously re-set the levels, preserving trust and possibly recovering the delegation. Re-running delegation poker on every area before understanding the cause simply ratifies the erosion as the new baseline and re-litigates the two areas that are not in dispute. Displaying the gap at the system demo weaponizes transparency to pressure the director in front of senior stakeholders, which damages the relationship and invites defensiveness rather than dialogue. Coaching the team to keep exercising the original levels engineers a direct confrontation over authority while ignoring that the director may have legitimate new constraints.
questions.concept: Delegation levels and delegation-board interpretation
questions.question: An agile practitioner supporting a platform team reviews the delegation board shown in the exhibit and confirms with the team that the 'observed' column accurately reflects the engineering director's behavior this quarter. Several responses are possible. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Meet with the director to explore what has changed for the two decision areas where behavior has shifted toward 'Sell,' then facilitate re-aligning the board with the director and the team together
Re-run delegation poker with the team and the director across every decision area, so the board is refreshed to match observed behavior and everyone shares a picture of where authority now sits today
Display the delegation board at the next system demo so senior stakeholders can see the gap themselves, creating the visibility needed for the director to honor the launch agreement
Coach the team to keep making technical-stack and deployment decisions at the levels originally agreed, since the board is the standing agreement and nothing about it has been renegotiated

questions.explanation: Running short, parallel spikes converts an unwinnable opinion contest into an inexpensive experiment: real data flowing through thin slices of both designs produces evidence the whole team can accept, and the timebox caps the cost of learning. Handing the choice to the enterprise architect resolves the stall by authority rather than evidence and leaves the team less committed to the outcome. A comprehensive quality-attribute analysis document is big-bang, speculative evaluation — it extends the delay and still produces predictions instead of observed behavior. Deferring to tenure substitutes hierarchy for empiricism and teaches the team that seniority, not results, settles technical questions.
questions.concept: Set-based spikes to resolve technical uncertainty with evidence
questions.question: Two senior engineers on a logistics team have spent three weeks deadlocked over whether the shipment-ETA service should be built on an event-streaming design or a batch pipeline. Design meetings keep growing in size and length, whiteboard arguments repeat, and delivery of the surrounding features has stalled. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Timebox parallel spikes that push realistic shipment data through a thin slice of each design, then let the measured results drive the decision
Have the enterprise architect choose between streaming and batch so the stalled surrounding features can restart without further design meetings
Commission a comparative analysis scoring both designs against the organization's quality attributes so the choice rests on documented criteria
Adopt the design favored by the engineer with longer domain tenure, since team harmony matters more than the gap between two workable options

questions.explanation: Read the trend rather than any single row: Test work in progress climbs from 2 to 18 while weekly completions fall from 4 to 3, 2, 2, and finally 1, and average cycle time more than doubles from 9 to 23 days - the tabular form of the widening band a cumulative flow diagram shows above a bottleneck. Stopping the intake, swarming as a whole team to drain the queue, and then setting a Test limit from what the data shows addresses the constraint directly and stops it re-forming. Asking a manager for two more testers hands the team's problem to someone else, takes weeks to arrive, and treats a queueing problem as a staffing shortage before the team has even tried limiting its own work in progress. Pulling more items into Analysis feeds the very queue that is starving throughput and will drive cycle time higher still. Switching the report from cycle time to velocity would conceal the deterioration the exhibit reveals - and completions are in fact declining week on week, not stable.
questions.concept: Reading WIP, throughput, and cycle-time trends to locate a bottleneck
questions.question: The team says everyone is fully occupied and that delivery 'feels about the same as usual.' Based on the exhibit, what should the agile practitioner recommend the team do next?
choices: Stop starting new Analysis work, swarm as a team to drain the Test queue, then agree a work-in-progress limit for Test
Ask the functional manager to assign two additional testers so the Test column can keep pace with Build
Increase the number of items pulled into Analysis so the cumulative Done line climbs faster over the coming weeks
Switch the team's reporting from cycle time to velocity, since the number of items finished each week has stayed broadly comparable

questions.explanation: Facilitating agreement on shared success criteria and a short comparative spike is the collaborating mode of conflict resolution: it moves the argument from positions to evidence, produces a decision the two developers own, and often surfaces a better design than either starting point. Choosing the stronger design personally is forcing — it restarts work fast but leaves one developer resentful and teaches both to lobby the practitioner instead of resolving conflicts themselves. Blending elements of both designs is compromising on a technical question where a spliced architecture can be worse than either coherent option; it optimizes for feelings, not for the product. Handing the matter to the enterprise architect escalates before team-level collaboration has been attempted and strips the two people closest to the problem of ownership of its solution.
questions.concept: Conflict management modes and collaborative (evidence-based) resolution
questions.question: Two senior developers on a hybrid team building hospital-pharmacy software have argued for a week over competing data-migration designs. Related backlog items are stalling, and each developer has privately lobbied the agile practitioner to endorse their approach. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Review both migration designs and pick the stronger one yourself so the stalled backlog items can restart this iteration
Facilitate a session where both developers agree on shared success criteria and design a small test of each approach
Propose merging elements of both designs so each developer sees part of their own approach adopted and the dispute ends
Refer the migration choice to the enterprise architect, whose ruling both developers have said they would accept

questions.explanation: Coaching the team to pull the next prioritized Ready item within the board's work-in-process limits restores the behavior a Kanban system depends on: the team decides who takes what, guided by visible priority and explicit flow policies, so idle time disappears because no one is waiting to be told. Assigning the Ready items for a few more weeks before handing the job to a team member keeps a dispatcher in place and merely changes who holds the clipboard later. A column policy naming the specialist who owns each ticket type is the closest alternative, and making policies explicit is genuine Kanban practice, but this policy encodes push: it routes work to the current expert, narrows skill growth, and prevents swarming on a blocked item. Lowering the limits misreads the cause — people are idle because nobody has told them to start, not because too much is in flight, so tighter limits would leave more of them waiting.
questions.concept: Self-organizing teams and pull-based work selection
questions.question: An agile practitioner joins a municipal permit-digitization team that uses a Kanban board. The previous team lead assigned every ticket to a named developer each morning, and now team members sit idle whenever no one tells them what to work on, even though prioritized items are waiting in the Ready column. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Assign the Ready items herself for a few more weeks, then hand the assignment task to a team member once delivery looks steady
Add a column policy naming the specialist who owns each ticket type, so members can see at a glance which waiting items belong to them
Coach the team to pull the next highest-priority Ready item themselves, within the board's WIP limits, whenever they have capacity
Lower the board's WIP limits so fewer items sit waiting, since less work in progress will draw idle members back into the flow

questions.explanation: Explaining that welcoming changing requirements, even late, lets the product capture more value for members applies the Agile Manifesto directly: short delivery cycles and a continuously refined backlog keep the cost of change low, so responding to new member needs is a strength rather than disorganization. Baselining requirements at design approval and batching later requests into the next release buys predictability by keeping the product wrong for longer. Routing every change through impact analysis and formal sign-off is the most defensible alternative, since it keeps the door open and gives the director the control she wants, but a heavyweight gate on every request raises the cost of change until the team behaves as though scope were frozen anyway. Promising deeper upfront analysis concedes the false premise that member needs should have been settled once.
questions.concept: Agile Manifesto principle: welcome changing requirements
