questions.question: During a quarterly business review at a regional credit union, an operations director asks an agile practitioner why the development team "keeps letting members change the mobile-deposit requirements" instead of locking scope at the start of the release, arguing that constant change makes the team look disorganized. What is the BEST response?
choices: Explain that requirements are baselined once the design is approved, and that later member requests will be batched into the next release to keep the release predictable
Agree to route every requirement change through an impact analysis and formal sign-off, so members can still request changes while the team is shielded from unplanned late rework
Explain that welcoming changing requirements, even late in development, lets the product capture more value for members, and that short delivery cycles keep the cost of change low

Explain that the late changes reflect gaps in the original requirements gathering, and commit to deeper upfront analysis with member representatives so that mobile-deposit scope settles earlier next time

questions.explanation: Flow efficiency is touch time divided by total lead time, so 3.5 of 21 days is about 17 percent, meaning roughly 17.5 days are pure waiting; queues, handoffs, and approval delays are the non-value-adding time and therefore where the leverage sits. Coaching the team to shave the active 3.5 days attacks the smallest slice of the timeline and could at best remove a fraction of a day from a three-week lead time. Reading the ratio as 83 percent inverts the calculation, and pushing velocity higher would simply feed more items into the same queues. Concluding that the team is understaffed ignores the finding entirely — adding people to a system dominated by waiting typically raises work in progress and lengthens lead time further.
questions.concept: Flow efficiency as a measure of waiting waste in a value stream map
questions.question: A team maps the value stream for its internal support-tooling requests and finds that a typical request receives about 3.5 days of active work spread across a 21-day lead time from request to done. Which interpretation is best supported by these numbers and most useful to act on?
choices: The team works too slowly while items are active, so coaching should target the 3.5 days of hands-on effort each request takes.
Flow efficiency is roughly 83 percent, which is healthy for knowledge work, so attention now belongs on lifting the team's throughput instead.
Flow efficiency is roughly 17 percent, so the largest available gain lies in the 17.5 days of waiting — queues, handoffs, and approvals.
The 21-day lead time shows the team is short of people, so two more engineers should be requested to absorb the standing demand.

questions.explanation: A blameless joint mapping of the deployment flow is best because the failures span the boundary between two teams: only a shared end-to-end view can surface the real contributing causes, the experiments the teams design together are the ones they will actually carry out, and the session directly counters the blame dynamic leadership is amplifying. Getting the two leads to agree how upgrade notices are published and acknowledged is the strongest alternative, being concrete and cheap, but it adopts one side's account of the cause before any shared analysis and settles for two leads speaking for the people doing the work. Separate retrospectives followed by an exchange of improvement actions avoids another argument, yet it keeps the two narratives apart, and causes living in the handoff appear only when the flow is examined end to end. A temporary approval step and joint checklist impose governance before anyone understands the failures.
questions.concept: Blameless cross-team root-cause analysis
questions.question: After the third failed nightly deployment in a month, the checkout stream team publicly blames the platform team's pipeline changes, while the platform team counters that the stream team ignores its upgrade notices. Tempers are high, leadership is asking for "someone to be held accountable," and both teams have asked the agile practitioner to get involved. What is the BEST response?
choices: Bring the two team leads together to agree how upgrade notices will be published and acknowledged before each change, since notice handling is the concrete dispute both sides have already named as the cause

Have each team retrospect separately on its own contribution to the three failures and then exchange improvement actions, so each side can see what the other has committed to without the conversation turning into another argument

Facilitate a blameless joint session where both teams map the deployment flow end to end, identify systemic contributing causes across the three failures, and agree on experiments and working agreements they will own

Introduce a temporary approval step for pipeline changes together with a joint deployment checklist, so nightly deployments are protected while tempers cool and the underlying disagreement is worked through calmly

questions.explanation: A community of practice is the lightest structure that connects practitioners across team boundaries so hard-won lessons flow voluntarily and continuously, and opening with the pain point every team shares makes participation immediately valuable. Commissioning an integration handbook from the most experienced integrator turns knowledge sharing into documentation: it captures one person's explicit knowledge once, goes stale, and does nothing for the next unfamiliar failure. Consolidating all customs-API work into one specialist team is an organizational-design escalation that creates a bottleneck and removes the learning from the delivery teams. Adding a shared certificate-expiry alert to every board is the strongest alternative — it is a real countermeasure a community would likely build — but it solves exactly one failure while leaving four teams with no channel for sharing what they learn, so the next surprise still gets diagnosed four separate times.
questions.concept: Communities of practice for cross-team learning
questions.question: Four Kanban teams at a freight-forwarding company each integrate with the same national customs API. During a flow review, an agile practitioner notices that every team has independently spent days diagnosing the identical certificate-expiry failure this quarter, and each team's fix lives only in its own chat history. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Have the most experienced integrator write an integration handbook the four teams adopt, so the certificate fix is documented once for everyone
Recommend consolidating all customs-API work into one specialist team so the same failure is never diagnosed four separate times
Invite volunteers from each team to launch a community of practice around customs integration, starting with a session on the shared failure
Add a shared certificate-expiry alert to every team's board so the failure is caught automatically before it blocks anyone's flow

questions.explanation: Cause and effect that is knowable only in retrospect places this work in the complex domain, where the fitting approach is to probe with safe-to-fail experiments, sense the results, and respond by amplifying what works and dampening what does not — exactly the empirical stance agile methods embody. Engaging experts to analyze and select a good practice fits the complicated domain, where cause and effect are discoverable through analysis, which is not true here. Matching the situation to an established best practice fits the clear domain of well-understood, repeatable work, and no such practice can exist when outcomes are emergent. Acting immediately to impose stability is the response to the chaotic domain, where there is a crisis and no time to experiment — this team faces uncertainty, not an emergency.
questions.concept: Cynefin framework — complex domain and probe-sense-respond
questions.question: A startup team is creating a wellness service in which both what users actually want and how the enabling technology behaves are still evolving; the relationship between actions and outcomes becomes clear only in hindsight. According to the Cynefin framework, which way of working best fits this situation?
choices: Sense, analyze, and respond - commission expert analysis and adopt the good practice the analysis identifies
Probe, sense, and respond — run safe-to-fail experiments, observe the results, and amplify what works
Sense, categorize, and respond - match the situation to an established best practice and apply it
Act, sense, and respond - take decisive stabilizing action first, then look for the practice that emerges

questions.explanation: Training is the right tool for a defined skills gap — structured instruction and guided practice can teach a toolchain she has never seen — and mentoring is the right tool for the career question, because she has explicitly asked for guidance from someone with lived experience of the path she is considering, which is precisely what a mentor provides. Coaching the toolchain gap fails because coaching is non-directive and draws out answers the person already holds; she cannot discover syntax and tooling she has never encountered. Mentoring the toolchain gap misapplies a relationship built for sharing experience and judgment to a need that is really about skill acquisition, and pairing it with training for the career question inverts both needs. Coaching the career question is the most tempting near-miss — coaching can serve career exploration — but she asked for experience-based guidance from someone who has walked the road, and a coach deliberately withholds exactly the advice she is seeking.
questions.concept: Coaching versus mentoring versus training distinctions
questions.question: A tester who has just joined a hybrid delivery team tells the agile practitioner two things: she needs to learn the team's behavior-driven development toolchain quickly, because she has never used it, and she would value ongoing guidance from someone who has already made the move from testing into quality architecture — a path she is weighing. Which combination correctly matches a development approach to each need?
choices: Coaching for the toolchain gap; mentoring for the career question.
Mentoring for the toolchain gap; training for the career question.
Training for the toolchain gap; mentoring for the career question.
Training for the toolchain gap; coaching for the career question.

questions.explanation: Little's Law relates average cycle time to average work in process divided by average throughput; at 24 items and 4 per week, cycle time is 6 weeks, so halving work in process to about 12 while throughput holds at 4 per week yields roughly 3 weeks — and lowering WIP limits with a stop-starting, start-finishing discipline is the lever the team actually controls. Raising throughput to eight through sustained overtime attempts the one thing the scenario explicitly rules out, and sustained overtime erodes quality and sustainable pace, typically reducing real throughput across a quarter. Starting a fresh item whenever one blocks feels productive and keeps nobody idle, but it is exactly the move that drives work in process up: with throughput fixed, more items in flight means every item waits longer. Reclassifying the smaller items into their own class of service changes what gets averaged rather than how fast work flows; the reported arithmetic improves while customers wait exactly as long.
questions.concept: Practical Little's Law applied to WIP reduction
questions.question: A support-engineering team using a Kanban system currently has 24 items in process and finishes an average of 4 items per week; average cycle time is about 6 weeks. Leadership wants average cycle time cut to roughly 3 weeks within a quarter. Throughput capacity cannot be increased in that timeframe. Applying Little's Law, which action is most consistent with the goal?
choices: Reduce work in process to about 12 items by lowering WIP limits and finishing started work before starting new work
Raise throughput to about eight items per week through sustained overtime while work in process holds at twenty-four
Start a fresh item whenever an existing one blocks, so nobody waits and all twenty-four items keep moving toward done
Reclassify the smaller items as their own class of service so the reported average covers fewer, faster items

questions.explanation: Bringing the compliance specialist into the next refinement session treats the regulatory bulletin as new information to be welcomed and ordered by value and urgency, which is the agile stance that changing requirements, even late, are harnessed for the customer's advantage. Slotting the wording change into the current iteration as a trivial text edit is tempting and may prove right, but calling regulator-mandated disclosure wording trivial skips the person who can say what the bulletin actually requires and pulls unrefined work into a committed iteration on one member's sizing. Routing the bulletin through a change control board and pausing the feature adds governance delay to a decision the product owner and compliance specialist can make in refinement. Deferring to next quarter protects predictability while leaving a top-priority feature specified against superseded wording.
questions.concept: Welcoming changing requirements through collaborative backlog reprioritization
questions.question: An insurance product team working in a hybrid model is mid-iteration when a regulator publishes a bulletin changing the required disclosure wording for a policy-comparison feature sitting near the top of the backlog. A team member says, "Log it for next quarter's planning cycle — we've already committed this quarter." What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Slot the wording change into the current iteration as a trivial text edit, since the comparison feature has not been built yet anyway
Invite the compliance specialist to the next backlog refinement session so the change can be reprioritized based on its value and urgency
Route the regulatory bulletin through the change control board and pause the comparison feature until formal approval comes back from governance
Agree with the team member, since reopening a quarter that is already committed costs the predictability stakeholders were promised at quarterly planning

questions.explanation: Several responses here are technically defensible, which is what makes the choice hard — but with psychological safety actively bleeding in the room for the third time, the facilitator's first duty is an in-the-moment repair. Neutrally re-opening the idea protects the analyst without shaming the engineer, models the working agreement in front of the same witnesses who watched it violated, and still leaves room for a private conversation afterward; facilitator silence would itself teach that the agreement is decorative. Letting the review finish and speaking to the engineer privately is the strongest alternative and belongs in the plan, but as a first move it lets the room disperse having watched dismissal win again. Putting interaction norms on the next retrospective delays the signal for weeks and asks the most junior person to relive the moment in a group setting. Coaching the analyst to return with supporting data shifts the burden onto the person who was cut off, as though weak evidence, not a norm violation, was the problem.
questions.concept: In-the-moment facilitation of dismissive behavior; protecting psychological safety
questions.question: During a fortnightly service-delivery review on a Lean support team, a senior engineer cuts off a junior analyst's suggestion for reducing ticket-reopen rates with 'we tried that before you got here — next topic,' drawing laughter. The analyst goes quiet. The practitioner facilitating recalls that this is the third review in which the same engineer has dismissed a junior voice, despite a working agreement stating 'every idea gets examined.' What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Intervene in the moment — neutrally return the group's attention to the problem the suggestion targets and invite examination, quietly reasserting the working agreement
Let the review run to its end and hold a private conversation with the senior engineer afterward, so the working agreement is reinforced without a public correction in the room
Note the exchange and put team interaction norms on the next retrospective agenda, letting the group surface the pattern itself and repair its own working agreement
Follow up with the analyst after the review and encourage her to bring the reopen-rate idea back with supporting data, so it is harder for anyone to wave away

questions.explanation: Several responses here are technically workable, but only one follows the agile decision rules. A facilitated session that puts the affected teams and the customer in one (virtual) room converts conflicting opinions into a shared picture of impact, lets the people who own the work make the trade-offs, and produces an early thin increment against the most urgent need — collaboration, empowerment, and early value in a single move. Escalating to the steering committee outsources the decision to people furthest from the work and typically resolves slower and worse than direct collaboration. Directing the confident team to proceed ignores that two other teams depend on the same component; their unexamined impacts would surface later as integration failures. A multi-week impact analysis before any commitment is big-bang analysis that delays feedback on a regulatory change whose cost of delay is high and rising.
questions.concept: Cross-team coordination in response to change
questions.question: Midway through a quarter, the largest client of a distributed analytics program demands that a shared data-ingestion component support a new regional privacy regime. Three teams in different countries depend on that component: one says the change is trivial, one says it threatens its committed roadmap, and one has not responded. The program sponsor asks the agile practitioner to "sort it out this week." Which action is BEST?
choices: Ask the sponsor to have the steering committee rank the regional privacy work against each roadmap, so all three teams receive one authoritative priority before any of them commits to anything
Facilitate a short working session where representatives of the three teams and the client map the impact together and slice a first increment that satisfies the most urgent regulatory need
Assign the change to the team that called it trivial, since it has both the confidence and the capacity, and let the other two teams protect the roadmap commitments they have made
Commission a full cross-team impact analysis of the new privacy regime and hold every commitment until it is complete, so no team is asked to plan on an incomplete picture

questions.explanation: The feedback loop is wired to the wrong people. Enthusiastic feedback from administrators alongside near-zero clinician usage says the team is validating with proxies, and the direct remedy is to put genuine end users into the loop, both in the review and, more revealing still, by watching them work with the product. Telemetry alerts shorten the time to learn that a feature is unused, which is worth having, but they report the symptom faster without explaining it; the team already knows three features went unused and still has no clinician contact. Asking the two department heads to rank the backlog hands prioritization back to proxies who rarely touch the schedule. Mailing a release note and a feedback form to every clinician is the strongest alternative because it finally reaches the right audience, yet it collects stated opinions from people given no reason to try the software, and observed use answers questions a form cannot ask.
questions.concept: Validating with real end users versus proxy stakeholders
questions.question: A team building a clinician scheduling tool demonstrates its work every two weeks. Attendance is high, with 14 people from the hospital administration office, but the only clinicians present are two department heads who rarely use the schedule themselves. Feedback at demonstrations is consistently positive, yet three features released last quarter show almost no usage in production telemetry. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Add usage telemetry alerts so the team learns within a week whenever a newly released feature is not being opened by the clinical staff
Ask the two department heads to rank the backlog for their departments, since they are accountable for how the schedule is used
Send a release note and a short feedback form after each demonstration to every clinician on the scheduling system's current user list
Bring a few nurses and residents who use the schedule daily into the demonstrations, and sit with them in short observed usage sessions

questions.explanation: The rework came from a gap between what the proxy could describe and what the work actually looks like at the gate, and the cheapest way to close that gap is to put the increment in the hands of the people who do the job, on the hardware they use, while the membership-scanning work is still cheap to change. Asking the analyst for fuller acceptance criteria asks the same proxy to imagine harder; the coach-party problem was invisible on paper precisely because it lives in the physical rhythm of the counter, not in a written rule. A formal user acceptance testing phase before go-live moves feedback to the point where changes are most expensive and turns validation into an end-of-project gate. Having the analyst shadow gate staff for a week is the strongest alternative and real observation, but it still routes everything through the proxy and produces documented notes rather than staff reacting to the increment, when the supervisors could simply attend the next review.
questions.concept: Direct end-user participation versus proxy representation in reviews
questions.question: A museum is replacing its ticketing and admission system. The sponsor has assigned a business analyst to represent the box office, and she attends every iteration review; the box-office supervisors and gate staff who will actually use the system have not seen an increment. After the last release, the group check-in flow had to be rebuilt because staff could not process a coach party while the kiosk was mid-transaction. The next iteration adds membership scanning. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Arrange for two box-office supervisors to join the next review and work through the membership-scanning increment on the real kiosk hardware.
Ask the analyst to write fuller acceptance criteria for each story, so edge cases such as coach parties are captured before the team builds them
Add a formal user acceptance testing phase before go-live, so gate staff can exercise the finished system on the kiosks and sign it off
Have the analyst shadow the gate staff for a week and bring documented observations of their real workflow into the next review

questions.explanation: A single widening band on a cumulative flow diagram identifies the constraint, and this constraint is owned jointly with a partner outside the team. Showing the reviewer the same data, agreeing smaller batches and a turnaround expectation, and limiting what the team pushes into that queue both shrinks the accumulated inventory and treats the vendor as a collaborator whose own workload matters. Escalating to the account manager reaches for authority before anyone has tried to understand the reviewer's constraints, and contractual pressure rarely improves a flow problem it did not diagnose. Consolidating into one large monthly review optimizes for the reviewer's utilization while making the batch bigger, which lengthens the queue and delays feedback further. Adding a buffer column relabels the queue rather than removing it and explicitly licenses more starting, which raises work in progress and, by Little's Law, lengthens cycle time.
questions.concept: Cumulative flow diagram queue interpretation, WIP limits, and external handoff waiting
questions.question: A data-migration team moving a utility's meter records depends on an external vendor to sign off each migrated batch. The cumulative flow diagram shows every band thin and stable except "Awaiting Vendor Sign-off," which has widened steadily for six weeks; items now sit there an average of nine days. Developers have kept starting new batches to stay busy, and the board shows 21 items in progress. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Raise the nine-day average with the vendor's account manager and ask for a contractual turnaround commitment, so that the delay has an agreed remedy in place before the team changes the way it works.
Group the waiting batches into one large monthly sign-off session, so the vendor's reviewer uses their review time efficiently and the team can plan around a single known date.
Invite the vendor's reviewer to a short joint session to look at the queue data together, agree smaller batches and an expected sign-off turnaround, and cap work in progress ahead of that column.
Add a buffer column ahead of sign-off and keep starting new batches, so the developers stay productive and the board shows clearly where the waiting work is sitting and how long it has been there.

questions.explanation: The diagram has already localized the problem: work is finishing at the same rate but queuing after "Done," so the monthly deployment batch is the constraint. Making that visible to the people who control the change window and trialling smaller, more frequent deployments attacks batch size directly, and re-measuring lead time validates whether the change worked. Lowering work-in-progress limits targets the upstream stages, whose bands are stable; it would starve the team without draining the release queue. Commissioning an organization-wide value-stream map is a large piece of analysis that delays action when the evidence needed to act is already on the chart — map later if the trial reveals deeper constraints. Asking the steering group to fund a release engineer buys capacity to service the delay rather than removing it, and it escalates before the team and stakeholders have tried the cheaper experiment together.
questions.concept: Reading a cumulative flow diagram to locate queues and reduce batch size
questions.question: Over eight weeks, the cumulative flow diagram for a hotel-booking platform shows the "Done, awaiting release" band steadily widening while every other band holds roughly constant width. The team deploys once a month inside a change window. Lead time from commitment to release has grown from 12 days to 31 days, even though the time for an item to reach "Done" has not changed. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Ask the team to tighten its work-in-progress limits until the awaiting-release band stops widening, then keep that policy through the next change window.
Commission a value-stream map of the whole organization before changing anything, so the release constraint is understood in its full context first.
Bring the diagram to the team and the release stakeholders, propose trialling smaller and more frequent deployments, and re-measure lead time afterwards.
Report the lead-time trend to the steering group and ask them to fund a dedicated release engineer, since deployments clearly need more skilled attention.

questions.explanation: Splitting by architectural layer produces parts that cannot be reviewed, tested against acceptance criteria, or released, so all feedback is deferred until the last of the four lands; narrowing scope to one pollutant for one region delivers a thin but complete slice a fleet manager can actually run and react to. Demonstrating the data model and the calculation engine each iteration puts a manager in front of artifacts they cannot evaluate, which yields polite nods rather than feedback. Keeping the item whole across two iterations preserves end-to-end value but forfeits early feedback, and it confuses a thin slice with an incomplete filing. Splitting along the manager's workflow is the strongest alternative because the steps are user-facing — but entering data, reviewing totals and filing are sequential stages of one job, so the first two still file nothing.
questions.concept: Vertical slicing and INVEST when decomposing large items
questions.question: An XP-influenced team is decomposing a large item: "As a fleet manager, I can generate regulatory emissions reports so that I can file quarterly compliance returns." The item is far too large for one iteration. The team proposes splitting it into "build the data model," "build the calculation engine," "build the PDF renderer," and "wire up the UI." What is the BEST response from the agile practitioner?
choices: Accept the four-part split but have the team demonstrate the data model and the calculation engine to the fleet manager each iteration, so feedback on the emissions work still arrives before the report is finished
Point out that none of the four slices can be demonstrated to a fleet manager, and coach the team to split by narrowing scope instead — for example, one pollutant type for one region, end to end
Keep the item whole across two iterations, since a partial emissions report would let a fleet manager file an incomplete quarterly compliance return and risk a regulatory penalty
Split along the fleet manager's workflow instead — enter machine data, review the calculated totals, then produce the filing — so every slice matches a real step of the quarterly filing job

questions.explanation: The beta produced exactly the evidence prioritization exists to consume, and re-walking the story map with the sponsor, product owner and real clinics turns that evidence into a shared re-slicing decision — it maximizes customer value while keeping the sponsor inside the decision rather than on the receiving end of it, and it fits comfortably inside four days. Honouring a six-month-old list treats a snapshot judgment as a contract and knowingly ships two capabilities the market has already declined, which erodes trust more than an evidence-based change would. Demoting items and then informing the sponsor gets the content right but the collaboration wrong; presenting a fait accompli at a steering review invites the sponsor to defend the original scope instead of reasoning about the data. A full Kano survey is a sound technique in the abstract, but here it delays a decision that live usage from 40 clinics already informs and pushes the answer past the steering review.
questions.concept: Re-prioritizing an MVP slice from validated learning versus a stale MoSCoW commitment
questions.question: A veterinary practice-management SaaS team is preparing its first paid release. Six months ago a scoping workshop produced a MoSCoW list, and the executive sponsor treats its nine Must-haves as the release commitment. A six-week closed beta with 40 clinics has now finished: usage telemetry and interview notes show two of the Must-haves (a bulk-import wizard and an in-app chat widget) were opened by fewer than 5 percent of beta clinics, while an unranked reminder-scheduling capability was requested repeatedly and used daily by the clinics that had a rough prototype of it. The sponsor's steering review is in four days. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Commission a Kano survey across the whole customer base to classify the disputed capabilities objectively, so that any change to the scope the sponsor already treats as committed rests on more than a single forty-clinic beta

Prepare the beta evidence and facilitate a joint session with the sponsor, product owner and a few beta clinics that re-walks the story map and re-slices the release around what the evidence shows customers actually use
Honor the agreed Must-have list for this release so that the sponsor's trust in the team's commitments is preserved, and carry the beta evidence forward as input to the release that follows this one

Support the product owner in demoting the two barely used items to Could-have and adding the reminder-scheduling capability, then inform the sponsor of the revised release list at the next steering review

questions.explanation: Two things reliably grow safety: explicit shared norms and visible leader behavior. Working agreements the team writes together make raising concerns a defined, expected act with a promised response, which lowers the personal risk of speaking; leaders who share their own mistakes and thank problem-raisers prove with behavior that candor is safe and valued. Publishing per-member impediment counts weaponizes a metric — it pressures people to perform participation and adds fear rather than removing it. Making the coach a permanent anonymizing intermediary institutionalizes the workaround: information flows, but the team never practices direct candor, and safety never has to develop. Restricting attention to the official tracker adds a procedural gate that punishes informal early signals, which is exactly the behavior a safe team wants more of, not less.
questions.concept: Building psychological safety in distributed teams
questions.question: An agile coach supports a recently merged product team distributed across three time zones. Impediments and concerns are almost never raised in shared channels or team events; instead, members send them privately to the coach and ask not to be named. Which TWO actions would most effectively build psychological safety on this team? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Publish a per-member count of impediments raised to encourage broader participation
Co-create team working agreements that define how concerns are raised and how the team commits to respond to them
Route all impediments through one-on-one calls with the coach, who will anonymize and relay them to the team
Institute a rule that only impediments logged in the official tracking tool will be addressed
Ask visible leaders to model fallibility by openly sharing their own mistakes and publicly thanking members who raise problems

questions.explanation: Having the whole team revise its own working agreements addresses the actual defect — decisions are invisible to half the team — and does it in a way the team owns, for example by agreeing that decisions move to a shared, asynchronous, visible channel before work starts. A mandatory weekly ratification meeting in one site's hours adds ceremony, delays decisions, and privileges the larger office again, deepening the imbalance it is meant to fix. Sending a representative to the larger office is a workaround that funnels information through one person instead of making decisions transparent to all, and it leaves the underlying practice unchanged. Escalating to the site managers hands a team-level collaboration problem to hierarchy before the team has tried to solve it, weakening self-organization and possibly hardening the two-site divide.
questions.concept: Working agreements for distributed decision-making
questions.question: A product team is split between two offices nine time zones apart. Members in the smaller office complain that key design decisions keep being made in spontaneous hallway conversations at the larger office, and that they learn of decisions only after work based on them has already begun. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Facilitate a whole-team session to update the working agreements on how design decisions are raised, recorded, and made visible to everyone
Require every design decision to be ratified at a weekly synchronous meeting that is scheduled inside the larger office's normal working hours
Advise the smaller office to send a rotating representative to work alongside the larger office for the next few months of the effort
Ask the two site managers to align on how design decisions get communicated and to pass the agreed approach down to their own staff

questions.explanation: With 21 items in progress and 7 finished per week, Little's Law gives an average lead time near three weeks, and the arithmetic says the lever is WIP, not effort. Making that visible converts "we're working flat out" into a shared, testable model; letting the team choose its own new limit keeps ownership where the work is, and re-measuring turns the change into an experiment rather than a decree. Promising one week to a single partner while nothing else changes just creates another expedite path — the promise is kept by pushing everyone else's items further back, so total lead time worsens. Adding engineers to a system already drowning in concurrent work usually raises WIP faster than throughput, and it answers a flow question with a capacity purchase. Publishing three weeks as a committed service level is honest but passive: it records the current system instead of improving it, and it abandons the partner's legitimate need.
questions.concept: Practical application of Little's Law to a delivery commitment
questions.question: A platform-services team measures an average of 21 items in progress and completes an average of 7 items per week; its delivery times are reasonably stable and arrivals are steady. A partner team asks whether the platform team can commit to a one-week turnaround on its requests. Several team members respond that they are already working flat out. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Commit to the one-week turnaround for this partner alone and expedite its requests to the front of the queue each morning, since a single fast lane can be honored without changing the amount of work the platform team already carries.

Show both teams that average work in progress divided by throughput implies about a three-week wait today, and facilitate the platform team's own decision about how far WIP would have to fall to make a one-week average plausible — then run it and re-measure.

Ask for two more engineers so that throughput climbs toward twenty-one items a week, on the reasoning that a one-week turnaround follows once the team can finish in a week as many items as it currently holds in progress at any given moment.

Publish the measured three-week average as the platform team's service level and track variance against it each month, since an honest published figure sets the partner team's expectations correctly without asking anyone on either side to change how the work flows.

questions.explanation: Test-driven development pairs with writing a failing unit-level test before the code that satisfies it, because its distinguishing feature is the developer-level red-green-refactor loop that shapes design in minutes, not the existence of tests. Acceptance test-driven development pairs with the three-way agreement on concrete examples before the story is built, because its defining move is business, development, and testing converging on a shared definition of correct behavior up front, which prevents the requirement misunderstandings unit tests cannot catch. Continuous integration pairs with daily merges to a shared mainline behind an automated green build, because it is an integration discipline that keeps the codebase always releasable rather than a test-authoring technique. Exploratory testing pairs with simultaneous test design, execution, and learning, because its value comes from human investigation of behavior nobody thought to specify, complementing rather than replacing the automated checks the other three practices produce.
questions.concept: Building quality in through layered feedback loops
questions.question: Match each quality and feedback practice on the left with the description that best distinguishes it on the right. Several of these practices produce automated tests, so match on when the feedback happens and who creates it, not merely on the presence of tests.
pairs: Test-driven development
A failing unit-level test is written before the production code that makes it pass, so design pressure and regression protection arrive together
Acceptance test-driven development (specification by example)
Business, development, and testing agree on concrete examples of correct behavior for a story before it is built, and those examples become the tests
Continuous integration
Every developer merges into the shared mainline at least daily, and an automated build with its test suite must run green before work proceeds
Exploratory testing
A skilled tester designs, runs, and learns from tests at the same time, probing for behavior no scripted case anticipated

questions.explanation: Local optimization alongside global slippage is a shared-purpose problem: when the groups jointly define success in terms of patient and user outcomes and trace their own work to it, alignment comes from a vision they helped build rather than from pressure, and the blame dynamic loses its fuel. Having the sponsor mandate one metric set may change what is measured, but a vision imposed from above is complied with rather than owned, and the underlying divergence of purpose survives untouched. A practitioner-designed integration-readiness metric repeats the same mistake one level down — it prescribes an answer nobody helped shape, so the groups will optimize the new number instead of the outcome. Reorganizing reporting lines is a slow structural gamble that addresses hierarchy rather than purpose, and groups can blame each other just as effectively inside a single reporting line.
questions.concept: Stakeholder alignment around shared outcomes
questions.question: A hybrid medical-device program includes firmware, mechanical, and application-software groups. Each group is hitting its own milestone metrics, yet the integrated prototype has slipped twice, and status meetings have turned into rounds of cross-group blame. The agile practitioner is asked to help. What is the BEST response?
choices: Facilitate a session where the three groups and key stakeholders co-create a shared definition of program success in patient and user outcomes, and trace each group's work to it
Ask the program sponsor to mandate one common set of delivery metrics that all three groups must report against, so progress can be compared across firmware, mechanical, and software
Define an integration-readiness measure yourself and have each group report against it weekly, so prototype slippage becomes visible before the next integration attempt
Recommend placing the three groups under a single reporting line so one manager owns integration end to end, and hold that manager accountable for the prototype dates

questions.explanation: A high-impact, high-uncertainty assumption sitting three months out is the definition of a risk worth retiring early; a bounded spike buys the information for a few days of effort and lets the backlog be re-ordered while changing course is still cheap. Adding a schedule reserve accepts the risk without reducing it — the reserve absorbs damage rather than preventing it, and the team still discovers the truth at the worst possible moment. Pushing the epic later increases exposure rather than reducing it: the later the assumption is tested, the more dependent work will have been built on it and the less room remains to respond. A written vendor statement is contractual comfort, not evidence; it does not tell the team how partial refunds behave in their own integration, and treating a document review as validation is exactly the big-bang analysis that empirical practice replaces with a working test.
questions.concept: Spikes and risk-adjusted backlog ordering for high-uncertainty assumptions
questions.question: A payments team's highest-value epic assumes a third-party tokenization service can process partial refunds; no one on the team has verified this, and the vendor's documentation is ambiguous on the point. The product owner has ordered the epic for the middle of the release — roughly three months out — because other work is ready now. The team's risk log rates the assumption high impact and high uncertainty. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Keep the current ordering and add a schedule reserve to the release plan so the impact can be absorbed if the service turns out not to support partial refunds.
Move the epic later in the release so the team has as much time as possible to learn about the service, and start now with the work that is already ready.
Ask the vendor's account manager for written confirmation that partial refunds are supported, and record that confirmation as the mitigation for the risk log entry.
Propose a short timeboxed spike in the current iteration that calls the vendor sandbox with a partial refund, and let what the team learns re-order the backlog.

questions.explanation: A wide estimate spread is a signal of a shared-understanding gap, not an estimation problem. Facilitating a conversation that splits the vague item into thin, decision-specific slices addresses the root cause — the item fails INVEST on small and negotiable — and re-estimating afterward produces numbers the team actually believes. Asking the product owner to rank the reporting needs by urgency is the strongest alternative, because it begins to break the item apart — but ordering needs nobody has yet articulated skips the conversation that reveals them, and the most urgent one could still be a forty-point fog. A second estimation round against a reference story forces convergence on a number while the ambiguity that caused the spread survives to mid-iteration. Recording the largest estimate buys padding and conceals the risk instead of removing it.
questions.concept: INVEST and story splitting driven by estimation divergence
questions.question: A team building a veterinary clinic scheduling platform has a backlog item written as "As a clinic manager, I want reporting so I can run the practice." During refinement the developers cannot agree on what to build, and estimates from the group range from 3 points to 40 points. The product owner is present and available. What should the agile practitioner do FIRST?
choices: Ask the product owner to rank the reporting needs by urgency so the team can estimate only the most urgent one and leave the rest for later refinement
Facilitate a conversation with the product owner and team to split the item into thinner slices tied to specific manager decisions, then re-estimate
Run a second estimation round against a reference story of similar complexity so the group converges on a single number before the item is pulled in
Record the largest estimate as the item's size for now, so the team is not over-committed and the detail can emerge during the iteration

questions.explanation: The stalls share one cause: items are being started before the team knows the rules or has what it needs to verify them. Lightweight, team-owned readiness checks surface exactly those gaps at the moment of pull, and because the team owns them they stay proportionate rather than becoming ceremony. Bringing the customer representative and subject-matter expert into refinement to walk through concrete examples produces the acceptance criteria that would have settled the rounding rule and prevented the review rejection, and it builds shared understanding rather than transferring documents. Having an analyst write complete specifications up front reinstates a handoff, front-loads detail that feedback will invalidate, and removes the team from the conversation where understanding is actually formed. A governance board that signs off readiness adds an external approval queue on top of a flow already suffering from waiting, and moves the decision away from the people who need it. Lengthening the iteration to four weeks gives ambiguity more room to hide, delays feedback, and grows batch size without addressing why items start unready.
questions.concept: Readiness criteria and collaborative acceptance criteria
questions.question: A hybrid product team runs two-week iterations while pulling work across a flow board. Of the last eight items started, three stalled mid-iteration: one waited four days for a decision on how partial refunds should be rounded, another could not proceed because no anonymized customer records existed to test against, and a third was rejected in review over a rule nobody had written down. The team's cycle time is now dominated by mid-flight waiting. Which TWO actions should the agile practitioner take? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Facilitate the team in agreeing lightweight, team-owned readiness checks — such as agreed acceptance rules and available test data — applied as a guideline when pulling an item.
Ask a business analyst to write complete written specifications for every backlog item before the team is permitted to pull it.
Invite the customer representative and the subject-matter expert into refinement to work through concrete examples and write acceptance criteria with the team.
Establish a governance board that formally signs off each item as "ready" before it may enter the board.
Lengthen the iteration to four weeks so the team has more time to resolve ambiguity while the work is in progress.

questions.explanation: The increment produced output but not outcome, and the fastest correction is to surface the evidence immediately, bring real users into the feedback loop that internal applause substituted for, and let that evidence re-order the backlog before more capacity is spent on the same unvalidated bet. Continuing with the next dashboard because the roadmap was agreed treats a forecast as a commitment and repeats a hypothesis the data has already contradicted. Adding a usability specialist improves craft but presumes the problem is design rather than demand — it prescribes a remedy before the cause is understood, and could produce a better-built feature nobody wants. Commissioning an in-app promotion campaign tries to manufacture adoption for something customers never asked for, treating 4% usage as a marketing shortfall rather than as a value hypothesis that failed.
questions.concept: Outcomes versus outputs; validating delivered value with real users
questions.question: A team delivering a subscription analytics product completed all planned items for the iteration. At the review, the product owner demonstrates the new cohort-retention dashboard to internal stakeholders, who applaud. Three weeks later, usage telemetry shows only 4% of accounts have ever opened the dashboard, and no customer has mentioned it. The team is about to start the next planned dashboard from the roadmap. What should the agile practitioner do NEXT?
choices: Continue with the next dashboard as planned, since the roadmap was agreed with the same stakeholders who applauded the demonstration, and reopening it in mid-quarter would create churn that the team cannot absorb

Bring a usability specialist onto the team to redesign the cohort-retention views before the next release, since low usage of an accepted feature usually points to a discoverability and design problem

Raise the telemetry finding with the team and product owner now, propose inviting actual account users into the next review, and re-examine whether the remaining dashboard items still merit their backlog position

Ask marketing to run an in-app campaign highlighting the cohort-retention dashboard so adoption climbs before the next roadmap item starts, then re-check the usage telemetry three weeks later before changing the roadmap

questions.explanation: Keeping the chart visible and using the worsening trend to open a conversation about impediments is best: an information radiator exists precisely to make uncomfortable truths visible so the organization can act on them, and an executive visit brings people who can remove obstacles. Moving the chart to a dashboard and giving the executives the full defect numbers afterwards is honest in intent and the data does eventually arrive, but it removes the signal from the room during the one visit when it could prompt help, and delayed disclosure invites the question of why it moved. Adding a note framing the trend as a temporary dip pre-empts the inquiry with an interpretation the data does not yet support. Swapping the defect count for build pass rate retires the measure that is saying something inconvenient.
questions.concept: Information radiators and transparency under pressure
questions.question: An XP team displays a wall chart in its work area showing build pass/fail history and the count of unresolved defects. After a rough week the chart shows a clearly worsening trend, and a line manager asks the team to move the chart into a private folder before an executive site visit. What should the agile practitioner do?
choices: Move the chart to a team dashboard for the visit and give the executives the full defect numbers in a follow-up
Keep the chart up and add a note framing the trend as a temporary dip, so visitors read the week in context
Swap the defect count for build pass rate this quarter, since the longer trend is fairer to the team
Keep the chart visible and use the worsening trend to open a conversation about the impediments behind it

questions.explanation: Bringing actual users into the review and watching them work in their real context closes the gap between the sponsor's beliefs and the users' behavior, and it does so within one iteration so the learning changes the very next increment. Having the operations director run a survey and bring consolidated results keeps the same proxy whose confidence produced the misjudgment, and filters the signal a second time through the person least likely to hear that his own picture is wrong. Making in-app booking a condition of gate entry would certainly lift the adoption number, but it forces hauliers onto a product they have avoided for three releases and converts a product-fit problem into a compliance one, so the published percentage then measures the mandate rather than the fit. Adding a feedback form and holding the design steady for two releases postpones learning available this week, and self-selected responses miss the drivers who never got far enough to comment.
questions.concept: Direct end-user engagement versus proxy stakeholder assumptions
questions.question: A team is delivering a truck-appointment application for a container terminal. The terminal's operations director sponsors the work, attends every iteration review, approves each increment enthusiastically, and relays what he believes drivers want. Three releases in, only about eleven percent of hauliers book appointments in the app; the rest still phone the gate office. Reviews continue to end in sign-off. What is the BEST response?
choices: Ask the operations director to run a structured survey of the hauliers he deals with daily and bring the consolidated results to the next review, so driver needs reach the team without extra scheduling.
Make in-app booking a condition of gate entry and publish a monthly adoption percentage on the sponsor's dashboard, so hauliers move off the phone line and uptake becomes visible to everyone.
Add an in-app feedback form and hold the design steady for two more releases until enough responses accumulate to analyze, then bring those findings to the review as evidence of what drivers want.
Arrange for several drivers and a gate clerk to join the next review, and observe a few drivers booking appointments in their own working conditions, feeding what is learned into the next iteration.

questions.explanation: A story map's two dimensions each carry meaning: the horizontal axis is the user's narrative flow and the vertical axis is depth of support within each step, so a horizontal slice defines a release that is coherent end to end and any missing step in the journey becomes visually obvious. Sorting the items by estimate arranges the backlog by cost rather than by user journey, which reveals nothing about coherence or gaps. Grouping by component team organizes around the delivery structure instead of the user and encourages release slices that no single user can actually complete. Ranking everything into one prioritized column with a capacity cut line is ordinary backlog ordering; it yields a set of high-scoring items that can still leave the user's journey broken in the middle.
questions.concept: Story map structure and release slicing
questions.question: A product team inherits a flat list of roughly 200 backlog items. Stakeholders complain they cannot tell which items make up the first usable release or where the product has gaps. The team decides to build a story map. Which arrangement applies story mapping correctly to this problem?
choices: Sort all the items by estimate from smallest to largest so the team can see how many of them fit inside the release timebox, then draw the release boundary at the point where the accumulated estimates reach the capacity the team forecasts for the coming period

Group the items under the component team that will build them, place each group in its own column, and let every team plan and sequence its own portion of the release independently so the map shows how the work is spread across the organization

Rank all the items in a single prioritized column using a weighted value score, draw a cut line where the release capacity is exhausted, and treat everything above that line as the release content, since the highest-scoring items deliver the most value for the release

Lay the user's activities left to right in the sequence a user performs them, stack the supporting stories beneath each activity in order of necessity, and draw a horizontal line across the map marking the thinnest slice that lets a user complete the whole journey.

questions.explanation: The rework is caused by an absence of real usage evidence, not by an absence of meetings. Putting each increment in front of a small opt-in cohort of genuine applicants generates that evidence inside the existing governance; agreeing the pilot and its scope with the sponsor first answers the concern about public exposure by bounding who sees the work, and it turns the gate from an opinion review into an inspection of what actually happened. Circulating a traceability pack between gates substitutes documents for working software, and reading specifications is precisely what generated the misunderstandings at the last two gates. Raising internal demonstrations to weekly and inviting committee delegates is the strongest rival, since some drift would surface earlier — but attendance is optional, the audience is still internal, and nobody is using the service to do real work. An acceptance checkpoint two weeks before each gate shrinks the surprise without shrinking the batch, and walking written criteria item by item tests conformance rather than fitness for applicants.
questions.concept: Obtaining real-user feedback within fixed governance constraints
questions.question: A publicly funded program is delivering a permit-application service. Governance allows the customer's steering committee to review progress only at quarterly gates. The team's flow metrics are healthy and internal demonstrations happen fortnightly, yet each of the last two gates generated rework that consumed most of the following quarter. The committee will not change its meeting cadence. The sponsor is supportive but wary of "showing unfinished work to the public." What is the BEST action for the agile practitioner?
choices: Ask the steering committee members to review a detailed requirements traceability pack between the gates, so that any misunderstanding about scope surfaces in writing well before the team reaches the next quarterly review.

Increase the internal demonstrations to weekly and invite committee delegates to attend them as optional observers, so feedback on the increment arrives more often and rework is caught long before each gate.

Add an acceptance checkpoint two weeks before each gate where the team walks the committee's written criteria item by item, so that the increment can be corrected against those criteria before the gate opens.

Propose a controlled pilot, agreed with the sponsor, that releases each increment between gates to a small opt-in group of real permit applicants, and bring the observed usage evidence into the next gate.

questions.explanation: The board is an information radiator: it already broadcasts the truth about the work continuously, so the best move is to connect the stakeholder to that transparent source and confirm which of its views answer her real questions, which maximizes transparency while eliminating waste. Automating the deck from the board's export is the strongest alternative and recovers nearly all of the lost half day, but it preserves a second, lagging channel beside the live board and never establishes what she is actually trying to learn. Asking the product owner to take on the deck redistributes the waste instead of removing it, and the document stays as stale as before. Replacing it with a monthly written summary saves time by making the information older, when the stated problem was visibility.
questions.concept: Transparency and information radiators
questions.question: A Kanban team building warehouse-automation software spends nearly half a day each week converting its board data into a formatted status deck because a senior operations manager says she "needs visibility." The team's electronic board already shows work items, blockers, cycle-time trends, and WIP limits in real time. What should the agile practitioner do next?
choices: Automate the deck from the board's export so the manager keeps her weekly document and the team loses almost no capacity
Invite the manager to a short walkthrough of the live board and agree on which of its views answer her questions directly
Ask the product owner to take on the weekly deck, since stakeholder reporting is her accountability rather than the team's
Replace the weekly deck with a monthly written summary so the manager still gets a narrative and the team recovers time

questions.explanation: Co-creating the vision in a workshop that mixes all three former teams with key stakeholders gives every 'tribe' a hand in shaping the purpose, which is what turns three roadmaps into one direction. Radiating the agreed vision together with its customer-outcome measures, and visibly using it to order the shared backlog, keeps that purpose alive in daily decisions — directly countering stand-ups that never mention customers — instead of leaving it as a one-time event. Publishing the executive statement on the intranet and counting page views is one-way broadcast: exposure is not commitment, and view counts measure nothing about shared purpose. Rating vision adherence in individual appraisals converts purpose into compliance pressure, rewards performative alignment, and erodes the intrinsic motivation shared purpose exists to create. Quarterly PMO alignment audits add inspection overhead and hand ownership of the vision to a control function rather than to the people doing the work.
questions.concept: Building shared purpose across newly merged teams
questions.question: Three product teams working under a shared Lean-Kanban model have just been merged into one product group after an acquisition. Members describe the group as 'three tribes with three roadmaps,' and stand-up conversations rarely reference customer outcomes. Which TWO actions would most effectively build shared purpose across the new group? (Choose TWO.)
choices: Publish the executive vision statement on the intranet and track how many people from each former team view the page
Facilitate a collaborative visioning workshop where members of all three former teams and key stakeholders draft the product vision together
Include adherence to the product vision as a rated factor in every member's individual performance appraisal
Ask the PMO to audit each former team's alignment to the vision at the end of every quarter
Display the agreed vision and its customer-outcome measures on a highly visible radiator and reference them when ordering the shared backlog

questions.explanation: Inviting the department head into the flow review is best because it assumes positive intent, surfaces the real information need behind the request, and uses transparency and live data to show why flow-based measures beat resource utilization — the practitioner promotes the agile mindset by demonstrating rather than arguing, and builds a relationship instead of a battle line. Having the product owner absorb the request shields the team but keeps the new leader at arm's length; the buffer holds only until he asks again, and his assumption about utilization is never examined. Automating the report makes a harmful measure cheap and permanent, and utilization pressure rewards busyness over value. Supplying the figures while coaching the team to stop inflating estimates is honest and the most tempting alternative, yet accurate numbers make testers look idle precisely when they are collaborating on refinement, confirming the wrong conclusion instead of correcting it.
questions.concept: Shifting leadership from utilization thinking to flow and value metrics
questions.question: A newly hired department head with a plan-driven background begins requesting weekly individual utilization percentages from each member of a Lean software team and asks why testers appear 'idle' while they collaborate on story refinement. Team members quietly start inflating task estimates so their numbers look busier. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Ask the product owner to absorb the utilization request and answer it from the delivery numbers already reported to the business, so the team is shielded from the weekly reporting
Automate the utilization report from the team's board so the numbers are produced with no effort from anyone and the testers can go back to refining stories together
Invite the department head to attend the team's flow review and explore together how throughput and cycle time reflect value delivery better than individual utilization
Supply the weekly utilization figures as requested and coach the team to stop inflating estimates, since accurate numbers will show the head that refining together is productive

questions.explanation: Bringing the skeptical stakeholder into reviews lets him see working software and live transparency, and jointly mapping his underlying governance needs onto iterative evidence models the agile mindset while tailoring practices to the organization — collaboration over confrontation, and working product over speculative documents. Maintaining the gate documents alongside the backlog and updating both every iteration is the strongest alternative, since it genuinely satisfies governance, but it buys peace with permanent duplicate bookkeeping and never tests whether the increments themselves could serve the need. Offering a detailed monthly written status report swaps one document for another and keeps him at arm's length from the working product, so his confidence still rests on narrative rather than evidence. Complying with the full twelve-month plan for the first release concedes a heavyweight forecast that anchors expectations for the rest of the pilot and delays the feedback the pilot exists to generate.
questions.concept: Tailoring governance while modeling agile values in a hybrid pilot
questions.question: An insurance company is piloting a hybrid delivery approach for a claims-automation product. The head of actuarial services insists the pilot team produce a fully detailed twelve-month plan plus sign-off documents at every phase gate, "the way real projects do." The team worries this will erase the benefit of iterative delivery. What is the BEST response by the agile practitioner?
choices: Maintain the gate documents alongside the team's backlog and update both every iteration, so corporate governance is satisfied without changing how the team works
Offer the actuarial head a detailed monthly written status report in place of the phase-gate sign-offs, so his oversight need is met another way
Comply with the full twelve-month plan and the gate documents for the first release, then use the delivery record to renegotiate the burden
Invite the actuarial head to iteration reviews and work with him to map which of his governance needs each increment and information radiator can satisfy

questions.explanation: Meeting the VP to understand the intended outcome, presenting the observed behavior changes as evidence, and proposing team-level flow and outcome measures serves the VP's real goal of transparency while removing a measure that ranks individuals and destroys collaboration and safety; it is understand-first, evidence-based, and collaborative. Removing the display unilaterally and declaring it against agile values wins the argument and loses the sponsor, inviting a power struggle rather than a shared solution. Coaching teams to calibrate estimates treats the symptom and legitimizes the ranking, and inflated estimates would simply be gamed more skillfully. Annotating the rankings with explanations keeps the harmful individual measure in place, and no context note stops people from avoiding hard stories that would drag down their number.
questions.concept: Choosing measures that illuminate work at the team level without destroying psychological safety
questions.question: A vice president championing 'radical transparency' directs that a large wall display show every developer's completed story points for the month, ranked from highest to lowest. Within two sprints, pairing has almost stopped, difficult stories sit unclaimed, and estimates are visibly inflating. Several responses are possible, and the VP is proud of the initiative. What should the agile practitioner do first?
choices: Coach the teams to calibrate their estimates together so that the point totals become comparable across people and the ranking at least stops rewarding whoever inflates their own numbers the most
Take the display down and tell the VP that ranking individuals conflicts with agile values, so the damage to pairing and to story selection stops before another sprint goes by
Keep the display but add a short note beside each name explaining why individual output varies, so the transparency the VP values survives with the unfairness openly explained
Meet the VP to understand the outcome the display is meant to achieve, share the behavioral effects observed, and propose team-level flow and outcome measures that provide genuine transparency
